Furthermore, the "Chapter on Dedication" states: "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally non-dual; even non-duality is further absent.
This is the emptiness of emptiness itself.
Regarding the phrase "the traces of speech are cut off," it means that both emptiness and existence are severed, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Because the sphere of activity has ceased, its traces cannot be sought.
This means that if there were existence that could be existent, then there would be non-existence that could be nonexistent.
Now, since there is no existence that can be existent, there is likewise no non-existence that can be nonexistent.
Using non-existence to dispel existence—non-existence itself is a trace.
Using emptiness to dispel emptiness—emptiness is also a trace.
Because one uses existence to dispel [existence], one dispels again and again until there is nothing further to dispel.
If one uses non-existence to dispel existence, that "dispelling of non-existence" is also a trace; because there is something attained, it is like a bird walking upon sand.
If there is nothing attained, the very phrase ceases at once.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "To thoroughly know that the nature of all phenomena is quiescent is like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace.
Thus it is said: "Emptiness within emptiness leaves no trace."
Because emptiness is empty and does not obstruct form, it leads to the statement "although.
The character "although" gives rise to the meaning that the celestial bodies of the stars are brilliantly radiant;
this means that by relying upon the clear sky, they do not obstruct the brilliant radiance of the stars.
The clear sky is itself the Dharma-realm (Arthadhātu); relying upon this ultimate Dharma-realm, the constellations of the unobstructed Dharma-gates appear.
Furthermore, it is precisely because these constellations are unobstructed that one knows this empty, unobstructed Dharma-gate to be the true ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
The "Superior" (the ultimate) takes emptiness as its root and the Dharma-gates as its branches.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Profoundly still and beyond words, yet the waves of the ocean of teaching surge vast and boundless,” this second point concerns how the wordless does not obstruct speech.
Thus, taking non-speaking as the root and speaking as the branch:
that which is profoundly still is the appearance of the ocean water’s clarity and congealment; this signifies that movement depends upon stillness, and that non-speaking does not obstruct speaking.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "Although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness.
If one is obstructed by speech, Śāriputra was rebuked; if one is not obstructed by speech, Mañjuśrī is praised.
Moreover, since the nature of words is detached from them, speech itself vanishes; thus, although there is no speech, within the ocean of the teachings the waves are vast and surging.
A great wave is called a *lán*.
Therefore, while the Buddha realizes that which transcends words, he causes the eightfold tones to flow forth for the ears to perceive.
The Dharma is fundamentally ineffable, yet it was expounded as the Great Canon within the Dragon Palace.
Thus we know that the ultimate destination is not distant; when one’s mental activities attain it, it is profoundly deep.
Words and symbols are not near, yet by embodying them with an empty mind, one perceives them directly.

The principle of severing speech is not itself severed; the profusion of profound scriptures does not itself arise. Thus, by means of speech, one transcends speech; when the constant mind is harmonized, there is nothing to be discarded.

The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'If the thousand gates flow secretly, they form a great source for all scriptures,' this discusses the primary and secondary aspects by contrasting the various teachings; thus, the *Avataṃsaka* is taken as the fundamental wheel of Dharma."
The text contains two pairs [of meanings]:
the first pair constitutes the foundation for opening the way to the gradual [teachings].

This means that the diverse meanings of the thousand gates flow secretly through all the scriptures, like the hidden currents of the ocean beneath the lands of the four continents; thus, those who dig with the drill will inevitably find water.
Thus we know that because all streams depend upon the seawater, the sea is the source of all waters; likewise, the *Avataṃsaka* is the fundamental source of all teachings.
When the lower [teachings] correspond [to it] as a means of subsuming the branches and returning to the root, then the myriad virtues converge, just as the hundred rivers flow back into the sea.
The ocean is able to universally receive all things because it is their very source.
As an ancient said:
"The nine schools of thought converge here; the myriad sages meet in mystery here."
The former [assembly] ultimately converges upon *nirvāṇa*, while this assembly ultimately converges upon the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, the *Dilun* states: "There is nothing that does not flow from this *dharmadhātu*, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this *dharmadhātu*."
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches three.

The One Vehicle is the very foundation of the Three Vehicles; the Single Buddha Vehicle is precisely the *Avataṃsaka*. To harmonize the three and return to the one is to subsume the branches and return to the root.
The fifth sutra states: "Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I preach, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This refers to the *Avataṃsaka* as the root.
"To set aside those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna" refers to what flows from the source.
"I now also cause them to hear this sutra so that they may enter the Buddha-wisdom" refers to gathering the branches back to the root.
This sutra is none other than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* subsumes all other sutras and returns them to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* also points to the *Avataṃsaka* as its ultimate foundation.
The meaning is clear and distinct;
the remainder is as explained below.
From the sixth section, "As for its purport," onwards, the underlying intent is profound and subtle.
This sentence serves as the heading for the commentary;
the section following "Ming zhen ti" (Concealing the True Essence) correctly elucidates the underlying intent.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena is clarified; subsequently, the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena is revealed.
Although this sutra extensively explains both phenomena and principle, they are all mutually unobstructed; therefore, its fundamental purport is the non-obstructed *dharmadhātu*.
This section corresponds to the meaning within the "Delimitation of Meanings" (Arthaviniścaya).
Within the first part, the "Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena," there are also two sections:
first, the demonstration of the three great natures; second, the integration of the true and the delusive.
In the preceding section, it was asked:
"Since the three great aspects—beginningless and endless, and so forth—have already been clarified, why are they stated again here?
The answer is:
There are three points of meaning that differ from what preceded.

First, whereas previously the Three Greatnesses were elucidated by taking the Dharma-realm as the primary tenet and explaining it according to its significance, here they are explained in full according to the sūtras that serve as the expressive medium; thus, they are different.
Second, whereas previously the characteristics of the three greatnesses were analyzed, here the locations of the three greatnesses are clarified.
That is to say, where does the essence reside?
It is said to be in the myriad transformations and so forth.

Third, the previous section clarified that the three great natures (tridharmadhātu) are fused and swept away to establish one's own school; this section clarifies that the three great natures exist mutually to refute divergent interpretations, and demonstrates their inseparability to define the meaning of non-obstruction.
As an ancient said:
"As for its essence, it is neither born nor extinguished, neither departing nor arriving.
Taking non-extinction as non-birth and taking non-birth as non-extinction, and so forth, constitutes its characteristics.
Thus, the distinct entities of similar and dissimilar categories can be contained within subtle forms;
the separate substances of similar and dissimilar categories can be successively and repeatedly manifested.
The principle of subtlety is difficult to perceive, and it is compared to a mustard seed within a jar.
The manifestations of its re-manifestation are easy to contemplate, being illustrated by metaphors such as Indra’s net.

As for its function: it is pervasive without being divided, and reaches everywhere without moving; within the interplay of the one and the many, the large and the small, the long and the short, and the tranquil and the turbulent, their mutual presence remains equal. This specifically reveals the characteristics of the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*).
Now, to clarify only that they are not separate is profound and mysterious; this is termed the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*).
The first phrase clarifies the essence (*ti*).

Since the essence exists within the midst of the myriad transformations and is not outside of phenomena, it is said that "the true essence is darkly unified with the realm of the myriad transformations."
"Darkness" refers to the dark seal (míngqì), which is also profound stillness.

"The myriad transformations" is a general term for phenomenal phenomena; thus, Master Xuǎnxiǎo’s *Preface to the Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "To investigate the essence of the Mahāyāna: it is spontaneously empty and still, profoundly serene and mysterious."
"Profound after profound—how could it transcend the realm of the myriad phenomena?
Stillness after stillness—it remains within the discourses of the hundred schools.
It is not beyond the realm of forms; even the five eyes cannot behold its countenance."
"Even within words, none of the four types of eloquence can describe its form.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that the true essence is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena.
Now, this commentary merely states that it is "unimpeded," which means it is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena.
Thus, Master Zhao said:
"Is the Way far away?"
"Whatever it encounters is the Real," which also means that the essence itself is the myriad transformations. The commentary states,
"Manifesting the attributes of virtue at the gate of the profound mystery," clarifying that the attributes do not obstruct the essence.
The "Twofold Mystery" (chóngxuán) is the very essence of principle (lǐtǐ); the characteristics of sublime virtue (míngdéxiàng) reside solely within this essence.
If characteristics were to exist apart from the essence, those characteristics would not be profound and wondrous.
The characteristics of supreme virtue are termed "characteristics of virtue" (déxiàng).
The term "double mystery" (chóngxuán) refers to the "emptiness of emptiness" (kōngkōng); the phrasing borrows from the *Laozi*.
The *Laozi* states: "Mystery upon mystery is the gate of all wonders."
He [Zhuangzi] treats both that which has a name and that which has no name as equally "mysterious" (*xuan*).
He Shanggong says, "The Mysterious is Heaven; within Heaven, there is yet another Heaven.
The *Zhuangzi* says, "Heaven is spontaneity (*ziran*); thus, spontaneity is itself spontaneous."
"All phenomena arise in dependence upon this; therefore, it is called the gateway to all wonders.
Now, within the midst of emptiness and emptiness, there is no virtue that is not complete.
The commentary states: "The manifold arisings of function are eternally such," which clarifies that function does not depart from the essence.
Though manifold phenomena arise, they are eternally suchness.
The essence, characteristics, and function—these three—are never separated from one another; all are that which is realized and that which is observed.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Wisdom universally reflects while remaining eternally quiescent,” this refers to that which realizes and that which observes.
If the phrase clarifies this, then stillness (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are without obstruction.
"Universal discernment" is insight;
"constantly abiding in stillness" is the universal observation of both principle and phenomena.
The characteristics of delusion are all quiescent, and thus the provisional and the real are unimpeded.
Universal discernment is the provisional;
eternal stillness is the real.

Regarding the preceding three phrases, they constitute the non-obstruction between object and wisdom; because the observed object is already characterized by the non-obstruction of essence and function, the observing wisdom likewise flows as both quiescence and illumination.
If one considers them individually in relation to the three great aspects, each possesses its own essence and function, and each includes both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
For instance, when the essence conforms to the true essence, it is essence and it is *śamatha*;
when it pertains to the realm of myriad transformations, it is function and it is *vipaśyanā*.
The manifestation of the characteristics of virtue is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
The gate of the twofold mystery is cessation (*śamatha*).
The profuse arising of function is contemplation.
To be ever thus is cessation (*śamatha*).
If one explains this by way of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*): using wisdom to discern that the essence is empty is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);
discerning its functional activity is the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*).
"Discerning appearances" (*jianxiang*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Because the three truths are observed simultaneously, it is called "universal discernment.
In contrast to these three contemplations, there are likewise three forms of *śamatha* characterized by constant stillness:

First, it is quiescent because its single essence is true; second, it is quiescent because skillful means follow conditions without grasping; third, it is quiescent because it is free from the discrimination of the two extremes.

When the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are fused into a single mind, they accord with the unimpeded principle of the three truths; thus, mind and object are fused and integrated, yet remain eternally distinct and clear.
In the commentary, the passage “where truth and delusion interpenetrate, one perceives the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind” integrates truth and delusion.
The text contains two pairs:
the first pair correctly elucidates their mutual integration, while the second pair demonstrates that they manifest simultaneously without mutual obstruction.
Now, first:
"Reality" refers to principle and to the Buddha;
"delusion" refers to affliction and to birth, as well as to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
To speak of "mutual penetration" means that the Truth encompasses the extremities of delusion, while delusion penetrates to the source of Truth; hence it is called mutual penetration.
It is like waves and moisture: there are no waves that are not moist, and there is no moisture apart from the waves.

If we discuss their mutual penetration, it is likewise appropriate to say that by means of the sacred mind one perceives the mundane mind, just as one perceives waves within moisture; therefore, the Tathāgata does not sever his inherent evil.
Furthermore, within the Buddha’s mind there are sentient beings and so forth.
If one relies on this meaning, it should be said that truth and delusion penetrate each other, and ordinary beings and sages mutually encompass one another.
If it were not thus, then from the perspective of the fusion of principle and reality, truth and delusion would exist within one another.
Now, based on the characteristic of non-disintegration, it is merely clarified that the ordinary person is identical to the sage because they are identical with the Truth;
yet the sage is not identical to the ordinary person because he is devoid of afflictions.
Just as waves are wetness, yet wetness is not necessarily waves because there is pure water.
Therefore, when pure water is said to be "waves," it possesses the nature of movement but lacks the actual occurrence of movement.
As it is said regarding waves, moisture and movement exist together.
Furthermore, to say that ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas is beneficial for ordinary beings;
however, to say that Buddhas are themselves ordinary beings leads people to false understanding. Therefore, it is simply stated that by means of the ordinary mind, one perceives the Buddha-mind.
However, the reason why the true and the false interpenetrate is that these two dharmas—true and false—are of one and the same mind.
The false is formed by grasping at the true, for there is no separate false;
the true manifests in accordance with the false, for there is no separate true.
The names "true" and "false" differ, yet they possess no dual substance.
If the false existed apart from the true, it would contradict the principle that [the true] is all-pervasive;
if the true existed apart from the false, it would lack a basis for its manifestation.

Yet, some speak of the false as empty and the true as existent, while others speak of the false as existent and the true as empty; whether both are empty or both are existent, or whether they are both negated and both affirmed—though there are many such approaches, they all interpenetrate one another.
What is the meaning of this?
For now, let us explain: what dharma is considered true, and what dharma is considered false?
Reality and falsehood each possess two meanings:

first, explained in terms of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is reality, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is falsehood, and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) partakes of both reality and falsehood—the pure portion being identical to reality and the defiled portion being falsehood.
Second, it is explained in terms of the two truths: the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is taken as true, and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is taken as false.
There are many gateways to these two truths, which shall be explained extensively below.

For now, we shall briefly rely on the two gateways of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*): principle is the ultimate truth and is thus true; phenomena are the conventional truth and are thus false.
The activities of the pure portion are established because delusion has not yet been exhausted.
Question:
Between the two dharmas of reality and delusion, which is empty and which is existent?
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, if one regards the parikalpita (the imagined nature) as false, then falsity is empty and reality is truly existent.
If, however, one regards the kliṣṭa-manas (the defiled mind) as false, then both the real and the false are equally present.

If, as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states, that which is empty refers to saṃsāra and that which is non-empty refers to Mahāparinirvāṇa, then the defiled portion of the dependent nature is empty, while the pure portion exists as both the dependent and the perfected natures.
If one relies on the Three Treatises, things exist according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and are empty according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one takes the false as conventional truth and the true as ultimate truth, then the false is existence and the true is emptiness;
if one speaks of the two truths in accordance with worldly convention, then both the true and the false encompass both emptiness and existence.
If, in terms of all objects of contact, they are all "middle," then both the true and the false are neither empty nor existent.
Question:
When the true and the false interpenetrate, what is the nature of their manifestation?

Regarding the statement that "all things mutually penetrate one another," this is explained according to the *lakṣaṇa* school (the School of Characteristics); in schools such as *vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only), mutual penetration cannot be established.
Now, from the perspective of the *Avataṃsaka*, all the aforementioned meanings attain mutual penetration, because they fully possess the principle of "the oneness of mind" and so forth.

If one considers the thoroughly imagined nature to be false, then "existence from the perspective of phenomena" (qing you) is precisely "non-existence from the perspective of principle" (li wu); thus, the false penetrates the true.
"Non-existence from the perspective of principle" is precisely "existence from the perspective of phenomena"; thus, the true penetrates the false.

If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) in its defiled aspect is considered delusion, then because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature, delusion penetrates to the ultimate truth;
because that which lacks intrinsic nature is established through conditions, the ultimate truth penetrates to delusion.
If explained in terms of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvana, birth-and-death is itself nirvana; thus, delusion penetrates to the ultimate truth.
Nirvana is precisely birth-and-death; it is the ultimate penetration through delusion.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of birth-and-death is itself the limit of reality of nirvana."
"The ultimate reality of nirvāṇa is itself the limit of birth-and-death.
These two limits are without the slightest difference.
This refers to their mutual interpenetration.
The scripture below states: "That which has contention is called birth-and-death; that which is without contention is called nirvana.
Both birth-and-death and nirvana are unobtainable.
This also refers to the principle of mutual penetration, wherein both are empty and both are existent.
If one relies on the two truths, taking the delusory as the conventional truth and the real as the ultimate truth.
As for what is called "mutual penetration," it is because the conventional is identical to the real, and the real is identical to the conventional.
Therefore, Master Ying said:

"However, when one summarizes the essential point, it converges upon the two truths: because of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no existence; because of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is no non-existence."
Because it is true, it does not exist; thus, although it is non-existent, it exists.
Because it is conventional, there is no non-existence; thus, although it exists, it is non-existent.
Although it exists while being non-existent, it is not burdened by existence.
"Though it is non-existent, it exists; thus one does not stagnate in non-existence.
By quiescing these extremes, it is called the Middle Way.
This refers to the mutual penetration of the real and the false.
Because it is true, there is non-existence; thus, although there is non-existence, there is existence, whereby the true thoroughly penetrates the delusive.
Because it is conventional, there is no non-existence; thus, although there is existence, there is non-existence, whereby the delusive thoroughly penetrates the true.
The remaining points may be inferred accordingly.
If one speaks according to conventional truth, both the real and the false are fundamentally empty, and thus they interpenetrate naturally.
Since both the real and the false are ultimately real, the root and the branches are of a single flavor, and thus they interpenetrate naturally.
If all objects touched are central, they naturally interpenetrate.
Next, the reason for this interpenetration is explained.
Question:
Truth and falsehood are mutually opposed, like water and fire.
How can they penetrate one another?
Answer:
This has several meanings.
First, because the two dharmas of truth and falsehood are one within the single mind, they are unified by this oneness; thus, they penetrate one another.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Based on the dharma of the single mind, there are two gates:"
"First is the gate of the suchness of the one mind; second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind.

Yet these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena without exception. Because these two gates are not separate from one another, it is said that they do not depart from the one mind; thus, they penetrate one another completely.
Second, the false is formed by grasping the true, for there is no separate false apart from it.
This is also the purport of the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Since True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions to form all phenomena, the true penetrates the false.
The statement, "The true manifests in accordance with the delusive, for there is no separate true," means that the delusive penetrates to the true.
If there were no delusion, in relation to what would one speak of the true?
It is like how, if there were no dependent origination, there would be no such thing as the absence of intrinsic nature.

Third, regarding the statement "The names 'true' and 'delusive' differ, but their substance is not two": as cited previously, when both that which is characterized by contention—namely saṃsāra—and that which is free from contention—namely nirvāṇa—are found to be unattainable, then their substance is non-dual.

Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "If one pursues provisional names and clings to these two dharmas, this is an inverted view that lacks true meaning, and one will be unable to perceive perfect enlightenment.
This clarifies that non-duality is the reality; how could this not be mutual penetration?
4. "Because the principle that there is delusion outside of reality is not pervasive," and so forth, reverses [the previous argument] to establish two meanings.
This phrase indicates that reality penetrates through to delusion.
5. There is reality outside of delusion, because delusion would otherwise have no basis.
This is precisely the delusion penetrating through to the real.
This is also the doctrine of the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-naya*): all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); how could there be reality apart from delusion?
True suchness pervades all things; how could there be delusion apart from reality?
Thus we know that truth and delusion are constantly interpenetrating, yet the characteristics of truth and delusion are not destroyed.
Truth that encompasses delusion is not "truth" in a literal sense, but is profound stillness;
delusion that penetrates to truth is not "delusion" in a literal sense, but arises like clouds.

The Commentary states: "Cultivating both phenomena and principle, one seeks Buddha-wisdom by relying on fundamental wisdom. This means that these two are not mutually obstructive and both are preserved.

Since the preceding discussion has focused on the meaning of their mutual penetration without obstruction, this statement is raised lest people mistakenly cling to the notion that the two characteristics are obliterated.

Furthermore, those who are deluded cling to dhyāna, asserting that one relies on the original nature which is without action or cultivation, like a mirror that is inherently bright and requires neither wiping nor polishing.

Conversely, those who cling to dharmas must initiate active practice, seeking the Tathāgata and relying on superior external conditions to accomplish their own virtue; both of these constitute biased attachments.

Therefore, regarding these two practices for one who relies on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they are explained from the perspective of principle (*tattva*): because the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is inherently complete.

However, regarding the pursuit of the Buddha-wisdom, they are discussed from the perspective of phenomena (*vastu*): "Within that which is nothing to seek, I therefore seek it. This is because the mirror of the mind is fundamentally pure yet has long been obscured by the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*); because the ocean-like inherent virtues are all buried within the sands of afflictions; because one practices giving (*dāna*) and other perfections in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to eliminate stinginess and greed; and because all Buddhas have already realized this while I have not yet realized it.
Furthermore, principle does not obstruct phenomena, for there is no hindrance to seeking;
phenomena do not obstruct principle, for seeking is itself non-seeking.
Cultivation such as this is called "non-cultivation."
"Cultivation that is non-cultivation—wherein cultivation is itself non-cultivation—is true cultivation.

Regarding the commentary’s passage, "When principle accords with the transformations of phenomena, there is the boundlessness of the dependent origination of the one and the many," this second section clarifies that the intent of the sutra is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
This shall be analyzed in detail within the section on the "Delimitation of Meaning" (*arthaparyāya*); here it is explained only briefly.
It is also divided into two parts:
the first pair clarifies the basis for non-obstruction.
The reason why all things are different yet attain non-obstruction is that principle harmonizes with phenomena.
Within this, the first phrase clarifies how phenomena are established based on principle; thus, the one and the many mutually function as *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination).
This still pertains to the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; it is mentioned here because it follows upon the preceding and gives rise to what follows.
It is only through the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle that one attains the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
If phenomena were not identical with principle, and phenomena were established apart from principle, they would obstruct one another;
now, because they are identical with principle, they attain non-obstruction.
The following phrase uses principle to harmonize phenomena, hence it says that when phenomena attain harmony with principle, the thousand differences interpenetrate without obstruction.
This correctly explains the reason for the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*).
Since phenomena are established by encompassing principle (*li*), there is no phenomenon that is not principle; thus, principle is used to harmonize phenomena.
Once principle is pervasive and unobstructed, phenomena likewise follow suit; therefore, a thousand differences may interpenetrate without obstruction.
Because they are identical with phenomena (*dharmas*), there are a thousand distinctions;
because their principle is harmonious, they interpenetrate one another in layers.
This corresponds precisely to the "Gate of the Harmonious Integration of Rational Nature" within the context of the Ten Mysterious Gates.
The remainder will be clarified below.

In the commentary, the passage beginning with "Therefore, the ten bodies are distinct yet mutually interpenetrating" correctly reveals that the characteristics of non-obstruction possess the ten gates of mystery (daśa-guhya-dvāra).

Because this follows the convenience of the phrasing of the text, the order is slightly unconventional. The sequential order is as follows: first, the gate of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence;

second, the gate of unimpeded mastery over the vast and the narrow; third, the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion; fourth, the gate of the mutual identity and sovereignty of all phenomena; fifth, the gate of the secret and hidden being simultaneously perfected; sixth, the gate of subtle containment and establishment; seventh, the gate of the realm of Indra’s net; eighth, the gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena to generate understanding; ninth, the gate of the distinct perfection of phenomena across the ten periods of time; tenth, the gate of the sovereign and its companions being perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues.

The sequence of the current text is evident from its arrangement; however, as for the single section on the primary and attendant [deities], since the principles and phrasing have already been fully set forth in the preceding ritual manual, it is not repeated here.
The various scriptural collections differ greatly in their purity or mixture of content and in their antiquity; since this present text repeats these themes, it likewise consists of ten gates.
First, this is the Gate of the Mutual Identity and Sovereign Freedom of All Dharmas.
The text contains two sentences:
the first sentence generally clarifies that the three worlds are mutually constituted; therefore, the ten bodies are clearly distinct yet functionally interdependent.

Regarding the phrase "thereby attained," it means that because the phenomena of the preceding stage have attained the integration of principle, one is then able to possess the ten profound gateways described below.
Although the two characters "hence attained" (*gode*) appear at the beginning of the text, their meaning extends through the following ten [sections].
Regarding the "ten bodies," the *Eight Stages* (*Aṣṭabhūmika*) states: "This bodhisattva, having distanced himself from all conceptualizations of bodily marks, abides in equanimity."

This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, the body of the land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of śrāvakas, the body of pratyekabuddhas, the body of bodhisattvas, the body of Tathāgatas, the body of wisdom, the body of phenomena, and the body of space.

Regarding the "activity of signs," the subsequent sutra states: "This bodhisattva knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings; he is able to take the bodies of sentient beings as his own body, and likewise takes on the bodies of lands, the bodies of karmic retribution, and even the bodies of empty space."

Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, they are able to manifest the body of a buddha-field as their own body, and likewise manifest the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of karmic retribution, and even bodies of empty space.

Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, they are able to manifest their own bodies as the body of karmic retribution, and likewise manifest them as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even up to the bodies of empty space.

Furthermore, knowing the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings, one is able to manifest one's own body as the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of lands, and even the bodies of space; according to the differing inclinations of those beings, one manifests such forms within these bodies, and so forth.
The commentary states:
The four preceding categories have been individually explained, while the final one serves as a concluding illustration, namely the manifestation of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
It is said to be "distinctly clear" because its characteristics are indestructible.
To act by destroying their characteristics is not inconceivable.

It is like a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru; yet the original characteristics of Mount Sumeru remain as they were. Therefore, the seventy-seventh sutra below states: "This is the dwelling place of those who cause one land to enter all lands without destroying their respective characteristics."
It further states: "This is the dwelling place of those who cause one Buddha to enter all Buddhas without destroying their respective characteristics.

The fifty-sixth sutra says: "That which is called taking the body of sentient beings to become the body of a buddha-field, without destroying the body of sentient beings—this is the playful mastery (*vikrīḍita*) of a bodhisattva."
"To transform the body of a buddha-field into the body of a sentient being without destroying the body of the field—this is the 'play' (*vikrīḍita*) of a bodhisattva.

Thus, the Buddha-body and the marks of the two vehicles interact; the body of bodhisattva practice and the body of perfect enlightenment interact; and within nirvana, they manifest birth and death and so forth, yet without destroying their respective characteristics. Therefore, it is said that "they interact while remaining distinct."

Regarding the statement, "The six stages are not disordered, yet they are further subsumed," the six stages refer to the three levels of worthiness (the *śaikṣas*), the ten stages of the sages (*āryas*), and the two types of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhas*); thus, both cause and fruit are entirely mutually inclusive.
It is as if one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the mind of awakening, without destroying the characteristics of that initial mind.
If there were no initial mind, how could it be said that "at the very moment of first generating the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment"?
Therefore, the ten faiths encompass all stages, and within each stage, the ten faiths are clearly manifest.
The ten abidings encompass all stages, and within each stage, the ten abidings remain undisturbed.

When they are undisturbed, there is sequential unfolding (*xingbu*); when further integrated, there is perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), as will be explained below in the analysis of the causal stage.
This phrase is also an entry into mutual inclusion (*xiāng rù*), because there is mutual inclusion below it.

Therefore, this single phrase serves merely as mutual identity (*xiāng jí*); just as when milk is poured into water, it abandons its own nature to become identical with the other, it is thus called mutual identity.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra of the Flower Ornament of the Great Vaipulya Buddha, Scroll One.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra of the Flower Ornament of the Great Vaipulya Buddha,
Scroll Two.
The Commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty states:

"The vast and great immediately enters the infinitesimal; the dust mote and the hair encompass all without exception. This refers to the second gate: the Unobstructed Gate of Sovereignty over the Vast and the Narrow.

The first phrase means that the large can enter the small; the second phrase means that the small can contain the large. Although there is "immediate entry," the intended meaning concerns breadth and narrowness.
"Without interval" refers to the small; when something is made small, it has no interior, and because it has no interior, there is no middle space.
To have no exterior is called "great";

when one expands to the point where there is no exterior, that which has no exterior is precisely the body and land of vast magnitude. This is to enter the dust-motes and hairs of that which has no interior; therefore, it is called the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow.
Whether they are identical with or enter into [the object], both attain the unimpeded mastery of the vast and the narrow.
As the Sūtra says: "The countless mountains of the Vajra-perimeter can all be placed upon the tip of a single hair."
"If one wishes to know that the ultimate great possesses small characteristics, it is by means of this that a bodhisattva first resolves their mind.
That "the ultimate great possesses small characteristics" refers precisely to the non-obstruction between the vast and the narrow.
It further states: "One can transform a small world into a large world, and a large world into a small world," and so forth. The commentary says:
"Vividly appearing together like mustard seeds in a bottle" refers to the third gate, the Gate of Subtle Mutual Containment and Establishment.
One being able to contain many is called "mutual inclusion" (xiāngróng).
Because the one and the many do not intermingle, it is termed "establishment" (ānlì).
"Bǐng" means clarity.
There are three kinds of subtlety:
first, the subtlety of containment.

This is like a lapis lazuli jar filled with many mustard seeds, which appear vividly and simultaneously without obstructing one another, neither preceding nor following; this is what is taught in the *Tathāgataguhya-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata).
However, there are two versions:
one version reads "white mustard seeds," while another simply reads "mustard seeds"; for now, I follow this latter version.

This means that a single phenomenon accords with its true nature and encompasses all things exhaustively; therefore, all phenomena, according to the principle they contain, are present within this one.

Furthermore, it is through the actual virtue of dependent origination—its unimpeded sovereignty—that they are made to coexist; this is not something created by gods or humans, but is established as it is.
As within each of the eight aspects, all eight aspects are fully contained; this is called "subtlety.
Second, it is subtlety in terms of that which contains the subtle.
Third, it is subtlety in terms of its difficulty to know.

The Commentary states: "To be fully endowed with [all things] simultaneously is like comparing them to drops in the ocean" refers to the fourth gate, the Gate of Simultaneous Endowment and Correspondence.
Just as a single drop of the great ocean possesses the flavors of all rivers and the ten kinds of virtues, so too does each individual dharma encompass all inexhaustible dharmas.
Regarding the subsequent nine gates, since this one gate serves as their general heading, they are simultaneously clarified without chronological sequence, fully encompassed without omission.

As for the ten virtues, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "First, it becomes progressively deeper; second, it does not harbor corpses; third, when other waters enter it, they all lose their original names; fourth, it is everywhere of a single taste; fifth, it contains immeasurable treasures; sixth, it is deep and its bottom is difficult to reach; seventh, it is vast and immeasurable; eighth, it is the dwelling place of great beings; ninth, its tides do not exceed their limits; and tenth, it universally receives great rains."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It is like a person who enters the great ocean to bathe; they thereby make use of the waters of all rivers.
If one practices in accordance with this principle, the virtues within even a single practice will be inexhaustible.
The Commentary states: "Unity and multiplicity are unimpeded, like a thousand lamps in a single room" refers to the fifth gate, the Gate of Mutual Interpenetration of Unity and Multiplicity.

Because unity and multiplicity arise through mutual conditionality (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and their functional powers penetrate one another, they are able to intermingle; this is called "mutual inclusion."
Because their characteristics are not destroyed, they are said to be "not the same.
It is like a thousand lamps illuminating together within a single room: as the lamps follow the differences of their individual bowls, each is distinct;
yet as the lamps follow the pervasiveness of their light, each ray of light interpenetrates the others—ever distinct and ever merged.
The Sūtra states: "Within one, understand the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, understand the one.
By comprehending their mutual arising, one shall attain fearlessness.
This analogy of the lamp may also serve as a metaphor for mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
If one looks directly at the light, no distinct characteristics are seen, for it is solely a single light.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Both concealment and manifestation are established together, like a crescent moon in the autumn sky,” this refers to the sixth gate: the Gate of the Simultaneous Establishment of Secrecy and Manifestation.

It is like the moon on the eighth or ninth night, half-hidden and half-manifest: when it is fully manifest, it is immediately hidden; when it is fully hidden, it is immediately manifest. This is unlike the moon during the dark fortnight, when it is hidden and has no manifestation, nor unlike the full moon at the end of the month, when it is manifest and has no concealment.
When the one subsumes the many, the one is manifest and the many are hidden;
when the many subsume the one, the many are manifest and the one is hidden.
When a single hair subsumes the Dharma-realm, then the Dharma-realms of all other hairs are hidden.
Each of the remaining individual hairs likewise interpenetrates one another, and their appearance and disappearance are the same.
Furthermore, during that half-month, it is not only the case that light and darkness coexist, but also that there is darkness beneath the light and light beneath the darkness.
For example, entering right concentration in the east constitutes one half of light;
arising from concentration in the west constitutes one half of darkness.
Yet the very place where one enters in the east is precisely where one arises in the east, just as there is darkness beneath the light.
The place where it arises in the west is precisely its entry from the west, like light appearing beneath darkness;
therefore, it is called the "Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of Secrecy and Manifestation.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Layer upon layer they reflect one another, like pearls suspended from Indra’s net,” this refers to the seventh gate, the "Indra’s Net Realm Gate."

It is like the celestial palace of Indra, covered above by a net of pearls; within each single bright pearl, the myriad images are all manifested, and this is true for every pearl. Furthermore, they mutually reflect one another’s images, and these reflections again produce further reflections, layer upon layer without end.

Although a thousand lights and ten thousand colors interreflect in successive layers, they remain clearly distinguished; it is like two mirrors reflecting one another, where each layer penetrates the next, transmitting and mirroring light so that they emerge from one another in an infinite succession.

The Commentary states: "Each thought-moment is perfectly interfused, like a dream lasting through an entire lifetime. This refers to the Eightieth Gate, the Gate of the Accomplishment of Differentiated Dharmas Through the Separation of Worlds.

It corresponds to the ten ways in which Bodhisattvas speak of the three periods of time as taught in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*): namely, speaking of the past as the past; speaking of the past as the present; speaking of the past as the future; speaking of the present as the past; speaking of the present as equality; speaking of the present as the future; speaking of the future as the past; speaking of the future as the present; speaking of the future as the inexhaustible; and speaking of the three periods of time as a single thought-moment.

The preceding nine [eons] are the particulars, while a single thought-moment is the totality; thus they are called the "ten eons," because the three periods of time are mutually inclusive through their causal interdependence.

Since a single thought-moment contains all ten, this reveals their inexhaustibility; therefore, a single thought-moment is itself immeasurable kalpas, and immeasurable kalpas are themselves a single thought-moment.
The "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" states: "Immeasurable and incalculable eons, when understood, are but a single thought-moment.
Knowing that this thought is itself non-thought—thus one perceives the world."
"Just as in a single night's dream, one may pass through many lifetimes.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In a dream, one thinks years have passed, yet upon awakening, it is but a brief moment."
Therefore, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
The "Chapter on Transcending the World" states: "It is like a person in a dream who performs all manner of deeds; though they pass through billions of years, a single night has not yet ended."
Thus, when Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, his slumber lasted for a hundred years.
Such instances are numerous.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The dharma-gates are layered like clouds rising in the vast sky,” this refers to the ninth gate: the Gate of Manifesting the Dharma through Events to Generate Understanding.
The term "redundant" (or "layered") is intended to reveal that the one and the many do not obstruct one another; thus, for each and every phenomenon, there are manifold dharma-gates.
Since each individual phenomenon is itself the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and because the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible, phenomena are likewise inexhaustible.

The "Chapter on Dedication" states: "These flowers arise from the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas," and so forth. This intends to clarify that all causes give rise to a single fruit, and that this single fruit inherently contains all causes; it does not mean that these [flowers] are relied upon to symbolize something else.

The Commentary states: "The myriad practices unfold like flowers blooming upon brocade" refers to the tenth gate, the Gate of the Endowment with Virtues through the Pure and Mixed [Teachings] of All Treasuries (*sarvakośa*).

This name appears among Zhixiang’s Ten Profundities (*daśa-gambhīra*), yet because it carries two meanings, Xianshou changed it to the Gate of the Unobstructed Freedom between the Broad and the Narrow.

First, if one considers that accord with principle constitutes the "pure" while the myriad practices constitute the "mixed," this refers to the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*shili wuai*), not the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishu wuai*).

For example, if a Bodhisattva’s great compassion were the "pure," and throughout the limits of the future they perceived only the practice of compassion while all other practices were like empty space; [this would be an instance of the former].

If one speaks according to the "mixed" gate (*miśra-mukha*), wherein all myriad practices are cultivated together, these two gates differ and thus do not constitute the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).
Second, as in the case of the single gate of giving (*dāna*), all myriad dharmas are entirely termed "giving"; therefore, it is called "pure."
Furthermore, this gate of giving already encompasses the practices of all the perfections; therefore, it is called "mixed.

In this way, the pure and the mixed do not obstruct one another, which is why it is termed "endowed with virtues," thereby establishing the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena in phenomena (shishi wuai).
Furthermore, within a single [practice], all the pāramitās are complete; when these pāramitās are maintained, it is called the "Gate of Characteristics and Identity" (sō-soku-mon).
If the pāramitās are dissolved, it again resembles the "Gate of Identity" (soku-mon).
Therefore, rather than maintaining [the former], it is revised as the "Gate of Broadness and Narrowness" (kō-kyō-mon).

Now, regarding the ultimate characteristic (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*), there is a slight difference in that it is defined solely by its activity; since this section lacks the primary and its attendants (*sahāya*), it is presented again here to complete the ten meanings.

As for the phrase "comparable to flowers blooming upon brocade," the intention is to take up the five-colored threads: although the colors of the flowers differ, each and every thread passes completely through them.
The universal analogy refers to purity, while the particular analogy refers to mixture; thus, being both constant and variable, and both uniform and diverse, it is called "unimpeded.
This is not merely a difference like that between embroidery and painting, for it does not encompass the ten mysteries mentioned above.
This provides a brief outline of the general framework; for a detailed account, refer to the subsequent section on the "Delineation of the Scope of Meaning" (*yifenqi*).

Regarding the commentary’s passage: “If [the goal] is so lofty that it cannot be looked up to, then the Bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices will find their gills and scales exposed at the Dragon Gate,” this refers to the seventh stage: the immediate transcendence of benefits.
The text contains ten meanings.
The first two meanings collectively reveal its loftiness and profundity, clarifying that those of provisional or limited capacity cannot fathom it;
the subsequent eight correctly clarify the immediate and perfect fulfillment of benefits.

Furthermore, the first two [aspects] are profound and sublime; they function by way of contrast to manifest the benefits, clarifying that the provisional and the small vehicles cannot fathom them, and thus, because there was no prior cause, they conversely exhort sentient beings to have faith and understanding.
The latter eight [aspects] manifest the benefits through direct correspondence, meaning they are both sudden and perfect, ensuring that [the benefits] are necessarily received.
First, this clarifies loftiness and distance.

If Mount Tai leaned toward heaven and the Min and Eme ranges brushed against the Milky Way, their summits would be difficult to look up at; thus, the *Analects* says: "The more one looks up at it, the higher it seems; the more one drills into it, the harder it becomes."

Regarding the Bodhisattva who has accumulated practice, the "Chapter on Appearance" states: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment."

If one has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majestic power of the Tathāgata, or if, having heard it at some time, one does not believe or understand it, does not follow or enter into it, such a person cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.

If one hears this Dharma gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, and having heard it, believes, understands, accords with, and awakens to its entry, you should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
It is like a fish ascending the Dragon Gate: if it succeeds in ascending, it immediately transforms into a dragon, which corresponds to those with the capacity for the *Avataṃsaka*.

If it fails to ascend, its gills and scales are exposed beneath the Dragon Gate; this corresponds to the "provisional-name bodhisattvas," namely those who practice according to the stages of the provisional teachings.

The Commentary states: "Profound and thus impossible to fathom, the śrāvakas of supreme virtue close their eyes and ears at this auspicious assembly" refers to the second [section], which reveals the profound and wondrous, namely, the "Dharmadhātu Chapter."
First, Śāriputra and the five hundred śrāvakas praised his virtues, saying:
"He has fully awakened to the ultimate truth and realized the limit of reality; he has deeply entered the nature of phenomena and forever emerged from the ocean of existence."
Relying on the virtues of the Buddha, they are freed from the bonds of the fetters and abide in the state of non-obstruction.
Their minds are tranquil like space.
Having forever severed doubt and confusion regarding all Buddhas, they enter with deep faith into the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The commentary states:
This refers to the aforementioned excellence.
To be present at the Tathāgata’s sublime assembly in the Jeta Grove without seeing or hearing it is called "obstructing the sight and sound."
"Du" (to block) means to obstruct.
When it pertains to the eyes, it is called "seeing"; when it pertains to the ears, it is called "hearing.
Although he was present at the assembly, he was as if deaf and blind; therefore, it is said that he "blocked his sight and hearing."
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the foremost great Śrāvakas—
Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Revata, Subhūti, Aniruddha,
Nanda, Kapphiṇa, Kātyāyana, Pūrṇa, and other such great Śrāvakas..."
In the Jeta Grove, they all failed to see the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, the Tathāgata’s magnificent adornments, the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity,
the Tathāgata’s playful manifestations, the Tathāgata’s miraculous transformations, the Tathāgata’s supreme excellence,
the Tathāgata’s wondrous conduct, the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, the Tathāgata’s sustaining presence, or the Tathāgata’s pure buddha-field. Furthermore—
Furthermore, they do not see the inconceivable realm of bodhisattvas, the great assemblies of bodhisattvas, the universal entry of bodhisattvas,
the universal arrival of bodhisattvas, the universal approach of bodhisattvas, the spiritual transformations of bodhisattvas, the playful sports of bodhisattvas,
the retinues of bodhisattvas, the locations of bodhisattvas, nor the majestic lion-thrones of bodhisattvas.
The palaces of bodhisattvas, the abodes of bodhisattvas, the mastery of samādhis entered by bodhisattvas, the observations of bodhisattvas,
the yawns of bodhisattvas, the valor of bodhisattvas, the offerings of bodhisattvas, the predictions of bodhisattvas,
the maturation of bodhisattvas, the courage of bodhisattvas, and the purity of the dharma-body of bodhisattvas.
The purity of the bodhisattva; the perfection of the wisdom-body of the bodhisattva; the manifestation of the vow-body of the bodhisattva; the accomplishment of the form-body of the bodhisattva;
the complete purity of the bodhisattva’s possession of all marks; the adornment of the bodhisattva’s constant radiance with various colors;
the bodhisattva’s emission of great light from a jeweled net; the bodhisattva’s arising of clouds of transformations; and the body of the bodhisattva.
Throughout the ten directions, the various practices of bodhisattvas are perfected;
yet none of such matters are seen at all. Why is this?

Because their roots of goodness differ: because they originally did not cultivate the roots of goodness for witnessing the sovereign power of the Buddhas; because they originally did not praise or proclaim the pure merits of all Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions; because they originally did not extol the various miraculous transformations of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; because they originally did not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while transmigrating within the flow of birth and death; because they originally did not cause others to abide in the bodhicitta; and because they originally were unable to ensure that the lineage of the Tathāgatas would not be severed, and so forth.
The preceding section first enumerates the persons, who are the śrāvakas of superior virtue.
The subsequent clarification regarding "not seeing" and so forth refers to the closing off of sight and hearing.

As for the explanation following "Why is this? which states that the cause for not seeing is inferiority: "not seeing" alone is not yet profound; it is only when those of superior virtue do not know [it] that it becomes truly mysterious and wondrous.

In the commentary, following the passage "Seeing and hearing serve as the seeds for transcending the eight difficulties and the stages of the ten grounds," there are eight sections that correctly reveal the characteristics of the perfect and pervasive attainment of benefit.

This first section clarifies the benefit of seeing and hearing, which is also termed the "benefit of planting seeds. This refers to the threefold simultaneous fulfillment of the hell-dwelling devaputra in the "Anuvyañjana-parivarta," as well as the statement in the first bhūmi: "Even if one dwells amidst the waters of the ocean or within the kalpa-ending conflagration, if one is capable of receiving this Dharma, one will certainly hear it."
"Those who harbor doubts and do not believe shall never hear such a teaching as this.
This statement that they neither believe nor hear serves, by contrast, to reveal that those who do believe and hear will indeed attain benefit.
The seawater is a dragon, subsumed within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
The kalpa-fire is a celestial being; when the fire disaster reaches the first dhyāna heaven, those born in the second dhyāna heaven, such as the Ābhāsvara gods, [are not burned].

The difficulty of being born in the Heaven of Long Life is such that one may hear [the Dharma] here; furthermore, the celestial sons of the upper realms and those in hell already face three difficulties.
Even for spirits and ghosts in the Buddha’s assembly, hearing [the Dharma] is sufficient to resolve the three miserable paths.
At the time of the fire disaster, it encompasses both before and after the Buddha’s appearance.
Although the paths of humans and devas differ, those who have already attained combined intelligence are not excluded from the northern continent.
The deaf can see with their eyes, and the blind can hear with their ears; thus, the eight difficulties are fully present.
All may listen to the sutras for the purpose of planting the seeds [of enlightenment].
To transcend the stages of the ten bhūmis lies precisely within the realm of the sons of heaven in hell; this is a case of weighing the heavy against the light.
If even those in the Avīci Hell can attain sudden and perfect realization, how could one who is honored by birth among human beings fail to remain and listen?
Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Minor Marks and Radiance," it says: "The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying:
'O Son of the Buddha!
On the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet there is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, named King of Universal Radiance.'"
He possesses an auspicious mark named King of Perfection.

He constantly emits forty kinds of light rays, among which is one called Pure Merit. This ray can illuminate worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred billion nayutas of Buddha-fields, causing the various karmic actions, conducts, and aspirations of all sentient beings to reach full maturity.
Sentient beings in the Avīci Hell who encounter this light all reach the end of their lives and are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Once reborn there, celestial drums resound, extensively expounding the Dharma for them.

It continues: "At that time, because the sons of the gods heard this teaching on the vast and universal dedication of Samantabhadra, they attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and acquired the samādhi adorned with all powers. By means of pure threefold action (*trikarma*) equal in number to all sentient beings, they repented and eliminated all heavy obstructions. Thereupon, they immediately beheld lotuses made of the seven precious jewels, as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-fields. Upon each lotus, there was a Bodhisattva sitting in the full lotus posture, emitting great radiance, and so forth, until they scattered flowers over the Bodhisattvas."
It further states: "Those clouds of incense rain universally upon worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable Buddha-fields.
If there are sentient beings whose bodies are touched by this fragrance, their bodies become peaceful and blissful; it continues until it says that eighty-four thousand afflictions are extinguished."
The conclusion states: "Having known thus, one accomplishes the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of Fragrant Banner Clouds.
The commentary explains:
This refers to attaining the ten stages (bhūmis) in a single succession.

Next it says: "If there are sentient beings who see its canopy, they plant roots of goodness equal to those of a Wheel-Turning King with Pure Golden Rims, as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River.
The commentary states:
This refers to attaining the tenth stage (bhūmi) for the second time.
The subsequent passage states: "This bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the position of a Wheel-Turning King with a Pure Golden Rim, emitting the pure radiance from his maṇi-crest.

If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they all attain the tenth stage of a bodhisattva, accomplish immeasurable wisdom-light, obtain ten kinds of pure eyes up to ten kinds of pure minds, and become fully endowed with immeasurable, profound samādhis."
The commentary states:
"This refers to the third stage of attaining the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, 'When understanding and practice are embodied, the fruit of vast kalpas is perfected in a single lifetime,' this refers to the benefit of the second stage, understanding and practice."
In the seventy-eighth sutra, Maitreya praises Sudhana, saying:

"Other bodhisattvas must pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas before they can fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva, and before they can draw near to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas."

Within a single lifetime, this son of a householder is able to purify Buddha-fields; to transform sentient beings; to penetrate the Dharma-realm with wisdom; to accomplish all the pāramitās; to expand all practices; to fulfill all great vows; to transcend all demonic activities; to serve all spiritual friends; to purify all bodhisattva paths; and to be fully endowed with all the practices of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, Prince Mahātejas also represents the fruit of many kalpas perfected in a single lifetime.
The two aforementioned cases both clarify swift realization through direct evidence.
Moreover, the central tenet of this sutra clarifies the perfection of the three lifetimes:
First, arising from seeing and hearing;
second, arising from understanding and practice, which corresponds to the two preceding lines;
third, arising from realization and entry, which corresponds to the two subsequent lines.
The Commentary states: “The Lion’s Rush, where the multitudes of the ocean suddenly realize [enlightenment] within the forest” refers to the third benefit, sudden realization.

The beginning of the sixtieth sutra says: “At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the bodhisattvas, took great compassion as his body, great compassion as his gate, and great compassion as his head; employing the dharma of great compassion as his skillful means, he pervaded empty space and entered the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Lion’s Stretch).”
The old translation says "exertion" (*visphūrjita*); this meaning of exertion is applied to the lion because it is convenient for that context.

However, at the beginning of the sixty-first sutra, after Samantabhadra has made his manifestation, the Tathāgata emits light from between his eyebrows. Consequently, the great assembly of bodhisattvas in the Jeta Grove all see every Buddha-field throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm; within each and every atom, there are Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-fields, with various names, various colors, various purities, various dwellings, and various forms.

In all such lands throughout these various world-systems, there are great bodhisattvas seated upon lion thrones at sites of enlightenment, having attained equal and perfect awakening, surrounded before and behind by assemblies of bodhisattvas.
They made offerings to the various lords of the world, and so forth, until it was said:

"Therefore, they all enter the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and profound samādhi; through the great supernormal powers that exhaust the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, they may enter the Dharma-body, or enter the form-body, or enter the practices accomplished in the past, or enter the perfection of the *pāramitās*, or enter the wheel of pure conduct and adornments, or enter the various bodhisattva stages, or enter the power of attaining perfect enlightenment, or enter the undifferentiated great transformations of the samādhis in which the Buddha dwells, or enter the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and wisdom, or enter the ocean of the Buddha’s unimpeded eloquence."
This was immediately and fully realized, as explained at length in the *Vana-samādhi-sūtra*, by means of the ten modes of entry (*daśa-praveśa*) entering this object of entry.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The elephant king turns in circles; the six thousand paths are accomplished beneath a single word,” this refers to the fourth [stage], the benefit of transcending expedient means (*atīta-kuśala-mūla*).
This refers to the beginning of the final assembly in the sixty-first sutra, where there was a gathering of six thousand bhikṣus.
Śāriputra had these six thousand bhikṣus contemplate the ten virtues of Mañjuśrī; the six thousand then requested to go and see Mañjuśrī, and Śāriputra directed them to do so.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, surrounded by immeasurable and sovereign bodhisattvas as well as his great assembly, turned to look at the bhikṣus like an elephant king; therefore, it is called "the turning of the elephant king."
Regarding the statement that "six thousand attained the Way beneath these words": when the bhikṣus gave rise to their vows, Mañjuśrī caused them to develop ten kinds of tireless minds.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the bhikṣus attained a samādhi called "The Unobstructed Eye that Beholds the Realm of All Buddhas."
By attaining this samādhi, one sees all the Buddha-Tathāgatas and their respective assemblies at their places of enlightenment throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions;
one sees all sentient beings within every realm of existence in those worlds of the ten directions, and one also sees all the various distinctions among those worlds of the ten directions.
Furthermore, they clearly see all the atoms within those entire worlds;
they also clearly see all the palaces where sentient beings dwell in those worlds, adorned with various kinds of jewels;
and they also hear the various voices and sounds of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they expound the various dharmas, including their phrasing and explanations.
He fully understands and comprehends them all; he is also able to observe the faculties, minds, and desires of all sentient beings in that world;
he is also able to recollect the ten prior and ten subsequent births of all sentient beings in that world;
he is also able to recollect the events of ten eons past and ten eons future in that world; and he sees them all.
The ten original birth stories of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the ten attainments of perfect enlightenment, the ten turnings of the wheel of Dharma,
the ten kinds of supernormal powers, the ten kinds of preaching the Dharma, the ten kinds of admonitions, the ten kinds of eloquence,
as well as the accomplishment of ten thousand bodhicittas, ten thousand samādhis, and ten thousand pāramitās.

All were completely purified; they attained the perfect radiance of great wisdom and acquired the ten kinds of supranormal powers of a bodhisattva—supple and subtle—and dwelt in the bodhicitta, firm and unshakable.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva exhorted the bhikṣus to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra; having abided in the conduct of Samantabhadra, they entered the ocean of great vows; having entered the ocean of great vows, they accomplished the ocean of great vows.

Because they have accomplished the ocean of great vows, their minds are pure; because their minds are pure, their bodies are pure; because their bodies are pure, their bodies are light and agile; and because their bodies are light and agile, they attain great supernormal powers from which there is no regression.

By virtue of attaining this supernormal power, he never leaves the presence of Mañjuśrī’s feet, yet manifests his body before all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, fully accomplishing all Buddha-dharmas.
The commentary states:
This refers to the accomplishment of the Path; within a single samādhi, there are ten universal functions, all of which provide perfect benefit.

Regarding the sub-commentary’s statement, “When the light is opened at the Eastern Temple, the perfection of wisdom is no different from the initial aspiration,” this refers to the fifth stage: the accomplishment of the benefit of wisdom.

Regarding the "Eastern Temple of the Illuminator," it refers to what is stated in the sixty-second scripture: "At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he gradually traveled south through the human world until he reached the east of the City of Blessings (Puṇyavatī). There he stayed within the Śāla Grove of the Adorned Banner (Vyūha-dhvaja), at the site of a great stūpa where, in the past, various Buddhas had taught and transformed sentient beings."
The commentary states:
This refers to the Eastern Temple.

At that time, when the people of Puṇḍravardhana heard that the youth Mañjuśrī was at the great stūpa in the Śāla Grove of the Banner of Adornment, a vast multitude emerged from the city and went to where he was.
In the detailed enumeration that follows, there are five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred young men, and five hundred young women; Sudhana is one among them.

Thereafter, Mañjuśrī gazed alone upon Sudhana; having observed him, he comforted and instructed him, expounding all the Buddha-dharmas for him, even saying: "Having taught this Dharma, he earnestly exhorted and encouraged him to increase his power, causing him to rejoice and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and further causing him to recollect his past roots of goodness."
Having performed these deeds, he again preached the Dharma to all sentient beings at that place as was appropriate for them, and then departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard from Mañjuśrī such various merits of the Buddha, single-mindedly and diligently sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and following Mañjuśrī’s lead, spoke in verse, etc.; this refers to the opening of the Eastern Temple.
To say that the perfection of wisdom is no different from that of a beginner means that, as stated at the beginning of the eighty-first sutra, wisdom illuminates the non-dual nature.
The sutra says: "At that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar, across a distance of one hundred and ten yojanas, and placed it upon the crown of Sudhana’s head, saying these words:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"Good son! If one is separated from the root of faith, the mind becomes inferior and filled with regret; one’s meritorious practices remain incomplete, and one falls away from diligent effort.

One develops attachment to even a single root of goodness and considers a small amount of merit sufficient. Unable to skillfully initiate vows and practices, one is not sustained by spiritual friends nor remembered by the Tathāgatas. One cannot understand such a nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such a principle (*naya*), such a Dharma-gate (*dharmamukha*), such a practice (*caryā*), or such a realm (*viṣaya*). Whether it be knowing them universally, knowing them in their variety, exhausting their source, comprehending them, entering into them, explaining them, discerning them, realizing them, or attaining them—one is utterly incapable of any of these."
The commentary states:
"Thoroughly knowing the nature of phenomena" and below refers to the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna*).

If one is separated from faith, this cannot be attained; conversely, this reveals the preceding meaning: because of faith, one attains it without departing from the initial resolve to practice. Thus, faith and wisdom are non-dual.
If one takes immovable wisdom (*aniñjya-jñāna*) as the starting point, then the preceding and succeeding two wisdoms are non-dual.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Seeking southward through successive stages, the perfection of causes does not exceed a single pore,” this refers to the benefit of the sixth stage, the Stage of Accomplishment (*niṣpanna-bhūmi*).
That is to say, Sudhana’s initial meeting with Mañjuśrī is assigned to the stage of the Ten Faiths;
from Meghashiri to Gopā, they are assigned to the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Sainthood;
and from Māyā onwards, they are all assigned to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
Later, upon seeing Samantabhadra, he immediately attained the perfection of the cause without exceeding a single pore.
The text says: "At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw himself within the body of Samantabhadra, teaching and transforming sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions."

It further states: "From the time the youth Sudhana first resolved his mind for enlightenment until he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, all the oceans of Buddha-lands he entered during that interval are now surpassed by the oceans of Buddha-lands entered in a single thought-moment within a single pore of Samantabhadra—by a factor of unspeakably unspeakable times the number of atoms in a Buddha-land."
"As it is with one pore, so it is with all pores.
It further says, "The youth Sudhana, within the world-systems of the pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, may pass through an eon in a single world-system, proceeding in this manner."
Thus they practice for as long as it takes—even for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

Yet they do not pass away from this field to appear in that field; rather, in every thought-moment, they pervade the ocean of boundless fields to teach and transform sentient beings, leading them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the youth Sudhana successively attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; he became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas. A single body of his filled all worlds, being equal in terms of buddha-lands, practices, perfect enlightenment, spiritual powers, wheels of Dharma, speech, voices, powers and fearlessnesses, the abodes of Buddhas, great compassion, and the inconceivable mastery of liberation—all were entirely equal.
The commentary states:
"This refers to the perfection of causes within a single pore. The sub-commentary says:

"'Opening the sutra-scrolls within a minute atom, the fruit is accomplished in every thought-moment'—this seventh point reveals the benefit of the fruit resulting from the causes; it corresponds to the metaphor of the great sutra hidden within a mote of dust in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata)."

A verse in the sutra says: "Suppose there were a great scripture, equal in measure to the three thousandfold world system, contained within a single speck of dust; and so it is with every speck of dust.
A person of wisdom, with pure eyes that see all clearly, breaks open the dust and brings forth the scripture, universally benefiting all sentient beings."
