That is to say, beyond the aforementioned four faults, the fifth asks: "Why is the Hīnayāna not established?

Regarding the four sections that address this difficulty: first, it sets forth the basis for the names of the Tripiṭaka, thereby resolving the fault of contradicting the ultimate teachings as well as the fault of indiscriminately conflating them with the Mahāyāna.
This means that since both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises establish this name, the fault of indiscriminate confusion does not lie with us.
If someone were to raise the objection:

"Within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the term 'Hīnayāna' follows the terminology of its own school, while the designation 'Tripiṭaka' follows the terminology of other schools; it is not a common name."
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* follows the terminology of others.
But why is it that even the Hīnayāna of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* is called the "Three Baskets" (Tripiṭaka)?
How could this be following another school?
It is precisely because of the aforementioned principle that it does not contradict the ultimate teaching; for Kumārajīva’s translations of the sutras mostly rely on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
To ensure the textual integrity of the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, both terms are presented together.

The fault of the Hīnayāna does not lie in the Tripiṭaka itself, but rather in its narrow-mindedness; therefore, when the Hīnayāna is criticized, it is not the Tripiṭaka—the subject matter it expounds—that is being censured.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, confronting the old physician,” this second section clarifies the reason for establishing the Tripiṭaka.
At the beginning of the four teachings, these are set in opposition to the three [teachings] of the "old physician"; therefore, it is necessary to establish the Tripitaka as a distinct category.
Furthermore, since these three are categorically different, they do not overlap with the Mahāyāna; for this reason, they are designated by their specific titles.
It is just as all five sense objects are "form" (*rūpa*), yet the term "form" alone serves as the general designation for them;
thus, although the Tripiṭaka masters employ this general name, it has come to function as a specific designation for the Hīnayāna.
Regarding the "old physician," this refers to the analogy of the two physicians—the old and the new—in the second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The old physician is a metaphor for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
As for the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, each of these likewise has two aspects.
The first is false and the second is correct.
The former, false precepts, refer to those such as those of the chicken and the dog;
the latter, correct precepts, refer to the ten paths of wholesome action.

The "old heterodox certainties" refer to the methods of ghosts and spirits taught by the ninety-five types of heretics, which may allow one to know the fortune or misfortune of the world and manifest supernatural transformations;
the "orthodox" refers precisely to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the development of the five supernormal powers.

Those with former false wisdom, based on the view of a self and what belongs to a self, give rise to various forms of false knowledge; they deny cause and effect, such as those who eat excrement or go naked.

Those who are correct, likewise based on the view of a self and what belongs to a self, give rise to various forms of worldly knowledge; they assert that there are causes and effects and various wholesome dharmas.

Now, the Buddha teaches the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), wherein the precepts, concentration, and wisdom are elucidated; this is precisely what the new physician who has come from afar, well-versed in the eight branches of medical art, has been taught by the Tathāgata.

First, regarding precepts: this refers to the five ways of attaining the precepts, which give rise to all forms of restraint, both unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and manifest (*vijñapti*), such as those found in the five divisions of the Vinaya.

Second, regarding concentration: this refers to entering the nine successive concentrations based on the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), thereby giving rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

The three types of wisdom refer to the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing; they involve the destruction of the two views of self and body as well as the sixty-two views, the manifestation of true outflow-free wisdom, and the accomplishment of the eleven knowledges and the three outflow-free faculties.
Regarding these [three]—precept, concentration, and wisdom—even all non-Buddhists have not heard their names, let alone possess them in part.
Therefore, it is said that "first, they are contrasted with the old physician," and so forth.

To say that "the three matters are categorically different" means that the former are contrasted with the old physician, while the latter are contrasted with the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings.
The names of the Three Piṭakas are established on account of their distinct differences; it is precisely for this reason that many schools extensively elucidate the Three Piṭakas.
Names are established based on what is predominant, so there is no fault of indeterminacy.

The commentary states: "Because the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) integrates the three [vehicles]," etc. This third section clarifies why the latter three [teachings] are not termed "Tripitaka," thereby correctly demonstrating that the Mahayana lacks the deficiency of being a Tripitaka.

This means that although the Mahāyāna possesses the three piṭakas, each contains meanings such as "integration" (*róng*) and "dispelling" (*fú*); therefore, specific names are not established for them, yet their substance is not absent.
As for the statement that the intent of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) integrates the three, it is because they are integrated into ultimate emptiness and quiescence.

Thus, the *Dharmapada* says: "If one speaks of those who uphold the precepts, yet lack goodness and dignified deportment, their mark of morality is like empty space; those who uphold them would be deluded."
"If one studies various samādhis, this is movement and not sitting meditation; if the mind flows following external objects, how can it be called concentration?
Only when there is neither wisdom nor attainment is it termed true wisdom.
"Prajñā is without cognition," "as wisdom and [ignorance] are both quiescent," and so forth—all these are instances of the third [meaning], the integration of the three in intention.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The Separate Teaching manifests the three based on a single dharma-nature": because they are unified by this single dharma-nature, they cannot be considered as being distinct from one another.

Since each and every dharma-gate does not depart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is said: "Because one knows that the nature of phenomena is free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) in accordance with it."
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from disordered conceptualization, one practices the dhyāna-pāramitā in accordance with this truth.

Because one knows that the nature of phenomena is originally endowed with the radiance of wisdom and devoid of the darkness of delusion, one practices the prajñā-pāramitā in accordance with this truth, and so forth.

The Commentary states: "In the Perfect Teaching, the three and the one are without obstruction" means that they are three while being one, and one while being three; it is not merely a single entity that unifies them, for within a single study, all three are fully encompassed.
"If even a single practice possesses all [qualities], how much more so the three?
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning "The reason it is not called Hīnayāna," this is the fourth section clarifying why it is not termed Hīnayāna, which addresses the fifth objection.
That is to say, there may be an objection stating:
"Why not simply call it the Hīnayāna, rather than arbitrarily establishing the Tripiṭaka and thereby inviting many errors?
Therefore, we now respond as follows:
Because there exists the Mahāyāna, it cannot be called "Small.
Within that teaching, there are also bodhisattvas, and thus it is termed Mahāyāna.
Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, all such teachings are designated as the "Small Vehicle" Tripiṭaka.

Regarding the term "Six Perfections Bodhisattva" (*ṣaṭpāramitā-bodhisattva*): this refers to one who separately cultivates the six perfections throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, each reaching its fulfillment at a specific time. These stages are all with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and have not yet entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). By means of the wolf of impermanence (*anityatā*), which lies in wait for the sheep of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the fat of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is made to diminish while the body of merit (*guṇakāya*) is made to grow plump, continuing thus until the foot of the Bodhi tree. There, through thirty-four moments of mind, the fetters are severed all at once. This consists of the sixteen moments of the Path of Seeing—eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*)—plus the nine grades of the delusions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) on the single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Each grade has nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), totaling eighteen; thus, there are thirty-four moments in all.
This is explained in detail in such works as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "becoming a true Buddha," the Mahāyāna explains that this attainment of Buddhahood through the severance of afflictions refers to the eightfold manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
The Hīnayāna considers these to be truly established; therefore, they belong to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this adherence to reality is termed the "crooked view" of the two vehicles.

The Commentary states: "Therefore, regarding the meanings of the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings]," and so forth. This is the second section, which generally explains the difficulty concerning the four teachings.
It refers to the following objection:

"If the Tripitaka teaching also possesses the meanings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect, and even the Perfect teaching also possesses the meanings of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct, why can they not be designated interchangeably, rather than being restricted and fixed?"
Therefore, the present response states:
although all four teachings possess these four meanings and each contains the other three to some degree, they do not establish their primary meaning as a secondary matter.
This is like the Great Virtuous Chan Master Sanxue, who, despite possessing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, established only the meaning of Chan because Chan was predominant.
The others are merely supplementary and do not fully embody the wondrous; therefore, they are not called the "Dharma of Vinaya.
The same applies to the other two [collections].
As for the phrase "mutually possessing," even within the Tripiṭaka teaching, the principle of impermanence is universally present and is equally received by the three vehicles.
Furthermore, because the Four Great Vows and the Six Perfections were specifically taught for bodhisattvas,
and because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) was also taught for bodhisattvas, there are thus three divisions within the Tripitaka teaching.
As for the three divisions within the Shared Teaching, since it also teaches the Tripitaka, it should likewise be called the "Tripitaka."
Furthermore, because it also teaches the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*), it should be called the Distinct Teaching;
because it also teaches the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it should be called the Perfect Teaching.

The Distinct Teaching possesses these three aspects: it also teaches the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), it also teaches the principle of non-arising emptiness, and it also teaches the Middle Way and the Knowledge of All Modes.

Since the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) also speaks of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), speaks of the principle of true emptiness, and speaks of practicing through the stages and ranks over successive kalpas, it too should possess the other three names.
Therefore, the general answer is:
although each of the four teachings incidentally possesses elements of the others, upon critical examination, they do not establish [a definitive system].
Why do they not establish it?

Regarding the initial point that the commonality of the Tripitaka teachings and so forth is not established: although both [the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas] equally receive the teaching on impermanence, the two vehicles attain the realization of truth and sever their fetters in a single lifetime, whereas the bodhisattvas do not realize it for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; therefore, the meaning of "commonality" is not established.

Although for Bodhisattvas there are the separate explanations of the Four Great Vows and the Six Perfections, these do not expound a distinct principle nor sever distinct delusions; since they arise from views based upon the four truths of arising and ceasing, how can they be called "distinct"?
Although it is said that one possesses "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā), a bodhisattva in the causal stage cannot yet fully possess this all-encompassing wisdom.
Furthermore, since this all-encompassing wisdom illuminates only the two truths and does not illuminate the Middle Way, how can it be called "perfect" (pūrṇa)?
Thus, according to this [interpretation], the latter three meanings cannot be established; it merely establishes the meaning of the Tripiṭaka within the specific teaching.
As for the three meanings being unestablished in the Shared Teaching, although it speaks of the Tripiṭaka, this is because all things are of a single characteristic and without characteristics.

Furthermore, it is said that because [the former two] have already been attained, although they speak of the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*), they only illumine the conventional within the realms, and do not pertain to the Tathāgatagarbha’s merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although they speak of the Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they only illumine the Two Truths, and do not illumine the Middle Way, the inconceivable Two Truths.
Therefore, the meaning of the three distinct teachings cannot be established; they merely establish the meaning of the Shared Teaching.

As for why the three [aspects] of the Distinct Teaching are not established: although it speaks of the Buddha-dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and of immeasurable precepts, concentration, and wisdom, these differ from the three [aspects of] arising and ceasing.

Although the principle of non-arising emptiness is taught, it is the emptiness of the unattainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), for this is not merely emptiness as perceived in common by the two vehicles.
Although the Middle Way and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are taught, one does not possess the knowledge of all modes immediately upon generating the mind in the first stage.
Therefore, the three meanings of the Tripitaka, the Shared, and the Perfect teachings are all not established; only the Distinct meaning is established.

As for why the three [other] teachings are not established in the Perfect Teaching: although the Tripitaka is spoken of, it is because they all refer to True Suchness, the Real Mark, Buddha-nature, and Nirvana.
Although there is the principle of true emptiness—which is the very emptiness of Buddha-nature—the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know it, much less attain entry into it.
Although distinct stages and positions are taught in the Dharma gates, there are none that do not correspond to the true mark (dharmatā), for the one encompasses all.
Thus, the meanings of the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct teachings are all not established; it is solely the meaning of the Perfect Teaching.
Therefore, it is said: "If one examines its definitive reality, the other three are not established; they only establish the meanings within their own respective teachings."

The commentary states: "But [the passage] 'only judging the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*' and below constitutes the third section, which reconciles the Perfect (*yuan*) and Distinct (*bie*) teachings by determining what is to be accepted or rejected, using those [teachings] to judge all other sūtras.
To say that the *Avataṃsaka* is 'comprehensive' means it is comprehensive of the Distinct Teaching."

This would mean that one is confused regarding the sequential arrangement (xingbu) and thus labels it the Separate Teaching (biejiao), while taking only the perfect fusion (yuanrong) to be the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
To separate them results in two distinct teachings, each losing one side;
only by combining and harmonizing them can the definitive meaning (liyi) be realized, in accordance with the Huayan school, because the sequential and the perfect mutually encompass one another.

As was explained in the preceding section on the stages of practice (*caryābhūmi*), if one adopts this [position], it is merely a difference in terminology with the same underlying meaning, and thus there is no great fault.
However, if one rejects it, one loses the fundamental intent of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; therefore, we do not accept that view here.
Therefore, this section is titled "Determining What to Adopt and What to Reject.
The remaining meanings are found extensively in the *Four Teachings*; their essential points have already been fully prepared.

Regarding the commentary’s section “Third, during the early Tang dynasty, from海东 (Haidong),” there are two parts: first, the formal establishment of the position, and second, the [discussion of] conformity and contradiction.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the formal establishment [of the position], followed by the explanation beginning with "the Three Vehicles study together.

This does not clarify that the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) constitutes a distinction; rather, it clarifies that the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth do not constitute a distinction. It fully elucidates the two types of emptiness as being universal (*sāmānya*), because it does not take up the "study common to the Three Vehicles" as a distinct category.

The first two [interpretations] differ slightly based on the Tiantai school, as they explain the One Vehicle through its unique (asādhāraṇa) characteristics rather than by merging the three vehicles into one.
The commentary’s section beginning with "However, this" distinguishes between what is concordant and what is discordant.
The preceding section presents the essential meaning.
From the words "speaking for oneself" (*svayam-ukti*) onwards, there is a formal discussion of what is concordant and what is contrary.
This is because, by humbly acknowledging that one's own [view] does not encompass everything, one remains free from error.
If there were another principle [for this], it would be inferred from its inclusion within the category of "that which is not fully encompassed.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "Fourth, the disciples of Xianxiu," there are also two parts:
first, the formal establishment [of the position], and second, the reconciliation of contradictions.

The preceding section consists of five parts: first, a general introduction; second, citing the treatise as authority, beginning with "The Treatise says"; third, clearly explaining the established doctrine, beginning with "Regarding the four teachings"; fourth, specifically indicating their characteristics, beginning with "The initial teaching refers to..."; and fifth, concluding by summarizing the extensive details, beginning with "As extensively explained... and so forth.
That commentary further clarifies:
This established teaching reveals the expressive medium (the teaching) by relying upon the expressed nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
In the first stage, the nature of phenomena is entirely hidden; in the second, it is partially revealed; in the third, it is again partially hidden; and in the fourth, it is fully revealed.
Although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is one, its manifestations differ; thus, it is established as fourfold.
If categorized according to the vehicles (*yāna*), the second teaching corresponds to the Hīnayāna, the third to the Mahāyāna within the Three Vehicles, and the fourth to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is also largely the same as Guangzhai’s [theory of] the four vehicles.

In the commentary, from the words "However, now" onwards, there is a discussion of compliance and contradiction, which first provides a specific refutation and subsequently concludes with the demonstration of its fallacy.
Within the former, there are two parts:
First, the initial [point] is refuted, and subsequently, the latter three are refuted.
Now, regarding the first: there is the fault of the intermixture of the heterodox and the orthodox.
The section beginning with "If one were to address the Teacher" serves to refute and prevent such a defense.
One might fear that someone would offer this rebuttal:
"If one does not recognize the heterodox, how can one know the orthodox?
Only through the dialectical confrontation between the heterodox and the orthodox are black and white made distinct."
Therefore, we now refute this by saying:

if you wish to do so, you must first distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox in general; only thereafter can you differentiate their "Great" and "Small" [vehicles] within the categories of the heterodox and the orthodox.

Therefore, I have established this system: first, the three teachings are distinguished; within Confucianism, the nine schools and seven classics are analyzed; within Daoism, the differences between the *Daode jing* and other texts are discussed; and within Buddhism, the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the provisional and the real, are examined. Thus, there shall be no confusion or overlapping.
Otherwise, it is as in the Western Regions, where one first distinguishes between the "inner" and "outer"; within the outer, there are six masters or ten schools, and so forth.
The term "and so forth" includes the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles within the inner teachings.

Regarding the term "Six Teachers," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "First, Pūraṇa by name and Kāśyapa by clan; second, Maskarī by name and Gośālīputra [son of Gośālī]; third, Sañjayin by name and Vairāṭīputra [son of Vairāṭī]; fourth, Ajita by name and Keśakambalin [wearer of hair-cloth]; fifth, Kakuda by name and Kātyāyana by clan; sixth, Nirgrantha by name and Jñātiputra [son of Jñātī]."
These six each give rise to a particular view. One gives rise to the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), asserting:
"All phenomena are empty; there is no way of sovereign and minister, father and son, loyalty and filial piety."
Second, Makkhali Gosāla gave rise to the view of eternalism, asserting:
"All suffering and pleasure do not arise from karma; they exist inherently by their own nature.

Third, he gave rise to the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), maintaining that the Path need not be cultivated, for after eighty thousand kalpas of suffering have ended, one is spontaneously liberated—just as when a ball of thread is cast from the summit of a high mountain, it unwinds until it is exhausted and stops of its own accord.
To establish liberation as the cause means to take liberation itself as the cause.
To regard what is not a cause as a cause is a false cause.
To repudiate the Path and claim it need not be cultivated is wrong view.
The fourth refers to ascetic non-Buddhist practitioners who believe that liberation is attained by plucking out their own hair or by scorching themselves with the five fires.
To regard what is not the Path as the Path is likewise the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Fifth, they give rise to extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), clinging to the notion that all phenomena both exist and do not exist. This differs from the Buddha-dharma, according to which things exist because of causes and conditions, yet lack intrinsic nature and are thus non-existent.
By clinging to existence, one grasps at existence as having a fixed nature, which is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*);
by clinging to non-existence, one grasps at non-existence as having a fixed nature, which is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
To deviate from the Middle Way by clinging to either annihilationism or eternalism constitutes the formation of the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The sixth [view] holds that all fruits of suffering and pleasure result entirely from past karma and do not depend on present conditions; thus, when the karma of previous lives is exhausted, suffering is exhausted, and even if one practices the Path in the present, it cannot bring about its cessation.
This person believes that past karma serves as the cause [of present existence], which is not a false view; however, to deny the efficacy of present conditions is a partial false view.
One may believe that the Path can bring an end to suffering, yet deny its capacity to do so.
To regard the path as non-path is likewise a false view.
The calculations of the six masters are fully detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Each of these six gives rise to a single view, as cited in the Sixth Ground.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, based on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as being 'half and full,'" and so forth, it refutes the latter three teachings.

However, the intention of that master was that True Suchness (*tathatā*) has two aspects: to speak of both aspects together is the "complete aspect," while to speak of only the unchanging aspect is the "partial aspect."
It is merely the elucidation of the emptiness of persons that constitutes the "half," while the complete manifestation of both types of emptiness constitutes the "full.
Now, regarding the difficulty concerning "half" and "full," there are two senses:
first, if it were referred to as "full" based on the second sense alone, it would be improper for it to be obtained as only one part.

If even that which is "full" possessed but a single part of its meaning, then the "full" letters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* would likewise possess only a single part and thus would not be full; therefore, it is said that there should be no further mention of "one part."
The phrase "one part" intends the third teaching.
A second person offers this defense:
"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* discusses 'half' and 'full' only in terms of the two kinds of emptiness, and not in terms of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth."
This would contradict the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states: "That which is empty is called saṃsāra; that which is not empty is called Mahāparinirvāṇa."
How can it be said that the distinction between the "half" and the "full" is discussed solely in terms of the two kinds of emptiness?
One should know that these two kinds of emptiness are still the "half-letters" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; only the simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and non-emptiness constitutes the "full."
Therefore, that sutra states: "The śrāvaka perceives only emptiness and does not perceive non-emptiness, whereas the bodhisattva perceives both emptiness and non-emptiness.
Thus, the commentary says: "How could it be that he does not speak of wondrous existence while disparaging emptiness?"
The phrase "Therefore, that which is established" below is a general refutation.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "First, the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman," the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* (Lamp of Wisdom Treatise) preface states: "The Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman from Central India; in the language of Tang, his name means 'Friend'."

He studied both the *Hīnayāna* (Half) and *Mahāyāna* (Full) teachings, extensively mastering all commentaries. Having relinquished the self to delight the spirit and sought the profound to nourish his nature, he kept traveling abroad in mind and cherished benefiting sentient beings as his purpose. Thus, he was able to carry his body upon wooden pegs and summon companions by raising smoke; braving frost and ice, he crossed the Pamir Mountains, and enduring wind and snow, he traversed the River of Sands. After five years had accumulated and a journey of forty thousand *li* was completed, on the twentieth day of the eleventh month in the year of the *Jue* lunar station—the first year of the Zhenguan era of the Great Tang—he arrived at the imperial capital carrying the Sanskrit texts upon his head.

In the past, the State of Qin summoned Kumārajīva through the bitter use of arms, and the Han dynasty invited Kāśyapa Mātanga by dispatching envoys from afar; how can these be compared to the present, where the Way is harmonized through spiritual resonance and a hidden accord, such that auspicious signs prevail for both family and state, and a man of virtue has descended?
When the officials presented him for an audience, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

That year, an imperial edict was issued to station him at Daxingshan Monastery, and he was further requested to translate the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī Sūtra*, the *Prajñāpradīpa Śāstra*, the *Vyavahārasiddhi Śāstra*, and other works.
The Commentary states: "Āgama" is fully rendered as *āyāmā*, which here means "teaching.
In the section of the Commentary beginning with "This explanation of the name is restrictive," the author distinguishes between what is concordant and what is contrary.
The above propositions each cite a specific sutra, yet within each of these sutras there are practices such as the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

For instance, both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtras contain chapters on the "Four Noble Truths" that extensively elucidate their characteristics; thus, it is not the case that Mahāyāna sutras lack such contemplative practices.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, the system established by Xianshou,” and so forth: since the subsequent text relies upon this, it is now briefly indicated here.
However, in the past, there was also the Dharma Master Qisheshan who established six types of teaching:
first, the Teaching on Causal Conditions (hetu-pratyaya);...
Second is the religion of provisional names;
third is the religion of non-reality, which refers to the teaching of the principle that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations;
fourth is the religion of reality, which refers to the teaching of the principle of the true emptiness of all phenomena.
The teachings of the Five Constant Virtues speak of the truth and the eternality of merits such as the sands of the Ganges;
the teachings of the Six Perfectly Round Teachings are those which the various masters do not include in their current systems.
The first four names correspond to Master Yan’s exposition of the four doctrinal schools (*zong*) at the beginning of his establishment of tenets;
the fifth corresponds to the fifth period;
and the sixth corresponds to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of various masters, and is therefore omitted here without citation.

Furthermore, the True School (Shinshū) teaches the principle of true emptiness, while the Constant School (Jōshū) teaches that the truth possesses eternal merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Since the truth of the True School is not the same as the constant [truth] of the Constant School, it should likewise be impermanent.
Furthermore, as [sections] three and four are merely distinguished by being the dharma and its metaphor respectively, they are not cited here.
The preceding section concludes the establishment of the teachings in this land.
Second, regarding the introduction to the Western Regions, the text is divided into two parts:
First, the correct sequence; second, the conformity and deviation.
Regarding the former, Master Xianshou’s *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* arranges them within the initial section on "The Delimitation of Principles.
This section contains two parts:
First, a general preface regarding the origins; second, a dual explanation of what has been established.
Now, for the first:

although the three Tripitaka masters—Paramārtha, Dharmagupta, and Vajrabodhi—all hailed from the Western Regions, they personally resided here in this land to divide and transmit the teachings; therefore, they are included within the tradition of this region.
The latter two Great Virtuous Ones were originally teachers of the Western division; thus, they are referred to as being from the "Western Regions.
As for Nālandā, it means "Inexhaustible Charity" in this language.
However, according to the *Biography of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang*, it appears that Jñānaprabha was actually a disciple of Śīlabhadra.

As for the term "simultaneous" used here, one might fear that while the names are the same, the persons are different; or perhaps they were teacher and disciple, yet the tenets upon which they respectively rely are nonetheless distinct.
Furthermore, according to the letter of Chan Master Wuxing, it also says: "In the Western Regions, two schools coexist: one school is that of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu;
the other school is that of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva."
"When the profound banner of Nāgārjuna’s school is merely raised, Asaṅga leads the sheep;
when his wings and feathers briefly soar, Dignāga disrupts the tracks.
Thus, it is certain that two schools existed simultaneously.
Furthermore, according to the *Record of the Western Regions*, when the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty first encountered the master Nāgārjuna and wished to study the Dharma under him,
the master commanded him to take medicine to attain longevity before he could fully investigate the teachings.
The Tripitaka Master reflected to himself that his original desire was to seek out the sūtras; he feared that if he did not succeed in the art of the immortals, he would fail his lifelong aspiration.
Consequently, he ceased studying this school and instead studied the school of Dharmalakṣaṇa.

Regarding the second point, concerning the completeness or deficiency of the teaching: the first [period] spoke only of the Small Vehicle, and the second spoke only of the Great Vehicle; since each was deficient, they were not definitive.

Within the second section, there are also two points of interpretation.

During the third period, one universally attains great benefit, and it is only then that [the teaching] is considered definitive (*nītārtha*).

Regarding the increase or decrease in the manifestation of principles: the first [period] taught that dependent origination is substantially existent, and the second taught that it is conventionally existent; therefore, these were not definitive.

Based on this, one may interpret the two schools as each having both definitive and non-definitive meanings;

That is to say, according to the first perspective, the Dharmalakṣaṇa school is definitive while the Dharmatā school is non-definitive.
If we consider the latter perspective, then the Dharma-nature school (Faxingzong) is considered "perfected" while the Dharma-character school (Faxiangzong) is not.
Since both schools are thus "perfected" in one sense and "unperfected" in another, they are equal in principle.
Now, observing the intention of the Worthy Leader (Bhadramukha), it largely elucidates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Why?
Because there are two meanings.

First, when contrasting the breadth and narrowness of "gathering living beings" (*saṃgraha-sattva*) with the gradual progression of "benefiting beings" (*anugraha-sattva*), then "gathering living beings" being broad is taken as definitive, whereas "benefiting beings" alone being great is not taken as definitive.

Second, when contrasting the completeness or deficiency of verbal expression with the increase or subtlety of the revealed principle, then verbal expression being complete is taken as definitive, whereas the revealed principle being fully manifest is not taken as definitive.
This can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the second point, although it is said within the words that each has both the definitive and the non-definitive, according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, even those two types of definitive meaning become non-definitive.

Why is this? For instance, within the process of gathering and producing [gold], if one considers the second stage as "incomplete" because it gathers only the great [essence], and the third stage as "complete" because it gathers everything, then how could the pure gold obtained there possibly compare to that mixed with iron?
How can a community consisting solely of bodhisattvas be compared to one where ordinary beings and śrāvakas dwell together?
How can the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), which is intended exclusively for bodhisattvas, be compared to the teachings of the past that were addressed to the three vehicles?
Therefore, it should be said that [the *Lotus Sūtra*] exclusively gathers those of great capacity as "perfect" (niṣpanna), while gathering all three capacities in general as "imperfect" (aniṣpanna).

Furthermore, regarding the presence or absence of scriptural authority: if one holds that the second turning is "incomplete" and thus not definitive, while the third turning—which fully explains the three vehicles—is "complete" and therefore definitive, then it would follow that statements lacking scriptural authority are non-definitive, whereas those mixed with unverified elements should instead be considered definitive.
One who sells only pure gold should be a poor man, while one who deals in miscellaneous goods such as tiles and wood should be a wealthy merchant.
The *Lotus Sūtra* speaks only of the One Vehicle; how does this differ from the three distinct vehicles opened up in the past?

Therefore, one should say that only the teaching of a single ultimate vehicle (*ekayāna*) constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), whereas the mixed teaching of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) is non-definitive (*neyārtha*).
The two aforementioned [teachings] were originally considered definitive by the Dharmalakṣaṇa school; now, they have all become non-definitive.

That is to say, if one establishes the five natures as the ultimate reality, then the meaning of the three vehicles being the ultimate reality is naturally revealed: because there are those of the two fixed natures—śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha—they constitute the two vehicles;

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, in the first two fascicles" below demonstrates that the One Vehicle is provisional.
The subsequent citation from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* likewise serves only to demonstrate that the One Vehicle is provisional.

In the commentary, following the phrase "The Great Prajñā," the second section clarifies that the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are definitive, thereby establishing the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This, in turn, reveals that the single nature (*ekagotra*) and the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) are both not definitive.
Within this section, five passages from the sūtras are cited, with three treatises appended; thus, it is divided into five parts:

first, citing the *Prajñāpāramitā* to explain that there are five natures—though the fifth may be non-existent, since the former four exist, the nature of being without nature (*abhāva-dhātu*) is necessarily established.
The first three [points] can be understood.

Regarding the fourth, which states, "although they have not yet entered the state of right determination and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*): this refers to persons of indeterminate lineage who have not yet entered the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); for them, there remains the possibility of being indeterminate.
However, once they have entered the Path of Seeing, they are termed those in the group of right determination (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), and it is no longer possible for them to be indeterminate.
Just as those who have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Śrāvakas never turn their minds back to become Bodhisattvas,
so too is it said that they are "separated from birth," for the faults and afflictions of the delusions of seeing are like raw food remaining in the belly.
If one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is able to be free from that birth; therefore, it is called "leaving birth" (*vairāgyaja*). This will be explained further below.
Regarding the phrase "The second [chapter] of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*," the commentary cites the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
This section has two parts:

first, pointing out that this is identical to the preceding text; second, from "Furthermore, it says 'all [beings] are pacified in their destiny'" onwards, proving that there is a destiny of pacification.
If there is a destiny of pacification, then the doctrine of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) is established.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding the 'Ten Wheels' [Sūtra] below," this is the third section, which cites the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* to clarify that there are three vehicles within meditative concentration, thereby establishing the existence of the five natures;
for if the five natures did not exist, the three vehicles would likewise not exist.
The commentary states: "Therefore, in the *Laṅkāvatāra*," and so forth, is the fourth section, which correctly elucidates the five natures (*pañca-gotra*).
This is consistent with the two treatises, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The commentary states:

"In the *Śīlasamvara*," and so forth, is the fifth section, which cites the *Śīlasamvara* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to establish that there are two natures, thereby substantiating the preceding point regarding the absence of nature (*agotra*).
Therefore, that treatise states: "There are two types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
first, those with the lineage; second, those without the lineage.

The commentary on that treatise explains: "'Spiritual lineage' refers to that which is beginningless and natural (*dharmatā*), consisting of the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) transmitted in succession," and so forth.

As for the phrase "it is also said," it is entirely identical to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. Since the explanation from that sūtra was not cited previously, it is now explained by analogy, so as not to burden the text with excessive detail.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “If it is the Dharma-nature school,” the text is also twofold:
first, it indicates the school’s tenet; second, from “The Lotus Sūtra” onwards, it cites evidence to establish that position.
The long section consists of ten parts:
first, citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it elucidates both the One Vehicle and the One Nature;
second, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it elucidates the mutual perfection of the vehicle, nature, and characteristics.
Third, citing the *Lotus Sūtra* three times, it clarifies that there is no entry into quiescence.
Fourth, citing the ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it clarifies that there is no absence of nature.
Fifth, citing sūtras and śāstras, it concludes with the established correct meaning.
Sixth, by extensively citing various sūtras, he refutes the defense of those with fixed natures.
Seventh, by citing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he refutes the defense of those without nature.
Eighth, by citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he refutes the defense of those who incline toward quiescence.
Ninth, the commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* reconciles the skillful means of the One Vehicle.
Tenth, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is used to conclude the process of refuting [false views] and establishing [the truth].
Now, for the first [of these], there are two parts:
First, the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is established; subsequently, the One Nature (Eka-dhātu) is established to explain and perfect the One Vehicle.
Now, for the first part:
the passage beginning with "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions" refers to the verse from the first chapter, the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-parivarta).
The first three phrases establish the position, while the fourth phrase resolves doubts.
Regarding the statement, "neither two nor three," there have been many ancient interpretations.
Master Dharma of the Mahāyāna School said:
The second is indeed the second, and the third is indeed the third; however, because the Bodhisattva vehicle is superior, it is designated as the first.
This reflects the intention of Master Daosheng, yet it does not fully exhaust the underlying meaning.
Master Daosheng said:
"If there were a second vehicle and a third vehicle, there should likewise be no first vehicle.
Yet, because the 'first' does not contradict its nature as the Great [Vehicle], it is not non-existent."
Since there are neither two nor three, even "one" has departed.
The meaning is this:
today, the One Vehicle possesses a profound and mysterious depth; for this reason, it is called "Great."
That which is "Great" is so because its principles and meanings are profound.
In the past, within the Three Vehicles, the Mahāyāna had not yet been fully integrated; thus, the other two were established as provisional.

If one considers them in terms of compassion and wisdom, the myriad practices do not conflict with the "One" of today; therefore, it is said that they do not conflict, and for this reason they are Great, and thus they are not non-existent.

Regarding the statement that "since neither two nor three exist, one also departs": previously it was said there were three [vehicles]; since the second is not established, how could the first alone remain?

This is because the two vehicles are not included, and because they were expediently pointed out; furthermore, it is the same as in the case of the sheep and deer [carriages], both of which are ultimately unattainable, as explained in the Guangzhai school’s teaching on the Four Vehicles.
According to the view of Tiantai and others, "no two" means there are no two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"No three" means that, in total, there were no three vehicles of the past, because all of them are not ultimately real.
The tenets and the explanations differ, so one may choose and reject according to one's own inclination.

However, from the perspective of the intended meaning of the sūtras, only the establishment of a single reality is accepted as the true goal; the positing of two or three [realities] is entirely disallowed, regardless of whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.
As it is said that this person in the world stands alone with no one to compare him to, it does not necessarily refer specifically to two individuals, such as Zhang and Wang.
The following sentence resolves this doubt.
The doubt is as follows:
If there were only one, why did you previously speak of three?
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In some lands, the One Vehicle is taught; in others, two, three, four, or five; and so on, even up to an immeasurable number."
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
If one relies upon the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*), then both the "many" and the "few" are attained.
That there are ten directions and worlds, as well as the previous teaching that there are three [vehicles], is merely a skillful means; it is not the ultimate reality.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage in the sutra states: "Only by means of provisional names does one guide sentient beings.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "It further says that initially [he used] the three vehicles," etc., this cites the second sutra to re-establish that all three are expedient means (*upāya*).

To cite it in full, the sutra says: "Just as that elder first used the three carts to entice his children, and later gave them only the great carts, adorned with precious objects and foremost in security."
Yet that elder was free from the fault of falsehood.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is without falsehood. Initially, he taught the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and only thereafter did he deliver them by means of the Great Vehicle alone.
The commentary states:

This passage clarifies that the first three are provisional while the last one is the ultimate reality; even if one integrates the two into the one, it is still the case that the three serve as skillful means and only the one is the reality.
In the commentary, from the phrase "Because the nature is unique" onwards, two passages are cited to clarify that the nature is unique and to establish the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This sentence summarizes how the single nature establishes the One Vehicle.
If there were multiple natures, there might be multiple vehicles; since there is but a single nature and all equally become Buddhas, there is only the One Vehicle.
The commentary states, "Therefore it says, 'The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet,'" which serves as a scriptural citation.

First, citing the chapter on the first future Buddha, that verse says: "Though the Buddhas of the future world may preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality, they are for the sake of the One Vehicle."

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature; yet the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions, and for this reason they preach the One Vehicle.
This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant; having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher speaks through skillful means.
Now, by citing only two lines, it is revealed that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), thereby establishing the meaning of the single nature (*ekasvabhāva*).
However, regarding the three preceding verses, various interpretations differ.

Here, I shall provide a direct exegesis of the scriptural text: the first verse clarifies that the Buddha, in opening the provisional (*upāya*) teachings, ultimately returns to the single reality; hence it says, "In truth, there is but one vehicle."
The following verse explains the reason for teaching the One Vehicle (ekayāna): it is because there is only a single nature.
That is to say, if there were two natures, there might be two vehicles;
since there is only a single nature, it is therefore called the One Vehicle.
"Knowing that phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature" means that knowing is itself the realization; "phenomena" refers to that which is realized.
These phenomena consist of all things, such as form and mind.
"Eternally without intrinsic nature" refers to the principle that is realized, namely the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) being without intrinsic nature, because it awakens one to all phenomena.
What is meant by "the eternal absence of intrinsic nature"?

It refers to the fact that from the very beginning, the nature and characteristics of form, mind, and so forth are empty and quiescent; they are neither self nor other, neither identical nor separate, and are profoundly and eternally still. Therefore, it is called the absence of intrinsic nature.

As for what is called "constant," it means that [the nature] has been non-existent from the very beginning; it is not made non-existent through some external effort. Therefore, it is said to have the nature of constant non-existence.
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," there are two meanings:
first, in terms of the causal seed, the causal seed is precisely the true causal Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is the seed of the Middle Way within unsurpassed bodhi.

This seed is precisely the principle of the eternally non-existent nature mentioned previously; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further states: "Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)."
The absence of intrinsic nature is the meaning of emptiness.
Conditions refer to the myriad practices of the six perfections; these are the conditional Buddha-nature that gives rise to the causal Buddha-nature, enabling one to attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, when the One Vehicle is taught, it is solely because Buddhahood arises from Buddhahood, and there is no other nature; thus, the One Vehicle is taught, which is an exposition in accordance with reality.
Identity of essence is called "nature" (*dhātu*), while similarity is termed "seed" (*gotra*); thus it is said in Guanzhong:
"Just as rice naturally produces rice and not other grains—this is what constitutes nature."
"The sprouts, stems, flowers, and fruits are of the same kind without distinction; this belongs to the category of seeds.
Regarding the second, the nature of the fruit-seed, Guanzhong says:
"The Buddha-retribution is only for the Buddha; its principle is without error, which is precisely the meaning of 'nature' (xing)."
"The preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is, in its essence, similar in all cases; this is the meaning of 'kind' (*gotra*).
The nature of the fruit arises from the True Principle; therefore, it is said to 'proceed from conditions.'"
Therefore, the commentary on this verse states: "The Buddha arises by taking principle as his object; since principle is non-dual, it is for this reason that he speaks of the One Vehicle.
The intended meaning is:
attaining Buddhahood through the realization of principle, one speaks of the One in accordance with that principle.
Regarding the verse herein that understands phenomena as eternally devoid of intrinsic nature, it is identical in its entirety to the *Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna* (The Appearance Chapter).

The *Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna* states: "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvāṇa; they are all of one single nature, namely, the absence of nature."

It continues until it says: "Because one knows that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, one attains omniscience and, with great compassion continuously manifesting, delivers sentient beings.
This means that by knowing the absence of intrinsic nature, one realizes that the Buddha-nature is identical [to theirs].

According to the subsequent sutra, by knowing that there is no fixed nature, one can achieve everything through the achievement of even a single thing; how much more so when there is nothing that is not taught as the One Vehicle to deliver and liberate beings.
The subsequent verse further states, "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas," and so forth; this is a re-explanation of the preceding verse.
The phrase "this dharma" refers precisely to the dharma that was previously known.
The reason they are eternally without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is that they abide in the true state of *tathatā*.
Because they take non-nature as their object, dependent origination is itself reality;
because it is itself reality, it is therefore said above to be without intrinsic nature.
What is called the "dharma-position" (dharmasthiti) is precisely the true position of suchness (tathatā).

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Dharma-nature (dharmatā), dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), dharma-abiding (dharmasthiti), and dharma-position (dharmasthiti) are all synonyms for suchness."
The worldly dharmas are themselves suchness, and therefore they are all eternally abiding.
This means that because causes deviate from the principle of constancy, the three realms become impermanent.
If one understands the reality of impermanence, then impermanence itself becomes permanence.
Thus, the two principles of permanence and impermanence are not partial; therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* compares them to two birds.

Now, at this site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one realizes that the impermanence of all worlds is itself the principle of true permanence—just as when a mirror is suspended in a high hall, the myriad forms are all reflected therein.
"Duality and non-duality are ineffable; they are expressed through conventional speech by the power of skillful means.
If even 'one' is but a provisional designation, how much more so 'two' or 'three'?

Therefore, we know that the preceding verse is a textual passage concerning the single nature (*eka-svabhāva*); in the commentary, for the sake of brevity and essentials, only a single line has been cited."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, the third [point]" and below cites the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter to prove the meaning of the single nature (*eka-svabhāva*).
Thus, that sūtra says: "Sentient beings dwell on various levels; only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, clearly and without obstruction."

Just as those herbs, trees, forests, and medicinal plants do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures, the Tathāgata knows this Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation; it is the ultimate nirvana, the eternally quiescent characteristic, which ultimately returns to emptiness.

Now, I shall briefly cite two lines as proof; this clarifies that while those of the three vehicles do not know that differentiation is itself unity, only the Buddha has thoroughly realized it as being neither three nor two.
What is called liberation is true liberation.
Thus, the verse of the second sutra says: "One practices the Path for the sake of the Truth of Cessation; being freed from all bonds of suffering is termed attaining liberation."
"By what means does this person attain liberation?
Merely being free from falsehood is called liberation; in reality, they have not yet attained all-encompassing liberation.
The commentary states:
All liberations are true liberation; true liberation is the single flavor of liberation. Therefore, since there are no two flavors, how could there be three vehicles?
Thus it is further said: "The mark of eternal quiescence is precisely the nirvana of intrinsic purity."
"This refers to the eternal abiding nature of the supreme mundane realm; therefore, all possess a single nature.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Nirvāṇa also says," this is the second section, which cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to clarify the mutual establishment of the vehicle (*yāna*), its nature (*prakṛti*), and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
It is not merely because of a single nature that the One Vehicle is taught;
the sutra clarifies that this single nature is itself the One Vehicle.
As the twenty-seventh sutra states: "Good son!..."
There are two kinds of ultimateity (*atyanta*):
first, the ultimateity of adornment; second, the ultimateity of finality.
First, the worldly ultimateity; second, the supramundane ultimateity.
Ultimate adornment refers to the six *pāramitās*.
Ultimate consummation refers to the One Vehicle attained by all sentient beings; this One Vehicle is called Buddha-nature.

For this reason, I say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all sentient beings truly possess the One Vehicle, yet because they are shrouded by ignorance, they are unable to see it for themselves.
The commentary states:
Because all possess the Buddha-nature, there is but a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Furthermore, the Buddha-nature is precisely the principle of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); since this principle is capable of conveying [beings] to liberation, it carries the meaning of a "vehicle."
The Commentary states: "The 'Lion’s Roar' refers to definitive teaching. This refers to the twenty-seventh chapter of the sutra, the "Chapter on the Lion’s Roar.
The Explanation says:

If one does not proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, that is merely the howling of a jackal; even if one remains within the Buddha-dharma for a thousand million years, one will ultimately never be able to let out the lion’s roar.
The commentary states: “Regarding the passage ‘Furthermore, it says... and below, this cites evidence that Buddha-nature is precisely the One Vehicle;

it is not only the same in terms of the cause, but the fruit is also the same. This is also from the *Siṃhanāda-parivarta*; therein it clarifies that the ocean possesses eight qualities, which are subsequently matched with the [eight] analogies. This specifically matches the third meaning: ‘one flavor.’”
In the sutra, it is merely added that "the third is of one flavor," with the explanation as given in the commentary (*shu-wen*).
"The first is ambrosia" (*amṛta*) precisely reveals this single flavor;
ambrosia is used as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Seven Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Eight
The Sub-commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty.
From the passage beginning "Furthermore, the third [chapter] of the Lotus Sūtra says... onwards, the third section clarifies the absence of a tendency toward quiescence.
Since there is no such thing as "entering quiescence," there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature; thus, the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is also clearly established.
The Commentary cites three texts—namely, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-upadeśa*—to substantiate this point.
First, this refers to the "Parable of the Magic City" chapter, which brings together the disciples transformed by the World-Honored One.

The sutra states: "Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—these are you, O bhikṣus, and the śrāvaka disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa."
The passage beginning with "After my parinirvāṇa" is identical to the commentary [of Jizang].
Regarding the phrase "other lands," some say that any land outside of this Sahā world may be cited as an example.
As for Tiantai, when he speaks of "other lands," he refers to the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*).
He establishes four lands:

first, the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages (*pṛthagjana-ārya-sahāvāsa-bhūmi*), which corresponds to the land of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bhūmi*) within the *dharmalakṣaṇa* [school].
Second is the land of skillful means with remainder;
third is the land of true recompense and non-obstruction, which is the land of recompense within the Dharma-characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) and encompasses both self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment;
fourth is the land of eternal quiescent light, which is the land of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The "expedient means" (upāya) of a single land is something that does not exist within the characteristics of dharmas; this was established by Tiantai based upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Śāstra* refers to the ninety-five passages cited below.
The treatise says: "The segmented body received by an Arhat due to causes and conditions from previous lives must necessarily perish; dwelling in what state, then, can one fulfill the Buddha-way?"
Answer:
Having attained arhatship, one is no longer reborn within the three realms. There exist pure buddha-fields outside the three realms where even the name of affliction does not exist.
In such lands, in the presence of a Buddha, one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and fully realizes the path to buddhahood.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: “There are arhats whom I [have placed] in other lands,” and so forth; the full citation is identical to that in the previous commentary. It further asks:
“If this is so, and these arhats receive the dharma-nature body, they should swiftly attain bodhi; why then do they linger?”
He replied:

"Because they have abandoned sentient beings and abandoned the path to Buddhahood, and furthermore, they speak falsely of attaining the Way; although they do not undergo birth and death, their faculties regarding Bodhi are dull and they cannot attain it quickly, unlike the bodhisattvas who proceed directly."
The commentary states:

The text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clearly accords with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. One can therefore know with certainty that although they have emerged from the triple world, they do not proceed toward quiescence; hence the concluding remark in the sub-commentary: "They definitely turn their minds [toward enlightenment]."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Within the *Dharmapada-śāstra*, among the four types of śrāvakas,” etc., this cites the treatise to establish the aforementioned meaning that there is no inclination toward quiescence.
First the citation, then the explanation.
This is the first [part].
However, the treatise states: "Regarding those spoken of as śrāvakas who receive the prediction [of enlightenment], there are four kinds of śrāvakas:

first, the śrāvaka of fixed destiny; second, the śrāvaka of overweening pride; third, the śrāvaka who has regressed from the bodhisattva mind; and fourth, the śrāvaka who is a manifested transformation."
The Tathāgata bestows predictions upon two kinds of śrāvakas: namely, the emanated śrāvaka and the one who, having fallen back, again resolves to attain bodhicitta.

As for the other two kinds of śrāvakas—the one who is fixed in their destiny and the one with overweening pride—the Tathāgata does not bestow predictions upon them because their faculties are not yet matured.
"The Bodhisattva bestows the prediction (vyākaraṇa).
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s bestowal of the prediction, it is because he employs skillful means to cause [beings] to resolve upon bodhicitta.
This is a brief citation from the commentary.

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva’s mind regressed and he attained remembrance," this refers, for example, to Śāriputra, who had already received transformation under twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas.
Furthermore, it says below: "I now wish to cause you to recollect the path you practiced according to your original vow."
It was not only Śāriputra;
furthermore, the four great śrāvakas personally confessed that they had fled from their fathers, and thus they had already been converted previously.
In the third week, [the Buddha] cited the case of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who had already extensively converted those who had all regressed from the bodhicitta.
Regarding those who are "transformed and manifested," they are like Pūrṇa, who secretly maintains the practices of a bodhisattva within while outwardly appearing as a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, it is said: "For this reason, all bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, Ānanda recalled his own original vow, as stated in verse: "I serve as an attendant through skillful means.
Regarding Rāhula, the verse says: "The secret practices of Rāhula—only I can know them; he is now my eldest son."
All of them were transformed śrāvakas.
Thus we know that those who can respond to and propagate the holy teachings, manifesting their traces as reflections, are without exception expedient means (*upāya*).
To claim that only Pūrṇa was a transformed being is likewise to disparage the various arhats of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva bestows predictions," the Master [Vasubandhu] previously stated himself: "As it should be understood in the chapter 'On the Unconquerable' (*Anupalipta-parivarta*):
when one prostrates, praises, and speaks these words—'I do not dare to slight you;
you shall all become Buddhas'—it is to reveal the Buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings."
The above constitutes the treatise.

However, Master An-guo does not accept this interpretation, asking: "How could there have been bodhisattvas in former times who already predicted that the śrāvakas present at today’s assembly—namely, those such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others who propagate the Dharma—would receive their predictions?"
The commentary states:

Since this is what the Master himself said regarding the granting of the prophecy to the Bodhisattvas, and since it is also the Master’s own explanation of the treatise, how could one not rely upon it?
Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary beginning with "Since it says 'not yet mature,'" the author explains the scriptural passage cited above.

If it were certain that śrāvakas of fixed destiny would never attain Buddhahood, then one should say that the other two types of śrāvakas did not receive a prediction because their faculties were not yet matured.
Since it is said they are "not yet matured," this does not mean they will remain immature forever.
If a Mahāyāna Dharma Master says:
"It should have been stated as 'not mature.
This was an error by the translator; it should have been said 'not yet mature.'"
Therefore, the Commentary concludes its critique by stating:
"One must not, simply because one's own school does not maintain that there is definitely a realm of quiescent nirvana, judge the treatise to be erroneous.

Furthermore, regarding the previous statement about "expedient means causing the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment," the aforementioned treatise has a question immediately preceding it which says:
Are those śrāvakas and others given the prediction because they will truly attain Buddhahood,
or are they given the prediction despite not attaining Buddhahood?
If they were to truly attain Buddhahood, for what reason would bodhisattvas cultivate immeasurable and boundless varieties of merit over immeasurable kalpas?
If they do not attain Buddhahood, how can one grant them a false prediction of enlightenment?
The answer is:
when those śrāvakas receive a prediction, it is because they have attained a mind of certainty; it does not mean that the śrāvakas have perfected the *dharmatā*.
Because the Tathāgata teaches the One Vehicle Dharma based on the three kinds of equality.

Since the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is equal and no different from the Dharma-body of those śrāvakas, he bestows predictions upon them; it is not because they have already fully cultivated meritorious practices. Thus, while bodhisattvas are complete in their merit and virtue, śrāvakas are not yet complete in their merit and virtue.
The commentary states:
Based on this scriptural passage, it is therefore said above that [the Buddha] employs skillful means to inspire the arousal of the mind.
Regarding the "threefold equality," it refers to the equality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), because there are no two vehicles.
Second, the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
third, the equality of the dharmakāya.
This present case refers to the third equality.
The sub-commentary states: "The *Laṅkāvatāra*," and so forth, also establishes the meaning of entering into the quiescence of non-destination.
As for the term *Laṅkāvatāra*, it refers to the translation by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty, consisting of ten fascicles.
The World-Honored One entered the city of Laṅkāpura; hence, it is said that he "entered.

As the three-fascicle version of the scripture likewise cites this, all of which speaks of a nirvāṇa that lacks substantial reality, it is clear that there is certainly no [attainment of] quiescent extinction.
If that is so, why is it said that they attain *nirvāṇa*?
From the perspective of their respective stages, this is called *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

However, viewed from the standpoint of the Mahāyāna, this is merely a deep entry into *samādhi*; having remained submerged in emptiness for a long time, it is provisionally termed "nirvāṇa" only to attract those of inferior capacity.
The Commentary states: "The meaning in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* is also the same as this," and thus it is identical to the view that there is no real nirvāṇa.
In the commentary’s explanation of the seven parables, the fourth—the parable of the conjured city—is taught for those of fixed nature.
The treatise states: "Fourth, although it does not exist in reality, there are those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Because they possess worldly, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa where no nirvāṇa exists; thus they grasp it through inversion."
"To counteract this, it should be understood that the parable of the conjured city was taught.
The commentary states:
Since it is said that there is no real nirvāṇa, it is clearly known to be a provisional designation; therefore, it is the same as what preceded.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Although I have previously said that you have attained extinction (nirvāṇa), this merely exhausts birth and death; in reality, there is no extinction.
Next, it cites the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, which likewise establishes that the aforementioned nirvāṇa is not ultimate.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* all state that the two vehicles enter extinction,” etc.: the first fascicle of the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* says: “Ānanda!...”
All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained mastery are unable to obtain the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya due to four kinds of obscurations.
First, the delusion that conditions birth; second, the delusion that causes birth; third, existence within existence; and fourth, non-existence.
What is the delusion that conditions birth?
It is the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), which gives rise to all formative activities (*saṃskāra*), just as ignorance gives rise to karma.
What is the delusion that serves as the cause of birth?
It is the various formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), just as various karmas are produced by ignorance.
What is "existence" (*bhava*)?
With the ground of ignorance as the condition and the ground of ignorance as the cause, the outflow-free formations that arise give rise to the three kinds of mind-made bodies.
This is just as, with the four graspings as the condition and the three types of tainted karma as the cause, the three kinds of existence arise.
What is it that does not exist?
It is the subtle cessation that occurs in dependence upon the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), which is imperceptible.

This is analogous to how, within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), there is moment-to-moment aging and death in dependence [upon them]. Because the dwelling-place of all afflictions—the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*)—has not been severed, the various *arhats*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and bodhisattvas who have not yet attained mastery are unable to reach the ultimate extinction of the turbid stains of afflictions and the foul stench of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). This is the Great Purity Perfection (*mahāviśuddhipāramitā*).

Furthermore, because the afflictions of subtle characteristics within the ground of abiding ignorance cause false and delusive activities to remain unextinguished, one cannot yet attain the perfection of the Great Self—supremely quiescent, non-active, and non-conditioned.

Conditioned by the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) and caused by subtle, false conceptualizations, one gives rise to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*). Because the various aggregates born of the mind (*manomaya-skandha*) have not yet been completely eliminated, one cannot attain the perfection of great bliss (*mahāsukha-pāramitā*), which is characterized by ultimate cessation and total detachment.

If one has not yet attained the permanent and complete exhaustion, without remainder, of all afflictions, karmas, and the difficulties of birth, then for those Tathāgatas who constitute the realm of ambrosia (*amṛtadhātu*), the transformation-death (*pariṇāmikī-jarāmaraṇa*)—with its continuous flow of arising and ceasing—will remain immeasurable; thus, one cannot reach the vision of the supreme, unchanging, and great eternal *pāramitā*.
Ānanda! Within the triple world there are four kinds of difficulties:
first, the difficulty of afflictions; second, the difficulty of karma; third, the difficulty of retribution for birth; and fourth, the difficulty of faults.
The *upāya-bhava* (birth-and-death through effort) arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) is like the difficulty of the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms;
the *hetu-pratyaya-bhava* (birth-and-death through causes and conditions) arising from the ground of the abiding of ignorance is like the difficulty of karma (*karman*) within the three realms.
The existence of birth-and-death arising from the ground of abiding ignorance is difficult to overcome, like the retribution of birth within the triple world.
The non-existence of birth-and-death arising from the ground of abiding ignorance is difficult to overcome, like the faults within the triple world.
It should be understood in this way: Ānanda!
Because the four kinds of birth-and-death have not yet been eliminated, the three kinds of mind-made bodies lack the fruits of the perfections of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
"Only the Buddha’s Dharma-body is the perfection of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; you should know this.
The commentary states:

Based on the above scriptural passage, it is clarified that both those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained mastery undergo transformation and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-vaipākika*).
Outside the three realms, the existence of karma, afflictions, and suffering is extremely evident; how can one categorically state that they are eternally extinguished without remainder?
The sub-commentary clarifies the four types of birth-and-death, which may be consulted therein.
In the subsequent sections of the treatise, the characteristics of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are explained in detail; thus, one may also know their ultimate destination.
As for the mention of the "Two Treatises on the Jewel Nature and Buddha-nature" below, their general meaning is the same as that of the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* corresponds to the fourth [section], and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* corresponds to the second; this fascicle also extensively discusses the four types of birth and death.
The commentary’s phrase “such sūtras and śāstras” and following concludes that there are no śrāvakas with a fixed nature.
In the sub-commentary (*śūtra*), following the phrase "Nirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Nine," the fourth section clarifies the nature of non-existence.
After that sūtra has extensively explained that icchantikas lack roots of goodness, it states: "Furthermore, son of good family!..."
For example, just as lotus flowers are all made to bloom when touched by the sun’s rays, so it is with all sentient beings:
