This very statement is not accepted either, for it is utterly transcendent and without support, beyond the reach of words or conceptual understanding, because the arising of the mind and the movement of thought deviate from the essence of the Dharma.
The first eight gates distinguish emotional afflictions to reveal the principle.
The third gate explains the ultimate orientation toward practice.
The fourth gate correctly establishes the essence of practice; through understanding, practice is perfected, and as practice arises, conceptual understanding is transcended.
The above constitutes the meaning of the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm.

The reason why it is not extensively cited in the Commentary is that the third [contemplation], "the non-obstruction of form and emptiness," would overlap with the second [contemplation], the "non-obstruction of phenomena and principle."
The reason it is established is that the fourth [stage] extinguishes all attachments and, by extinguishing the preceding three, is therefore called "True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics.
Now, taking the general meaning of this single gate, it likewise constitutes the extinction of all attachments and the absence of any locus of reliance.

Furthermore, it is because one wishes to establish four kinds of dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) through the four gates: the first gate is phenomena (dharma); the second is principle (li); the third is the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; and the fourth is the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
Therefore, within the third section on the "Unimpeded Contemplation of Principle and Phenomena," the commentary is divided into three parts:
first, a general introduction; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "First, principle pervades phenomena"; and third, a summary beginning with "The ten phenomena mentioned above."

First: regarding the statement "the ten pairs are all unimpeded," this refers to: first, the unimpededness of teaching and meaning; second, the unimpededness of phenomena and principle; third, the unimpededness of practice and stages; and so on, up to the tenth, the unimpededness of response and resonance.

Now, to briefly summarize by way of phenomena and principle: phenomena and principle constitute the totality within the dharmas that are explained; furthermore, they are extensively elucidated in various places as the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle; and this is for the purpose of establishing the four dharma realms.
In the commentary, following the section "First, principle pervades phenomena," the second part provides a detailed explanation of the ten gates, which constitutes ten distinct sections.
Within each gate, there is generally first a direct explanation and subsequently a reconciliation with the preceding meaning.

These are the aforementioned natures and characteristics, which differ from the meanings of the ten pairs [of categories] discussed previously; whether a single section synthesizes a single meaning, two sections together synthesize a single meaning, or a single section synthesizes multiple meanings, these shall be understood as they appear in the text.
Furthermore, among the ten pairs, only those that accord with the *dharmatā* are included, because they represent the definitive scope of the meaning of the "Teaching of the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*).
As previously stated, while there was a distinction between the three vehicles and the one vehicle, here we only harmonize the one vehicle;
and while there was a distinction between the five natures and the one nature, here we only harmonize the one nature.
This applies to all ten pairs.
Now, regarding the first:
they do not meet at the first gate, but meet simultaneously at the second gate.
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, the heading of the section;
second, the formal explanation beginning with "That is to say, it has no limits," and so forth.
This means that because principle (*li*) cannot be divided, it has no boundaries;
yet because phenomena (*shi*) differ according to conditions, their respective states are clearly distinct.
Nevertheless, as they do not interfere with one another, they are able to be mutually pervasive.
Now it is clarified that principle is not different from phenomena; therefore, it pervades all phenomena.
The subsequent passage, beginning with "Therefore, each and every minute speck of dust," concludes the meaning of this pervasive nature.
If it did not pervade completely, then the principle would be divisible.
Phenomena are not fully subsumed [by a single principle], nor are they identical to that principle.
Just as it is with a single speck of dust, so it is with every phenomenon.
At the very moment it is present in one place, it does not preclude its presence elsewhere; therefore, it is not the case that there is no principle in other locations.
The entirety of this and the entirety of that are likewise not two distinct principles.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two matters pervade the gate of principle,” there are two parts within the text:
first, the formal elucidation; second, the reconciliation with what preceded.
The reason why the preceding and middle [sections] must be entirely identical is that phenomena have no separate essence, as they are themselves the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
If they were not entirely identical, they would not accord with the nature of reality, and the meaning that "form is not different from emptiness" would not be fully established.
However, the two gates of the pervasive characteristic transcend the realm of ordinary cognition and are difficult to perceive. Why is this so?
It is because while phenomena possess parts, principle is partless; how, then, can it be pervasive?
If the object were to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, the object would not be small;
yet since principle pervades while sharing the same activity, it should be like the small object.

Now it is clarified that because there is a sense of being neither identical nor different between the phenomenon and the principle, they are entirely identical due to non-difference, yet remain undestroyed due to non-identity.
When differentiated, phenomena and principle are divided into two; yet they are like the waves of the ocean: a single wave completely pervades the great ocean because it is identical to the ocean;

and the great ocean is entirely contained within a single small wave because the ocean is non-dual—it is entirely present in one wave and entirely present in all waves, for they are one and the same ocean.
The Commentary states, "By means of the two preceding meanings," and below this, it reconciles the previous meanings.
This section contains two parts:
first, it reconciles the single nature; second, it reconciles the single vehicle.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, clarifying the single nature and the five natures; second, clarifying whether one attains Buddhahood or not; and third, clarifying that the absence of nature is itself Buddha-nature.
Within the first part, there is first the formal explanation and subsequently the citation of evidence.
Regarding the preceding [distinction]: phenomena (*dharma*) have limitations, whereas principle (*li*) has no limitations.
The five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are categorized according to phenomena, while the single nature (*eka-gotra*) is categorized according to principle.
Now, since principle pervades phenomena, the principle of the single nature is entirely present within the five natures.
The phenomena pervade the principle, such that the five natures are identical to the one nature.
Therefore, it is said: "Because they mutually encompass and penetrate one another, they are all of the same single nature.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "Hence, the Manifestation," the second section provides scriptural evidence.
This passage explains two meanings:
first, it is precisely the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*), because both sentient beings and Buddhas are all phenomena.
Now, by taking the meaning of the explanatory text—that they are all of one single nature—it serves as proof for the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle (*shili wuai*).
Because principle pervades all phenomena, sentient beings exist within the Buddha in accordance with that principle.

In the commentary, following the passage "Because principle pervades phenomena, when one is perfected, all are perfected," the second section clarifies the meaning of attaining Buddhahood and not attaining Buddhahood.
This means that because principle has no dual reality, it encompasses many phenomena and thus all are established;
yet because principle is like empty space, phenomena are identical to that principle and thus have no establishment.
The passage beginning with "The Sūtra says, 'For example, like empty space'" cites scriptural evidence.
This is also cited from the meaning within the "Chapter on Manifestation" regarding the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
The text says: "O Son of the Buddha!
For example, just as space neither increases nor decreases whether all worlds are forming or disintegrating."
Why is this? Because space is without arising.
The bodhi of all Buddhas is likewise; whether one attains perfect enlightenment or does not attain perfect enlightenment, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because bodhi has no marks and no non-marks; it is neither one nor manifold.
This is precisely the meaning of having nothing to be accomplished.

Based on these two meanings, if one wishes for [enlightenment] to be achieved, it is achieved at every moment; if one wishes for it not to be achieved, there would be no one achieving Buddhahood throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time. Therefore, achievement and non-achievement are sovereign and unimpeded.
The Commentary states: "That 'one nature and non-nature' is itself Buddha-nature" refers to the meaning of Buddha-nature in the third assembly.
First is the formal exposition; following this, from "Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa*... onwards, scriptural citations are provided as proof.

Since the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is itself the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the general purport is simply this; however, because I wish to exhaustively investigate the source of the Dharma, I shall briefly cite further passages.
Now, in the twenty-seventh chapter of this sutra, the "Lion’s Roar" (*Siṃhanāda-parivarta*), there are six questions concerning the Buddha-nature:
the first asks what constitutes the Buddha-nature, and the second asks about its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
1. By what meaning is it called "expounding the Buddha-nature"? (This is the first question regarding the meaning of the name "nature.
2. Why is it further named "permanence, bliss, self, and purity"? (This is the third question regarding the virtues of nature. 3.

If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, why do they not see the Buddha-nature possessed by all sentient beings? (This is the fourth question regarding the reason why sentient beings do not perceive it.)
In what dharmas do Bodhisattvas abiding in the fifty stages dwell such that they do not clearly perceive the Buddha-nature?
In what dharmas does the Buddha dwell such that he clearly perceives it? [These are] five questions concerning the distinctions among the dharmas of the stages.
[Question: With what kind of eye do Bodhisattvas at the sixty stages see indistinctly?
With what eye does the Buddha see clearly? [These are] six questions concerning different eyes.

[Answer: In response to the first question, the Sūtra says: "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called wisdom (*prajñā*)."
That which is called "emptiness" does not perceive emptiness or non-emptiness.
The wise person perceives both emptiness and non-emptiness, permanence and impermanence, suffering and pleasure, and self and non-self.
"Emptiness" refers to all of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
"Non-emptiness" refers to Great Nirvāṇa (*mahāparinirvāṇa*).
It continues, saying: "That which is 'selfless' (*anātman*) is birth-and-death; that which is 'self' (*ātman*) is Great Nirvāṇa."
"To see all things as empty and not see them as non-empty is not called the Middle Way.
It continues, "To see all things as selfless and not see a self is not called the Middle Way."
The Middle Way is called Buddha-nature.
For this reason, Buddha-nature is eternal and constant, without change or variation.
Because it is shrouded by ignorance, all sentient beings are unable to perceive it.
Jianfu Shi said: "However, there are two kinds of Buddha-nature:
first, that obtained by nature; second, that obtained through cultivation.
Buddha-nature is named 'emptiness of the ultimate truth' (paramārtha-śūnyatā), and emptiness of the ultimate truth is named 'wisdom' (prajñā)."
"Wisdom" refers to the awakened nature of wisdom attained through one's inherent nature, which is the Middle Way.
As the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s pure treasury is also called stainless wisdom; it is eternally abiding without beginning or end, transcending the discourse of the four extremes."

Furthermore, as stated in the subsequent sutra: "The wisdom of signlessness and the unimpeded wisdom are fully present within the bodies of sentient beings," and so forth; it is not that wisdom is named "wisdom" merely because it arises from conditions.
Because it possesses the meaning of the light that universally illumines the dharma-realm by its own nature, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
From the passage beginning with "the emptiness that is spoken of" below, the nature attained through cultivation is clarified.

One who has cultivated and realized the awakened nature contemplates the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), seeing neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, because they are free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
From the passage "The wise see emptiness" downward, it clarifies those who perceive the Middle Way.
"The wise" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
From the passage "From emptiness" downward, it clarifies the dharmas of the equality of emptiness and existence.
Emptiness refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

non-emptiness refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). As the subsequent text states: "All dharmas are merely provisional; wherever they cease is ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)," and so forth. Thus, one should know that ultimate emptiness is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, not the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate both the ultimate and the conventional truths simultaneously, and illuminate both existence and non-existence equally; therefore, this is called the Middle Way.
Furthermore, according to the subsequent passage, it asks: "In what sense is Buddha-nature empty?"
Because it is emptiness in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Why is it not empty?
Because it is eternal.
"What is meant by 'neither empty nor non-empty'?
It is because it can serve as the seed for wholesome dharmas.
According to this scriptural passage, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is not the same as the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The preceding recommendation of the meaning of "benefiting" also possesses profound道理 (principle).
However, the current formal explanation differs slightly from the former.

When it first states that "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called wisdom," this is a simultaneous designation of both emptiness and wisdom.

Because ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) pervades both mind and objects, "clarity" (*prabhāsvara*) is identified as wisdom (*jñāna*), thereby distinguishing it from insentient matter such as rubble.
From the passage beginning with "As for that which is called empty," the Sūtra itself provides a dual explanation of these two meanings:

"As for that which is called empty" refers back to the aforementioned ultimate emptiness; since ultimate emptiness is so named only when both existence and emptiness are transcended, it says, "one does not perceive either emptiness or non-emptiness."

"Where it says, 'The wise see both emptiness and non-emptiness,' the following explains the aforementioned wisdom; the scriptural text is somewhat abbreviated, for if it were complete, it should state: 'That which is called wisdom is that which can perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness.'"
Therefore, the word "in this" (*asmin*) does not refer to a person; it is merely a reference to the preceding statement.

The expression "seeing in this" does not refer to seeing through cultivation, but clarifies the seeing of the nature (*prakṛti*), because the inherently existing wisdom-nature (*jñāna-dhātu*) is capable of realizing both the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness.
If there were no fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), who would know whether something is empty or not empty?
The same applies to the self and non-self.

Regarding those who practice and see, it is only within the Buddha’s answers to the fifth and sixth questions in the subsequent sutra—specifically in the sections concerning "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*) and "being shrouded by ignorance" (*avidyā-āvṛta*)—that the matters of seeing and not seeing are discussed.
Now, because wisdom itself is luminous emptiness, it is called the "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
This very wisdom that is emptiness is precisely the eternally constant nature of wisdom; it is permanent because it does not arise, and it is everlasting because it does not cease.
The ancient masters cited the two gates of "emptiness" and so forth from the sutra below to prove that the ultimate emptiness is not the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Now, observing what was cited, it actually proves the meaning of the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

How so? It is not that one first realizes emptiness and subsequently attains what is called the meaning of wisdom; rather, it is when emptiness and wisdom mutually accomplish one another that they constitute the true meaning of Buddha-nature.

Thus, one knows that the two stores (the storehouse of phenomena and the storehouse of wisdom) are likewise inseparable: because Buddha-nature is untainted by deluded dharmas, it is called "empty"; because it possesses sands-of-the-Ganges-like sublime virtues, it is called "not empty."
One must empty all delusions before the non-empty virtue can manifest; therefore, they are not separate.
Reflect on this.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): because emptiness is discussed in relation to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is clearly understood that the nature of emptiness and the nature of wisdom are of a non-dual nature. Thus, what was stated at the outset is itself the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, it is said that seeing all things as empty while not seeing them as non-empty is not called the Middle Way; the Middle Way is what is termed Buddha-nature.
If this were so, then Buddha-nature would exist only when both [emptiness and non-emptiness] are seen simultaneously, and there would be no Buddha-nature at times when they are not seen together.

Therefore, one should know that all such statements as "all is empty" or "not empty" encompass both the subject and the object; with respect to what is seen—emptiness and non-emptiness—it is the Middle Way and Buddha-nature, while with respect to that which sees it, it is wisdom.
If one does not see both [aspects] simultaneously, one does not recognize the Buddha-nature; if one sees the Middle Way, it is called seeing the Buddha-nature.
The rest is as stated in that sutra and its commentary.

Regarding the passage in the *Shu* (Commentary) beginning with "Furthermore, the *Chuxian* says 'not a single sentient being... and continuing to the second section on how the One Vehicle exists in all, this explains the meaning of the One Vehicle.
If there is a person who lacks the nature of wisdom, there are only the two vehicles or the three vehicles.
Regarding the third [point], the gate of "the principle giving rise to phenomena," there are two parts: first, a general explanation; second, reconciling it with what preceded.

Regarding the preceding section, the statement "it must be established by means of reasoning" is because all dependent originations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is precisely through the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature that things are established.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Because emptiness exists, all phenomena are established.
Furthermore, because there is no separate essence apart from the true mind.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Within this, there are two [points]," the second section correlates these with the two meanings mentioned above.
Because, as previously established, there is no separate essence apart from the true mind, the first stage, the "complete" aspect of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), is established.
Because the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) has been established, the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) conforming to conditions is established.

First: Regarding the term "complete aspect" (*sakalabhāga*), the non-arising-and-ceasing and the arising-and-ceasing are conjoined, being neither identical nor different; this is named the *ālayavijñāna*, which is precisely the complete aspect.

Because it possesses both that which arises and ceases and that which neither arises nor ceases, this non-arising and non-ceasing is the Tathāgatagarbha; this refers back to the previous discussion on the distinction between the true and the false within "Mind-Only," wherein it is identified with the True Mind.
If one does not rely entirely upon the true mind, then phenomena do not rely upon principle;
thus, to speak only in terms of arising and ceasing is not a complete teaching. Some say:

If it is held that there is a substance external to the reflection, this constitutes "half-cognition-only" (*ardhavijñaptimātra*); if both the substance and the reflection are manifest, this constitutes "complete [cognition-only]" (*sakalavijñaptimātra*). This, then, is the "complete" position within the Vijñānavāda school.
Next, he cites the verse from the "Forest of Enlightenment" (Bodhivṛkṣa), which is the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Yāma Palace.
It begins with a metaphor: "For example, like a skilled painter who distributes various colors..."
"Grasping at false and distinct colors, while the great elements remain without differentiation," and so forth.
The verse cited in the commentary combines the first half [of the original verse].
The first line corresponds to "just as a skilled painter," and the following three lines all correspond to "distributing various pigments."
Next, the verse on the complete manifestation is cited as proof, which likewise involves the distribution of various colors, as explained in the "Praise in Verses of the Yāma Heaven" chapter.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, to clarify that True Suchness (tathatā) becomes [phenomena] through following conditions,” this integrates the meaning of “following conditions” from the previous discussion on the distinction between True Suchness following conditions and remaining immutable.

Because conditions arise from the Truth, they are established by means of principle; for apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*, no phenomena whatsoever can be found, as explained in the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Knowledge" (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*).
The Commentary states: “The four matters can manifest the gate of principle. This section is divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Within the former, the phrase “because phenomena are formed by grasping the principle” refers back to the third gate.
The statement that “the phenomenon is empty while the principle is real” means that phenomena are established by grasping the principle.
Since there is no phenomenon apart from the principle, the phenomenon is empty and the principle is real.
Because phenomena are empty, they can manifest the true principle.
If phenomena were real, the true principle would remain hidden.
Because phenomena are empty, the principle within them is revealed in its full, unobstructed clarity—just as the emptiness of the characteristics of waves allows the water to appear.
Because waves are formed from water, the waves are illusory while the water is real; therefore, the waves can manifest the water.
If one were to speak of water apart from the waves, it would be like explaining emptiness outside of actual phenomena.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The dependent lacks intrinsic nature,” and so forth: this explains and establishes the preceding meaning; that is, it reconciles the sense of identity within the distinction between emptiness and existence regarding the prior dependent nature.

Since it is stated that "the absence of nature is itself the perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), this clarifies that it is not merely the absence of the imagined false nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
rather, there exists separately the perfected nature, which is the principle revealed [by the emptiness of the former].
The subsequent section beginning with "Yāma" cites scriptural evidence.
In total, three passages are cited:
first, the verses from the *Yāma* [chapter], which are the verses of the Bodhisattva Balakalpa; these three verses follow one after another.
Second, the citation from the "Chapter on the Ten Endurances" (*Daśakṣānti-parivarta*), specifically the "Endurance like an Echo" (*Pratiśrutkā-kṣānti*).
The third verse, which cites Mount Sumeru, is the verse by Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa; its second half states: "One who understands the nature of phenomena in this way sees Vairocana.
Prior to this is another verse that explains by contrast: "Those who are deluded and ignorant falsely grasp at the characteristics of the five aggregates."
"One who does not understand that true nature does not see the Buddha.
Regarding the profound meaning therein, it follows the text of the commentary (*śāstra*).
As for the commentary’s section on "The Fifth Gate: Substituting Principle for Phenomena" (*li duō shì mén*), it is divided into two parts:
First, the formal explanation; second, the reconciliation with what preceded.
Now, for the first:

regarding the statement, "Since phenomena are entirely identical to principle, phenomena are exhausted without remainder," this is because apart from true reality, not even a fragment of a phenomenon can be found.
This means that while the water remains, the waves have already ceased.

Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "Therefore it is said that the Buddhas are neither increasing nor decreasing," this is the second section, which reconciles the preceding [statements].
It consists of three parts:

First is the main assembly, second is the citation of scriptural evidence, and third—beginning with "It is not in reference to only one portion of sentient beings"—is the selection [of this teaching] as distinct from provisional schools.
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "The 'Appearance Chapter' says" cites the scriptural evidence.
I shall briefly cite two sutras.

First, regarding the citation from the *Avataṃsaka* which says, "Even if one were to say 'all things,' etc.," what is included within that "even if" should be stated as follows: "Bodhi is without marks and not without marks, because it is neither one nor manifold."
O Son of the Buddha!

Suppose there were someone who could manifest as many minds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each of those minds further manifested as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—all of whom were without color, without form, and without marks.
In this manner, they continue without rest for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Son of the Buddha!
What do you think?
"If this person, through their transformative mind, were to manifest as a Tathāgata, how many instances of the arising of the Tathāgata-nature would there be?
The Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue replied,
"As I understand the meaning of what you have said, the manifested and the non-manifested are equal and without distinction."
"What do you mean by asking how many there are?
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva replied,
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!"
"It is as you have said.

Regarding the phrase at the end of the commentary on the section "If all sentient beings" which states, "All because of the equality of signlessness," the meaning should be interpreted as "equal and without difference."
Why is this? Because awakening is without marks.
If there are no marks, then there is neither increase nor decrease.
In the sub-commentary (*śū*), following the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra*, there are two citations from other sūtras;
although the wording differs slightly, their textual meaning is largely identical.
The sub-commentary’s phrase “the six matters that can obscure the principle-gate” refers to a specific aspect within the context of “following conditions.”
Because phenomena arise in accordance with conditions, these phenomena pervade the ultimate truth; thus, while the phenomena are manifest, the truth remains hidden.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "Therefore, the Dharmakāya," this is a citation of supporting evidence from the *Dharmakāya Sūtra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The verse by Vasumitra says,” it refers to the *Vimalaprabhā-parivarta* (Chapter on Inquiring about Wisdom): “There has never been a single dharma that can enter into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The explanation states:
because the substance of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is empty and non-existent, there is nothing that can enter [into it].

Regarding the "Gate of the Seven Truths as Phenomena": because phenomena necessarily depend upon principle and lack a substantial essence of their own, this principle, in its entirety, is itself phenomenon;
only then does it constitute true principle.
Just as water is the waves—there is no movement that is not moist, and thus water is the waves—the commentary states:
"Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not violate the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa)," where the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the remaining textual passages.

The full text states: "The Dharma-nature does not contradict phenomena, and phenomena do not contradict the Dharma-nature; arising does not contradict the Dharma-nature, and the Dharma-nature does not contradict arising.

These two pairs clarify that there is no contradiction between phenomena and principle: that phenomena do not contradict the nature and arising does not contradict the nature belongs to the capacity of phenomena to manifest the principle.
Furthermore, the eighth matter is the principle-gate (*naya-mukha*); therefore, only the single phrase "the nature does not contradict the characteristics" is briefly cited here.
This refers to the twenty-ninth sūtra.
In the commentary following the words "The two preceding gates," the seventh and eighth gates are combined to synthesize the five previous meanings.
The first assembly [discusses] the two truths of emptiness and existence; this refers to the meaning of their mutual identity within the context of their distinction and separation.
Moisture is a metaphor for the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and waves are a metaphor for the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
As for the "Verses of Yāma," these are the verses of the Bodhisattva of the Forest of Diligence (Vīryavana).
The first verse states: "All phenomena are without distinction, and there is no one capable of knowing them.
Only Buddhas know [them] with other Buddhas, because their wisdom is ultimate.
The subsequent passage then says: "Just as gold and the color of gold, their nature is without distinction."
"Whether dharmas or non-dharmas, their essential nature is likewise without difference.
Now, regarding "dharmas and non-dharmas," there are two meanings:
first, wholesome dharmas are "dharmas" and unwholesome dharmas are "non-dharmas"; this accords with the statement in the heading that all dharmas are without distinction.

Second, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as being the phenomenon and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as being non-phenomenon: here, the gold serves as a metaphor for the nature of phenomena, while the color serves as a metaphor for the characteristics of phenomena.
The present text correctly employs this latter sense; therefore, it demonstrates that phenomenal dharmas are identical with principle, and that the two truths are mutually identical.

The Commentary states: "This also serves as a metaphor for the fact that the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna are mutually indistinguishable. This reiterates the meaning of the true mind within the previous discussion on the distinction between the true and the false aspects of "mind-only. Here, gold is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha, while color is used as a metaphor for birth-and-death and the like.

Thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s pure store and the worldly *ālayavijñāna* are like gold and a finger-ring; they differ only in manifestation, yet are fundamentally without distinction."
The word "also" (*api*) is used because this has already been reconciled in the third section above.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, because phenomena are identical to principle,” and so forth, this reconciles the [extremes of] discontinuity and permanence; it is likewise derived from within the gateway of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, because principle and phenomena are mutually identical, arising and ceasing are simultaneous. This reconciles the meaning of the four characteristics being either sequential or simultaneous, and their being distinct yet simultaneous.
The principle is entirely the same for phenomena; therefore, when a phenomenon arises, it is simultaneously extinguished.
This is because phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic substance.
The cited verse refers to the Bodhisattva Śubhamati.

In the commentary, the passage beginning with “Also causing [them] to reach the ultimate” harmonizes the subject and object of what is severed and realized; this is precisely the meaning of their mutual identity within their distinctness.

However, regarding the citation from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* concerning the severance of delusions, only the first phrase describes the characteristic of severing delusions, for it states that there is no severance during the three periods [of time], and only then does it speak of severance;
the subsequent phrase, however, describes the characteristic of *prajñā*.
Since *prajñā* is also that which effects severance, it is cited here as a matter of course.
Thus, the treatise explains this phrase by stating: "This is the aspect of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā-lakṣaṇa*).
This means that the essence of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) transcends all names and language; true wisdom arises internally, unlike the Śrāvakas who awaken by relying on sound.
Since it is true wisdom, it is capable of severing delusions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ‘Dedication Chapter’ says there is no suchness outside of wisdom,” this also proves that the subject and object of the severance of delusions are non-dual; the meaning is as previously explained.
The scriptures cited above will all become clear by themselves in the main text that follows. Regarding the commentary’s “Ninth Gate:

The Principle of Reality is Not Phenomena,” this means that while it is the principle inherent within phenomena, it is not the phenomena themselves; for truth and delusion are distinct, the real is not the unreal, and the supported is not the supporter.
Just as water that is waves is not [simply] waves, because moisture is not motion;
so too, this is the true emptiness (śūnyatā) that is not different from existence, wherein emptiness persists.

Regarding the commentary’s “The Gate of Phenomena Being Non-Reason in Ten Points”: it means that phenomena which are entirely identical to principle are nonetheless eternally non-reason, because their nature and characteristics are distinct, and because the dependent is not the supported.

Therefore, while the entire substance is the complete principle, the phenomenal characteristics remain distinct, like waves on water; yet the waves are never identical to the water, because movement is not wetness.
Thus, it is no different from illusory phenomena within emptiness, for the phenomena persist.

The Commentary states: "From 'the two preceding sections, seven and eight' onwards, the first four sections are used to harmonize the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the previous distinction between the conditioned and unconditioned aspects of the Buddha-body.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also says: "Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
If this Dharma is equal and without high or low,
is it conditioned or is it unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
"It is neither a conditioned dharma nor an unconditioned dharma. Why is this?"
Apart from conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
"Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
These are all its meanings.
In the commentary, the section following "The ten matters above" constitutes the third part, the general conclusion, which summarizes and explains the ten gates.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general heading; second, from "In terms of principle relative to phenomena" (*yueli wangshi*) onwards, the ten gates are specifically grouped to form eight characters.

Regarding the statement, "In terms of principle relative to phenomena, there is establishment and destruction, identity and separation": first, "establishment" refers to the third gate, the Gate of Establishing Phenomena Based on Principle (*yili chengshi men*).
Second, "that which has destruction" refers to the fifth gate, the sublation of phenomena by principle;
once those phenomena are sublated, the phenomena are destroyed.
Third, "that which is identical" refers to the seventh gate, the identity of ultimate truth with phenomena.
Regarding "the fourth, that which possesses separation," this refers to the ninth truth-gate of non-phenomena (*avastu*).
The commentary states: "When phenomena are viewed in relation to principle (*tattva*), there is manifestation and concealment, as well as identity and difference. This also comprises four gates:
first, "that which possesses manifestation," which is the fourth gate of phenomena being able to manifest principle.
The second, "that which has concealment," refers to the sixth category: the door of phenomena that can conceal the principle.
The third, "that which has unity," refers to the eighth category: the door of phenomena that are identical to the principle.
The fourth, "that which has difference," refers to the tenth category: the door of phenomena that are not the principle.
The preceding discussion regarding formation, destruction, and so forth is spoken in terms of functional efficacy (*kāritra*).
For instance, that which is "formed" refers to a phenomenon established through principle; it does not arise spontaneously by itself apart from principle.

Thus, within each and every gate, there is the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle; therefore, it is said that one may view phenomena from the perspective of principle, or view principle from the perspective of phenomena.
The remainder may be considered accordingly.
Thus far, through mutual comparison, there are four pairs of eight meanings.

As for why the first pair, "pervasive characteristics" and "two gates," is not combined here: it is because the meaning of pervasiveness is similar in all cases, and does not involve such distinctions as one arising while another perishes; therefore, it is not explicitly presented.

Furthermore, as for "pervasion by characteristics," this is the reason for the latter eight gates; that is to say, it is only through pervasion by characteristics that there can be arising and ceasing, and so forth.
If one wishes to subsume these, they are contained within the two meanings of the mutual identity of phenomena and principle.

Regarding the statement that "the later [section] does not treat them as identical," it means that only when the subject and object are not destroyed can there be mutual pervasion (*xiāngbiàn*); because there is mutual pervasion, one can then discuss their non-identity.

As for the commentary’s phrase "freedom in the inverse and direct," among the four meanings each when comparing phenomena (*shì*) and principle (*lǐ*), two meanings are inverse and two meanings are direct.
This means that when phenomena are established based on principle, true principle is identical to phenomena; this is "conformity.
When principle subsumes phenomena, true principle is not the phenomena; this is "reversal.
When phenomena can manifest principle, the dharmas of phenomena are identical to principle; this is "conformity."
Phenomena can obscure principle; since the nature of phenomena is not the principle itself, this constitutes opposition.
Because they can manifest when one wishes to manifest and perish when one wishes to perish, they are said to be "sovereign.

Since manifestation does not obstruct perishing and perishing does not obstruct manifestation, and visibility does not obstruct invisibility and invisibility does not obstruct visibility, they are said to be "unimpeded."
The very moment of formation is itself the moment of destruction and so forth; therefore, they are simultaneous.
Since all four pairs lack temporal sequence, it is said that they arise instantaneously (*tunqi*).
Furthermore, regarding the four pairs above, why does the text refer to principle in relation to phenomena only by saying "formation" and so on, rather than "manifestation" and so on?
When considering phenomena in relation to principle, why do we speak only of "revealing" and so forth, rather than "accomplishing" and so forth?
There is a profound reason for this. Why is that?
Phenomena arise from principles; thus, it may be granted that they are "established.
Principles do not newly come into existence; they can only be said to be "manifested.
Since phenomena, once established, must perish, they can be said to "disintegrate."
Since the Truth is eternally abiding, it is said merely to be "hidden.
As for its identity with or separation from [the phenomenal], and its oneness or difference [from it], the general principle is the same, yet when explained in detail, they differ.
Principle has no form or appearance; it can only be accessed through phenomena.
Since phenomena exhibit ten thousand variations, one may say that words and principle are in profound unity.
Because principle transcends all characteristics, it is said to be detached from phenomena.
Because phenomena possess differences, they are said to differ in principle (*li*).
The above was based on distinctions in meaning, resulting in these variations.

If one were to comprehensively synthesize them, there should be five pairs of meanings regarding non-obstruction: first, the pair of mutual pervasion; second, the pair of mutual formation; third, the pair of mutual harm; fourth, the pair of mutual identity; and fifth, the pair of non-identity.
Among the five [points], the first four clarify that phenomena and principle are not separate, while the last one clarifies that phenomena and principle are not identical.
Furthermore, within these five pairs, there are three meanings; the pair that establishes and manifests the two meanings is the meaning of phenomena and principle acting upon one another.
The two pairs—“separating what is hidden” and “not being immediate”—represent the sense of contradiction between phenomena and principle.
The two pairs—“mutual pervasion” and “mutual identity”—represent the sense of non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
Furthermore, because of the operation of the second characteristic, there is the identity of the fourth characteristic; because of this identity, the characteristics are mutually pervasive.
Because of the existence of the third characteristic of sublation, there is the fifth characteristic of non-identity.
Furthermore, if there were no non-identity, there could be no pervasive characteristic; therefore, it is said that "True Emptiness" and "Wondrous Existence" each possess four meanings.
With respect to principle in relation to phenomena, these are the four meanings of True Emptiness:
first, the meaning of discarding oneself to become another, which corresponds to the gate of "establishing phenomena based on principle."
Second, the meaning of submerging the other to manifest oneself, which is the gate of truth eclipsing phenomena.
Third, the meaning of the coexistence of self and other, which is the gate of truth not being phenomena.
Fourth, the meaning of the simultaneous submergence of both self and other, which is the gate of truth being identical to phenomena.
Because they are identical, they mutually dissolve into one another.

Furthermore, in the first and third [cases], it is the principle that pervades the phenomena; because it exists in its own right, it constitutes the other with its entire essence, and thus it pervades the other.
Subsequently, when considering phenomena in relation to principle, there are four meanings within the "wondrous fourfold" (miaosiu):
first, the meaning of manifesting the other while exhausting itself, which is the gate of phenomena being able to manifest principle;
second, the meaning of manifesting itself while concealing the other, which is the gate of phenomena being able to conceal principle.
Third is the meaning of the coexistence of self and other; this is the gate of phenomena being non-identical with principle.
Fourth is the meaning of the simultaneous sublation of self and other; this is the gate of phenomena being identical with principle.
Furthermore, the first and third are gates in which phenomena pervade principle: because they exist as themselves, they are able to manifest others, and thus they pervade others.
Therefore, it is said that regarding the existence or non-existence of phenomena, there is no obstruction; within true emptiness, concealment and manifestation are sovereign.
Regarding the fourth contemplation on universal inclusion and containment, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the topical outline; second, the detailed explanation according to the sections.

First: However, this name for the contemplation is precisely the name used within the "Contemplation of the Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā), as it corresponds to the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai).
Because principle possesses the two meanings of universality and expansive containment, it can permeate and fully encompass all phenomena through its harmonious integration.
The numerous categories of meaning all exist by virtue of these two principles.
However, the ten contemplations established in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* differ from the Ten Mysterious Gates (*shí xuán*).
Therefore, the present commentary states: "For now, I shall rely on the ancient masters to manifest the ten mysterious gates," which refers specifically to Master Zang.
The essential characteristics are already present, yet there are slight differences.
Below the phrase "Within this, there are two," the chapter is opened.
In the commentary, from "Now, first, the simultaneous" onwards, there is the second part: the detailed explanation according to the chapters.
The explanation of these two chapters constitutes two distinct sections.
Now, for the explanation of the first chapter, the commentary text is divided into three parts:
first, listing the names to provide a general overview; second, pointing to specific instances to explain them individually; and third, concluding with examples to demonstrate the benefits.
Now, the first ten names rely entirely upon Xianshou; therefore, it was stated above that "for now, we rely on the ancient masters.

Within the listing of these names, the second, the Gate of the Sovereignty of Extent and Narrowness, shares the same meaning as the "vast capacity and universal pervasion" found in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, though the terminology differs slightly.
This gate was newly established by Xianshou to replace Fazang’s "Gate of the Ten Mysterious Gates of the Pure and Mixed Endowment of All Treasuries.
Its intent is as follows:
a single practice is "pure," while myriad practices are "mixed," which constitutes the meaning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

If one principle were considered pure and the myriad practices impure, then phenomena and principle would be unimpeded; however, fearing that this might be confused with the doctrine of the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and principle, [Zhi]yi revised it.
The "Gate of the Principal and its Companions" was absent from Zhiyi’s work, though he did include the "Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment through the Revolving of Mind-Only."

Now, for the sake of the Profound Gate (the Chan school), these are not established; however, the enumeration of their names is also different from that [of the Avatamsaka Sūtra]. That [Sūtra] states: 1. The gate of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence;

2. The gate of the realm of Indra’s net; 3. The gate of the secret and the manifest being simultaneously accomplished; 4. The gate of subtle containment and establishment; 5. The gate of the distinct accomplishment of phenomena separated by the ten periods of time; 6. The gate of all treasuries possessing virtue through purity and mixture; 7. The gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion; 8. The gate of the sovereign interpenetration of all phenomena; 9. The gate of the excellent accomplishment of the turning of mind-only; 10. The gate of generating understanding by relying on things to reveal the Dharma.
Now, these ten gates do not follow the *Zhixiang* [commentary], because Xianshou’s established sequence possesses a specific order.
First is the Gate of Simultaneous Perfect Correspondence; as this is the general principle, it is placed at the beginning of the nine gates.
Regarding the second section, the gate of breadth and narrowness:

the reason for specifically discussing this first among the distinct gates is that because phenomena and principle are mutually pervasive within the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle mentioned above, the subsequent gates arise therefrom.

Furthermore, in terms of phenomena, because they pervade according to principle, they are "broad," yet because they do not destroy the characteristics of phenomena, they are "narrow"; thus, this constitutes the beginning of the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena.
Third, because breadth and narrowness are unobstructed, there are many things that are pervaded; since one is viewed in relation to many, there is the mutual containment of the one and the many.
When they are mutually compatible, both entities coexist, yet their functional powers interpenetrate.
Because this contains that, that is immediately this; because this pervades that, this is immediately that, and so forth—therefore, there is the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
Fifth, by way of mutual inclusion, there is a mutual alternation of concealment and manifestation.
That is to say, when including the other, because the other is visible, there is the "entrance of the appearance" (xiāngjiàn mén).
Furthermore, when including the other, because the other lacks intrinsic substance, there is the "entrance of identity" (xiāngjí mén).
Because they encompass others, yet those others exist without being visible, there is the "gate of concealment and manifestation.
Since these serve as distinct gates, all three of these gates exist through mutual inclusion.

Mutual entry is like two mirrors reflecting one another; mutual identity is like waves and water encompassing each other; and concealment and manifestation are like fragments of the moon illuminating one another.
Because these six aspects subsume others, all things are simultaneously subsumed, and their subsumption is likewise so; thus, there is the "Gate of Subtle Mutual Containment and Establishment."
Seventh, because they mutually encompass one another in ever-deepening layers, there is the inexhaustibility of the Indra’s Net (*indrājāla*).

Eighth, because it is like the Indra’s Net, wherein each single element is itself the entirety of the inexhaustible whole, there is the gateway of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena (*dharmatā*) to give rise to understanding.
Ninth, because the preceding eight are all supports (*āśraya*), and once the supported phenomena have been integrated, one next examines the supported (*āśrita*).
At the time of examining the supported, it is likewise so.
Tenth, because every phenomenon is thus, whichever one is raised becomes the primary subject; through their mutual connection and dependent origination, there is then a principal and its retinue.

This is explained in detail below. However, the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) divides the ten mysteries (*shixuan*) into three categories: the ten mysteries of the characteristics of qualities (*dexiang*), the ten mysteries of function (*ye-yong*), and the ten mysteries of each [category].

Regarding the ten mysteries of the characteristics of qualities: first, the quality of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence; second, the quality of mutual identity; third, the quality of presence and absence; fourth, the quality of concealment and manifestation; fifth, the quality of principal and attendant; sixth, the quality of identity through the same essence; seventh, the quality of inexhaustible fullness; eighth, the quality of purity and mixture; ninth, the quality of subtlety; and tenth, the quality of Indra’s net.

The ten aspects of the second, the function of karma, are: first, the simultaneous and complete mutual function; second, the function of mutual manifestation; third, the function of mutual inclusion; fourth, the function of mutual penetration; fifth, the function of mutual activity; sixth, the function of purity and mixture; seventh, the function of concealment and revelation; eighth, the function of principal and attendant; ninth, the subtle function; and tenth, the Indra’s net function.

Within the gate of the attributes of virtue (*guṇalakṣaṇa*), there are no gates of karmic function; within the gate of karmic function, there are no gates of the attributes of virtue (the fifth and sixth gates).
The intention of that master is as follows:

since karmic function is established in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings (*yathābhavyatā*), there is mutual inclusion and mutual operation; for while they were originally not included, they are now seen to be included.
Originally, sentient beings are not Buddhas; because they now manifest as both Buddha and sentient being, this is the functioning of karma.
The marks of virtue are not like this; therefore, there is no mutual manifestation of marks through interpenetration.

Because its virtuous characteristics (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) are inherently present, it possesses the same essence (*samāna-svabhāva*), namely, the virtues of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-guṇa*) and the possession of inexhaustible virtues.
Its karmic activity (*karma-vyāpāra*) is not thus; therefore, these two [attributes] do not exist therein.
Since these four are mutually inclusive, each possesses ten aspects.
When enumerated exhaustively across all categories, they total twenty.
Now, although the characteristics of virtue, substance, activity, and function differ, this does not preclude their being one within the Ten Mysterious Gates, wherein nothing is not encompassed.
Because the marks of virtue also function through mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*),
when those marks exist, they are precisely mutual inclusion;
when those marks function, they are precisely mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
The names differ while the meaning remains the same.
What is now seen as entering and exiting is the gate of karmic function (*karmayoga*).
Their constant mutual interpenetration, like mirrors reflecting one another, is the gate of virtuous marks (*guṇalakṣaṇa*).
Taking sentient beings as Buddhas, birth itself is the Buddha;
taking the Buddha as sentient beings, the Buddha himself is birth. Thus, one knows that "mutual production" is precisely "mutual identity."
If categorized according to the capacity of the recipient, it is called the Gate of Functional Activity (*karmaprayoga-mukha*).
If they are fundamentally identical in nature, it is called the Gate of Virtuous Characteristics (*guṇalakṣaṇa-mukha*).
Although distinguished based on this, there is not a lack of slight difference between them.
When one comprehends the essence and function of these matters, there is nothing further to distinguish them.

Thus we know that "mutual identity" and "mutual functioning" differ only in name; though the two names are distinct, they do not constitute two separate gates. Their entry points may differ slightly, yet their beginning and end are fundamentally one.

Furthermore, if the characteristic of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) were unable to enter [into activity], then True Suchness (*tathatā*) would lack this virtue and consequently could not possess the virtue of universally encompassing all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-saṃgraha*).

Moreover, the virtue of pervading all phenomena would likewise lack the capacity to establish a stable foundation, as well as the virtues of sustaining the world and accomplishing all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is logically consistent that it constantly enters [into activity].
As a verse says: "The Buddhas are like a pure, bright mirror; my body is much like a mani jewel. The Buddhas constantly enter my being, and my body pervades the bodies of all Buddhas."
This refers precisely to constant entry.
Furthermore, since True Suchness (Tathatā) follows conditions to manifest as all phenomena, how could there be no activity?
If one were to effect entry according to emotional views, it would possess only the meaning of karmic function.
That their identical substance constitutes "attainment" (de) is precisely the "gate of generating understanding by relying on phenomena to manifest the Dharma" within this context;
it is merely a difference in terminology. Thus, he himself explains: "Each and every one is all dharmas."
Therefore, this is identical in meaning to the subsequent explanation of "relying on phenomena.
That which is fully endowed with inexhaustible virtues is precisely the gate of the Indra-net (Indrajāla).
It is also subsumed under the subtle gate,
as detailed below in the assembly.
Furthermore, it does not maintain distinctions between broad and narrow, but maintains the distinction between pure and mixed.
It is also as in the previous assembly;
however, that [system] lacks the "Gate of the Accomplishment of the Distinction of Dharmas Separated by Ten Ages," because it takes time as the substantial basis for phenomena.
Therefore, those entities and phenomena also consist of ten types:
namely, matter, mind, time, place, person, direction, teaching, meaning, practice, and stage; these encompass all phenomena without exception.
This also has its道理 (dili).

Now, it is clarified that because time has no separate essence, it does not serve as a basis; rather, it is established based upon phenomena, and thus enters the profound gate (xuánmén), as also explained in the subsequent section.
In the commentary, from the passage "Now, first among the ten [categories] above," the second section provides a specific explanation by citing actual instances.
This is divided into two parts:
first, a general discussion of the basis, which refers to one specific dharma among those previously shown to be unimpeded; and second, a detailed explanation of the specific instances.
Below the passage "as in the following section, 'a single lotus petal,'" ten distinct gates are separately revealed, constituting ten individual sections.
The first is the Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment; because it stands nearest to the initial listing, its sequential number is not explicitly marked.
In this passage, there are two parts: first, the direct clarification; second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Within the first part, there are again two sections:
first, clarifying that the present category is complete in itself; second, clarifying that it encompasses the remaining nine categories.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Thus, the ten pairs such as teaching and so forth are simultaneously corresponding, complete, and perfect,” this refers to their completeness within the initial section of the gates.

Here, the primary intent clarifies that these possess the ten pairs of dharmas previously mentioned: teaching and meaning, principle and phenomenon, object and wisdom, practice and stage, cause and fruit, and so on.
The preceding ten pairs encompass all phenomena and non-phenomena; therefore, when these are possessed instantaneously, there is nothing that is not possessed.
As for the reason they are so possessed, there are ten causes at length, but briefly stated, it is because the *dharmadhātu* is interfused.
However, the ancient masters established these ten meanings based on a single flower.
The *Tanyuan ji* states: "This single lotus flower symbolizes the generation of understanding and serves as the teaching that expresses it."
Thus, that which is expressed is called "meaning" (*artha*).
As stated in the *Padmadhātu* chapter of the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā*:
"The two lotus-forms constitute the phenomenon (*dharma*), while the essence of the lotus constitutes the principle (*tattva*)."
The third flower is that which is observed, and it is also that which observes;
for within this sutra, internal practice is treated as an external object.
The fourth is the flower of active practice, which brings about the formation of the stages, as in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct."
Fifth, the flowers are manifestations of causal phenomena, for they encompass the fruition of results.
Sixth, the bases upon which the flower-pedestals rest also enter into the correct [reality], as in the case of the bodies of the Buddha-lands and so forth.
Seventh, the substance of the flowers is identical to the True [Suchness], while their function responds to the capacities of sentient beings.
Eighth, because the entirety of the eightfold path is taken as the person, it is eternally the Dharma.
Ninth, because the [five] rebellious acts correspond to the five heats and the [five] compliant acts correspond to the ten perfections.
Tenth, because it responds to the various capacities of sentient beings, it is also capable of eliciting a response.
Just as it is with this single matter of the flower, so should all other matters be understood by analogy.
Just as it is with these phenomena, so it is with all other teachings, meanings, and so forth.
This can be understood through reflection: just as it is with each of the ten pairs being complete, so too is it for each single petal of the flower, which likewise possesses the ten gates.
The commentary states:

According to the ancient masters, this principle means that within a single flower there already exist these ten meanings; furthermore, upon each of the preceding ten pairs there are again ten, such that a single flower instantaneously possesses ten times ten.
There is indeed this principle.
The intent of this commentary (*śāstra*) is merely to ensure that the ten preceding [sections] are all simultaneously present, such that nothing remains uncollected.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It also contains the nine subsequent sections and the teachings contained within those sections, because it is a comprehensive whole,” this second point clarifies that it contains the remaining nine sections, thereby further establishing its status as a comprehensive whole.
If one were to possess only the "future gate," it would not constitute a comprehensive [classification],

for the phrase "the teachings and so forth possessed" indicates that each of the nine subsequent gates possesses its own respective categories of teaching, meaning, principle, phenomenon, object, and wisdom.
Now, since that which is fully possessed by all gates is entirely present in the first gate, it is evident that what is possessed by each gate resides here.
Nevertheless, although the nine gates are identical in their possession of the teachings and so forth, they differ individually in their meaning.

That is to say, regarding the gates of breadth and narrowness, all ten are both broad and narrow—namely, the breadth and narrowness of the teaching, the breadth and narrowness of the meaning, the breadth and narrowness of the principle, the breadth and narrowness of the phenomena, and so forth.
"If one enters through the characteristics, then all ten mutually enter.
The following seven examples are likewise so.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "Therefore, the text below says," this is the second section: citing scriptural evidence.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, I cite the "Chapter on Sublime Adornment," specifically the verse by the Heavenly King Vast Fruit of Universal Wisdom-Eye (*Samantajñānacakṣurvipulaphala*).
The second half of that verse says: "Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as taught by the Buddha; the eye of wisdom can clarify these skillful means."
This clarifies that within a single gate there are inexhaustible dharmas, such that nothing is not fully contained.
Subsequently, it quotes the second half of a verse from the *Avataṃsaka*: "The jewel-lights manifest Buddhas gathering like clouds; this is the sovereign mastery of the Tathāgata’s realm."

Now, citing that a single dust mote contains the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is itself the comprehensive meaning; for the teachings, meanings, principles, phenomena, objects, wisdom, and the mutual interpenetration of the vast and the narrow are all the dharma-realm.
Question:
Since it simply says "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu), how can we know that this is not the "reality dharma-realm" (tathatā-dharmadhātu)? Answer:
The latter half states: "The Buddhas of Jewel Light appear like gathering clouds; this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field.
It is clearly understood that this refers to the phenomenal dharma-realm (sāṃvṛtika-dharmadhātu).

The Commentary states: "If even a single mote of dust possesses [all qualities], how much more so a single leaf? This uses the subtle to illustrate the coarse, thereby explaining and establishing its profound subtlety.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Sublime Adornments" uses a metaphor for the Buddha’s body, saying: "It is like empty space, which contains all forms within it."
This refers to the Buddha-body, which is fully endowed with all dharmas.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (*Xingqi pin*) in the Jin translation states: “All kalpas of the three periods of time, the Buddha-fields and all dharmas, the various faculties, the mind and its mental concomitants—all these are false dharmas.”
"Within the body of a single Buddha, all these dharmas are fully manifested.
Therefore, it is said that bodhi is immeasurable and boundless.
This also refers to the perfection of the Buddha’s body and mind.
Furthermore, the "Samantabhadra Samādhi" chapter states: "It can cause all the atoms within every land to be able to contain the entire boundless Dharma-realm."
According to the phrase "that which enables," it is simply that the function of activity arises entirely from the aspect of qualities (*guṇalakṣaṇa*).
Being inherently complete is itself the aspect of qualities; causing sentient beings to perceive this is what constitutes the function of activity.
The application of the lower activities follows this principle.
The tenth practice states: "This bodhisattva, within his own body, manifests all buddha-fields, all sentient beings, and all buddhas."

The *Śrī-bhadracarī-praṇidhāna-rāja-ṭīkā* (Eighty Fascicles) states: "When Sudhana beholds each and every limb and each and every pore of Samantabhadra, there appear within them all the worlds of the ten directions, including the earth, water, and other wheels, as well as the mountains, rivers, oceans, and palaces of humans and devas within the trichiliocosm; and he sees the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout all kalpas, just as if seeing the present world."
In this way, they clearly perceive everything from the past limit to the future limit throughout all worlds.

Even within the atoms of the lands of the ten directions, they manifest all realms of the three periods of time: all Buddha-lands, all sentient beings, the appearance of all Buddhas, and all Bodhisattvas; and they hear the voices and sounds of the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"These both constitute the gate of simultaneous fulfillment and correspondence.

Regarding the commentary's passage, "Second, those flower petals universally pervade the Dharma-realm without losing their original positions," this refers to the second gate: the gate of unimpeded mastery over the vast and the narrow.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the broad and the narrow; second, the reconciliation of the pure and the mixed.
Within the former, there are three sections:
First, the explicit clarification; second, the citation of evidence; third, the enumeration of categories. Now, for the first:
the first two lines set forth the characteristics of breadth and narrowness.
The statement, "That which is differentiated is itself non-differentiated; that which is non-differentiated is itself differentiated," sets forth the reason why this is so.
Due to these phenomena, their boundaries are clearly distinct;
yet because they are identical to true nature, they have no boundaries and are thus vast and boundless, for phenomena accord with principle.
"That which has no parts is itself the part" clarifies that the broad is identical to the narrow, because their characteristics are not destroyed.
Below the "Ten Samādhis Chapter," there are two citations as proof;
these are the passages from the tenth [samādhi], the Unhindered Wheel Samādhi (*anāvaraṇacakra-samādhi*), corresponding to the forty-third [fascicle].
“There is a lotus flower that reaches to the limits of the ten directions” is the scriptural passage; however, it is still somewhat brief.
To speak in full: “O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has a lotus flower, and this flower is so vast that it extends to the limits of the ten directions.”
"It is adorned with unspeakable leaves, unspeakable jewels, and unspeakable fragrances," and so forth.
The subsequent statement, "yet this does not preclude the existence of external objects that can be perceived," is an interpretive citation.
That sutra states in full: "All sentient beings who see it pay homage and show respect; thus we know that there is also an external form visible [to the senses].
In the seventy-seventh sutra, Sudhana praises the pavilion, saying: "It is the dwelling place of one who, without moving from their original location, is able to visit all Buddha-fields."
In the seventy-sixth sutra, Queen Māyā said: "Furthermore, noble son!
When that wondrous radiance entered my body, although the dimensions of my physical form did not exceed their original size, it had in fact already transcended the world."
Why is this? Because at that time my body was equal in measure to empty space, being able to fully accommodate the various palaces adorned for the births of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions.
Passages such as these all demonstrate the freedom to expand or contract at will.
Regarding the three phrases following "Therefore, sometimes it is only expansive" in the Commentary (*Sū*), they are distinguished numerically as follows:

first, because phenomena are identical to principle, there is expansion; second, because their original characteristics are not destroyed, there is contraction; third, because these two occur simultaneously, there is both expansion and contraction at once; fourth, because they mutually negate one another simultaneously, both are subsumed; fifth, possessing the preceding four, there is simultaneous illumination and realization.
Therefore it is said: "The realm is understood, practice arises, and understanding ceases.
Thus, there is a sixth stage that universally transcends the preceding five; who then would allow distinctions of breadth or narrowness, existence or extinction, to occupy one's inner mind?

The Commentary states: "However, this [distinction between] broad and narrow is also termed 'pure and mixed'... This refers to the second section, the Gate of Pure and Mixed in the two assemblies, because the ancient Ten Mysteries (Shi-xuan) bear this name.

Master Xianshou’s intention is that the purity and mixture of the myriad practices encompass both the unimpeded interfusion of phenomena and principle as well as cases discussed solely in terms of phenomena; therefore, he has set them aside here.

This means that because they share the same dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they are "pure," yet because their phenomenal characteristics (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) are not destroyed, they are "mixed"; this is the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*jili wuai*).
Because one practice is the long-form practice, it is "pure," yet because it does not obstruct other practices, it is "mixed"; this refers only to phenomena.

Therefore, although in the past these were discarded in favor of establishing the broad and the narrow, if one now seeks to synthesize them, they accord with reality and are all-pervasive; thus they are "pure" because they do not destroy the unity of the many, yet they are "mixed" because they do not destroy the multiplicity of the one. In this way, there is indeed the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena.
If one takes them by way of their entry gates, they are "pure" because everything enters therein; yet they are called "varied" because there are many dharma-gates within that entry.
As stated in the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornments," the oceans of assemblies each obtain only a single gate of liberation—this is purity.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra attained the inconceivable gate of liberation; this is the "Miscellaneous" section.
In the sixty-fifth scripture, the maiden Maitrīcāriṇī says:
"I cultivated and attained this Dharma in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers."
"Those Tathāgatas each, by means of different gateways, have caused me to enter this gateway of the universal adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā.
This refers precisely to the non-obstruction between the pure and the mixed.
Furthermore, because each of the spiritual friends sought by the youth Sudhana states,
"I know only this single dharma-gate," and further says, "For many kalpas I have cultivated only this one gate," this refers to the "exclusive gate" (the *chunmen*).
All the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) collectively urged:
"The various knowledges and views, the various practices, and the various realizations of all bodhisattvas"—this is the section on miscellaneous topics.

To say that one knows for oneself while inferring that others possess much—though self and other differ, they both belong to the single principle—this is also the gate of the unimpeded interfusion of the pure and the mixed.
Furthermore, Sudhana’s universal attainment of the understanding, practice, virtue, and realization of all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is likewise the gate of the mixed.

However, most of the scriptural passages cited above concern practice—whether as a single practice or multiple practices being pure or mixed—and they all explain this by referring to both combined and individual phenomena.

However, regarding the general characteristics of these virtues, if we follow the *Avivāda-avibandha-vimokṣa-pariṇāmanā* (The Dedication of Liberation Without Attachment or Bondage), it says: "By means of a mind that is without attachment or bondage, one manifests within a single gateway for unspeakably unspeakable eons without end, causing all sentient beings to attain awakening and entry."
"By means of a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, one accomplishes the sovereign power of Samantabhadra and manifests through various gateways.

Throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, this is never exhausted, causing all sentient beings to attain awakening and entry, while his body appears universally before all Buddhas"—this refers to the purity and interpenetration of function.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The same applies to the myriad practices,” this refers to explaining purity and mixture in terms of practice; it encompasses both the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and principles, as well as cases where it refers solely to phenomenal practices.
Regarding the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*): for example, when a single act of giving encompasses all acts of giving, it is called "pure" (*chun*).
When within that single act of giving all various practices are fully present, it is called "mixed" (*za*).
This is the third gate: the mutual inclusion of the one and the many without confusion.
Within this, there are three sections:
first, the formal explanation; second, the citation of evidence; and third, a further investigation and selection.
Within the first section, there are two parts:
The preceding section provides the formal explanation, namely the pervasion according to principle and the encompassment according to principle;
the subsequent section, beginning with "expansion and contraction are simultaneous," analyzes the number of phrases.
Since this follows the pattern of the aforementioned broadness and narrowness, it says, "reflect upon this."
If one possesses these functions, there are three possibilities: first, it may be merely "entering," because by means of one [entry], all are entered;
second, it may be merely "encompassing," because by means of one, all are encompassed;
third, it may be both entering and encompassing simultaneously, because they are without obstruction at the same time.
Fourth, they are neither entrances nor inclusions; because an entrance is itself an inclusion, it is not an entrance, and because an inclusion is itself an entrance, it is not an inclusion.
Fifth, they may possess all four [characteristics], as they are the objects of understanding.
Sixth, it may exclude the preceding five, because these are the objects of its activity; since activity arises, understanding is severed.
