"In my land, the Tathāgata does not preach by means of written words; rather, he causes devas and humans to enter into the practice of the precepts solely through various fragrances.
Each bodhisattva sits beneath a fragrant tree, and upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues."
"One who attains samādhi is fully endowed with all the merits of a bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
This uses fragrance as a metaphor to manifest samādhi.

Furthermore, the preceding text states: "He was sitting and eating together with various bodhisattvas; there were also sons of gods, all named Gandhavimāna, who had all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This refers to the benefit of the flavor of the food.

Furthermore, in the "Bodhisattva" chapter below, it clarifies how long the meal will take to digest, stating: "For those who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) and eat this meal, it will only be digested after they have entered that stage of certainty."
It further states: "Those who have already resolved upon the Mahāyāna and eat this food shall attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), after which it will be digested.
The commentary explains:

This is the Buddha’s work through the flavor [of the teaching]; therefore, the sub-commentary (*śū*) comprehensively gathers the intent of the sūtra, encompassing it within two passages of the scripture.

The Commentary states: “In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one achieves right mindfulness by listening to the wind rustling through the branches” refers to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, which says: “Śāriputra!

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, when a gentle breeze stirs the various jeweled rows of trees and the jeweled nets, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds, like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously.”
Those who hear this sound will naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness toward the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha. Śāriputra,
the land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious virtues as these.
By comparing the sutra with its commentary, the meaning of the text becomes clear.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that “stringed and wind instruments can transmit the mind,” this refers to an account found in the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian).
Incorporating these various matters, it is said that Lu Yue conveyed his intentions to the Lord of Qin and indeed escaped the hands of Jing Ke;
Sima Xiangru sent word to the family of Zhuo and ultimately won the devotion of Wenjun.
Śakra has the minister of the Dharma-pleasure, and Aśvaghoṣa has the musician Haradatta;
both transmit the mind through stringed and wind instruments.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “One preserves the Way by witnessing with the eyes,” this refers to an episode from the *Zhuangzi*.
"Master, you wished to see Wen Bo Xuezi and for a long time did not meet him.
When you finally met him, he was silent and did not utter a single word.
Upon his departure, Zi Lu was astonished and asked:"
"I have long desired to see Master Wen Bo Xuezi.
Why is it that upon meeting, you remain silent and do not utter a single word?
The Master said:
"Regarding such a person, the Way exists in a single glance; it is something that cannot even admit the sound of a voice.
Commentary: From "Since speech and silence... onwards, the second section establishes the nature of speaking and listening.
"Speech, silence, gazing, and blinking all constitute preaching" concludes the preceding passage.
"Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all listening" clarifies the subsequent meaning.
"Sensing" (jue) encompasses the three faculties of the nose, tongue, and body.
Since the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) were all explained above, the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are now all addressed as "listening.
In the commentary, from the words "If one can... onwards, the meaning of listening is explained.
Above, it was merely the manifestation of the Dharma that constituted "speaking"; here, it is merely the attainment of the Dharma that constitutes "listening."
The Commentary states: “Moreover, as for the *Avataṃsaka*,” and so forth. This third section provides a further illustration regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Above, it was shown that this principle applies universally to both the internal and external teachings of the Three Vehicles;
how much more so, then, for the perfectly consummate school of the One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka*—what dharma therein is not a teaching?
This section consists of four parts.
First, the explanation of the phenomena and the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "canopy of jewel nets on a cloud-platform," this refers to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*: "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted pure light from between his eyebrows... and it further illuminated this Sahā world, including the Buddha, the great assembly, and the body and lion throne of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva; thereafter, in the space above, a great canopy of radiant clouds and jewel nets was formed."
At that time, from within the Hall of Radiance, by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, a verse was spoken:

"The Buddha is unequaled, equal to space; his ten powers and immeasurable, supreme merits are the most excellent in the human realm and the highest in the world. May the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas be bestowed upon them. Such is the text.
Furthermore, regarding the "Jewel Net," the first sutra states: "That lion throne has a platform made of maṇi jewels and a net of lotus flowers.
Below it says: "Furthermore, sustained by the majestic power of all Buddhas, it expounds the vast sphere of the Tathāgata."
This is also the wording [of that scripture].

Furthermore, regarding the word "clouds," it refers to the beginning of the sixth sutra, where sounds spontaneously emerge from within clouds of all manner of offering implements to preach the Dharma, and so forth.
The Commentary states: "The light from the pores is all capable of preaching the Dharma" refers to the fact that even the aforementioned *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* teaches through light.

Furthermore, the ninth stage says: "At times, the mind desires to emit great radiance to expound the gates of the Dharma; at other times, the mind desires for every single pore upon its body to produce the sounds of the Dharma."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "At that time, from within the radiance of all the bodhisattvas, a voice simultaneously issued forth, reciting these verses:

'From within the various radiances emerge wondrous sounds, which pervade all lands throughout the ten directions; they proclaim the manifold virtues of the Buddha-sons, who are able to enter the sublime path to enlightenment,' and so forth."

Furthermore, at the beginning of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," it says: "The bodhisattvas who have come from below—namely, the Bodhisattva named Sarvāvaraṇavikiraṇavegajñānadhvajārāja, together with as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds—approached the place where the Buddha was. From all his pores, he emitted clouds of sounds of the ocean of languages of all sentient beings, and clouds of sounds of the ocean of skillful means for the practice of all bodhisattvas throughout the three periods of time. And so forth.
The phrasing is not uniform.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Flower-scented clouds and trees are themselves the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm,” this second point clarifies that phenomena are themselves the Dharma; what further explanation could there be?
This is because there is a "gate for generating understanding by manifesting the Dharma through reliance on specific phenomena.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The lands and sentient beings are fundamentally the true essence of the ten bodies,” this third section clarifies that these very phenomena are the speakers; how could it be that they merely manifest the Dharma?

The *kṣetra* (buddha-field) is the body of the land, and sentient beings are the body of sentient beings; these two out of the ten bodies are mentioned briefly. If even these two inferior ones are already the ten bodies, how much more so the others that are superior?
"Regarding 'in what sense is it not the teaching,'" this is the formal conclusion of the argument.
Since even that which is capable of speaking [is not the teaching], how much more so that which lacks the essence of the teaching?
*Da fangguang fo huayan jing su shu yan yi chao*, Scroll 12.
*Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
Fascicle Thirteen,
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
The sub-commentary states, “As stated below,” which is the fourth section, citing scriptural evidence.
First, it cites the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," as was analyzed previously in the section on the conditions for the teaching.
Regarding the sub-commentary’s phrase, “The sixth [section], ‘The Essence of the Mind-Only Comprehension of Objects,’ etc.,” the commentary is divided into two parts:
First, there is a general clarification;
subsequently, from "However, there is... onwards, the chapter is opened for a detailed explanation.
Within the former section, there are also two parts:
First, the correct explanation; second, the citation of evidence.
Now, for the first:

the preceding five substances are all transformations of the mind; there is no phenomenon external to the mind. Just as sound is form, it is a reflection manifested by the mind itself, let alone names and so forth that are conventionally established based upon sound.
The meanings elucidated by that teaching and the manifest significance of all phenomena are both devoid of intrinsic nature apart from the mind.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," etc., constitutes the second part: citing scriptural evidence.
These three cited passages encompass the four teachings.
The first citation from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) represents the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
Thus, that treatise states: "It merely negates external objects; consciousness expresses the internal mind, and apart from consciousness, there are no other dharmas."
He cites numerous scriptures to establish *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), also citing the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as detailed in that treatise.
Regarding the term "etc. (*ādi*), there are two meanings:
first, it refers equally to other treatises; second, it refers equally to other sūtras.
Regarding the first [category], this refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and so forth.

Thus, in the fourth chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, it is said: "Among those who have not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, how do they infer [the nature of] consciousness-only?"
This should be understood through both scripture and reasoning.
Regarding scripture, as the Bhagavān stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*: "The three realms are nothing but mind."
Furthermore, the Bhagavat’s explanation in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also speaks in this way.

Regarding the statement in the commentary that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* refers to the ten kinds of stages (*bhūmi*) taught for bodhisattvas within that sūtra, this is precisely the collection of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) that establish the characteristics of the ten stages; it has as its essence the aggregation of what is manifested by consciousness.

This refers to the fact that the noble Lord Vajragarbha, taking the reflected image manifested upon his purified consciousness as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), caused a reflection resembling that Dharma-gate to appear upon the consciousness of the listeners. Thus transmitted from one to another down to the present day, it is called "teaching" (*śāsana*).
Therefore, in all the treatises, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited to establish Vijñaptimātratā.
The scripture cited is precisely the "Gate of Being Subsumed within One Mind" from the sixth stage (*Ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
All that exists within the triple world is but this single mind.
It is upon this single mind that the Tathāgata relies to analytically expound the twelve links of existence; thus are they established."
Now, since all these [scriptures] have already been cited in various treatises, the present commentary cites only the *Brahmacarya* [Sūtra].

Second, regarding the phrase "these and so forth," it refers to the meaning within the sudden teaching (dun-jiao) of sūtras such as the *Laṅkāvatāra*, which states that although the eight consciousnesses are empty, they are called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
The sub-commentary states: "The *Awakening of Faith* also says... and so forth; this refers to the realization within the Final Teaching (*zhōngjiào*).
This passage is from the section on "Revealing the Correct Meaning" within the "Explanatory Division" (*shìshìfēn*) of that treatise.
However, within the section on the "Establishment of the Meaning," it says: "The Mahāyāna, when stated in general, is of two kinds.
What are these two? First, the Dharma; second, the meaning."

That which is called "Dharma" refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas, and it is based upon this mind that the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed.
This concludes the clarification of the meaning of "Mind-Only.
Now, by taking up the section on "Exegesis" which reveals how the characteristics of the nature of mind—truth and falsehood—interpenetrate, we know this to be the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao).
According to that treatise, Xianshou’s Commentary states: "The 'one mind' is the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
It contains two meanings:
first, in terms of its essence, it is devoid of all marks; this is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*)."
"The second, following conditions to arise and cease, is the gate of arising and ceasing.
This meaning shall be analyzed in detail in the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications"; for now, we merely provide a brief scriptural proof that the essence of the teaching is mind-only.

In the commentary following the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," the author cites the relevant scripture to substantiate the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) that all phenomena are but the mind itself.
One should understand that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind; it is not merely a matter of the mind’s transformations as asserted by the Dharma-character school (Xiangzong).

In the commentary, from the words "However, there are... onwards, within the section on the detailed explanation of the opening chapters, there is first the opening of the chapters and subsequently the detailed explanation.
Within that explanation, the four propositions concerning the primary image and its reflection are first explained as four distinct points.
The second sentence is divided into two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of coexistence; second, the explanation of the manifestation of the aggregate.
Within the former, there are also two [subdivisions]:
First, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* is cited to establish each [of the two] individually; subsequently, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is cited to corroborate the preceding arguments together.
Regarding the former, first, it is because the Tathāgata truly exists and preaches the Dharma that it is called the "original substance" (*maulika*).

The "text" (*vyañjana*) encompasses the six types of literary expression, and the "meaning" (*artha*) encompasses the ten types of meaning; these all serve as the basis for manifesting the text and meaning herein.

Because in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) both speaking and listening depend upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), in the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*) it is likewise solely the mental consciousness; therefore, it is said to be the "pure consciousness associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna-saṃprayukta-viśuddha-vijñāna*). Since in the resultant stage wisdom is predominant and consciousness is subordinate, this consciousness is described as being associated with that wisdom.
This wisdom can rain down the great Dharma-rain within the great assembly, and thus it is able to preach the Dharma.
The King upon which this wisdom relies is the sixth consciousness; therefore, it is said to be manifested by pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
Regarding the term "pure," it refers to being exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The *Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Since it is manifested by an untainted mind, its substance consists of the true, untainted words and meanings."
Therefore, the World-Honored One truly has taught the Dharma; his statement that he has not taught it is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).

The commentary states: "In the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, under the heading 'There is one interpretation,' the scriptural citations are provided, which may be understood [by the reader]."

The Commentary states: “If it is upon the consciousness of the listener,” and so forth, clarifying that the teaching as a reflected image relies upon the Buddha’s primary substance (mūla-vastu), because it is a transformation of one’s own mind.
When transformed by a contaminated mind (sāsrava-citta), it is then termed contaminated (sāsrava).
In the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is cited as scriptural evidence that there is a reflection (*pratibimba*).

This is also because, in the preceding fascicle, the Buddha was taken as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the textual meaning of the mental image (*svacitta-pratibimba*) was established as the result.
The sub-commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'the characteristics of this textual meaning' below, [this] explains [it] and also addresses potential objections.
One might fear an objection being raised as follows:"
If this is a transformation of one's own mind, why is it called "the Buddha’s teaching"?
Therefore, the text reiterates and explains:
with one's own virtue as the cause and the Buddha’s power as the condition, the mental image is the result.
Now, following from conditions, it is merely called "the Buddha's teaching.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Therefore, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*," this second section cites treatises to provide dual proof for the preceding two points.
Thus, both the primary object (*maulika*) and its reflected image (*pratibimba*) are equally present in the two teachings.
This means that if the listener serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), then the appearance of the words and their meaning arises upon the Buddha’s mind;

if the Buddha serves as the dominant condition, then the appearance of the words and their meaning arises upon the listener’s mind. Therefore, it is said that they arise through the successive power of mutual dominance.

The consciousness of the Tathāgata and the consciousness of the listener are called the "two consciousnesses," which definitively establish the teaching of the original and its reflection (*mūla-pratibimba*).
Regarding the phrase "the Master Dharmapāla" and so forth: this is because all masters of the *Vijñaptimātra* school establish [this doctrine] in the same way.

The *Commentary* by the Mahāyāna Dharma Master states: "However, since this master of the treatise does not fail to explain the teaching, we adopt this interpretation. Regarding the passage in the *Commentary*:

"Furthermore, as the text and its meaning arise together, it further explains the five mental states as a collective manifestation," and so forth, this second section clarifies the manifestation of the collection.
This section has two parts:

first, a general clarification of the characteristics of their aggregation; second, a detailed explanation of the number of the five consciousnesses, beginning with the passage "However, in the Western [tradition]...
Regarding the statement "However, there are many explanations in the West," it is traditionally said that there are briefly four interpretations, and the present commentary follows the first.
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Weishi shu) as well, only this interpretation is given; as it represents the general intent, the commentary preserves it.
Following the phrase "The rest is as in the separate chapter," there are the explanations of three masters.
One explanation states:

When the initial sounds of the various characters are uttered, the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) arises spontaneously, and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perceives only their sound, because this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Within the mind of investigation (*paryeṣaka-citta*), one seeks only the object perceived by the ear-consciousness; thus, it likewise perceives only the sound and does not perceive the characters or names.

Although these three minds have names and words upon the sounds they transform—just like the characteristics of arising and so forth—they do not take them as objects; it is only when reaching the mind of determination that they take the sounds, words, and names as objects, whereupon the three characteristics appear.

When the second syllable "sa" is uttered, the sudden auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the mind of seeking (*paryeṣaka-citta*) likewise take only the sound as their object.

Upon reaching the mind of determination (*niścaya-citta*), which takes the sound, the syllable, and the name as its objects, six aspects appear; this is because each of the two preceding syllables possesses its own sound, syllable, and name.

When the three "letterless" (a) syllables are uttered, the spontaneous auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*) likewise take only the sound as their object.

Upon reaching the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*), which takes the sound, the letter, and the name as its objects, nine aspects appear; this is because each of the preceding three syllables possesses its own sound, letter, and name.

When the fourth syllable, "nitya" (constant), is uttered, the spontaneous ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*) likewise take only the sound as their object.

Upon reaching the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*), which takes the sound, the syllable, and the name as its objects, twelve moments of mind have elapsed, comprising fourteen aspects—namely, four sounds, four syllables, four names, along with the phrase and its meaning—which is termed the "assemblage."
If there is no distraction, then minds such as those of defilement or purity, as well as their resultant mental continuities (*nisyanda-citta*), arise;
if there is distraction, the arising of the mind is indeterminate.

One school asserts that the sudden auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and its simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perceive only sound, because this constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In the mind seeking [an object], one takes sounds, syllables, and names as conditions;

because this is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it passes through at least twelve moments of mind. Within these, there appear three, six, nine, or fourteen aspects, which is termed "aggregation" (*saṃnipāta*).
If there is no distraction, a determinate mind arises;
if there is distraction, the arising of the mind is indeterminate.

One view holds that while the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) merely takes sound as its object, the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the sound, the syllables, and the names as its objects.
If this were not the case, what would the seeking consciousness (*manovijñāna*) be seeking?
Regarding this, there are two interpretations of the "crookedness" (*vaṅka*):

first, it is said that the four types of sudden auditory consciousnesses (*śrotravijñāna*) merely take the sound as their object, while the simultaneous mental consciousness takes the sound, the syllable, and the name as its objects; this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because when taking the constant sound as its object, it does not take various similar sounds or the syllables and names as its objects.

Because the five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness all constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding sounds and other objects, it is only through the subsequent four types of seeking minds that [the process] becomes complete.
When these twelve minds manifest in three sets of six, nine, and four aspects respectively, this is termed "aggregation" (*saṃnipāta*).
One explanation states:

The simultaneous mental consciousness may not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it can take the past as its object and apprehend eight types of mind; namely, the four sudden auditory consciousnesses and the four simultaneous mental consciousnesses.
When the three, six, nine, four, and ten signs appear, it is called "aggregation.
Question:
Since the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it take words and names as its objects?
Answer:
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) also takes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of names and so forth as its object, as stated in the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra*.
As for that which does not take them as its object, it is because it does not take the name and its referent as objects when they are related to one another.

The above summarizes the fourfold explanation of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*) in order to distinguish the varying numbers of names for the five mental states (*pañca-citta*).

The commentary (*śāstra*) provides the general meaning, which can be understood from the context; however, regarding the statement, "By the power of the preceding syllables, through successive perfuming (*vāsanā*), the subsequent syllable arises," when one utters these various syllables, the three characters *saṃskāra* and so forth are all yet to come in the future.
When the character "xing" (行) is pronounced, the two characters for "impermanence" (無常) are likewise yet to come in the future.

Although all those individual characters have already passed away and currently lack an intrinsic essence, by the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and the power of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), they nonetheless manifest upon the mind at this very moment when the character "xing" is being spoken.
The subsequent discussion on "concomitance" (saṃprayoga) may be understood by analogy with this.

Now, regarding this collection [of phonemes], according to the *Fayuan* (Dharma Garden), based on the five characters "mò zuò wǔ zì" (do not commit the five [evils]), there are one hundred and five aspects for each phrase. That is to say, when pronouncing the character "zhū" (諸), it possesses two aspects: namely, one character and one name.

Next, when pronouncing the syllable *aḥ*, there are seven aspects: namely, two syllables and two names, together with one single-syllable body as the fifth; by taking these two preceding aspects, there are thus seven aspects in total.

Next, regarding the syllables: when pronouncing the word, there are sixteen phases; three syllables constitute three names, along with two instances of single-syllable bodies and one instance of a double-syllable body—these comprise nine phases.
Including the aforementioned seven, there are thus sixteen.

Next, when pronouncing the syllable *ma*, there are thirty aspects; that is, four characters and four names, consisting of three instances of the single-syllable body, two instances of the double-syllable body, and one instance of the triple-syllable body, totaling fourteen aspects.
Adding these sixteen to the previous, there are thus thirty.

Later, when pronouncing the syllable *va*, there are fifty characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); that is to say, five characters with five names, four instances of single-syllable bodies, three instances of double-syllable bodies, two instances of triple-syllable bodies, and one instance of a quadruple-syllable body. Combining these twenty characteristics with the aforementioned thirty, there are thus fifty characteristics.
The total number of characteristics across the five positions is one hundred and five.
These one hundred and five characteristics concern only two matters: syllables and names.
As for the fourteen characteristics mentioned above, these include sounds, phrases, and meanings as well.
Furthermore, if one considers only the individual characters, it is said that there are four characters and four names.
Now, by taking them as connected units, they form one hundred and five aspects (*lakṣaṇa*).

If one considers only the four characters, there are merely fifty-five aspects; however, the twelve minds are not treated as connected units here. Nevertheless, among these five minds, the first and last pertain to all six consciousnesses, while the middle three pertain exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, the first three are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), while the latter two may be either wholesome or unwholesome.

Moreover, following the five sense-consciousnesses of sudden encounter (*ābhoga*), there must necessarily arise a mind of seeking (*paryeṣaka*); thereafter, it may be distracted or undistracted. If distracted, one again gives rise to the consciousness of sudden encounter; if undistracted, one gives rise to the third stage, the consciousness of determination (*niścaya*), and so on up to the consciousness of natural outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Furthermore, there are two types of sudden, impulsive mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*):
first, the sudden mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, which takes present objects as its domain;
second, the independent sudden mental consciousness, which takes only past objects as its domain.
Herein, for now, only simultaneity is discussed; the other meanings are explained extensively in a separate chapter.

However, all of these refer to the manifestation of the five mental states as a collection when one is in a state of non-mastery; in a state of mastery, they are fully manifested within a single moment.
Reflect upon this according to the principle.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The three are merely images without an original,” the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* points to the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* as making such a claim, but this is not accepted as the correct view.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The schools of Nāgārjuna and others mostly establish this doctrine,” the term “and others” includes the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras of the Sudden Teaching.
As for the phrase “mostly establish,” it does not mean that they do so exclusively, because these schools also maintain the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
This merely clarifies one aspect of emptiness.
The commentary states that "the previous four explanations" must be integrated into a single flavor (*ekarasa*) before they accord with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).
If considered in terms of encompassing sentient beings, however, there are differences in their depth and shallowness.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second [section] on the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener,” there are three parts in the text:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion regarding their mutual integration.

Now, concerning the initial heading, the reason for establishing two sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) is that when the true mind integrates these two, phenomena and principle appear to be without obstruction; therefore, they are further divided.

In the initial section on the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*), the first two phrases indicate that because sentient beings and Buddhas are identical within the single true mind, they mutually encompass one another.
The third phrase indicates that because they do not obstruct each other, both can coexist.
The fourth [point] is that because they are mutually identical, they are thus mutually subsumed;
this is easily understood.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, concerning the Separate Teaching (biejiao)”: the four propositions of the Separate Teaching pertain exclusively to the non-obstruction between phenomena (shishi wuai).
This is because the two aspects of sentient beings and Buddhas are clearly distinct yet mutually inclusive.

Furthermore, the former may be considered the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*), while the latter is the gate of mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*); since the gate of mutual identity contains the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*lǐshì wú'ài*), it is merely designated as the "teaching of commonality" (*tóngjiào*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, all sentient beings are entirely within the Buddha,” and so forth: the first sentence has two parts—the initial formal establishment of the position, followed by the citation of scriptural evidence.
This is the first part.

This is because the fruit of Buddhahood accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); thus, it encompasses all phenomena without exception, for there is not a single phenomenon that transcends the nature of reality.
Since the entire nature constitutes the Buddha, there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed within it.
The commentary states: "Therefore it appears" and below is the subsequent citation of scriptural evidence.
First, the citation from the sutra itself has already been explained as before; it will be further clarified in the main text below.
Below the section beginning with "Furthermore, the Buddha-nature," the treatise is cited to establish the proof.
Now, within this chapter, the Tathāgatagarbha is explained according to three meanings; this present [section] is one of them.
Regarding the three meanings, the treatise states: "Furthermore, it should be known that there are three meanings of the *tathāgatagarbha*. What are these three?
First, the *garbha* as that which is contained;
second, the *garbha* as that which is concealed; and third, the *garbha* as that which contains."
The commentary cited herein refers precisely to the first category of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because it is encompassed by the Tathāgata, it is called the "Tathāgata-garbha.

Thus, that treatise states: "Regarding the first category, termed 'garbha,' the Buddha taught that, with respect to the abiding suchness (*tathatā*) of their own nature, all sentient beings are the Tathāgata-garbha."
Regarding the term "suchness" (tathatā), there are two meanings:
first, the wisdom of suchness; second, the object of suchness.
Because both are non-erroneous, they are called "suchness."
As for the term "coming," it refers to the process from the self-nature arriving at the attainment of the fruit; this is called the *tathāgata-gotra*.

Although it is a single cause designated as "that which should be attained" and the fruit designated as "that which has been reached," their essence is not dual; they differ only by virtue of being clear or turbid.
While in the causal stage, one violates the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; thus, ignorance arises as an affliction.
Because it is intermingled with and confused by these, it is called "defiled turbidity.
Although not yet manifest, it is certain to appear in the future, and is therefore termed "that which is to be attained."
When one reaches the stage of fruition, it merges with the two kinds of emptiness; being free from further afflictions and entanglements, and untainted by defilements, it is called "pure.
Because the fruition has already been manifested, it is termed "attainment."

For example, the nature of water is neither inherently clear nor turbid; it is only due to the presence or absence of impurities that it receives the names "clear" or "turbid. The same applies to the two meanings of "attainment" (*prāpti*)—namely, "attainment as acquisition" (*pratilambha-prāpti*) and "attainment as possession" (*samanvāgama-prāpti*).
And so forth.
Regarding the term "treasury" (*garbha*), it is identical in all respects to the *Vyākhyā* (the Commentary).
The subsequent section of the treatise states: "Furthermore, there are three kinds of treasuries:
first, the treasury of the incomparable manifestation of the true object, because apart from the realm of suchness (*tathatā*), there is no other distinct realm that transcends this realm."
Second, it reveals the incomparability of correct practice, because apart from this wisdom, there is no other superior wisdom that surpasses it.
Third, it manifests the incomparability of the correct fruit, because there is no single fruit that surpasses this fruit.
Therefore, it is called "without peer.
Because this fruit is able to encompass and conceal all sentient beings, sentient beings are said to be the *tathāgatagarbha*.

In the present commentary, I have cited only the beginning and the end of this passage to capture the sense that the Buddha contains sentient beings; below, I shall further briefly cite the next two *garbhas*.
Second, it is called a "store" (*garbha*) because of concealment: prior to the Path, sentient beings do not perceive it because it is still shrouded by afflictions.
Third, it is called a "store" because of its capacity for inclusion: within the stage of fruition, all merits are already fully contained within its nature at the time of its attainment.
Now, because it is subsumed under the "attainment of the fruit" (*phala-saṃgraha*), it likewise does not lead to the inclusion of the latter two *piṭakas*.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Furthermore, below 'appearance'": thirdly, it further cites the present sutra by way of analogy to demonstrate the inclusion of the listeners.
All phenomena are encompassed; why then speak only of sentient beings who listen to the Dharma?
Within this, there are two further layers of illustration:
first, clarifying that a single body instantaneously encompasses all sentient beings.
Second, the wisdom of clarity and vastness is identical to space; since all sentient beings and their environments fundamentally abide within this wisdom, by what means could they be "gathered"?

Nevertheless, the first passage, namely the verse from the *Samantabhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* (The Chapter on Manifestation), states: "Just as throughout the kalpas and lands of the three periods of time, all mental thoughts, faculties, and desires [of sentient beings]—such bodies as these are all manifested; therefore, the Perfectly Awakened One is called 'Immeasurable'."
The present commentary on the first two phrases merely abbreviates the characters "ru" (如) and "ji" (及).
The statement "even all [appear] instantaneously as a single body" conveys the meaning of the prose section.
The Sūtra says: "When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he entered the Samādhi of the Wisdom of Excellent Awakening through a single skillful means.
Having entered this samādhi, within his single, vast body of perfect enlightenment, he manifested bodies equal in number to all sentient beings and dwelt within them."
"Just as it is with the body of one who has attained perfect enlightenment, so it is with all the vast bodies of those who have attained perfect enlightenment.
Thus, while that sūtra’s prose section describes the inclusion of bodies by means of bodies, its verse section clarifies their comprehensive inclusion.
Now, I shall take but a single instance from the prose and contrast it with the extensive summary found in the verse to demonstrate its inconceivability.
Thus, when it says "even a single body appears instantaneously," this single character "even" (shàng) serves as a rhetorical comparison.

First, regarding those who hear the Dharma: to further illustrate the vastness of the Buddha’s wisdom by comparison with inferior states, we turn to the beginning of the verses of praise to the Buddha by Samantabhadra in the eightieth sutra.

The sutra says: "The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast as space, pervading the minds of all sentient beings; it fully understands all the delusions of the world, yet gives rise to no various false discriminations."
Regarding the citation in the Commentary: its intent encompasses the first half [of the verse], yet it specifically takes "Great Wisdom" (*mahāprajñā*) to serve as a metaphor for the "One Body.

Therefore, it cites only the first line. As for the Commentary’s statement, "The two Buddhas abide within sentient beings," and so forth: sentient beings are the cause; the cause is termed the *dharmadhātu*. Since the *dharmadhātu* encompasses all phenomena without exception, sentient beings are likewise encompassed without exception.
Next, from "Therefore, he appears" onwards, there is the citation of scriptural evidence.
Following that, from "This clarifies the Buddha’s realization" onwards, there is the explanation.
This means: why does the Tathāgata not depart from the mind of arising?
The commentary states:
Because the *tathatā* within the minds of sentient beings is that which the Buddha has realized.
If this is so, it is merely the principle of equality; why should it be considered "mysterious"?
Therefore, it is further stated:
"Because fundamental enlightenment is without distinction.
This means that the fundamental enlightenment of the Buddha and the fundamental enlightenment of sentient beings do not have two separate essences, for they are one and the same enlightenment.
Because original enlightenment (benjue) is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and because the Dharma-body is identical [in all beings].

Regarding the phrase "by means of the initial [awakening]," if this is so, since the essence of the Dharma-body is the same, what connection does the Buddha have with sentient beings who have not yet realized it, while he himself has realized the Dharma-body?
Therefore, it is said next:
"Because the beginning is identical to the fundamental source, they are collectively present within the minds of sentient beings.
This means that since the *Awakening of Faith* states that initial awakening is identical to fundamental awakening, there is no longer any distinction between the beginning and the fundamental.

Since the original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical, when a Buddha’s present awakening (*ādi-awakening*) becomes identical with that original state, it is entirely identical to the original enlightenment of sentient beings; therefore, it is fully present within the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is a question:
"Although they are identical in terms of their essence (*tattva*), their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*) are naturally distinct; how can they be entirely the same?
Therefore, it is said next:
Function arises from essence, yet function is not different from essence.
Since essence is the essence of sentient beings, how could function be separate from sentient beings?
Therefore, the arising of function based on essence is precisely the Great Function of True Suchness within the minds of sentient beings; there is no other Buddha apart from this.
If that is so, since this meaning already exists within the *Awakening of Faith*, why is only the *Avataṃsaka* designated as the "Distinct Teaching" (biejiao)?
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:

although the *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual and that the three great aspects are identical, it speaks of each person's own mind cultivating and realizing [enlightenment] individually; it does not state that the sentient being and the Buddha are mutually and completely inclusive of one another.
This is to employ the text of the *Awakening of Faith* to establish the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; it is the ultimate in subtlety.
The commentary (*shu*) is worth contemplating.

Regarding the passage in the commentary following "Third, because the preceding Buddhas are mutually inclusive," it merely combines the previous two [points] to form this phrase, which is both real and not empty.
This means that when the original Buddha gathers sentient beings, he gathers them entirely at once, without before or after; therefore, it is real and not false.
That the gathering of beings is not false means the teaching resides in the minds of the beings;
that the gathering by the Buddha is not false means the teaching resides in the mind of the Buddha alone.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the Buddha within the minds of sentient beings," and so forth, which clarifies the aspect of their simultaneous existence.
This means that although they mutually encompass one another, it does not hinder the fact that speaking and listening remain perfectly distinct.
While this appears obscure in the literal text, its meaning is extremely clear.
Please allow me to illustrate this with analogies; briefly, two examples may be cited.

First, it is like a single bright mirror: when a teacher and disciple face it together to speak and listen, if the teacher takes hold of it, it is the teacher’s mirror; if the disciple takes hold of it, it is the disciple’s mirror.

The mirror is a metaphor for the one mind; the teacher and disciple are metaphors for the Buddha and sentient beings. This is called the master within the disciple’s mirror preaching the Dharma to the disciple within the master’s mirror, while the disciple within the master’s mirror listens to the master within the disciple’s mirror preaching the Dharma.
May all those who possess wisdom examine this analogy in detail.
Although this analogy has been set forth, I fear it may still not be fully understood.
It is further like water and milk mixed together in one place, wherein each acts as both the agent that blends and the object that is blended.
Furthermore, let us explain this according to the principle of harmony: that which brings about harmony is called "speaking," and that which is brought into harmony is called "listening.
Let us take water as a metaphor for the Buddha and milk as a metaphor for sentient beings.
One should say that there is water within the milk and milk within the water; although the milk and the water share a single flavor, the agent and the object remain distinct.
Although the subject and object appear distinct, they exist within one another, mutually pervasive and mutually inclusive; reflect upon this principle accordingly.
Furthermore, let us clarify the commentary on the text:

"The Buddha within the minds of sentient beings" means that while sentient beings are universally pervasive according to their true nature (*dharmatā*), the Buddha’s unimpaired characteristics reside within the minds of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement, "To preach the Dharma for sentient beings within the Buddha's mind," this clarifies that while the Buddha-mind universally pervades in accordance with its true nature (*dharmatā*), sentient beings do not lose their distinct characteristics even as they abide within the Buddha's mind.
The Buddha who can preach is simply the Buddha within the minds of sentient beings;
the sentient beings who listen to the Dharma are simply the sentient beings within the mind of the Buddha.
The lower [position] is the opposite of the upper; there is no further distinct principle, for it is merely a difference between speaking and listening.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “Fourth, because birth is entirely present,” etc., this sentence brings both [positions] to cessation, making the meaning even easier to understand.
Within this, the preceding section provides the formal explanation;
the passage beginning with "Therefore, O Worthy One" below cites scriptural evidence, namely the fifteenth sutra.
This, however, only corroborates the meaning of the fourth pair of negations: that which is produced by causes and conditions has no production, for production is extinguished.
"The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is not a body"—this is the Buddha’s dissolution.
The second half [of the verse] says: "The nature of phenomena is eternally abiding like space; thus is the light of its explained meaning."
This is because it is precisely the first two lines that are relevant here; therefore, this [passage] has not been cited.

Furthermore, the "Verses of Praise" chapter (*Gāthā-stava-parivarta*) also serves as evidence for the "neither-nor" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*) perspective found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, as was already explained in the preceding section.
The Commentary states: “Therefore, these four,” and so forth, summarizes and integrates [the preceding discussion]. Whenever one mentions even a single phrase, all four must be present.
Thus, whether it be a single passage or a single sentence—be it from a Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna text—it must necessarily possess these four, encompassing the principle in its entirety.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The seventh [section] on entering the true substance through conditions,” the text is divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words “There is also.”
The sub-commentary states: "In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is called 'the twelvefold teaching flowing from True Suchness'";
this is a citation of evidence from the seventh chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrabhāṣya* and the tenth chapter of the Liang dynasty translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Next, he cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, Chapter Ten. That treatise explains the third stage among the ten types of true suchness (*tathatā*).

As its commentary explains: "Because in this stage one attains the three kinds of wisdom that illuminate the Mahāyāna teachings, and contemplates the fundamental true suchness of these doctrinal teachings, it is called the 'True Suchness of Superior Outflow' (*viśeṣa-niṣyanda-tathatā*)."
"Alternatively, it is because the teaching of this *tathatā* is superior.
The commentary states: "Although that school does not establish... and so forth, which explains a potential objection.
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
In that school, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is immutably quiescent; how, then, could there be any sense of "flowing"?
Therefore, the commentary explains: "It speaks of the Buddha’s realization of the essence," and so forth.
Within this context, there are four dharmas—both regressive and progressive—which mutually depend upon one another.
If one traces back in reverse, from what is this teaching established?
Answer:
It is established from the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna).
Upon what does this subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) depend for its arising?
It arises from fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
Therefore, the treatise states: "The conventional is understood by virtue of realizing the ultimate; therefore, it is called 'subsequently attained.'"
From what does this fundamental wisdom arise?
Because it accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*), True Suchness is named the most fundamental.
To explain it in its positive sense:
The commentary on the tenth fascicle of the *Liang* [translation] states: "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the most supreme among all phenomena.

Because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises by taking True Suchness as its object, and this non-conceptual wisdom is that which flows from True Suchness, this wisdom is the most supreme among all forms of wisdom."

From this wisdom flows forth the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and from that subsequently attained wisdom arises great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This great compassion is the most supreme among all meditative concentrations.
Because of this great compassion, the Tathāgata, desiring to establish the True Dharma to rescue and deliver sentient beings, has preached the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
This Dharma flows from great compassion; this Dharma is the most supreme among all dharmas.

For the sake of attaining this Dharma, a bodhisattva is able to practice all that is difficult to practice and endure all that is difficult to endure; by contemplating this Dharma, they enter the third stage.
This can be understood from the text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second assembly clarifies the nature through its characteristics”: previously it was taught that suchness (*tathatā*) is the basis of the teaching, yet the teaching is not identical to suchness.
Now it is taught that the teaching is itself suchness; thus, the characteristics of the twelvefold division of the teaching are subsumed within the nature that is suchness.
In the commentary, the section beginning with “The Tathāgata’s speech” provides a further explanation that the teaching is itself suchness (*tathatā*).
Above, it was clarified that the teaching arises from conditions and lacks intrinsic nature; therefore, the teaching is itself suchness.
Now it is clarified that the Teacher is called "Suchness" (tathatā); therefore, all his teachings are Suchness.
The *Vajrasamādhi* corroborates this meaning, stating that both the signified meaning and the spoken words are in accord with Suchness.
The following citation from the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) serves to corroborate the preceding meaning.
The phrase "up to and including" (*nàizhì*) is used because the text is abbreviated;
were it complete, the sūtra would read: "King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:"
"How is it that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas practice the characteristics of all dharmas without departing from words? "Great King!

The Wheel of Dharma consists of the Suchness of the *Dharmapada*, the Suchness of the *Geya*, the Suchness of the *Vyākaraṇa*, the Suchness of the *Gāthā*, the Suchness of the *Udāna*, the Suchness of the *Nidāna*, the Suchness of the *Avadāna*, the Suchness of the *Itivṛttaka*, the Suchness of the *Jātaka*, the Suchness of the *Vaipulya*, the Suchness of the *Adbhutadharma*, and the Suchness of the *Upadeśa*."
These are called phrases of flavor, the fruit of sound, and recorded phrases of syllables; all are suchness.
If one grasps at syllables, one does not practice emptiness.
"O Great King!
Just as these very syllables cultivate the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
The above is the scriptural text.
Within it, it says: "The *Śīla-sūtra* is, in fact, the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
Since the precepts were established based on specific events, it constitutes one doctrinal meaning within the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, what is called the 'Tathatā of the Dharma-realm' refers to the *Jātaka-sūtra*."
Since "realm" (dhātu) has the meaning of "cause," the rest may be understood accordingly.
The names and meanings of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures] are explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Stores" (Daśaka-vastu).
The Commentary states: "This sutra clarifies that the teaching is itself Suchness," and below this, it further distinguishes between the universal and the specific.
This means that if one simply says the twelvefold teaching is Suchness, then this Suchness is restricted to being within those twelve divisions.
If it is said that "suchness is itself the Buddha's teaching," then since all phenomena are suchness, all things would be the Buddha's teaching; this principle is thus universally applicable.
Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "If one takes all phenomena to manifest the essence of the meaning," which clarifies that everything is the teaching.
Since all things are thusness, and thusness is the Buddha’s teaching.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “The eighth [section], the essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena,” it may be seen directly in the text.
Regarding the commentary on the section "Ninth, the Non-obstruction of Phenomenon by Phenomenon," the text is divided into three parts:
first, the dual introduction; second, the main exposition of the text; and third, the illustrative explanation of the meaning.
First, the text and its meaning are presented together; here, we distinguish the meaning to extract the text.
Next, from "The text is... onwards, the perfection of the text is explicitly revealed.
"Text" refers to names (nāma), phrases (pada), and phonemes (vyañjana).
Regarding the term "perfect sound" (*yuan-yin*), there are two meanings.

First, as an analogy, the aforementioned names and so forth are devoid of sound and lack substantiality; now, the substance of the perfect sound and its written characters likewise depend upon this principle.
Second, since it is called the "perfect sound" (paripūrṇa-svara), the phrases and sentences must all be complete to truly merit the name "perfect.
If it were merely a single uniform tone, the previous interpretation would not be correct.
Below, various sūtras are cited to establish that this teaching-body possesses the ten gates of mystery (daśa-guhya-dvāra).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The Buddha, with a single wondrous voice,” and so forth: the scriptural text contains three sections in brief;
the first concerns how a single voice is heard everywhere, merely manifesting its pervasiveness.

Next, regarding the statement that "all sounds are fully possessed," this means that within each preceding single sound, many sounds are instantaneously present—namely, the diverse sounds of the ten thousand categories, such as those of the goddess Śubhavyūha.

Regarding the third point, that "the rain of Dharma pervades all": this means that according to each individual sound, there are expounded all the inexhaustible Dharma-gates of the Great and Small Vehicles, the provisional and the real; furthermore, each and every Dharma fills the entire Dharmadhātu.
The three sections encompass four meanings:
"three" signifies the unfolding of the one to pervade all, while "two" signifies the gathering of all into the one.
This unfolding and rolling up are unimpeded and entirely simultaneous; thus, what sound or what dharma is not fully contained within them?

The passage immediately following that sutra states: "The ocean of all speech, all sounds according to type, throughout all lands, constantly turning the unsurpassed wheel," and so forth; thus, the repetitions are even more numerous.
Now, citing just one verse is sufficient to manifest their simultaneous and complete perfection.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "For example, like written characters," this is a partial quotation intended to convey the essential meaning from the *Tathāgata-dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*; hence, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used.
To cite it in full, the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata’s Wheel of Dharma enters entirely into all speech and writing, yet abides nowhere.
It is like written characters, which universally enter into all things, all speech, all calculations, and all mundane and supramundane realms, yet abide nowhere."
The voice of the Tathāgata is likewise: it universally enters into all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, all karmas, and all retributions, yet it abides nowhere.
The various languages of all sentient beings are entirely not apart from the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma.
Why is this? Because the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of speech and sound is itself the discourse on the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*).
"O Son of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand the Tathāgata’s turning of the Wheel of Dharma in this way.

This very scriptural passage already contains a concise illustration through both the dharma and its metaphor; therefore, I have here briefly cited it according to the essential meaning in my commentary.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This ‘mutual entry’ (*xiāngrù*) is also ‘mutual containment’ (*xiāngróng*,” it refers to the meaning of mutual entry based on the cited text.
This very mutual entry constitutes the gate of “the different ways in which one and many mutually contain one another” (*yīduō xiāngróng bùtóng mén*).

That which can enter is called "entry," and that which is entered is called "receptacle. That which can contain is itself that which is entered, and that which is contained is itself that which can enter; though their names differ according to their respective meanings, the underlying sense of "receptacle" and "entry" is one and the same.

The Commentary states: "In the *bodhimaṇḍa*, all hear [this] without it going outside the assembly" refers to the analogies of Brahmā and the multitude within the "Manifestation" (*prādurbhāva*) section on sound.
To cite it in full, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"... [and so forth].

It is, for example, like the Great Brahmā King dwelling in his Brahma palace who utters a Brahma voice; all the Brahma hosts hear it without exception, yet that sound does not go beyond their assembly.
All the hosts of Brahmā deities each formed this thought:
"The Great Brahmā King is speaking to me alone.
It is the same with the Tathāgata’s wondrous voice: the entire assembly at the site of enlightenment hears it, yet its sound does not issue beyond the gathering.
Why is this? Because those whose faculties are not yet mature should not hear it.
Those who hear the sound all think to themselves:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks with me alone.
O Son of the Buddha!
The voice of the Tathāgata neither issues forth nor abides, yet it is able to accomplish all activities; this is the fifth characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice.
The commentary states:
Regarding those who hear the assembly, those whose faculties are matured are considered "within the assembly," while those whose faculties are not yet matured are considered "outside the assembly.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
That which should be heard is heard; this is manifestation.
That which should not be heard is not heard; this is concealment.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "each according to their understanding," there are further distinctions within the act of hearing itself.
If one hears of the Mahāyāna, the Mahāyāna is revealed;
if one does not hear of the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), the two vehicles are concealed.
It should be understood that if one hears of the Hīnayāna, the Great [Vehicle] is concealed and the Small [Vehicle] is revealed, and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it says 'the words and sounds of the Tathāgata,' etc.; this refers to the sixth characteristic immediately following that [in the sutra].
The Sutra says: 'O Son of the Buddha!

For example, all waters are of one and the same taste; yet because they follow the differences of their vessels, the water appears to have distinctions. The water has no thoughts and no discrimination.'"

The speech and sounds of the Tathāgata are likewise thus: they are of but a single flavor, namely the flavor of liberation; yet, because the mental capacities of sentient beings differ, they appear in immeasurable varieties, while remaining free from thought and devoid of discrimination.
However, this single passage establishes two meanings:
if one takes it as each vessel receiving [the water] individually such that they do not know one another, this constitutes "concealment and manifestation";
if one takes it as a single flavor conforming to the vessels, this constitutes "purity and mixture."
The goddess Suvaktrā also belongs to that same category.
The sūtra states: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!
It is as if the Heavenly King Vaśavartin had a celestial consort named Suvaktrā."

From within his mouth issued a single sound, which was in perfect harmony with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music; within each of these musical instruments, there were again hundreds of thousands of distinct variations of sound.
"O Son of the Buddha!
Just as that woman of virtuous speech produced such immeasurable sounds from a single voice, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so:

from within a single sound, he produces immeasurable voices; according to the differences in the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, these voices reach them all and cause them all to attain understanding."
"Thus, the fourth characteristic is suddenly and fully present within one [moment], which is precisely what is meant by 'subtle.
Regarding the commentary's statement, 'From the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* to 'unspeakable' (*anabhilāpya*) and so forth,' the 'and so forth' includes the remainder of the sūtra text."

The Sūtra says: "Each and every Buddha-dharma is unspeakable; their various purities are unspeakable; the production of wondrous sounds is unspeakable; and the turning of the true wheel of Dharma is unspeakable."
Within each and every wheel of Dharma, there are unspeakable numbers of sūtras expounded; within each and every sūtra, there are unspeakable numbers of dharma-gates distinguished.
Within each and every one of those dharma-gates, it is further taught that all dharmas are unspeakable; within each and every one of those dharmas, the taming of sentient beings is unspeakable.
The preceding scriptural passage already contains multiple layers, yet it speaks of only a single dharma.
Since every dharma is likewise so, they interpenetrate one another in successive layers, thereby becoming inexhaustible.
Furthermore, it says therein: "The pure true reality is ineffable; the teaching of the sūtras is ineffable.
Within each and every sūtra, the expounding of the dharma-gates is ineffable."
Within each and every one of those dharma-gates, it is further taught that all dharmas are ineffable;
within each and every one of those dharmas, there is that which is definitively ineffable.
Within each and every such certainty, there are unspeakably many sentient beings to be tamed;
unspeakably many similar dharmas and unspeakably many similar minds;
unspeakably many dissimilar dharmas and unspeakably many dissimilar minds.
"Inexpressible are the various types of faculties; inexpressible are the various types of speech.
Moment by moment, throughout all spheres of activity, the taming of sentient beings is likewise inexpressible"—such passages are also of this same category.
The Commentary states: "To expound instantaneously in a single thought" means that within a single thought-moment, one instantaneously expounds the teachings of immeasurable kalpas;

how could the ten periods of time not be mutually integrated? As the fifth scripture says: "The tree-spirits, as numerous as the atoms of all lands, all together rely upon this site of enlightenment; each, before the Bodhi tree of a Tathāgata, proclaims the gates of liberation from moment to moment," and so forth.
The sub-commentary states: "This, for now, concerns... and below, it explains the meaning by way of examples from the text.
The first sentence concludes what preceded; all subsequent parts explain what follows.
The sub-commentary states: "With these ten gates... and below, the third section provides a general summary, which is clear.
The section on the essence of the teaching is concluded.
Regarding the sixth section, "The General and Particular Aspects of the Fundamental Tenets," the commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the title and the presentation of the headings; second, the detailed explanation according to those headings, beginning with the phrase "Within the former... and so forth.

Regarding the preceding section, "zhong" (中) means "to honor," hence it is called "that which is esteemed" (*shàng*); it is also termed "venerable" (*zūn*), "principal" (*zhǔ*), or "abundant" (*duō*).
Below the phrase "the general discussion in the preceding section," the second part provides a detailed explanation according to the chapters.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the general school; second, the explanation of the specific school.
Within the former, there are three sections:
First, a general statement of the main intent; second, an account of past views and their refutations; third, the presentation of the present correct interpretation.
Regarding the first:
the phrase "the divergent tenets of the various schools" refers to the twenty schools.
Regarding the phrase "the eighteen are fundamentally two," this refers to the names of the eighteen schools, which shall be enumerated below.
As for "fundamentally two," these are the Sthavira (Theravāda) school and the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Therefore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The eighteen [sects] and the two original ones all emerge from the Mahāyāna.
There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; I say they will arise in the future."
Regarding the phrase "following according to the principles," this refers to the combination of the twenty schools together with the various Mahāyāna traditions to form ten systems.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "However, during the Sui dynasty" constitutes the second part, which recounts past accounts to clarify discrepancies.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, an account of the past; second, a discussion of conformity and contrariety.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
First, the formal establishment; second, the alternative names.
Within the former [section], each is named according to what it establishes.
Within these four, there are two phrases for each:
The preceding phrase establishes the thesis, while the subsequent phrase provides the instruction. The sub-commentary states:

"Furthermore, regarding these four schools," the following distinguishes their different names; they do not go beyond the categories of Nature (svabhāva) and Characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Among them, the first three follow what is being refuted, while the last one proceeds from what is revealed.

In the commentary, from "The first two [categories] are the Small Vehicle" onwards, there is a differentiation of what is concordant and what is discordant. Within this section, there are two parts: first, a concordant explanation, which clarifies what accords with principle; second, a discordant explanation, which clarifies what contradicts principle. Regarding the first part, there are further two sections: first, a general explanation of the meaning; second, a specific explanation of the text. As for the general explanation of the meaning, it is as follows: the first two categories are the Small Vehicle, while the latter two are the Great Vehicle. This is because the former two do not transcend the realm of birth and death, whereas the latter two transcend that realm. Furthermore, the former two are merely expedient means, while the latter two constitute the true reality. This is because the former two are established based on the latter two. Moreover, the former two are provisional teachings, while the latter two are definitive teachings. This is because the former two are taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, whereas the latter two reveal the ultimate truth. Furthermore, the former two are inferior, while the latter two are superior. This is because the former two are characterized by limited merit and wisdom, whereas the latter two are characterized by immeasurable merit and wisdom. Furthermore, the former two are incomplete, while the latter two are complete. This is because the former two lack the perfection of the Buddha-qualities, whereas the latter two possess them fully. Furthermore, the former two are subject to regression, while the latter two are irreversible. This is because the former two may fall back due to various conditions, whereas the latter two are firmly established and cannot be overturned. Furthermore, the former two are mundane, while the latter two are supramundane. This is because the former two remain within the cycle of birth and death, whereas the latter two transcend it entirely. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by duality, while the latter two are non-dual. This is because the former two involve the distinction between self and other, whereas the latter two realize the equality of all phenomena. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by grasping, while the latter two are free from grasping. This is because the former two cling to the notions of existence and non-existence, whereas the latter two have abandoned all attachments. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by obstruction, while the latter two are unobstructed. This is because the former two are hindered by afflictions and ignorance, whereas the latter two are free from all hindrances. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by suffering, while the latter two are blissful. This is because the former two are subject to the three types of suffering, whereas the latter two abide in the supreme bliss of nirvana. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by impermanence, while the latter two are permanent. This is because the former two are subject to arising and ceasing, whereas the latter two are eternally abiding and unchanging. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by emptiness, while the latter two are non-empty. This is because the former two are empty of self and what belongs to self, whereas the latter two are not empty of the Buddha-nature. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by non-self, while the latter two are the true self. This is because the former two deny the existence of a self, whereas the latter two reveal the ultimate self of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by impurity, while the latter two are pure. This is because the former two are defiled by the outflows of passion, whereas the latter two are stainless and immaculate. This is because the former two arise from causes and conditions, whereas the latter two are beyond cause and condition. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the finite, while the latter two are infinite. This is because the former two are limited by time and space, whereas the latter two pervade all dharmadhātus. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the conventional, while the latter two are the ultimate. This is because the former two are established through worldly consensus, whereas the latter two accord with the true nature of reality. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the relative, while the latter two are absolute. This is because the former two depend upon one another, whereas the latter two are independent and self-sufficient. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the partial, while the latter two are universal. This is because the former two apply only to specific cases, whereas the latter two encompass all phenomena without exception. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the limited, while the latter two are vast. This is because the former two are restricted to a narrow scope, whereas the latter two are expansive and boundless. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the shallow, while the latter two are profound. This is because the former two are easily understood, whereas the latter two are difficult to fathom. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the superficial, while the latter two are deep. This is because the former two are easily perceived, whereas the latter two are hidden from ordinary view. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the derivative, while the latter two are fundamental. This is because the former two are secondary manifestations, whereas the latter two are the primary source. This is because the former two rely on external conditions, whereas the latter two are self-so and spontaneously present. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the constructed, while the latter two are unconstructed. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the conceptual, while the latter two are non-conceptual. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the dualistic, while the latter two are non-dual. This is because the former two maintain the distinction between subject and object, whereas the latter two realize the non-duality of all things. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the differentiated, while the latter two are undifferentiated. This is because the former two manifest in diverse forms, whereas the latter two are uniform and identical. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the fragmented, while the latter two are integrated. This is because the former two are disjointed and inconsistent, whereas the latter two are harmonious and coherent. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the unstable, while the latter two are stable. This is because the former two are subject to fluctuation, whereas the latter two are firm and immovable. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the unreliable, while the latter two are reliable. This is because the former two are deceptive and false, whereas the latter two are authentic and true. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the illusory, while the latter two are real. This is because the former two are like dreams and phantoms, whereas the latter two are the actual reality. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the deceptive, while the latter two are honest. This is because the former two mislead sentient beings, whereas the latter two lead them toward enlightenment. This is because the former two increase suffering, whereas the latter two bring about peace and happiness. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the destructive, while the latter two are constructive. This is because the former two destroy wholesome roots, whereas the latter two cultivate them. This is because the former two are subject to decay, whereas the latter two are eternal and indestructible. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the perishable, while the latter two are imperishable. This is because the former two are subject to extinction, whereas the latter two are never extinguished. Furthermore, the former two are characterized by the changing, while the latter two are unchanging. This is because the former two undergo transformation, whereas the latter two remain as they are. The subsequent section provides a summary to clarify the contradictions in the text. First:

regarding the statement that "each is shallow at the beginning and deep at the end," this is because the initial stage reveals the conditions for the true cause (zheng yinyuan), establishing the existence of the nature of cause and effect; therefore, it is considered shallow.
Second, it subverts the notion of fixed nature; because all things exist solely through conditions, it is profound.
Since the myriad dharmas arise from conditions, they lack any fixed reality.
It is like the hardness of iron, which melts when it encounters fire.

Just as the moisture of water becomes solid when it encounters cold, one clearly understands that because things arise from conditions, they have no fixed nature and are merely provisional designations; therefore, this constitutes the profound aspect of the Hīnayāna.
