Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “the analogy of stealing an ox while in a state of nirvana,” this refers to the third chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which answers the questions of Kāśyapa.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
What is the difference between the supramundane Dharma and mundane dharmas?'"
As the Buddha has said:
"The Buddha is the eternal dharma, the unchanging dharma.

The world also says that Brahmā is eternal, that Īśvara is eternal and without change, that the self (ātman) is eternal, that primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal, and that atoms (paramāṇu) are also eternal.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is an eternal dharma,
why does the Tathāgata not manifest eternally?
If he does not manifest eternally, what distinction is there [between him and other things]?
"Why is this? Because from Brahmā down to a mote of dust, even the nature of the world does not appear.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"It is, for example, like a householder who has many cows of various colors, all belonging to a single herd. He entrusts them to a cowherd, instructing him to let them graze where there is water and grass, seeking only the *ghṛta* (clarified butter) and not the milk or curds; yet that cowherd, having milked them, consumes it himself."
When the elder passed away, all his cattle were plundered by a band of robbers.
Having seized the cattle, the robbers had no women with them; they therefore milked the cows themselves and ate the milk.
At that time, the bandits said to one another:
"That great elder raises this cow not for the sake of milk or curd, but for the sake of the *ghṛta-maṇḍa* (the finest cream).
By what means should we now obtain it?"
"Now, ghee is known as the foremost and most excellent flavor in the world.
We lack the proper vessels; even if we were to obtain milk, we would have no place to set it down.
Thus they spoke to one another.
"There is only a leather bag that can hold it.
Although there is a place to contain it, if one does not know how to churn it, even whey will be difficult to obtain, let alone fresh butter.
At that time, the bandits added water to the clarified butter (ghṛta) for its sake; because of the excess of water, the milk, curd, and clarified butter were all lost.
It is the same with ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*): although they possess wholesome dharmas, these are all merely remnants of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.

Why is this? Because after the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, those who secretly steal the Tathāgata’s remaining wholesome dharmas—such as morality, concentration, and wisdom—are like those bandits who plunder a herd of cattle.
Although ordinary worldlings may attain this morality, concentration, and wisdom, they lack skillful means and are unable to explain them.
For this reason, they cannot obtain the constant morality, constant concentration, constant wisdom, and liberation.

Just as those bandits, not knowing the proper method, lost the *amṛta* (clarified butter), and just as those bandits added water to it for the sake of the *amṛta*, so too are ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*).

For the sake of liberation, they speak of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a soul, a celestial being, Maheśvara, atoms, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and the nature of the world; they speak of precepts, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, and claim that the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is itself *nirvāṇa*. Yet, in reality, they do not attain liberation or *nirvāṇa*.
Just as those bandits did not obtain the clarified butter (sarpis),

so too these ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana), by virtue of practicing a small measure of pure conduct (brahmacarya) and making offerings to their parents, are born in the heavens and experience a small degree of peace and happiness, like those bandits who had milk mixed with water.

Yet these ordinary people truly do not know that by practicing even a small amount of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and making offerings to their parents, one may be reborn in the heavens; nor can they know of the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and taking refuge in the Triple Gem. Because they do not know this, they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; though they speak thus, they truly do not understand it.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata appears in the world, he expounds for them permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
It is like a wheel-turning monarch appearing in the world: by the power of his merit and virtue, the throngs of bandits disperse and retreat, and not even a single cow has its life harmed.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King entrusted the cows to a cowherd who was highly skillful and resourceful; by means of his expedient methods, this man obtained the finest cream (sarpis), and because of that cream, all sentient beings were free from affliction and suffering.

When the Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, those ordinary persons who are unable to expound upon morality, concentration, and wisdom immediately retreat and disperse, just as thieves scatter.
At that time, the Tathāgata skillfully expounded both worldly and world-transcending dharmas; for the sake of sentient beings, he caused all bodhisattvas to follow and proclaim them.

Having already attained the *amṛta* (the supreme essence) themselves, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further enabled immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to obtain the flavor of the unsurpassed *amṛta*-dharma, namely: the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, son of good family, the Tathāgata is eternal and a phenomenon that does not change;
he is not like the Brahmā and other deities whom worldly, foolish, and ignorant people claim to be eternal phenomena.
This constant Dharma-name must belong to the Tathāgata and not to any other dharma.
Kāśyapa, you should know the body of the Tathāgata in this way.
The commentary states:
By correlating the Dharma with these metaphors, the meaning of the text becomes clear.
Thus, one knows that the teachings of Confucianism and Daoism are identical in expression, as they both originate from the Buddha-Dharma.
The commentary states, "How much more so regarding the churning of donkey's milk," which refers to the third passage of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Its meaning is that the Buddha’s teaching is like cow’s milk, while the cultivation and attainment of liberation are like the churning of milk to produce curds, fresh butter, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and so forth.
If one does not understand how to practice, one will not even obtain curd, let alone the teachings of non-Buddhist paths, which are like donkey's milk.
The Buddha is likened to a cow, while non-Buddhists are like donkeys.
Donkey's milk is inherently incapable of producing curd; likewise, the teachings of non-Buddhists lack the flavor of liberation, so that churning donkey's milk only results in excrement and urine.
"Practicing according to the teachings of external paths merely invites bitter fruits and yields no benefit.
Regarding the commentary’s section "Extensively Clarifying Divergent Views," the fourth point indicates that the detailed exposition follows from the brief summary.
For fear of prolixity, I have been brief; wishing to know the source, I have merely pointed to where it emerges.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Now, however, I shall only speak...,” this is the fifth section, which concludes by demonstrating that its merit is transcendent and supreme.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-dharma is shallow," this is because among its ten schools, each preceding one is shallower than the succeeding one, while each succeeding one is deeper than the preceding one. When compared to the tenth school, the first two possess eight layers of depth; they are already capable of refuting all non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas), let alone the third school, let alone the fourth, up to the tenth, which becomes increasingly profound and subtle.

However, all that was cited above belongs to the profound and mysterious depths of non-Buddhist schools; now, by means of the second [point], one can surpass them all. Therefore, it is said: "The shallowest of the Buddha-dharma already excels the deepest of the non-Buddhists."

However, the non-Buddhist outsiders of the West clearly expound upon the three periods of time and largely believe in cause and effect; they know to weary of birth and death and aspire to seek nirvana. Yet, because their understanding of the true source is slightly deficient, they remain at a vast distance from the Way.
Moreover, the Confucians and Daoists of this land excel only at regulating the single person; even if they observe lifelong mourning, they have no concern for other worlds.

Although they may equate life and death and forcibly unify the withered and the flourishing, they simply regard life and death as ordained by Heaven and the withered and the flourishing as matters of one's lot.

Heaven is the principle of spontaneity; one's lot is received from the void. The gathering and dispersing of qi constitute birth and death, while returning to non-existence constitutes the ultimate Way.
Compared with the teachings of the Śākya school, these cannot be considered contemporaneous.
Briefly distinguishing the differences between the Buddhist and Daoist traditions, ten points of divergence are set forth.
First is the difference regarding the beginning and the absence of a beginning.
This means that Buddhism establishes the causal conditions of arising and ceasing, which have no fixed origin.
In Confucianism and Daoism, there are the concepts of "Great Beginning" (Taichu) and "Great Commencement" (Taishi), which exist prior to all things.
The Great Beginning is the precursor to the myriad phenomena, and these phenomena arise spontaneously through the process of transformation.
Dependent origination (yinyuan) is the root of all dharmas; their arising and ceasing depend upon human action.
The two qi are not different from qi itself.
[The Buddhist] explains that the mind is the root of all dharmas, and the myriad practices rely upon conditions.
[The Daoist] holds that the Way takes the transformation of qi as spirit, spontaneously manifesting through non-action.
If one transforms through self-nature, there is neither cultivation nor practice; wisdom is discarded and the sage is severed.
If one relies upon conditions, one must necessarily depend on cultivation to achieve completion, so that the myriad practices converge with the source.
Throughout the three periods of time, there is no difference between the three periods.

The Buddhists explain that one’s nature consists of form and mind, which are linked through spiritual resonance; they arise and cease according to conditions, flowing through the three periods of time.
The Confucians and Daoists hold that life is the gathering of vital energy (*qi*) and death is its dispersal; once dead, one returns to heaven and earth, neither continuing nor persisting.
Since it resides in but a single body, how can one know the three periods of time?
The four types of conditioning differ from non-conditioning.

This is explained by the fact that good and evil arise from karma, while folly and wisdom are born of habituation; thus, through cultivation over accumulated kalpas, the numinous consciousness becomes profound and subtle.

The Confucians and Daoists maintain that good and evil are distinguished by human nature, while folly and wisdom arise from Heaven: those who receive a pure and harmonious endowment become sages and spirits, whereas those who receive a turbid endowment become foolish and obscure.
Even if one speaks of being cautious in one's habits, this applies only to a single lifetime; how could it be said that the accumulation of functional capacity assists one in future lives?
Fifth, there are differences in the conditions received and the vital energy inherited.
This is explained by observing that the myriad phenomena of the universe all arise through conditions.
The Confucians and Daoists hold that wealth, honor, fortune, and misfortune all arise from *qi* and destiny.
That which is received through *qi* cannot be altered; however, that which is received through conditions (*yuan*) can be augmented and cultivated.
These six internal factors are not identical to the internal [self].
The Buddhists explain that the heavens, the earth, and the myriad things arise from the transformations of internal consciousness.
The Confucians and Daoists maintain that all humans and creatures, whether crawling or flying, are produced by the transformations of Heaven and Earth.
For us [Buddhists], one can transform defilement into purity; for them [Confucians and Daoists], the transformations belong to Heaven, which must simply accept its own heights and depths.
Seventh is the distinction between conditions and non-conditions.

The commentary explains that the constant flux of the four characteristics—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—and their nature of being insubstantial, empty, and subject to transformation and destruction, all arise through the power of conditions; they are not said to be spontaneous.

Confucians and Daoists maintain that because days change and months shift as things move toward novelty and renewal, this power is entirely inherent (*zì'ěr*) and does not derive from the power of the mind.
The eight heavens and the asuras differ.
Confucianism and Daoism divide the flow of calamity and fortune, good and ill, into two:
first, Heaven; second, Earth.
That which is wrought by the earth can be obstructed and cut off; therefore, when a plot has not yet manifested its signs, it is dispersed and rendered fragile and minute.
That which is wrought by Heaven cannot be evaded or avoided; therefore, one accepts it with joy and, having forgotten it, returns to it.
Therefore, those who find peace in Heaven abandon the human realm; those who sever ties with the sages follow the Way—this is the purport of Laozi.
Buddhism explains this through the causes and conditions of karmic retribution, its fundamental sources being twofold:
first, suffering and its accumulation (duḥkha-samudaya); second, cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga).

Regarding cessation and the path: they abide nowhere and are unstained; they transcend both annihilation and permanence, rising high above the extremes of emptiness and existence, and soaring far beyond the realm of birth and death.

Regarding suffering and its accumulation: they revolve according to the mind, ascending or descending with one's karma, wandering to and fro within the six destinies and lingering within the three realms of existence.
Therefore, those who are weary of suffering sever the origin [of suffering], and those who rejoice in cessation cultivate the Path; this is the essential tenet of the Śākya school.
The principles of these two traditions are as clear as the palm of one's hand.
Households differ in their thousand gates, returning to distinct lineages; how could they be compared to the One?
The nine stains are not truly stains.
Laozi [criticized] benevolence as being contrary to the Dao; by severing benevolence, the Dao naturally comes to rest, for it does not reside in deliberate action.
Desire harms one's nature; by removing desire, nature attains itself spontaneously—this does not depend on cultivation.
Advantage burdens one's life; by setting aside advantage, life completes itself spontaneously—this does not depend on augmentation.
Ritual arises from disorder; if one abandons ritual, disorder naturally disappears—it does not depend on its creation.
Principle is rooted in the Dao; when the Dao exists, principle arrives of itself—it does not depend on a sage.
Attainment lies in timing; when the time comes, the position establishes itself spontaneously, for it does not reside in contention.
Therefore, it is attained naturally without seeking, and accomplished spontaneously without striving.
Those who strive will surely fail, and those who seek will surely lose—this is the teaching of the Old Master (Laojun).
Śākyamuni explained that goodness is the foundation of the path to blessings; by cultivating goodness, one receives the rewards of humans and devas.
Unwholesomeness is the root of the evil paths; by accumulating unwholesomeness, one sinks and wanders through the three evil realms.

Loving-kindness is the path to harmlessness; desire is the source of birth and death. By severing desire, birth and death will surely be eliminated; by practicing loving-kindness, one's lifespan becomes long and far-reaching.
Therefore, those who do good will surely attain [their goal], while those who do evil will surely fail;
those who detach from desire will surely transcend it, while those who do not detach from desire will surely fall into it—this is the teaching of Śākyamuni.
Since the methods of teaching have been distinguished, their differences are now clearly delineated.
They are like the metaphors of cold and warmth; in principle, they cannot be merged.
The "Ten Returns" and the "Non-Return" are distinct.
The Buddha explained that the suffering of birth and death takes form through deluded conceptualization;
it is the defilement of craving, which arises because of ignorance.
Since it arises because of ignorance, it can be cut away and eliminated.
Arising from delusive conceptualization, they can be pulled up and eradicated.
Their pulling up depends on the provisional nature [of phenomena], while their excision depends on the falsity of the essence.
One who knows the falsity of the essence quiets delusion and realizes nirvana.
Those who realize that nature is provisional abandon the provisional and return to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

Thereupon, they control the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and navigate the raft of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); they cross the bitter sea of birth and death and emerge from the vexing cage of the burning house. They ascend loftily to the terrace of Prajñā and wondrously enter the garden of Nirvāṇa. Here, profound and eternal bliss coexists with empty space, and the majestic, perfect luminosity merges environment and wisdom into a dual stillness; this is the ultimate destination of the Śākya teachings.
That old age, birth, and death are matters of destiny is entirely due to the workings of the Dao;
that one is sagely or unworthy is a matter of nature, which is simply what Heaven has bestowed.
What Heaven bestows cannot be escaped; what the Dao brings about cannot be resisted.
One who knows that the Way of Heaven cannot be obstructed by delusion is able to dwell at ease within birth and death while preserving the integrity of their nature and emotion (*xingqing*).

When nature and emotion are complete, Heaven is not destroyed; when one dwells amidst birth and death, the Way is not diminished. When the Way is not diminished, the anxieties of pleasure and aversion vanish; when Heaven is not destroyed, the mind of joy and anger is extinguished. Thereupon, one departs from the realm of clamor and dust to roam the land of the Way and Virtue; one’s principles are solitary and resolute within the world, while the spirit is uniquely concentrated beyond the mundane sphere. Being profoundly tranquil and silent, no burdens or harms can disturb them; being calmly non-active, no depraved energies can assail them. Thus they may attain longevity and fulfill their natural lifespan—this is the ultimate destination of the Laozi teaching.
Since their ultimate destinations differ and their initial departures are likewise distinct, they are separated by a vast distance; yet even a thousand li is not far [in comparison].
These ten aforementioned differences—please examine them with care and hold them deeply in your heart.

If one frequently uses the causes and conditions of the Hīnayāna to refute the profound and subtle tenets of external schools, how much more so must this apply to the wondrous reality of true emptiness, wherein phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated, defilement and purity encompass all, the one and the many are without obstruction, and each layer reflects the others in mutual resonance, achieving perfect fusion in every moment of thought.
Do not seek the petty fame of a single moment, but merge the three teachings into their ultimate unity;
do not cultivate the poisonous seeds of false views, which serve as the profound cause for the hells;
do not open the source and flow of ignorance, which blocks the mysterious path of the wisdom of all modes.
"Caution! Caution!
Those who transmit [this teaching] must be carefully selected.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* (Sū) stating, "The school that maintains the three dharmas have no coming or going is the Mahāsāṃghika," etc., the first part sets forth the tenet (*siddhānta*), while the section beginning with "asserting the existence of the present" provides the explanation.
The phrase "and so forth" includes seven schools in their entirety and one school in part;
that is to say, these eight schools in their entirety and one school in part all share this same tenet.
They are: (1) the Mahāsāṃghika, (2) the Haimavata, (3) the Kaukkuṭika, (4) the Caitika, (5) the Aparaseliya, (6) the Uttaraseliya, (7) the Dharmaguptaka, and (8) the Kāśyapīya.

The prefaces to the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* by Jetavana, West Mountain, and North Mountain state that "in most other matters, [the Mahāsāṃghikas] are largely the same," and the account regarding Dharmagupta is likewise.
The introduction to the *Kāśyapīya* states: "As for the remaining doctrines, they are mostly the same as those of the Dharmaguptaka.
The aforementioned eight classes of schools follow this calculation.
The phrase "a small portion" refers to the inclusion of the Mūlasarvāstivāda.
He says: "The past and future worlds do not exist; only the present and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) exist.
The Xueshan Zhuan states: "In most other points, its tenets are largely the same as those of the Sarvāstivāda, and it likewise does not admit the existence of the past and future."
Master Sugu of Beijing said:
"Based on the preceding reasoning, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* represents the doctrine of the Dharmaguptaka school,
while the *Catur-āgama* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* represent the doctrine of the Mahāsāṃghika school."
Both of these belong to the third school, which maintains that dharmas have neither coming nor going.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The fourth [school] is the school that distinguishes between the provisional and the real regarding the supernormal powers,” one [school] holds this in its entirety while the other holds it only partially.
The "one whole" refers to the Prajñaptivāda school.
The "one partial" refers to the Sautrāntika school, because the Mūlasarvāstivāda is subsumed under the first of these two schools.

Regarding the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, its author was originally a disciple of the Sāṃkhya school who held that the "effect" is pre-existent within the "cause"; later, upon renouncing the world and entering the Buddha-dharma, he became affiliated with the Sautrāntika school.
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master said:

"In the Sautrāntika school, the subtle is real while the coarse is provisional; since the meanings of 'provisional' and 'real' are identical, both the manifest and the pervasive are subsumed under the categories of the provisional and the real.
This explanation of the provisional differs from the "One-Exposition" (Ekavyavahārika) and the "Transcendent-Exposition" (Lokottaravādin).

This means that within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there exist both the conventional and the real. Regarding the meaning clarified through the gateway of the aggregates (skandha): it is "real" because it is a real accumulation.
Regarding the meaning clarified through the gateways of the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana): it is "conventional" because it is a conventional accumulation.
The current commentary states: "That *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* is precisely a partial branch of the Sautrāntika school.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the five schools of conventional falsity and ultimate reality," it means that the conventional is provisional; being provisional, it is false.
That which transcends the world is the truth; since the truth is not false, it is real.
This bears some resemblance to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, though it only goes halfway toward it.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Sixth, all dharmas are merely names,” this reveals that even that which transcends the world is but a provisional name.

Therefore it is said that all self and dharmas are likewise; as stated in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "If there were a mundane world, there would be a supramundane world; since there is no mundane world, how could there be a supramundane world? and so forth.
Commentary 7: "The School of the Emptiness and Existence of the Three Natures" refers to the School of the Perfectly Rational and Ultimate Reality established by Master Mahāyāna.
Commentary 8: "The School of True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics" refers to Master Mahāyāna’s School of the Mutual Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ninth [section] concerns the thesis of the non-obstruction between emptiness and existence,” this means that because they are mutually interfused, existence is existence-as-emptiness and emptiness is emptiness-as-existence; thus, when speaking of emptiness it necessarily includes existence, and when speaking of existence it necessarily includes emptiness. Therefore, it is called mutual interfusion.
Regarding "the simultaneous transcendence of both": because existence is itself emptiness, existence is transcended; because emptiness is itself existence, emptiness is transcended.

To say "without obstructing their coexistence" means that because their characteristics are not destroyed, existence is itself emptiness yet existence is not obliterated; emptiness is itself existence yet emptiness does not perish.

Regarding the phrase "True Suchness follows conditions": since the previous statement that emptiness and existence contain one another might be confused with mere emptiness, it is said that True Suchness is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself True Suchness.
Furthermore, it is distinct from being merely static; therefore, it is said to "follow conditions" (suiyuan), yet this does not mean it lacks "unchanging nature" (bubian).
As for "possessing virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," this belongs exclusively to the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong) and is not merely a state of empty quiescence.
The above are all the meanings within the teaching of ultimate reality (*śuddha-dharma*), as distinguished previously in the section on the establishment of the teachings.
Regarding the "Tenth: The School of Perfect Interfusion and Endowment with Virtue," it is explained extensively in the *Yifenqi* (Delineation of the Scope of Meaning).
The Commentary states: "Now, these ten schools are successively deeper than those preceding them," which marks the third section: the systematic analysis (*liao-jian*).
This section contains two parts:
first, a general analysis of the ten schools; second, the resolution of objections.
The preceding section has five parts:
first, it generally clarifies that the later stages are progressively deeper than those that precede them.
Regarding these ten schools, the first six are entirely identical to those of Master Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

In the Mahāyāna, there are eight schools: seven are named "Ultimate Emptiness" (paramārtha-śūnyatā), and the eighth is named "Conformity with Principle and Perfect Reality" (yukti-sampanna-tattva). That is to say, the Dharma-characteristics (lakṣaṇa) constitute "Conformity with Principle and Perfect Reality," while the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) constitutes "Ultimate Emptiness."

Now, the seventh is shifted to become the eighth and the eighth becomes the seventh; this is like the two differing schools previously mentioned in the Western Regions. Here, it accords with the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), and the final two [stages] are added to manifest its profound depth.

The Commentary states: “The first four are exclusively of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while the fifth and sixth pertain to both the Great and Small Vehicles. This refers to the second section: the comparative analysis of the Great and Small Vehicles.

However, although the fifth and sixth [categories] are established within the Small Vehicle, their meaning extends to the Great Vehicle; therefore, it is said that the fifth and sixth pertain to both.
In the commentary, from "The seventh is the Dharma-character [teaching]" onwards, there is the third section: the discernment between the provisional and the real.
In the commentary, from "Furthermore, the seventh is the Initial Teaching" onwards, there is the fourth section: the discernment by means of the five teachings.
I shall merely cite the four teachings; the first six, which are the Small Vehicle, correspond to the first, the Small Vehicle Treasury Teaching (*śrāvakapiṭaka*).
Since the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles has already been established previously, it is omitted here without further mention.
In the commentary, from the passage "Furthermore, the seventh is also called the school that maintains both truths exist" onwards, there is a fivefold discernment of the two truths.
This is also an exegesis provided in response to specific difficulties; it specifically discerns three schools because they contain divergent meanings, and thus they are explained again.
It can be understood that, from the outset, both truths exist as the primary tenet.

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "As in the *Karatalaratna-gatha*," this refers to a treatise composed by the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka, which consists solely of an exposition of this single verse.
Within this, there are two levels of inference (*anumāna*):
the first half constitutes the inference regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

That is to say, it is established as follows: "Conditioned phenomena" is the subject (*dharmin*), and "they are definitively empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)" is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The reason is stated: "Because they arise from conditions.
The concordant example is stated: "Like illusory phenomena.
Illusory phenomena arise from conditions; illusory phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Conditioned phenomena arise from conditions; conditioned phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature.
Here, the order of the cause and the example is reversed, or perhaps the phrasing is incomplete.
As for the term "true nature," it refers to the nature of the conditioned; thus, one should also say that the true nature of the conditioned is empty.
Second is the inference by analogy regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To state it: "The unconditioned is a subject that possesses a property; it is necessarily devoid of substantial reality" is the thesis (*pakṣadharma*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it does not arise."
The concordant example is as follows:
"Like a flower in the sky, the flower in the sky has no arising; the flower in the sky has no reality.
So too, the unconditioned has no arising; the unconditioned also has no reality."
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If conditioned phenomena existed, then unconditioned phenomena would exist.
Since conditioned phenomena do not exist, how could unconditioned phenomena exist?"
The details are as found in that treatise.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This is a portion of the meaning within the three treatises on Prajñā,” it means that in the three treatises, prior to the *Catuḥsatya-pariccheda*, existence is negated by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereas within the *Catuḥsatya-pariccheda* itself, existence is established by means of emptiness.
Therefore, the verse says: "Because of the meaning of emptiness, all phenomena are established.
If there were no meaning of emptiness, nothing at all would be established.

Furthermore, the title is designated as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way) to signify that it does not stagnate in either emptiness or existence, but rather clarifies emptiness alone.

Furthermore, a verse states: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Thus, the three contemplations proceed in unison and the three truths are mutually unimpeded; how could it be that only emptiness is emphasized?
Therefore, the claim that studying the school of Nāgārjuna leads to falling into the evil destinies through emptiness is a terrifying statement. Thus it is said:
"the meaning of one part" refers precisely to the meaning of the single contemplation of emptiness among the three contemplations.

The Commentary states: "The ninth, the thesis of the non-obstruction of the two truths," means that the ultimate does not obstruct the conventional, and the conventional does not obstruct the ultimate; while they are always dual in terms of the truths themselves, they are always one in terms of their realization.
To penetrate this non-duality is the true entry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The two truths are not a duality; they are eternally distinct yet never separate—this is their meaning.
Now, to briefly indicate its essential point, I refer back to the preceding text.
The reason why there is no tenth school is that the tenth could also be called the "School of the Inexhaustibility of the Two Truths.
However, because it must be integrated with the preceding [schools], it is not established separately.
Furthermore, as for the preceding three schools, each was established by various masters; therefore, they are now set forth.
As for the tenth school, it was not a point of contention among them, and thus it is not mentioned.
In the commentary, following the phrase "However, regarding the ten schools and five teachings," the second section explains away potential objections.
This refers to an objection that asks:
"In what way do the ten schools differ from the five teachings, such that they must be discussed again?
Therefore, this response is provided.
However, there are two meanings:
first, the difference between the universal and the specific; second, the distinction in their essential forms.
Regarding the first, we shall first present both points together.
Below the section on "The Principle of Teaching," both are explained together to clarify that while the two [aspects] are universal, the other two are specific.
The preceding sentence states, "According to the principle of teaching, a single sūtra may contain multiple teachings," which clarifies the universality of the teaching.
Just as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* contains all five teachings, so too do the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other scriptures; thus, the specific tenets emerge as reflections thereof.

The *Vimalakīrti* is exclusively a school that emphasizes the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*shili wuai*), for it does not extend to schools such as those concerning the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) or emptiness and existence.
When it is said that "a school (zong) may encompass many scriptures," this clarifies the penetration of the school (*zongtong*).

Because within the school of the unimpeded interfusion of phenomena and principle, the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and others are all subsumed, it is therefore projected that the teachings are provisional and limited.
"Just as within a single sutra there are five teachings that do not interpenetrate," and so forth.
The commentary states, "Furthermore, in establishing a teaching, one must necessarily rely on realization and verification," and so on; this second point clarifies that their essential forms differ.
This also serves to further address an objection.
The objection states:
"If each possesses both the universal and the particular, why can one not take the tenet as the teaching, or take the teaching as the tenet?"
Therefore, this general explanation is provided.
Because the teachings contain distinctions such as the stages of severance (*prahāṇa*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), there are only five schools.
However, when categorized according to their respective specific tenets, there are ten schools.

Therefore, while the six preceding [schools] differ in what they esteem, forming six distinct sects, their realization of cessation and verification is equal; thus, as they constitute merely the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, there is no contradiction among their doctrinal tenets.
The commentary states: "The second section, 'Revealing the Distinct Tenets,' below, provides two explanations of the distinct tenets.
Within the commentary, this is divided into two parts:
first, a general clarification of the underlying intent; second, an opening of the chapters for detailed explanation."
Regarding the first [section], there are two parts:
first, it formally establishes that each scripture has its own specific tenet; therefore, this section specifically clarifies the tenet of this present sutra.

For example, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* takes the One Vehicle as its tenet, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the permanence of Buddha-nature and so forth as its tenet; thus, it is said that each has its own tenet.
Although these [teachings] mutually encompass one another, they are designated as distinct schools because of their respective emphases.
The commentary states, "However, regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra*," and so forth, to resolve an objection.
The objection is as follows:
The second fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Mahāmati!
All dharmas are unborn; one should not establish this as a thesis.
Therefore, we now provide a comprehensive explanation:
These words are intended merely to dispel obstructions.
If one were to never establish a tenet at all, why would there be both the "penetration of the tenet" (*siddhānta-praveśa*) and the "penetration of the teaching" (*deśanā-praveśa*)?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The penetration of the tenet is for one's own cultivation; the penetration of the teaching is to instruct those who have not yet awakened."
An ancient said:
"When the principle is realized but the teaching is not, it is like the sun obscured by clouds.
When both the principle and the teaching are realized, it is like the sun in the void."
Since there are these two forms of penetration, it is not that there is no thesis.

This is the thesis of having no thesis; it is established while being without establishment. Thus, both the thesis and its exposition are thoroughly elucidated; this is what is called "dwelling in emptiness."
The commentary states: "Briefly distinguishing by means of two gates. This marks the second section: the opening of chapters for detailed explanation.
Within this, there are also two parts:
first, the presentation of the chapter headings; second, the detailed explanation according to those headings, beginning with the phrase "Among the former... and so on.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the first chapter, ‘Inexhaustible Equality’ and so forth,” this refers to the verses of the Great Sovereign Heavenly King Ocean of Good Light (Sūryaprabha-sāgara-mahendra-rāja) in the second [chapter] of the Jin translation.
The second half of the verse says: “Without grasping and without arising, it is also quiescent; for the sake of being the refuge of all, he appears in the world.”

This is precisely what the verse of the Celestial King Subhavyūha-sāgara in the present sutra says: "The Buddha-body is omnipresent throughout all great assemblies, filling the dharma-realm without end," and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “Because the characteristics of dependent origination mutually penetrate,” this refers to the meaning of the gate of the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination.
Regarding the section of the commentary beginning with “The ten [stages] prior to the Wise Head (Bhadramukha),” there are two parts within the commentary for this single master:
first, the presentation of the underlying intent and its general establishment; and second, the specific exposition.

The subsequent section, beginning with "That is to say, the two preceding masters," serves as an explanation; it interprets the statement regarding mutual omissions and reveals the intent behind their new formulations.
This section further consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of the mutual omissions, and second, the clarification of the reasons for those formulations, beginning with "Therefore, the intention of Xianshou."
Although this relies upon Master Guangtong, it has been further augmented.
Within this, there are three parts;
first, the general heading.
Second, from "By Master Dīpaṃkara" onwards, the intention of Master Dīpaṃkara is presented, explaining the reason why he does not posit the *dharmadhātu* as the dependent origination;
third, from "Xianshou" onwards, the reason for Xianshou’s addition is presented.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation of the reason, because while that [preceding section] attained the specific, it lacked the general;
second, from "By means of the dharma-realm" onwards, the presentation of the characteristics of the general and the specific.
The Dharma-realm has four aspects, yet in reality it is one; thus it is said to be "distinct.
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the general principle, which possesses two meanings:
first, original dependent origination (*mūla-pratītyasamutpāda*), as in the term *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive).
The Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings) represents functional activity, for it is all-pervasive by virtue of being primordially existent.
The Buddhāvatamsaka (Flower Ornament Sūtra) represents cause and fruit; that is, the dependent origination realized through cultivation.
Furthermore, dependent origination refers to the underlying principle, whereas cause and fruit refer to the stages [of realization].
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “Second, presenting the present interpretation,” the text contains two parts:
first, a general explanation of the establishment [of the system]; second, from “Now, explaining the previous meaning” onwards, a detailed explanation through the opening of specific chapters.
The preceding section has five parts: first, the general presentation;

second, the manifestation of its inclusion; third, the clarification of the reason for the addition; fourth, the resolution of potential objections; and fifth, the further elucidation of alternative formulations.
Regarding the first point, the intention is as follows:
if one were to be brief, the tenth master’s words would be too numerous.
Since Master Guāngtǒng distinguishes the specific without subsuming the general, one should instead speak of the "dharmadhātu-dependent origination."
Since the general principle subsumes the particular, the phrase "the reality of the principle of cause and effect" should no longer be retained.

If one were to adopt the extensive explanation, it would again lack the "inconceivable. Therefore, it is said: if one adopts the former meaning, one should speak of "cause and effect arising through conditions"; however, the true principle is that the Dharma-realm is inconceivable, which constitutes the thesis.

If one follows the sequential order, one should state that the principle of the *dharmadhātu* is, in reality, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), taking the inconceivability of cause and effect as its central tenet.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This then subsumes the general title,” the second section clarifies its inclusiveness.
The character "fang" (square) is used in two senses: when directed upward, it signifies the Great Square; since the Great Square has no corners, it is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
When directed downward, it signifies vastness; since its karmic activity is the dependently originated Dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is said that the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm) comprehensively encompasses the preceding two.
In the commentary, from the phrase "As for the words 'the Dharma-realm, etc.'", the third section clarifies the reason why inconceivable power is bestowed.
To distinguish this from other sutras, the text additionally cites scriptural evidence.

Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "The *Vimalakīrti* merely clarifies...", this is the fourth part, which explains away potential objections; that is, it addresses the difficulty raised by following immediately upon the previous point.

That is to say, even if one were to add the "inconceivable" (acintya) in order to distinguish this from other sutras, it would still be identical to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*; how then could it be considered different?
Therefore, this explanation is provided.
This is because [the *Śrīmālā*] attains the functional activity (*karmayoga*) but does not attain the marks of excellence (*guṇalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, that sutra says: "There is a liberation called 'Inconceivable.
Abiding in this liberation, a bodhisattva can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed," and so forth.

It has never been said that True Suchness possesses inexhaustible virtues, nor that the virtues of the Buddha-body—which is undivided yet pervades every atom and hair—are inexhaustible; therefore, it [the Buddha-body] constitutes but a single part [of True Suchness].
Therefore, Nāgārjuna refers to this sūtra as the *Mahā-acintya-sūtra* (The Great Sūtra of the Inconceivable), thereby indicating that the other is the *Aṇu-acintya* (The Minor Inconceivable).
Although the inconceivable itself has no distinction of great or small, within the teachings it is manifested with varying degrees of breadth and narrowness.
The Commentary states: "If one proceeds from within the title," and so forth; this is the fifth section, which further clarifies the alternative categories.

What has been discussed above merely demonstrates that the essential tenets of the sutra are already fully contained within its title. However, according to the interpretation of the Tiantai Master Zhiyi regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, a single title contains the essence (*tǐ*), the tenet (*zōng*), and the function (*yòng*).
Now, taking examples for explanation, there are thus three [aspects].

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “mutual application is universally pervasive,” this means that when one does not disrupt the nature (性) and characteristics (相), then it is the principle-dharmadhātu (理法界); here, the meaning of "nature" (性) is termed "dhātu" (界).
If one takes the dharmadhātu as the referent, "dhātu" (element) signifies the meaning of differentiation.
If nature and characteristics interpenetrate such that the characteristic is identical to the nature, then differentiation is identical to nature; for nature is itself the characteristic.
That which is without parts is itself the part; therefore, it is said that they interpenetrate.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary stating, "Within the second section on manifesting the meaning, there are four sub-sections," this section has three parts:
first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; and third, a summary conclusion.
The initial heading is self-evident.
The detailed explanation of the four chapters constitutes four distinct sections.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, the separate opening of the Dharma-realm,” etc., this segment of the commentary contains four distinct parts:
First, a brief clarification by means of the headings;
second, a detailed explanation through the opening of chapters, beginning from "Among these, ten matters";
third, the reconciliation of the central themes, as indicated by "And this cause and effect mutually serve as the central themes."
However, there are two interpretations:
first, all five cycles take cause and effect as their central tenet. If one takes the cultivation of causes as the central tenet, then the attainment of the fruit is the ultimate goal;
[if one takes the fruit as the central tenet, then the cultivation of the causes is the ultimate goal].
Taking the fruit as the thesis is for the purpose of causing one to cultivate the cause;
taking the causal relationship of what is believed as the thesis is for the purpose of causing one to attain the differentiated fruits and causes;
taking the differentiation as the thesis is for the purpose of establishing that which is believed.
To take differentiation as the thesis is to have the attainment of equality as the goal;
to take equality as the thesis is to have the integration of differentiation as the goal;
to take equality as the thesis is to have the accomplishment of practice as the goal.
To take the sudden accomplishment of all practices as the primary tenet is to have faith in equality as the goal;
to take the accomplishment of practice as the primary tenet is to have realization and entry as the goal;
to take realization and entry as the primary tenet is to have the forgetting of realization and cultivation as the goal.
Therefore, it is said that "they are mutually [the cause and effect].
In the commentary, from the passage "Throughout the beginning and end of one sūtra" onwards, the fourth section establishes the relationship between cause and effect.
This synthesizes the meanings of the four masters—numbers five, six, seven, and eight—since their views do not transcend the framework of cause and effect.
Therefore, this cause and effect do not contradict the *dharmadhātu*, because it is through this *dharmadhātu* that cause and effect are established.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “Second, harmonizing cause and effect by their identity with the *dharmadhātu*,” there are also four parts:
first, the heading;
Second, from "Within the Gate of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-mukha*) onwards, the chapters are opened for explanation;

third, from "The Five Pairs Explained Individually" onwards, the six types of interpretation are harmonized and integrated—namely, because cause and effect are neither destroyed nor obstructed, and because they mutually penetrate one another;
fourth, from "The Above Five Cycles of Cause and Effect" onwards, the discussion is concluded by returning to the Dharma-realm, thereby subsuming the views of the two masters Yan and Yu.
Regarding the summary and conclusion within the *dharmadhātu*, there are two intentions: first, returning to the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena and principle.
This refers to the fifth [pair], cause and fruit, which is the aforementioned cause and fruit.
Furthermore, the preceding four pairs all encompass both cause and fruit, because both cause and fruit possess objects, wisdom, and so forth.

Furthermore, within the third pair, one element is principle (li), while the remaining nine matters are all subsumed under phenomena (shi); thus, the five cycles of cause and effect do not transcend these ten.
Second, from "How much more so, cause and effect lack intrinsic nature" onwards, the discourse returns to the principle of the Dharma-dhātu.
The Commentary states: "The third [section] clearly displays the cause and effect of the Dharma-dhātu. This passage also consists of four parts:
first, the general heading;...
Second, from "There are also ten meanings" onwards, there is the detailed explanation;

third, from "These five preceding pairs" onwards, there is the reconciliation of the fundamental intent (*abhiprāya*): for example, taking the *dharmadhātu* while still enmeshed as the fundamental intent, and causing it to emerge from its entanglements into purity as the goal (*prayojana*), with the other four cases to be understood by analogy;

fourth, from "Furthermore, among the preceding five" onwards, there is the summary demonstration of the characteristics of cause and effect within the *dharmadhātu*, which incorporates the position of Master Guangtong.
Only the first pair constitutes the ultimate principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); all others are the causes and effects of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the commentary’s section “The Fourth: The Mutual Fusion of Cause and Effect in the Dharma-realm,” this chapter consists of only two parts:
first, the general heading; second, the detailed explanation.
First: because of the mutual fusion of the two, both are transcended; because of their mutual fusion, they are blended as one.
Since transcendence does not obstruct existence, it is called "unimpeded."
Because it is able to preserve and able to transcend, it is called "sovereign.

Although the *dharmadhātu* encompasses both phenomena and principle, here we take the actual principle; thus, the *dharmadhātu* is its nature (*svabhāva*), while cause and effect constitute its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

In the commentary, from the passage "First, by way of being free from characteristics" onwards, within the detailed explanation, the first pair [of verses] clarifies that both are abandoned together, while the third and fourth pair clarify that there is no obstruction to their coexistence.
However, as for nature (*xing*), it is indestructible and thus merely said not to perish;
as for characteristics (*xiang*), they are destructible, and thus it is said they do not perish.

The fifth [category] combines the first two, and the sixth combines the fourth and third; all are due to the mutual identity of nature and characteristics, such that the two pairs are not distinct from one another.
Seventh, it reunites the six and the five; that is to say, the six pertain to existence and the five pertain to cessation. Since existence itself is precisely cessation, they are not different.
Eighth, it integrates the preceding cause and effect so that they are identical with the Dharma-realm.
Ninth, because factors of the same dharma-realm mutually encompass one another as cause and effect;
tenth, because the distinct dharmas of cause and effect are each individually encompassed.
Having understood the general meaning, we shall next explain it point by point in response to potential difficulties.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This takes the characteristics as the thesis,” and so forth: the intention in citing the characteristics is to cause them to be forgotten, for they do not reside in the characteristics themselves.
Subsequently, these are conjoined with the aforementioned transcendence of characteristics, together forming the thesis.
Regarding the phrase "causing the loss of cause and effect": previously, by departing from signs, it was clarified that the nature of cause and effect is fundamentally detached;
now, by causing the loss of cause and effect, it causes one to depart from the mind that grasps at signs.

Regarding the statement "the lower nine follow the contemplation," it should be said that within the two [middle] stages, the nature is taken as the thesis to be raised, with the goal being to cause one to depart from that nature;
and departing from that nature is taken as the thesis, with the goal being to cause one to transcend the dharma-realm.

The third [aspect] takes "separation from nature" as its thesis (*pakṣa*) and "the non-extinction of nature" as its goal (*prayojana*), because nature is inherently separate and does not depend upon extinction.

Furthermore, it takes "separation from nature and the non-extinction of nature" as its thesis, with the aim of causing the loss of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to be no obstacle to the dharma-realm.

Fourth, taking the detachment from characteristics as the primary tenet and the non-destruction of characteristics as the goal, because characteristics are fundamentally detached by nature and do not depend on being destroyed.

Furthermore, taking the detachment from characteristics while not destroying characteristics as the primary tenet, and causing the cessation of [clinging to] cause and effect while not destroying cause and effect as the goal.
The thesis is the departure from characteristics; the goal is non-difference from the nature of departure, because nature and characteristics are not different.
If there were difference from the nature of departure, it would not be the true departure from characteristics.

Furthermore, the thesis is that being free from characteristics is not different from being free from nature, leading to the goal where both nature and characteristics are simultaneously fused and extinguished.
The sixth thesis is that the characteristics are indestructible, leading to the goal where they are not different from and do not vanish into nature.
If there were something that, being separate from [the other], was neither obliterated nor destroyed, it would necessarily exist as a fixed entity.
Furthermore, our thesis is that there is neither destruction, nor difference, nor obliteration; our aim is to bring about their simultaneous presence before us.
The principle is that the dual persistence is not different from the dual extinction; for it is precisely through the state of extinction that there is true persistence.

Furthermore, the principle is that the dual persistence is not different from the dual extinction, while the goal is to transcend sight and hearing and sever thought and deliberation, such that seeing, hearing, speech, and recollection remain unimpeded.

However, the wondrous Dharma that transcends sight and hearing is explained in terms of *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), while the profound meaning that is beyond thought and deliberation is explained in terms of *dharmatā* (essential nature).

Since the natures of the eight realms of existence are fused and cannot be divided, they constitute the fundamental principle (*śāstra*); thus, cause and effect each encompass the entire dharma-realm as their respective goals (*prayojana*).
The ninefold cause and effect each fully encompassing the Dharma-realm is their primary tenet; causing cause and effect to exist reciprocally is their ultimate purpose.
The twelve stages of differentiation all encompassing the Dharma-realm is their primary tenet; the inexhaustibility of every single practice and stage is their ultimate purpose.
The sub-commentary states: "The four preceding gates" [refers to] the third section, the summary.
This contains four parts;
first, they are subsumed under essence and function: "essence" refers to the aforementioned nature (*svabhāva*), and "function" refers to the aforementioned characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
2. "Furthermore, 'the first is itself cause and effect'" and below, these are subsumed within the eleven characters of the central thesis.
3. "'Since the fourth [gate] has already integrated the preceding ones, the four gates are of one principle'" refers to the comprehensive integration of the four gates.

4. From "Therefore, it immediately illuminates" onwards, [the text] returns to the contemplation of the mind. In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there is detachment; in terms of the mind, there is cessation. In terms of phenomena, there is no destruction; in terms of the mind, there is illumination.
"Obstruction" refers to the first two gates, while "illumination" refers to the third and fourth gates.
However, the initial obstruction is the obstruction that is itself illumination, and the subsequent illumination is the illumination that is itself obstruction.
The fifth is the simultaneous negation of both;
the sixth is the simultaneous illumination of both;
the seventh is the correct simultaneous negation while correctly simultaneously illuminating both.
The eighth [gate] is the unification of the four gates into a single principle, a single contemplation of perfect luminosity.
The ninth and tenth [gates] encompass the preceding four within each individual phrase; they likewise constitute a single contemplation.
Furthermore, the simultaneous illumination of the ten gates is termed "shining," while being without mind regarding these ten is termed "cessation."

The dual illumination illuminates both the preceding illumination and the negation; the dual negation negates both the preceding negation and the illumination. Where words fail and thought ceases, there is perfect clarity and distinctness.
Thus, only when the ten gates are unified within a single contemplation of perfect luminosity does one truly accord with the intent of the ten gates.
This concludes the summary of the essential principles of the four preceding sections, intended to provide a brief overview of the thematic connections within the text.
*The Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra Following its Sub-commentary* on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Scroll Fourteen.
*The Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra Following its Sub-commentary* on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Scroll Fourteen.
Fifteenth:
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty, as a Commentary (*śāstra*).
Part Seven: "Categories, Chapters, and Assemblies," Second Section. This chapter has two parts:
First, the intent of the introduction is explained; subsequently, from the passage "Among these, four... onwards, the chapters are opened for detailed exposition.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The Mahāyāna Piṭaka is Mañjuśrī," and so forth, this refers to the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka.
The Sūtras state that there are three Ānandas:
first, Ānanda, here translated as "Joyful Celebration" (Qingxi), who preserves the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second, Ānandabhadra, here translated as "Virtuous Joy" (Xixian), who preserves the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka; [and third, Ānandottara, who preserves the Mahāyāna-piṭaka].
Third is Ānanda-gara, here translated as "Ocean of Joy" (Xǐhǎi), who upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Although he is but a single person, his names differ according to his various virtues.

Because this Ānanda possesses vast learning, he maintains what he has heard; having accumulated the three types of wisdom and perfected both the letter and the meaning, he universally upholds the teachings of the Tripiṭaka with mastery over dhāraṇī.
Regarding the phrase "between the Iron Ring Mountains," the *Zuǎnlíng jì* states: "However, this record was originally composed by Master Zàng; it was later revised and embellished."
"Whatever is not found in the sūtras and śāstras was all questioned of the Tripiṭaka Master Sīlabhadra; it is merely what has been transmitted from the Western Regions.
Yet, both the *Zuǎnlíng jì* and the *Kāndìng jì* state that this is taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, though I have not yet seen the relevant passage.

The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* (Jingangxian lun) also speaks in this same way, stating that the Buddha prophesied that outside the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), between the two worlds, eighty billion nayutas of arhats and immeasurable, boundless bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would be summoned to assemble for the compilation of the teachings.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “When Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace, he saw that this Great Inconceivable Sūtra existed in three versions,” etc., the *Zuǎnlíng jì* cites the account from Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s *Xīyù jì*, and the *Biézhuan of Nāgārjuna* also describes the circumstances of his entry into the Dragon Palace and his vision of the sūtras, as detailed in other sources.
However, according to the seven-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the Tathāgata’s prophecy states: "Mahāmati,

you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there will be in a future age one who upholds my Dharma— a bhikṣu of great fame and virtue in the land of South India named Nāgārjuna, who will be able to destroy the schools of existence and non-existence."
"In this world, he manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma, attained the first stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), and was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
The *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* by the Tripiṭaka Master also provides a detailed account of his life and deeds.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the fact that the kingdom of Cakpan possesses its original text," according to the *Sui Kaihuang Sanbao Lu*, more than two thousand li to the southeast of Khotan lies the kingdom of Cakpan.

The kings of that country have transmitted their devotion to the Mahāyāna through successive generations; whenever renowned monks from other lands enter their territory, they all undergo examination and trial. If they are students of the Hīnayāna, they are sent away and not retained; if they are followers of the Mahāyāna, they are invited to remain and provided with offerings.
Within the royal palace there were eleven sūtras, including the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāmegha*, totaling one hundred thousand verses.

The King personally received and maintained [the sacred objects], holding the door-keys himself; he made offerings of incense and flowers with various adornments, hanging up multicolored banners interspersed with seasonal fruits, thereby inducing the princes to enter and pay homage to the deity, causing them to dedicate their merit toward enlightenment.

Furthermore, about twenty *li* to the southeast of this country there is a mountain. Within it are deposited eleven sections of Mahāyāna scriptures, including the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Vaipulya Ratnakūṭa*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Vistara*, the *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī*, the *Puṣpasaṃcaya-dhāraṇī*, the *Tuṣāra-piṭaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāmegha*. Each consists of one hundred thousand *gāthās*. According to the laws of the country, these have been handed down through successive generations and are protected as precious treasures.

In the early Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Zhi Falin, who delighted in the Mahāyāna and was determined to seek the Dharma even at the cost of his life. Packing provisions and taking up his staff, he traveled until he reached the kingdom of Cīnakupa.

Through sincere and earnest prayers, he was able to obtain the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consisting of thirty-six thousand stanzas; these were brought here and are the very ones translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

However, while Nāgārjuna possessed the complete original and ascended to the heavens, Fǎlǐng obtained only half of the pearl and subsequently brought it to the Eastern Land. Because the realizations of sages and ordinary beings differ and the sounds of Chinese and Sanskrit are distinct, the long journey was cut off and the subtle purport fell into obscurity; with scrolls lost and manuscripts discarded, only a mere portion has been transmitted.

Furthermore, according to the present edition brought from Khotan, it comprises more than forty thousand verses; whereas the text of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) as expounded in the first assembly of the Chinese *Dīrgha Āgama* is largely deficient and abbreviated, leaving no means for one to attain realization.
Reaching the eightieth fascicle, it is clearly visible in its entirety.
Although the hundred thousand verses are not yet complete, forty thousand lines of text are already mostly present; this is precisely the aforementioned abbreviated version.
The Commentary states: "That which is held by Sāgaramegha" refers to the third spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of Sudhana, as described in the sixty-second fascicle [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*].
Regarding the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma," the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching have already been cited within the section on the natural law (*dharmatā*) of causes.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Form and non-form, speech and non-speech,” and so forth: form and non-form are contrasted with sound and names (nāman), etc. This means that among these, that which takes sound as its substance is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha);
whereas that which takes names and so forth as its substance constitutes the non-form aggregates.
Now, neither of these can be definitively established. The terms "non-utterance" (*avyākṛta*) and so forth simultaneously address all phenomena (*dharma*) to manifest their meaning and essence;
while sound, name, phrase, and syllable all belong to "utterance," the function of manifesting the meaning of all phenomena is precisely what constitutes "non-utterance" and the like.
Now, because different realms and categories [of beings] exist, it cannot be fixed [in one way].

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The seventy-third is named the Wheel of the Cause of Perfection,” the Jin translation simply calls it the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*. This refers to when the Night Goddess Great Vow and Diligence Power (*Mahāpraṇidhānavīryabalā*) recounted how, in the past, as the Crown Prince Subduer of Good (*Kalyāṇasubha*), she rescued prisoners from a jail by practicing giving for half a month. When the time for their execution was imminent, the Tathāgata entered the assembly and preached this sūtra for her.
In the second section, "The Differences among the Assemblies," there are two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed analysis beginning with "Now, this sutra has nine assemblies.
Within this, the differences between the assemblies are explained first, followed by the distinctness of the chapters beginning with "Now there are thirty-nine chapters."

First, regarding the "nine assemblies," they are fully enumerated below in the word-by-word commentary; here I shall provide a brief indication: the first three assemblies each have six chapters; the fourth has four chapters; the fifth has three chapters; the sixth has one chapter; the seventh has eleven chapters; and the eighth and ninth each have only one chapter. Thus, there are thirty-nine chapters in total.
Regarding the "nine assemblies": the first, the Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment, comprises the first through the eleventh scriptures;

the second, the Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance, comprises the twelfth through the fifteenth; the third, the Assembly in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, comprises the sixteenth through the eighteenth;
the fourth, the Assembly in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven, comprises... [the nineteenth through the twenty-first].
Nineteenth to Twenty-first: The Fifth Assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace; Twenty-second to Thirty-third:
The Sixth Assembly in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; Thirty-fourth to Thirty-ninth:
The Seventh Reassembly in the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall; Fortieth to Fifty-second.
The eighth, the Third Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance, from the fifty-third to the fifty-ninth;
the ninth, the Assembly in the Jeta Grove Garden, from the sixtieth to the eightieth.
The names of its nine assemblies will be explained in detail below in the commentary (*śū*).

Regarding the phrase "thirty-nine chapters" in the commentary: this is because when the assemblies are grouped by assembly, each contains its own introduction (*nidāna*), main discourse (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), and so forth.

What is the sequence? The first assembly consists of six chapters: first, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Rulers"; second, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs"; third, the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra"; fourth, the "Chapter on the Formation of the World"; fifth, the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World"; and sixth, the "Chapter on Vairocana."

The six chapters of the second assembly are: the seventh, "Chapter on Names and Titles"; the eighth, "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths"; the ninth, "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance"; the tenth, "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity"; the eleventh, "Chapter on Pure Conduct"; and the twelfth, "Chapter on the Wise Leader."

The third assembly consists of six chapters: the thirteenth, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; the fourteenth, "Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; the fifteenth, "The Ten Abodes"; the sixteenth, "Pure Conduct"; the seventeenth, "The Merit of First Resolving for Enlightenment"; and the eighteenth, "The Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma."

The fourth assembly consists of four chapters: the nineteenth, "Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven"; the twentieth, "Chapter on Verses of Praise within the Palace of Yāma"; the twenty-first, "Chapter on the Ten Practices"; and the twenty-second, "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries."

The three chapters of the fifth assembly are: the twenty-third, "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace"; the twenty-fourth, "Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace"; and the twenty-fifth, "The Ten Dedications."

The first chapter of the sixth assembly is the twenty-sixth, the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta). The eleven chapters of the seventh assembly are: the twenty-seventh, "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (Daśa-dhāraṇī-parivarta); the twenty-eighth, "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (Daśābhijñā-parivarta);

the twenty-ninth, "Chapter on the Ten Endurances" (Daśakṣānti-parivarta); the thirtieth, "Chapter on the Incalculable" (Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta); the thirty-first, "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgata-āyuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta); the thirty-second, "Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattvas" (Bodhisattva-vihāra-parivarta); the thirty-third, "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgata-acintya-dharma-parivarta); the thirty-fourth, "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgata-daśa-kāya-lakṣaṇa-sāgara-parivarta); the thirty-fifth, "Chapter on the Merit of the Minor Marks and Radiance" (Anuvyañjana-prabhā-guṇa-parivarta); the thirty-sixth, "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" (Samantabhadra-caryā-parivarta); and the thirty-seventh, "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (Tathāgata-utpatti-parivarta).
The first chapter of the eighth assembly is the thirty-eighth, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*).
The first chapter of the ninth assembly is the thirty-ninth, the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dharmadhātu-praveśa-parivarta*).

The reason for this sequential order is that when sages establish their teachings, there must necessarily be a gradual progression. Desiring to enunciate the subtle words [of the Dharma], he first speaks of the adornments of the three kinds of worlds; this serves as the general preface for the nine assemblies and provides the origin of the Great Dharma. Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornments of the World Rulers," which corresponds to the introductory section (nidāna) found in other sutras.

2. Since the preliminary causes have been manifested, the formal exposition is about to be presented. The ocean-like assembly gives rise to thoughts and initiates the inquiry; the Tathāgata, about to provide the response, first manifests auspicious signs: light from his mouth summons the Bodhisattvas from afar, and light from his ūrṇā-kośa illuminates everywhere to indicate the Master of the Dharma. He shakes the network of worlds to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings, and a flower appears before the Buddha to symbolize the fruit upon which the teaching relies. From his white ūrṇā-kośa, a multitude emerges to signify that the teaching flows from the Buddha. These constitute the initial signs of the preaching of the Dharma; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs."

Third, as the manifested signs have become manifest and the Lord of Dharma is about to proclaim the teaching, the Tathāgata’s eldest son—namely Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—manifests the light from his ūrṇā-kośa to reveal the enlightened mind of liberation. Desiring to manifest the inconceivable, he first clarifies his entry into samādhi; internally contemplating the principles of phenomena and internally examining the capacities of sentient beings, he moves the Buddhas above to bestow their empowerment and serves as a model for beings below. Therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi."
4. Having entered this ultimate meditative concentration, all Buddhas praise him; upon emerging from concentration, he speaks, and his words are invariably true and appropriate.

First, he describes the *parivṛta* (supportive environment) of the Tathāgata, providing a general account of the origins of the ocean of lands; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Formation of Worlds."

Fifth, the "Chapter on the Accomplishment" provides a general exposition of the ocean of lands; it subsequently details the infinite adornments established by the Original Teacher through his past purification and arrangement—adornments as vast as space and containing the Dharma-realm within every atom. Therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World."

Sixth, the excellence of the dependent retribution must necessarily have its cause; it is like a distant source yielding a long-flowing stream, or deep roots producing lush fruit. Therefore, it is said that in the past, as a prince, he served inconceivable [masters], fully cultivating superior causes and purifying the ocean of lands. This thus cites the person to manifest the Dharma; hence, it is followed by the "Vairocana Chapter."

The first six chapters above collectively clarify the causes and effects of what is to be believed; this constitutes the First Assembly, also titled "The Section on Presenting the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith. Next, regarding the six chapters of the Second Assembly:

seventh, following that which was previously believed, the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*) is now presented. Since one wishes to give rise to profound faith, it is further necessary to recognize the correct [teachings]; therefore, the three karmas of the Tathāgata’s direct retribution—namely body, speech, and mind—are clarified first. Because the body is the totality, it is explained first. As he manifests bodies in accordance with sentient beings and establishes titles as appropriate to their needs, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Names and Titles of the Tathāgata."

8. As for the eighth point, "Speaking in Accordance with the Desires of Beings": To expound the Wheel of Dharma extensively, one unfolds the dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths so that its name pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Since each and every world possesses four hundred billion ten-thousand names, the text proceeds with the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths."

9. Since the physical and verbal [karmas] have already been manifested, the mental karma is about to be revealed. Although the mind is profound and unfathomable, it still manifests through the body; therefore, the wheels on the soles of the feet emit light to illuminate phenomena and awaken sentient beings. Mañjuśrī universally expounds the light of wisdom, illuminating both phenomena and principle simultaneously to awaken them and lead them into realization. The two illuminations of body and wisdom merge into a single light, causing the two types of awakening to be perfected equally; hence, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance."
