Therefore, it is further said: "All dharmas are without arising; all dharmas are without cessation.
If one can understand them in this way, such a person sees the Tathāgata.
The Preface states: "As for its characteristics, there is neither going nor coming," which is the second praise of the greatness of its characteristics (xiang-da).
The Sūtra says: “The Tathāgata does not take marks as his essence; he is rather the markless, quiescent Dharma.
Though his physical marks and majestic deportment are fully perfected, they are seen by those in the world according to their inclinations.”
Since non-characteristic itself serves as the characteristic, it is profoundly still and devoid of coming or going.
Furthermore, because its virtue pervades the Dharma-realm, it likewise has no coming or going.
The Preface states, "The foundations of mindfulness extend to many strands," which is the third praise of the greatness of its function.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, explaining the function in terms of the manifested phenomena; second, clarifying the function by means of the manifested essence.
This is the first.

The methods of transformation are profound and subtle; they differ from the previous methods of transformation within the realm in that their practice consists solely of the category of "creation" and their mind consists solely of the four immeasurables. Their many gates of skillful means respond perfectly and unfathomably, as described in detail in the sutras.
Regarding the term "perfect correspondence" (*yuánduì*): the body is perfectly pervasive and universally responsive, like the moon reflected in a hundred rivers;
the voice accords with all things and is heard everywhere, like the wind blowing through the myriad pipes;

the mind awakens instantaneously in a single moment, like the brilliant clarity of the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). Therefore, it is said that there are many strands [of manifestation].
The Preface states: "Merging with the great void as its measure. Below this, the second section clarifies the function by way of the essence of transformation.
This means that when expanded, there is nothing external; when contracted, there is nothing internal.
The Sūtra says: "For example, it is like space, which pervades all places, whether material or non-material.
It is also like space, which contains all phenomena; though their measure is as vast as the atoms of all lands, they are incalculable and beyond knowledge."
Therefore it is said: "How could numerical calculation ever exhaust [this]?

The subsequent phrase, "Entering the subtle realm of a single fine mote, it cannot be described by names or words," refers to what the Sūtra says: "Just as one sees the Buddha seated in this assembly, so it is within every atom of dust."

Within a mote of dust there is a world-system, and within that world-system there are further motes of dust; within each mote of dust there are again world-systems, layer upon layer without end. This is not an object of mental consciousness or discursive thought, and therefore it transcends the realm of names and words.
To express its meaning, names and words are difficult to describe; it is where the path of language is cut off.
To manifest its realm, names and words do not know it; it is where the movements of the mind cease.

Furthermore, the former phrase clarifies that the locus of transformation universally pervades the Dharma-realm, while the latter phrase indicates that there is nothing so subtle into which it does not enter.
The Sūtra states: "Each and every tip of a hair can accommodate boundless worlds without obstruction, manifesting the taming of immeasurable sentient beings.
The Preface says: "He who possesses no merit yet is praised—can this be anyone other than the Great Awakened One? This is the fourth conclusion, attributing all virtue to the Tathāgata.
This means that since the three preceding sections all pertain to the Tathāgata, his praises are inexhaustible.
The *Analects* states: "Tàibo may indeed be called one who possesses the ultimate virtue."
"Third, he yielded the empire to the world, yet the people have no virtue by which to praise him.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The thoughts in the minds of beings as numerous as motes of dust may be counted; the water in the great oceans may be drunk up; space may be measured and the wind may be bound; but none can fully describe the merits of the Buddha."
This refers precisely to that matter.

The *Preface* states: "In past kalpas I planted the causes and have humbly received the Buddha’s prediction. From this point downward, the third section expresses his own joy at having encountered the right time and being able to hear the teachings of the Voice.
This section has three parts:

first, receiving the Buddha’s prediction; second, enjoying the peace and prosperity [of the reign]; third, the ten thousand nations paying court and presenting tribute through successive translations.
This is the first.
Because he had planted causes over a long period of time, he received the personal prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Great Awakened One.
*Tāo* (叨) means to have received an undeserved honor.
From the phrase "Gold Mountain" (*Jinshan*) downward, the specific characteristics of the prediction are clarified separately.
First, it clarifies that there may be doubts regarding the authenticity of the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*.
Subsequently, under the entry for "jade screen" (*yuyi*), it clarifies the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states: "The *yi* is a screen."
"The screens of the Son of Heaven are adorned with jade.
The *Ratnavarṣa-sūtra* consists of ten fascicles and is included in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*.

In the first fascicle, it says: "At that time, there was a son of heaven from the east named Candrasūryavimalaprabha. He came to the place where the Buddha was riding upon a five-colored cloud; he circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side."
The Buddha addressed the devaputra, saying:
"Your radiance is most rare indeed,
O devaputra!"

In the past, before immeasurable Buddhas, you have already venerated and made offerings with various kinds of incense, flowers, precious gems, articles for adorning the body, clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions, thereby planting many roots of goodness.
"O Son of Heaven!
It is because you have planted immeasurable roots of goodness in the past that you now obtain such radiant and brilliant light.
O Son of Heaven!"

For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, during the fifth five-hundred-year period when the Dharma is about to perish, you shall be in the land of Mahācīna in the northeastern region of this Jambudvīpa; established in the stage of *avaivartika*, you are truly a bodhisattva, and thus manifest in the form of a woman as a sovereign ruler.
Having ruled according to the True Dharma for many years, he nurtured sentient beings as if they were his own infants and caused them to practice the ten wholesome deeds.

He was able to extensively uphold my Dharma by establishing stūpas and monasteries, and furthermore, he provided śramaṇas with offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, constantly practicing the pure conduct throughout his entire life.
"Furthermore, all women are subject to five obstacles, yet this son of heaven is not hindered by two of them:
first, that of becoming a Wheel-Turning King; second, that of being a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva."
The remainder is as in that sutra.
The commentary states:
At this time, there is no other female ruler who establishes such [a state of affairs]; these words are not false.

The *I Ching* says: “In a family that accumulates goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings; in a family that accumulates evil, there will surely be an abundance of calamity.”
Now, by virtue of the accumulation of merit, the earth has become level and the heavens perfected; the rivers have cleared and the seas have been pacified.
"Pacified" (yàn) means tranquil and secure.

The *Preface* states that following the "extraordinary portents and rare omens," thirdly, the myriad nations came to court like tributaries of a river, bringing their offerings after translating their texts twice over.

first, two pairs that set forth the topic; second, two pairs that explain it.

Regarding the former: people from all quarters look up to his virtue, and extraordinary portents, marvelous omens, and wondrous auspicious responses arrive day after day and are recorded month after month.
"Books" refers to historical records.
"The auspicious texts on shell-tablets also arrive seasonally and harmonize year by year" means they are received with consistent abundance every year.

At the beginning, "zhēngxiáng" (auspicious omens) is formed above;
at the end, below "jiàxiǎn" (crossing over peril), "bèidié zhēnqià" (bamboo slips arriving in abundance) is formed.

The Preface states: From "Mahāvaipulya" [Dafangguang] onwards, the fourth section separately extols the profound and subtle purport of this scripture.
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, a general praise; second, a specific praise.
Now, for the first part: the first two lines indicate its profundity and vastness, while the subsequent lines beginning with "Those who behold it" establish the meaning of those two preceding lines.
Since it is a secret treasury, one cannot see it when looking at it;
since it is called the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*), how could its boundaries be measured?
Regarding "drawing from" (*yi*), the *Zhu cong* states: "It refers to drawing water into a vessel by means of a ladle."
Thus, the "Stele of Toudousi" in the *Wenxuan* states: "I have heard that those who draw from a pond that rises and falls at dawn and dusk cannot fathom its depth;
those who look up at the azure color of the heavens find it difficult to know its distance."
Therefore, those who attempt to gauge it now are like one peering at the heavens through a tube or scooping up the ocean with a clam shell.
Following the passage in the Preface which states, "Those in training and those beyond training have severed their desire for such peering," the second section provides a specific eulogy.
Within this, there are three sections:

first, praise by way of persons; second, praise by way of the Dharma; third, praise by way of the location. Within the first, there are two parts: 1. Praise by way of persons 2. Praise by way of the Dharma 3. Praise by way of the location Regarding the first [praise by way of persons], there are two parts:
First, the superiority [of the Buddha] is manifested in contrast to the inferior; subsequently, his superiority will be manifested through the essence itself.
Regarding the former, the first phrase applies universally to the three vehicles, while the latter phrase speaks specifically.

This is because those of the two vehicles were as if deaf and blind while seated there, and even the bodhisattvas of the third vehicle, despite having accumulated practices over many kalpas, were unable to fathom it.
Regarding *kuī* (to spy/gaze), the *Zuozhuan* states: "It means to look while lifting one's feet.
Regarding *yú* (to covet/aspire), the *Zhucóng* states: "It means to have expectations or hopes for something."
Below the phrase "supreme knowledge of all modes" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), the excellence of its essence is revealed.
The preceding sentence refers to the perfection of the fruit, wherein the fulfillment of the two adornments (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*) constitutes the knowledge of all modes.
Regarding the phrase "Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī" in the subsequent line, it signifies the perfection of the causes.
Both the conduct of Samantabhadra and the vows of Mañjuśrī are fully perfected.
It is also possible for the practices and vows to extend to the two aforementioned sages.
The *Preface* states, "Within a single phrase," and so forth; this is the second section, which praises [the Dharma] by way of its principles.

Within this, the first line refers to the profundity and vastness of the expressive medium (*vyañjana*); thus, the meaning of a single phrase could not be exhausted even if one were to use as much ink as the waters of the ocean.

Following this, from the phrase "within a single hair" (*yī háo zhī zhōng*) downward, the third section praises [the Buddha] by way of the location, based on the principle that the phenomena of the phenomenal world are mutually unimpeded (*shìshì wú'ài*);
thus, although a buddha-field (*zhàtǔ*) is placed within a single hair, it is not cramped. The *Preface* states, "The Kingdom of Magadha," and so forth.
The mention of "Makuta" (Magadha) refers to its being the fundamental site of the nine assemblies, where one need not arise from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to reach everywhere.
The mention of "Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabhā) indicates its proximity to the field of bodhi.
Furthermore, it explains that the gate of faith encompasses the ocean of fruition; thus, it says, "Herein is spread the principle of quiescent extinction."

The preface states: "Reflecting deeply upon the profound meaning," and so forth. Fifth, the transmission and translation [of this work] and the joy felt at encountering it across ancient and modern times.
This section has two parts:
first, clarifying the many omissions in previous translations; second, clarifying the many complete elements in the present translation.
First: "Mian" means distant;
"wei" means to contemplate.
The "six dynasties" refer to the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, and Sui.

Regarding the statement, "Only Kai [the founder of the Liang] glimpsed half of a pearl, yet had not yet beheld the entire treasure," this refers to the passage in the "Chapter on the Noble Conduct" (*Ārya-caryā*) of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where the youth in the Snowy Mountains hears a transformed rākṣasa say:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing."
Startled, he wished to look closely and saw only a rākṣasa.
He asked the rākṣasa,
"Great Being!..."
"Great Being, where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by the one who was free from fear in the past?
Where did you obtain such a half-jewel of wish-fulfillment?"
The commentary states:
The latter half of this verse is missing, as its meaning is therefore incomplete.
[It continues: "When birth and death have ceased, extinction is bliss. If one hears these words...
This refers to the "complete jewel.
Now it is clarified that since the earlier translations were largely deficient and omissions, they constitute the "half-jewel.
The *Preface* states, "I have heard that its Sanskrit original... and so forth; this second section clarifies that the present translation is largely complete, which is the "complete jewel."
The text contains six sections: first, the invitation;
second, the actual translation; third, the response to the inquiry; fourth, the conclusion of the work; fifth, the praise of its benefits; and sixth, the celebration of the encounter.
Now, for the first section, the details are as explained in the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse).
The preface states: "In the first year of Zhengsheng," and so forth; this is the second verified translation.
"The moon travels through Guxi" refers precisely to the third month.
Regarding the phrase "personally receiving the pen and the eraser," it means that Empress Wu personally performed the editing and revision.
As for the term "pen and eraser" (*bishuo*), the *Han shu*, in the "Biography of Wei Qing," states: "If it was to be erased, she would erase it; if it was to be written, she would write it."
"Shao" (shaving) refers to deletion; "bi" (brush) refers to addition.
Some say: "In the case of texts based on principle, one examines and receives them, shaving [the redundant] and annotating [the essential]."
This is because the ancients wrote on bamboo and wooden slips using knives to shave the surface.
The passage in the Preface, "Thus the sweet dew flowed its essence," refers to the third sign of spiritual response.

The fourteenth day was Xin-you; Geng-shen was the thirteenth day, and Ren-xu was the fifteenth day. On each of the days preceding and following [the central day], there were respective signs of spiritual response.
That is to say, on the night of the thirteenth day, Empress Wu dreamed that nectar descended everywhere throughout the heavens;
on the fourteenth day, Tan-k’ai began the translation of the scriptures; and on the fifteenth day, a sweet rain fell from the sky.
As for the character *qín* (覃), the *Erya* states: "It means 'to reach' (*jí*) and 'to extend' (*yán*.
Guo Pu’s commentary says: "This refers to spreading and creeping so as to cover and reach one another.
Following the phrase "thus opening" (*shìkāi*), this forms an auspicious omen for what precedes.
These two lines may also be understood to apply to the preceding two auspicious omens, as they are all the moisture of the single flavor.
Alternatively, "opening the true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the ambrosial medicine of immortality, all the more so because true reality is eternally abiding.
"The grace of a single flavor" forms the aforementioned copious rain, for there is no difference in flavor between a single cloud and a single raindrop.
"Shi" (式) means "to employ.
In the *Preface*, from the phrase "in the second year of the Shengli era" onwards, the fourth matter concludes with the year Jihai.
Beginning from the years Yiwei, Bingshen, Dingyou, Wuxu, Jihai, and Gengzi, it took five years for the transcription to be completed.
Regarding the term "transcription" (shen): the *Shuowen* states, "To supplement."
The *Zhucóng* states: "To repair the old and create the new is collectively termed 'shàn' (to mend).
The preface says: "Adding to the waves and billows of the ocean of nature," which concludes the fifth section on praising the benefits.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, clarifying the benefit of the teachings and principles.
A great wave is called a "lan" (wavelet).
The *Xuanyan* says, "To 'expand' (kuò) means to stretch what is small and make it large.
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Liji* states, "'Boundaries' (jiāng) refers to demarcations.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* says, "'Territories' (yù) refers to enfeoffments."
This means that once the profound words have been bestowed, they augment the ocean of nature and open wide the dharma-realm.
Following this, under the section "The Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna," the second part distinguishes the capacities of sentient beings who receive these benefits.
The preface states, "How could it be said that [this occurs] in the latter five hundred years," and so forth; this is the sixth section on rejoicing in the encounter.
Within it, there is first the rejoicing in the encounter, followed by the making of vows.
Regarding the first point: the preceding phrase concerns obtaining the hearing [of the teaching] during an evil age; this is the first blessing.
The subsequent phrase concerns obtaining the hearing [of the teaching] in an evil place; this is the second blessing.

Regarding the initial mention of "the latter five hundred years," there are five periods of five hundred years following the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. The first five hundred years were characterized by the firmness of liberation and so forth; we are now in the fourth five hundred-year period, which is why it is called "latter," as it occurs after the third five hundred years.
Therefore, in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is said that those who can believe and accept [this teaching] during the final five hundred years will be difficult to find.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly opening the secret of the jewel casket," the sixty-fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Prajñā is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), and the śarīra [relics] are like the casket."
"Although there is no Prajñā within the relics, because they have been permeated by Prajñā, one who makes offerings to them is reborn in the heavens for a thousand lifetimes.
Applying this principle to the present case, the Tathāgata is like the casket, while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The preface states: "What is hoped for is to propagate [the Dharma] throughout the sands of the world-system. Below this, there are two sections on making vows.
Within these, there are two parts:
first, the initial lines describe universal pervasion.
"Sand-grain worlds" refers to pervasive gross forms.
"Dusty regions" clarifies pervasive subtle forms, as it pervades every area within minute particles.
The final two lines, beginning with "Hanging long alongside the two luminaries," clarify vertical thoroughness, for they hang perpetually and are spread eternally.
The "two luminaries" refer to the sun and moon, which serve as metaphors for the Tathāgata’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

In the section following "A Single Glimpse of the Jewel Verses" in the Preface, the sixth part comprehensively clarifies the intent of the preface, praising the principle while expressing self-effacement.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, two lines formally establish the preface, because the joy is profound as one searches through, contemplates, and savor[s] [the text].
The commentary on the *Mao Shi* states: "Fu (復) means 'repeatedly'."
The *Zhucóng* states: "‘Fù’ (again) means to re-examine; this refers to Nánróng’s ‘threefold repetition of the white jade tablet.
This has already been cited in the commentary.
Second, regarding the passage beginning with "Although there is no speaking and no showing," it praises how the principle transcends words while necessarily relying on words for its manifestation.
"Neither speaking nor demonstrating" refers to the passage from the Maudgalyāyana chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
"The gate of non-duality" refers to the "Chapter on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, as also explained in the commentary.
Regarding "revealing speech through speech": if there were not the words of Mañjuśrī praising silence, how could one know that wordlessness is sublime?
Thus, the mark of quiescent extinction is provisionally expressed by means of verbal explanation.

Regarding the meaning of the "great trichiliocosm," this refers to the analogy of the dust particles containing sūtras from the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), which has already been cited in the commentary.
Thus, while the sūtra-scrolls hidden within the dust of the great trichiliocosm provide no benefit, when opened by those of wisdom and discernment, they are able to benefit all beings.
Now, by resorting to provisional words to manifest the meaning, one should open the dust [of ignorance] and point it out within the scriptures, whereby there will be accomplishment and benefit.
The section beginning with "I now venture to submit" below expresses humility and brings the composition to its conclusion.
The preceding brief explanation of the preface is concluded.
Among its contents, those that accord with reason have been adopted as appropriate, while others have been set aside.
Regarding the commentary’s section titled “Tenth: Separate Explanation of the Textual Meaning,” the commentary is divided into two parts:
First is the general outline, followed by the commentary on the sutra.
Within the former, there are three parts: the heading, the enumeration of names, and the explanation.
Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "First, the three divisions of the primary section," the following explains the three [divisions] for each of the ten levels.
The first part is divided into two sections:
first, the explanation of the introduction and the main body; second, the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*).
From the words "existence and non-existence" (*yǒuwú*) onwards, there is a specific explanation of the dissemination.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, an introduction to the previous explanations; second, an introduction to the previous meanings; and third, the presentation of the present interpretation.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "The seven interpretations above," the second part [of this section] reconciles the previous meanings.
Furthermore, by combining the previous seven masters, they are fused into four propositions:
the first corresponds to the seventh master, and the third corresponds to the first six masters, with the second and fourth meanings added.
As for the second point, "only the orthodox teaching," the intention is to take the realization and entry into the manifestation of principle as the orthodox teaching.
Therefore, Dao Lang of Hexi said:
"If one attains awakening by means of the initial division, then the initial division is the primary.
If one attains awakening by means of the subsequent division, then the subsequent division is not secondary."
This is precisely that meaning.
In the commentary (*shu*), from "Now, based on possessing the three" onwards, the third section presents the current correct interpretation.

This means that while the preceding exposition of the principles may, in its full scope, result in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), when explaining the meaning according to the text, one may rely upon the three divisions.
If there were no introductory section (āgamana), how could the main body (samyaktva) be established?
If there were only the main body, the beginning and end would not be clear.
If one were to rely solely on the absence of words, how could it be explained? Regarding the commentary text, there are four parts:
First, establishing the source and basis;
second, from "As for why there are three" onwards, distinguishing the characteristics of the three;

third, from "It is not merely one section" onwards, corroborating the preceding argument by analogy—meaning that if even the text of a single chapter requires these three divisions, how much more so must a complete section establish them?
4. "Although all six interpretations are generally applicable" and below, the section establishes and determines the circulation [of the correct meaning].
This contains three parts:
first, adopting the correct meaning; second, examining the preceding points of conformity and contradiction; and third, concluding with the definitive explanation.

In the commentary, the passage beginning with "The first of the four interpretations" and following constitutes the second section, which examines the preceding [arguments for] conformity and contradiction, thereby explaining the reason why the previous five interpretations were not adopted.

Regarding the phrase "causing the main body of the teaching to lack the proof of entry," this refers to how Guangtong [Tanying] regarded the "Dharmadhātu Chapter" as the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding dedication).

The *dharmadhātu* is the cause and fruit of realization; it is a great inquiry by the ocean-like assembly. As the new assembly gathers from afar, the Buddha enters samādhi, and the ocean-like assembly suddenly attains realization.

Having already suppressed the scriptural text by classifying it as the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section, how much more so in the *mūla-prakaraṇa* (authentic teaching), where there are only the three stages of faith, understanding, and practice, but no realization or entry.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The third belongs only to the single aspect of Sudhana,” this refers to Master Yu’s classification of the verses following the *Dharmadhātu* chapter as the *pariṇāmanā*.
However, within the five characteristics of the *Śrīkaranda-vyūha*, only half of the characteristic of the vastness of the cause is revealed; therefore, it does not circulate as a complete section.

Regarding the phrase "the latter two verses" in the Commentary (*Ṭīkā*), it merely states that some say so, which implies that the primary intent of the *Kanding ji* (Commentary on the Determination) employs this interpretation.

Regarding the statement, "Only the virtues of the Buddha within the verses are summarized," it is because Samantabhadra was unable to exhaustively praise the Tathāgata; therefore, he concludes by saying: "The atoms in all lands may be counted, the waters in the great oceans may be drunk up, space may be measured and the wind bound, yet no one can fully describe the Buddha’s merits."

If one were to take this concluding verse as praising the Buddha’s virtues and judge it to be the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section, then there would be no description of the Bodhisattva’s virtues within the entire work.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “At the end of the ‘Ten Practices’ and other similar sections, these verses appear,” the former [point] refutes [the opponent’s view] by means of meaning (*artha*), while this refutes it by means of the text (*vyañjana*).

Since this verse does not appear at the conclusion of that sutra, it is not intended as a general circulation verse for the entire work; rather, it serves specifically as a verse for the circulation of this particular assembly and this specific chapter.
Regarding the "Verses at the End of the Ten Practices," the verses state: "The merits of the Bodhisattva are boundless; all practices are fully perfected.
Even if immeasurable and infinite Buddhas were to speak for immeasurable eons, they could not exhaustively describe them."

How much less could the gods and humans of the world, or any of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, ever reach the ultimate end in praising and extolling [this] throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas?
The commentary states:

At the end of the verse on the *dharmadhātu*, the inexhaustibility of the Buddha’s virtues is concluded; here, it is the inexhaustibility of the virtues of the bodhisattvas of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) that is concluded.
As for the mention of "the ten practices and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

The conclusion of the tenth dedication states: "All sentient beings may be counted, and the mental dimensions of the three periods of time may also be known; yet the limits of the merit of such sons of the Buddhas, Samantabhadra, can never be measured."

One might reach the limit of space by measuring it with a single hair; one might know the number of atoms in all the lands; yet the conduct, dwellings, vows, and practices of these great sages, the sons of the Buddhas, are immeasurable.
"This dedication of the fetters toward practice and vows is inexhaustible.

At the end of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, it says: "The lands of the ten directions could be ground into dust, and their number known in a single thought; the space traversed by a hair-tip could be measured, yet even speaking of this for billions of eons, it could never be exhausted."
The reason for stating this is to clarify that the virtues of these aforementioned ten stages (*bhūmi*) are inexhaustible.
Thus, we know that at the conclusion of each stage, rank, category, and virtue, the term "inexhaustible" is appended; therefore, this is not merely the concluding transmission of a single section.
The Commentary states: "That 'the arrival of the sutras is not yet exhausted does not necessarily mean they will follow later' refutes the fifth master.

The phrase "not necessarily" allows for the possibility that more may follow, though it is not certain; as seen, for example, at the end of the "Vairocana Chapter" or the end of the "Anuvyañjana Chapter," and so forth.
Since it is not necessarily the case [that they exist], it is difficult to establish them with certainty.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The retinue and the circulation are spoken of only in terms of their meaning," this refers to the sixth master. Because he speaks of the three vehicles as a differentiation within the One Buddha Vehicle based on doctrinal principles, the fundamental wheel of Dharma subsumes those retinues; thus it is said that the various scriptures are gathered as its retinue. Why, then, must those [scriptures] be taken as this specific circulation?
Within this [text], there is an established order; why rely solely on that [other] order for its circulation?
The commentary states, "Therefore, following Master Huiyuan," which concludes the three points by returning to the correct meaning.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ancients said that within these nine assemblies, there are five instances of major thematic questions and answers,” the intention of the commentary is to maintain four such instances; thus it cites the ancient explanation because the fifth lacks a major thematic question and answer.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the narration of the past; second, from "The ancient masters [say] that Sudhana... onwards, the secret revelation of the present meaning.

There are two underlying intentions, and thus [the sections] are only four: first, because the fifth does not have a major thematic position as a question; second, because the fifth belongs to the *Pravartana* (Circulation) section. Therefore, it says: "Since it is now judged to be included in the *Pravartana*, there are only the preceding four."
The fourth section should be titled "The Section on Entering through Realization Based on Persons and Accomplishing Virtue.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Taking the propagation [of the teaching] together makes five sections," this accords with the ancient interpretation. Since the first section already encompasses the introductory portion (*nidāna*) of the entire work, it is not divided into five sections within the main body (*śarīra*) itself; therefore, taking the propagation as the fifth section is logically consistent and without contradiction.
However, because there was no question regarding a "great position" (*mahāsthāna*), the commentary combines them into four.

The commentary states, "Third, classifying according to the meaning following the text," which means that based on the extant text, there are only four [sections], as these are the four great questions concerning the four positions.
Within the second division, there are two meanings—differentiation and equality—hence it is divided into five cycles of cause and effect.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The first five stages clarify the cause, while the latter eight characteristics clarify the fruit": this is based on one perspective; since the eight characteristics are the manifestations of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are subsumed under the category of the fruit.

If one speaks according to the ultimate reality, it is only from the fourth door downward among the powers of the Tathāgata that they constitute the fruit; the preceding one hundred and ninety-six doors are all subsumed under the category of causes.
If the eight aspects are taken as the fruit, there are nineteen categories for the fruit, while all others belong to the cause.
It is called "transcendental cause and fruit" because the title of this chapter signifies its departure from the mundane world.
Regarding the statement, "It is also called the cause and effect of accomplishing practice," this is because the designation of the stages is set aside, as the intent lies in the practice itself.

As for the commentary’s phrase, "The fourfold scheme of sequential folding," although there are ten layers, they are collectively divided into two parts; one folds them backward from the end, removing the subsequent sections at each stage and dividing the preceding portion into two.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the first stage, the ten stages of faith and practice,' this explains the meaning by means of the forty-two stages.

Since the ten faiths have not yet constituted formal stages and serve merely as the causes for abiding, the *Renwang jing* designates the ten abidings as the ten faiths; it takes that which can establish faith to designate the abidings that are established thereby."
The commentary’s section titled “Five: The Interlocking Chain of Antecedents and Consequents” represents a new interpretation.
This section consists of two parts:
first, a general heading; second, the formal explanation.
The commentary states: "First, the first assembly constitutes the causal and resultant environment (*niśraya-vipāka*)," and so forth; this is the second section, the formal explanation.
Furthermore, the text contains ten sections: first, the five chapters at the beginning of the sutra;
second, the "Vairocana Chapter"; [and so on].
The three chapters from "Names" (Nāman) downward constitute one section;
the twenty-three chapters from "Inquiry into Knowledge" (Prajñāparipṛcchā) to "Abodes" (Vihāra) constitute one section;
and the three chapters from "Inconceivable" (Acintya) to "Secondary Marks" (Anuvyañjana) constitute one section.
Six, the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," constitutes one section;
seven, the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata," constitutes one section;
eight, the "Chapter on Transcending the World," constitutes one section.
The ninth chapter, "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*), constitutes a single section.
Since the beginning and the end are not repeated, there are only eight layers of cause and effect in total.
Because the ninth, "Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), and the tenth, "Dharma Realm," each constitute their own layer of cause and effect, the work thus comprises ten chapters.
Below the "Chapter on the Inconceivability of the Five Appropriations" in the Commentary, this section on cause and effect consists of four parts:
first, the formal exposition; second, the resolution of objections; third, the citation of scriptural evidence; and fourth, the concluding summary.
The initial text is clear.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because ‘inconceivable’ and so forth serve as the fruit for what precedes,” there are two ways to resolve the objection.
That is to say, there may be a question such as this:
The two meanings of differentiation and perfect interfusion are not identical; how then can the previously mentioned differentiated fruit become a perfectly interfused fruit?
Therefore, the general intent is this:

although the scriptural passages such as those in the *Acintya-sūtra* are one and the same, because the perspectives from which they are viewed differ, the fruit is distinct from the cause, thereby establishing differentiated causes and effects.
The fruit itself is perfectly interfused, thereby accomplishing the fruit of perfect interfusion.
What is called "perfect interfusion" means that each and every virtue pervades the Dharma-realm;
furthermore, within each of the thirty-six gates, ten phrases are contained.
Because the characteristics described therein are difficult to measure;
and because the title of this chapter is designated as "Inconceivable" (*acintya*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "However, there are six meanings," the third section provides scriptural citations as proof.

It is established that the three chapters beginning with "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) constitute the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct, while the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct" constitutes the cause of the inconceivable and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the section on the mutual connection between cause and effect, causes are generally presented after effects”: within the five cycles of cause and effect, the two effects—namely, that which is believed and that which is realized—occupy the preceding positions; furthermore, even prior to the specific causes, there is already an effect. Therefore, it is said that “causes are generally preceded by effects.”
Now, here too, the effect precedes the cause; the principle of classification is the same.

As for what is called the "section on the mutual connection of cause and effect," this refers to the third section above, "Classifying Text According to Meaning," meaning that five sections are established based on the meaning of the mutual connection between cause and effect.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “After the twenty-four and forty-eight [marks], there is no further proof,” etc.: from the *Acintya* chapter up to the *Anuvyañjana* chapter, these belong exclusively to the fruits of differentiation.
Once cause and effect have reached their conclusion, there ought to be the manifestation of auspicious omens as a sign of their fulfillment; yet now, there are none.

Since the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" pertains solely to the causes for the manifestation [of the Buddha-body] and has not yet spoken of the fruit, how could there be any such sign of fulfillment?
It is known that the *Samantabhadra-caryā* has a concluding summary, as it belongs to the preceding sections such as the *Acintya*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Third, at the beginning of the *Samantabhadra-parivarta*, there is no separate introductory narrative”: if this chapter did not belong to the preceding sections, there ought to have been a separate introduction at its start;
since there is no such introduction, it is clear that it belongs to what precedes.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Fourth, by means of the meaning,” and so forth: the merit of the fruition is inconceivable; it cannot be regarded merely as a differentiated fruit.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Fifth, although there was a question previously,” and so forth: this refers to the question at the beginning of the second assembly.
Furthermore, the reason for asking again is that one wishes to show that the "inconceivable" section below [the preceding text] is the beginning of the perfectly interfused cause and effect.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Sixth, at the beginning of the second assembly there are already the three karmas,” etc., it means that if there were no fruit previously, one must take the "inconceivable" section and others as the distinct fruits.

Since [the preceding] already exists, this section on the "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) and so forth belongs entirely to the subsequent part; the differentiation of cause and effect in the preceding section is also sufficient.
The commentary’s phrase "by these six meanings" and below constitutes the fourth conclusion.
Regarding the third interpretation in the commentary, the phrase "attaining Buddhahood and entering Nirvāṇa are also causes for manifestation" serves to refute an external objection.
One might fear an objection being raised such as:
"The 'Chapter on Leaving the World' (Lokottaraparivarta) possesses its own internal cause and effect; how can it be taken as the general cause for manifestation?"
Therefore, this general explanation is provided.
Regarding the commentary’s statement "By departing from the world," etc., it explains the meaning of the cause for manifestation. Regarding the commentary’s "Eight:

Departing from the World," etc., it means that within this very assembly, the self-arising cause and effect are established; "Nine" means that the two assemblies are entirely combined into a single cause and effect; and "Ten" means that the *Entry into the Dharma Realm* constitutes the self-arising cause and effect within this very assembly.

However, although the eighth assembly does not link back to the preceding [sections], the previous "Chapter on Manifestation" has already linked this tenth [assembly] regarding cause and effect; while it does not link to the eighth assembly, the eighth assembly has already linked to the ninth. Therefore, all are termed "linked chains of cause and effect."

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “As for ‘That Sudhana... and so forth,” it is because Sudhana’s successive encounters serve as the cause, while Samantabhadra’s exposition of the Buddha’s virtues serves as the fruit.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “The sixfold division of the *Anugata-parivarta*,” this does not involve a detailed sub-division; rather, it simply divides the thirty-nine chapters directly into ten sections.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The section ‘II. The Manifestation of Signs’ and below clarifies the boundless great function of the Buddha-fruit”: the meaning of the “great function” in the *Manifestation of Signs* chapter is readily apparent.

Regarding the "great function" of the Samantabhadra-samādhi: it is because Samantabhadra, through his shared empowerment, arrives without coming; because there is no obstruction regarding the unity and multiplicity, or the extension and contraction [of time and space]; and because the light from a single pore in praising his virtues reaches everywhere without exception.

The accomplishment of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha) explains that the Tathāgata pervades the pure Dharma-realm and universally responds throughout the ocean of lands, causing the environment and its inhabitants to interpenetrate and every atom to contain the Dharma-realm; all of these are boundless, great functions.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “The tenth section, ‘The Instruction and Realization of the Good Friends by Sudhana’”: if one were to follow the heading which states, “according to their respective assemblies,” there would be one section for each assembly, resulting in only nine sections.
To manifest the fulfillment of ten, the final one is divided.

According to the actual facts, there should be ten assemblies to represent the perfection [of the teaching]; however, as perhaps the scriptures have not yet arrived in their entirety, I shall for now provide an explanation based on the extant text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one were to open up the assemblies of the various nāgas and the three vehicles,” etc.: if the text were divided into one hundred and twenty sections, then the assemblies of the various nāgas and the three vehicles would all be subsumed under the assembly of Sudhana.
Because the initial arrival at the City of Blessings was primarily for the sake of Sudhana, no separate assemblies for the various vehicles were established there.

Now, although [the Buddha] has reached the City of Blessings, Sudhana and the other two thousand four hundred members of the assembly have not yet left the city; therefore, he first preaches the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm* to benefit the dragons and those of the three vehicles, and thus establishes a separate vehicle for them.
The remainder may be understood.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ten preceding examples each manifest a single principle, yet they are nonetheless inexhaustible,” this constitutes the second section: the formal explanation of the sūtra text.
This section contains three parts:
First, a general summary of the preceding meaning; second, an outline based on the three divisions; third, an exegesis of the sūtra based on the four divisions.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "If one relies on the common usage," this is the second section: a brief outline based on the three divisions.
This section has two parts:
first, a general classification into three divisions; second, a detailed explanation of the two prefaces, beginning with the statement, "In the preface, the text is divided into two.
This [detailed explanation] has three parts:
First is the general outline. Regarding "2.
Connecting the General Application," the text appears at the end of the fifth fascicle; that passage consists of three parts:
first, connecting this world-system; second, connecting the interior of the Flower Treasury World; and third, connecting the exterior of the Flower Treasury World.
Next, from "Now, as for these two prefaces" onwards, they are collectively indicated as being elsewhere.
Third, from "First, regarding the *śraddhā-prasāda*" (the testimony of faith) onwards, the text is divided into three parts:
first, the origin of establishing the preface; second, the reason for establishing the preface; third, a brief explanation of the preface text.

First, regarding the brief statement in the text that "Ānanda requested [instruction]," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he lay down with his head to the north between a pair of śāla trees in Kuśinagara, desiring with single-minded intent to enter nirvāṇa."
Ānanda’s kinsmen had not yet eliminated their affection nor abandoned their desire; their minds were submerged in an ocean of grief from which they could not emerge on their own.
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"You are the one who guards the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha; you should not, like an ordinary person, sink into an ocean of grief."
"All conditioned phenomena are characterized by impermanence; do not grieve.
Furthermore, the Buddha has entrusted the Dharma to you; yet now, out of sorrow and distress, you are neglecting that which was entrusted to you."
You should ask the Buddha:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should we practice the Path?
First, who shall serve as our teacher?"
Second, how should one dwell together with the ill-natured Chandaka?
Third, what words should be uttered at the beginning of a Buddhist sūtra?
Fourth, such various matters of future concern should be asked of the Buddha.

Having heard these words, Ānanda’s heart was somewhat relieved from its distress; aided by the power of mindfulness and the Way, he went to the side of the bed where the Buddha lay at his final rest and questioned the Buddha regarding this matter.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Whether in the present or in my past, rely again upon the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and do not rely upon anything else.
This is explained at length regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, in order to eliminate worldly craving and attachment.
Furthermore, it says:
"From this day forward, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* shall be your teacher.
As taught in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, you should conduct yourself in body, speech, and mind accordingly."
Furthermore, the bhikṣu Chandaka shall be disciplined according to the Dharma of Brahmā.
If his mind becomes supple, he should subsequently be taught the Kātyāyanāvavāda Sūtra, and he will then be able to attain the Way.
Moreover, this is the treasury of the Dharma-jewels accumulated by me over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; as the very beginning of this treasury, it should be spoken thus:
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in a certain region, in a certain country, in a certain grove of trees.
This is my gateway to the Dharma; at the beginning, it should be spoken in this manner.
Why is this? Because the sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time all begin with these words.
Now, at the beginning of my sūtra as well, it should likewise state: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling... and so forth.
Therefore, it is said as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "and as stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*," according to the fifth fascicle of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, it says: "The Buddha told Ānanda:
'I now entrust this treasury of the true Dharma to you; do not allow it to be destroyed.'"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should I now cultivate the Dharma-eye?
Furthermore, how should I compile the Dharma-eye?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when the great assembly of bhikṣus gathers to compile the Dharma and Vinaya, those great virtuous ones will have Mahākāśyapa as their leader."
"Ānanda! Those venerable bhikṣus should ask in this way:
'In what place did the World-Honored One speak the Mahāpadāna?'"
"In what place was the Mahānidāna spoken?
And so on, up to: in what place were the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka spoken?
"Ānanda! [the Buddha replied.]
When the bhikṣus have asked thus, you should answer:
"Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying under the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having newly attained perfect enlightenment."
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the city of Gayā.
Thus, and so forth, until it says: "Thus have I heard."
At one time the Buddha was staying at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara, by the banks of the Ādira-vatī River, between a pair of śāla trees. ...
[omitted] ... When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire great assembly rejoiced greatly, received it with reverence, and practiced accordingly.
"Ānanda! You should compile the Eye of the Dharma in this manner.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
The above constitutes the origin; that is, it sets forth the original reasons for the work.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one examines the reasons why [this was written], there are six points,” this refers to the second purpose for establishing the introduction.

The commentary states: “Now, setting aside my own views and following what I have heard” and below, the text above is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhilun), while the section below represents Master Seng’s intention, which establishes the meaning of the treatise.
The commentary states: “If one follows the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*” and below, this is a brief explanation of the third part of the preface.
This section has two parts:

first, citing two treatises to show the differences in their methods of categorization; second, from "However, regarding the two matters of faith and hearing" onwards, distinguishing between the general and the specific.

This means that while the phrase *evam mayā śrutam* (Thus have I heard) appears only at the beginning of a sutra, its meaning extends throughout all nine assemblies, signifying that "I have heard all such dharma-meanings."
Regarding "the time and the subject both being general," at the beginning of every assembly it is said, "At that time, the World-Honored One," and so forth.
Regarding "the location and the assembly both being specific," [examples include] Makhadeva’s assembly, which is not the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; thus, the location is specific.
Because the names of the bodhisattvas from the ten Buddha-fields differ, and because the new and old bodhisattvas are likewise distinct.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one follows the phenomenal aspects, it is so,” and so forth: since a single assembly is in fact all assemblies, how could there be a multitude that is not universally pervasive?
The sub-commentary states: "The section 'Above, briefly based on the three divisions' and below marks the third part, which uses a four-part topical outline (ko) to explain the text.
The sub-commentary has two sections:
first, a general clarification; second, a specific explanation beginning with 'Regarding the first.'"
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the preface to the past;

second, the exposition of what has now been heard. Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "If one follows the meaning according to the text, it may be divided into three," and continuing with "The meaning of a sūtra such as this," the commentary text consists of two sections.
First, a preliminary introduction to the previous interpretation; second, clarifying what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, a combined explanation of faith and hearing; second, a separate explanation of faith and hearing.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation of its characteristics, beginning with the passage: "Such statements proceed according to four meanings.
First, regarding the statement "proceeding by way of analogy," it is as some say:
In wealth and nobility he is like Vaiśravaṇa; the Dharma thus transmitted and heard is as the Buddha has taught.
This means that what the Buddha has taught is like Vaiśravaṇa.
What I now transmit is like a wealthy and noble person; thus, the Buddha’s teaching serves as the analogy.
There is also a saying:
"These words and phrases are just as I heard them in the past"; this uses what was heard in the past as an analogy for what is being heard now, and is therefore called an "illustration" (aupamya).
Therefore, some have explained it as follows:
"Like" (*yathā*) refers to the similarity between two phenomena, while "is" (*iti*) refers to the non-deviation of a single phenomenon;
"similarity" is merely a metaphor.
The Commentary states: "Second, 'relying on the instructions' means that one should listen thus to what I have heard in the past; this refers to the instruction of the transmitter of the Dharma.
There is also a tradition which says it refers to the Buddha's own instruction."
That is to say: "This is what my Buddha has taught; you should listen attentively.
It is like someone saying:
"You should recite the sūtras and śāstras in this manner."
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Third, based on questions and answers," it means that the assembly asked:
"What you are about to say—did you hear it previously?
Therefore, he answered as follows:
Thus have I heard.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "permission for the four reliances," it means that at the time of the compilation, the assembly of bodhisattvas collectively requested:
"Just as you have heard it, so should you speak."
The Dharma-transmitting Bodhisattva then granted permission, saying:
"It shall be spoken thus, just as I have heard it.
Speak these words accordingly:"
"I shall act for you in this way, I shall do this, and I shall speak thus," and so forth.
Furthermore, "granting permission" means that one may say with confidence, "This matter is indeed thus."
That is to say, regarding such teachings as I have heard in the past:
this matter is exactly thus; it should be explained precisely to this extent, and there is certainly no difference.
For these four reasons, the phrase "Thus have I heard" is placed at the beginning of every sutra.
However, the general intent of the preceding [passage] pervades these four meanings and does not constitute a separate meaning.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Other interpretations exist, but their intent is no different from the former," the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text) separately enumerates nine meanings:
first, it takes the general explanation as one meaning.
Next, by using the four specific [explanations] above, the five meanings are established in sequence.

Regarding the sixth, the second interpretation within the "Permission" (*anujñā*) section states: "Furthermore, 'permission' may mean that one can speak with faith. This is the Great Dharma Master’s re-explanation of the fourth "Permission," not a separate meaning;
even if there were alternative interpretations, they would largely coincide with this "Permission."

Furthermore, citing the *Guṇavatī-śāstra* as the seventh explanation, it says: "The phrase 'Thus have I heard' indicates that this sutra was expounded by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, based on his direct realization, and was not composed by himself."
This is likewise merely a summary of the general intent of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.

Regarding the eighth [point], the citation from the Tripiṭaka Master Dīrghanakha’s explanation based on the Three Jewels: if a Mahāyāna master were to employ it, it would constitute an analytical explanation (*vibhāga-vyākhyā*) such as this, which shall be cited below.

The ninth citation from Dharma Master Yun of the Liang Dynasty states: “Regarding ‘Thus have I heard’ (evam mayā śrutam): when about to transmit the Dharma as it was heard, one must first set forth the title of the work, stating that such-and-such a sutra-teaching is what I heard from the Buddha.”
This is also entirely consistent with the general purport of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.
Therefore, it says: "There are further alternative explanations," meaning that their intent does not differ from what preceded.
Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary beginning with "If one explains by way of separation," this is the second section: the separate explanation of faith and hearing.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the two characters "ru" (如是) are explained together as terms signifying faith and compliance.
However, the treatise states in full: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma: faith is that by which one enters; wisdom is that by which one crosses over."
Such a state is precisely pure faith.
If there is pure faith within a person's mind, that person is able to enter the Buddha-dharma;
if there is no pure faith, one should know that such a person does not enter the Buddha-dharma.
The non-believer says that this matter is not so; this is the characteristic of non-belief.
The believer says that this matter is thus; this is the characteristic of belief.

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, “Therefore, Master Zhao said,” the following is Master Zhao’s explanation. It merely employs the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidulun) and does not represent a separate principle; for this reason, the commentary states, “Therefore, Master Zhao said.”

Furthermore, there are those who add the following before the passage concerning Zhaoseng: "Faith is the primary foundation for entering the Dharma; wisdom is the profound art of ultimate realization.
When faith is present, the principles of what is taught accord with reality; when they accord, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected."
"Because of faith, the Dharma that is taught can be followed; because of this following, both the teacher and the disciple are established through the two paths of speaking and listening.

This was also added later by others based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and subsequently further supplemented by Master Zhaokong. Although the words are many, they do not deviate from the truth.

Therefore, the Commentary collected these divergent interpretations and established them as separate expositions; where the intent was identical despite the difference in wording, these were all omitted and not preserved.
Later generations, unaware of this, followed suit through successive generations, listing them all as distinct interpretations.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Some say that the Sage preaches the Dharma,” and so forth: the following section explains by proceeding from the narrow to the broad.
This first point is the most restricted, taking only the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as its basis; it is the interpretation of Liu Qiu for the *Wu liang yi jing*.

The Commentary states: "If one says 'such words as these'... This and what follows is the interpretation of Emperor Wu of Liang; here, it refers to the expressive capacity (*vācaka*) to comprehensively express both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

The Commentary further states: "'Some say that 'as such' refers to words that accord with the truth'"; this encompasses both the expressive and the expressed (*vācya-vācaka*), including both phenomena and principle.
"Principle" (li) refers to the underlying logic, not merely *tathatā* (suchness).
This concerns Master Sheng’s commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Under the section "This clarifies that when explaining phenomena, they are explained according to the phenomena," this represents a supplementary explanation by Master Yuan based on the Dharma within Master Sheng’s own interpretation; its intent is to clarify that Master Sheng’s meaning is identical to Master Yuan’s.
However, that text explains it as follows: "First, it is explained in terms of the Dharma.
It is called 'Tathā' (Thus) because Ānanda said that what was spoken by the Tathāgata is 'thus' with respect to all dharmas.
He speaks of principle as it truly is, speaks of phenomena as they truly are, speaks of causes as they truly are, and speaks of effects as they truly are."
Words that accord with the Dharma are consistent with principle; therefore, they are called "thus" (*evam*).
Since that which deviates from the Dharma is termed "not-so" (*na-evam*), words that accord with the Dharma can be designated as "so."
Although his words are numerous, they are merely words of principle; thus, he does not differ from Master Sheng. The Commentary states:

“Rong says that ‘suchness’ (ru-shi) is the beginning of response and stimulus. This means taking the character *ru* (such) as the Buddha’s response and the character *shi* (this) as the sentient being’s stimulus; therefore, it is broader than what preceded it.
From the passage "Based on the Sūtra, regarding response and stimulus" (*yīnggǎn*) onwards, he addresses potential objections.
He anticipates an objection, saying:
"If the 'as-it-is' (*rú*) is itself the response (*yìng*), and this is itself the stimulus (*gǎn*), why is it not called 'my hearing of the stimulus and response' (*gǎnyìng wówén*)?"
Therefore, this general interpretation is provided.
As for those who cite this as an explanation from the *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, that commentary is merely Master Liu’s [Zhiyi] exposition based on the principles of Master Yong (Sengrong).
Following the section "The various interpretations above," the second part sets forth the present selection and rejection.
Within this [section], there are two parts:
first, a general admission; second, the formal presentation of what is to be accepted and rejected.

Regarding the former, the statement "there are further commentaries whose words differ but whose meaning is the same" refers to the explanation given by the Tripitaka Master Dīrghaśravaṇa concerning the Three Jewels: "First, with respect to the Buddha, because the Buddhas of the three periods of time all teach without difference, it is called 'Tathā' (Thus)."
"Because they are taught in the same way, they are called 'is' (shì).
This is largely the same as the Emperor of Liang's [view].
Second, regarding the Dharma, it says: "The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not differ between past and present; therefore, it is called 'suchness' (*tathatā*)."
"The Tathāgata spoke for this purpose; therefore, it is called 'is' (evam).
This is the same as Master Liu’s view: when the Sage preaches the Dharma, he does so solely to manifest the *tathatā* (suchness).

Third, regarding the Saṃgha, the commentary explains: "Because Ānanda heard [the teachings], and compared them to what the Buddha taught, what was transmitted did not differ; therefore, it is named 'as' (*yathā*, i.e., *tathā*)."
"Because it is forever free from faults and errors, it is called 'thus' (*tathā*).
This accords with the general purport of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, and thus it is said that while the words differ, the meaning is the same.

Furthermore, Master Baohui explains this in terms of being free from the five types of slander, stating: "The first phrase is 'thus. Because this sūtra is free from the attachment of the superimposition slander (*samāropa-paryādāna*), it says 'thus.'"
The second phrase is thus; this sutra avoids the second attachment, which is the denial of existence (apavāda).
The third phrase is thus; this sutra avoids the third attachment, which is the contradictory denial of both existence and non-existence.
The fourth phrase is thus: this sutra avoids the fourth clinging—the deluded denial that [reality] is neither existent nor non-existent.
The fifth phrase is thus: this sutra avoids the fifth clinging—the conceptual proliferation of denial that [reality] is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent.
"These five types of denial above are fully encompassed by words that accord with reason.

Furthermore, since the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s explanation based on the two truths maintains that once one is free from existence and non-existence, one is likewise free from both [existence and non-existence] and neither [existence nor non-existence], it does not differ from the previous explanation.
Therefore, it is said that "the words differ but the meaning is the same.

I have briefly outlined several points; there are further explanations, which also show that while the phrasing differs, the underlying intent is largely identical. Fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them here.
In the commentary, from "If one relies on the faith of those who produce [sentient beings]" onwards, the second section correctly presents the criteria for adoption and rejection.
This section contains two parts:
first, a general adoption of three meanings; second, a definitive selection based on the central tenet. The text for both parts is readily intelligible.
Regarding the statement, "The adversary opposes the *āyū* of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)," the *Śata-śāstra* says, "The non-Buddhists establish *āyū* as auspicious.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "In the past, the Brahmā King possessed seventy-two characters with which he instructed the world and taught sentient beings."

In later times, as the merit of sentient beings became increasingly diminished, the Brahma King consequently swallowed back seventy characters; he left only one character at each of the two corners of his mouth, which are "a" and "u. These are simply variations in the weight of the Sanskrit vowels, also referred to as "a" and "o."
The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If it is according to the Huayan school," this is the second section, which uses the specific school to establish the definitive meaning; that is, it provides an exegesis based on the teachings (*jiao*).
The preceding [section] applied universally to all teachings.
Now, first I shall present the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), and subsequently, from the passage "one should follow the gates of the teachings" onwards, I shall explain according to the five teachings.

Since these words are thus established as being in accord with principle and clarify the two truths, then for the Śrāvaka vehicle, the person and dharmas constitute the conventional truth, while the emptiness of persons constitutes the ultimate truth.

Within the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching for the gradual), the four levels of truth involve the simultaneous operation of the ultimate and the conventional; in the Final Teaching, the phenomena and principle, as well as the ultimate and conventional, mutually penetrate one another.

As understood by the True Truth (Paramārtha), in the Sudden Teaching, both the ultimate and conventional are transcended; only when words are extinguished and thought is cut off can one be said to accord with the principle.

As in the *Anityatā-sūtra*, terms such as "certainly to be reviled" regarding birth, old age, sickness, and death should be called words that accord with reason; otherwise, what is explained here cannot be so designated.
The other teachings may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary stating, "Second, 'I heard' explains the accomplishment of hearing," the commentary text consists of three parts:

first, a general clarification of the underlying intent; second, a brief explanation beginning with "I am Ānanda"; and third, a resolution of objections and a further explanation beginning with "Why is he called 'I'?"
Within this, there are two parts:
first, an interrogation and explanation of "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*); second, an explanation of what was heard.

Regarding the former, first is an interrogation and explanation of "I," which refers to the conventional person (*pudgala*) composed of the aggregates (*skandha*), a principle that applies across all teachings.
Below the passage "By what means was this heard? there is a re-examination of the term "heard" (wen) to provide a comprehensive explanation that applies to both "I" and "heard.
Within this, first comes the interrogation, followed by a specific explanation according to the teachings, beginning with the section "If one relies on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna."
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); second, the signless (*animitta*); and third, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Within the first, the characteristics of phenomena, both the Hīnayāna and the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*) are included.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation by the former kings (the masters), and second, the resolution of objections.
Now, regarding the first, concerning the "three [aspects] of the Hīnayāna," the Sarvāstivāda school itself maintains three meanings:
The master of treatises Dharmatrāta maintains that hearing is not consciousness.
He asserts that although it is one's own consciousness that hears, it does so only by depending on the sense organ;
however, the essence of hearing is the organ itself, not the consciousness.
As it is with hearing, so it is with seeing and the other senses. Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"The eye itself sees form; it is not the visual consciousness that sees, nor is it wisdom, nor is it their conjunction; therefore, it does not see forms obstructed by barriers."
Second, the teacher Subhūṣaṇa [Miaoyin] maintains that it is consciousness and hearing that perceive, not the ear, because the sense organ lacks sentience.
Third, the teacher Tattvika [Chengshi] maintains that the auditory faculty and its object combine to enable hearing.
These three views are all as explained in the *Dhātunirdeśa* chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Regarding the three aspects of the Mahāyāna, the first is that hearing is not consciousness (*vijñāna*). As the second chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "What is the characteristic of the auditory element (*śrotra-dhātu*)?
It is that which is capable of hearing sounds."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (35) states: "Because one repeatedly applies attention (*manasikāra*) to sound until it reaches the point of being able to hear.
Thus, it is consciousness that hears, not the ear. The Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "There are three meanings of 'hearing':
first, the essence of hearing, which is the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*)."
Second is the equipment for hearing, which refers to sound.
Third is the fruit of hearing, which refers to the wisdom of hearing itself.
It is solely this auditory consciousness that constitutes "correct hearing," though it can hear through the conjunction of the three factors.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness to perceive and receive sound-objects.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Hearing refers to listening; that is, the ear-faculty generates the ear-consciousness, thereby hearing and receiving the teachings."

The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'either possessing four conditions or eight conditions,' this is a general explanation of the meaning of 'hearing through harmony' in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
The previous mention of 'harmony' referred only to the harmony between the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
here, because we are taking up the completeness of the conditions, we speak of 'four' and 'eight.'"
However, these four and eight [factors] are the conditions for the arising of consciousness;
if one includes that which hears as well as the consciousness it engenders, they become either five or nine.
The commentary states that the phrase "or four" refers to the Hīnayāna, namely: first, emptiness; second, the faculty; third, the object; and fourth, attention (*manaskāra*).

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At that time, the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and there is an intention to hear. When the sensory object, the mind, and the attention coincide, auditory consciousness arises; following the arising of auditory consciousness, mental consciousness arises, whereby one is then able to discern various causes and conditions and finally succeeds in hearing the sound."
The commentary states:
Sound exists where it is audible; its locus is emptiness.
The second is mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Because "feeling" (qing) is precisely the sense-faculties (gen).
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* internally designates the "Chapter on the Six Sense-Faculties" as the "Chapter on the Six Feelings.
As the ancients said:

The sense organs (indriya) contain the meaning of consciousness and are termed "sentient" (qing); the objects (viṣaya) are the sensory domains; and the mind (manas) is the mental faculty (manendriya). Adding these makes five, which give rise to auditory consciousness.

When it is said that [consciousness] arises following auditory consciousness, this refers to the arising of mental consciousness (manovijñāna)—that is, the simultaneous mental consciousness performing discrimination—and not the causal condition itself.
If one considers the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) in terms of its conceptual differentiation, then the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is also a condition for it.
"Hearing is attained through various causes and conditions" summarizes the above.

Regarding the "eight conditions," in addition to the previous four, four more are added: first, emptiness; second, the faculty; third, the object; fourth, mental attention (*manasikāra*); fifth, the fundamental support, which is the eighth consciousness; sixth, the support for defilement and purity, which is the seventh consciousness; seventh, the support for discrimination, which is the sixth consciousness; and eighth, the seeds.
The seeds serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) support; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rely upon this support, for they would necessarily not arise were it lacking.
The support of discrimination (*vikalpa*) is the sixth consciousness.
The supporting basis for defilement and purity is the seventh consciousness.
The fundamental supporting basis is the eighth consciousness, because the "root" (indriya) is identical to the supporting basis for the common object.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 4, states: "Therefore, the simultaneous supporting bases of these five consciousnesses are definitely fourfold—namely, the five material sense organs and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses—because they will certainly not function if any one of them is missing, and because their supporting bases differ as the common-object basis, the basis for discrimination, and the basis for defilement and purity."

As a verse says: "Visual consciousness arises from nine conditions; auditory consciousness arises only from eight; those of nose, tongue, and body arise from seven; and the latter three arise from five, four, and three respectively.
If the equal-and-immediate condition is added, one is added to each of the aforementioned."
The commentary states:
Regarding the nine conditions for the eye, "illumination" is added because there is no seeing in the dark.

For the ear, "illumination" has already been excluded; furthermore, "space" is excluded from the remaining seven, because these three [ear, sound, and consciousness] function through their conjunction.
The latter three are the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses].
The six consciousnesses have five conditions; furthermore, they exclude the defiled-pure and the discriminative.
"Discriminative" refers to the consciousness that is produced, while "defiled-pure" refers to the supporting faculty (indriya).

The seventh consciousness has either three or four [aspects].
