Since it is said that one observes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction, this clarifies the ability to universally observe all phenomena with equanimity; thus, it is called "observing equality."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done brings universal benefit through impartiality,” the *Śāstra* says: “This mental state, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, universally manifests various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions.”
"This is the meaning of universal benefit; since it makes no distinction between enemy and kin, is this not impartiality?
Regarding the commentary's statement, "The four wisdoms are perfectly interfused and subsumed within a single phrase," this is an expression of praise for its excellence.

Regarding the statement, "The lower body and speech are all manifestations of the four wisdoms," this clarifies the intent behind employing the four wisdoms here. Since the Buddha’s virtues described in the subsequent text correspond to the explanation of the four wisdoms in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it is said that they are all manifestations of the four wisdoms; therefore, it is appropriate to employ the four wisdoms as the interpretation for the general [section].
The Commentary states: “Because the four wisdoms are perfectly interfused and non-dual in nature. This concludes the third section, which addresses potential objections.
It refers to a challenge that might be raised as follows:
“The four wisdoms of enlightenment are conditioned and untainted; they are not the tenet of our scripture. How can they be intermingled in the explanation of this profound principle?”

Therefore, it is now generally stated that both the Nature (xìng) and Characteristic (xiàng) schools possess the four wisdoms of bodhi; they differ only slightly in their interpretation, yet there is no error in their application.
This is because "perfect fusion without duality" is one of its meanings; thus, that school maintains that the four [wisdoms] must not be conflated.
Now it is clarified that a single wisdom inherently possesses the four wisdoms; therefore, below in the "Appearance" chapter, the four precious jewels are used as a metaphor for these four wisdoms.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"
For example, the great ocean possesses four precious jewels endowed with immeasurable virtues, which are able to produce all the rare treasures within the sea.
If these jewels were not present in the great ocean, not even a single treasure could be found.
What are the four?
First is named Accumulated Jewels; second is named Inexhaustible Treasury; third is named Free from Blazing Heat; and fourth is named Fully Adorned.
O Son of the Buddha!
These four precious jewels cannot be seen by any ordinary beings, nor by devas, nāgas, spirits, and the like. Why is this?
Sāgara, the Dragon King, places this precious jewel—stately, upright, and square—within the most secret and secluded part of his palace.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same with the great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; within it there are four great jewels of wisdom, complete with immeasurable merit and wisdom. From these, the jewels of wisdom of all sentient beings—whether Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, those in the stages of training or beyond training, and all Bodhisattvas—are produced.
What are these four?

First, the Great Jewel of Wisdom of the Great Perfect Mirror-like Cognition (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is free from all conceptualization and is called "untainted" because its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know; due to its skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it never forgets nor is it deluded regarding the characteristics of any object.

Second, the Great Jewel of Wisdom of the Equality of Nature (*samatā-jñāna*), which skillfully discriminates between conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; observing the characteristics of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—whether pertaining to oneself or others—is called "skillful means," while the equality in benefiting others is called "skillful discrimination."

The Great Wisdom Jewel of the Threefold Sublime Discerning Wisdom, which differentiates and explains immeasurable dharmas without destroying the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is this wisdom that skillfully observes the specific and general characteristics of all dharmas and functions without obstruction; therefore, it is said that it explains immeasurable dharmas without destroying the nature of phenomena.

Regarding the "immeasurable dharmas," this refers to the teaching that encompasses the gateways of the inexhaustible *dhāraṇī* and meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it rains down the great Dharma rain to sever all doubts.

It is the great jewel of wisdom—the fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done—which never errs regarding the appropriate or inappropriate time, because it acts as it ought to act by knowing the capacities of beings and the proper timing.
If these four jewels did not exist within the great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgatas, it would be impossible for even a single sentient being to enter the Mahāyāna.
These are called the Jewels of Wisdom, which sentient beings of meager merit are unable to see.
Why is this? Because they are established within the profound and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Each and every wisdom is described as even, upright, pure, and exquisite, for it possesses the virtues of the four wisdoms.
How much more so when they share the same nature and are clearly interpenetrating?

As for the statement that "cultivation gives rise to that which is originally present because they are neither identical nor different," this second point differs from the tenets of that [other] school.
In that school, the four wisdoms are produced through cultivation, while nirvana is inherently existent.

Now, these four wisdoms are precisely the wisdom of original enlightenment; the four wisdoms produced through cultivation do not possess a separate substance, just as when gold forms images, the gold and the image are not distinct.
The Commentary states: "However, from 'the superior is able to awaken' onwards is the third section, the summary.

The reason for this summary is that it seeks to clarify that a single *bodhi*-body already possesses both the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*; how much more so, then, does it possess the [remaining] nine below."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, its lower body and bodily karma,” etc., the commentary consists of two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words, “The Dharma-body is universally pervasive.”
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the individual pervasiveness according to characteristics; second, the pervasive totality through perfect fusion.
Now, the first.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, by means of the three bodies, [the ten are] clarified" explains that the ten are subsumed into three.

Here it is clarified that the fundamental essence of the *dharmakāya* is all-pervasive; the *jñānakāya*, being accomplished through cultivation, is pervasive in accordance with that essence; and the *rūpakāya* is pervasive as the function of that essence.
The *dharmakāya* is pervasive like space; the *jñānakāya* is pervasive like sunlight; and the *rūpakāya* is pervasive like the shadow of the sun.
The commentary states: "All are perfectly pervasive," which below serves to specifically demonstrate the characteristic of pervasiveness.
Since all three bodies are as described below, it says "all are.
To say "all are perfectly pervasive" means that whether great or small, they are all complete and perfect.
Regarding "pervasion that is not by parts," this does not mean analyzing and dispersing [the object] so as to cause it to pervade.
The phrase "referring to all" below indicates the characteristic of perfect pervasion:
even a minute speck of dust is perfectly pervasive; if it were coarse, it would be easy to perceive.
Regarding "viewing as a whole, it also appears": throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is only a single Buddha, for the Buddha-body pervades the dharma-realm.
Regarding "viewing individually, it also appears": one then perceives the entire body within each and every land and within each and every atom.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "Just as one sees the Buddha seated in this place, so it is in all atoms of dust.
The Buddha’s body neither goes nor comes, yet all lands appear clearly within it. This is precisely that.

Furthermore, regarding the perspective of the general and the particular: generally, the entire body is present in every location; specifically, each limb and faculty—such as the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue—is individually pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Thus, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "How is it that the Buddha’s eye is immeasurable? His ears, nose, tongue, and body are likewise so," and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, 'the lands and so forth are precisely my own body' and below" refers to the second [section], the universal inclusion through mutual interpenetration.

This means that while the preceding section clarified that the three bodies (trikāya) are the pervader and not the pervaded lands, the present section clarifies that the pervader is precisely the pervaded, because the subject and object are mutually fused.
Furthermore, it clarifies that each individual bodily form is fused, harmonized, intermingled, and pervasive. Moreover,
whereas the preceding section discussed the ten bodies of the Buddha— namely, the bodies of enlightenment, vow, transformation, power, adornment, and so forth—
this section clarifies the ten bodies of unimpededness within the three worlds, namely the bodies of the land, sentient beings, and so forth.
How could the ten bodies and their manifestations not be harmoniously integrated? Therefore, it is said they are "like the light of a lamp.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, if there are hundreds of thousands of lamps in a dark room, the light of each lamp pervades the entire room; so too is it with the bodies and wisdom of all Buddhas."
The Commentary states: "The phrase 'For example, the following illustrations clarify' [is divided] into two parts within the commentary:
first, a general explanation of the main intent; second, a detailed explanation by opening the chapters.
This is the first."

Regarding the statement, "The three karmas of the Buddha cannot be illustrated by any analogy," the end of the eightieth fascicle says: "All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent within the triple world, cannot serve as metaphors for the Buddha."
For example, among the birds and beasts of the mountains and forests, there is none that dwells by relying upon space.

Only such true dharmas as the emptiness of space (*ākāśa*), true thusness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and quiescence (*śānti*) can be manifested within the Tathāgata.
This is precisely the text [of that sūtra].

Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "As it is said in the sūtras: 'Even all the designations and metaphors employed to illustrate the merits of the Tathāgatas are entirely slanders of the Tathāgatas.'"
"Except for one single analogy— that of empty space— which can serve as a metaphor for the Tathāgata,
because his immeasurable merits such as morality are identical to empty space.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "However, regarding empty space as a metaphor, there are similarities and differences," the first two lines present the heading, while the subsequent part explains these two aspects.
First, the explanation of the distinction refers to the passage on the fifth dedication.
This clarifies that the Buddha possesses the virtue of self-benefit, which is unlike empty space, which cannot benefit itself.

As for the phrase "and so forth," it includes the subsequent scriptural passage which states: "In all places, causing all sentient beings to accumulate roots of goodness until they are fully satisfied."
This clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses the virtue of benefiting others, which is not shared by empty space.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Now, taking up the similarities,” the two explanations of the meaning of “similarity” refer only to partial similarity.

Regarding the statement, "The various meanings of 'sameness' are as follows in the Chapter on the Ten Patiences," this refers to the tenth patience, that of the likeness to space. The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva realizes that all dharma-realms are like empty space, because they are without marks."
All worlds are like empty space, because they are without arising.
All phenomena are like empty space, because they are non-dual.
The conduct of all sentient beings is like empty space, because there is no place for it to proceed.
All Buddhas are like space, because they are without discrimination.
All powers of the Buddhas are like space, because they are without distinction.
All meditative concentrations are like space, because they are equal throughout the three periods of time.
All dharmas that are spoken of are like space, because they cannot be expressed in words.
All Buddha-bodies are like space, because they are unattached and unimpeded.
The commentary states:
Regarding the passage cited above, if one takes it in its general sense, "signlessness," "non-arising," and so forth all possess many meanings of emptiness (*ākāśa*).

If one takes them in their specific characteristics, they refer exclusively to non-conceptuality, non-differentiation, and non-attachment/non-obstruction, as these are used as metaphors for the Buddha, the Buddha’s powers, and the Buddha’s body.
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage on that patience, it says: "For example, like space, all phenomena depend upon it; it neither arises nor perishes.
It further states: "It is indestructible."
It further states: "That which is the support for all worlds, yet has no support itself.
It also states: "Without birth or cessation, it is able to sustain the birth and cessation of all worlds."
It is further said: "Without direction or corners, yet it can manifest all directions and corners.
It is also said: "Neither moving nor staying, yet it can display various modes of deportment."
It is further said: "Neither form nor non-form, yet it can manifest all manner of forms.
It is also said: "Neither distant nor near, yet it can abide for a long time and manifest all things."
It is further said: "Neither pure nor defiled, yet not apart from purity and defilement.
It is also said: "All worlds appear before it, yet it does not appear before all worlds."

Furthermore, it is said: "Universally entering all things yet being without limit," and so forth; these all metaphorically represent bodhi. The sūtra contains the corresponding applications, which are now omitted for brevity.

The analogy for the Buddha also possesses all the aforementioned meanings; since the stage of the ten kinds of patience (*daśakṣānti*) is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it may be equated with the Buddha.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "Now there are two analogies," this is the second section, which opens the chapter for a detailed explanation.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a general manifestation of the characteristics of the analogy; second, the analogy of that which is being analogized; third, the concluding demonstration of its ultimate resort.
Now, for the first part, it may be understood.
The Commentary states: "Using these four similes to illustrate the mental karma" (*manas-karman*) and below, it provides the similes for what they illustrate.
These distinct similes for the three types of karma are divided into three sections.

Ancient commentators used only the preceding similes to illustrate mental karma, while using the subsequent similes for bodily and verbal karma; they used the general simile for the body and the specific simile for speech.
Now, all three types of karma are illustrated by metaphors; however, by citing the scriptural texts as evidence, they can be clearly understood.
First, regarding the metaphor for mental karma (*manas-karma*), the text is divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation citing the sūtra; second, a detailed clarification according to its specific characteristics.
First: Regarding the statement, "The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space," this applies to both the two wisdoms and the four wisdoms.

However, the subsequent three lines state: "Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, fully understanding all the delusive thoughts of the world, and not giving rise to various different discriminations."
To realize that worldly delusions are themselves the wisdom of measurement (pramāṇa-jñāna) is non-arising discrimination, which is precisely the wisdom of principle (naya-jñāna).
Now, by taking only the vastness that is equal to space, both [the two and the four] are equally vast; therefore, it is called "total" (zong).
In the commentary, following the phrase "the wisdom of measure encompasses and pervades," the second section provides a detailed explanation according to their specific characteristics.
This consists of two parts:
first, an illustration of the two wisdoms; second, an illustration of the four wisdoms.

From the preceding [analogy], one takes the sense of "inclusion" contained therein; from the subsequent analogy, one takes the sense of "pervasiveness. These two senses together illustrate the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).
Because valid cognition knows specific distinctions, it resembles the sense of inclusion;
because there is no phenomenon it does not know, this is the sense of pervasiveness.

Regarding the statement, "The wisdom of principle and phenomena enters [reality] without discrimination," the former analogy illustrates the meaning of non-discrimination, while the latter analogy illustrates the meaning of entering into equality; taking both meanings together, they serve as metaphors for the wisdom of principle and phenomena.
"Intellect" (jili) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), for it alone is capable of realizing suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Furthermore, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom," the second section employs metaphors to illustrate the four wisdoms.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the initial metaphor illustrates the perfect mirror and the wisdom of equality; second, the subsequent metaphor illustrates the latter two wisdoms.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
First, the characteristics of the metaphors are explained individually; second, the overall meaning of the metaphors is summarized.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the metaphor for the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); second, the metaphor for the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, citing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to prove the sense of inclusion; second, citing the present sutra to simultaneously prove both senses.
This is the first part.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 10, states: "The first is the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). This mental complex is free from all conceptual discrimination; its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to discern. It does not forget nor is it deluded regarding any objective phenomena. Its nature and characteristics are pure, being free from all defilements. It serves as the support for the seeds and manifestations of purely virtuous qualities. It can manifest and generate the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom. Without interruption and without cessation until the end of the future, it is like a great perfect mirror manifesting various forms and images."
The commentary states:
"Pure" means unmixed; "clean" means free from defilement; "perfect" means the sense of fulfillment.

Regarding "the support for manifest and seed": it is the support for manifest virtues and the sustainer of seed virtues, capable of manifesting and generating the reflections of the three wisdoms within the bodies and lands.
The remainder of the text may be understood.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The subsequent scripture says: ‘Bodhi-wisdom manifests universally... and so forth, this is the second section, which cites the current scripture to provide dual proof for two meanings.

First, the scripture says: “For example, it is like the great ocean, which can universally reflect the physical forms and images of all sentient beings within the four continents; therefore, it is collectively called the great ocean.”
"The enlightenment of all Buddhas is also like this.
From "Universally Manifesting" onwards, it is the same as the commentary.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "The phrase 'nothing manifested' means there is no discrimination": the previous manifestation of the mind, desires, and so forth was to demonstrate the meaning of inclusive integration; now, it demonstrates the meaning of non-discrimination.

However, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of *vijñaptimātra* also possesses the meaning of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), as this was already cited in the previous general commentary; therefore, it is omitted here.
Furthermore, regarding the absence of that which is manifested, there are two meanings:
first, that which is manifested is itself empty; second, it manifests without [the presence of] a mind.
Now, we adopt the latter interpretation.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "The Wisdom of Equality," the text itself is twofold:
first, it cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and second, it cites the relevant scripture.
First, the treatise states:

"The mental state associated with the second wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, observes that all phenomena, as well as oneself and other sentient beings, are entirely equal. It is constantly associated with great compassion and other such qualities, and manifests various distinctions of enjoyment-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), lands, and forms according to the inclinations of sentient beings."
"The wisdom of wondrous observation is the unique support [of the Buddha], established by the nirvana of non-abiding, a single flavor that continues uninterruptedly to the end of the future.
The commentary states:
"Because of the grasping at a self during former causal stages, there was the distinction between self and other."
Now that the grasping at a self no longer exists, all things are equal.

Within the inclinations of sentient beings across the ten stages, the state of non-abiding nirvana is established; this consciousness is constantly associated with compassion and wisdom, being of a single flavor and untainted.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is also non-conceptual”: although the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* does not employ the term “non-conceptual” within its discussion of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the present statement that it is “also non-conceptual” carries two intended meanings.
First, according to the *Vijñaptimātratā* system, all four wisdoms universally take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object; therefore, this [wisdom of equality] is non-conceptual.
Second, it is called "non-conceptual" because there is no differentiation with respect to its object.
Regarding the first point, the treatise states: "Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom takes True Suchness as its object, it is non-conceptual."
Because it takes other objects as its conditions, it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Its essence is one, though it is divided into two according to its functions.
Since the understanding of the conventional arises from the realization of the ultimate, it is called "subsequently attained."
"The remaining three parts and two [aspects] should be understood accordingly.
The commentary states:
According to this treatise, each of the four wisdoms encompasses two wisdoms, and all equally encompass both the ultimate (paramārtha) and conventional (saṃvṛti) objects.
Now, for the sake of brevity and emphasis, two superior metaphors are each correlated with two types of wisdom.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The term ‘non-conceptual’ manifests non-differentiation,” this refers to the second meaning.
However, because the two objects of observation are non-conceptual, the observing wisdom is likewise non-conceptual; thus, the term "non-conceptual" indicates the absence of differentiation.
This reveals the meaning of non-conceptuality in the Wisdom of Equality, which differs from the Mirror-like Wisdom.

While the Mirror-like Wisdom is non-conceptual like a clear mirror that has no mind, the Wisdom of Equality is non-conceptual like the sun merging with space—wherein space has no distinct characteristics and is termed "undifferentiated," meaning it does not differentiate between distinct features.
Therefore, the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "One should know that all phenomena are by nature non-conceptual;
because the object of conceptualization does not exist, the subject of conceptualization also does not exist."

The Commentary states: "Therefore, the subsequent scripture says, 'Regarding all meanings, there is nothing to be observed,' and so forth. This is the second citation from the current sutra, specifically from the section on the characteristics of Bodhi within the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*).
The Sūtra states: "O Son of the Buddha!
When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he does not observe any phenomena.

The term "and so forth" (etc. refers to other sūtras which state: "Regarding all dharmas, he is equal and free from doubt; they are non-dual and signless, without activity and without cessation, immeasurable and boundless, far removed from the two extremes and abiding in the Middle Way, transcending all written characters and verbal expressions."
The commentary states:
"Without observation" realizes the non-conceptual meaning of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
From the phrase "equality toward all phenomena" downward, it realizes the non-conceptual meaning of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), while the remaining meanings are simultaneously present.
In the commentary, from "Therefore, the great void" onwards is the second section, which summarizes the meaning of the metaphors; this is clear from the text.

In the commentary, from "Second, the metaphor of pervasiveness" onwards is the second section, which uses the second metaphor to illustrate the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done.
The commentary consists of four parts:
first, citing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*; second, citing the present sutra; third, concluding with the intended meaning of the analogy; and fourth, summarizing the inconceivability.
Now, the first part.

Regarding the term "wonderful observation," the *Treatise* states: "The mental complex associated with the three kinds of wonderful observing wisdom refers to this mental complex which functions without obstruction in skillfully observing the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena. It encompasses and contemplates immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī and meditative concentration, as well as the precious jewels of the merits they produce. Within great assemblies, it can manifest boundless varieties of activity with total mastery, raining down the great Dharma rain to sever all doubts and causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness."
The commentary states:
The functioning of the spirit is without fixed direction; it is termed "subtle" (miao).
To take the specific and general characteristics as conditions is called "contemplation" (guan cha).
The "individual" refers to the distinctness of form, mind, and so forth, while the "shared" refers to their commonality, such as impermanence and the like.

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the shared characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
Regarding the phrase "comprehensively observing" (*saṃgraha-vipaśyanā*): "comprehensively" (*saṃgraha*) has the meaning of "storing" (*kośa*), while "observing" (*vipaśyanā*) means "investigating.

The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) constitute the jewels of merit, while the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth constitute the distinctions of their functional activities.
Since one has already observed the specific and general characteristics of sentient beings, it is clear that there is nothing not known by them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) accomplishes all things without omission; this is the meaning of ‘following entry’,” the treatise says: “The mental state associated with the fourth wisdom, the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, refers to this mental state which, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, universally manifests various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions to accomplish the tasks that ought to be performed through the power of its original vows.”
The commentary states:
Since it is said that the various activities of the three karmas constitute "accomplishing what is to be done," is this not a thorough and detailed accomplishment of things without omission?

This statement corresponds to what is said in the *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*): "It encompasses the transformations of heaven and earth without overstepping them; it completes all things in their particularity without leaving anything out."
The commentary states: "To 'encompass' means to model oneself after Heaven and Earth so as to fully perfect their principles.

To 'accomplish all things through their particularities' means to respond to phenomena by following transformations, rather than being restricted to a single perspective; thus, each thing shall find its proper place."
This explains the virtue of the *I Ching*; it is now used as a metaphor for the virtues of the Buddha.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* concludes: "Although these four classes of consciousness associated with wisdom each definitely possess twenty-two mental factors—wherein the transforming and the transformed, seeds and manifestations, arise together—their cognitive function is predominant, and thus they are designated by the name 'wisdom. Therefore, these four classes collectively encompass all conditioned merits of the Buddha-stage without exception."
The reconciliation of the two schools' doctrines has already been explained above.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The subsequent scripture says, 'The Buddha's wisdom is vast and great,'" this constitutes the second section: citing the relevant scripture to provide an explanation.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and second, the explanation of entry (*anupraveśa*).
In the former, there are four kinds of pervasion:
First, the pervasiveness in terms of the essence of wisdom; second, the pervasiveness in terms of the function of wisdom—these two are precisely from the eightieth sutra, as previously cited.

Third, the pervasiveness in terms of realization through accord, wherein the mind and its object merge in darkness; this refers to the text on Bodhi in the "Manifestation Chapter" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*).
Fourth, regarding the universal nature according to principle: this refers to the meaning cited from the *Awakening of Faith*, which states: "Question:
If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is free from material forms, how can it manifest material forms?"
Answer:
Because this very Dharmakāya is the essence of form (*rūpa*), it is able to manifest as form.

That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual; because the nature of form is itself the nature of wisdom, the essence of form is formless and is therefore called the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
Because the nature of wisdom is identical to the nature of form, it is said that the Dharma-body pervades all places.

The forms manifested therein have no boundaries; according to the mind, they can manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions an infinite variety of bodhisattvas, reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and adornments, each distinct from the others, yet all being without boundaries and mutually non-obstructive.
"This cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of mind-consciousness, because it is the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The commentary states:

This passage can also serve as proof for the pervasiveness of the body below; however, we now take only the sense of the non-difference between its two natures to clarify the pervasiveness of the nature of wisdom.
The previous statement held that the essence of wisdom takes wisdom itself as its substance; now, this refers to the nature of reality (dharmatā), which is vastly different from the former.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "How does it universally enter," there are two explanations for the term "following entry" (anupraveśa).
Now, first, I shall provide the correct explanation.
Regarding the statement "not destroying subject and object," there are two meanings due to the preceding term "universal" (pervasive):
first, there is the pervasion of subject and object, which refers to pervasion by way of essence (*tattva*), because sentient beings are, in fact, objects within wisdom.

Second, there is neither the object nor the subject. If one considers this in terms of the pervasiveness of principle, since that which is pervaded is entirely the essence of that which pervades, then the subject and object are non-dual.
Therefore, in this present sense, the distinction between subject and object is not destroyed; the two—the realized and the realizer—mutually interpenetrate.

The commentary states: "Therefore, the subsequent sutra" introduces supporting evidence, specifically the passage from the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications" (*Prajñā-prasāda-parivarta*) concerning the answer within the section on the profound realm of the Buddha.
However, the intended meaning therein is that there are two senses of "entry":
first, entry by means of the form-body (*rūpakāya*); second, entry by means of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). Here, we take the entry by means of wisdom.
The body-entry (*kāyāyatana*) is visible, whereas the wisdom-entry (*jñānāyatana*) can only be known by wisdom; therefore, it is said that it cannot be seen by them.

In the commentary, the passage beginning with "By following suchness" (*tathatām anugataḥ*) explains the term "entry into equality. This is a citation of the meaning from the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, in the chapter concerning Maudgalyāyana, which states: "Dharmas follow suchness, because there is nothing to be followed."

This means that if there is something followed, that which is followed must exist outside of that which follows it; thus, the dharma that follows exists outside of the suchness of that which is followed. Since the suchness of the followed does not pervade that which follows, it follows that there is no suchness in the very substance of that which is followed.
If one speaks in terms of contemplative practice, when the mind does not arise in accordance with suchness, one truly accords with suchness.

As it is also said in the "Inquiry into Knowledge" chapter below: "The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space; all sentient beings enter it, yet in reality there is nothing entered."
This is precisely that meaning.
In the commentary (*shu*), the section beginning with “Therefore, empty space pervades the lands” constitutes the third part, which concludes the intended meaning of the analogy.
Within this, first the analogy is concluded, followed by the application to the Dharma.

In the preceding section, first the universal entry (*sarvatraga*) is established; subsequently, from the passage "As space relates to the lands" onwards, the meaning of equal entry (*samatā-anupraveśa*) is established.
In the commentary, from the phrase "Space may be used as a metaphor for Buddha-wisdom" onwards, the two dharmas are correlated.
Within this, there are further two parts:
first, the synthesis of the "pervasive entry" (vyāpti-praveśa), and second, the synthesis of the "conforming entry" (anupraveśa).
Now, the first.

Regarding the statement, "In whatever place the three periods of time exist, the Buddha’s wisdom must be present therein," it means that because the Buddha’s wisdom penetrates both defilement and purity without obstruction, observing immeasurable eons in a single thought-moment, one knows that there is nothing the Buddha’s wisdom does not universally know.
Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are boundless, his prior contemplation has no beginning and his subsequent [contemplation] has no end.

As for the statement, "The Buddha-wisdom knows that the three periods of time may lack their own substance," this means that True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Reality Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), Nirvāṇa, and the Dharma-nature are realized by Buddha-wisdom, and these lack the three periods of time.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “The Buddha’s wisdom, in relation to the three periods of time,” the two explanations of the term “entering accordingly” can be understood from there.
As for the commentary’s statement, “This is still explained by means of the non-dual as dual,” etc., this is the fourth point, which summarizes the inconceivable nature [of the Buddha’s wisdom].
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the conclusion based on the meaning of "entering accordingly"; second, the analogy for universal application; and third, the summary of the two metaphors.
Now, the first part.
Based on the preceding phrase "following and entering," which refers to the non-differentiation of subject and object, it is said that although they are non-dual, they are spoken of as two.
Thus, in the analogy, space is the subject that enters, and the land is the object entered.
Within the Dharma, Buddha-wisdom is that which enters, and the three periods of time are that which is entered.

That which is entered cannot be that which enters; yet now, as they all mutually enter one another, the lands likewise enter into empty space, and the three periods likewise enter into Buddha-wisdom. Therefore, it is said: "Lifting up one, the whole is encompassed."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The same applies to pervasiveness,” this refers to two examples of pervasiveness.
Previously, it was only the Buddha’s wisdom that pervaded the three periods of time; now, the three periods of time also pervade the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “The three worlds are perfectly interfused,” etc.: this simultaneously concludes the meaning of the aforementioned inclusion and the fact that all things, being non-discriminative, are entirely interfused; therefore, it says, “inconceivable.”
In the commentary, the section beginning with "Therefore it is called" summarizes the two metaphors.
The passage "Next, two metaphors are used to illustrate bodily action" constitutes the second section, which likewise possesses four meanings.

The first meaning cites scriptural passages as illustrations to explain the sense of "inclusion"; thus it says: "If even a single hair can contain the Dharma-realm, the entirety must surely contain all phenomena."

The "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds" states: "Within a single pore are inconceivable lands, dwelling in various ways as numerous as atoms; in each one resides a Universal Illuminator, proclaiming the sublime Dharma amidst the assembly."
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "It is as if a person were to take a measuring rod to measure space, and another were to follow along to calculate its extent.
One might perhaps find the limits of space, but there is no bound or limit to a single pore of the Buddha."
The subsequent passage states: "Each and every tip of a hair can contain all worlds without obstruction.
This refers precisely to the principle that a single hair contains the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

In the commentary, following the section "The Second: Manifesting Physical Action," this single analogy is cited to prove that the preceding [discussion] encompasses both [aspects] and is free from conceptual discrimination; however, the combined text is not yet complete.

The full text states: "The body of the Tathāgata is likewise; because it universally illuminates with the light of wisdom, it causes all the mundane and supramundane roots of goodness and karmic deeds of all sentient beings to be fully accomplished. Yet, the body of the Tathāgata is without discrimination and without conceptual proliferation."
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, all attachments and all conceptual proliferations have been eternally severed.
This may be understood by referring to the text.
The Commentary states: "The Buddha’s body fills the Dharma-realm" refers to the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs.

The following three lines say: "He appears universally before all sentient beings; responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him, there is nowhere he does not reach, yet he ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi."
These four phrases all carry the meaning of "pervasive"; for now, it suffices to use the first phrase alone as proof.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, it says: ‘For example, just as space pervades everything,’ etc.,” this single passage is cited to likewise prove two meanings.
The two similes of "universality" and "pervasion" are explained next within the similes, following the scripture which asks: "For what reason?
Because space has no body."
This is a brief citation from the *Zhèhé* (Combined Editions).
The full text states: "The body of the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it pervades all places, pervades all sentient beings, and pervades all lands; it neither arrives nor does it not arrive."
Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is no-body, he manifests that body for the sake of sentient beings.
Now, I have merely cited this briefly, which is sufficient to prove the meaning of its universality.
"Neither reaching nor not reaching; this is that which enters into equality" means: because there is no body, it does not reach, and this non-reaching is itself equality;
because it does not fail to reach, it is not obstructed by reaching—this is the meaning of "entering into."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Next, the four meanings are illustrated by way of analogy for verbal karma,” this constitutes the third section, which sequentially establishes these four meanings.
The phrase, “Because the Tathāgata possesses all languages within a single utterance,” establishes the meaning of inclusion and integration; it is also an implicit citation of that meaning.

This corresponds to the fourth analogy of the celestial maiden of virtuous speech within the section on the manifestation of vocal karma, which states: "One should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so.

From a single sound, he produces immeasurable voices; according to the differences in the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, these voices reach them all and cause them all to attain understanding."
The commentary states:
Based on its final phrase, it can be proven that [the term] signifies "pervasive arrival.
However, here we take only the preceding part, which already contains the sense of "inclusion."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Sublime Adornment" states: "Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
This, too, refers to the sense of inclusion and integration.
The Commentary states: "Because the celestial drum of Śacī produces sound without intention" serves as proof for the second meaning, non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*).
This is illustrated by two metaphors.

First, regarding Śacī: in the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," the patience of being like an echo states, "It is like Śacī, the consort of Śakra and daughter of the Asuras, who from a single sound produces hundreds of thousands of kinds of sounds, yet does not intentionally think, 'Let these be produced in such a way.'"

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: having entered the realm of non-conceptuality and achieved skillfulness in accordance with the various types of sounds, they constantly turn the wheel of Dharma throughout boundless worlds.
The celestial drum is the third [example] concerning the manifestation of vocal karma; it is the analogy of the celestial drum’s awakening.
It concludes: “O Son of the Buddha!
That sound of the celestial drum has no master and no agent, neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.”
Having concluded the application of the lower dharma, it states: "The voice of the Tathāgata does not abide in any location and is without verbal expression.
This refers to the meaning of arising without mind.
Furthermore, as in the "Chapter on the Minor Marks," the celestial drum preaches the Dharma for the sons of gods in the hells, saying:
"O sons of gods!
Just as I speak of 'self,' yet I do not cling to a self, nor do I cling to what belongs to a self."
"All Buddhas are likewise; though they call themselves Buddhas, they do not cling to a self, nor do they cling to what belongs to a self.
This is because they are of the nature of no-mind.
All treatises state:
the Buddha’s body is like a mani jewel, manifesting colors without thought;
the Buddha’s mouth is like a celestial drum, producing sound without thought.
All these signify the absence of conceptual discrimination.

The Commentary states: "Because the Tathāgata’s voice reaches everywhere. This also refers to the first characteristic of the vocal activity (*vākkarman*) in the *Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa*, which says: "One should know that the Tathāgata’s voice is all-pervading, because it universally extends throughout immeasurable sounds."
This proves the third meaning, that of universality. The commentary states:

"One should know that the Tathāgata’s voice is uninterrupted because it universally enters the dharma-realm. This fully proves the meanings of equality and conformity; for it is because [the voice] universally enters [the realm] and because the dharma-realm is equal.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it says, 'The Tathāgata’s voice is without crookedness or deviation,'" and so forth. Below this, two passages are cited to specifically substantiate the two meanings of "equality" and "conformative entry.
Those passages state in full: "It should be known that the Tathāgata’s voice is without crookedness or deviation, because it is produced from the Dharma-realm."

Regarding the statement, "Causing them to rejoice according to their faith and understanding," it should be understood that the Tathāgata’s voice causes all beings to rejoice in accordance with their mental inclinations, because he teaches the Dharma with clarity.
The four preceding passages all concern the verbal karma (*vākkarman*) of the *Samantabhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The metaphor below [the section on] ‘emptiness’...”, this is the third point, which serves as a concluding demonstration of where the meaning resides.

This means that since it is clearly stated that [all three karmas] are fully present, one must not hold that the first metaphor represents only the mental karma (*manaskarman*), nor that the subsequent metaphor represents only the bodily and verbal karmas.
Regarding the commentary from "The second [section], the constancy of the body" onwards, this passage consists of three parts:

first, the presentation of the heading; second, the general explanation by quoting the treatise from "That is to say, according to all... onwards; and third, the specific explanation of the text from "As for 'all sites of enlightenment'... onwards.

Regarding these two, this refers to the function of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; it clarifies the meaning by means of the four bodies (*catur-kāya*), specifically corresponding to the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Although this is spoken in reference to the land, the intent actually refers to the body.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle ten, states: "First is the Body of Enjoyment for Others, which refers to the various Tathāgatas manifesting a subtle and pure body of meritorious qualities through their wisdom of equality. Abiding in a purely pure land, they manifest great supernormal powers and turn the wheel of the true Dharma for the assembly of Bodhisattvas dwelling in the ten stages, resolving the nets of doubt among them and causing them to enjoy the vast joy of the Dharma."
The commentary states:
That [previous passage] referred solely to the Pure Land; now, with the ten bodies perfectly interfused and the defiled and pure realms mutually penetrating, it differs slightly from that.
Regarding the phrase "all sites of enlightenment" (*sarva-maṇḍala*) in the *Śāstra*, the following is a word-by-word exegesis of the scripture.
The preceding section assigned the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) to a distinct category for the sake of conforming to the characteristics of the Dharma;
here, however, according to the ultimate reality, it is said that all ten bodies sit upon the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As for the statement, "These four meanings come for the sake of convenience," this is to conform to the specific distinctions among the ten bodies.

If one assigns the ten bodies to the ten sites of practice, the first two are readily understood; the third consists of the body of merit, the body of vows, and the body adorned with the marks and signs.
This is because "merit" refers to the great ocean of all virtues practiced throughout the three periods of time, as these constitute the myriad practices.
Aspiration is the root of all practices, for it is through practice that one fulfills aspiration and thereby attains universal pervasiveness.
The adornment of the marks and signs is accomplished by means of practice;

therefore, among the ten types of Buddhas, he is called the Buddha of Karmic Retribution (*karmavipāka-buddha*), because the marks and signs are obtained as the retributive fruit of the activities of the ten thousand practices.

As it is said: "For inconceivable oceans of great kalpas, he made offerings to all Tathāgatas; universally bestowing his merit upon all living beings, he is therefore most peerless in his majestic beauty. All such passages refer to the accomplishment of the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) through causes.
However, regarding the term "Dharmakāya," this is a designation established by Tiantai based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, referring to the Dharmakāya of merit.

As for the four types of *nirmāṇakāya*—namely, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), and the body sustained by power (*baladhārakakāya*)—these three are all subsumed under the category of the transformation body.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) serves as the totality, and it is also subsumed within this Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
These four bodies possess the nine qualities; when combined with the subsequent majestic power (*prabhāva*), the ten bodies are complete.
The above has been explained according to their individual distinctions.
Since the ten bodies are perfectly interfused, raising any single body immediately entails the presence of all ten; thus, sitting in one site of enlightenment is itself sitting in all ten categories.
It is only because we are currently addressing them according to their manifested characteristics that they are described as being distinct.
Having already identified the locations where the ten bodies reside, we shall next provide a detailed explanation of the meaning of their "pervasive seating.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The wisdom-body pervasively seats itself at the Dharma-nature altar,” Dharma-nature is that which is realized; it is because the realizing wisdom is established therein.
The Commentary states: "The Dharma-body does not sit, yet it sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Since the Dharma-body is devoid of subject and object, it is said that it does not sit.
This sitting that is non-sitting is a state of profound, tranquil abiding; thus it is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment."

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the body of the three dharma-gates" and so forth, it refers to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, in the chapter on the youth Prabhāvyūha, which says: "The Buddha said to the youth Prabhāvyūha:
'Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.'"
Prabhāvyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
Why is this? I recall that in the past, when I was leaving the great city of Vaiśālī, Vimalakīrti was just entering it.
I immediately paid him homage and asked him:
“Householder, from where have you come?
He replied to me,
“I have come from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).”
I asked: "What is this so-called 'site of enlightenment'? He replied:
"The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), because it is free from hypocrisy.
The practice of undertaking deeds is the site of enlightenment, because it can accomplish all tasks.
The profound mind is the site of enlightenment, because it increases merit."
The bodhicitta is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), because it is free from error.
Generosity is the site of enlightenment, because it does not expect recompense.
Upholding the precepts is the site of enlightenment, because one fulfills one's vows.
Patience is the site of enlightenment, because the mind is unimpeded toward all sentient beings.
Diligence is the site of enlightenment, because there is no slackening or retreat.
Meditative concentration is the site of enlightenment, because the mind is pliant and supple.
Wisdom is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it directly perceives all phenomena.
To speak at length, it is said that knowing all phenomena in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment, because it accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
In this way, good son!

If a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings in accordance with the various pāramitās, you should know that all their actions—whether lifting a foot or setting it down—are derived from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and abide within the Buddha-dharma.
The commentary states:
Prabhāvyūha, taking the *bodhimaṇḍa* (site of enlightenment) in its literal sense, asked what constitutes the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Vimalakīrti, representing it through the Dharma, explained that the ten thousand practices (*sāhasracaryā*) are the place where the Way is attained; this is the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Therefore it is said: "The body of the Dharma-gate sits upon the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) of the myriad paths.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The four types of illusory transformation bodies sit peacefully upon the site of practice of the water-moon," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "This body of mine is now an illusory body."
Thus, the locus where the Way is attained is like the moon in water.
Therefore, an ancient said:
"Cultivate the myriad practices as empty flowers; sit peacefully in the water-moon dharma-arena; subdue the mirror-image celestial Māras; and realize the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream."
The meaning is this:
both cause and effect arise from conditions and are like illusions or dreams.
Second, the citation.

The Commentary states: "If one specifically addresses 'majesty and power' (*vaibhutva*)... and so forth, separately explaining how each of the ten bodies occupies six types of *bodhimaṇḍas*. This proceeds from the narrow to the broad:

since majesty and power extend to both transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and other-enjoyment bodies (*sambhogakāya*), when considered across various lands, they gradually expand until they pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*, even reaching the stage of infinite mutual inclusion (*anavaśeṣa*).

The commentary states, "As explained in the 'Chapter on Names' and so forth"; the phrase "and so forth" includes the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance," and the "Chapter on Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace."

This means that throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, there are billions of sets of four continents and so forth, all of which are of a similar class; because the Buddhas pervade them all.
This has already been cited previously.

Regarding the "Names" and the "Four Truths," in both cases, one billion are first enumerated and then concluded as being all-pervasive; since each consists of ten thousand names and so forth, it is known that these are all realms of the same kind.
The five categories below will be seen later in the text.
Regarding the phrase "among the assembly of bodhisattvas" and so forth, this passage demonstrates that it is the Body of Majestic Power (*vibhūti-kāya*), which outshines the bodhisattvas.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “appearing and disappearing amidst the mountains” and so forth: this means that appearing and disappearing amidst the mountains is like the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
“Without concealment or manifestation” refers to the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) sitting at the site of enlightenment.
"Manifesting completely in every place" below refers to the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) seated at the site of enlightenment.
Because the responsive and the true are identical, it is complete in every location without any difference in essence.
In the commentary, from the phrase "The Great Radiance flows through space" onwards, there is a formal explanation of majestic power (*vibhūti*).
"Great Radiance" refers to the sun; "remaining effulgence" refers to the stars, the moon, and so forth.
The sun is a metaphor for the Tathāgata; the moon is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas; and the stars and other celestial bodies are used as metaphors for the remaining sentient beings.
"Correctly grasping and eclipsing" is the meaning of *vaibhutva* (sovereign power), and that "even Bodhisattvas cannot fathom it" is also a meaning of *vaibhutva*.

As for the statement, "The radiance of the blazing sun is difficult to fathom to its limits," this refers to the verse by the Bodhisattva Jayasenānanda in the *Yāma-pariṣad*: "It is like the month of midsummer, when the sky is pure and free from the veil of clouds."
The brilliant sun shines with radiant light, filling the ten directions without exception.
Its radiance is limitless and immeasurable; none are able to fathom it. If this is so even for those with eyes, how much more so for those who are blind and in darkness?
"The Buddhas are likewise; their merits are boundless, such that throughout inconceivable eons, none can discern or know them.
This is visible [in the text].
Regarding the commentary's passage beginning with "Since it says 'illuminating the world,'" this serves to resolve potential objections.
This refers to a question such as:
"If the ten bodies are perfectly interfused, they should universally respond to all beings; why then do they appear only among the assembly of Bodhisattvas?

Therefore, taking the metaphor from the text regarding the rising of the solar disc, it benefits everything without exception; thus it is said: "In the end, it benefits those born blind and illuminates the high mountains."
All of these are from the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), as previously cited.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Now the three temporal limits have been severed," this below explains the meaning of purity.
If there were characteristics of the three periods of time, merit would not be pure.

Because it is cultivated in accordance with the dharma-realm, it has no three limits; that is to say, it does not come from the past limit, it does not go toward the future limit, and it does not abide in the present.
The Dharma-body is already purified; since it has severed the three periods of time, how could its merit be measured?
Above the myriad practices, defiled habits have perished; thus it is called "pure," meaning that afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have all been exhausted.
The Commentary states: "Fourth, 'constantly taking birth according to one's will below' refers to the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
There are two meanings for 'mind-made':
first, it is a metaphor, meaning that it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as the mind."
Second, this dharma has two meanings:
first, following one's own intention; second, following the intentions of others.
Generally, it is called "following intention" because it is accomplished with swift ease.
The remaining meanings will be discussed in the "Chapter on Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā-parivarta*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "That is to say, compassion and *prajñā* are constantly in mutual association," this refers to the function of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. What follows below assigns this to the *nirmāṇakāya*, briefly citing one of its characteristics.
In reality, this body also includes the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), as it arises in accordance with the mental dispositions of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages.

Furthermore, because compassion and wisdom mutually guide one another, it functions as a transformative application; thus, the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the great function of non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

The Commentary states: "Being stirred and thereby attaining penetration" refers to what is said in the *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*): "Now, the *Yi* has no thought and no action.
It is still and unmoving, yet when stirred, it penetrates the affairs of the world."
"If it were not for the Ultimate Spirit, who could participate in this?
The commentary states: "The Ultimate Spirit is quiescent yet nothing fails to respond.
This is the mother of all functional efficacy, and that from which the forms and numbers arise."

This means that it is by the mind’s non-existence of the elephant that one can control the elephant; by the transcendence of numbers that one can exhaustively master numbers; and by non-movement that one can respond to movement.

Because the "emptiness and non-being" of the *Yi Zhuan* is devoid of movement, it is able to be unmoving yet omnipresent; I now borrow these words as a metaphor for the Tathāgata, whose inner essence is perfect stillness while his outer manifestation responds to all living beings.

Having ascended the body purified by the myriad blessings, one abides in stillness; yet while remaining silent, one constantly manifests birth. Thus it is said: "In stillness there is no movement, yet upon being stirred, all things are penetrated. This is precisely the Dharmakāya, which is unborn and yet does not fail to give birth to anything.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That is, the Body of Vow manifests the Dharma,” etc., this passage consists of three parts:
first, the formal indication.

This refers to raining down the great rain of Dharma and severing all doubts; it cites the passage on the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful discerning wisdom) from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to establish this meaning.
Second, "Therefore, the subsequent sutra says," cites the text to provide proof.
In the commentary, from "Third, as for the two phrases of the sutra" onwards, the sutra is restated and explained in detail.
Within this third section, there are five general points:

The single cloud is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, and the rain is a metaphor for the preaching of the Dharma; as for the "abbreviated" metaphor of the reflection, it is explained extensively in the tenth chapter on the vocal activity (*vākkarman*) of the *Samantabhadravyūha* (Chapter on the Appearance), within the parable of the rain falling from the Dragon King Sāgara, where it is stated that the colors of the clouds differ in various places and the rain likewise varies accordingly.
The *Compendium* states: "O Son of the Buddha!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, is likewise.

Desiring to teach and transform sentient beings with the True Dharma, he first spreads clouds of his body to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting various forms according to their needs. That is to say, he may manifest for sentient beings clouds of mind-born bodies; or clouds of transformation bodies; or clouds of power-sustaining bodies, form-bodies, marks-and-signs bodies, merit-bodies, wisdom-bodies, indestructible power-bodies, fearlessness-bodies, or Dharma-realm bodies."
Each instance contains the phrase "manifested for the sake of sentient beings.
Following this, it further states: "Once these signs have manifested, the bodies and minds of all sentient beings attain refreshing clarity."

Thereafter, from the "Great Dharma-body Clouds of the Tathāgata," the "Great Compassion Clouds," and the "Great Inconceivable Clouds," there falls the inconceivable rain of the vast Dharma, causing the bodies and minds of all sentient beings to be purified. Specifically, for the Bodhisattvas seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), there falls a great rain of Dharma called "The Non-differentiation of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-aviśeṣa*). From this, it is known that the clouds represent the manifestation of the body and the rain represents the preaching of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma, the metaphor, and the shadow are abbreviated": in the section on the Dharma, there is only the teaching of the Dharma; in the section on the metaphor, there is only the arising of clouds.
If it were complete, it should state: "Extensively manifesting transformation bodies, he expounds all dharmas, like spreading great clouds and raining down the great rain of Dharma."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, first raising the clouds of compassion and subsequently pouring down the rain of Dharma" refers to the passage cited above from the "Appearance" chapter.

The Commentary states: "That which is moistened by a single cloud and a single rain differs" refers to what is said in the "Parable of the Herbs" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Moistened by the rain from a single cloud, [the plants] grow according to their respective natures, producing flowers, fruits, and seeds; though they are born from the same earth and moistened by the same rain, each of the grasses and trees has its own distinctions."
This is an analogy.
To apply it to the meaning, one should say: "Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this.
His appearance in the world is like the rising of a great cloud."
"With a great voice that pervades the world of devas, humans, and asuras, it is like that great cloud which universally covers the trichiliocosm.
The commentary states:
"The 'above' refers to the union with the clouds."

Next, it says: "At that time, the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of these sentient beings, as well as their diligence or indolence; according to what they are capable of, he preaches the Dharma for them in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits."
The commentary states:
"Above, it should indeed rain.
How do we know that this is one [rain]?"

Next it says: "The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation—which ultimately culminates in all-knowledge."
This is precisely the meaning of "one cloud and one rain.
As the verse says: "The cloud emits water of a single flavor, yet the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests receive its moisture according to their respective capacities."
Furthermore, it is not the case that what is moistened by a single cloud and a single rain is different [in kind].
As stated below: "For the great assembly, he preaches the pure Dharma of ambrosia.
That Dharma is of a single flavor—liberation and nirvana—and he expounds this meaning with a single wondrous voice."
Even unto the point of distinguishing right view from wrong view and sharp faculties from dull faculties, he rains down the rain of Dharma equally without weariness.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide in various stages, whether as humans, devas, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or the Brahmā kings.
"These minor medicinal herbs and so forth all receive different degrees of nourishment from the same cloud and the same rain. The commentary states:
"The clouds and rains also differ according to the capacities and needs of sentient beings," which likewise reflects the intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The passage from the *Lotus Sūtra* cited above—where clouds and rain provide different degrees of moisture to various things—is a metaphor for the fact that the Buddha’s body and its preaching of the Dharma are never at variance; the difference lies solely in the objects [to which they are directed].
Now it is explained that the Buddha is able to possess distinctions, namely, manifesting clouds of ten kinds of differentiated bodies and raining down ten kinds of Dharma rains.

This is like the Dragon King Sāgara raising clouds, which may manifest the radiant color of Jāmbūnada gold, or the radiant color of vaidūrya, or the radiant color of white silver, or the radiant color of crystal, and so forth; thus, the clouds are not the same.
Next, it says: "That which is called 'the rain of pure water in the great ocean' is named 'uninterrupted';
that which rains 'various musical sounds such as flutes and pipes in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations' is named 'exquisite,' and so forth. This refers to the diversity of the rains.
Therefore, it is said that clouds and rain are each distinct.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “Shrouding the dust and obscuring the sun, universally covering with no mind,” this reflects the intent of both the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the Dharma-Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), it says: "O Son of the Buddha!

At this stage, the Bodhisattva, through the power of their own vows, raises great clouds of compassion and thunders the great Dharma-thunder. With penetrating clarity and fearlessness as lightning flashes, and merit and wisdom as dense clouds, they manifest various bodies, traveling back and forth everywhere. In a single thought-moment, they pervade as many lands as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* worlds throughout the ten directions, expounding the Great Dharma and subduing the hosts of Māra and enmity."

Furthermore, surpassing this number, throughout lands as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds, he pours down the rain of ambrosia according to the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, extinguishing the dust and flames of all their delusions; therefore, this stage is named the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā).
The commentary states:
This refers to the meanings of "obscuring the dust" and "universally covering.
The meaning of "mindlessness" is a general exposition, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka*: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!"

For example, within the ocean there is a great dragon king named Great Adornment; when he sends down rain upon the great ocean, he may send down ten kinds of adorned rain, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand kinds of adorned rain.
O Son of the Buddha!
Water is without discrimination; it is merely through the inconceivable power of the dragon kings that it is made magnificent, even unto hundreds of thousands of immeasurable varieties.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise; when he teaches the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, he may speak using ten distinct types of tones, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or eighty-four thousand sounds to explain eighty-four thousand kinds of practices, even up to explaining the Dharma individually through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sounds, causing all who hear it to give rise to joy.

"The Tathāgata’s voice is without discrimination; it is simply because the profound Dharma-realm of all Buddhas is perfectly pure that it can accord with the capacities of sentient beings' faculties, producing various sounds and voices that cause them all to rejoice," and so forth—this is the meaning of being "without mind."

Furthermore, in the parable of Sāgara raising clouds, it is also said: "Although that dragon king’s mind is impartial and free from distinctions between self and other, there are nevertheless differences because the roots of goodness of sentient beings vary."
This is also the meaning of being without mind (*acitta*).

The *Lotus Sūtra* likewise states, "I have no greedy attachment and no obstruction," and further says, "I rain down the rain of Dharma equally without weariness"; both express the meaning of being without mind.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'in the great assembly,' etc., this cites the function of the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful investigative wisdom) from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to explain the manifestation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Regarding the phrase "first clarifying extensive containment," the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) has two aspects, like space:
first, extensive containment; second, universal pervasion.
Now, because a single atom contains the entirety of the dharma-realm, it is "vastly inclusive.
In the commentary, the phrase "because vast inclusion does not obstruct universal pervasion" explains the reason why [the world] is produced within a single hair-pore.
This means that when [the hair] is expanded to contain the entire Dharma-realm, it is contained within a single pore; when it is universalized, it extends a single pore throughout the Dharma-realm.
Now, at the very moment the hair correctly contains boundless lands, because it is simultaneously universal, it pervades the entirety of those lands it contains.
The Commentary states: "If [the Buddha] manifests extensively throughout the ten directions," and so forth; this second section provides an explanation by means of an illustration.
It means: if [the manifestation] already pervades even within a single hair, how much more so outside?
This passage from the Commentary is precisely the wondrous function of the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom).
The Commentary states: “The Dharma-body pervades and encompasses” is the heading.
“Pervades and encompasses” (mílún) carries the meaning of being all-pervasive and inclusive.
“Taking the Dharma as the body,” and so forth, first clarifies that the Dharma-nature Dharma-body is omnipresent and devoid of coming or going.

Below the section "Manifesting Form According to the Dharma," the reason why there is no coming or going is clarified in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
This interpretation is used because, as will be shown below, [the three bodies] are subsumed [within these two], and this [specific case] belongs to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Regarding the phrase "sustained by power" (*li-chi*) and so forth, the commentary consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation of "sustained by power," which divides this sutra into two sections;
second, from "above, based on the ten bodies" onwards, the summary by means of the three bodies.
Within this section, there are five parts:

first, the formal inclusion [of the Buddha] within the three or four bodies; second, the explanation of the reason for such inclusion; third, the discernment between the provisional and the real; fourth, the harmonization of the lands and other bodies; and fifth, the concluding praise of its inconceivability.

First: Thus, when the ten bodies are compared with the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), they are both pervasive and limited. *Bodhi* is the totality and is also the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body);
among the remaining nine bodies, those sustained by the power of the vow and emanation are exclusively the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The power of the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*) pertains to both the enjoyment body for others (*para-sambhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The marks and signs resulting from merit and wisdom pertain to both types of retribution and the transformation body.
The Dharma is restricted to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); here, we have provisionally adopted this sequential correspondence and thus made this assignment.

Therefore, previously the *bodhi-kāya* was used to clarify the *tathatā-kāya*, and just now the *dharma-kāya* was used to clarify the *rūpa-kāya*; this is merely for the purpose of conforming to the sequence of the present arrangement.

Regarding the two [points] within the commentary’s passage beginning with “Because in various teachings there are three bodies,” etc., it provides the reason for the inclusion of the second [category].
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
"What is the purpose of further subsuming the ten bodies within the three bodies?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:

Since the various teachings differ widely regarding the three or four [bodies], we now clarify that in the perfect fusion (yuanrong), a single body possesses all three; thus, there is a distinction between the provisional and the real.
As for the statement that the three bodies are established as distinct: the Dharma-body has no "establishment," for it is only through the removal of obstructions that it is said to be established.
The Sambhogakāya is "perfected" when the four wisdoms are first perfected;
the Nirmāṇakāya is "perfected" beneath the Bodhi tree through the eight phases [of enlightenment].
Regarding the distinctions among the three bodies: the Dharmakāya has no teaching.
The Reward Body Buddhas perceive one another, yet there is no discourse;
the Transformation Body possesses discourse.

If one reabsorbs the derivative into the fundamental, then the responsive and transformational bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma; it is the Reward Body that speaks.
That which is taught as identical to what is realized is the teaching of the *dharmakāya*.
