fifth, knowing the suffering of birth and death yet not feeling weary or loathing it;
sixth, contemplating the profound Dharma and attaining immeasurable fruits.
Seventh, they preach the Dharma of the Two Vehicles for the sake of all sentient beings, yet they do not personally realize or grasp the liberation of those vehicles;
eighth, they contemplate unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) with joy but do not abide within them, giving rise to no dualistic notions regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned;
ninth, they reach the realm of non-arising yet manifest birth therein.
"10. Although they have realized all-knowledge, they initiate the bodhisattva practices and do not sever the lineage of the bodhisattvas.
In each case, there is the phrase "sustained by the Buddha."
Regarding "the empowerment of suchness" (yathābhūta-adhiṣṭhāna), there are many such instances.
This refers, for example, to manifesting multiple bodies according to what beings wish to see;
or to the fact that by making offerings even once to the fragmented bodily relics (śarīra-dhātu), one is reborn in the heavens a thousand times.

The entire-body relics (sarīra) are like those of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; they are precisely the bodies sustained by the power of the Tathāgata, as illustrated in the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) through the analogy of the King of Physicians who leaves behind his body, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the second is like Jīvaka," it refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 30 (fascicle 28 in the Southern edition), which states: "At that time, I went to the city of Campā."
At that time, there was a great elder in that city who had no heir; he served the six teachers in hopes of obtaining a child.
Not long thereafter, his wife became pregnant. Upon learning this, the elder went to the six teachers and said with joy, "My wife is pregnant;
will it be a boy or a girl?"
The six teachers replied,
"It must certainly be her daughter.
Upon hearing this, the elder felt sorrow and distress arise within his heart.
Furthermore, a friend came to the householder and said,
"For what reason are you so distressed as this?
The householder replied:
"My wife is pregnant, but I do not yet know whether it will be a boy or a girl; therefore, I asked the six masters.
The six masters replied to me, 'According to our method of physiognomy, she will certainly give birth to a girl.'"
"Upon hearing these words, I reflected that I am old and possess immeasurable wealth; yet if this child is not a boy, there will be no one to whom I can entrust it, and for this reason I am grieved.
The friend then said, "You lack wisdom," and so forth, extensively praising the virtues of the Buddha to encourage him to question the World-Honored One.
The elder then went to where the Buddha was and asked the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"My wife is pregnant, and the six teachers have said that she will certainly give birth to a girl.
What do you say to this? The Buddha replied:
"Householder!
Your wife is pregnant; there is no doubt that it will be a son.
Once the child is born, his merit and virtue will be beyond compare."
Upon hearing this, the six teachers conceived feelings of jealousy. They then mixed poisonous drugs with mangoes and gave them to the elder, instructing him to have his wife consume them, saying:
"If she takes this medicine, the child will be handsome, and there will be no harm to the mother during childbirth."
Having taken it, he died immediately; they were sent outside the city and cremated with fire.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, went to the cemetery.
The elder rebuked him, saying:
"What you call 'non-duality' may indeed be named the World-Honored One.
Since your mother has already passed away, how could she have given birth to a son? I said:
“O Householder!
At that time, you did not inquire at all about the length of your mother’s life, but asked only whether the child she bore would be male or female.
Since the words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are never equivocal, you should know for certain that you will surely obtain a son.”
At that time, the corpse was consumed by fire until its belly split open, and the child emerged from within, sitting upright amidst the flames like a ruddy sheldrake in a lotus pond.
I immediately commanded Jīvaka:
"Go into the fire and bring this child here."
The six teachers tried to stop him, but Jīvaka said:
"Even if the Tathāgata were to send me into the Avīci Hell where fierce fires blaze, they could not burn me, much less the fires of this world."
At that time, Jīvaka entered the mass of fire as if entering the cool waters of a great river; he took up the child and returned to my place, handing the child over to me.
Having entrusted my son to him, I said to the elder:
"The lifespan of all sentient beings is uncertain, like a bubble upon the water.
If a sentient being has the retribution of heavy karma, fire cannot burn them and poison cannot harm them."
"This child's karmic retribution is not something created by me.
The elder then requested the Buddha to bestow a name upon him.
The Buddha said:
"This child was born from within a fierce fire; as the fire is named Jyotiṣka, he should be named Jyotiṣka.
At that time, those in the assembly witnessed my supernatural transformations, and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore it is said that it is like Jīvaka entering the fire.
Thus, the phrase "entering the fire" encompasses two matters:
one is as previously explained.
Second, as Jīvaka stated, the Buddha caused [Devadatta] to enter the Avīci Hell, yet the fierce fires did not burn him.
There is another account concerning this very entry into hell, which concerns the inquiry into Devadatta’s affairs.
Regarding the commentary on "The Four Practices of the Buddhas," the text has three parts:
first, the formal explanation of the names; second, the differentiation of categories; and third, the elimination of confusion.
From the passage beginning with "Alternatively, ten kinds are taught," the second part—the differentiation of categories—is presented.
Within this, the first part explains through the act of transformation, while the latter explains through that which is transformed.
Now, for the first:
regarding the "ten kinds of transformations that do not miss their time," the forty-sixth sūtra states: "O Son of the Buddha!..."

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of transformations that do not miss their proper time. What are these ten? They are: first, all Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment without missing the proper time;

second, they bring those with whom they have a karmic connection to maturity; third, they bestow the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhy-avyākaraṇa*); fourth, they manifest spiritual powers in accordance with the minds of sentient beings; fifth, they manifest the Buddha-body in accordance with the understandings of sentient beings; sixth, they abide in great equanimity (*upekṣā*); seventh, they enter various villages; eighth, they gather in those who possess pure faith; ninth, they discipline sentient beings who are wicked; and tenth, they manifest the inconceivable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all Buddhas.
Above all [phrases], there is the phrase "all Buddhas," and below, the words "not missing the proper time.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This is also the practice that is performed," etc., the second point explains this in terms of what is practiced.
Within this, there are two further parts:
first, the citation of the text; second, the interpretive explanation beginning with "Alternatively, great compassion encompasses sentient beings.
Regarding the first: the passage "That which is unimpeded practice is the practice of the Tathāgata," and so forth, refers to what the *Fifty-two [Chapter] Sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha!"...
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand the conduct of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Son of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know that unimpeded conduct is the conduct of the Tathāgata; they should know that conduct of true suchness (*tathatā*) is the conduct of the Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!
Just as True Suchness (tathatā) is unborn in the past, immovable in the future, and unarisen in the present, so too is the practice of the Tathāgata: unborn, immovable, and unarisen.
The bird soaring through the void below, with no bounds before or behind, serves as a metaphor for the practice of *tathatā* (suchness);
the golden-winged bird parting the ocean serves as a metaphor for unimpeded practice.
These are explained in detail below.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Alternatively, great compassion gathers in sentient beings," there are two examples of interpretation that also establish the preceding meaning.
"Great compassion gathering in sentient beings" is the practice of non-obstruction, while "great wisdom creating conditions" is the practice of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Accomplishing matters without thought" establishes the two aforementioned meanings and also encompasses the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

In the commentary, the section beginning with "In terms of the person looking toward the practice" constitutes the third point, which clarifies potential confusion; for the *sūtra* states that "the conduct of the Tathāgata might be confused with the objective realm, as it is the conduct of compassion and wisdom."
In this passage, the first part provides the formal distinction and the latter part cites scriptural evidence.
This means that the Buddha is the "practitioner" (the agent), while the practices of compassion and wisdom are the "practices" (the objects).

It is not as in the case of an object, where compassion and wisdom are the practitioners and True Suchness or sentient beings are the objects; therefore, it is said: "In terms of the person looking toward the practice, it is designated as the 'practice'."

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, as for 'the expectations being different,' the superior practice encompasses both the subject and the object, whereas the objective realm is restricted solely to the object; this already constitutes a difference.

Even if one were to adopt compassion and wisdom equally, with respect to the practiced action, one would employ compassion and wisdom as the objective realms, while with respect to the practicing agent, one would employ compassion and wisdom [as the subjective faculties]."
It is like a person who is called "father" when looking toward his son, and called "son" when looking toward his father; though one person serves two functions, how could they be confused?
The passage beginning with "If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*" constitutes the second part, which cites scriptural evidence to explain that the two characteristics are not identical.
The sūtra should be the fifth; the five elements are entirely identical to those in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

However, since the *Yogācārabhūmi* transcribes the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in its entirety as its treatise, when I now cite the *Yogācārabhūmi*, I do so because I wish to cite both the sūtra and the treatise together.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That is to say, the ‘vast powers’ and so forth are as described in the ‘Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas,’” this refers to what is stated in the forty-seventh [chapter]: “O Sons of the Buddha!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of vast power, supreme power, immeasurable power, power of great majesty and virtue, power difficult to obtain, non-retrogressive power, firm power, indestructible power, inconceivable power for all worlds, power that no sentient being can move, and the courageous dharma of the great Nārāyaṇa banner.”
"What are the ten? They are:
the body of all Buddhas being indestructible, and so forth, as the first.
These aforementioned ten powers pervade ten kinds of heroic dharmas, as detailed in that text.
Now, to briefly enumerate their names: first, the power that the body and life cannot be destroyed;

second, the power of containing and sustaining within a single pore; third, the power of supporting great mountains with a single hair; fourth, the power of sovereign mastery over the application of meditative concentration; fifth, the power of constantly and universally expounding the Dharma; sixth, the power of the marks and signs of virtue to subdue Māra; seventh, the power of the perfect voice to penetrate everywhere; eighth, the power of a mind free from obstruction; ninth, the power of the subtle and secret Dharma-body; tenth, the power of fully endowed wisdom and conduct.
Within each of these powers there are many principles and meanings, which are fully detailed in the subsequent text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ‘Chapter on Transcending the World’ speaks of ten kinds of fearlessness,” this refers to what is said in the fifty-sixth [chapter]: “O Son of the Buddha!...”
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of fearlessness.
What are these ten?

Although the scriptural text is vast and extensive, I shall now cite its meaning: namely, first, the fearlessness of hearing and retaining; second, the fearlessness of eloquence. These former two do not involve being unable to answer difficult challenges.
The third and fourth are the fearlessnesses regarding emptiness; these do not fear deluded thoughts.

The fourth is the fearlessness of having no deficiency in the four modes of deportment; the fifth is the fearlessness of having no transgression in the three karmas. The former two are fearlessnesses regarding external censure.
The sixth is the fearlessness of external protection; this does not fear celestial Māras or non-Buddhists.
Seventh is the fearlessness of right mindfulness, being fearless regarding forgetfulness;
eighth is the fearlessness of skillful means, being fearless regarding birth and death;
ninth is the fearlessness of all-knowledge, being fearless regarding the two vehicles.
The ten types of fearless conduct do not fear being unable to transform and bring forth sentient beings.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Alternatively, four kinds are taught,” this is explained in the *Daśacakra-parivarta* (Chapter on the Ten Stores), namely: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the path that transcends obstacles; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the path that transcends suffering.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is not necessarily the case that it is entirely so,” this does not mean that the ancient interpretation is disallowed;

rather, it simply clarifies that the meaning is all-inclusive. Regarding the passage below, “Such as the Lion’s Stretching [Samādhi],” etc., sixty-one sūtras briefly list one hundred gates: the first is named the Samādhi of Universally Adorning the Dharma-realm, the second is named the Samādhi of Universally Illuminating the Unobstructed Realm of All Three Times, and the last is called the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi. It concludes by stating: “By means of such samādhis, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, one enters the great ocean of supernatural transformations of the Tathāgata Vairocana’s samādhi, which in every thought-moment fills the entire Dharma-realm.”

The Commentary states: "Briefly stated, there are ten kinds, as explained in the 'Inconceivable' Chapter regarding the Buddha’s immeasurable and inconceivable samādhis. This refers to the forty-seventh sutra, which says: "That is to say: first, all Buddhas are constantly in right concentration, pervading all places within a single thought-moment, universally expounding the wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings;
second, they universally expound the limit of non-self for all sentient beings;
third, they universally enter the three periods of time..."
Fourth, universally entering the vast Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
fifth, universally manifesting immeasurable and diverse Buddha-bodies;
sixth, manifesting body, speech, and mind in accordance with the various mental inclinations and understandings of all sentient beings.
Seventh, they proclaim that all phenomena are the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) free from desire;
eighth, they expound the self-nature of all dependent origination;
ninth, they manifest immeasurable, vast adornments of both mundane and supramundane realms, causing all sentient beings to constantly behold the Buddha.
"10. To cause all sentient beings to fully penetrate all Buddha-dharmas and immeasurable liberations, ultimately reaching the unsurpassed shore.
Each phrase contains the statement: "All Buddhas eternally abide in samādhi, pervading all places within a single thought-moment," just as in the first phrase.

The Commentary states: "Or it is said that there are ten [supernormal powers], as in the 'Chapter on the Ten Pervasions'": 1) the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds; 2) the supernormal power of the divine eye; 3) the supernormal power of knowing past lives throughout kalpas; 4) the supernormal power of knowing kalpas extending to the limits of the future; 5) the supernormal power of the unimpeded, pure divine ear; 6) the supernormal power of traveling to all buddha-fields without substance or activity; 7) the supernormal power of discerning all speech and terminology; 8) the supernormal power of innumerable form-bodies; 9) the supernormal power of all dharmas; and 10) the supernormal power of entering the samādhi of the cessation of all things. These are explained in detail in the sūtra text.

The Commentary states: "The 'Inconceivable Chapter' says that all Buddhas possess boundless and unimpeded liberation, manifesting immeasurable great supernormal powers. This is an interpretation citing the scriptural text.

The single phrase "unimpeded liberation" (*anāvaraṇa-vimokṣa*) cites the sūtra to demonstrate that this liberation is a liberation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting immeasurable great supernormal powers—
just as the inconceivable liberation in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* enables one to place Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed and so forth.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "What are the ten? They are:

first, all Buddhas being able to manifest within a single atom unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas appearing in the world; second, turning the pure wheel of Dharma; third, sentient beings receiving transformation and being tamed; fourth, the Buddha-lands; and fifth, Bodhisattvas receiving predictions [of enlightenment]."
In each of the first five [phrases], there is the expression: “All Buddhas are able, within a single atom, to manifest unspeakably unspeakable [things],” exactly as in the first sentence.

In the subsequent five phrases, the expression “unspeakably unspeakable” is omitted, while the remainder is the same as above; namely: (6) manifesting all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; (7) manifesting all world-systems of the past, future, and present; (8) manifesting all supernatural powers of the past, future, and present; (9) manifesting all sentient beings of the past, future, and present; and (10) manifesting all Buddha-activities of the past, future, and present.
The commentary states:
Since all [phenomena] manifest instantaneously within a single atom, this clarifies that it is the power of great supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the sub-commentary’s statement, “The ten powers (*bala*) are restricted exclusively to Bodhisattvas,” this is intended to introduce the six supernormal knowledges below, which are common to both the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The six are: the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, mastery of supernormal powers, and the exhaustion of outflows.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "there are immeasurable [powers] in detail," this is because they are explained individually according to their specific functions.
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'or speaks of a hundred kinds,' this refers to the fifty-six sutras. At the beginning, ten gates are listed, stating: 'O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of unimpeded functions.'"

What are these ten? They are: first, unimpeded function regarding sentient beings; second, unimpeded function regarding lands; third, regarding phenomena (dharma); fourth, regarding bodies; fifth, regarding vows; sixth, regarding spheres of activity; seventh, regarding wisdom; eighth, regarding supernormal powers (abhijñā); ninth, regarding spiritual power; and tenth, regarding the powers (bala).
All [of these] contain the phrase "unimpeded function" (*anāvaraṇa-vṛtti*).
Below, nine [sections] explain each [of the ten masteries], each having ten gates; thus, they total one hundred.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Briefly, there are ten kinds, namely, mastery over life (*jīvita-vaśitā*) and so forth," this refers to what is said at the end of the fifty-fifth sutra: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of mastery.
What are these ten? They are:
mastery over life, because they can abide for an unspeakable number of kalpas;
Mastery over the mind, because wisdom can enter incalculable samādhis;
mastery over requisites, because one can adorn all worlds with immeasurable ornaments;
mastery over karma, because one receives retribution according to the appropriate time;
Mastery over birth, because they manifest birth in all worlds;
mastery over resolution, because they perceive all worlds as filled with Buddhas;
and mastery over vows, because they attain perfect enlightenment in various lands according to their desire and at their chosen time.
Mastery over spiritual powers, because they manifest all great supernatural transformations;
mastery over phenomena, because they manifest boundless Dharma gates;
and mastery over wisdom, because in every thought-moment they manifest the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses to achieve perfect enlightenment.
These are the ten.
If bodhisattvas abide in these dharmas, they will attain the perfection of all the pāramitās of all buddhas, as well as wisdom, spiritual power, and mastery over enlightenment.

The Commentary states: "The 'Chapter on the Inconceivable' also speaks of ten [kinds of mastery]," and so forth. This refers to what is said in the forty-sixth chapter: "What are the ten? They are as follows:

All Buddhas have attained complete mastery over all dharmas; they clearly understand various *padakāya* (phrases) and *vyañjanakāya* (syllables); they expound all dharmas with unimpeded eloquence. This is the first dharma of mastery belonging to all Buddhas."

The latter part is abbreviated for its essential meaning; the former refers to mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*). These are: first, mastery over mind; second, mastery over resolve (*adhimuktivaśitā*); third, mastery over requisites (*pariṣkāravaśitā*); fourth, mastery over life (*āyurvaśitā*); fifth, mastery over supernormal powers (*ṛddhivaśitā*); sixth, mastery over knowledge (*jñānavaśitā*); seventh, mastery over karma (*karmavaśitā*); eighth, mastery over rebirth (*upapattivaśitā*); and ninth, mastery over vows (*praṇidhānavaśitā*). (Note: The tenth is typically *jñānavaśitā*, but here it appears as *praṇidhānavaśitā*; the list provided in the source text contains nine items, with the tenth being implied by the context of the ten masteries.)
However, the two preceding sūtras are identical in their entirety to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the commentary’s [section on] "The Ten Inabilities to Comprehend," the text has two parts:
first, the explanation of the names; second, from "Briefly, there are ten" onwards, the classification of types.
Regarding this, there are two parts;
first, an explanation based on the *Fó zuìshèngfǎ* (The Buddha’s Most Supreme Dharma) from the Jin translation.

The commentary states: “As in the ‘Inconceivable Chapter,’ the Buddhas possess ten kinds of most supreme dharmas. This refers to the forty-sixth sutra; it cites this passage because it accords with the expression *fó zuìshèngfǎ* found in the Jin translation.
The Sūtra says: "That which is called the great vows of all Buddhas are firm and indestructible; what they say must be done, for their word is without duality.
Second, in order to fulfill all merits, they cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva throughout all future kalpas without ever giving rise to weariness."
Third, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, they go to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, acting thus for all sentient beings without interruption.
Fourth, regarding the two types of sentient beings—those who have faith and those who are hostile—he universally contemplates them with great compassion as equal and without distinction.
Fifth, from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of Buddhahood, he never regresses or loses the bodhicitta.
Sixth, they accumulate immeasurable meritorious virtues and dedicate them all toward the nature of omniscience, remaining forever free from defilement or attachment to any worldly realm.

Seventh, they cultivate the three types of action under the guidance of the Buddhas, practicing only the conduct of Buddhas and not that of the two vehicles, dedicating it all toward the nature of omniscience to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

They emit eight great rays of light; these rays shine equally upon all places and illuminate the teachings of all Buddhas, causing the minds of all bodhisattvas to attain purity and fulfill all-knowledge.

Ninth, they relinquish worldly pleasures without craving or attachment, universally wishing for the world to be free from suffering and attain happiness, devoid of all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

Tenth, out of compassion for all sentient beings who undergo various sufferings, they protect the lineage of the Buddhas, practice the realm of the Buddhas, transcend birth and death, and reach the stage of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
"These are the ten.
In each phrase, the words "all Buddhas" appear at the beginning, identical to the first phrase.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "If one takes it in the sense of being indestructible," etc., this is the second section explaining the dharma of great courage and valor according to the present sutra.
As previously cited, the meaning encompasses both aspects.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "it mostly appears in the 'Inconceivable Dharma' chapter," the inclusion of the term "mostly" is because there are also sections such as the "Leaving the World" chapter.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the 'Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas,' the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of dharmas that universally pervade the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-realm. This refers to what the forty-sixth sutra says: "What are these ten?"
That is to say: all Buddhas possess boundless physical forms and marks that are pure, entering universally into all realms of existence without defilement or attachment;
second, they possess unobstructed eyes, clearly seeing all phenomena.
Third, they possess unobstructed ears, capable of fully understanding and comprehending all sounds.
Fourth, their noses reach the sovereign other shore of all Buddhas.
Fifth, they possess broad and long tongues, which produce wondrous sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Sixth, his six bodies appear to sentient beings, causing them all to behold him.
Seventh, his mind abides in the unimpeded and equal Dharma-body.
Eighth, through unimpeded liberation, he manifests inexhaustible great supernormal powers.

In nine pure worlds, he manifests various Buddha-lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings; these lands are fully endowed with immeasurable and diverse adornments, yet he gives rise to no defiled attachment toward them.
Through the ten bodhisattva practices and vows, they attain perfected wisdom, sport with mastery, and are able to thoroughly penetrate all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!
These are the ten kinds of Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which are universal and boundless.

Upon each and every one of these phrases, there are the words "All Buddhas have no boundless limit," exactly as in the first phrase; however, in the fifth tongue, the words "no boundless limit" are replaced by the term "broad and long."

The commentary states: "The 'Chapter on Transcending the World' explains each [topic] by means of ten gates," referring specifically to the fifty-seventh sūtra, namely the ten eyes, ten ears, and so forth.

As for the ten eyes: first, the fleshly eye; second, the divine eye; third, the wisdom-eye; fourth, the dharma-eye; fifth, the buddha-eye; sixth, the knowledge-eye; seventh, the light-eye; eighth, the eye that transcends birth and death; ninth, the unimpeded eye; and tenth, the all-knowing eye.
The details regarding the ten ears, ten noses, and so forth are extensively explained in that text.

However, since those refer to the eyes and other faculties of a bodhisattva, while the concluding statements below all say "then one attains the Buddha-eye" and so on, they encompass both cause and fruit; thus, they may be interpreted as referring to the Buddha-eye and the rest.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the 'Ten Meanings for Each of the Three Karmas in the Chapter on Manifestation,' the body is treated in fifty sūtras, while speech and mind are treated in fifty-one; each has ten meanings, all illustrated by means of ten metaphors."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The constant, wondrous radiance is ineffable,” etc., this refers to the seventh of the ten kinds of adornments in the forty-sixth scripture. The text states: “All Buddhas possess immeasurable, constant, wondrous radiance, adorned with ineffably ineffable varieties of color and form.”
It is the treasury of light, from which it produces immeasurable, perfect radiance that shines universally throughout the ten directions without obstruction.
This is the seventh supreme, unsurpassed, eternal, and wondrously radiant adornment of all Buddhas.
The Commentary states: "However, 'the emission of light' and below serves to resolve potential objections.
One might fear an objection being raised:
'If the constant light extends one fathom, it must be distinct from the emitted light.'"
Now, since the constant light (nityaprabhā) pervades the entire dharma-realm, how does it differ from the emission of light?
Therefore, this [section] provides a comprehensive explanation.
Regarding the passage beginning with "As for those who make distinctions," the commentary also addresses potential objections.
Regarding the statement that "the superior [marks] universally emit light, which is different from ordinary light":

if it were the case that they emit light only at times and not otherwise, how could one distinguish them now, given that the Ocean of Marks (lakṣaṇasāgara) emits light constantly? How then can one grasp their distinction?
Therefore, this general explanation is provided.
The commentary states: "The Buddha's wisdom is vast, that is, immeasurable," because it is boundless according to its various objects.
"Briefly stated, there are ten" refers to what is found in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata."

In the fifty-first sutra, which clarifies mental karma (*manas-karman*), it is stated that the Tathāgata’s heart, mind, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) are all unknowable; yet, because his wisdom (*jñāna*) is immeasurable, one knows the Tathāgata’s heart. This refers to the teaching of the ten types of wisdom (*daśa-jñāna*) and the ten similes.

The Commentary states: "The essence does not exceed five" means that both the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* state that the nature of Great Enlightenment is subsumed within five dharmas: namely, the one true dharma-realm and the four wisdoms of enlightenment; thus, one is principle and not wisdom.
Presently, pure wisdom is the single true *dharmadhātu*; pure wisdom is the primordial nature of wisdom.
The *Vajraśekhara-yoga* speaks of five wisdoms, of which the first, the wisdom of the purity of the *dharmadhātu*, is precisely the single true *dharmadhātu*.
The commentary states: “The ocean established within the universally manifest Dharma-realm,” etc.; this has three interpretations.
The first is the intended meaning of the commentary itself.
As for the term “universally manifest” (tōmyō), it means that the world-ocean is spoken of solely in terms of its fruition.

The ocean of the established Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vyavasthāna-samudra*) encompasses both cause and fruit, for it is by means of arising and possessing the causal conditions that one is able to establish the Dharma-realm.

Second, regarding the phrase "if it refers to causes and conditions," Xianshou says they are the dharmas of those to be converted; this is another interpretation, taking them as referring exclusively to the dharmas of conversion.
Third: "Furthermore, these are also the former two" refers to the third meaning.
Because it establishes the world of sentient beings, the "former two" refer to the ocean of worlds and the ocean of sentient beings.
Within this, first there is the correct elucidation, followed by the formal establishment (*vyavasthāpana*).
However, following the term "formal establishment," a Sanskrit citation is provided; this is a scriptural proof cited by Xianshou.

The latter two meanings regarding the ritual format (*vidhi*) refer to the method of transformation birth (*upapāduka*); since "formal establishment" is the third meaning, the conclusion states: "that is, the ritual format of formal establishment."

Fourth, regarding the "Chapter on the Ocean of Buddhas, the Inconceivable, etc.": the term "etc. includes the oceans of marks and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), as these are all the manifestations of the Buddha’s virtuous qualities and functions; they constitute the state of wondrous enlightenment.
5. Regarding the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Pāramitās Pointing Beyond the World": it is because each and every one of the two thousand dharmas of practice reaches the other shore (*pāra*).

6. Regarding the "Chapter on the Dharmadhātu": it is because the Buddha has personally realized and entered the liberation that is free from obstructions, as well as the great activities, all of which are liberation.
The "Seven-Finger *Saṃghī*" refers to the *Saṃghī-gāthā*, which extensively reveals the Buddha’s virtues as infinitely layered and vast in their function.
"Equal" means it is equal to the various passages concerning transformations throughout the beginning and end of a single sūtra.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “Because his virtues are profound and vast,” the text consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the sūtra; second, the analytical selection of the meaning beginning with “Now, these ten phrases.”
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion.
The commentary states, "As for the specific [classification], the first two," and so on, which explains the specific classification.
First, the vertical explanation distinguishes [the stages] because of their varying degrees of depth.
The statement, "This refers to all bodhisattvas discussed from a horizontal perspective," concludes the preceding section on the specific meanings.

To discuss the distinctions among the stages of practice, such as the levels of faith (*śraddhā*) and abiding (*vihāra*), is to speak in terms of vertical progression; this refers to the practitioners themselves.
To say that each individual stage encompasses many bodhisattvas is to speak in terms of horizontal inclusion of all bodhisattvas.
The Commentary states: "If explained according to the general sense," and so forth; this constitutes two explanations for the term "general" (*tong*).
To explain it according to the dharmas practiced, wherein each stage (*bhūmi*) is cultivated identically, is the meaning of "general.
Alternatively, to explain it according to a single individual who traverses all stages and cultivates these ten throughout, is the vertical discussion of all bodhisattvas.
The commentary states: "Therefore, these ten phrases apply throughout the stages of practice" refers to the third pair of conclusions.
This is because while they were explained individually in terms of their assigned stages, they are now explained collectively in terms of their application to practice.
Below the section "The forty phrases of the response," the text provides a detailed analysis of the answers given in response to the questions.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the heading and inquiry;
second, the explanation of the characteristics, beginning with "The 'pervasive' refers to all assemblies," where one first explains the pervasive and subsequently explains the specific.
The general explanation consists of two parts:
first, the general explanation of the characteristics; second, the combined and individual explanations.
Within the former, there are four sections:
First, the explicit clarification of the comprehensive response, meaning that the nine assemblies provide a comprehensive answer.
Second, from "The aforementioned ocean-like assembly" onwards, the establishment of principles.
This contains three principles:
First, the "ocean-like assembly" follows [the teaching] constantly; since this extends through the nine assemblies, the questions and answers are thus collectively comprehensive.
Second, from the words "How could it be... onwards, because the wisdom of the ocean-like assembly is profound, they are able to inquire exhaustively.
Third, "Therefore, we know that the first assembly is the general [teaching]" and below, this combines the general inquiry;
by means of these three principles, the question and answer are harmoniously resolved.
Third, "And as for the divisions" and below, this explains away potential objections.
This refers to the previous question:

"If it is said that the assembly's inquiries are exhausted across the nine assemblies and the responses are given collectively in those nine assemblies, why are there three further stages of great questions in the subsequent text?"
Therefore, this general explanation is provided.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This reveals that within each respective part, both cause and fruit are fully present,” it means that although the questions differ in their relative detail, the causes and fruits are complete in each case; thus, these are merely repeated inquiries.
4. From "Then from this, the light is exhausted" onwards is the actual response. The commentary states:
"Furthermore, regarding the forty questions," which is the second section, explaining them in terms of both the general and the specific.

The ten oceans constitute the general [category], while the remaining thirty phrases are specific instances all subsumed within those ten oceans; therefore, having answered the ten oceans as the general response, the other thirty questions are thereby answered.
This section consists of two parts:
first, the actual response to the ten oceans by means of the nine assemblies;...
Below the section "The Order in the Questions," the text answers the questions to demonstrate the differences in their sequence.
Regarding the statement in the questions, "First there were the world and sentient beings," this indicates that, fundamentally, there are three oceans:
the world itself is the World-Ocean (*lokadhātu-samudra*), which also includes the Ocean of Establishment (*vyavasthāna-samudra*).

Next, regarding the passage "Then there is the appearance of a Buddha, who attains the fruit through the cultivation of causes," this refers to the "cultivation and accomplishment" mentioned in the heading, which signifies the meaning of one's own practice (*svayam-ācāra*).
The statement "The remaining four [perfections] all constitute great functions applied according to the occasion," etc., refers to the "transforming others" (*parārtha*) mentioned in the heading.
In the commentary, the section beginning with “In the answer, one first [benefits] others and later oneself” indicates that one first benefits others.
To employ the great function throughout the four seas is precisely to benefit others first.
As for the term “four seas,” there are four meanings: first, the sea of names; second, the sea of the Four Noble Truths; third, the sea of transformations; and fourth, the sea of lifespan.

Regarding the statement that "the two oceans of self-benefit are placed last," this refers to the ocean of the *pāramitās* as the cause and the ocean of the Buddha’s liberation as the fruit; since these are answered in the eighth and ninth assemblies, they are placed last.

Regarding why only the six oceans are reconciled here while the four oceans are not: it is because the World-Ocean (*lokadhātusāgara*) and the Establishment-Ocean (*vyavasthānasāgara*) were addressed previously in response to questions, and because both the Buddha and sentient beings fundamentally abide within them.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, 'the single ocean of sentient beings' and below" further explains the ocean of sentient beings through another method.
Because [the author] previously wished to fully encompass the ten questions, he attributed the causes of the answers to the ocean of sentient beings.
Now, taking "sentient beings" as the general subject, this refers back to the previous answer concerning the "Ocean of Exposition," which explains the various stages [of the path].
The preceding section concludes the general explanation.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "If one speaks in terms of the specific," this is the second part: the explanation of the specific answers to the questions.
Regarding the phrase "the sūtra has not yet come to an end," it is because there is no concluding section following the "Vairocana Chapter.
If it had been completed, the response should have fully answered [all questions].

As for the statement "two answers encompass two others and the remainder," this means that while the primary responses concern the establishment [of the world] and the world-system itself, they also concurrently address the remaining thirty-eight questions.

The Commentary states: "It also signifies that the body serves as an offering. This refers to the verse spoken by Upādhyāya Vimukti in praise of the Buddha: "With palms joined as flowers, the body as an offering, the fragrance of a virtuous and sincere mind, and the spreading incense of eulogies."
"When the Buddhas hear this fragrance, they will come at the sound of it to deliver us; you all must exert yourselves with diligence and never again fall into doubt or error.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "If one were to explain them individually, one should contemplate them according to the text," this means that for instances such as these, the manifestation of meaning is not limited by fixed methods; one may simply cite them as corroborative evidence provided their analogies are similar.
The commentary states: "The 'face-gate' (mianmen) is the mouth. This is because there was formerly an interpretation which said:
"The face-gate is the primary countenance of the face, not the mouth itself.
Furthermore, it was said: [and so forth].

Below the nose and above the mouth, the term *mukha*—pronounced with a Brahma-voice (*brahmasvara*)—is used to refer to the face, the mouth, and the opening; for this reason, translators who understood the meaning have not been uniform in their choice of wording.
Now, because there are many teeth, the mouth serves as the fixed locus of understanding.
"The Manifestation of the Forty Questions" refers to the presence of forty teeth.
"The Path of Teaching Extends Afar" refers to the light of the wisdom of the teaching.
"True sons are born from the mouth" is said because it refers exclusively to the meaning of the "mouth.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma, they obtain a portion of the Buddha-Dharma."
Therefore, below the section on "Manifestation," the light of Samantabhadra is added as it enters the mouth.
Below the phrase "chewing the flavor of the Dharma," the meaning is clarified in relation to the teeth.
Regarding the term "general locus": the mouth is the locus for preaching the Dharma, for all dharma-gates are collectively expounded from it.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “listing the ten titles in general,” and specifically “attaining perfect, universal knowledge” (*samyak-saṃbodhi*): in principle, being free from partiality or deviation is termed “perfect” (*samyak*), and being such that no phenomenon remains unilluminated is called “universal knowledge” (*saṃbodhi*). This is the title for the ultimate realization of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "one endowed with knowledge and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): "knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to realized practice, while "conduct" (*caraṇa*) refers to taught practice. When these two practices are perfected, one is called "endowed with knowledge and conduct," which is a title signifying the fulfillment of spiritual cultivation.
Regarding the term "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*): it signifies the clear understanding of the world, and is thus a title for the perfect clarity of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "he may be called the Well-Gone One" (*sugata*): "well" (*su*) means excellent, and "gone" (*gata*) means departed; this means that he does not depart toward the other three realms or the vehicles of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but departs only toward Great Bodhi—thus, it is a title for one who proceeds directly to enlightenment.

Regarding the statement "this is precisely the meaning of 'Buddha'": "Buddha" means awakening. One who awakens themselves and awakens others, whose awakening and practice are perfected, is named Buddha. Because of this, he is honored by both gods and humans alike, and is thus called the World-Honored One (*Lokanātha*); this is the title for one who has attained self-awakening without a teacher.

Regarding the phrase "the Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara-puruṣa*): "One" (*puruṣa*) refers to a person (*puruṣa*). Among all the sages, there is none who surpasses him; thus he is named the Unsurpassed One, a title that transcends all other designations for the sages.

Regarding the term "Tamer of Men" (*purusa-damya-sārathi*): "taming" (*damya*) refers to training and refining, while "controlling" (*sārathi*) refers to guiding and restraining; thus, it is called "Tamer," which is a designation for one who gathers and guides sentient beings.

Regarding the term "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*): "teacher" (*śāstṛ*) refers to a model or guide; because he teaches the doctrines of the five vehicles to benefit sentient beings, this is a title for one who guides and instructs sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), it means that he is capable of receiving the vast offerings of devas and humans; thus, he is designated by the title "Field of Merit.
Regarding the concluding term "Tathāgata," it means that he has come to achieve perfect enlightenment by means of the path of reality as it is; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.

He immediately followed the precedent of his predecessors, proclaiming that the Buddha’s virtues are boundless; thus, the ten titles are briefly exhausted. Therefore, the third chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"I am the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha Bhagavān. Those who have not crossed over, I cause to cross over; those who have not been liberated, I cause to be liberated; those who have not found peace, I cause to find peace; those who have not attained nirvāṇa, I cause to attain nirvāṇa. I know the present world and future worlds as they truly are."
I am the all-knowing one and the all-seeing one; you, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
This is precisely what is manifested by citing the Ten Epithets.

However, the initial statement merely says that the Tathāgata likewise appears in the world like the rising of a great cloud that universally covers the trichiliocosm; thus, there is a difference between the general and the specific.
Furthermore, in the assemblies of the lower classes, it is merely stated that there are devas, humans, asuras, and so forth; the differences are simply minor matters of superiority and inferiority.
Now, adopting their perspective, I shall explain the sutra by means of the ten epithets.
The meaning of the ten titles will be explained in detail in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because [the assembly] has already arrived at the gathering, the first three matters—the ocean of lands, the ocean of worlds, and the names of the Buddhas—are omitted": (1) the ocean of lands, (2) the ocean of worlds, and (3) the names of the Buddhas.
It does not come from elsewhere; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
*The Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra Following the Sub-commentary on the Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-three.
*The Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Sūtra Following the Sub-commentary on the Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Fascicle [Twenty-three].
The twenty-fourth section,
"Detailed Explanation," composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty, states:
Regarding the "three detailed explanations," the preceding two explanations consist of one that correlates each item individually and another that correlates them collectively as a whole.

If these were not contrasted with what precedes them, the meanings of the two sections on the "seventh" and "eighth" would not be related; for the seventh is explained in terms of awakening through the Dharma, while the eighth is explained in terms of attaining benefit through the body, and since the body and the Dharma are different, they would not correspond.

Regarding the statement above that "the preceding is threefold because it is in contrast [to what follows]": the first two are called "contrasts" because they depend upon one another; now, being distinct from those, this too is a contrast to the preceding.

In the commentary, following the phrase "This concludes the beginning and end of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-transformation," the previous section explained according to the natural order (*anuloma*), whereas here we gather [the points] in reverse order (*pratiloma*) to manifest its profound subtlety.
This can be easily understood through careful investigation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, compassion and wisdom guide one another, so that one delivers sentient beings without weariness”: if compassion lacks great wisdom, it becomes merely attachment and biased views.
One who possesses compassion based on attachment develops a sense of weariness and exhaustion toward birth and death.
That one now practices through oceans of eons without weariness or exhaustion clearly demonstrates that they are guided by wisdom.
If wisdom lacks compassion, one tends toward excessive quiescence, which is termed "inferior.
Now, to liberate sentient beings from suffering with a mind free from inferiority is precisely what it means to be guided by compassion.
"Because of compassion, one is able to deliver others; because of wisdom, one is without weariness.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The next verse concerns the simultaneous contemplation of emptiness and existence," etc.: the simultaneous contemplation of emptiness and existence constitutes the first half [of the verse]. Emptiness has no measure, while existence is boundless.
Entering the gateways to the dharmas while remaining constantly quiescent constitutes the latter half.
In the former, there is the entry into all gateways to the dharmas through internal contemplation of existence; by means of the prior contemplation of emptiness, one remains eternally extinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent verse" and so forth: the two benefits for oneself and others throughout the three periods of time are all cultivated through aspiration; this is what is meant by being unimpeded regarding both things and self, thereby accomplishing the latter half [of the path], which consists of transforming others and purifying oneself.
The Commentary states: "Briefly similar to what preceded" means that while there was previously entry into the atoms (*rajas*), it is absent here.
Furthermore, such things as abiding on a single hair-tip while simultaneously shaking all lands, or the instantaneous manifestation of many bodies within every atom, are all omitted therein.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because both the differentiated and the undifferentiated are unimpeded, and so forth, each constitutes four propositions,” this is said in terms of general characteristics: the differentiated is phenomena (*dharma*), while the undifferentiated is principle (*li*). Since phenomenon and principle are already fused, there is no obstruction.
Regarding the statement that each [category] has two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), this is because both phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*li*) each possess four aspects.
As for the four aspects of principle: first, it is without spatial limitation, because it pervades all things;
second, it is not non-limiting, because within a single phenomenon there is nothing that is not fully present.

Third is both having parts and being partless: it refers to the single flavor of having parts and being partless, because the entire body resides within a single dharma while remaining eternally pervasive in all places—just as when one observes a single atom, one sees the dharma-realm in all places.

Fourth is neither having parts nor being partless: this is because its own essence is beyond dependence and is perfectly interfused; thus, these two meanings are a single characteristic and not two separate gates.
Regarding the four propositions concerning phenomena (*dharma*): first, "having parts" (*sabhāga*), because each phenomenon has its own distinct limits according to its specific characteristics;
second, "without parts" (*asabhāga*), because the entire entity is identical with the principle (*tattva*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "As with form, its prior limit is unobtainable and its posterior limit is unobtainable.
This refers precisely to the absence of divisions.
Regarding the three together: because the former two meanings are mutually unimpeded, it is only when these two meanings are fully present that there is a phenomenon.
The fourth is "neither [one nor many]," because the two meanings are fused, because they are equal, and because the two characteristics are transcended.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the body and so forth are not merely partial,” it means that by virtue of the aforementioned meanings, the principle of nature is not merely without parts; therefore, while existing in all places, its entire substance resides within one.
Because it is not merely partial, while constantly residing within one, it is entirely present in all places.
Since the phenomena of reality are not merely divisible, they are eternally present in this location while constantly existing in all other directions;
since they are not merely indivisible, they pervade all places without shifting from their original position.
Furthermore, because the principle of reality is not merely non-differentiated, it does not exist outside of any single phenomenon;
because it is not merely differentiated, it does not exist within any single phenomenon.
Since phenomena are not merely differentiated, they always abide in this very place yet have no fixed location.
It is not merely because it lacks parts that it eternally abides in all places while being nowhere absent.
Therefore, being neither localized nor non-localized, there is no obstruction in its being here or there.
However, within this there are two pairs of phenomena and principles, each consisting of four propositions, thus forming eight propositions in total.

The commentary (*śāstra*) cites only two of these propositions; namely, the statement above that "realizing the principle is not merely the absence of differentiation," which constitutes one proposition concerning the principle from the first pair.
That "all dharmas are likewise" is merely an illustration.

Now, when it says that the body and so forth are not merely parts, this refers to the phrase "in terms of phenomena" (*vastu*) from the subsequent section on "correspondence," for the body and so forth are themselves phenomena.
The remaining six phrases are omitted for brevity;
therefore, the previous general statement that there are "two sets of four phrases each" implicitly includes them.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “not reckoning the two extremes of existence and non-existence with respect to the essence”: this is because the essence of all phenomena does not transcend existence and non-existence.

Regarding the phrase "not clinging to permanence in meaning" and so forth: this refers to the meanings of permanence and impermanence inherent within a single existence (*bhava*). That is to say, arising and ceasing constitute the meaning of impermanence, while non-arising and non-ceasing constitute the meaning of permanence; furthermore, non-arising and non-ceasing may also constitute the meaning of impermanence, and so on.

As soon as there is a "dharma-nature" (dharmatā), there immediately arise permanence and impermanence, self and non-self, suffering and pleasure, purity and impurity, and so forth; therefore, it is said that "the characteristics of all dharmas are pervasive."

Regarding the phrase "not practicing suffering or pleasure within conduct": this means that those who sever the view of annihilationism—which calculates pleasant conduct as pleasure—and the view of eternalism—which calculates painful conduct as suffering—and who abide in the Right Path, do not discriminate between what is heterodox and what is orthodox, because cause and effect are mutually penetrating.
The emptiness of the nature of the world is itself the supramundane.
By observing conventional truth in accordance with reality, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within the truths, there are always two; within understanding, there is always one. Therefore, for those not yet capable of receiving the true teaching, the provisional is taught as threefold. Once the great faculties have matured, the true is then taught. This is because the provisional is the provisional that is identical to the true, and the true is the true that is identical to the provisional.

The Commentary states: "Illuminating the first two treasuries causes Bodhisattvas to realize them" means: first, the *tathāgatagarbha* within the state of entanglement (*saṃvṛta*), because it contains the dharmas of fruition;
second, the *prakṛtiviśuddhagarbha*, because it remains unstained even while in the state of entanglement.
Since these two exist as the basis, they cause that [realization] to be proven.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Illuminating the next two treasuries causes the Bodhisattvas to achieve [their goal],” the first is the Dharma-body treasury (*dharmakāya-garbha*), which refers to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), because it serves as the locus for all merits.
The second is the "Supreme Treasury of the Transmundane," which refers to those who have emerged from the entanglements (*vīta-āvaraṇa*), as they surpass both the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
Because they have all already emerged from the entanglements, the term "accomplished" (*siddha*) is employed.

The Commentary states: "Illuminating the fifth treasury to transform and purify" means that the fifth, the Dharma-realm treasury (*dharmadhātu-garbha*), pervades both cause and fruit; externally it sustains all defiled and pure conditioned phenomena, and thus is called the "Dharma-realm.
Internally it contains all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and for this reason it is further called a "treasury" (*garbha*).
They transform [beings] because there is causality; they purify them because there is defilement; the rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Of the three, the latter two are as in the section on lower karma,” this refers to the three meanings of the *garbha* (womb/storehouse), specifically the latter two meanings:
first, shaking the nets of lands; second, manifesting countless Buddhas within each and every atom.
The third is the rain of the Dharma-rain, which is the third meaning.
The cloud of the sublime wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgatagarbha; thus, it is that which is realized.
The second is the cloud of renunciation, which causes transformation and purification.
The "clouds of the three great vows" mean that they cause [beings] to attain and accomplish [the goal].

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Form is like a cloud of lamps,” the *Chapter on the Ocean of Marks* says: “Between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows there is a mark of a great man called ‘Cloud of Radiance Pervading the Dharma Realm.’”
Adorned with mani-jewel flowers, it radiates great light endowed with the colors of all manner of jewels, as penetratingly pure as the sun and moon.
Its light shines universally upon the lands of the ten directions, wherein the bodies of all Buddhas appear, and further, wondrous sounds emerge, proclaiming all dharmas.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it possesses the ten gates such as 'simultaneous fulfillment' (*yugapat-paripūrṇa*) as well as the teachings and meanings. Regarding these ten gates, they may be considered as follows:
however, the Dharma is the essential substance that serves as the basis.
Regarding the single matter within the matters: because this matter of the lotus flower is integrated by principle, it possesses ten pairs that cause them to be simultaneous and so forth.
Master Kangzang, however, explains its establishment according to the limits of its meaning, saying:
"First is the meaning of the teaching, which means that seeing this lotus flower enables the arising of understanding."
Second is the flower of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*), which means that the substance of phenomena is identical with the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
Third is the flower of object and wisdom (*ālambana-jñāna*), because that which is observed is identical with the nature of wisdom.
Fourth is the flower of practice and stages (*caryā-bhūmi*), which refers to the flowers of the myriad practices, as they differ according to their respective stages.
Fifth, cause and effect: these are the blossoms of causal phenomena, as one contemplates the fruit accomplished through causes.
Sixth, the environment and its inhabitants: these are entirely that which is cultivated, for they are also the basis upon which one relies.
Seventh, essence and function: the essence is identical to true nature, while the function responds to the capacities of sentient beings.
The Dharma of the Eight Persons is constantly observed by others because it is gathered as the Dharma.
The nine [categories of] inverse and conforming: the inverse is identical to the five heats, while the conforming refers to the ten perfections.
The ten [categories of] response and induction: they respond universally to all things, and are likewise capable of inducing [a response].

The Commentary states: "And its fundamental intent is precisely to manifest the meaning. This is because, through the ten mysteries and ten pairs, whenever a single matter is raised it necessarily encompasses all ten mysteries, and every single mystery-gate necessarily includes all ten pairs; thus, when a single dharma is explained in general terms, each one is perfectly and completely subsumed.
If one were to act as a teacher, it would merely be a secondary matter; however, the fundamental intent is solely to manifest the meaning.
Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "Suddenly appearing," this is an exegesis that restates the point in response to an objection.

According to the second fascicle of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, it is explained that when the light of the white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) appears on the ground of diamond, by the power of this mark, precious lotuses spontaneously manifest beneath the roots of the Buddha’s Bodhi tree. These flowers are forty *yojanas* in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions, and their golden petals have pedestals made of golden diamond.
"The light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows illuminates this flower pedestal; that light descends directly to the adamantine limit," and so forth.
This is largely the same as the present text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "It is also like the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* saying 'milk comes from a cow,'" this refers to the fourteenth fascicle (the thirteenth in the Southern Edition), which says: "At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbharāja. He possessed great majestic power, had accomplished supernatural faculties, attained great dhāraṇīs, was fully endowed with samādhi, and had obtained fearlessness."
Immediately rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, the merits and wisdom accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, boundless, and numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis; they are truly ineffable."
In my view, it still does not equal such Mahāyāna sūtras. Why is this?
It is because, by the power of these Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one is able to give birth to the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.

Although these Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras possess immeasurable merit, they cannot be compared to this sūtra; even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold, or even by any calculation or analogy, they cannot approach it.
"Good son! It is like this:
from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the finest cream (ghṛta)."
Ghee is the most supreme; if there are those who consume it, all their many ailments will be eliminated, for all medicinal herbs are contained within it.

Good son, the Buddha is also like this: from the Buddha flow forth the twelve divisions of the scriptures; from the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerge the sūtras; from the sūtras emerge the Vaipulya sūtras; from the Vaipulya sūtras emerges the Prajñāpāramitā; and from the Prajñāpāramitā emerges the Mahāparinirvāṇa, which is like the finest ghee.
What is called "ghee" (sarpis) is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
The Buddha-nature is none other than the Tathāgata.
O son of good family!
"For this reason, it is said that all the merits possessed by the Tathāgata are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
The commentary states:
This refers to the excellence of the praised Dharma, which can proceed from the subtle to the manifest.
Now, we shall simply take the teachings issued from the Buddha as a comparison for the multitude of ears emerging from between his eyebrows.
However, there are differing interpretations regarding this passage of the sutra.
According to Zhezhou, within the "Explanation of the Questions Addressed to the Bodhisattvas," there is a question that states:
This sutra is its teaching, and *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is its realized fruit.
Since the teaching is shallow while the realization is profound, why would *bodhi* not surpass this sutra?
The commentary states:
herein, that which specifically expresses the terminology for Buddha-nature and the teaching of the Dharma-body is designated as a "sūtra.
That which is realized is the cause and fruit of intrinsic purity, and the bodhi that arises therefrom is its expedient means.
The nature of cause and effect takes purity as its root and skillful means as its branches; because the branches do not equal the root, the merits of the Buddha’s bodhi cannot be attained.
This is the meaning according to the subsequent answer of the Buddha.
Next, the following explains the Buddha’s response; the "correspondence" (*he*) therein states:
the Buddha corresponds to the ox, referring to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) Buddha;
the twelve divisions of the scriptures correspond to the milk, referring to the preaching of the Hīnayāna sūtras.
The *sūtras* combined with the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) are called the Mahāyāna teachings.
Because they rely on the Small Vehicle to open up the Great Vehicle, they are termed "emergence" (*niryāṇa*).
The latter four [categories] are all Mahāyāna teachings that explain matters; they are called *sūtras*, referring to matters such as giving (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The *Vaipulya* (fangděng) corresponds to clarified butter (*sarpis*); it refers to the teaching of the emptiness that destroys marks within the Mahāyāna.

Because it reveals the principle through phenomena, it is called "emergence. The *Prajñā* corresponds to ghee (*ghṛta*); the wisdom that ultimately abandons marks and realizes the truth is named *prajñā*. Because this wisdom arises based on the principle, it is called "emergence"; furthermore, when distinguishing the teachings according to practice, it may also be termed "emergence."
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This prajñā is precisely the aforementioned essence of bodhi.

By uniting the *amṛta* (clarified butter) with nirvāṇa, prajñā serves as the cause of illumination; it illuminates that beginningless dharma-nature which is nirvāṇa, and for this reason, it is called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
In terms of ultimate reality, the teaching may also be called "emergence.
When the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata," this refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, not the Saṃbhogakāya Tathāgata.
The merits of the *Sambhogakāya* do not equal those of this sutra; therefore, [the Buddha] did not immediately [reveal it].
The above points represent Master Huiyuan’s intention.
