the five are the ocean of all sentient beings' karma; and the five are the wisdom that enters the ocean of all inclinations, understandings, and faculties.
The ocean of liberation of the six Buddhas; the wisdom of the various samādhis of the profound, non-differentiated liberation of the Buddhas abiding in the sixth stage;
the ocean of the faculties and desires of all sentient beings; and the wisdom that universally knows all three periods of time in a single thought-moment.
The ocean of the transformations of the seven Buddhas; the wisdom of the seven entries into the ocean of the faculties of all bodhisattvas;
the ocean of the wheels of Dharma of all Buddhas of the seven [aeons]; and the wisdom of the seven manifestations of the ocean of the immeasurable vows of all Tathāgatas.
The ocean of the teachings expounded by the eight Buddhas; the wisdom of eloquence in turning the wheel of Dharma through the ocean of the languages of all sentient beings and the eight wisdoms;
the ocean of all three periods of time; and the wisdom of manifesting the ocean of all Buddhas' supernatural transformations.
The ocean of the names of the nine Buddhas; the ocean of the wisdom of the bodies that universally enter all oceans of worlds within the Dharma-realm;
the ocean of the power of the vows of all Tathāgatas; and the wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma.
Ten oceans of the lifespans of Buddhas constitute one attainment of the wisdom of the voices of all Buddhas;
ten oceans of the spiritual transformations of all Tathāgatas constitute one establishment of the wisdom that expounds oceans of teachings.
The ten dharmas practiced therein are also ten oceans, as already explained in the previous assembly.
Although the word "ocean" does not appear in the text, it is omitted here for brevity.
Now, correlating these with the four textual passages, they are divided into four sections:

Regarding the first section, which praises wisdom by correlating it with the ocean-like eloquence in sequential order: the first wisdom contemplates the first ocean; the second wisdom contemplates the second ocean and the fifth ocean; the third contemplates the fourth; the fourth contemplates the third; the fifth contemplates the sixth; the sixth contemplates the eighth; the seventh contemplates the ninth; the eighth contemplates the tenth; and the ninth and tenth both contemplate the seventh. This can be understood simply by observing the sequence listed above.
The correlation presented in the Commentary is precisely this correspondence.

Second, if one correlates the "Praise of Wisdom" with the "Successive Stages of Wisdom," that which is praised as first corresponds to the fourth stage of wisdom: the world’s formation and destruction;
and the second corresponds to the fifth: the wisdom regarding the ocean of karma.
Three is two; it enters the immeasurable Dharma-realm.

Four is three; five is seven; six is six; seven is nine; eight is six; nine is eight; ten is that very ten, because that contains a comprehensive statement; within those six, these six and eight are included.
Third, if one were to correlate the praise of wisdom with the ten oceans of questions, it would for the most part be identical to the first correlation regarding the ocean of contemplation.

To explain in detail: the first four correspond respectively to the first four oceans; the fifth corresponds universally to the latter five; the sixth is that very sixth; the seventh is the ninth and tenth; the eighth is the seventh; and both this ninth and the tenth are that very eighth.

Fourth, if one were to correlate these ten contemplations of the ocean with the ten oceans themselves: this first contemplation corresponds to the first ocean; the second to the second; the third to the fourth; the fourth to the third; the fifth also to the second; the sixth pervades the latter five and may likewise be considered the second; the seventh corresponds to the eighth; the eighth corresponds to the sixth; the ninth corresponds to both the ninth and the tenth; and this tenth ocean is the seventh ocean itself.
Furthermore, one should again correlate the ten oceans by means of the "Contemplation of the Ocean" (Guan hai), as was done in the previous correlations.
Moreover, one should further correlate them with "Wisdom" (Zhi) to inquire about the ten oceans, as has already been correlated in the previous section on Wisdom.

If one were to further correlate the ten oceans with the ten dharmas of the "object of practice" (yōsho-chū), it would be as already explained in the preceding chapter regarding the object of practice;
therefore, I shall now briefly present only four gates.
The remaining meanings are fully explained in the commentary (*śāstra*), which can be easily understood through careful study.

Regarding the passage in the commentary stating, "By means of the general, the particular is subsumed; this merely expands upon the bodily radiance and so forth": it means that by means of the generality of the three types of action (*trikarma*), the particulars of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are encompassed.
Regarding the phrase "merely the extensive body-light and so forth," the term "and so forth" (等) includes the aforementioned light, voice, and wisdom.

The two types of light pertain to the body, the voice belongs to the mouth, and wisdom is that of the mind; since this text now possesses all of them, the word "and so forth" is employed, thereby opening the three karmas into ten.

The Commentary states: "If it is said that [the text] explains everything in full, why does the subsequent section speak only of the 'establishment' and the 'ocean of worlds'? This concludes the question; what follows below is the response and analysis.
The answer has two intentions:
first, because the scripture has not yet reached its conclusion, the response is given in terms of what is currently manifest;
for there is no final conclusion at the end of the "Chapter on Vairocana."
If the sūtra were complete, one should further answer the remaining thirty-eight questions.
Second, from "Furthermore, although two are mentioned" onwards, the answer addresses these two while including the others.
Within this, first the heading is established, and subsequently, from "That is to say, the realms must necessarily arise," the characteristics of what is included are set forth.
Briefly stated, there are three oceans: first, sentient beings; second, Buddhas; and third, karmic actions.
When these are combined with two others, there are already five oceans.

Regarding the phrase "the remainder may be sought as desired," this refers to the other five oceans and so forth: namely, (1) wherever there are sentient beings, there must be faculties and desires; (2) wherever there is a Buddha, it must be by means of the power of vows; (3) there must be spiritual transformations that are universally pervasive; (4) there must be the turning of the Dharma to benefit living beings; and (5) there is the function of liberation.
Thus, the ten oceans are fully possessed.
Just as it is with the possession of the oceans, so it is with the possession of the others by analogy.
This is explained according to the separate answers to the forty questions.

If the ten oceans are taken as a whole, this [text] answers only two of them, while the remaining eight are answered individually, as already explained in the "Manifestation of Signs" chapter; thus, within these ten oceans, the other thirty are also included.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “These ten also correspond to the preceding ten oceans of the ten wisdoms,” the first [ocean] is intended to cause one to possess all ten wisdoms immediately; thus it says, “for the purpose of causing sentient beings to enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.”

The remaining nine constitute the ten oceans: the first is the ocean of Buddhas and the ocean of spiritual transformations; the second is the ocean of worlds; the third is the ocean of the three periods of time; the fourth is the ocean of the dharma-realm; the fifth is the ocean of turning the wheel of Dharma; the sixth is the ocean of the faculties of sentient beings; the seventh and eighth are both the ocean of sentient beings; and the ninth is the ocean of vows. Thus, the ten oceans are complete.
As it is with the ocean, so it may be understood regarding wisdom, for they are like the ocean.
The four praises of excellence and the exhortation to listen follow.
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "However, this applies to these ten" is a re-explanation of the verse.
The conclusion states: "I wish to provide a detailed correlation and explanation, but fear it may weary the reader with excessive detail. I shall now correlate them.

The first verse cites the stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*) and the merit of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya-guṇa*), while simultaneously encompassing the ten phrases beginning with "essence" (*svabhāva*) and "manifest characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-prasphuṭatva*), because it speaks of the universal manifestation of light throughout the ten directions and its pervasive illumination.
The second verse concerns the ocean of worlds and their manifestation.
The third verse restates the Buddha’s realm.
The fourth verse restates the Buddha’s empowerment.
The fifth verse concerns the ocean of karma, the ocean of aspiration, and the ocean of discipline.

The first half of the sixth verse concerns the ocean of *pāramitās* as well as the Buddha-bhūmi; the next line concerns the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*; and the final line concerns the sphere of practice.
The seventh verse concerns the ocean of supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*).
The first half of the eighth verse concerns the ocean of sentient beings, and the second half concerns the ocean of eloquent exposition (*deśanā*).
The ninth verse concerns the ocean of the Buddha’s liberation (*vimukti*) and the three masteries (*vaśitā*).
The tenth verse concerns the ocean of great vows;
all others contain [elements of] both [aspects], which can be understood through reflection.
As they do not benefit contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), they are omitted from this brief commentary.
Because I wish to provide a detailed explanation following the text, I have excerpted and reissued it.
Second, the fundamental meaning is extensively set forth.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "Wisdom is still difficult to fathom," it is divided into three parts:
First, the general objection; second, the selection and discrimination beginning with "Now, as for the ten matters above"; third, the explanation of the text.
Within the second [section], there are three parts:
first, the ten [matters] corresponded to lands; second, the ten corresponded to lineages; third, the ten corresponded to oceans.
The first four points at the beginning are as follows:
first, the direct response;
second, from "Some say" onwards, the narration of past views, which represents the intent of the *Kanding* (Determining the Text).
3. From "then it would contradict" below, there is the analysis of the contradiction.
4. From "if one relies on" below, there is the conclusion regarding the fault.
This means that since the entirety of the ocean of world-systems is rendered without distinction, there would be no distinct phenomena within the ocean of lands.
The remainder may be understood.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "As for the phrase 'as numerous as the atoms in the oceans of worlds,' etc.," there are three explanations of the text.
Within this, there are four parts:
1. Correctly explaining the meaning of the sūtra; 2. Reiterating the general refutation of past views; 3. Revealing the reason for the refutation; 4. Proactively blocking past defenses.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "Some say," this is the second section: reiterating the general refutation of past views.
Regarding the phrase "exceedingly reckless" (*mènglàng zhī shèn*): *làng* means to drift or wander; *mèng* also means violent or impetuous.
The "Qi Wù" chapter of the *Zhuāngzǐ* states: "Jiūquè Zǐ asked Chángwù Zǐ, saying:
'I have heard from you, Master:'"

The sage does not engage in worldly affairs; he does not pursue advantage nor avoid harm, he does not delight in seeking nor follow the conventional path. He treats "non-being" as "being" and "being" as "non-being," and thus wanders beyond the realm of dust and defilement.
"The Master considers these to be reckless words, yet I consider them the practice of the wondrous Way.
What do you think of this?
The commentary states:
I do not take up the specific matter here, but merely what was stated in a careless manner.
"Careless" refers to hasty and superficial speech; it clarifies that such statements are inappropriate.
Xiang Xiu said:
"Vastly pervasive and having no place of resort or abandonment—this is what is meant.
These two characters must be used in conjunction.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "For what reason," the three points clarifying why [it is not so] can be understood by following the intent.
Yet, fearing it may still be difficult to perceive, I shall clarify this through a metaphor.
Suppose there is a single platter containing ten plates, and within each of those ten plates, there are ten marbles.
One platter is like an ocean of lands, one dish is like a world-system, and a pellet is like a single land.
If one says that within one platter there is another platter and its pellets, they are equal in number to atoms without any difference.
How can one claim that because the pellets within a single bowl are indistinguishable, they may suffice as the required number?

A single bowl contains but one hundred pellets; yet the dust particles of even one pellet are difficult to count, let alone the dust produced by grinding all one hundred pellets into powder—their number would be immeasurable. To take the number "one hundred" and equate it to the number of dust particles in a bowl is therefore reckless.
If one grasps the meaning of this analogy, it becomes easy to understand upon immediate reflection.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Nor can it be said that [the teaching] universally applies to all oceans of worlds," this is the fourth point, which serves as a counter-objection to previous defenses.
One might fear that there would be an objection, saying:
"The lands within a single ocean of lands do not suffice to fill the dust motes of one ocean of lands.
Now, if we take all the lands within every ocean of lands to fill the number of dust motes in one ocean of lands, would this not be possible?"
It is like the number of pellets in a single bowl, which cannot fill the dust of even one bowl.
If there were many bowls of pellets, would they not suffice to fill the dust of a single bowl?
Therefore, we now refute this by saying:
although the meaning may be roughly consistent with this interpretation, how can it contradict the subsequent passage?
The subsequent passage states: "Within a single world-ocean, there are as many world-oceans as there are atoms in a world-ocean."
It cannot be said that all world-oceans together constitute a single world-ocean with a number of atoms; how then could this be used as a defense?
It is just as when one bowl of pellets has a number of atoms equal to that bowl of pellets, yet one does not say that many bowls possess the same number of atoms as a single bowl.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “However, as for the meaning of Buddha-lands,” there are three parts to the text:
first, the classification of types; second, the integration and inclusion; third, the explanation of the text.
Now, for the first, the three lands are explained.
The two open into three to become four;
the three merge with the four to become two;
the four dissolve into the two to become one.
The first two [categories] correspond to the meaning of the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
However, the initial explanation of three [bodies] is based on the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Since the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) includes both self and others, it constitutes four bodies; these four bodies, in turn, rely upon the four lands (*catasraḥ kṣetrāḥ*).

The treatise states: "Furthermore, the svabhāvakāya relies upon the dharmatā-realm (dharmatā-kṣetra). Although there is no difference in essence between this body and its realm, they are distinct in terms of their respective Buddha-nature and its characteristics."

This Buddha’s body and land are both not comprised within form; although their dimensions—whether large or small—cannot be described, their extent is nonetheless boundless according to their phenomenal characteristics, just as space pervades all places.
The commentary states: This meaning was already cited in the preceding chapter; it is cited again here in full detail for the sake of its application in the subsequent text. The treatise says:

"The Body of Self-Enjoyment resides within the Land of Self-Enjoyment. That is to say, the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—due to the maturation of the causes and conditions for the self-benefiting, untainted, and purely immaculate Buddha-land cultivated in the past—continuously transforms from the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future into a purely immaculate Buddha-land that is circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels. The Body of Self-Enjoyment constantly dwells in reliance upon this."

Just as the measure of the pure land is, so too is the measure of the body; each of its sense faculties and marks of excellence is boundless, for it is produced by the guidance of limitless roots of goodness.

Since merit and wisdom are not material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), although their physical dimensions cannot be described, they may nonetheless be said to pervade all places in accordance with what is realized and the body upon which they rely.
The commentary states:
"Merit follows the body upon which it relies; wisdom follows the suchness (tathatā) that has been realized.
The rest may be understood accordingly."

The treatise states: "The Body of Enjoyment for Others also relies upon its own land. This refers to the Great Compassion and the Wisdom of Equality; through the maturation of the causes and conditions for the pure, untainted Buddha-land cultivated in the past for the benefit of others, it transforms into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages. These lands may be small or large, inferior or superior, changing and shifting from one period to another."
The Enjoyment Body (sambhogakāya) dwells in dependence upon this [Dharmakāya], and the dimensions of that dependent body are likewise without fixed limit.

As for the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya), it relies upon a transformation land; that is to say, through the power of the wisdom of accomplishing activities and great compassion, and by virtue of the maturation of causes and conditions from previously cultivated pure and impure Buddha-lands for the benefit of others, it manifests as a Buddha-land according to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the stages (bhūmi). These lands may be pure or impure, large or small, and they change and transform over time.
"The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha abides in dependence upon it, and the dimensions of this dependent body likewise have no fixed limit.
Commentary: The above are all from the treatise; the text is straightforward and easy to understand.
When applying this in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), one must know its location.

Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary: "The categories are only two kinds, namely purity and defilement, as well as nature and characteristics," this means that the three [categories] subsume the four [aspects] into two.
In various sūtras and śāstras, there are two types of these two categories. Regarding the prior inclusion of the aforementioned four as either pure or impure, there are many reasons.
Since the four contain both the pure and the impure, three and a half categories are pure and half a category is impure.

The first two and the preceding three are pure because, having severed the obstacles of conceptual discrimination through the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*), they have realized true suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, they are called "pure.
Transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are all impure; even if they possess the seven treasures, they are inhabited by defiled sentient beings, and thus they are not pure either.
The latter two of these three are both defiled. The *Renwang jing* states: "The Three Sages and Ten Saints dwell in the retribution of fruition; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
Master Sheng, however, said: "That which has form is entirely defiled; that which is formless is pure."
Thus, it is only the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) that is pure.
If this is so, could the land of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) be called defiled?
Since this [land] is in profound accord with true nature (*tathatā*), its dimensions—whether large or small—cannot be specified; therefore, it is likewise subsumed under the category of purity.
Regarding the subsumption of the former four as nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are briefly two approaches:
first, that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is the nature while the other three are all characteristics;
second, that the self-enjoyment realm (*svasaṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), which is identical to true nature, may also be called "nature," while the remaining two are exclusively characteristics.

The fourth [characteristic] is that they are fused into one; thus, the nature and characteristics of the pure and the defiled, as well as the three lands and four lands, are all perfectly interfused. This is precisely the meaning of this sutra, which is why it says, "it differs from other schools."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, this Pure Land does not consist of a single substance," and so forth; this is the second section on integration and subsumption.
Because of the aforementioned fourth point, this integration is briefly provided here.
However, Master Dong’an Zhuang originally had only three propositions, which did not include "non-substantiality does not constitute [existence].
Now, by adding this phrase, two pairs are formed. That is to say:
the realms of purity and defilement are utterly distinct and cannot be said to be one; [and so forth].
Principle is of a single flavor and cannot be said to be diverse.
It is identical in its hidden nature to emptiness and cannot be said to exist;
yet it is established according to conditions and cannot be said to be non-existent.
However, "one" is used to eliminate difference, and "non-characteristic" is used to eliminate existence.
Yet, within that explanation, "one" is also applied according to principle; in reality, it carries the meaning of "one.
There are two types of this:
First, unity in terms of principle; second, unity in terms of phenomena.
For example, regarding self-enjoyment, the pure lands of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are equally possessed by all; they cannot be said to be non-existent, and thus may be called "one."
Therefore, the commentary establishes four propositions, consisting of two pairs of differing aspects.
Furthermore, while the above briefly cites four propositions that exclusively negate errors, in reality, [the nature of things] is both different and identical, and both existent and non-existent.
If they mutually negate one another, then both unity and difference vanish, and both existence and non-existence are simultaneously stilled.
If they are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, then they are identical with both the one and the many, and identical with both existence and non-existence.
There is this non-abiding existence and this abiding non-existence; the many are the one-many, and the one is the many-one.

Existence and non-existence are the unimpeded interfusion of phenomena and principle, while the one and the many constitute the unimpeded interfusion of phenomena with phenomena. Through these successive layers, every single atom within each land of the Flower Treasury World reveals the entire Dharma-realm.
The remainder is as in the *Xuanzhong* [section].
*Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Following its Sub-commentary*, Scroll Twenty-Five.
*Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Following its Sub-commentary*, Scroll [Twenty-Five].
The twenty-sixth [section],
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty,
as a commentary: from the phrase "Since the lands are not the same" onwards is the second part, the explanation of the text.

Within this, there are four sections: first, the sequential arising based on what preceded; second, the formal explanation of the scriptural text; third, the selection and resolution of difficulties; and fourth, the sequential interlocking.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "The first three," this constitutes the second section: the formal explanation of the scriptural text.
The commentary on the first phrase consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation; second, the resolution of objections.
This is the first [part].

Regarding the phrase "all that is pure and defiled," this refers generally to the three lands, with the sole exception of the dharma-nature (dharmatā), because these are established through the power of universal wisdom.
This corresponds to the verse line: "The power of wisdom and supernormal faculties is thus."
Regarding the statement, "Taking [the body] for the sake of beings so as to respond universally," this means that, excluding what is for one's own enjoyment, it is all for the sake of beings.
The commentary, from "The Buddha should preside over them" onwards, explains away potential objections.
There are two objections to this:
first, the objection that all [realms] would be called Buddha-fields.
That is to say, there are pure and impure lands; how could an impure land be a Buddha-field?
Therefore, the present answer states:
"Defilement is also a Buddha-land.
The dilapidated house of the triple world belongs to a single person; the Sahā world, with its mixed evils, dwells within the Flower Treasury World (Huazang), and this is my Buddha-land.
Secondly, speaking from the perspective of the Buddha himself, there is no land that is not pure.
Even when referring to impure lands, they are designated as "pure" in a conventional sense.
This is based on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, wherein Ratnākara requested to hear how one attains a pure buddha-field, to which the Buddha replied:
Regarding the phrase "the classes of sentient beings," this does not distinguish between the pure and the defiled;

even the defiled is a Pure Land. Therefore, one may harbor doubt, thinking that what is called "defiled" is actually named a Buddha-land, and that which is called "defiled" under the governance of the Buddha is in fact named a Pure Land.
Furthermore, on what basis is this answer given?
Indeed, all Buddha-fields are pure; it is for this reason that when Śāriputra saw hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, the Buddha said:
"This land of mine is pure, yet you do not see it."

Regarding the statement that "speech is both defiled and pure, and is therefore inconceivable," this means that the preceding meaning is applied to the subsequent verse. The verse states: "The realm of the World-Honored One is inconceivable."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If this is the dharma-nature, it is the fundamental consciousness,” and so forth: this refers to how the Tathāgatagarbha, by following conditions, establishes all pure and impure lands, as cited from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in the "Samādhi" chapter.
This is spoken in terms of general characteristics; it is neither restricted to sentient beings nor restricted to Buddhas.

If one speaks of "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), this refers to the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Therefore, the commentary reconciles these two passages, and the underlying principle is thus evident.
In the commentary, from "Karma has good and evil" onwards, there is first a general explanation;
subsequently, from "The Pure Name" onwards, there are scriptural citations.
Three sūtras and four passages are cited; two of these are from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, both from the "Buddhakṣetra" chapter.
Regarding the initial statement, "taking the myriad practices as the cause," the Sūtra says: "Baoji!
You should know that the straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will come to be born in his land."
The profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with complete merit will come to be born in that land.
The bodhicitta is the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings of the Mahāyāna will come to be born in that land.
Next, because the six perfections and so forth are enumerated, it is said that "the myriad practices are the cause.
Second, as for the statement, "The class of sentient beings is the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva," this is also from this same text.
Next, the passage beginning with "Although the dharma-nature is one" provides a dual explanation for the two preceding points.
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, [the section on] "becoming diverse according to karma" explains that the myriad practices mentioned above serve as causes; these are the causes for the land.

The two Buddhas, according to their respective classes of beings, take up the earth to gather in and nurture sentient beings; this explains the previous passage stating that "the various classes of sentient beings are the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva," which constitutes the conditions for that land.
Third, following the section on "Nirvāṇa," other sūtras are separately cited to establish the first meaning.
Within the second [section], the text is also cited in full.
In the "Buddhakṣetra-parivarta" chapter, when Ratnākara offered a parasol, the Buddha manifested the signs of a transformed pure land for him, whereupon Ratnākara sought its cause.
Therefore, the initial question states, "I wish to hear about attaining the purity of a Buddha-land," which cites the fruit.
It continues, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the practices for purifying the lands of bodhisattvas," which inquires into the cause.
The Buddha replied:
"The various classes of sentient beings are the hallmark of a bodhisattva’s buddha-field. This is followed by the detailed explanation of the text. Why is this so?
"A Bodhisattva takes up a Buddha-field according to the sentient beings he transforms; he takes up a Buddha-field according to the sentient beings he disciplines.
The commentary states:
The first two lines generally clarify that the act of taking up a land is solely for the sake of sentient beings.
The Sūtra says: "According to whatever lands sentient beings should enter through in order to attain the Buddha’s wisdom, he takes up that buddha-land.
According to whatever lands sentient beings should arise in through in order to develop the roots of a bodhisattva, he takes up that buddha-land."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the reason for the differences between the lands.
The subsequent sutra text poses a question and provides an explanation, saying: "For what reason?"
"The Bodhisattva takes up a pure land solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.
This explains the meaning of the sutra:
the Bodhisattva cultivates causes and takes up a land entirely conditioned by sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, what would be the use of taking up a land?
These are all due to the conditions of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (other-enjoyment) land and the *nirmāṇa* (transformation) land.
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, both lands are established through altruistic practice; they are clearly intended for the sake of sentient beings, as that scripture provides an analogy:
"To construct a palace, one must rely on vacant ground."
If there were no space, it could never be accomplished.
To cultivate a pure land, one must necessarily rely upon sentient beings;
if there were no sentient beings, there would be no place to cultivate a land.
The commentary states: "Regarding 'the subtle goodness of nirvāṇa' and below, [the author] separately cites another sutra to establish the initial meaning.
This refers to the twenty-first sutra, the *Bodhisattva Gao-gui-de-wang Pin* (Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gao-gui-de-wang)."
When the Bodhisattva Vairocanaraśmiprabha had come from the world-system Akṣobhya, the Bodhisattva Abhaya asked the Buddha:
"What karma must the sentient beings of this land perform in order to be reborn in that world-system Akṣobhya?"
The Buddha answered in verse, extensively enumerating the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), each of which leads to rebirth.

Regarding "even a slight wholesome deed," there is a verse that says: "If one makes an offering of even a single incense stick or lamp, or even presents a single flower to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one shall be born in the Land of Immovability (*Acalā*)."
"If one writes even a single verse of this sutra for the sake of fear, for gain and honor, or for the sake of merit, one will be born in the Immovable Land (Acalā).
It also says: "If one creates an image or a stupa even as small as a thumb, while constantly giving rise to a joyful mind, one will be born in the Immovable Land. This is it.

Regarding the *Commentary*’s mention of “the three minds of the *Contemplation Sūtra*,” there are three sets of three minds. First, after the Buddha had manifested the Pure Land for Vaidehī, Vaidehī made a vow to seek the causes for rebirth there.
The Buddha said:
"Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three kinds of merit:
first, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten virtuous actions."
Second, to receive and uphold the Three Refuges, to be complete in all the precepts, and not to violate the rules of dignified conduct.
Third, to resolve upon Bodhicitta, to have deep faith in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahāyāna sutras, and to exhort practitioners to advance.
"These three matters are called pure karma.
The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī:
"Do you now understand?"
"These three types of action are the primary causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The commentary states:
"If one possesses these three, what purity could one fail to attain?"

Nevertheless, because those who are born [in such lands] proceed toward Buddhahood, they are collectively referred to as "born. As cited above: "A straightforward mind is the Buddha-land of a bodhisattva; when that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings free from flattery will come to be born in his land."

In the second section on the highest grade of rebirth, it says: "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, they will attain rebirth immediately upon giving rise to three kinds of mind.
What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; and third, the mind of dedication and aspiration."
"One who is fully endowed with these three minds will certainly be born in that land.
The third [section] says: "Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain birth in the Pure Land.
What are these three?"
First, to possess a compassionate heart and refrain from killing while maintaining all precepts;
second, to read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras;
third, to practice the six remembrances, dedicate the merit, and make vows to be reborn in that land.
"Endowed with these merits, after one day up to seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth there.
The commentary states:
The third set of three minds is largely the same as the first three phrases; however, it combines the first two and expands upon the last one.

These aforementioned mental states not only serve as the cause for birth in that land, but can also function as the cause for cultivation to achieve that Pure Land; therefore, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states that they are "the direct cause of the pure karma of the Buddhas of the three periods. Thus, they are now cited as the causes for the Buddha-land.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the first three: the first is one cause, the second is two conditions, and the third is one cause,' there are briefly two kinds of causes:
first, the transformative cause, which is the first [cause], the Tathāgata’s supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*)."
The second is the cause for perceiving a pure land, which is the third [topic].
Its conditions are also twofold:
first, taking sentient beings who benefit others as the object-condition; second, subsuming the object within the mind, such that all are transformations of one's own consciousness.
Among these, the second meaning is that the true mind merely transforms in accordance with conditions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The next four [points] specifically clarify that there are both causes and conditions”: for example, that which is accomplished by the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is the condition; the transformation land is the cause. This applies to both causes and conditions: the Buddha takes birth as a condition, and birth takes the Buddha as a condition.

The Commentary states: "Sentient beings and bodhisattvas together construct a single object-condition. This has already been explained in general above as being that the straightforward mind is itself the pure land of the bodhisattva and so forth.
If a bodhisattva personally cultivates a straightforward mind, how could the flattery and crookedness of sentient beings possibly arise?
For this reason, he exhorts beings to collectively cultivate a straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*).

Thus, by means of the cause of a straightforward mind, the Bodhisattva takes a land of straightforwardness; responding to sentient beings with straightforward minds, they share a common karmic condition to be born in that realm.
All myriad practices are likewise thus; therefore, it is said that they "accord with their respective karmic actions.
As for the phrase "ordinary beings and sages dwell together," this refers to the land of transformation.
If it were the land of other-enjoyment, it would be inhabited by sages alone.
Regarding the land of transformation where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, there are two meanings:

first, it is because [the Buddha] transforms according to the capacities of sentient beings; second, even those who have newly realized the fruit of sainthood within an ordinary body still reside therein.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two kinds of causes for the other-enjoyment lands (he-shou-yong-tu) are three and four,” this is briefly as cited above from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

While the *Vijñaptimātratā* consistently speaks of the causes in reference to the Buddha alone, here it applies them generally to Bodhisattvas as well; that is to say, when the Buddha cultivates these two causes during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), they result in the other-enjoyment [body], and thus constitute the Buddha’s own causes.
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the two stages cultivate these two causes and thereby attain the enjoyment for others; this is in terms of the bodhisattva cause.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* explains in detail [the distinctions between] the first stage and the eighth stage.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) holds [the object] and transforms according to the mind”: resolute conviction has the nature of holding [the object] with respect to its focal point; it holds all objects such that they transform according to the mind.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “the cause that flows from a single root of goodness,” this refers to the unimpeded practice of the twofold benefit of self and others through perfectly integrated cultivation; it is for this reason that such a state is attained.
In the Commentary, from the passage "That Dharma-nature land" onwards, the third section provides a critical analysis of potential difficulties and objections.
Question:
Since the ten preceding phrases encompass all four lands, why is it that the causes for only three lands are specifically explained here?
Therefore, this explanation was provided.
Next, it is further asked:
"Apart from the four lands, if the perfectly integrated (yuanrong) land is mentioned separately, there should be five lands."
Therefore, the present response states:
Thus, the latter three merely integrate the former four; this is our own school's tenet, and they do not possess a separate substantiality.
The cause of such perfect integration is also as explained above.
Furthermore, it is said that there are generally two meanings of the Pure Land:
first, taking the purification of karma as the cause to evoke the fruit of pure appearances;
second, taking virtuous deeds as the cause to evoke the fruit of sovereign purity.

The practice of deeds begins with ordinary beings and culminates in the tenth stage; the meritorious activity begins with the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) and culminates in the state of a Tathāgata.
This second section provides a specific clarification regarding the purity of these practices.
The third [section], "Integration," refers to the purity of mastery.
Since the first [section], "General Clarification," possesses these two purities, the commentary (*śāstra*) establishes three [categories].
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "Furthermore, these ten matters," it appears within the "Chain of Verses" (*gāthā-śṛṅkhalā*).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “The Establishment of Consciousness-Only” (*Cheng weishi lun*) and below: the preceding text has already been cited in its entirety; now it shall be briefly explained.

The pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is precisely the eighth consciousness at the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*); this serves as the basis for the cause, because [the transformation] occurs instantaneously in dependence upon it.
The section beginning with "From what was cultivated in the past" explains the causes of the practice.
The section beginning with "From the initial attainment of Buddhahood" distinguishes the characteristics of its fruit.
First, it clarifies the vertical length; subsequently, from the term "circumferential," it clarifies its horizontal breadth.
The Commentary states:
"That which is called the wisdom of equality," and so forth; this has already been cited in full above.
Wisdom preceding practice and practice following wisdom are both conditions as objects (ālambana-hetu).
Furthermore, because practice serves as the cause and wisdom serves as the condition, they are called "causes and conditions.

Moreover, both of the aforementioned [practice and wisdom] are causes, while the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages serve as the conditions; as described above, manifesting transformations according to the beings to be converted constitutes the characteristic of the fruit, namely the Pure Land.
On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one perceives a hundred [world-systems] such as the *trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*; therefore, it is called "small.
On the second stage, there are a thousand; on the third, ten thousand, and so forth.
Each subsequent stage is greater than the preceding one; thus, each preceding stage is inferior, while each subsequent stage is progressively superior.
The meaning of the stages cited below is consistent with that of this chapter.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, the seventh verse relies on the basis of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),” it provides a systematic analysis of the meaning to establish the gateway of unimpeded practice.
This is precisely the contemplative intent of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* as taught by the Venerable Master Xianshou.
That [contemplation] consists of five gates:
first, establishing the causal conditions, which corresponds exactly to this gate of giving rise to the complete causal conditions.
Second, the array of characteristics, namely the wind-circles, fragrant oceans, and so forth as described in the *Puṣpakūṭa* chapter;
third, the perfection of endowed virtues;
fourth, the integration of the environment and its inhabitants.
The five [factors] comprise the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
This commentary has two parts:
first, a brief explanation based on the sūtra, which corresponds to the fourth [section] therein.
The second section, from "However, its unimpeded [knowledge] has ten kinds" onwards, corresponds to the third [section] of that [text].
It explains these two alone so as to naturally constitute the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), and thus the fifth [section] is omitted.
However, that virtuous one points to a single fragrant tree, which also clarifies ten meanings: first, this fragrant tree is the merit of the Buddha’s body of wisdom;

second, it is the turning of the wheel of Dharma; third, the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; fourth, the merit of compassion and wisdom; fifth, inconceivable merit; sixth, the non-obstruction between essence and function; seventh, the non-obstruction between meditative concentration and distraction; eighth, subtle merit; ninth, the merit of the Buddha’s realm; and tenth, the merit of the non-obstruction of dependent origination.
While the internal and external aspects were previously combined to form ten gates without citing supporting evidence, I shall now follow the sutras;

for all additions, subtractions, omissions, and establishments, I will cite textual proofs so that phenomena and principle are fully integrated, with each phenomenon and principle being mutually unimpeded.
The commentary consists of four parts:
first, a general heading;
second, from "The various teachings describe the lands" onwards, the establishment of the thesis.
The phrase "or it is impermanent" applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

The statement "or it is a transformation of the mind" pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna; since it posits a vast separation between principle and phenomena, it is clear that this is not the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
Third, from "The Unimpededness of Phenomenon and Principle" (*dharma-artha-avyāghāta*) onwards, the gates are opened for a detailed explanation.

Within the first [section], a scriptural citation is provided; specifically, the final line of the verse in the tenth sutra states, "Abiding in emptiness. Here, we take "ornamentation" (*vyūha*) as the phenomenon (*dharma*) and the "Dharmadhātu" as the principle (*artha*); the term "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*) refers precisely to this unimpededness.
Regarding the two points concerning formation and destruction, no scriptural citations are provided because the meaning is easily understood.
Furthermore, as these are also [contained within] this verse, it says "each one.
Within the world-systems (*kṣetraprakāra*), though inconceivable eons of conflagration occur and what is manifested may be ruined and corrupt, those places remain eternally pure.

Regarding the phrase in the third [section], "The sūtra says: 'The essence and characteristics are as they were in the original,'" etc., this refers to the eighth sūtra, which explains the verse on the chapter of the world-systems (*kṣetra-vyūha*).

Furthermore, that which is cited within the subsequent fourfold mutual entry is the first half of the aforementioned verse, which states in full: "One world-system enters into all, and all enter into one without remainder; their essence and characteristics remain as they were, without distinction, peerless, immeasurable, and universally pervasive."
The five characteristics are thus unimpeded; the realization of the text corresponds to the seventh sutra.

Sixth, the passage beginning with “Pure pearls and gems” refers to the eighth verse on the River of Fragrant Water, which reads in full: “Pure pearls and gems are spread like clouds, completely covering all the fragrant rivers; those pearls, equal to the Buddha’s mark between the eyebrows, vividly manifest the reflections of all Buddhas.”
Now, we shall take only the first and last phrases to clarify the meaning of subtlety.
Among the seven instances of concealment and manifestation, I have omitted citations from the sūtras because their meanings are numerous.
This refers precisely to the meaning of the verse therein: "Karma created according to the mind is inconceivable;
all lands are established thereby.
It is inconceivable because different perceptions arise within the same location.

Furthermore, the Verse on Form says: "The lands manifested within every atom are all the power of original vows and spiritual penetrations; according to the various inclinations of beings' minds, they can be produced everywhere throughout space."
The commentary states:
Since a single atom can manifest as various things according to one's wishes, its concealment and manifestation are sovereign.
Nevertheless, the sub-commentary briefly sets forth two types of concealment and manifestation:

First, regarding the concealment and manifestation of the defiled and the pure: for those who perceive the Sahā world, when they face the Flower Treasury World (Huazang), the pure is concealed and the defiled is manifested;

for those who perceive the Flower Treasury World, when they face the Sahā world, the defiled is concealed and the pure is manifested. Thus, it is said that the land of Magadha is composed of vajra and so forth.

Second, to clarify the concealment and manifestation of different types: for example, when the world-sphere in the form of Mount Sumeru is manifested as a single type, those in the form of rivers and so forth are all concealed.
When long *kṣetras* are manifested, short *kṣetras* are then concealed.
The remaining points may be understood by analogy.

I shall not cite textual passages regarding the eightfold manifestation of non-obstruction, as I have already cited them repeatedly in the passage: "Within every single atom of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm."

If one cites further passages, the *Gāthā on Abiding* states: "There are lands that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, pure and free from defilement, manifesting from the mind; like shadows and like illusions, vast and boundless, each distinct like those in Indra’s net," and so forth.
The "nine things induced" refers to the eighth sutra, which explains the verse on the "Minor Ocean" within the ten [verses].
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, the text below says," this refers to the eighth sutra, the verse on the river and forest grove.
The Commentary states: "These ten non-obstructions," and so forth, constitutes the fourth section, which summarizes and explains the meaning of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*).
A brief account is as previously stated; a detailed exposition is found in the separate chapter on the *Daśabhūmika*.
In the commentary, from the phrase "How is it vast and great? onwards, each difficulty is explained individually.

Regarding the eighth and ninth [points], there are two levels of explanation: the former applies generally to all teachings, while the latter, beginning with "By means of the untainted," pertains specifically to the school of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).
Therefore, Samantabhadra said above: "All lands enter my body, and the Buddhas who dwell therein are likewise so.
You should observe all my pores; I now reveal to you the realm of the Buddhas," and so forth.

The Commentary states: "Because the manifested lands resemble that retribution, they appear in successive layers without departing from a single hair. This is like ten lamps illuminating a single hair together; thus, upon that single hair, there are a thousand layers of light.
This is analogous to the contemplation of the dharmas.

Regarding the passage in the *Sū* (Commentary) beginning with “In the fourth [section], the essence of the realm (*dharmadhātu*) differs according to various teachings,” there are two intended meanings for the explanation of how the five teachings define their essence (*tattva*):

first, the individual assignment of the eight subtle elements (*aṣṭau paramāṇavaḥ*) to the Hīnayāna; “mind-only” (*cittamātra*) to the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*); “dharma-nature” (*dharmatā*) to both the Final and Sudden Teachings; or “all phenomena” (*sarvadharma*) to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).

Secondly, the Comprehensive and Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) fully possesses all four meanings; the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao) consists solely of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā); and the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) consists solely of the eight subtle particles (aṣṭau paramāṇavaḥ). The two teachings of Beginning and End both encompass the first three [meanings]. If these three are distinct, then the [latter] two constitute the Beginning Teaching (Shijiao); if the three are unimpeded and the nature and characteristics are perfectly fused, this is the End Teaching (Zhongjiao). Therefore, it is so called.

Regarding the distinctions in the determination of the essential nature (*tattva*) according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school: first, the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature realm), which takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence.

Second, the *sambhoga-kṣetra* (Enjoyment-realm), which takes all merits such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), as well as the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*), as its essential nature; however, if one subsumes the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into the nature (*dharmatā*), it likewise takes True Suchness as its essence.
The three-colored land (*tri-varṇa-bhūmi*) subsumes the objective realm within the mind, as its essence is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) for one's own benefit.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Its characteristic is the most supremely sovereign pure consciousness."
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are themselves the essence and the marks.
If distinguished according to their marks, the four sense-objects constitute the essence.

Regarding the four lands of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), they take as their essence the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that benefits others, subsuming the objects within the mind.
When subsuming characteristics back into their nature, it likewise takes true thusness (*tathatā*) as its essence.
If distinguished according to its characteristics, it is also composed of the four sense objects.
As for the five transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*), they share the same essence as the aforementioned land of others' enjoyment (*para-sambhogika*).

Thus we know that while the Initial Teaching fully employs the three dharmas [of nature, characteristics, and function], the Perfect Teaching uses nature to harmonize characteristics; because characteristics are non-obstructive, they penetrate all phenomena, such that the mutual non-obstruction of all things constitutes its essence.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "Now, all of these are fully present.
Next, it cites the sutra to encompass them completely, followed by their seamless integration.

Regarding the passage in the fifth section on the adornment of the lands, from "or using jewels as adornments" and so forth: however, there are three kinds of adornment, which are termed the "three purities":
First is the purity of the site, which is adorned by various jewels;
second is the purity of the sentient beings dwelling there, which is adorned by the "jewel of humans";
third is the purity of the dissemination of the Dharma-gates, which is adorned by the Dharma itself.
The meaning can be understood from the text.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The sixth section clarifies the purity of the buddha-field," the commentary consists of four parts:

first, a general indication of the main theme; second, a detailed exposition of its characteristics; third, a definitive selection based on the teachings; and fourth, a definitive selection to avoid confusion based on the text.
First, regarding the phrase "only in reference to purity": because it speaks of being pure, this differs from [the categories of] form and so forth, which apply to both the defiled and the pure.
Regarding the phrase "attained through practice," this is the intended meaning of Master Sheng.
That *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti* states: "Practicing leads to the Pure Land; it is not something created.
Those who create a land are among the class of sentient beings.
Within the fourteen sections, the meaning of "leading to" (*chi*) is explained as follows: "Question:"
What is it that is "attained" yet not "gained"?
Answer:
That which is called "attained" has its substance as a provisional designation for things; thus, although it is acquired, it does not belong to oneself.
The commentary states:
It is called "attainment" (*zhì*) because it is acquired through others.

That is to say, while the Buddha cultivated the myriad practices to directly course toward the ultimate truth, he did not grasp at the marks of form or the enjoyment-body for others; rather, because of other sentient beings, he took up the land out of great compassion for their sake. Therefore, it is called "attainment through practice."
Since one attains the land by means of the myriad practices, it must necessarily be pure.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "However, purity is of two kinds" constitutes the second part, which specifically elucidates its characteristics.
Expanding upon this further, it forms four layers, all of which take skillful means (*upāya*) as the cause and purity as the fruit.

In the first pair, it states that "the six practices constitute the skillful means"; this refers to the aversion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obscurations of the lower realms, and the aspiration for the purity, subtlety, and detachment of the higher realms; thus, the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) are taken as the pure land.
The commentary states: "This further consists of two kinds," which refers to the second pair, already clarified in the *Xuán* [section] regarding the Pure Land of the Two Vehicles.
The commentary states: "However, within the supramundane, supreme purity," which refers to the third pair.
Regarding the mention of the *Ratnarājasūtra* and other texts, this refers to the praise of the Buddha by King Prasenajit in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice.

The preceding one and a half verses state: "The Perfectly Awakened One is signless and pervades the Dharma-realm; his patience regarding non-arising and his knowledge of exhaustion are perfectly luminous."
Quiescent illumination is unimpeded true liberation; its compassionate manifestations are peerless.
Tranquil and unmoving, it is eternally peaceful; its radiance shines everywhere, yet there is nothing upon which it shines.
"The Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones dwell in the retribution [realms], while only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
This is easy to understand from the text.
Furthermore, the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* also says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
There are lands named as the abodes where all worthy ones and sages dwell.
Therefore, every sentient being and every saintly person each has their own land of karmic fruition as their dwelling place.
If ordinary sentient beings dwell within the five aggregates, these constitute their land of direct retribution;
mountains, forests, and the great earth are termed their land of circumstantial retribution.
The noble ones of the first stage likewise possess two lands:
First is the land of ultimate reality-wisdom (*tattvajñāna-bhūmi*), wherein prior wisdom constitutes the dwelling and subsequent wisdom constitutes the land;

second is the land manifested through transformation—whether pure or impure—which appears according to the measure of many kalpas, and this applies likewise even to the lands of the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
All sentient beings, up to those on the Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi), do not dwell in a pure land, for they abide in the retribution of their karma.

Only the Buddha alone dwells in the land of the Middle Way, the foremost Dharma-nature; therefore, in the past, while in the Hall of Universal Radiance, I extensively expounded the gateway to the pure land for all sentient beings.
Regarding the two sutras above, only the Buddha is pure.
In the commentary, from the phrase "within that which is not yet ultimate" onwards, this is the fourth pairing.

As for the statement "permanently severing the burdens of form," it refers to Master Daosheng’s fourteen-point exposition on the Pure Land, which states: "Those who have not yet escaped the burden of the physical form—those from the eighth stage downwards—remain within the contemplation of the emptiness of birth; when they emerge into the Pure Land, they still reside in a defiled land."

From the eighth stage upward, one constantly dwells in the emptiness of sentient beings, which is to say, one constantly dwells in the Pure Land; therefore, it is necessary to rely upon a land to establish one's own abode.

Since those from the eighth stage upward have forever severed the burdens of form, their enlightened essence stands alone and their spirit has no fixed location—what further need would there be for a land?
The meaning is this:

at the eighth stage, through the pure patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one attains mastery over form and abandons the fragmented existence of birth and death; therefore, it is said that the burdens of form are forever severed.
Since all mundane and supramundane mental states no longer manifest before one, it is said that the essence of illumination stands alone.
Because it accords with the nature [of reality] and is universally pervasive, it is said that "the spirit has no fixed location.
"Spirit" refers here to the mental spirit; as the *I Ching* states: "The spirit is that which speaks of the wondrousness of all things."
"Therefore, the Spirit has no fixed location and the Change has no form.
Since it is free from the constraints of form, its terrestrial manifestations are difficult to describe by name.

Regarding the phrase "those at or below the seventh stage" and so forth: those who have not yet emerged from the triple world and follow the direct path have not yet abandoned the *pariccheda* (segmented) death.

Regarding the statement that "untainted contemplative wisdom has interruptions," this refers to the stages from the sixth bhūmi downward; once one reaches the seventh bhūmi, contemplation becomes uninterrupted.

According to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, the six bhūmis and below are considered defiled (*saṃkliṣṭa*), while the eight bhūmis and above are pure (*viśuddha*). The seventh bhūmi is also termed "intermediate" (*madhya*); it may be called defiled, it may be called pure, or it may be neither defiled nor pure.
Now, taking the meaning of "defilement" (rañjana), it is not purely pure.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "If one relies on the *Yogācārabhūmi*," the third section clarifies the definitive selection based on the teachings; this may be understood.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "However, the pure means," the fourth section clarifies the distinctions to avoid confusion based on the textual passages.
Within this, there are two parts;
first, in response to this text.
In the four pairs mentioned above, all take purity as the fruit and skillful means as the cause.

Now, explaining this through the principle of universal application, the skillful means are themselves the fruit: drawing near to virtuous friends is the skillful means, while now obtaining the "human treasure" as one's adornment constitutes the fruit; thus, in lands such as Sukhāvatī, where various superior and virtuous persons assemble in one place, this is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The commentary states: "However, with regard to 'adornment'... and so forth; this is the second section, which distinguishes [the present passage] from the preceding text.

For instance, it is identical in meaning to the passage in the section on adornment that says, "Or, by means of the adornment of proclaiming all the merits of bodhisattvas," which corresponds to the current phrase, "because the vast clouds of increasing merit pervade the Dharma-realm."
Furthermore, that verse frequently cites the cause to reveal the result, which is the same as this prose section. This states:
"Compassion is vast and pervasive throughout all sentient beings; by means of this, he adorns the oceans of all buddha-lands."
This is the same as [the section on] "Adornment.
It establishes the causes and conditions for arising various pure lands; this is the same as the long prose section on cultivating the causes for purity.
Therefore, this distinction is made.
The commentary consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the distinction between the gates. This means that although the substance employed is one, the contexts of its application differ.
It is like preaching the Dharma: when situated within the gate of giving, it is called "Dharma-giving," whereas when situated within the gate of wisdom, it is called "expedient means," and so forth.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, from 'arising with the requisites' onwards, another principle is used to distinguish between the two gates: while possessing the conditions is universal, this specific case is restricted; therefore, the previous commentary stated, 'This refers exclusively to the pure [requisites].'"

Regarding their adornments, there are some differences: for example, when many medicinal ingredients are combined, they receive their name from the predominant one; likewise, when wisdom is present within concentration, it is merely supported by that concentration, and when concentration is present within wisdom, it is simply termed *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said that the former primarily concerns the fruit, while this primarily concerns the cause.

Regarding those who previously cultivated much merit, the "more" or "less" was discussed in terms of the cause relative to its result; here, however, it refers solely to the internal degree of "more" or "less" within the causes themselves.

The previous passage spoke of the "boundless ocean of a bodhisattva’s merits," and the "Universal Worthy Conduct" chapter states: "May all the Buddha-sons, throughout the kalpas of sentient beings, diligently practice and cultivate. These refer primarily to the extensive cultivation of wholesome qualities.

Now, the text states: "Purifying and cultivating vast and sublime resolute beliefs, one accomplishes the power of pure skillful means. This clearly indicates that [the practitioner] has extensively remedied their evils;
this is evident from the text.

The Commentary states: "As explained in the section on the Night Goddess where Sudhana encountered her" refers to the seventy-third scripture, the Night Goddess of Great Vows and Diligent Power. When Sudhana first beheld her, he gave rise to ten mentalities, such as regarding the spiritual friend as equal to himself, and immediately attained practices as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
What is called the "mind of identical mindfulness" is because it constantly recollects the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The "mind of identical wisdom" is because it discerns and determines all phenomena, and so forth.
The details are as explained therein.
The following sections are all according to the text of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “the first half concerns skillful means (*upāya*) and the second half concerns purity (*viśuddhi*”), this is because each of the subsequent phrases contains the terms "skillful means" and "purity."

Regarding the statement that "the first phrase refers to the fruit and the second phrase refers to the cause," this is said from the perspective of the majority of cases: thus, skillful means (*upāya*) is the cause and purity (*viśuddhi*) is the fruit.
If explained according to the general principle, both are common to both cause and fruit.
Skillful means, in terms of cause, skillfully brings forth the land.
Skillful means, in terms of fruit, purify the characteristics of the pure land through the functional activity of the environment and its inhabitants.
In terms of cause, it is purified by being free from all hindrances and obscurations.
Regarding the fruit [of rebirth], there are no three evil realms or eight difficult conditions.

The commentary states: "The first two follow their respective types. For example, when a Buddha appears in the Sahā world, he is only sixteen feet tall; yet if he were born in Sukhāvatī, he would be immeasurable *yojanas* in height. One cannot use a Tathāgata of immeasurable *yojanas* to transform sentient beings with bodies of only three feet, nor can a sixteen-foot Buddha transform a person ten thousand feet tall.
The same applies to lifespan: while those dwelling in this land do not exceed a hundred years, the lifespan of the people of Amitābha’s realm is all immeasurable.
However, this pair also corresponds to the extent of the capacities of those to be transformed.
Next, regarding "the breadth or narrowness of the object-condition": when the object-condition is broad, the land is broad, as in the realms of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;
when the object-condition is narrow, the land is narrow, as in the countries of Kāśyapa and Prabhāśrī.

Fourth, if one is fit to hear three [vehicles], then the wondrous treasure of the One Vehicle should be kept secret; if one is fit to hear only one, then the small carts of the sheep and the deer should be discarded.
Fifth, for those whose five faculties are matured, transformation is manifold, as in the case of Śākyamuni’s transformation;
for those not yet matured, transformation is limited, as in the case of the Tathāgata Suśānta.
This is also because the conditions within the causal state vary in breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "A single thought-moment and an eon," it explains the meaning of the expedient means of Mind-Only.
However, both a single thought-moment and an eon arise from the conceptualizing mind; this contains two points of significance:
First, because there is conceptualization, there are moments (*kṣaṇa*); through the accumulation of these moments, kalpas are ultimately formed.
If mental conceptions are extinguished, birth and death will be permanently severed.
This accords with the scriptural text.
Second, all objective realms exist with their distinctions based upon deluded thought; if one is free from mental ideation, then the characteristics of all objective realms do not exist.
This accords with the intent of the Sūtra in establishing the contemplation of Mind-Only; therefore, the Commentary states: "If thought does not give rise to long or short, where can they abide?
The absence of long and short is precisely the pure essence of the mind; thus, the Sūtra says, "By a single expedient means, all are pure."
This is because it refers to the true nature (*dharmatā*).
The third phrase signifies the meaning of the "unbreakable characteristic" (*akṣaya-lakṣaṇa*); it is the meaning of the ocean of lands where characteristics and nature are mutually unimpeded.
The Commentary states: "The second [point] concerns only the good and evil of the inhabitants during the abiding eon (*sthita-kalpa*)," which further has two meanings:
First, it is obtained through the inducing causes pertaining to sentient beings;
second, it pertains to the functioning of Bodhisattvas dwelling therein, for because their minds are purely wholesome, defilement and purity interpenetrate one another.

The commentary’s statement, “Because they encounter adverse conditions, the pure transforms into the defiled,” refers precisely to the fact that sentient beings within the kalpa abide in a state of defilement.
The Seventy-two Sūtras state: "In the past, when this city had not yet produced a great king, everything was devoid of joy, like the abode of hungry ghosts."

Sentient beings who kill and harm one another, steal, and indulge in sexual license; who engage in double-tongued speech, untruthful words, and meaningless or harsh language; who covet the wealth and possessions of others, harbor malice with poisonous intent, and hold wrong views while performing unwholesome deeds—upon the end of their lives, they fall into the evil realms.
"Because these sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and abide in inverted views"—
this refers to the adverse conditions above—

"the heavens do not send down moisture; because there is no rain in due season, the hundred grains do not grow at all, the grasses and trees all wither away, and even the springs and streams run dry."
"Before the Great King arose in this world, the rivers and ponds were all parched dry; the gardens and groves were filled with many bones, appearing from afar like a desolate wilderness.
This refers to the transformation at the end of the kalpa.

The Commentary states: "Non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously," etc., which refers to the subsequent passage in the aforementioned sutra: "When the Great King ascends the precious throne, he extensively relieves all living beings; like a thick oil-cloud covering the eight directions, rain falls everywhere in abundance."
This refers to transforming the ten non-virtues into the ten virtues.

Among them, the transformation of stealing is described as follows: "In the past, sentient beings were impoverished and lacked clothing; they sheltered themselves with grass, emaciated by hunger like hungry ghosts."
"When the Great King appeared in the world, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously, and wondrous garments emerged from trees; both men and women were adorned with finery.
This refers to that very event.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The third is that prior to the stages”: *śraddhādhimukti* (faith-understanding) is a general designation for the stage prior to the [bodhisattva] grounds (*bhūmi*). It is also called the dwelling of superior-understanding practice (*adhimukticaryā-vihāra*), because one has not yet realized *tathatā* (suchness) but practices by relying solely on the power of understanding.

The Commentary states: "Or, one may adorn a single land with many adornments. This refers to the fifth dedication, which is the vow to universally encompass all the adornments of every Buddha-land throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time to adorn each and every land, such that it is so for all of them as well.
Upon reaching the completion of the stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to fulfill these vows as described in the accounts of the eighth and tenth stages.

Regarding the statement, "Or, by means of a single adornment, one adorns many lands," the second dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) says: "Adorning all with a single adornment, yet not giving rise to conceptual discrimination regarding phenomena; thus awakening all sentient beings, [one realizes] that all things lack intrinsic nature and there is nothing to be observed."
Regarding the phrase "As above, the light from the mouth summons the assembly," this refers to the sixth sūtra.

Once those bodhisattvas had arrived at the assembly and manifested their sovereign powers, and were thus seated, from every single pore of each of those bodhisattvas’ bodies there emerged various kinds of radiant light of all manner of jewels, as numerous as the atoms within ten oceans of worlds. Within each ray of light appeared bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within ten oceans of worlds, all seated upon lion thrones within lotus treasuries.
"These bodhisattvas are all able to travel everywhere throughout the entire dharma-realm, reaching every single atom within the oceans of all established worlds.

Within each and every atom, there are vast lands as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds; within each of these lands, there are the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time. These bodhisattvas are all able to travel everywhere to approach, attend upon, and make offerings to them"—this refers to the adornment of lands within atoms.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “A hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, milk was not as [pure] as water,” the *Saṃgharakṣitavadāna* (or *Śrīsaṃghabhedavastu*) says:
King Aśoka constantly made offerings to the noble Saṅgha. One day, the Elder consumed a somewhat large amount of milk.
King Aśoka said to him, “If you consume too much milk, I fear it may cause illness.”
The Elder said:
"What power does this milk have?
It is not equal to the water when the World-Honored One was in the world."
"Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, all its refined essence has sunk beneath the earth.

King Aśoka wished to see the water as it was during the Buddha’s lifetime; the Elder reached his hand down into the earth and drew up the water. When the King tasted it, he found it truly surpassed even milk. He clearly understood that when those who possess merit pass away, their meritorious deeds likewise perish with them.

This was so even a hundred years ago; how much more so now that we are nearly two thousand years removed from the Sage? The Dharma has become increasingly thin and sparse, reaching its ultimate decline.
As stated in the *Lokaprajñapti* and other sutras: "Iron is considered the finest ornament, and weeds are considered the finest flavor."
The Commentary states: "The eighth [case], 'like Maitreya’s coming,' refers to what is taught in the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

'When the waters of the four great oceans have gradually receded by three thousand yojanas, at that time the land of Jambudvīpa will be ten thousand yojanas long and eight thousand yojanas wide, as level as a mirror. Various fragrant flowers and soft grasses will cover its surface, and all kinds of trees with abundant flowers and fruits will flourish; each of these trees will reach a height of thirty li. "
The cities and towns were situated so close together that a rooster could fly from one to the next.
The lifespan of humans was eighty thousand years; they were fully endowed with wisdom, majestic virtue, physical beauty, and strength, living in peace, security, and happiness.
There was a great city named Kinnaramati, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width.
That city was made of the seven precious gems; its towers, pavilions, doors, windows, and balconies were all covered with nets of various jewels and pearls.
The moat is twelve *li* wide; at every street, lane, and path there are pillars of bright pearls, and at every place there are heaps of gold and silver.
