When excrement or impurities fall upon the ground, the earth cracks to receive them, and having received them, it closes back up again. Furthermore, there is no suffering from water, fire, or military force, nor any calamities such as famine or poison.
The gardens, groves, ponds, and pools were filled with water of eight virtues and various flowers of diverse fragrances; no weeds or impurities grew there.
There was a single crop harvested seven times, which was exceedingly fragrant and delicious, increasing one's physical complexion, strength, and vitality—details as extensively described therein.

The Commentary states: “Vimalakīrti pressed the earth with his toe” refers to what is taught in the *Buddhakṣetraparivarta*: “According to the purity of one’s mind, so is the purity of the Buddha-field.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, had this thought:
“If it is the case that when a bodhisattva’s mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure, then when our World-Honored One was originally practicing the path of a bodhisattva, was his intention not pure?”
"Yet this buddha-field is as impure as this.
The Buddha then replied,
"This land of mine is pure, but you do not see it."
At that time, the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the trichiliocosm became a land adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels.
The entire assembly marveled at what had never occurred before, and each saw themselves seated upon precious lotus flowers and the like.
The commentary states: "The 'Three Transformations of the Pure Land' in the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to the 'Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa.'"
Mahāpratibhāna requested that the doors of the stūpa be opened, and the Buddha said,
"It is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies.
Mahāpratibhāna then requested that the emanated Buddhas be assembled.
The World-Honored One emitted light from afar to summon [the Buddhas], desiring to receive the buddhas who had manifested as emanations; first, he transformed the Sahā world;
second, in each of the eight directions, he further transformed two hundred myriads of koṭis of nayutas of lands, making them all pure, yet the seated Buddhas were still insufficient;
third, he further transformed another two hundred myriads of koṭis of nayutas of lands, making them all pure.
Therefore, it is said that there are "three transformations.

The commentary states: "'This refers to the preceding nine [sections] which explain the various worlds; because they differ in their characteristics yet all reach universal pervasiveness,' this explains the meaning of the title."
Within this, there are three points:
first, regarding the relative nature and characteristics—characteristics possess differentiation, whereas nature is without differentiation.
Second, from "Furthermore, regarding provisional establishment" onwards, it concerns the relative provisional and real; therein, the real is without differentiation.

Third: "Furthermore, because these are all that is utilized by the Buddhas," and so forth, gathers the differentiated and the undifferentiated, showing that both ultimately converge in the function of the fruit.
In the preceding two pairs, nature and characteristics, and the provisional and the real, were not mutually identical; now, they are fused and identical.
To speak of "the difference of non-difference" refers to the sequential arrangement within perfect interfusion;
to speak of "the non-difference of difference" refers to the perfect interfusion within sequential arrangement.
If one were apart from perfect interfusion, there would be nothing to differentiate; if one were apart from differentiation, there would be nothing to interfuse.
It is like gathering particulars to form a whole: this whole does not exist apart from those particulars.
Quoting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it clarifies only that these two are inseparable.
The section beginning with "By virtue of this meaning" below demonstrates that the eighteen [attributes] are perfected through this.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The dust motes of the entire ocean—each mote being a world-realm—is already the meaning of inclusion,” this is because the Sūtra says: “Within each and every ocean of world-realms, there are world-realms as numerous as the dust motes of an ocean of world-realms without distinction. This means that within a single ocean of world-realms, there are still world-realms as numerous as the dust motes of an ocean of world-realms; thus, the meaning is that each single mote of dust constitutes one world-realm.
By means of this single phrase alone, the integration [of all things] is already revealed, and the explanation of the meaning of non-differentiation is well established.
If one were to argue for non-differentiation by comparing realm to realm, such non-differentiation would be extremely limited.

Now, within each of these ten phrases, there are as many world-oceans as there are atoms; thus, within a single ocean, there are already as many instances of non-differentiation as there are atoms in ten world-oceans. Therefore, it is necessary to integrate them.
Reflect on this.

The commentary states: "As for the previous [passage] which 'merely refers to the uniformity without distinction,' it refers to the long prose section stating that 'the Buddha's majestic power throughout every world-ocean is without distinction. Now, however, it says in each and every atom there are immeasurable lights and so forth; this refers to the non-distinction of their overlapping."
The Commentary states: "If it is said that this refers to common matters," and so forth, concluding with a critique of past scholars.

This means that since the Sūtra cites ten matters all in terms of harmonious integration (*yongs su sbyor ba*), why—according to the former interpretation—does it not state that within each and every world-ocean there is no distinction between the defiled and the pure?
Is it because there is no difference in the suffering experienced by sentient beings in each individual world-ocean?
Since all world-oceans contain defilement and suffering, the commentary concludes: "How could it be that this [suffering] does not exist at all within the world-oceans?"

Since this scripture does not explicitly state it, we clearly know that it refers simply to the non-differentiation through integration and inclusion. This concludes the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World-System. **Chapter Five: The Flower Treasury World-System** Regarding the phrase "In the Sanskrit original, it says...

and so forth: In Sanskrit, *kusuma* means flower; *garbha* means treasury; *vyūha* means adornment; *alaṃkāra* means ornament; *lokadhātu* means world-system; *samudra* means ocean; *pariśuddha* means universally pure; *guṇa* means merit; *samudra* means ocean; *āloka* means light; and *parivarta* means chapter. Thus, this is translated as: "The Chapter on the Light of the Universally Pure Ocean of Merits of the Flower Treasury Adorned Ornament World-System. **Commentary on the First Part of the Second Assembly, the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas"** Regarding the phrase "In the Sanskrit original, it says... and so forth: In Sanskrit, *kusuma* means flower; *garbha* means treasury; *vyūha* means adornment; *alaṃkāra* means ornament; *lokadhātu* means world-system; *samudra* means ocean; *pariśuddha* means universally pure; *guṇa* means merit; *samudra* means ocean; *āloka* means light; and *parivarta* means chapter. This is translated as: "The Chapter on the Light of the Universally Pure Ocean of Merits of the Flower Treasury Adorned Ornament World-System."
However, the commentary consists of four parts:
first, the citation of the Sanskrit name;
second, the exposition of its meaning beginning from the phrase "The translator deems it too prolix," and so forth.
3. "Its Sanskrit original says... and below explains the preceding Sanskrit text;

4. "In terms of the facts, this may be so" and below examines its ultimate source. If one does not provide this explanation, how could one thoroughly understand the origins of the arising of the ocean of lands?
Regarding the three points of the essential purport:
as for the statement "there are ten virtues," four passages have already been cited in the preceding chapter.

As for the commentary’s remark, "First, it clarifies the self-substance of the Flower Treasury's cause and fruit": although the second section on the "arrangement and adornment" is also a characteristic of the fruit, one should therefore correlate the causes with the category of the fruit.
This is divided into two sections: first, clarifying the causes of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field); second, manifesting its resultant characteristics (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).

Since the prose of the first section contains both cause and effect, and the verse elucidates both cause and effect together, they are combined under the "causes" and subsumed within the "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).
The Commentary states: "That is to say, pointing to this ocean of lands as my original teacher. Below this, the commentary text has two parts:
first, a general explanation of the scriptural passage; second, a specific explanation according to the difficulties raised.
First: Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Not only [did he serve] Vijaya, Śākyamuni, and so forth,” the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter eighteen, states:

During each of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he made offerings to seventy thousand Buddhas; furthermore, he successively made offerings to five, six, and seven thousand Buddhas. Upon the completion of the three incalculable eons, he encountered, in reverse order, the Buddhas Vijaya, Dīpaṃkara, Ratnaśikhin, and first of all, Śākyamuni.
The commentary states:
Among these three verses, the first clarifies the number of Buddhas to whom offerings were made.

Specifically, during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas; during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas; and during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
The meaning of the subsequent verse clarifies which Buddhas were honored.

Regarding the "reverse order," this is explained by proceeding backward from the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa: at the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Vipaśyin; at the completion of the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; at the completion of the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin; and at the time of his initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha, making this vow:
"May I become a Buddha exactly like the World-Honored One."
"When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world during the final kalpa, the Dharma remained for a thousand years; now my Tathāgata is in every way the same as him.
Therefore, the present commentary states, "not only [the Buddhas of] Superior Contemplation," which refers to the Buddhas at the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Regarding the term "Śākyamuni," this refers to the Buddha at the initial stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
As for the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it carries three meanings:
first, it includes [Buddhas] such as Dīpaṃkara and Ratnaśikhin; second, it refers to the number of Buddhas to whom offerings were made; and third, it indicates those elucidated in other teachings.
Even if one were to say that making offerings to thirty-six or thirty-eight *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of Buddhas and so forth is not considered much, the Commentary states:
"Not only [the case of] Śuddhika and Anutpattika," as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
by offering five flowers to Dīpaṃkara, one attains the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If there were even the slightest dharma that could be apprehended, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me the prediction [of my future enlightenment]," and so forth.
That no dharma can be apprehended is the characteristic of non-arising (*anutpattilakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "and so forth" includes other dharma-gates.
As the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Merely through compassion, he gave universally; though his limbs were severed, his mind felt no anger; he praised Buddha Tiṣya."
Next, regarding unsurpassed enlightenment and the six pāramitās, within these four stages, one, two, and again one and two are cultivated to perfection respectively.
The commentary states:
The first four lines correspond to the four stages.
The completion of the first stage means that universal giving constitutes the perfection of *dāna* (generosity).

The second and third stages are fulfilled by two [perfections], namely ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*). One fulfills ethical discipline because one does not retaliate when harmed; one accomplishes patience because there is no internal anger.
In the third stage, only one degree is fulfilled, namely the perfection of vigor (*vīrya*).
In the fourth stage, both concentration and wisdom are fully perfected; hence it is said, "one and two, again one and two," and so forth.
As for *Tiṣya*, this is translated as "Fullness. A verse in praise of the Buddha says:

"Within heaven and earth, in this world, and in the abode of the learned (*Śakra*), throughout the palaces of the departed and the celestial realms of the ten directions, there is none equal to the Great Śramaṇa—the Hero, the Bull-King, who has searched the earth, mountains, and forests and found no peer."
For seven days and seven nights, he forgot to set down his foot while praising Tiṣya; therefore, he surpassed Maitreya by nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood first.
This is also stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Therefore, when the six perfections are fulfilled, there is not much difference between the beginning and the end.

In this sutra, at the site of each and every Buddha, one purifies vows as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds; how much more so for many Buddhas, and how much more so for many eons? Thus, the conclusion states: "Because of the three preceding layers, it is said to be profound and vast."

The Commentary states: "Now, regarding 'the arising of faith in Yoga' and below," this is the second section, which provides specific explanations in response to difficulties; it re-explains the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, reconciling them through the perspective of both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.
The phrase "pervading the ten directions" refers back to the aforementioned modes of transformation within a single direction.
The phrase "as well as realms in the form of trees and so forth" refers back to the aforementioned types of worlds.

Furthermore, if one eon in the Sahā world is known to be but a single day in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), then the World of Peaceful Nurturing would have already passed through three incalculable days.
This is still before even a month has elapsed in the world-system of Kāṣāyadhvaja; how much more so for those successive lands where an eon constitutes a single day?
Thus, one cannot definitively determine the number of kalpas required for attaining Buddhahood based on this single direction or single category.

Second, regarding different categories of lands (*kṣetra*): within a single realm, all realms are fully present yet do not see one another, and their kalpas also differ; how then could one know whether they are long or short?

Therefore, a morning mushroom does not know the difference between the end of the month and the beginning of the next; how much less could it recognize the spring and autumn, and how much less the years of the great cypress?
As for what is called the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, the sūtra says: "O son of good family!..."
Bodhisattvas cannot conceive of the realm of the Tathāgata; the realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.

It is only for the sake of shallow and limited sentient beings that he speaks of attaining bodhi through cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, whereas in reality, the time since his initial resolve has been incalculable.
The *Xiánshǒu* (Worthy Head) commentary states:
"Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) refers to an incalculable number of *asaṃkhyeyas*.
The *Yìfēnzhì* (Analysis of the Meaning) states:

In the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s teaching), the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are not calculated as ten times ten as they are in the Hīnayāna; rather, they are calculated by doubling each successive stage, and it is further taught that one cultivates the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) for a hundred kalpas.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes this separate cultivation of the marks and signs, not permitting their cultivation apart from the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; this is precisely the intent of the True Teaching (the Mahāyāna).
However, the meaning of the definitive teaching (nītārtha) inherently possesses two aspects:
first, it is because [the Buddha] employs the pedagogical method of a single direction over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, and second, because he is the actual Buddha.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Alternatively, he manifests the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment beyond the stages for the sake of sentient beings who are timid."
Some say that they shall attain the Buddha-way after immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; this is for the sake of sentient beings who are indolent.

They are able to manifest such immeasurable and inconceivable skillful means, yet in reality, those of the Bodhisattva lineage are equal in their faculties, equal in their aspiration, and equal in what they realize; there is no dharma by which one may surpass another, because all Bodhisattvas must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
This refers to the fixed [classification].
The second is the indefinite, which further comprises two meanings:
first, for the purpose of including other types of worlds, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* (or *Jin-tian-wang Sūtra*), namely those lands with the shape of trees and so forth.
Secondly, it is based on the fact that the Buddha’s actual virtues are limitless, as stated in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two kinds of incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*):
first, those consisting of days, nights, months, half-months, and so forth, which serve as a skillful means to manifest the immeasurability of time; [the second being the eons of practice].
The second point is as previously explained.
If one follows the first meaning, it takes immeasurable kalpas;
if one follows the latter meaning, it takes only three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas.

However, according to this interpretation, it differs from the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*. The *Ratnamegha* does not state that the great eons (*mahākalpa*) are taught for shallow and inferior beings, while the solar and lunar eons (*sūryacandramasakalpa*) are taught for those who are profound and superior; thus, it is clear that their intended meanings are distinct.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is also merely what is appropriate to be taught for a particular perspective.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, time has no separate substance,” this is explained through the integrative and inclusive teaching of the distinct vehicle (biejiao yisheng). For example, when the Rishi Vimala took Sudhana by the hand, many kalpas passed and they traversed boundless realms; therefore, it cannot be conceived in terms of duration.
If manifested in its transcendent excellence, it is perfected instantaneously in a single lifetime;
if considered in terms of its profound depth, it cannot be fathomed even over many kalpas.
Therefore, it is said that one must not adhere to fixed interpretations; what is prized is entry into the mysterious.
The Commentary states: "The second section, 'All Sons of the Buddha' and below, clarifies the characteristics of the essence of the fruit.

This commentary consists of four parts: first, the general arising of the characteristics; second, the clarification of its dimensions; third, the detailed explanation of the scriptural text; and fourth, the application of the meaning regarding its scope and limitations.
The Commentary states: "However, as for the measure of the land upon which [the Buddha] relies," and so forth, this is the second section, which clarifies its dimensions.

Regarding the phrase "transformations of large and small," it is as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: "Upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central lotus], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis"; this refers to the "great transformation."
"One flower contains ten billion lands, and in each land there is one Śākyamuni"—this refers to the minor transformation.
The minor transformation encompasses only a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*), whereas the major transformation includes all ten billion such systems.

Regarding the phrase "provisionally based on a single characteristic" and so forth: provisionally, based on one kind of phenomenal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there exist distinct oceans of Buddha-fields outside the lotus, with their boundaries and appearances remaining intact; however, in reality, these accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) such that they cannot be sought out horizontally [as discrete entities]. Therefore, it is said that "the Dharma-realm is without differentiation."
If one integrates the characteristics with their nature, then within a single atom, the dharma-realm is infinite.
The commentary states, "However, following what is specifically revealed below," referring to the third section that explains the scriptural text.
Regarding the statement "there should be ten matters," this is because the text provides an extensive explanation of these ten matters.

Since the prose section (*gadya*) here provides only a brief indication and enumeration, the ancient masters first divided the causes of the lands within a single chapter, and then divided it into ten sections based on the characteristics of the results (*phala*).

Regarding the current lack of adherence [to the standard division], each of the following six matters has its own prose and verse; however, since the first four matters share a single prose section, it would be inconvenient to divide the text into ten sections. Therefore, it is first divided into three parts, and only within the prose of the first part—the *Huazang* (Flower Treasury) itself—is it further divided into four.
In the commentary, from the passage "However, as for the causes of that land" onwards, the fourth section clarifies the scope—whether universal or restricted—of their functional application.

The phrase "as has already been seen in the preceding text" refers to the fact that within the section on the arising of the causal conditions, the universal meaning was easy to understand; therefore, it now demonstrates the specific characteristics.
Regarding the commentary in the list that states "the power of wind sustains from afar," there were two ancient interpretations:
first, it was said that one layer of wind-wheel sustains one heavy object.

However, because the *Samantabhadravyūha-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifestation) mentions ten wind-wheels sustaining the desire and form realms and so forth—all of which constitute sustaining from afar—the present [author] has determined this accordingly.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The ocean of incense he holds," the commentary provides two interpretations:
first, an interpretation based on the literal (factual) sense; second, from "Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna" onwards, an interpretation based on symbolic representation.
Within this second part, there are again two [sub-sections].
First, it concerns sentient beings; second, from the passage "Furthermore, buddha-nature is named water" onwards, it concerns both ordinary beings and Buddhas.
Because buddha-nature is the true dharma-nature (dharmatā), these three meanings are expressed by the ocean at the beginning of this chapter.
I shall now cite two instances, omitting for brevity the mention of compassion.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states, "There was a person who smelled a fragrance"; this refers to the seventh fascicle, which I shall quote in full when we reach the "Chapter on Inquiring about Wisdom."

The Commentary states: “Furthermore, regarding the ‘ten thousand practices that are brought forth’ and below,” the preceding section explained this in terms of concrete phenomena (*vastu*), whereas this section explains it in terms of symbolic dharma (*dharmanirdeśa*), representing the practices through general characteristics.
To explain them specifically, the ten virtues are briefly shown as symbolizing the ten *pāramitās*: (1) blooming with fresh splendor symbolizes the *dāna-pāramitā*;

(2) an inherently undefiled nature symbolizes the *śīla-pāramitā*; (3) fragrant aroma; (4) a firm precious stem; (5) luxuriant precious leaves; (6) radiant banners on precious filaments; (7) the skillful perfection of its marks; (8) containing lotus seeds within; (9) a firmly established precious pedestal; and (10) universally emitting light. The latter eight correspond respectively to the manifestation of the [final] eight *pāramitās*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *sūtra* consists of the prose [sections], while the *gāthās* consist of the verses,” herein the prose portions are designated as *sūtra* because they take up the prose narratives to elaborate upon the meanings that were briefly stated, constituting the specific characteristics of the *sūtra*.

Regarding the statement that the Sūtra is separated from the Verses: the "past causes" refer to the previously mentioned profound and vast manifesting causes; the "present conditions" refer to the previously mentioned wind-sustained fragrant ocean and so forth; these two are explained separately.
Regarding the correspondence between the prose and the verse: the first verse summarizes the whole; its first half concerns past causes, while its second half concerns present conditions.
As for the second verse, three lines concern past causes, and the fourth line concerns present conditions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The characteristics of the fruit attained are briefly stated in the sūtra and explained at length in the verses”: the prose passage stating, “That which dwells within this Flower Treasury World-Ocean” refers to the characteristics of the fruit attained; this text [of the sūtra] is thus brief.
Because each of the ten verses contains the characteristics of the fruit, it is said that "the verse is broad.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Third, regarding the present conditions: the wind-wheel is detailed in the sutra but summarized in the verse," the sutra enumerates ten kinds of wind-wheels, whereas the verse merely says, "Supported by the power of the wind, there is no shaking."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *Catuḥpariṣat-sūtra* contains the prose but lacks the verse,” this means that the long prose version says, “Mount Cakravāḍa of diamond wheels encircles [the world], and the lands, oceans, and various trees each have their distinct divisions”; thus, these elements exist in the prose, while it can be understood that they are absent from the verse.

Regarding the statement that there are four [types], there are merely four categories; only the single pair consisting of "extensive" and "concise" constitutes a true dyad, whereas "separation and combination" and "existence and non-existence" each constitute but a single category.
If they were to form pairs, there would need to be a combination of sūtras with verses and sūtras without verses to constitute three pairs;
otherwise, for the remaining four examples, there are two pairs, which do not exist here but do exist below in the verses.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This is the limit of the limitless; it does not obstruct principle while being identical to phenomena,” the intent is to clarify that principle has no boundaries and is therefore termed ‘limitless.
Phenomena have boundaries, and are thus termed ‘limited.’
If the principle establishes the phenomenon, the nature of the principle is entirely concealed, and thus the boundless is itself the finite.
If one realizes the phenomenon by returning to the principle, the phenomenal characteristics are entirely exhausted, and thus the finite is itself the boundless.
Now it is not so: when the principle is not lost and the phenomenon manifests, we speak of "the limit of the limitless";
when the phenomenon is not destroyed and the principle is revealed, we speak of "the limitless of the limit."
This refers to the principle of the non-obstruction between phenomena and reality (*dharmadhātu*), not the sense of mutual identity or mutual production; reflect upon this.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "But it says 'all adornments,'" this sentence is somewhat lengthy, so it is cited and explained as follows:
from "all various ornaments" (*sarva-vyūha*) onwards is the ninth phrase, and from "exquisite maṇi jewels" (*maṇi-ratna*) onwards are all the tenth phrases.

The Commentary states: "According to the subsequent *kṣetra-vyuha* and the Sanskrit original, there are ten [oceans]. This is because one central ocean governs ten oceans, and these ten oceans are arranged in a single line, forming an incalculable number of fragrant water oceans as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field.
The same applies to all ten paths; as they constitute a single ocean and a single category, there are ten "unspeakables.
Regarding the statement, "The same applies to the place where the category is designated at the lower level," it is designated thus: "O Sons of the Buddha!"
"In these seas of fragrant water, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, there are world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
The commentary states:
This is the designation of the locations where the world-systems reside; although the character "ten" (十字) is not present here, it should likewise be understood to exist by analogy.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “*Puṇḍarīka* is the white lotus,” this is the translation by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty and other masters.

As for the phrase, “It is also at the time of full bloom,” this reflects the intention of Master Fu; thus, Master Rui states in his *Preface to the Lotus Sutra*: “The flower has three distinct stages:

when it is blooming but not yet fully opened, it is called *kumuda*; when it is withered and about to fall, it is called *kāmala*; and when it is in its prime, situated between these two, it is called *puṇḍarīka*.”
Master Daosheng also said:
"In the exquisite beauty of forms and images, none surpasses the lotus flower.
As for the splendor of the lotus, its glory lies in its first unfolding."
Regarding the flourishing state when it first unfolds: "the interior is filled with seeds, and the color, fragrance, and flavor are complete; these are the *puṇḍarīkas*.
The meaning is essentially the same.

Fearing that a detailed exposition would be too cumbersome for the reader to grasp, the Commentary does not present them in full; however, this abridgment must exhaustively demonstrate each point according to the principle.

Regarding how this "Chapter on the Collection of Flowers" subsumes the "Chapter on Accomplishment": herein, the entry [into the realm] subsumes both the causal conditions for its arising and its purification; for entry is itself the three gates of liberation, which can serve as the cause for a buddha-field and thereby purify that field.

Among these, the "sustenance by power" encompasses the other three matters—namely, the appearance of a Buddha, the duration of the eon, and the transformation of the eon—for sustenance by power is itself the vast joy of the Dharma; without a Buddha, from what could one obtain such joy?
How much more so when there is the sustenance of the Buddha!
If the Buddha does not appear in the world, one is sustained merely by food;
but when the Buddha appears in the world, there is the sustenance of the Dharma.
If sustained by food, the duration of abiding is short;
if sustained by the Dharma, the kalpa of abiding is long.

Both types of sustaining power involve transformation: sustaining by the Dharma transforms the defiled into the pure, while sustaining by food transforms the pure into the defiled. Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that when the three calamities arise, there are two kinds of causes:
First is attachment to delicious flavors, and second is indolence; thus, by means of food, purity is maintained yet transformed into defilement.
The former [two] subsume the latter [five], and since the five matters are entirely identical, the ten are complete.

If the "Manifestation of Realization" (*Siddhi*) is subsumed under the "Flower Treasury" (*Kusumatalavyūha*), then as the former two gates subsume those five [aspects], so too do those five subsume these two. As for the remaining three matters—namely, location, extent, and arrangement—which of the [five] aspects do they subsume?

That is to say, among the five commonalities, it is subsumed under two matters: reliance upon a basis and shape; for where there is reliance upon a basis, there is spatial location and arrangement, and where there is shape, there is delimitation.
Thus, those seven [categories] subsume these five matters; since the five matters are entirely identical, the ten are likewise complete.

In both instances, each set of ten matters is cited such that nothing is excluded. Because they skillfully manifest multiple aspects, they alternate between concealment and revelation; in reality, they emerge from one another to manifest the eighteen [dhātus].
In the commentary, from "Furthermore, the preceding passages" onwards, the third section—which distinguishes and determines the tenet—is clear to understand.

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "This mutual penetration of this and that also refers to 'entering' (*praveśa*)," it is because the meaning of "entering" was explained in the aforementioned commentary as being interpreted in this way.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a brief correlation with the verses; second, a general explanation beginning from "all enter yet there is no entering.
Regarding the phrase "entering yet no entering" in the two verses, the meaning in the preceding verse alone extends to the subsequent verse; therefore, the word "all" is employed.
In total, there are three points of meaning:
the first is a comprehensive explanation that encompasses both the gate of mutual dependence in dependent origination and the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature.
Regarding the gate of dependent origination, all dharmas of dependent origination must possess three essential characteristics:
First, the meaning that the various conditions are distinct; second, the meaning that they mutually pervade and support one another; third, the meaning that they coexist without obstruction.
Now, when it says, "If one enters, then dependent origination is destroyed," this is an inverse explanation of "not entering."
If one enters [the state of non-differentiation], one loses the conditions; thus, there would be no principle of the various conditions being distinct from one another.
To say that "not entering destroys the nature and its function" is an inverse explanation of the meaning of "entering."

Thus, they must enter [into one another]; if they do not enter, their functional efficacy cannot be mutually pervasive. Consequently, there would be no principle of mutual interdependence through reciprocal penetration, and their functioning would be destroyed.
If both inclusion and non-inclusion are present together without obstruction, they constitute the gateway of dependent origination.
What is called the gateway of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature is precisely the single character "nature" (xing).

In all cases, the interpenetration of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) must consist in the non-disruption of phenomenal characteristics while simultaneously being identical to true nature. If one enters [the state of such identity] by destroying dependent origination, there would be nothing with which to interpenetrate; if one does not enter it by destroying [phenomenal] nature, then that nature would not be pervasive throughout all phenomena. Therefore, it is precisely by not disrupting phenomenal characteristics that one can achieve universality—this is the meaning of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature.
Second, regarding the statement, "Furthermore, it is precisely by not entering that one is able to enter," this is an exegesis in accordance with the principle.
It applies to both gates, though it is explained here specifically from the perspective of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

If we consider the gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is precisely because the various conditions do not enter one another in a distinct manner that they are able to mutually support one another and achieve universal mutual entry.

If one considers this from the perspective of the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature, it is only by virtue of the distinctness of phenomenal characteristics that they can subsequently accord with principle and merge into all dharmas; therefore, it is said that if one relies solely on principle, there is nothing into which one can enter.

Third, from "Furthermore, regarding emptiness of essence" onwards, it is also explained in accordance with the [preceding] sequence, yet it treats both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) together.
Regarding the aforementioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as for its characteristics, it does not enter; as for its nature, it is able to enter.

Now, regarding this single principle, neither the individual characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor the individual nature (*svabhāva*) can penetrate it alone; only when these two characteristics are fused can there be penetration. Therefore, when it is said that "if one relies on the emptiness of essence (*tattva-śūnyatā*), there is neither coming nor entering," this means that if one relies solely on the absence of nature (*svabhāva-abhāva*), there is no sense in which penetration is possible.

Regarding the statement, "If one relies on characteristics, they are not destroyed and remain as they were without difference," this means that if one relies solely on phenomena (*vastu*), one cannot immediately enter [the truth].
Both of the above points signify the sense of "not entering."
Regarding the statement, "Because nature and appearance are fused, they attain mutual entry," this explains the meaning of "entry" and clarifies the correct principle.

That is to say, when a single phenomenon that is non-different from reality fully encompasses the dharma-nature, it causes all the many phenomena that are likewise non-different from reality to simultaneously appear within that one, in accordance with the reality upon which they depend.
Since the principle of subsumption by a single phenomenon is thus, so too is the principle of subsumption by multiple phenomena.

Accordingly, each single phenomenon, in accordance with the principle upon which it relies, is simultaneously and instantaneously manifested within the many; thus they achieve mutual interpenetration, which constitutes the Gate of the Interfusion of Dharmadhātu.
Regarding the "delimitation of meaning," the commentary states:
"Because the ocean possesses flowers, it receives the name 'Flowers'"; this is because the name of the ocean is "Unbounded Light of Exquisite Flowers.
It is like a lotus pond, which receives the name of its flowers.

Regarding the phrase "the flower takes its name from the bottom of the sea upon which it rests": since the sea has a banner of the *maṇi* king as its floor, the flower is named "Adorned by the *Maṇi* King."
It is like a flower growing from mud; the flower receives the name "mud.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "There are only two hundred and ten," this means that the first layer consists of worlds as numerous as the atoms in one Buddha-field;
the second layer consists of two Buddha-fields, which, when added to the one above, makes three.
Adding three to the third layer makes six;
adding four to the fourth layer makes ten;
adding five to the fifth layer results in fifteen.
The sixth layer adds six, making twenty-one;
the seventh layer adds seven, making twenty-eight;
the eighth layer adds eight, making thirty-six.
The ninth layer adds nine, making forty-five;
the tenth layer adds ten, making fifty-five.

Below, there are five layers of ten that increase to fifty-five, while above, each of the ten layers increases by one in succession; the calculation likewise results in fifty-five, yet each consists of ten units, namely eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, and so forth.
The upper ten layers each have one hundred more, totaling one hundred and fifty-five;
when combined with the fifty-five of the lower layer, there are thus two hundred and ten.
Question:
Since there are twenty tiers, why is it said that only nineteen Buddha-fields serve as the principal fields?
Answer:

The very lowest layer is said to consist of only one world, not worlds as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-field; therefore, it is said that "from this one world," and because it is stated that "passing above this by a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a Buddha-field, one reaches the second layer," the two layers together comprise only a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a single Buddha-field.

It is like stacking two thousand coins to form twenty hundreds; if one takes a single coin from the very bottom—just as the lowest instant [kṣaṇa] does—one must pass a hundred coins above it to constitute the second layer, at which point they together total exactly one hundred.
Counting upward from this point by hundreds reaches the third layer, which is then two hundred.
Reaching the twentieth layer, there are exactly one thousand nine hundred units.
Therefore, twenty layers constitute nineteen Buddha-fields; reflect upon this.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The following shall be explained together,” this refers to the third assembly, which concludes by categorizing those who surround and those who are surrounded.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “six retinues,” this refers to what is stated in the sutra as “variously arranged and variously adorned,” which explains the characteristics and appearances of the lands belonging to these retinues.

The Commentary states: "Heaven is a circular vault. According to non-Buddhist (external) scriptures, heaven is sometimes said to have form; thus they say the shape of heaven is a vaulted dome, like the surface of a pan, and therefore heaven is round while earth is square.
If the *Zhuangzi* states that "Heaven is spontaneity (*ziran*)," then it possesses no form or substance.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "It is also as the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

'The Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings,'" this refers to what is said in the sixth chapter, the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta*), which states: "For example, the Great Brahmā Heaven King is the father of all sentient beings."
"This sutra is also like this, acting as the father of all sentient beings.
Just as when the Brahmā King was born at the beginning of the kalpa, later the various devas descended from him; yet ordinary people all falsely reckon the Brahmā King to be their father.
All the sūtras and śāstras refute this as being the conceptualization of non-Buddhists.
Now, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Tathāgata himself cites it as an analogy for the *Dharma-puṇḍarīka*; how could the Buddha not know that his father was speaking falsely?
Therefore, this was merely the World-Honored One speaking in accordance with worldly convention.
Now, as we likewise speak of devas having form in accordance with worldly convention, what contradiction is there to the underlying principle?

However, the present commentary does not deny the view of the Master Jing; rather, since certain points he has recorded in his commentary can be reconciled with the sūtras, I have provided an interpretation to harmonize them, wishing only to prevent people from lightly disparaging the holy teachings.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the erroneous translation of *loka-nāma*": *loka-nāma* means "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) in this language;
*akṣara* means "syllable" (*vyañjana*).
Because their sounds and forms are similar, an error occurred.
The Sanskrit original is *Śrīghana-lakṣaṇa*, which, when translated in full, means "the mark of the auspicious ocean-cloud.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "However, this mark is taken as... and so forth, the commentary explains that ancient masters took "Auspicious Ocean-Cloud" (*Śrīghana*) to mean "ten thousand marks" (*lakṣaṇa*). This establishes the correct interpretation of the Master Jingfa (Jñānaprabha).

Even if you, Śrīsamudramegha, were to express it through ten thousand combinations of words, it would be appropriate to say "ten thousand aspects" (*lakṣaṇa*), but not "ten thousand characters" (*akṣara*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The lands thus enumerated are certainly the principal lands,” this is because former masters have said:

“When the Sūtra speaks of ‘each and every world,’ it refers only to the lands numbering as many as the atoms within two hundred and ten Buddha-lands mentioned above, and not to the lands numbering as many as the atoms within the unspeakable Buddha-lands mentioned above.”

It is surrounded by two hundred and ten times the number of *rajas* (dust-motes) of lands; only after these two layers of encirclement are completed does the "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*) [number] begin.
Therefore, the established reasoning states:

if this were not used to reconcile the great numbers, first, within this single world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*), there would not be merely unspeakably many vast worlds equal to the number of dust-motes; second, the numerical descriptions given in three different locations would be mutually contradictory.
The commentary states:

The underlying intention here is that if there are already as many worlds as atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields surrounding [the central world], then adding two more layers of surrounding worlds would result in a multitude of worlds numbering as many as atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.

Regarding the statement that the numerical enumerations differ across three locations: first, in the introductory section, there is "the unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*); second, in the intermediate section, there are only two hundred and thirteen; and third, in the concluding text, there are two layers of "encirclers": the first has "the unspeakable," while the latter has "immeasurable unspeakables. Because the intermediate section does not reach the full count of "unspeakables," they are thus inconsistent.
This interpretation also appears to be reasonable.
However, these repeated phrases "each one" (一一) are separated by a vast distance from the preceding "two hundred and ten" [inexpressible Buddha-fields].

Since the text states, "In this way, there may be inexpressible numbers of Buddha-fields," and then immediately says, "Each of these worlds is surrounded on all sides by as many vast worlds as there are atoms in ten Buddha-fields," it is clear that they must surround the aforementioned "inexpressible" [Buddha-fields].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that there are two hundred and ten [buddha-fields] as those being surrounded: although the preceding intermediate section mentions only the skipping over [fields], it clarifies that there are indeed two hundred and ten.

According to the intent of the text, these fields—numbering as many as the atoms within nineteen buddha-fields stacked upward—are each individually surrounded by a multitude of buddha-fields; thus, they must be unspeakably unspeakable in number.

Why is this? For instance, the lowest single world-system is already surrounded by as many world-systems as there are atoms in a buddha-field; moving upward past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, one reaches the first world-system of the second tier, which is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in two buddha-fields.
Regarding these intermediate lands from the first tier up to the second tier, why are they not surrounded?

If the lands were not surrounded, the net of lands (*kṣetra-jāla*) would not be formed. Therefore, one should know that every single land among the number of lands equal to the atoms within a Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra-rajas*) must have its surrounding [lands]. It is impossible to describe them all in detail; thus, twenty tiers are mentioned as a representative example.

Since the first tier at the very bottom consists of as many world-systems as there are atoms in a single Buddha-field surrounding it, the second tier above this adds one more world-system as the surrounding layer; the third likewise adds one more. In this manner, ascending gradually, one adds a hundred to reach the hundredth tier, a thousand to reach the thousandth, and ten thousand to reach the ten-thousandth, until they fill as many world-systems as there are atoms in a Buddha-field.

Upon reaching the second tier, one additional number of lands equal to the atoms within a buddha-field is added as the surrounding [lands]; thus, there are lands equal to the atoms within two buddha-fields surrounding it.

This continues in the same manner up to the twentieth tier, with each successive tier gradually increasing. Therefore, by proceeding directly upward to a number of worlds equal to the atoms within one buddha-field, along with their surrounding [lands], there already exist a multitude of worlds—more than can be known even by the number of atoms in a buddha-field; for the sake of this single calculation, they are merely called "unspeakable. It is clear that those which surround must be the central lands.
If that is so, how is this not in contradiction with the introductory text?
For the introductory text merely states that within a single buddha-field there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields.
Since there are many instances where two layers are added as enclosures, [the question arises].
Answer:
There are two meanings to this.
The phrase "that which cannot be spoken of in a single word" serves as the primary heading.
These two layers of capacity to encompass do not, however, exist outside of the lands within the atoms of the unspeakable lands.
Why is this? Upon examining the meaning of the text, it is simply that these various lands serve as mutual leaders and companions, encircling one another.
It is like a hundred people gathered together: if one person is the leader, then the other ninety-nine surround him.
When each of the remaining ninety-nine individuals served as the central leader, they were all surrounded by ninety-nine others.

If it were not so, then even at the very bottom level, there would already be worlds as numerous as the atoms within a single Buddha-field surrounding it; and since this surrounding field itself has two further layers of surrounding fields, there would already be fields as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Reflect upon this.
If one clearly understands that [the worlds] are mutually principal and attendant, then the original number does not increase.

As for the loose statement that they "depart to the sides," the sutra explicitly describes them as being narrow below and broad above, like an inverted stupa; it further states that when arranged like a row of geese facing upward, they should also be described as tapering at the top and widening at the bottom, like a regular stupa. When arranged like a row of geese facing downward, the upper and lower tiers are interlaced like the teeth of a comb, completely filling the space without any gaps; only then do they constitute a *kṣetra-jāla* (net of lands).
The upper, lower, and four sides are all perfectly symmetrical.
Since the sutra cannot list every detail when distinguishing between various layers, it merely increases the count to describe the specific features surrounding the stūpa.
Furthermore, this statement was made so that they might appear aligned when viewed from an oblique perspective.
Therefore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "The worlds are not uniform, being like the holes of a net."
If one were to take only two hundred and ten as the number of encirclings, it would certainly not capture the intended meaning.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “According to this, it seems the translator’s prose is prolix and the principle is obscured”: if one says that "ten Buddha-fields" consists of only three characters, whereas saying "as described above" now consists of four characters, it is therefore considered prolix in its phrasing.
To merely state "as explained above" when the words are not explicit constitutes an obscuration of the principle.

The Commentary states: "If one relies on the former meaning, it is the excellence of the translator. Since the number of encirclers and the encircled is already great, to simply say "as above" is an abbreviation of the wording; therefore, it is called "excellent."

Although there are two interpretations, the intent of the commentary lies in the second interpretation; it employs a number equal to the dust motes of ten Buddha-fields as the "encirclers" because this accords with the sūtra’s fundamental principle of manifesting inexhaustibility, and because the structural pattern of the preceding and following sections is likewise consistent.
The rest is as found in the commentary (*śāstra*), which can be seen by careful examination.
Regarding the phrase "the *Abhidharmakośa* says" in the commentary, it is merely an abbreviation of its meaning.

The complete verse states: "The eastern continent, Pūrvavideha, is shaped like a half-moon; three of its sides are like those of Jambudvīpa, while the southern side is three hundred and fifty [yojanas]."
Jambudvīpa is shaped like a carriage; its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], and its southern side is three hundred and fifty.
Aparagoyānīya is circular and without defect; its diameter is two thousand five hundred, and its circumference is three times this.
"Uttarakuru is square, with each side measuring two thousand [yojanas].
To the east, it is wide in the north and narrow in the south; the rest may be understood accordingly.
Therefore, it concludes: 'The four continents differ in their characteristics.'"
From the phrase "Now, as for what is called 'thus' (*tathā*)," the preceding section raised the treatise as a question, which is now being explained and reconciled.

Regarding the statement "entirely resembling this realm," the arrangement of these four continents constitutes the domain of a single Buddha; thus, this present world is identical to the realm of those four continents.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In this section, there is no heading or conclusion indicating the total number,” etc., it follows the pattern of the intermediate oceans as seen at the end of the eighth scripture.

As for the tenth scripture taking the primary metaphor as its basis, it is because the bodies of sentient beings are used as a metaphor for the various lands (*kṣetra*), and it is also because the cause is used as a metaphor for the conditions (*pratyaya*).

The sixth section below states: "Karma is the field, and consciousness is the seed. This means that the mind itself is the seed of names and words; as the immediate causal condition, it is designated as the cause.
Karma is called a "condition" because it functions as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
the rest is as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The three verses [from 18.103–105] clarify both mind and karma together,” this serves as the heading.
"Conduct" (*caryā*) is synonymous with "action" (*karman*), and therefore it is explained.
Because it is manifested by the mind, it is not separately explained;
that is to say, "according as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-field pure," which means that due to differences in the mind, the visions of the lands (*kṣetra*) differ.

If one practices the ten wholesome deeds, then one will not meet with an untimely death and will be born in a land of great wealth and pure conduct; this is because the lands differ according to the diverse perceptions resulting from karma.
This passage thus simultaneously presents both the causes and conditions, as well as the two types of realms presided over by the King.

Regarding the statement, "It is also a metaphor for sentient beings sharing the same place yet having different perceptions": the Buddha is fundamentally non-dual, yet some perceive him as silver while others perceive him as gold;
the land is fundamentally one, yet some perceive it as pure while others perceive it as defiled.
Therefore, what Śaṅkhakuṇḍalī saw was like the palaces of the sixth heaven, while what Śāriputra saw were hills, mounds, pits, and ravines.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first [type of land] is coarse and destroyed while the subtle remains,” although that which is manifested is ruined and foul—this is precisely what is meant by "coarse destruction"—it is nonetheless a land of transformation (*nirmāṇakṣetra*).
That place is eternally stable and subtle; it refers to the enjoyment [realms] for oneself and others.
The first part briefly follows the scriptural text, while the second explains the reason.

Regarding the phrase "destruction results from evil karma," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "These sinful sentient beings, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."
Regarding the statement, "Its existence is due to two causes," this is the thesis.
"First, with respect to the Buddha" refers to the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment realm).
"Second, through virtuous karma" refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment realm), as well as the transformation-realm (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) and the pure realm.
Because their karmic actions differ, those in the same place perceive different things.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "All those who have cultivated merit and are gentle, supple, and upright shall all see my body here, preaching the Dharma."
The commentary states: "Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*," and so forth, citing scriptural evidence.
The phrase "my pure land is not destroyed" serves as proof for the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), thereby establishing the preceding point regarding the Buddha.

"Gods and humans are constantly filled" refers to the realization of the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*) and so forth, which is accomplished through the cultivation of superior wholesome karma.
Because these are realized in successive order, the meaning is thus derived from the scriptural passage.

If one were to cite the full passage, the Sūtra says: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, when it is consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, constantly filled with devas and humans."
The gardens and various halls and pavilions were adorned with all kinds of jewels; the jewel-trees bore many flowers and fruits, providing a place for sentient beings to roam and enjoy themselves.
The devas struck celestial drums and constantly performed various musical entertainments, raining down *māndārava* flowers which they scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
"My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as being consumed by flames; they are filled with such pervasive sorrow, fear, and suffering.
He then says, "These sentient beings who have committed transgressions," and subsequently, "Those who have cultivated merit," and so forth.

The Commentary states: "However, although cessation does not occur simultaneously," and so forth. This explains and establishes the preceding meaning, concluding by returning to the point that it is inconceivable; this is precisely the intention of Master Zhiyi (En).
Because one [aspect] ceases while the other exists, they are said not to be simultaneous.

Since existence does not persist apart from the locus of cessation, it is said that arising must necessarily share the same locus; this is like a person seeing water at a place where hungry ghosts see fire, or hungry ghosts seeing fire at a place where humans see water.

Regarding the statement, "Though they are said to occupy the same place, they are eternally non-existent [in one another]": within cessation there is no persistence, and within persistence there is no cessation; it is just as the palaces of rākṣasas and the palaces of humans, though situated in the same location, never see one another.
The land of communal enjoyment is likewise so: if it is the land of self-enjoyment, it is therefore all-pervasive; it is neither identical to the triple world nor separate from the triple world.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Not as the triple world, yet seeing within the triple world."
"If it is the land of the dharma-nature, it is moreover eternally as-it-is despite arising and ceasing.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "therefore it is inconceivable," this concludes the explanation of the sūtra passage on the inconceivability of the kalpa-conflagration; that is to say, one must not conceive of it in terms of existence and cessation, or defilement and purity.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The characteristics of the worlds are different,” this refers to the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (dharma-nature land) in contrast to the *sāmbhogika* (enjoyment) and *nairmāṇika* (emanation) lands.

Regarding the commentary on the sixth chapter, the *Vairocana-parivarta*, which states, “Thereafter, there are further great kalpas; this is not contrary to principle,” this serves to refute a potential objection.
Jingfa stated:
According to the subsequent text, a great kalpa consists of as many small kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
At the beginning of the second small kalpa, when the human lifespan is two small kalpas long, the Buddha’s lifespan is five billion years.
Vigour and Radiance (Weiguang) served three Buddhas in succession and, through the transformation of his karma, was reborn in heaven.

Now, regarding the statement that during the first kalpa there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten Mount Sumerus: does this mean that within that world-system there are further multiple great kalpas, and this refers to the first among them?
Does this refer to taking the initial [moment] of each minor kalpa?
The commentary states:
Based on the textual evidence cited above, both alternatives are established.
Next, it says:
If one considers the beginning of a *kṣudrakalpa* (minor eon), it would be unreasonable for him to encounter only three Buddhas within a single lifetime of such majestic radiance.
If one considers a *mahākalpa* (great eon), how much space could there possibly be within a single *kṣetra* (buddha-field)?
The commentary states:
This explains both points simultaneously.

That is to say, during the two intermediate kalpas of human lifespan, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within Mount Sumeru during each intermediate kalpa; therefore, it is not possible that a single lifetime of retribution would encounter only three Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "how could it be so vast," if one considers a single Bhadrakalpa, it is not particularly vast.
Next, it says:
"Therefore, we know that these three characters 'first kalpa' (chū-shou-chieh) in this text should be reordered to read 'kalpa first' (chieh chū-shou)."
It would still be no fault to move these three characters to the line below "appearing in the world" (出興於世).
The commentary states:

This formulation of the principle is complete in its inverted phrasing; it should properly read: "In that World of Supreme Sound, there appeared as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten Mount Sumerus, and the name of the first Buddha at the beginning of that eon was 'Sumeru-Victory-Cloud of All Merit Mountains'."
This is indeed most excellent.
I do not wish to laboriously cite the faults of the scriptural passage here; rather, I have merely used reasoning to explain the term "the first kalpa.

As for the statement that "there is yet more great," this refers in meaning to the intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*); it is spoken of as "great" in accordance with the intent of the *Śāntavimokṣa-sūtra*.

For example, in the Bhadrakalpa there are twenty periods of increase and decrease that constitute intermediate kalpas; since nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appear during the fifteenth kalpa, it is evident that many Buddhas can appear within a single kalpa.
However, because that Pure Kalpa is of long duration, there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of ten Mount Sumerus within a single kalpa.

Yet, one should not wish to disparage the sutras by claiming they do not urge immediate practice; thus, while retaining a concise principle for general understanding, it is certainly not the case that the Pure Dharma itself is being rejected.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Briefly clarifying that there are ten aspects,” the concluding text below says, “It is largely the same as at the beginning of the sutra,” which refers to the inconceivable ten-body aspects of the Teacher.

The first [body] is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Sūtra defines the Dharma-body as the unimpeded nature of body and wisdom, while the Commentary further integrates form and other characteristics into this single Dharma-body, because the first body serves as the totality.
The Dharma is nowhere not present and is inherently all-pervasive; this explains that the "pervasiveness of its body" mentioned in the sutra refers to the Dharmatā-kāya.

Next, the statement "Because wisdom merges with principle, it is equal to that true realm" explains the sutra’s phrase "equal to the true Dharma-realm"; this is the Saṃbhoga-kāya, which is likewise the wisdom of suchness.
Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Only suchness and the wisdom of suchness alone remain, constituting the Dharma-body.
Regarding the phrase "able to cause the physical marks [to be pervasive]," it means that because the true body is all-pervasive, its functional application is likewise all-pervasive.
This body of mine is now the eternal body, for it is the Dharma-body.
Thus, through the perfect interpenetration of the three bodies, they constitute the one true Dharma-body.
The following nine sections provide specific explanations.
The second is the aspect of compassion, which is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
The third is the aspect of fulfillment, which is the bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*).
Taking principle, practice, time, and place as the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is as described at the beginning of the sutra.

The four marks of physical form constitute the body of merit; therefore, the aforementioned sutra states, "The great ocean of all merits practiced throughout the three periods of time is entirely purified. Thus, exquisite physical form is the fruit of merit.

The aforementioned sutra further states: "Having made offerings to all Tathāgatas throughout inconceivable oceans of great kalpas, and universally bestowing these merits upon all sentient beings, he is therefore most peerless in his dignified majesty."
The five superior marks constitute the body of majestic power.
The six noble marks constitute the body adorned with the primary and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Furthermore, in accordance with the three vehicles, it is said that [the Buddha] "surpasses the holy emperors."
The *Abhidharmakośa* verse states: "Because his marks are not perfectly round and brilliant, he is not equal to a Buddha.
This explains the marks of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
Since this refers to the World-Honored One, it is said they are "distinct and clear"; in reality, he possesses marks numbering as many as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds.
The seventh is the characteristic of being sustained, which refers to the body maintained by power;
it is like the shadow left behind by a dragon, which is maintained by power so that it does not perish.
The eighth is the characteristic of non-obstruction, which refers to the body of vows.
The aforementioned scripture states: "The Buddha Vairocana’s power of vows pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel.
Therefore, all behold him with their own eyes.
The ninth is the mark of transformation, which is the nirmāṇakāya (transformation body).
The tenth is the mark of auspiciousness, which is the jñānakāya (wisdom body); it resides precisely within the light of wisdom, while incidentally encompassing the light of the body.
Thus, we know that the past causes and conditions cited in this sutra are likewise all perfect and subtle.

The Commentary states: "First, regarding the production of meritorious and immovable karma, one takes the three—generosity, patience, and wisdom—as the roots of goodness. There are three types of karma:
first, unwholesome karma, which is produced by the three unwholesome roots; this is not what is being clarified here.
The commentary enumerates the three types of action, which are produced from the three roots of goodness.
These three roots of goodness are non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
Now, not only does one refrain from clinging to objects, but one is also able to practice giving, thereby accomplishing the root of non-attachment.
Not only is there no resentment toward suffering, but one also practices patience; thus, the faculty of non-hatred is established.
Not only is there clarity regarding objects, but one further cultivates wisdom and understanding; this is the faculty of non-delusion.

Because these three roots give rise exclusively to the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), they constitute the roots of merit (*puṇya*) and the immovable (*āniñjya*).

Furthermore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, these three roots each have their own distinct nature and are subsumed within the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-citta-dharma*): non-attachment (*alobha*) has the nature of being without clinging toward existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence; non-hatred (*adveṣa*) has the nature of being without malice toward suffering (*duḥkha*) and the instruments of suffering; and non-delusion (*amoha*) has the nature of clear understanding regarding all principles and phenomena (*tattva-artha*).
Pervasive [factors] are exclusively wholesome wisdom (*prajñā*), each having its own distinct nature.
Now, according to the first chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, wisdom is taken as the nature of non-delusion (*amoha*).

However, the intention of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* understands wisdom to be the fruit of non-delusion; therefore, giving (*dāna*) and patience (*kṣānti*) are also designated by their resultant names, for giving and patience are accomplished through non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Therefore, the Commentary states: "Taking generosity, patience, and wisdom as its roots.
The two roots of faith and so forth will be explained in detail below.

Regarding the Commentary’s statement, "Third, seeking supreme wisdom, taking the four immeasurables and heedfulness—these five dharmas—as its roots," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All praise compassion and loving-kindness as the root of a bodhisattva."
Those who possess a compassionate heart and must joyfully renounce while remaining heedful consist of diligence, non-attachment, and so forth.
Thirdly, regarding that which is to be abandoned, their nature is the cultivation of guarding against what is improper; they are established as one [aggregate] by way of designation.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of the faculty of heedfulness (*apramāda*), whose roots are deep and difficult to uproot.
Because one relies on heedfulness to exert the preceding four [immeasurables] and thereby attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is designated as a "faculty."
Fourth, "The General Explanation of the Wholesome Roots" below refers to the common nature of the three aforementioned categories.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "First, for those whose ignorance is heavy, the wisdom of self-awakening opens," the text consists of two parts:
first, a detailed explanation, and second, a concluding interpretation.
Regarding the preceding section: first, the initial four [verses] eliminate obstacles;
the fifth causes liberation, benefiting all three vehicles;
and the sixth inspires faith in those who have not yet believed.
Seventh, to cause them to enter the three stages of the worthy ones;
eighth, to cause them to attain the first stage;
ninth, to cause those from the second stage upward to attain the eighth stage.
"Having already attained the eighth stage and realized non-arising, the Buddhas exhort them to arise so that they may attain the ninth and twelfth stages.
The commentary states: "This is based on distinctions," which marks the second section, the concluding explanation.
The preceding section on "differentiation" clarifies that this is a vertical explanation of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*); the preceding conclusion does not pertain to the three *siddhāntas*.
The phrase "If one applies them horizontally" below further concludes the alternative classification.

Arranged horizontally opposite the preceding vertical set, these ten phrases are universally applied to each stage; thus, they give rise to the realization of the True Dharma (Saddharma). To give rise to wholesome qualities by confronting the aforementioned antidotes is precisely the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the therapeutic teaching for individuals).
This means that giving rise to great faith and understanding, producing superior roots of goodness, and conceiving the mind to see the Buddha—all these constitute the production of goodness.
Seeing the principle is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint); it is like the wisdom of self-awakening opening the way toward all-knowledge—this is seeing the principle.
There should likewise be that which accords with worldly convention to bring joy;
because the world-siddhānta (worldly standpoint) benefits those nearby, the unimpeded nature of the horizontal and vertical [dimensions] is not discussed here.
This is the intended meaning regarding the four siddhāntas, which shall be analyzed in the "Inquiry on Knowledge" (*Prajñāpṛcchā*).
The sub-commentary states: "According to the *Sūtra on the Original Vows of the Śrī-mālā*," and so forth, citing the scripture to establish the point.
Five hundred is correct; twenty-five thousand is incorrect.
This section is divided into two parts:
First, it is refuted and then established through the "Exposition of the Teachings" (*yōkyō*).
Within the former, the phrase "upper fascicle" refers to the third chapter, the "Chapter on the Contemplation of the Worthies and Sages."
Therein, the Bodhisattva Revered Head asked:
"How should a bodhisattva train in contemplating the meaning and characteristics of names, and furthermore, how should they practice regarding the phenomena that the mind engages with?"
The Buddha first answered regarding names, enumerating the sublime titles of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
Next, he answered regarding the dharmas practiced by the mind, saying: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
Regarding what you previously asked about the "dharmas upon which the mind operates," namely the so-called ten minds— beginning with the first,
the Stage of Resolving the Mind— I have extensively explained the wondrous characteristics of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
Next, the Bodhisattva Revered Head again asked the World-Honored One:

"From the first stage to the final stage, there are two kinds of dharma-bodies: the dharma-body of retributive supernormal transformation and the dharma-body of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), as well as the dharma-body of responsive transformation."
"What are the characteristics of form?
What are the characteristics of the mind?
The Buddha replied:

"Regarding the prior explanation of supramundane fruits and rewards: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Buddha stage, there are two kinds of *dharmakāya* in each. Because they arise from the true nature within the stream of the *dharmadhātu* of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), true wisdom constitutes the *dharmakāya*; 'dharma' here signifies its own essence (*svabhāva*)."
"Accumulating the storehouses as the body," and so forth, while also explaining the Pure Land.
Next it says:
"O Son of the Buddha, the worldly retribution consists of the copper-jeweled necklace and the copper-wheel-turning king of the Ten Abodes, with a hundred-merit son as his retinue."
Born in one Buddha-field, he receives the Buddha’s teachings and practices, transforming and teaching two worlds.

As a silver-jewel-garlanded silver-wheel-turning king, with five hundred meritorious sons as his retinue, he is born within two Buddha-lands, receives the Buddha’s teachings and practices, and transforms three worlds.

The Vajra-jewel-garlanded Golden Wheel-Turning King, with a thousand meritorious sons as his retinue, enters the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to transform all sentient beings while dwelling throughout the four continents.

On the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), adorned with necklaces of a hundred jewels and seven-jeweled wheels, he is accompanied by the Four Heavenly Kings and ten thousand sons as his retinue; manifesting a hundred Dharma-bodies, he instructs the sons of the gods throughout the ten directions within a hundred Buddha-lands.
The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wears a necklace of a thousand jewels and a wheel of eight precious substances; he has twenty thousand sons as his retinue.
The King of the Yāma Heaven wears a necklace of ten thousand jewels and a wheel of nine precious substances; his retinue is likewise beyond counting.
The Tuṣita Heaven King, adorned with necklaces of a hundred million jewels and a ten-jeweled wheel-hub, has a retinue likewise beyond measure.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven King, adorned with celestial-light jewel necklaces and an eleven-jeweled wheel-hub, has a retinue likewise.
The Heavens’ Lord of Others’ Transformations wears a necklace of mani-jewel radiance with twelve jewel-marked wheels; his retinue is likewise adorned.
The Brahma Heaven Lord wears a necklace of thousand-colored dragon-jewel wisdom-light with thirteen jewel-marked wheels; his retinue is likewise adorned.
The Celestial King Great Response Jewel Sign Wheel Light of Radiance, with his retinue likewise;
and the Celestial King Pureness of White Cloud Jewel Sign Wheel, with his retinue likewise, both wear inconceivable jewel-light necklaces.
