However, it is not necessarily the case that all [afflictions] are so; thus, the word "many" is employed because even a single affliction can serve as a cause for the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, this is merely intended to provide a concise clarification; if one simply consults the commentary cited above, it will be easily understood.
"However, the causes for humans and devas encompass the three realms: first, humans; second, the desire-realm devas; and third, the two upper realms.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
From the phrase "There are two vehicles" onwards, the conclusion is established.
Thus, the preceding nine are considered false, while the final one is considered partial.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Among these, the correspondence with the four causes and four conditions can be understood through reflection”: deep-seated faith and understanding, as well as profound faith in all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma, constitute the first cause, which is the perfection of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
To reverently honor and respect all Buddhas is the second cause for being sustained by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, because of such reverence.
To act solely for the sake of eternally extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings is the third, which consists in frequently giving rise to compassion.

Constantly desiring to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings, to adorn the buddha-fields, and to make offerings to the Buddhas—this is the fourth [perfection], the long-term, intense, and difficult practice of asceticism.
The four causes are complete.

Regarding the statement, "As for the 'four conditions,' it is to revere and honor all Buddhas," this refers to the first condition, because one has seen and heard their miraculous transformations and majestic powers.
Those who uphold the True Dharma and cultivate wisdom do so because the hearing of the Dharma is subtle and profound; this constitutes the second condition.
Furthermore, those who uphold the True Dharma do so because they see that the Dharma is about to perish; this constitutes the third condition.
However, for one who seeks the eternal extinction of the suffering of sentient beings, seeing that birth entails the suffering of afflictions, karma, and retribution is the fourth condition.
Seeing suffering constitutes the condition, while extending compassion constitutes the cause; thus, although there is but a single phrase, the causes and conditions are complete.
In this context, because the four powers are not complete, they are not brought together.

The commentary states: "Furthermore, from 'not seeking the five desires' above," it re-explains the scriptural text, taking the previous interpretation and integrating it with the insights of the ancient masters.
From this point forward, the following represents entirely new interpretations that do not rely on previous commentaries.
The text itself consists of five sections:

first, concerning the virtue of faith; second, concerning the intention for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); third, concerning Buddha-nature; fourth, concerning the Four Great Vows; and fifth, concluding by returning to the true and correct [path].
Regarding the first [section]:
the five verses of the sūtra text should be divided into two parts;
the first verse indicates the arousal of the mind through faith, while the subsequent four verses manifest the virtues of that faith.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The present text contains all [the items] together, though they are not in sequence,” that sutra lists them in the following order: “First, drawing near to virtuous friends; second, making offerings to all Buddhas; third, cultivating roots of goodness; fourth, aspiring to seek the supreme Dharma; fifth, having a mind that is always gentle and flexible; sixth, being able to endure suffering when encountered; seventh, possessing profound compassion; eighth, having a deeply equanimous mind; ninth, loving and delighting in the Mahāyāna; tenth, seeking the Buddha’s wisdom.”
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the three characters for the four existences,' this is because the character for 'making offerings' (供養) is identical [to the first character] in its entirety.
The Commentary further states: "Moreover, these ten virtues are precisely the intent of seeking Bodhi"; this second section clarifies the intent of Bodhi.
Regarding the statement "generating the bodhicitta" and so forth, there is extensive textual material on this; here, fourteen instances are cited briefly to broadly represent the infinite.
Now, only one is mentioned to stand for the other thirteen, namely: "Because of the desire to serve and make offerings to all Buddhas without exception, one generates the bodhicitta."
The eight characters "its entirety without remainder" (其悉無餘) appear at the end of each and every one [of the preceding sections].

1. To adorn and purify all Buddha-lands; 2. To protect and uphold the true teachings of all Buddhas; 3. To fulfill the vows of all Tathāgatas; 4. To travel to all Buddha-lands; 5. To enter the assemblies of all Buddhas; 6. To know the succession of eons in all worlds; 7. To know the ocean of the minds of all sentient beings; 8. To know the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings; 9. To know the ocean of the karma of all sentient beings; 10. To know the ocean of the conduct of all sentient beings; 11. To extinguish the ocean of afflictions of all sentient beings; 12. To uproot the ocean of the habitual tendencies of afflictions of all sentient beings, leaving none remaining—for these reasons, they resolve upon Bodhicitta.
"Good son!
To state it briefly, it is by means of such hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* skillful practices that a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Good son!"
Because the Bodhisattva’s practice universally enters all dharmas and realizes them all, and because it universally enters all lands and purifies them all; therefore, O son of good family!
My vows will only end when the purification of all worlds is complete;
my vows will only be fulfilled when the afflictions and habitual tendencies of all sentient beings have been uprooted.
The commentary states:
All that precedes is brought about by the bodhicitta.
In light of the current scriptural passage, this can be understood through the meaning.
Below the phrase "The first line of the final verse," the third section discusses the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

This further clarifies, in response to the objection, the meaning of the complete possession of the three types of Buddha-nature within the lineage (*gotra*); it corresponds to the "Chapter on the Three Causes" (*Trihetuvarga*) within the "Section on Revealing the Essence" (*Tattvaprakāśanavibhāga*) of the second fascicle of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
The treatise states: "Furthermore, it should be understood that the essence of Buddha-nature has three kinds of meanings subsumed under the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
These three kinds refer to the three causes.
The three kinds of Buddha-nature and the three causes are: first, the cause of what is to be attained; second, the cause of application; and third, the cause of perfection."
The first is true suchness (*tathatā*) as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness; from this, one should attain the bodhicitta, up to the dharma-body after the path.

The second, the causal factor of application, is the bodhicitta; by means of this mind, one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten perfections, the ten stages, and up to the dharma-body after the path.
The cause of the threefold perfection refers to the cause of application (*prayoga-hetu*); by means of this, all perfections are attained.

Regarding the three kinds of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the cause that is to be attained inherently possesses these three natures: first, the nature of abiding in its own essence (*prakṛtistha-gotra*); second, the nature of being drawn forth (*samudānīta-gotra*); and third, the nature of attaining the fruit (*phala-prāpta-gotra*).
The commentary states:
"Abiding in the nature" refers to the stage of ordinary beings prior to the Path.
"Manifesting the nature" extends from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment upward, through to the final stage of the Śaikṣa (those still in training).
Regarding "attaining the nature of fruition," this refers to the stage of the noble one who has nothing further to learn (aśaikṣa).
In the commentary, the phrase "Furthermore, there are four great vows which can be understood through reflection" refers to the four [vows] in relation to the Four Great Vows.
Seeking nothing within the text such as the five desires, etc., manifests the vow to sever the boundless afflictions.
Acting solely for the sake of eternally extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings manifests the vow to deliver the boundless sentient beings.
To uphold the True Dharma and cultivate all forms of wisdom is the vow to study the inexhaustible Dharma-gates.
To realize Bodhi is the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Thus, the four [requisites] are complete.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, as it was said above: ‘With a profound mind of faith and understanding, ever pure’,” this is the fifth section, which concludes by returning to the true and correct [path].
This section has two parts:
First, the essence of the true and correct bodhicitta is revealed, followed by the formal conclusion.
Within the former section, there are three intended meanings:
first, it concerns the three types of bodhicitta; second, it concerns the three contemplations; and third, it concerns the four great vows.

Now, regarding the first [section]: first, the mind of great wisdom is clarified; next, from "Alas, sentient beings are deluded regarding this" onwards, the mind of great compassion; and finally, from "I lament that they did not know it in the past" onwards, the mind of great vows.
It is the lamp of the bodhicitta, with great compassion as its oil, the great vow as its wick, and great wisdom as its light; for this light illumines the dharma-realm.
These correspond, respectively, to the direct mind, the mind of great compassion, and the profound mind.
Second, regarding the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*): compassion and the vow constitute the contemplation of the conventional (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The preceding great wisdom-mind that directly clarifies the inherent purity of the fundamental nature constitutes the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
That afflictions are themselves bodhi and are fundamentally the Buddha constitutes the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*).

Third, regarding the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*): the initial section establishes the principle in general; because these are the four great vows of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), they are elucidated in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
From the passage "Believing that afflictions (*kleśa*) are identical to bodhi" onwards, the four great vows are specifically revealed.
The first is the vow to sever afflictions, which is boundless;
the second, from the passage "Because one generates the mind by invoking its fundamental nature," is the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
3. From "Alas, sentient beings are deluded regarding this" onwards is the vow: "I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. 4.
From "Lamenting that I did not know it in the past" onwards is the vow: "I vow to study inexhaustible Dharma gates."
This explains the Four Great Vows, referring collectively to the aforementioned four vows.
While the previous section merely pointed to the text, this passage now uses the term "profound mind" (shēn xīn) to harmonize and integrate these four, rendering them perfect and wondrous.
The commentary states: "Because there is compassion, one does not become extinguished in the infinite. This concludes the core point.

Although the preceding sections contain many meanings, they do not transcend compassion and wisdom; therefore, this now serves as a summary, concluding both the preceding commentary and the sutra itself.

Therefore, in the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, within the section clarifying the "Ten Dharmas that Form the Vehicle," the second point, "Truly and Correctly Arousing the Bodhicitta," states: "Having deeply realized that within the inconceivable realm, a single suffering is all sufferings, one personally laments one's own past sufferings—how one gave rise to delusions and became immersed in them. It continues until: "Contemplating the agonizing pain of both self and others, one immediately gives rise to great compassion and establishes two vows:
'I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings' and 'I vow to sever boundless afflictions.'"
Although sentient beings are like empty space, one vows to deliver those beings who are like space;
although one knows that afflictions have no existence, one vows to sever those afflictions which have no source—these two constitute the contemplation of emptiness.
Although one knows that sentient beings are exceedingly numerous, one delivers a multitude of sentient beings;
although one knows that afflictions are boundless and bottomless, one severs those boundless and bottomless afflictions through the provisional contemplation.
Although one knows that sentient beings are like the Buddha, one delivers sentient beings who are like the Buddha;
although one knows that afflictions are the true mark, one severs the afflictions that are the true mark—this is the Middle Way.
Why is this? If one were merely to uproot the causes of suffering and uproot the fruits of suffering, this vow would be mixed with poison; therefore, one must contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Yet, if one contemplates emptiness in a biased manner, one will not perceive sentient beings who can be delivered; such a person is called an "adherent of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-vādī*) and is one whom the Buddhas cannot transform.
If one views sentient beings as being exclusively capable of being saved, one falls into the great compassion of biased attachment; this is not the path of liberation.
Now, because it is neither poisonous nor artificial, it is called "True";
because it is neither the extreme of emptiness nor the extreme of existence, it is called "Right."

Just as a bird flying through the sky never dwells in the sky, yet though it does not dwell in the sky its tracks cannot be sought; though it traverses the sky, it is the sky, and though it traverses it, it is the sky—therefore, one who vows to contend with space is said to have truly generated the bodhicitta.
The commentary states:
The above explains the reason why three contemplations are required. It further says:

"Moreover, one recognizes the inconceivable mind, the single-minded joy, and the all-pervading joyful mind. Although I and other sentient beings have sought the causes of happiness in the past, we did not know those causes—like grasping at shards and pebbles while calling them wish-fulfilling jewels, or falsely pointing to fireflies and calling them the sun and moon. Only now do we finally understand; therefore, great compassion arises, giving rise to two vows: the vow to know the inexhaustible Dharma-gates and the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way."
Although one knows that the Dharma-gates are eternally quiescent like space, one vows to practice that eternal quiescence;
although one knows that bodhi is non-existent, one nevertheless seeks it within that non-existence—this is the contemplation of emptiness.
Although one knows that the Dharma-gates are like space and non-existent, one makes vows to paint and adorn space;

although one knows that the Buddha-way is neither something to be accomplished nor something already accomplished—like planting a tree in space to produce flowers and fruit—this is called "provisional contemplation."

Although one knows that the Dharma-gates and the fruit of Buddhahood are neither cultivated nor uncultivated, and neither realized nor unrealized, one attains the Madhyamaka by realizing through non-realization.
This is called neither false nor poisonous, and is thus termed "True";
it is neither empty nor a view of craving, and is thus termed "Right.
Such compassionate vows and the inconceivable realm of wisdom arise simultaneously, neither before nor after.

Compassion is wisdom, and wisdom is compassion; without conditions or conceptual thought, it universally covers all beings. Spontaneously uprooting suffering and naturally bestowing happiness, it is unlike poisonous harm, unlike mere emptiness, and unlike affectionate views—this is called the true and authentic arousal of the bodhicitta.
The commentary states:

"If one simply examines the passages cited above, the text of this sub-commentary is readily understood; thus, I have extracted its essential meaning to compose this sub-commentary that clarifies the profound and mysterious depths of the sutra."

However, the meaning of bodhicitta throughout this sutra is profound and vast in its literary expression; having observed its essential summaries, I have selected and utilized them, citing them as evidence.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second [section], ‘Faith as the Source of the Path,’ and below,” this passage is for the most part easy to understand.

However, as for the phrase, “First, the meaning of ‘source’ (ben): because it is the source of bodhi,” the intent is that the meaning of “source” refers to the source of the qualities of fruition, while the meaning of “head” (shou) refers to the source of the qualities of the cause.

The statement, “*Yuan* (the Origin) is the foremost of the good,” refers to the explanation of the four virtues—*Yuan*, *Heng*, *Li*, and *Zhen*—in the *Wenyan* (Explanatory Text) of the *Qian* hexagram in the *Book of Changes*: “*Yuan* is the foremost of the good; *Heng* is the assembly of the auspicious; *Li* is the harmony of righteousness; *Zhen* is the backbone of affairs.”

The superior man embodies benevolence and is thus sufficient to lead others in benevolence; he delights in auspicious assemblies and is thus sufficient to harmonize with ritual propriety; he benefits all things and is thus sufficient to bring harmony to righteousness; he is steadfast and firm and is thus sufficient to serve as the backbone for undertaking affairs.
"The superior man practices these four virtues; therefore it is said: 'Qian: Supreme Primacy, Success, Advantageousness, and Persistence.
Now, we employ only the meaning of one character [from each].
Regarding the commentary on the phrase 'Not believing in body and mind,' this conversely establishes the meaning of the preceding section."

The characteristics of knowledge and vision constitute bodhi, while the nature of knowledge and vision constitutes nirvana; therefore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* explains the "opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" as having the meaning of the unsurpassed, meaning that it simultaneously opens both bodhi and nirvana.
The Commentary states: "The wish-fulfilling gem has, in brief, five meanings," which refers to its correspondence with the meaning of faith.

If one follows the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the jewel has six meanings; as the verse says: "1) Reality, 2) that which is rare in the world, 3) clarity and purity, 4) power, 5) the ability to adorn the world, and 6) supreme and immutable."
Now, this ultimate truth (paramārtha) subsumes two meanings: the true and the supreme; the remaining four are identical [to those].
The fourth is power (prabhāva), and the fifth is adornment (vyūha), or alternatively, it may lack adornment, with the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) added to these.
However, the commentary’s five points all state that they contain both the dharma and the metaphor; this can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "one cannot even obtain a scabies-infested jackal," etc., it refers to the fourth fascicle of the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first three verses clarify the ten stages (*bhūmi*),” etc., it explains that all the stages contain the underlying principles and meanings, as detailed in this very chapter.

However, the specific mention of “superiority is the stage of non-retrogression” is because, whereas in the preceding stage of the Right Mind (*samyakcitta*) one remained unmoved by hearing praise or blame, here, even when hearing that such things do not exist—which is a deeper form of benefit or harm—one’s mind does not retreat; therefore, it is called “superior.”
The remainder is as found in the subsequent text; one should seek it there.

However, in all cases, the names of the stages are concealed while their practices are preserved—sometimes combined or separated, sometimes abbreviated or expanded—and they do not follow a complete sequential order. This is intended to clarify that the gate of perfect and harmonious faith is instantaneously and fully possessed.
This is also because, as in the "Chapter on Leaving the World," the six stages are fully possessed all at once;
thus, two thousand practices are also accomplished instantaneously, for they are cultivated all at once within each stage.
If one were to proceed solely by way of gradual succession, one would obtain only the meaning of the single aspect of sequential distribution.
The Commentary states: “Because if there is that, then there is this” serves to eliminate confusion. This clarifies that this is the meaning of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*):

as soon as one stage is attained, all stages are attained. It is like ten kinds of fragrant incense; when a single pellet is burned, ten scents are emitted simultaneously from a tiny mustard seed. If one smells the fragrance, all ten scents are perceived together. When the scent of aloeswood is perceived, the scent of sandalwood is also perceived; when the scent of ghee is perceived, the scent of camphor and so forth are likewise perceived.
Those who take the medicinal pill of ten flavors all obtain its benefits simultaneously; this should also be understood by analogy.
It is not like a chain, where one can only reach the subsequent link after reaching the preceding one;
nor is it like traveling a road, where walking one *li* results in reaching two *li*, or walking two *li* results in advancing to three *li*.
Therefore, within this stage, one does not abide in the name of a "stage"; whether opening or closing, it is precisely here that they reside.
Reflect on this, reflect on this.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “A brief exposition of the ten gates of the functional activity of samādhi”:

Nevertheless, the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) establishes six categories—first, the single essence; second, the two functions; third, the three pervasions; fourth, the four virtues; fifth, cessation; and sixth, contemplation—but these likewise do not transcend this [same principle].
Regarding the "single essence," this refers to the essence of self-nature purity and perfect luminosity, which serves as the common essence for all ten concentrations.
Regarding the "two functions": first is the function of the ocean-seal where all phenomena are eternally arrayed, which is the first samādhi;
second is the function of the eye of the dharma-realm’s perfect clarity, which is the Flower Adornment Samādhi (*Avataṃsaka-samādhi*).

Regarding the "three pervasions," they are: first, the pervasion of a single atom universally encompassing the Dharma-realm; second, the pervasion of a single atom producing inexhaustible manifestations; and third, the pervasion of a single atom containing both emptiness and existence. These three are all gates of the Indra’s Net Samādhi.

Regarding the four virtues: first, the virtue of wondrous and unimpeded function according to conditions; second, the virtue of maintaining dignified deportment with proper regulation; third, the virtue of gathering in sentient beings through gentleness and straightforwardness; and fourth, the virtue of universally taking upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings, which corresponds to the sixth samādhi gate mentioned below.

Regarding the five types of cessation: first, the cessation of illuminating the Dharma as pure and void, detached from conditions; second, the cessation of contemplating persons as tranquil and still, severing desire; third, the cessation of the spontaneous arising of nature as the natural law of phenomena; fourth, the cessation of the manifestation of radiant light through non-thought; and fifth, the cessation of the profound penetration of phenomena and principle beyond all signs.

Regarding the six contemplations: first, the contemplation of the true emptiness of all objects being subsumed within the mind; second, the contemplation of the wondrous existence of all objects manifesting from the mind; third, the contemplation of the secret, perfect fusion of mind and object; fourth, the contemplation of the reflection of the body of wisdom appearing amidst manifold conditions; fifth, the contemplation of many bodies entering into one like a mirror image; and sixth, the contemplation of the mutual manifestation of principal and attendant elements like a net of Indra.
The preceding *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are both gateways to the boundless samādhi of quiescence and function; therefore, these ten gates do not fail to encompass them all.
A detailed explanation of the single essence and the six contemplations, etc., is fully set forth as analyzed in the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source).
Regarding the commentary on the phrase "The Meaning of the Ocean-Seal" (*sāgarāmudrā*), the text is divided into four sections:
first, the presentation of the heading; second, a general explanation; third, a detailed demonstration of the categories of meaning; and fourth, a concluding summary and analysis.
The first point can be understood.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "As it says in the sutra below:
'Like the images of the fourfold army in clear water,'" this is the second section, which provides a general explanation.
He then cites this sutra as well as other sutras to demonstrate the characteristics of the "Ocean-Seal" (Sāgaramudrā) that manifests and that which is manifested.

Regarding the statement, "There is nothing that does not appear within the water," it further says therein: "Each is distinct and without intermingling; swords, halberds, bows, and arrows are of many kinds, and armor, helmets, chariots, and carriages are of various sorts. According to the differences in their respective forms, there is nothing that does not appear within the water; yet the water itself is fundamentally without discrimination, and the samādhi of the Bodhisattva is likewise."
This refers to the fifteenth sutra.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, it says that the ocean possesses wonders,” etc., this same fascicle later states: “For those who possess inexhaustible meditative concentration and liberation, the seal of equality is likewise; regarding all sublime practices of merit and wisdom, they cultivate them universally without ever becoming weary.”
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, fascicle 14, says...,” this cites the text of another sūtra.
The commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the actual citation; second, the explanation.
The preceding section corresponds to the beginning of the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha," where a good man says:
"It is also thus here. The sutra states, "It is likewise so," and all other parts are entirely identical.
The commentary states: "However, as for this scriptural passage," and so forth, which provides the explanation.
This refers to the aforementioned *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "manifesting images of the four continents" and so on, the text says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."

For example, just as the great ocean can universally reflect the physical forms and images of all sentient beings within the four continents, it is for this reason that it is collectively called the "great ocean."

The enlightenment of all Buddhas is likewise: it universally manifests according to the mental activities, faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of all sentient beings, yet nothing is manifested; therefore, it is called the enlightenment of all Buddhas.
The following verse states: "Just as the ocean seal manifests the minds of sentient beings, it is for this reason called the great ocean.
Bodhi universally seals all mental activities; therefore, it is called Perfect Enlightenment."
The commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'the ten meanings,' this is the third section, which specifically elucidates the categories of meaning.

As for the commentary’s citation, 'The Sūtra says: because it pervades the ten directions,' this refers to the present sūtra, wherein [the Buddha] pervades the ten directions in a single moment of thought."
Regarding the statement, "Universally encompassing all without rejection," this refers back to what was cited above.

The ten meanings cited are all from the sūtras quoted within the general introduction above, as well as the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna-parivarta); their texts are numerous and easy to understand.

However, as for the tenth [verse] stating, "Because it does not depend on a counterpart, it is eternally manifest," this uses the tenth to explain and establish the ninth, thereby serving to distinguish it from others.
Because ten [categories] establish nine, it is said that they "explain and establish" [the meaning].
However, since the nine are discussed vertically while the ten are explained horizontally, they serve as a distinction.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "Possessing the above ten meanings" constitutes the fourth part: the summary conclusion.
Within this, first is the formal conclusion;
subsequently, from "Question:
The Three Grades of Worthiness of the Benevolent Kings" onwards, there is a dialogue of inquiry and selection, with the question first and the answer following.
Question: This refers to the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Teaching and Transformation" in the preceding scroll.

The Sūtra states: "If a bodhisattva dwells within the lands of a hundred buddhas, acts as a king of Jambudvīpa, rules over the four continents, cultivates the hundred dharma-gates of illumination and the mind of equality regarding the two truths, and transforms all sentient beings."

The following verse says: "The Bodhisattva of Good Awakening, throughout the four continents, simultaneously illuminates the equal path of the two truths; through skillful means he transforms sentient beings as he travels among a hundred lands, and thus first ascends the signless path of the One Vehicle."
The commentary states:
There is no further textual passage regarding the attainment of Buddhahood prior to this.
Regarding the section in the sub-commentary beginning with "The answer is that which was cited above from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*," this constitutes the second response, which contains three parts:
First, citing the previous response; second, citing specific texts in response; third, illustrating through analogy the perfect interfusion.
Regarding the first:

since the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* cited above states that "consecration" corresponds to the tenth stage (*vihāra*), it says, "it speaks of the end of the stages. Thus, the first stage of the Noble Ones (*bhadra*) has already attained the eight aspects of manifestation; how then can one selectively cite the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (or *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*) while ignoring its lack of textual evidence regarding the three stages of the Noble Ones?
The commentary states: "Regarding the passage 'If one refers to the *Sūtra of the Divination of the Grounds of Practice*,' etc., it next cites a separate text to provide the answer.
This means that according to the *Sūtra of the Divination of the Grounds of Practice*, there are four ways of becoming a Buddha;
the first is the fulfillment of faith, which corresponds precisely to the present text, while the remaining three are mentioned incidentally."
Second, fulfillment through practice (*pratipatti-paripūri*) is identical to the empowerment and conferral of rank described previously in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.

Third, fulfillment through realization (*adhigama-paripūri*): the initial realization is termed "fulfillment through realization," hence it is called the "Stage of the Pure Mind" (*śuddhacittabhūmi*), which refers to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
The fourth is the ultimate stage of the Bodhisattva, which follows after the tenth stage.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted, the awakening-mind first arises; yet the mind has no initial characteristic, because it is far removed from subtle thoughts, and thus one perceives the nature of the mind."
"The mind is itself eternally abiding; this is called ultimate awakening.
This is [the scriptural passage]. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "The *Qixin* relies on this," the preceding section correctly cited the Sūtra, while this section now cites the Śāstra.
The accomplishment of the resolve through faith is precisely the first stage, the Stage of Fulfillment of Faith (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa-bhūmi*).
The Treatise states: "Because the Bodhisattva has generated this mind, he attains a partial vision of the Dharmakāya."

Because he has realized the Dharma-body, he is able to manifest eight modes of benefiting sentient beings according to his power of vows; namely: descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of the Dharma, and entering nirvana.
This refers to the passage concerning the eight aspects [of Buddhahood].

The commentary states: "Moreover, within the gate of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), one does not follow sequential stages. This is a threefold illustration of the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
Thus, what was cited above still pertains to the sequential teaching (*xingbu*), because the four stages of attaining Buddhahood differ in their depth and shallowness.
Now, the former inherently contains the latter; therefore, this is "perfectly interfused" (*yuanrong*).
Here, we speak in terms of the fulfillment of faith, which is still presented according to the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*).
Below the phrase "the non-obstruction of cause and effect" in the Commentary, there is a general response to anticipated objections.
This refers to an objection which states:
"If the beginning were identical to the end, it would subvert the relationship between cause and effect.
Therefore, this explanation is provided to clarify that there is no such impediment.

When the cause exists, the fruit is already present; the cause is within the fruit. Depending on the perspective from which one approaches them, they are designated as "cause" or "fruit," yet because their substance lacks temporal sequence, they attain perfect interfusion.
If both [cause and effect] are preserved, it is both cause and effect; if both are extinguished, the ocean of fruition transcends all words.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, this manifested transformation does not rely on a single stage or a single type of realm,” this serves as a further clarification of the preceding text. By stating that perfect interfusion is not restricted to a single stage, it reveals that it possesses all stages of attainment; by stating that it does not rely on a single type of realm, it reveals its pervasiveness across time and space.

The second is the Flower Adornment Samādhi (*Huayan Sanmei*). Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The myriad practices are like flowers adorning the Dharma-body; the rest is as explained elsewhere,” the *Yiwang ji* (Collection on Forgetting) states that there are briefly ten contemplations:

first, the contemplation of subsuming appearances into the ultimate truth; second, the contemplation of realizing the truth through the exhaustion of appearances; third, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between appearance and reality; fourth, the contemplation of subsuming the arising of beings according to appearances; fifth, the contemplation of the mutual inclusion of dependent origination; sixth, the contemplation of subtle containment; seventh, the contemplation of the identity of the one and the many; eighth, the contemplation of the infinite layers of Indra’s net; ninth, the contemplation of the perfect fusion of the principal and its attendants; and tenth, the contemplation of the equality of the ocean of fruition.
However, these ten contemplations integrate the four dharma realms: the first two are the realm of principle (*li-fajie*), which remains undifferentiated from beginning to end;
the third is the realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*shi-li wuai fajie*);
and the fourth is the realm that accords with phenomena (*suishi fajie*).

The next five [aspects] constitute the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*): the fifth is the gate of the mutual inclusion yet distinctness of the one and the many;
the sixth is the gate of the subtle mutual inclusion and orderly establishment;
the seventh is the gate of the sovereign interpenetration of all phenomena.
The eighth is the gate of the realm of Indra’s net;
the ninth is the gate of the perfect fusion of the principal and its attendants, endowed with all virtues;
and the tenth contemplation is the ocean of fruition, which transcends words.
When these are taken as the ultimate of the preceding four, then the four dharma realms and the ten profound gateways are all categorized according to the causal stage (*hetu-bhāga*).

Nevertheless, these ten contemplations briefly encompass all categories of phenomena; since they do not differ from the profound [ultimate] state, they are indicated as being contained within the remainder.
Furthermore, having extensively elucidated the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* within the explanation of its title, the *Huanyuan guan* (Contemplation for Returning to the Source) further explains:
"By extensively cultivating the myriad practices, one accords with reality to accomplish virtue; by universally pervading the Dharma-realm, one realizes Bodhi."
"Just as a flower possesses the function of bearing fruit, so too does practice have the power to evoke its result.
Now, by relying on this phenomenon to manifest the meaning, the flower is raised as a metaphor.

"Adornment" (yán) means that when practice is perfected and the fruit is realized, it accords with principle and corresponds to truth; both essence and appearance vanish, and subject and object are simultaneously severed. It is manifest, brilliant, and luminous; therefore, it is called "adornment."
Truly, without conduct that flows from the Real, one cannot accord with the Real; how could there be conduct that adorns the Real that does not arise from the Real?
Thus, the Real encompasses the extremities of the delusory, such that there is no practice that is not cultivated;

the delusory penetrates the source of the Real, such that there is no characteristic that is not quiescent. Therefore it is said that the sovereign, perfectly luminous, and unimpeded function of the Dharma-realm constitutes the Avataṃsaka Samādhi.
To provide a further general explanation: it is called *Huayan* (Flower Adornment) because all myriad practices collectively adorn the Dharma-realm and perfect the Dharmakāya.

These practices consist of both sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) and perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*). Correspondingly, the attainment of Buddhahood also involves the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), both in their collective and individual aspects. The distinct aspect is exemplified by the Elder Puyan, who adorned and perfected the ten bodies through the ten *pāramitās*. The aspect of interpenetration is illustrated by the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), where the ten perfections are cultivated perfectly within a single thought-moment; thus, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the ten bodies are unimpeded. Therefore, it is called *Huayan*.
The remainder is as indicated by the title.

Regarding the third [section], the *Indrājāla-samādhi*, the commentary states: "The subsequent half-verse cites one example to illustrate the rest; this also has two meanings. The first meaning corresponds to the first point previously discussed: since it was already explained that within a single atom there are many atoms, and that a single atom encompasses all lands (*kṣetra*), this now explains how the remaining atoms contained within that [first] atom likewise encompass all lands.

The subsequent mind confronts the preceding second mind; the objects exemplified here are not among the preceding objects, but are objects throughout the entire dharma-realm external to those preceding objects.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because in former times one offered worship with one's hands to the Buddhas and gave to others, [the merit] was said to pervade the dharma-realm,” this sets forth the cause.

Regarding the offerings to the Buddhas and gifts to others, they are measured by their practice; regarding the scope of the giving mind, it is said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm because it enters into profound contemplation.
The commentary states: "Therefore, the offering implements flowing from the Truth, etc., are inconceivable to all Buddhas," which reveals the present fruition.
The "true-flowing offering implements" manifest the mind at the time of offering as being commensurate with the Dharma-realm, because the offering implements emerge from the hands.
"Equal to the inconceivable [offerings] of all Buddhas" refers to the correspondence with the causal object.
Although the cause may be noble and superior, if the mind does not accord with the object, it is not true offering.
Because a cause that accords with reality brings about a fruit that accords with reality, one is able to offer to the realm of the True Buddha.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first half [of the verse] is the counteractive measure,” etc., the text concerning the counteractive measures is explicit.
As for “acting for the sake of the world according to what the mind delights in,” it means to bring joy by conforming to the mind.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction of conduct refers to those who are to be converted": because their mental dispositions differ and the wholesome states they produce vary, one should teach meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to those whose minds are tranquil, and explain wisdom (*prajñā*) to those whose minds are clear and sharp; all are brought to fulfillment through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). As for the phrasing, it is connected to the preceding section as belonging to the category of "conversion."
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) refers to the necessity of seeing the principle; only upon seeing the principle can one be said to have attained accomplishment.
Furthermore, the term "accomplishment" applies generally to the aforementioned three [Siddhāntas], for the first three Siddhāntas all serve the purpose of seeing the principle.

In the sixth section of the Commentary, regarding the "Samādhi of Gathering Beings through the Four Means of Integration," within the category of giving (*dāna*), the first two verses have a twofold explanation:
first, they are explained in terms of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*), as the royal throne required therein belongs entirely to external wealth.
The royal throne, as well as one's own body and life, also belong to internal wealth.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "Furthermore, regarding this stage of giving" constitutes the second layer, explaining the latter half-verse.
Giving away beloved objects is one of the three types of difficult practice.

Next, the giving of Dharma and fearlessness, together with the aforementioned three types of material gifts, constitute "all-encompassing giving" (*sarvadāna*); furthermore, the latter two are categorized as fulfilling the requests of others.

However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, each of the six perfections and the four means of integration has nine aspects. The verse states: "Essential nature, all [objects], difficulty, all gates, the virtuous person, all modes, fulfilling requests, happiness in both worlds, and purity."

The intrinsic nature is entirely one; all things are either two or three; difficult practices are entirely three; all gateways are entirely four; noble beings are entirely five; all aspects are entirely six; the fulfillment of aspirations are entirely seven or eight; happiness in both worlds is entirely nine; and purity is entirely ten.

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) correspond to the thirty-third fascicle; their specific characteristics will be explained further in the "Chapter on the Ten Practices" (*Daśabhūmikavarga*).
As for the current commentary’s statement that they are "difficult practices," there are three types of difficulty:

first, giving with few resources while possessing self-mastery; second, giving away objects to which one is deeply attached; and third, giving wealth obtained through extreme hardship. The present case refers to the second type of difficulty.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, from 'the latter two verses' up to 'granting immediately upon request' refers to giving in accordance with requests.

There are eight types of requests fulfilled: first, granting food and drink to those who beg while lacking food and drink; second, granting vehicles to those who beg while lacking vehicles; third, clothing; fourth, ornaments; fifth, articles of daily life; sixth, various ointments, perfumes, and garlands; seventh, dwellings; and eighth, light."
All [subsequent items] are like the first two phrases; the meaning can be understood by examining the text.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "all loving speech" (*sarva-priyavāda*) and so forth, the items listed below constitute the three types of loving speech:
first, consoling loving speech (*anuśāsanī-priyavāda*); second, joy-inspiring loving speech (*pramodana-priyavāda*); and third, supremely beneficial loving speech (*adhyātma-arthika-priyavāda*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The so-called ‘various Brahma-voices’ refers to the eight kinds of Brahma-voices,” the text fully enumerates the first two, while the commentary explains the latter six by merely citing their titles.
If one were to explain this, it should be said:
third, harmony, meaning that the great and small attain the middle;
fourth, gentleness, meaning the absence of coarseness or harshness.
Fifth, "without error" means his speech is free from mistakes.
Sixth, "not feminine" means his voice is powerful and resonant.
Seventh, "honoring wisdom" means his speech is devoid of agitation or fear.
Regarding the "eight profound [qualities]," the sound issues from the navel wheel.

As for the commentary’s statement, “The teaching of the Dharma according to the mind should be in the subsequent verse,” this is because the subsequent verse speaks of the eighty thousand dharma-gates as being words that accord with the teachings of the True Dharma; therefore, it should properly be said, “teaching according to the mind.”

Because the preceding verse mentions various *brahma-svaras*, this follows worldly conventions; thus, it is said that one should transform and guide others in accordance with what is appropriate for the world.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first verse [describes] all forms of *samānārthatā* (common purpose)”: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not list the specific characteristics of *samānārthatā* separately, but rather identifies it as being identical to *arthacaryā* (beneficial conduct). Therefore, since beneficial conduct is placed first, it demonstrates that sharing in both profit and loss constitutes "all," and by extension, includes praise and blame, fame and insignificance, and suffering and pleasure.

Regarding the phrase "enduring all sufferings for the sake of common purpose," there are three types of difficult practices that likewise possess no distinct characteristics; these are the three difficult practices of common purpose corresponding to the three types of beneficial conduct (*hitacaryā*). They are: first, the beneficial conduct practiced toward sentient beings who have not yet cultivated superior roots of virtue; second, the beneficial conduct practiced toward sentient beings who are currently attached to vast wealth, status, and the perfection of material requisites; and third, the beneficial conduct practiced toward those of external paths who hold heterodox views and engage in wrong conduct. The principle of common purpose (*samānārthatā*) is to be understood by analogy with these.
Now, regarding the three aforementioned common objectives (*samānārthatā*), one must endure suffering in all cases.
The commentary states: "First, the ten kinds of pure beneficial conduct" means that there are five based on external purity and five based on internal purity.

Regarding the five external types: first, beneficial conduct that is blameless; second, unchanging beneficial conduct; third, gradual; fourth, universal; and fifth, appropriate. The treatise explains their characteristics in detail.
Regarding the five types based on internal purity: first, bodhisattvas manifest a vast compassionate intention toward all sentient beings and carry out beneficial conduct;

second, bodhisattvas perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings such that, even while undergoing all manner of great suffering and toil, their minds feel no weariness and they give rise to deep joy as they carry out beneficial conduct for the sake of all beings;
third, though established in the most excellent and supreme station of wealth, they remain humble like children or servants, and free from pride, they carry out beneficial conduct.
Fourth, with a mind free from attachment and devoid of hypocrisy, they practice beneficial conduct out of genuine compassion;
fifth, they give rise to a mind of ultimate, irreversible compassion and practice beneficial conduct.
The Commentary states: “The next three phrases refer to the beneficial conduct of a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*).

There are five qualities of a virtuous person: first, encouraging sentient beings toward the ultimate truth; second, encouraging them at the appropriate time; third, encouraging them toward the practice of sublime and excellent meanings; fourth, encouraging them with gentleness; and fifth, encouraging them with a mind of loving-kindness.”
These five characteristics are all the dharmas of a Great Being; they exhort others with a compassionate heart, the latter being equal to the former.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The next two verses concern the practice of fulfilling the benefit sought,” the *Śāstra* says: “Briefly, there are eight [types of afflictions]: namely, when Bodhisattvas see sentient beings who, in situations requiring a sense of shame (*hrī*), are entangled by the fetters of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), they employ skillful means to resolve them and cause them to leave those fetters, just as one leaves the fetter of shamelessness.

Second is lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); third, lethargy (*styāna*); fourth, torpor (*middha*); fifth, restlessness (*auddhatya*); sixth, regret (*kaukṛtya*); seventh, envy (*īrṣyā*); and eighth, stinginess (*mātsarya*). All are explained in the same manner as the fetter of shamelessness.”
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the next two verses concern the beneficial conduct of all aspects,' that [text] explains them as either six or seven, totaling thirteen.

As for the six: first, properly gathering in those who should be gathered; second, properly disciplining those who should be disciplined; third, removing the resentment and affliction of those who hate and reject the Holy Teaching; fourth, causing those who dwell in the middle [neither hostile nor devoted] to enter the Holy Teaching; fifth, causing them to reach maturity within the Three Vehicles; and sixth, causing those already matured to attain liberation."

What are the seven types? They refer to the bodhisattvas establishing a portion of the sentient beings they seek to convert in the preservation and cultivation of the provisions for virtue. These are: first, relying on the departure via the Lesser Vehicle; second, relying on the departure via the Great Vehicle; third, regarding seclusion; fourth, regarding one-pointedness of mind; fifth, regarding the purification of hindrances; sixth, correctly establishing them in the two vehicles; and seventh, enabling them to be established in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The final verse refers to the beneficial conduct of all gates, meaning it causes those who lack faith to gain faith,” this consists briefly of four parts:

first, causing those without faith to gain faith; second, causing sentient beings who have violated the precepts to fulfill their ethical discipline; third, causing sentient beings with impaired wisdom to fulfill their wisdom; and fourth, causing sentient beings who are stingy to fulfill their generosity. In the present commentary, only one of these is briefly cited.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *Yogācārabhūmi* explains that beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) comes first,” the sequence of the two [beneficial conduct and concordant conduct] can be understood from this.
Regarding the reference to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 79, it says: “The *Vinaya* states:

‘At times the Blessed One, for the sake of the Four Heavenly Kings, taught the Four Noble Truths using the vernacular of a frontier country in South India; that is to say, he taught the Four Noble Truths using the Mleccha language of *i-ni-mi-ni-yu-bu-da-li-mo-li-chieh*.’”
This refers to "ma-śa-du-śa-saṃ-kṣepa-ma-saṃvarta-vilaya.
The treatise cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*’s teaching on the "perfect sound" (ekasvaranirghoṣa) as a challenge; the subsequent explanation contains seven points.
One says:
Some maintain this view.
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths using the noble language (*ārya-bhāṣā*), which enables all sentient beings who are to be converted to fully comprehend and understand them.
Why were such words spoken?
Answer:
To fulfill their wishes, for those devas desired to hear them.
The following citations are all taken according to their general meaning.
Second, furthermore, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate that he is fully capable of skillfully understanding all forms of speech and sound, addresses those who harbor doubts, such as:
"The Buddha cannot understand other languages," and so forth.
Third, furthermore, there are those to be transformed who receive transformation by relying on the Buddha’s unchanging form and speech;
and there are those to be transformed who receive transformation by relying on the Buddha’s transformed form and speech.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when the Buddha preaches the Four Noble Truths with a single voice, he cannot cause all sentient beings to be converted to understand them.

Although the World-Honored One possesses sovereign supernormal powers, he cannot transcend the limitations of the sensory domains; for example, he cannot cause the ear to see various forms and so forth.
Tong Yuan-yin said:
"There is no need to provide an explanation, for this is not the Tripiṭaka.
Many verses in praise of the Buddha exceed the facts; for instance, statements such as 'He is always in meditative concentration and never sleeps' all exceed the actual reality."
Furthermore, for a fifth reason, the Tathāgata’s vocal sounds pervade all realms of sound;
because he is able to produce whatever speech he desires, a verse says as follows:

Sixth, furthermore, because the Buddha’s speech is light, sharp, and swift in its transformation, it is said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand according to their own capacity."
Seventh, furthermore, although the vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are manifold, they are equally beneficial; therefore, it is said that he speaks with a single voice.
The commentary states:
Of the seven explanations above, the first three may be considered universal, while the latter four are shallow and mundane, as they are taught in the Tripitaka of the Śrāvaka-vehicle.
Regarding the term "Mleccha" in the Commentary: the Tripiṭaka Master says it means "the worst among the wicked," and also "the slave among slaves";
these are all literal translations of its meaning. *Dafangguang fo huayan jing su shu yan yi chao*, Scroll 35.
*Dafangguang fo huayan jing su shu yan yi chao*.
In the thirty-sixth section,
the *Commentary* composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty,

regarding the passage "Wisdom accords with the gateway of liberation" within the eighth [section], "The Samādhi of the Benefit of Light from the Hairs," it states that this generally sets forth the causes of the radiance, as it is endowed with both compassion and wisdom.

The preceding phrase above is explained in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), and it is also an explanation based on metaphorical representation (*vyañjana*); that is to say, the pores represent the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and the light represents wisdom.
Second, it explicitly clarifies wisdom; therefore, it says, "wisdom accords with the gates of liberation."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Compassion perfumes the actions of body, speech, and mind,” this is explained in terms of compassion and wisdom, because the Bodhisattva has cultivated these three types of action through the permeation of compassion over vast eons.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Subsequently possessing the fourfold total retention (dhāraṇī),” these are: first, retention of phenomena; second, retention of meaning; third, retention of mantras; and fourth, retention of the forbearance of non-arising, as explained in detail within the seventh stage.
"Since he possesses all four supports, why is he not sovereign?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Not because of failing to see him does one doubt that the Bodhisattva lacks radiance," and so forth: this section below provides a specific explanation of the meaning of severing doubt.
He severed three doubts:
first, because he did not see [the light], he doubted that there was any radiance;
second, because it did not rescue him from his acute suffering, he believed the light was of no benefit.
The scriptural passage uses the analogy of the blind not seeing the sun to simultaneously resolve two doubts.

Third, from the phrase "nor should one overestimate the function of the fruit" onwards, another doubt is dispelled: namely, that this activity is the activity of the Buddha-fruit and does not belong to the stage of the ten faiths.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Since it says that the lands and so forth are three thousandfold, the sequence is not destroyed,” this also serves to refute those who do not believe in the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the manifestation of enlightenment through the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-buddhotpāda*). It means that only at the tenth stage can [the bodhisattva] truly accomplish this; therefore, it is said that “the sequence is not destroyed.”
This refers to the bodhisattva of the tenth stage receiving his office, for whom there is a great lotus flower equal in size to ten million trichiliocosms;
whereas the "Ten Samādhis" chapter explains that for a bodhisattva of equal enlightenment, there is a single lotus flower whose extent encompasses the entire dharma-realm.
The Dharma-realm is solely vast; although there are hundreds of billions of worlds, it speaks only of "three thousand" [great thousandfold world systems], and thus it is inferior to the latter two.
Now, regarding the twelve verses in this commentary, which consist of six pairs—each pair containing ten meanings and five sub-pairs—the commentary text is divided into six parts:
first, the general introduction;
2. From "Desiring to distinguish the unimpeded" onwards, there is a general distinction between concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*);
3. From "Speaking of the five pairs" onwards, there is the explicit clarification of the unimpeded;
4. From "The aforementioned unimpeded" onwards, there is a general demonstration of the entryway.
5. From "Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the nature of form" onwards, it clarifies its inclusive subsumption;
6. From "This is the bodhisattva" onwards, it provides a concluding summary and exhortation to practice.
The first section is easily understood.
Regarding the second section, which provides a general exposition of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), there are three parts:
first, a general indication of the characteristics of concentration and wisdom as they appear in the present text;
second, from the passage beginning "Although concentration and wisdom are manifold," the demonstration of their various classifications.
Below the section beginning with "The reason why [one] has a restricted view," the text generally demonstrates gain and loss.
Within this second part, there are further two sections:
first, a general differentiation into two; second, the different applications of these two.
Now, first:

the commentary’s statement, “If one concentrates [the mind] in a single place, there is no task that cannot be accomplished,” is a passage from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching).
However, it may also be understood through principle, because its preceding and succeeding examples mostly concern practical matters.
This refers to the second of the Eight Great Persons' Awakenings in that same sutra, which clarifies diligence at its outset: "O Bhikṣus!
Having already been able to abide in the precepts, you should now restrain the five sense faculties and not allow them to become heedless."
It continues: "These five faculties have the mind as their master; therefore, you should well restrain the mind.
The mind is more fearsome than venomous snakes, wicked beasts, or vengeful thieves; even a great fire that leaps out of control is not enough to surpass it."
It is like a person holding a vessel of honey who, being restless and fickle in his movements, looks only at the honey and fails to see the deep pit.
It is like a mad elephant without a goad, or a monkey that has found a tree, leaping and bounding about so that it is difficult to restrain.
One must swiftly subdue it so that it does not become dissolute;
for if this mind is left to run wild, it will ruin one's wholesome deeds.
If it is restrained in a single place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should apply yourselves with diligent vigor to subdue your own minds.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "One who can contemplate the nature of the mind accords with principle and remains unmoving," the first phrase conveys the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The twenty-seventh chapter, "The Lion's Roar," states: "Because he establishes three grades of concentration.
The sutra says: "Good son!
All sentient beings possess three types of concentration, namely: superior, middling, and inferior."
The "superior" refers to the Buddha-nature; for this reason, it is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The "intermediate" refers to all sentient beings being fully endowed with the first dhyāna and so forth.
"The 'lower' refers to the determination of the mental factors within the ten universal ground-elements (*mahābhūmika*).
This is now merely cited for its doctrinal significance.
To remain unmoved in accordance with the principle is precisely what is meant by "doctrinal exposition" (*artha-vyākhyāna*).
To contemplate the nature of the mind is itself the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

As for why it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*): the nature of the mind is principle (*li*); contemplation is the realization of that principle. When one is in resonance with this principle, remaining profoundly still and unmoving, it is therefore termed concentration.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “clearly penetrating the contemplation of phenomena and their characteristics,” this refers to works such as the *Awakening of Faith*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “skillfully comprehending non-arising,” this refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*); as the Sūtra says, “To comprehend that phenomena are unarisen is called Prajñā.”

The Commentary states: “In various sutras and treatises, some speak only of the concentration of phenomena,” and so forth; this refers to the second point regarding the different applications of the two [methods]. The Commentary states:

“As in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, from ‘stopping all marks’ onwards,” and so forth; the Treatise says: “How does one practice the gates of stopping (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)?”
What is called "stopping" (śamatha) refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, as it accords with the meaning of śamatha-contemplation.

What is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to the discernment of the characteristics of arising and ceasing produced by causes and conditions, as it accords with the meaning of vipaśyanā-contemplation.
What is meant by "conformity"?
It is because these two meanings are cultivated gradually without being separated from one another, as they manifest simultaneously.
The subsequent treatise states: "Whether walking, standing, lying down, or rising, one should always practice both śamatha and vipaśyanā together."

That is to say, although one contemplates that all phenomena are by nature unarisen, one simultaneously contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed.
"Although one contemplates the karmic retribution of good and evil causes and conditions, one simultaneously contemplates that their nature is unattainable.
The commentary states:

Herein, first, cessation does not obstruct contemplation, and subsequently, contemplation does not obstruct cessation; cessation refers to entering into principle, while contemplation refers to observing phenomena.

In the first sutra, the text has already been extensively cited and its general meaning elucidated; thus, the relationship between the commentary (*śāstra*) and the sutra text can be understood by comparing them.

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "Alternatively, one may employ contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) in contrast to meditative concentration on phenomena (*shi-ding*)," the subsequent passage in the sutra, "With a single mind, unmoving, etc.," refers to the verse from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
However, the present sutra states: "To be unmoving on the Path is to cultivate dhyāna; to endure the non-arising [of phenomena] is named prajñā.
Thus, while the meaning is drawn from the same source, there are slight differences.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Meditative concentration holds the mind constantly upon a single object,” and so forth, this refers to the thirty-third sutra.

That text fully elucidates the ten perfections, stating: “Just as one practices giving through dedication, likewise one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts; with diligence over a long period, there is no retreat or cowardice; patience is gentle and the mind is unmoving. The same applies to meditative concentration below. Here, however, we take only the passage that clarifies concentration and wisdom.
In the commentary, from the passage "As for the statement 'five pairs,'" the third section correctly elucidates the unimpeded [wisdom].
Within this, there is first a detailed explanation and subsequently a summary.
Regarding the former, the five pairs constitute five distinct sections.
However, these five pairs are all based on the scriptural text, yet they select different passages.

The first pair selects the sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*), as in the first verse where the upper part is correlated with the eye faculty and the lower part with the form-object (*rūpa-dhātu*). Within this, there are three parts:
first, clarifying that the sense organ enters while the object emerges.
Second, from "In order to manifest" onwards, the reasons for why there is no obstruction are set forth; briefly, there are three meanings: first, because it is a manifestation of mind-only;

second, because of the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination; and third, because of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature. These are explained in detail in the *Xuan* (the Profound Commentary).
Because this is the first [case], the reasons are fully set forth; in the following instances, they are mostly summarized.
Third, regarding "the object enters and the faculty emerges, it is likewise," this is an analogical explanation of the subsequent verse.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase “the second pair,” this refers to establishing the meaning within the context of entering right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Within this section, there are four parts:
first, the formal explanation.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “discriminating the characteristics of phenomena” (*vastulakṣaṇavikalpa*) and so forth: since the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) emerges from the sense-object of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is clearly understood that its entry into the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is the fixed principle.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “desiring to contemplate the emptiness of nature” (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*) and so forth: since the arising of the object-condition from the eye and so forth is the arising of the principle, it is clearly understood that its entry into the sense-object of form is the entry into the phenomenon (*vastupraveśa*).
Second, from "Because [the seal] accords with the principle of the phenomenon" onwards, the reason is set forth.
This is explained solely by way of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*), and it consists of two parts:

first, establishing that one who has previously distinguished phenomena should enter the concentration on phenomena (*dharmasamādhi*) before entering the concentration on principle; second, from "The phenomenon of the mind being constrained to accord with principle," establishing that one who wishes to contemplate the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) should enter the concentration on principle before entering the concentration on phenomena.

Third, the passage beginning with "However, in the sūtra it merely says... explains the reason why these two concentrations receive their names, demonstrating that the preceding text regarding entering right concentration is so designated because of its contemplative object.

Fourth, "Furthermore, one should also correlate the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) with the principle [of non-obstruction] to distinguish their unimpeded nature" is the conclusion of the analogy.

This consists of two verses, which state: "Entering right concentration within the eye-faculty, Arising from concentration regarding forms with an undisturbed mind, One realizes that forms are unborn and have no arising; Their nature is empty, quiescent, and without activity."

Entering right concentration within the realm of form, arising from samādhi within the faculty of the eye, he discerns the inconceivable nature of the eye—something that neither gods nor people of the world can know.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the third [pair], the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena,' etc., this refers to the meaning established by correlating the latter half of the sūtra with the passage on arising from meditative concentration."
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, the direct exposition; second, from "By means of that which is observed" onwards, the explanation of the reason; and third, from "It should also... onwards, the counter-example.
Regarding the first part, the commentary provides only the initial verse and does not provide the subsequent verse.
If one were to state it fully:
wishing to comprehend ultimate truth, one ought to begin from the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), yet instead one begins from the contemplation of phenomena (*shi-guan*).

This means that the preceding verse demonstrates that the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*) is a phenomenon; thus, when samādhi arises within the sensory object of form, its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of principle.

The subsequent verse states that the eye is without birth and without arising; this is the principle of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, the preceding meaning—that the arising of the eye-faculty does not disturb the concentrated mind—should be understood as the contemplation of the object.
The reason for this can be known [from the context].

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “One should also compare the objects and principles with the faculties, matters, and principles to demonstrate their non-obstruction,” this is the third counter-example.
The meaning of this is somewhat obscure; one should first pose the question:

“In the previous analysis of the two meditative absorptions, it was merely stated that one should likewise compare the faculties and matters with the objects and principles; why does the present passage speak of comparing both objects and principles with both faculties, matters, and principles?”
Therefore, one should answer:

these two concentrations cannot be distinguished from one another by themselves; it is only by means of the arising of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) that one comes to know their respective objects and principles.

For example, when one enters a concentration through the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*), one does not yet know which specific concentration it is; it is only upon seeing the objects that one understands the differentiation of forms (*rūpa-viśeṣa*) to be its "contemplation of phenomena" (*vastu-vipaśyanā*), because one desires to be without obstruction.

In the discourse on the faculties (*indriya*), entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) therein refers to the certainty of principle; since the object enters the faculty and the nature of the faculty is realized as empty, it is said that one enters the concentration on phenomena (*vastu-samādhi*) within the object.

Thus, the scriptural passage has already distinguished the principle of the faculty in relation to the phenomenon of the object; therefore, we simply apply this analogy by correlating the phenomenon of the faculty’s concentration with the principle of the object.

Now, these two contemplations do not depend on distinct meditative concentrations; rather, there are two contemplations each regarding both the faculties and the objects. That is to say, when entering concentration upon the faculties, one gives rise to the contemplation of principle regarding the objects and thereby discerns phenomena; when entering concentration upon form, one gives rise to the contemplation of phenomena regarding the faculties and thereby discerns principle.

The sūtra text already contains these two [types of discrimination]: first, the arising of discrimination regarding phenomena from an observation of principles upon an object; and second, the arising of discrimination regarding principles from an observation of phenomena upon the sense faculties.
If one were to compose a verse, it should say:

Entering right concentration within the eye-faculty, the contemplation of phenomena arises regarding the objects of form; it is taught that form is unborn and without arising, its nature being empty, quiescent, and unconditioned.

Entering right concentration within the sphere of visible forms, he gives rise to contemplation of principle within the eye-faculty; he discerns all supreme and wondrous eyes, such that neither gods nor people of the world can know them.

This means that when phenomena arise within the objective realm, one contemplates principle; and when principle arises within the sensory faculties, one contemplates phenomena. Therefore, it is said: "One should also distinguish non-obstruction by correlating the phenomena and principle of the objective realm with the phenomena and principle of the sensory faculties."

The Commentary states: "The fourth pair, 'unimpededness in entering and emerging,' refers to the sūtra’s description of entering right concentration in contrast to arising from that concentration, as well as the sense of arising from concentration without confusion regarding one's purpose."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the classification by numerical categories starting from the phrase "If one compares phenomena and principles.

Regarding the four permutations of phenomena and principles, only two are explicitly presented here, while the remaining two are implied: namely, third, principle entering and phenomena arising; and fourth, principle entering and principle arising.
Above, we have briefly discussed four propositions; however, when considering the single and the multiple in relation to one another, nine propositions should be formed.

By adding five further propositions to the preceding four—namely: the entry of phenomena into phenomena arising from phenomena and principle, the entry of principle into phenomena arising from phenomena and principle, the entry of both phenomena and principle into phenomena arising from phenomena, the entry of both phenomena and principle into principle arising from principle, and the entry of both phenomena and principle into both phenomena and principle arising from both phenomena and principle—we arrive at nine propositions in total.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, four permutations are established. This refers to the four permutations formed by the entry and emergence of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*); however, only one is mentioned here. If they were fully enumerated, they should be stated as follows:

(2) when the objective fact enters, the faculty-fact arises; (3) when the principle of the faculty enters, the principle of the object arises; and (4) when the principle of the object enters, the principle of the faculty arises.

If these are further interwoven, ten propositions are formed: (5) the sense organ, the object, the entrance, and the principle arise; (6) the object, the sense organ, the entrance, and the principle arise; (7) the sense organ, the principle, the entrance, and the object arise; (8) the object, the principle, the sense organ, and the entrance arise; (9) the sense organ, the object, the principle, the entrance, and the object arise; (10) the object, the sense organ, the principle, the entrance, and the object arise.
Because these matters and principles correspond to the fourfold scheme of matters and principles mentioned previously, it simply says "four.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The fifth pair: the non-obstruction between the essence and function of the two benefits," there are two layers of non-obstruction:
