The initial statement, "Because the effect does not exist within the cause, there is no arising within the inverted [sequence]," is the explanation of the correct meaning in accordance with the principle.
Next, from "If necessarily" onwards, there is an inverse explanation to exclude what is not [the case], because [the effect] does not pre-exist.
Since the parikalpita (imagined nature) is the cause, and the effect exists within the cause, the paratantra (dependent nature) exists within the parikalpita.
Regarding the phrase "Because there is no cause within the effect, one gives rise to non-perversion internally," this explains the correct principle in its proper order.
The passage beginning with "If one wishes to make [it] exist" provides a reverse explanation to exclude what is incorrect.
If the effect existed because of a cause, then there would be sentient beings and so forth, which would entail the presence of inversion;
since there are now non-inverted sentient beings, we know that the cause does not exist within the effect.

Regarding the statement in the third pair, "not destroying cause and effect, nor the grasper and the grasped, nor pervasive imagination": the cause is the grasper (parikalpaka), and the effect is the grasped (parikalpya).
The grasped is precisely the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
From the section beginning with "From the preceding," the text concludes by returning to the Middle Way.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The fourth [section] distinguishes [the nature] based on its own essence," this is because it does not speak of inversions and so forth in relation to sentient beings.
In all cases, one first explains in accordance with the [opponent's] position and subsequently refutes it through reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
For example, the statement that "consciousness arises only by depending on an object, and therefore it is not internal" is the initial explanation in accordance with the position;
the subsequent passage beginning with "If it were internal... constitutes the refutation through reductio.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "Since one knows thus" concludes the two benefits [of self and others].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "In reality, the foolish person deceives themselves," it is like a monkey grasping at the moon; does the moon have any intention to deceive the monkey?
That fools grasp at the empty as real is clearly self-deception.
When the Sūtra speaks of "deceiving the foolish," it means that the objects of the foolish—being realms they do not understand—seem to deceive them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “the fruit accomplished by the aforementioned compassion and wisdom”: to understand it in this way means that awakening to all things equally is the fruit of wisdom;
penetrating both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa constitutes the possession of both fruits.
Because he possesses great compassion, he penetrates the cycle of birth and death; because he possesses great wisdom, he penetrates nirvana.
Furthermore, saving oneself and others equally is the fruit of wisdom, while enabling others to attain liberation is the fruit of compassion.
Both [the benefit of self and the benefit of others] are simply the fruits of compassion and wisdom.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is also the precept of happiness in both worlds among the nine precepts,” the *Śāstra* says: “One should know that these precepts are briefly of nine kinds: (1) when Bodhisattvas correctly prohibit sentient beings from what ought to be prohibited; (2) when they correctly permit them in what ought to be permitted; (3) when they correctly accept those sentient beings who should be accepted; and (4) when they correctly discipline those who should be disciplined. Within these, the two karmas of body and speech of the Bodhisattva always proceed in purity; this is called the four kinds of pure precepts.”
Furthermore, there is the pure ethical discipline that accompanies the remaining perfections of generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; these constitute five types.
Taken together, they are called the nine types of pure ethical discipline.
"It enables both oneself and others to attain peace and happiness in both the present life and future lives.
The commentary states:
This now provides a general explanation of the fruits of compassion and wisdom.
The fruit of wisdom comprehends all practices, which are thus associated with *prajñā*; therefore, it is said that they are also [the same]. If one were to assign them individually:

causing others to attain liberation and freedom from defilement corresponds to the prohibitions and permissions; these are the two types of precepts—prohibitive and permissive—by which one may achieve freedom from defilement and liberation. Causing others to abide in peace corresponds to "gathering" (*saṃgraha*), and causing others to be disciplined has the same name; both cause others to obtain the happiness of the two worlds.
The five perfections assist the precepts and are contained within them, as they encompass the gathering of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*).
The third is the practice of non-opposition (*avirodha*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Being humble when honored brings radiance; being lowly, one cannot be surpassed,” this refers to the *Qian* hexagram in the *Zhouyi*: “Humbleness leads to success; the superior man attains ultimate good fortune.”
The Tuan says: "Qian (Humility) brings success. The Way of Heaven descends to provide succor and is thus luminous; the Way of Earth is humble and yet moves upward.
The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble; the Way of Earth transforms the full and flows toward the humble."
The spirits and deities harm those who are full and bless those who are humble; in human relations, people detest the full and cherish the humble.
Humility is honored and radiant; though it may seem lowly, it cannot be surpassed—this is the ultimate end of the gentleman.
The *Xiàng* says: "Mountains within the earth constitute Qian (Humility). The superior man, accordingly, commends the many and benefits the few, weighing things to distribute evenly.
The commentary states:
The texts cited above clearly manifest this principle together.
This is the image of *qian* (humility): the earth is above and the mountain is below. A mountain normally emerges from the earth; that it is now submerged beneath the earth is the image of *qian*.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "praising the many," *bao* means "to gather. To gather what is abundant and thereby augment what is meager is the meaning of augmenting humility; therefore, it constitutes impartial bestowal.
Regarding the King’s annotation: "When the amount is large, using modesty serves as praise; when the amount is small, using modesty serves as an enhancement.
According to what is bestowed upon things, one does not lose the sense of balance."
"Humility is the root of patience.

Regarding the commentary's phrase "like the depths of the ocean," this refers to the *Laozi*, "De Jing" chapter, which states: "The reason the rivers and seas are able to become the kings of the hundred valleys is that they are skilled at placing themselves below; it is because they place themselves below that they can become the kings of the hundred valleys."
Therefore, the sage who wishes to be above others does so by making himself below them through his words; he who wishes to precede others does so by placing himself behind them through his person.

Thus, though he occupies a position of superiority, people do not consider him burdensome; though he stands at the forefront, people do not feel harmed by him. Consequently, all under heaven delight in supporting him and never grow weary of it.
The commentary states:
"It is solely through humility that the world turns toward one, and the world’s virtues gravitate toward them.
Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "In no way is there such a thing as harming oneself by means of external objects," the Tiānguān (Heavenly Palace) edition says:
Self-harm generally arises from five conditions: namely, greed, hatred, wrong view, delusion, and an unwholesome mind.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "if one praises others with a sincere heart," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states: "Śāriputra praised Subhūti for being a person of good character who speaks the Dharma well; he neither praised himself nor disparaged himself, nor did he praise or disparage others."
If one praises oneself, this is not the mark of a great person; to be self-flattering without being praised by others is to be vain.
If one disparages oneself, such a person is a sycophant.
If one disparages others, such a person is a slanderer and a villain.
If one praises others [for worldly gain], such a person is a flatterer.
Because Subhūti has realized the dharma of non-arising, although Śāriputra praised him, he was not being sycophantic, for his praise accorded with reality.
Furthermore, because they have severed attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), their minds are neither haughty nor attached; rather, it only increases the causes for non-obstruction.
That is to say, because all phenomena lack any basis of reliance, there is no obstruction.
Furthermore, it is said that "grasping" (*upādāna*) is itself "attachment.

In the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, within the explanation of the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it states: "Afflictions and suffering are called 'grasping,' because they consist of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*)."
"Taking" (*upādāna*) has the meaning of attachment; thus, karma cannot be called "attachment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that "taking" increases attachment. Chapter 74 states: "The initial defilement is called 'taking,' while the arising of craving is called 'attachment.'"

The Commentary states: "All that has preceded constitutes pure patience. The Treatise says: "Briefly, there are ten kinds: first, when Bodhisattvas encounter harmful acts, injury, affliction, or transgressions committed by others, they never retaliate;
second, they do not harbor resentment in their minds;
third, they do not feel malice or enmity."

1. The mental disposition is constantly present in the continuum, desiring to bring benefit without distinction between earlier and later stages, and not abandoning others after having benefited them once; 2. Toward those who harbor enmity, one spontaneously gives rise to remorse and apology, never causing them weariness or resentment before accepting their apology;
3. Regarding intolerance, one achieves a superior and intense sense of shame and dread of blame; 4.
Relying upon forbearance, one achieves a superior and intense love and reverence toward the Great Master.
Eighth, because of not harming or vexing any sentient beings, one achieves intense compassion and affection for them;
ninth, because all forms of intolerance along with their associated factors have been abandoned;
tenth, because of being free from the desires of the desire realm.
"By means of these ten characteristics, one should know that the patience practiced by a bodhisattva is pure and stainless.
The commentary states:
These cannot be individually correlated [with specific passages], as their general meaning is the same as that of the sūtra.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, enduring enmity and harm,” etc., the meaning of the three types of patience was briefly presented in the first assembly; now it is explained again based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The *Tattvārthā* states: "Those who endure enmity and harm are all sentient beings. Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:

"When one is able to endure the enmity and harm inflicted by others while diligently practicing deeds that benefit sentient beings, through the power of this patience, one is born by transformation; even amidst suffering, one does not regress."

Regarding the phrase "endurance in accepting suffering," this is the cause for attaining Buddhahood; it refers to being able to endure all manner of painful conditions, such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, without ever regressing.

Regarding the term "patience through the thorough investigation of phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya-kṣānti*), it is the basis upon which the preceding two types of patience rely, for it is the capacity to endure the exceedingly profound and vast Dharma.
Vasubandhu states: "It is the ability to examine all phenomena with precise scrutiny."

Regarding the statement that "thorough investigation serves as the basis for the former two," Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "By the power of this patience, one establishes the two types of patience previously described.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty states: "By means of the patience of investigating phenomena (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*), a bodhisattva is able to enter into the true principle of all phenomena."
"This patience is precisely the basis for the two preceding types of patience, because it is able to eliminate the dualistic grasping at persons and phenomena.
The commentary states: "This is also the 'patience difficult to practice' among the nine types. There are three kinds of what is difficult to practice:

first, enduring the lack of benefit from weak and inferior sentient beings; second, enduring the lack of benefit from one's own servants and subordinates; and third, enduring the lack of benefit from those of lowly birth and status."

This is now the same as the third [category]. Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one speaks of these benefits, it constitutes the conduct of a noble person (*satpuruṣa*),” the treatise says: “The patience of a noble person has five aspects: namely, that a bodhisattva first perceives the various benefits of patience—specifically, that a person capable of endurance will have few enemies and little estrangement in future lives, will possess much joy and happiness, will have no regrets at the time of death, and after the dissolution of the body, will be reborn in a happy destination within the heavenly realms. Having perceived these benefits, [the noble person] (1) practices patience themselves; (2) encourages others to practice patience; (3) praises the merit of patience; and (4) feels consolation and rejoices when seeing a person who is able to practice patience. It should include a fifth aspect—regarding those who are currently impatient, one should cause them to repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma—but this is omitted in the treatise. Fearing it may be a textual omission, I have now included it here.”
The commentary states, "Explaining these benefits," which precisely refers to the third [section], praising the merit of patience (*kṣānti*).
"Losing one's own essential purpose" is the first [point].
If one cannot endure it oneself and thus cannot cause others to endure it, this constitutes the second [case].
Since one now rejoices in it oneself and can also cause others to rejoice, these correspond to the fourth and fifth [cases].
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the 'Verses on Refinement'" refers to the three types of refining the mind, which constitute one of the four obstacles to be eliminated.
As the sixth chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, explaining the entry into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), says: "By what means can one enter?"
"Because it is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness—namely, by means of the three types of mental refinement (*citta-parikarman*), one eliminates the obstacles in four areas.

Thus, when the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, explains the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), it states that although the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two-fold grasping have not yet been subdued or extinguished, and although there may be three kinds of regression while practicing the sublime conduct, one is nonetheless able to refine the mind through these three matters so as to remain courageous and non-regressive in what is realized and cultivated.

Upon hearing of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the first time, their minds may immediately become discouraged; however, by using others as examples to demonstrate that they too can realize great enlightenment, they refine their own minds so that they remain courageous and do not retreat.
The commentary states:
"The first bodhi is vast, extensive, deep, and distant; because of these qualities, one may regress, and thus others are cited to refine oneself.

'Vast' means boundless; 'extensive' means unsurpassed; 'deep' means unfathomable; and 'distant' means long in duration. It is for this reason that one regresses, and others are cited to provide refinement."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* verse states: "May all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions swiftly realize the fruit of the Sugata in every thought-moment.
Since they are great men, so too am I; I should not disparage myself or succumb to despondency."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Second, upon hearing that the perfections such as giving are extremely difficult to practice, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
By reflecting that one's own disposition is capable of practicing giving and the other perfections, one refines and polishes one's own mind so that it becomes courageous and does not retreat."
The commentary states:

This refers to the second [stage], where one is weary of the difficulty of practicing the ten thousand deeds (*daśapāramitā*) and, through self-examination, increases one's cultivation and refinement.
The verse says: "In the past, you traversed the evil realms for many eons; though your diligent toil was without benefit, you were still able to transcend them."
"Now, by practicing even a small amount of goodness, one attains Bodhi; therefore, one should not give rise to despondency regarding this great benefit.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Third, upon hearing that the Buddhas' perfect transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is extremely difficult to realize, the mind immediately becomes despondent."
"If one can induce others toward coarse goodness, how much more so for one's own sublime causes? One should refine and temper one’s own mind with courage and never retreat.
The commentary states:
This refers to the third turning of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is difficult to realize; it uses the coarse to illustrate the sublime, thereby refining [the mind].
The verse says: "Even all ordinary beings on the vast ground aspire to realize the fruit of Bodhi at some distant time.
You have already undergone diligent toil through many kalpas; you ought not to retreat or sink back into delusion."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By means of these three matters, one refines the mind, making it firm and ardent as one cultivates all supreme practices.

The commentary explains: These are now the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), which constitute this very stage; therefore, the sub-commentary cites them. Regarding the phrase "severing the obstacles of the four bases," Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahopanibandhana* mentions only four, stating: "First, because of being free from the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas..."
First, because one is freed from doubt regarding the Mahāyāna by being able to permanently sever doubts concerning divergent views;
second, because one is freed from the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the teachings of the listener and the taught, thereby severing the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*);
third, because one severs all mental engagement and conceptualization regarding that which is manifest, present, and established, thereby severing discrimination; fourth.
The commentary states:
It is precisely because these four constitute the four bases (*catur-āyatana*).
However, the three refinements (*pariśodhana*) collectively remedy the four obstacles, all of which proceed by means of the three wheels of patience (*kṣānti*).
Regarding "enduring the three wheels," these refer to the conceptual distinctions of self, other, and fault.

In the commentary, from the section "Second, the emptiness of all phenomena" onwards, there are ten points concerning causing others to achieve patience until all things are purified, as previously cited.
The present passage concerns only the general characteristics; this is the intention of that [text], and it does not provide specific correlations.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the *Vyūha-śāstra*, [it is said] ‘by means of three reflections and five contemplations,’” this refers to the second treatise.

Regarding the statement, "These three exist within the patience of equanimity and acceptance": the various sufferings and afflictions experienced by previous thoughts throughout beginningless kalpas are precisely one's own karma and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
"Causing others also to attain this Dharma" refers, by extension, to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Regarding the phrase "to be considered in contrast to the former":

the former state of non-duality within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is ungraspable; that which lacks reality is impermanent (*anitya*); whether it be suffering or pleasure, it is the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*); and extensively preaching to others and so forth constitutes the perception of grasping (*parigraha-saṃjñā*). Briefly stated, there is no fundamental kinship [between these], as they are subsumed within beginningless birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

The Commentary states: "Compassionately pitying those who have fallen into perversion, how could one harbor a heart of resentment? This accords with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says: "Rāhula wept bitterly after being beaten by non-Buddhists."
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied, "My own suffering is but brief; what can I do about his long-term suffering?
Thereupon, he felt compassion for those who were drowning in the depths of affliction.
As for what is called "perversion," it is likewise out of compassion for its cause, which arises solely from inversion.

For example, when the Bodhisattva Deva had his abdomen opened by a non-Buddhist, his disciples wished to pursue him in retaliation. The Bodhisattva extensively expounded the emptiness of dharmas and admonished his disciples, saying:
"It is because these people hold perverted and false views of 'self' and 'person' that they give rise to such evil."
"...not understanding that the nature of things is empty and lacks any true reality," and so forth.

The Commentary states: "This refers to the 'joy of two lifetimes' among the nine. The Treatise says: "There are nine types of patience regarding the joy of two lifetimes: namely, first, the bodhisattva abiding in non-negligence;
second, being fully capable of enduring all wholesome dharmas..."
Third, being able to endure all cold and heat;
fourth, [enduring] all hunger and thirst;
fifth, [enduring] the touch of mosquitoes and gadflies.
Sixth, [affliction] from wind and sun;
seventh, [affliction] from the touch of snakes and scorpions;
eighth, various kinds of exhaustion and distress arising from all manner of toil, whether physical or mental.

"Regarding sentient beings who have fallen into the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth within saṃsāra, one practices the conduct of patience by manifesting compassion toward them.
In each of the preceding seven [cases], there is the phrase "fully able to endure."

The Treatise states: "In this way, compliant patience (anulomikī kṣānti) attains happiness in two worlds. This also refers generally to having compassion for sentient beings, causing them to attain happiness in both worlds.
Fourth is the practice of being unbending and unyielding.
The commentary states: "'Liao' means to bend and to be weak," which refers to the meaning of the *Dàguò* hexagram in the *Zhouyī*.
The *Yì* says: "Dàguò: the ridgepole bends; it is advantageous to have a destination; success."
The Tuan says: "Great Excess (Dàguò) means that the great has exceeded its proper measure.
'The ridgepole sags' because the foundation and the summit are weak.
The commentary explains:
Dàguò (Great Excess) has Dui on top and Xùn below; as both the top and bottom are yin, it is said that "the root and the tip are weak.
In the text of the *Yī*, "weakness" is used to explain "flexibility.
The *Yìnyì* states: "'Flexibility' means curvature."
"Bending" (*qu*) and "weakness" (*ruo*) have similar meanings. Now, if one takes the meaning of weakness to explain "not being bent or yielding," then that which is bent is also curved.
Since it is said to be "firm and strong," there can be no bending or weakness.

However, the Sanskrit term is *paryanta*, which here means "inexhaustible" (*wu jin*); this is the title used in the Jin dynasty scriptures, signifying that the power of the great vows is indeed inexhaustible.

This is also largely the same. Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This has three meanings: first, because it is great,” and so forth, this takes the ten phrases from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* to explain one another: the second, third, and fourth phrases explain the first phrase; the fifth, sixth, and seventh explain the second character, "Great" (大); and the eighth, ninth, and tenth explain the third character, "Supreme" (勝). The text is clear throughout.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That is ‘difficult practice’,” it is easy to understand from the text.
However, in all cases, this is because the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) have been eliminated.
As for the three spheres of diligence, they consist of the conceptual distinctions regarding the high and low status of sentient beings and their activities.
The Commentary states: "Fully containing three kinds of diligence. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains three types:
first, armor-like diligence; second, diligence in gathering wholesome qualities; and third, diligence in benefiting and bringing happiness to others.
Wu-xing’s commentary states: "First, donning the armor; second, application; third, being without cowardice, without regression, and without complacency.
The first refers to the initial moment when one exerts oneself, saying, 'I shall perform such-and-such a task'; this is precisely the interpretation of what is taught in the sūtras."
First is the phrase regarding "possessing power," followed by the phrase regarding "exertion in application.

"Being without cowardice" and so forth means that one performs virtuous deeds according to the circumstances and one's intention, not relinquishing them even until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
To have no mental despondency despite one's own weariness and suffering is called "absence of cowardice.
To remain unmoved by the afflictions of others is called "absence of regression.
To cultivate wholesome qualities with constant diligence and without indolence from now until enlightenment is called "absence of complacency."
"These three phrases explain what is taught in the sūtra: 'being courageous and not abandoning any wholesome dharmas.
Vasubandhu’s commentary on the three types of diligence is largely the same.
In his commentary on the five phrases of the sūtra, Asvabhāva further states: "Why is this so?

There may be those who initially seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; although they possess the capacity [for it], at the time of application they are unable to exert themselves. Therefore, it is said that they possess 'diligent application'."
Although one may possess diligence, it might still be timid or weak; to counteract this, "courage" is taught, and through courage, the mind does not succumb to retreat or discouragement.

Although the mind may lack cowardice, it might still regress when encountering the suffering of birth and death; because one would thereby lose the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood, "non-regression" is established as its antidote.
"One who does not regress" means being firm and fierce; therefore, one does not regress.
Xuanzang explains that "firm and fierce" means: because of being firm, one does not regress when encountering suffering; because of being fierce, one does not fear suffering.

Although one may encounter manifold sufferings and yet not regress, if one becomes complacent upon attaining a small amount of goodness, one will consequently fail to realize unsurpassed enlightenment; therefore, it is next stated that "one who is not complacent" is one who does not become complacent upon attaining a small amount of goodness.
This meaning demonstrates not abandoning the yoke of virtue.
For this reason, three types of diligence are taught.
Now, as for "donning armor," it is a designation established by way of analogy; just as a person entering battle must first don armor to defend against bows and arrows.
"Now, in seeking Bodhi, one must first make a vow to prevent regression or discouragement.
The *Benye jing* states directly: "First, give rise to the mind of the great vow; second, advance through skillful means; third, diligently transform sentient beings."

The Commentary states: "Now, the initial section is entirely identical to the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; however, that treatise takes 'donning the armor' as the first. This refers to what the forty-two-fascicle version of the treatise says: "First, donning the armor of the vow."

If I were to liberate even a single sentient being, I would remain in the hells for as long as a thousand great kalpas counted as a single day and night until I realized great enlightenment; even if this duration were multiplied a thousand koṭis of times, I would never harbor a mind of indolence, let alone endure such brief suffering or minor hardships.
"If there are those who, having conceived even a small degree of pure faith in this life, can nurture the immeasurable, courageous nature of great bodhicitta, how much more so those who achieve it?
Therefore, it is said: "Based on the self-vow of the previous mind."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “To possess profound merit constitutes difficult practice,” the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* identifies three types of difficult practice (*duṣkaravīrya*).

First, if bodhisattvas continuously remain free from all notions of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and their own bodies, and cultivate wholesome dharmas without interruption and without ever succumbing to indolence, this is called the first difficult practice.
If bodhisattvas exert such diligence throughout their entire lifespan, never flagging or desisting at any time, this is called the second type of difficult-to-practice diligence.

If bodhisattvas, possessing the merit of equal and thorough penetration, are neither lax nor hasty and are free from inversion, and thus achieve diligence that leads to meaningful benefit, this is called the third type of difficult-to-practice diligence.

Now, the text contains all three [aspects]: practicing without slackening throughout long kalpas, let alone for the duration of one's life, constitutes the second; not having a single thought of regret even at the moment of death and entering the Avīci Hell constitutes the first; and from "rejoicing in oneself" onwards constitutes the third.
The first [section] of the preliminary practices is "Initial Separation from Faults," which is also the first [of these].
The fifth is "Separation from Deluded Conduct.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "Generally termed 'Accomplishment,'" there are two parts to this explanation of the general phrase:
First, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of objections.
Regarding the former, this refers to the "meditation on intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-dhyāna*) among the nine gates of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The treatise states that regarding the "intrinsic nature of meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-svabhāva*), it is preceded by hearing and reflection; "all one-pointedness of mind" is the general definition.
First, the category of śamatha; second, the category of vipaśyanā; third, the path of their dual integration.
It should be understood that in the commentary, the text is cited and explained according to the convenience of the headings.

Regarding the phrase "skillfully understanding the world" and so forth, it is stated below: "By means of right mindfulness, one skillfully understands all worldly speech, is able to maintain the verbal expressions of supramundane dharmas, and even reaches a state where the mind is free from delusion and confusion."
The commentary itself correlates "freedom from delusion and confusion" with the state of union (*yuganaddha*).

Furthermore, because it skillfully explains that "discernment" (*vipaśyanā*) is the aspect of analytical understanding while "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) is the aspect of stability (*śamatha*), it constitutes their union.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the subsequent scripture says, 'Dhyāna-samādhi sustains the mind,' and so forth," which refers to the verses of the tenth dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Although there is *vipaśyanā*," this is the second resolution of an objection; it is evident from the text that this precisely presents the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of dhyāna according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The nine upper phrases are subsumed under the three dhyānas,” these three dhyānas refer to all the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
While the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* merely lists them without explaining their names, the *Yogācārabhūmi* provides an extensive explanation.

Now, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva, it says: "First is abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which means attaining dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), because one has abandoned pride, views, and craving, and has attained purity."
Second is the meditative absorption that brings forth [attainments], meaning it is able to bring forth sublime qualities such as the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Third is the meditative absorption that accomplishes what is to be done, meaning that, desiring to benefit all classes of sentient beings, it is able to pacify the sufferings of famine, pestilence, epidemics, and various fears.
In the Liang dynasty’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, the three concentrations are explained as follows: "There is the attainment of dwelling in peace in the present life. Why is this?
Because one is able to remain detached from all defiled phenomena."

First, for those who rely on this meditative concentration to produce benefit for themselves, it refers to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), by which one is able to bring about the accomplishment of the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Second, the concentration that produces the superknowledges brings about benefit for others; this benefit for others consists of the three wheels:

first, the wheel of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*), which refers to the power of transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), and the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); this wheel serves to lead those who follow wrong paths toward the right path so that they may return to correctness.

Second is the wheel of reading minds, which refers to the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, the supernormal power of the divine ear, and the supernormal power of the divine eye. This wheel serves to lead those who have not yet been converted back to the correct path, causing them to gain faith and acceptance if they have not yet done so.

Third is the wheel of the true teaching, which refers to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*). Through the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, one recognizes the faculties and dispositions of others; then, by means of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, one imparts the true teaching according to what one has personally attained, causing them to plant the seeds [of liberation], bring them to maturity, and achieve deliverance.
Because it possesses this meaning, it is said that there are definitively three grades for the purpose of abandoning deluded and distracted conduct.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Right mindfulness involves contemplation,” the sub-commentary consists of five parts:

first, the direct explanation in accordance with the text; second, from “Worldly speech is of no benefit” onwards, the exposition of the specific intent of the sutra; third, from “Transcendental [wisdom] does not understand” onwards, the establishment of reasoning to demonstrate its universal applicability; fourth, from “Therefore, although the text states” onwards, the conclusion establishing the universal meaning; and fifth, from “Understanding phenomena” onwards, the specific explanation of "skillful understanding."
In the commentary following the passage, "The second [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains the four ways of entering the womb," there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the phrase "without delusion or confusion"; second, the demonstration of the characteristics of delusion and confusion.
The preceding Chinese text clarifies this.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in the ninth chapter, poses a question: "It was previously stated that one enters the mother’s womb with a perverted mind; is it necessarily the case for all fetal gestations?"
The commentary states:

This reiterates the previous question concerning the inverted mind that inclines toward sensual objects, specifically regarding moisture-born and transformation-born beings being defiled by odors and locations.
The treatise answers: "It is not so."
The Sūtra states that there are four ways of entering the womb. What are these four?
The verse says:

"One is fully conscious upon entering [the womb], two are both conscious during the stay and the exit, and four are conscious throughout all stages; furthermore, those born from eggs are always without consciousness.

These first three types of entry into the womb refer to the Wheel-turning Kings and the two kinds of Buddhas, because their karma, wisdom, and both are respectively superior; the remaining four types of birth follow accordingly."
The commentary states:

One should simply consult the aforementioned *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as the verses are easy to understand; however, because both the karma and the wisdom are preeminent, they require a brief further explanation.
Regarding the first wheel-turning king, he possesses correct knowledge of entering [the womb] due to the excellence of his karma, having cultivated vast merit in previous lives.

The second, the pratyekabuddha, possesses correct knowledge of entering, abiding, and emerging because his wisdom alone is superior, due to his long-standing cultivation of extensive learning and superior analytical discernment.
The third, the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), possesses correct knowledge in all three respects because both his merit and wisdom are superior.
This refers to having cultivated superior merit and wisdom throughout vast eons.
Apart from these three [types of birth], there are the remaining ones:
womb-born, egg-born, and moisture-born.
"Because both merit and wisdom are deficient, all are deluded and confused.
Regarding the commentary's section "The characteristics of the delusion and confusion of ordinary beings," this constitutes the second part, which specifically demonstrates delusion and confusion.
First, its general characteristics are presented; subsequently, its source is indicated.
In the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, many passages are identical to those in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding the eighteenth [fascicle] of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the Southern Edition it is the sixteenth; the sūtra says: "Good son!..."
There are three grades of persons, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
When a person of inferior grade first enters the womb, they think:
"I am now in a latrine, a place where all impurities gather; I am amidst corpses, among many thorns, and in a place of great darkness."
Upon first emerging from the womb, he again thought:
"I have now emerged from a latrine, emerged from a place of manifold impurities, and even emerged from a place of great darkness."
A person of middling capacity thinks to himself:
"I shall now enter among the groves of trees, into the pure rivers, and into houses and dwellings."
The same occurs when emerging.
A person of superior capacity thinks to themselves:
"I am ascending a palace hall, dwelling amidst flowering groves, riding horses or elephants, and climbing high mountains."
The same is true when emerging.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first enters the womb, he knows he is entering; while dwelling there, he knows he is dwelling; and when emerging, he knows he is emerging. Throughout this process, he never gives rise to thoughts of greed or anger.
Yet they have not yet attained the stage of the first bhūmi;
for this reason, it is further called "inconceivable.
Twenty-ninth: in the Southern edition there are twenty-seven [sections], where the sūtra says, "There are two kinds of intermediate existence (antarābhava):"

There are two kinds of karmic results: those of wholesome karma and those of unwholesome karma. Because of wholesome karma, one obtains wholesome thoughts and reflections; because of unwholesome karma, one obtains unwholesome thoughts and reflections.

At the time when the parents are in union, following the conditions of their karma toward the place of rebirth, they feel attachment for the mother and aversion toward the father. When the father’s semen is emitted, they claim it as their own; seeing themselves [in this state], their minds are delighted and they give rise to joy.

"By means of these three kinds of causes and conditions for affliction, the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) perish and the subsequent five aggregates arise, just as when a seal is pressed into clay: the seal perishes and the impression is formed.
The commentary states:
This briefly cites the case of a male.
The ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the intermediate state being] possesses both male and female characteristics.

The commentary explains the "perverted mind" (*viparyāsa-citta*) directed toward the object of desire, saying: "This clarifies that the intermediate state being first gives rise to a perverted mind and rushes toward the object of desire. By the power of karma, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) produced therein, though remaining at a distance, is able to see the parents at the place of birth engaged in sexual union and thereby gives rise to a perverted mind."
If one is a male intermediate state being (*antarābhava*), one conceives desire for the mother and gives rise to a mind of lust.
If one is a female intermediate state being, one conceives desire for the father and gives rise to thoughts of lust.
Conversely, if one encounters both parents, one gives rise to a mind of aversion toward both.

Due to the arising of these two kinds of inverted thoughts, he imagines that his own body has united with the beloved; when the discharged impurity flows toward the womb, he considers it to be his own and gives rise to joy.
Once this mind has arisen, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases and one receives a body in the state of birth (*upapattibhava*).
The details are as explained extensively therein.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Regarding that fetal matrix (*garbha*), if it is to become a female, she dwells on the mother’s left side, leaning against the spine and facing the abdomen."
If it is to be a male, it dwells against the mother’s right flank, leaning toward her back.

Furthermore, as this embryo is produced by the power of karmic retribution, the "dividing wind" arises, causing the head to turn downward and the feet upward; enveloped by the fetal membrane, it moves toward the birth canal.
When it is about to emerge, the fetal membrane subsequently tears and divides between the two armpits.
The moment of passing through the birth canal is termed the "position of actual birth.
This may be understood accordingly.
The commentary states: "The 'distinct' refers to the four māras. These four are the celestial, the skandha, the affliction, and the death māras.
Regarding the statement, "The ten māras and their activities are as described in the *Lokottara-parivarta*," these refer to: first, the skandha-māra, because it gives rise to grasping and attachment;
second, the affliction-māra, because it is constantly defiling.
Third is the demon of the three karmas, because it can create obstacles;
fourth is the demon of the mind, because it gives rise to arrogance;
fifth is the demon of death, because it causes one to abandon the place of birth.
Sixth is the demon of arrogance, due to self-conceit and license;
seventh is the demon of wholesome roots, due to constant grasping and attachment;
eighth is the demon of samādhi, due to long-term indulgence in its flavor.
Ninth is the demon of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), because of giving rise to a mind of attachment;
tenth is the demon of the wisdom of the bodhi-dharmas, because of not wishing to relinquish them.
As for the ten demonic activities: first, forgetting the bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness is a demonic activity.

Second, giving with a malicious mind and maintaining precepts with a hateful mind; abandoning those of evil character and distancing oneself from the indolent; treating those with distracted minds with contempt and disparaging those of poor wisdom; and so on, up to the tenth: increasing self-conceit and lacking reverence, inflicting much harm upon sentient beings, not seeking the true Dharma or authentic wisdom, and having a mind so corrupt and evil that it is difficult to enlighten—these are the works of Māra.
The four māras are as commonly explained: namely, the celestial māra (devaputra-māra), the aggregate māra (skandha-māra), the affliction māra (kleśa-māra), and the death māra (mṛtyu-māra).
Therefore, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, although there are four māras, it speaks primarily of the celestial māra and the affliction māra.
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*": while other treatises contain extensive discussions on this, the present treatise is particularly clear and easy for people to consult;

therefore, I shall now provide a brief indication. Specifically, within the section on "Cultivating Faith," the treatise states: "There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness and are thus deluded and disturbed by various māras, non-Buddhists, ghosts, and spirits. These may manifest forms during their sitting practice to terrify them, or appear in the likeness of handsome men or beautiful women."
One should maintain the mindfulness that all is but mind; then objective realms will cease, and one will ultimately not be afflicted by them.

Sometimes they manifest in the form of devas or bodhisattvas, or even in the form of a Tathāgata complete with the primary and secondary marks. They may preach dhāraṇīs, or speak of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Or they may speak of equality, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of enmity and the absence of kinship, and the ultimate emptiness and quiescence of cause and effect as being true nirvāṇa. Alternatively, they may cause people to know the events of their past lives and to know future events, attain the knowledge of others' minds and unimpeded eloquence, and thereby cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit.

Furthermore, it causes people to frequently become angry and frequently become joyful, their nature lacking any constant standard; they may become excessively compassionate, or suffer from excessive sleep and illness; their minds may be indolent, yet suddenly give rise to diligence only to later abandon it; they develop a lack of faith, becoming full of doubt and overthinking; or they may forsake their original superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous, inferior karmas.

If one becomes attached to worldly affairs and is entangled by various distractions, one may still enable others to attain a semblance of various samādhis; however, these are all obtained by non-Buddhists and are not true samādhi.

Furthermore, it may cause a person to remain in a state of meditative concentration for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days; they will obtain naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink, their body and mind will be comfortable and joyful, free from hunger and thirst, causing others to feel attachment toward them.
Or it may cause a person to eat without moderation, such that their intake fluctuates between much and little, and their complexion changes.
For this reason, the practitioner should employ wise observation so that this mind does not fall into the net of error.
"One should diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging, so as to be able to remain far removed from these various karmic obstructions," and so forth.
The commentary states:
Although this passage is somewhat extensive, it is nonetheless of essential utility.
The inclusion therein of antidotes demonstrates that the Bodhisattva’s mind is free from delusion and distraction.

Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*’s statement, “The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* excludes the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*),” the treatise provides an analogy: “For example, a rope can grasp all objects, yet it alone cannot grasp a flame; for if it were to grasp a flame, it would be consumed by the fire.”

Māra is likewise able to take all phenomena as objects of his cognition, yet he alone cannot take the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as an object. If one enters into this true nature, Māra is then itself the true nature; what, then, could there be to delude?
Therefore, the treatise says: "The suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are a single suchness, not two suchnesses;
they are all the seal of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-mudrā). How could the seal of the Dharma-realm further destroy the seal of the Dharma-realm?"

Furthermore, section eighty-two states: "When Māra sees a bodhisattva who has realized prajñā, he is like a fisherman who sees a great fish enter deep, vast waters beyond the reach of hooks and nets; he then falls into despair and sorrow because [the bodhisattva] has escaped the net of the sixty-two views."
Furthermore, seventy-third: Māra may manifest as a great śramaṇa, possessing profound majesty and virtue, and at times say to the bodhisattva:
"The Prajñā and the three gates of liberation are the teachings of Māra."
However, this is emptiness; you have constantly practiced this emptiness, yet whether or not you attain realization within it, how can this constitute the Buddha-dharma?

The Buddha-dharma first requires the practice of giving, maintaining the precepts, and so forth, as well as the cultivation of the merit for the thirty-two marks; it is only when sitting at the site of enlightenment that one then employs emptiness.
"Whether a bodhisattva practices, has faith, or harbors doubt, they remain far removed from Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary states:
"In this world, Māras are exceedingly numerous."

Seventy-one: It further states, "Māra assumes the form of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and teaches the emptiness of Prajñā; although he speaks of the names of transgressions and merits, they lack any underlying principle, or he may say that emptiness is something to be grasped, which is itself Nirvāṇa."
The commentary states:

Regarding the previous seventy-three [points], Māra caused them not to cultivate emptiness but to practice ritualistic activities; here, however, it speaks of severing the emptiness of annihilation to lead them toward realization, and for this reason many people are confused.

If one realizes the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*), yet does not abandon emptiness to cultivate activities, nor claim that emptiness obstructs existence, nor take emptiness as a realization—then, by guiding all practices with the nature-emptiness of *prajñā*, one cultivates without anything to cultivate; thus, Māra cannot cause the Bodhisattva to become deluded or distracted.
The Commentary states: "Now, by means of wisdom one observes" indicates the reason why one is not subject to delusion and confusion.

"Like a person who awakens to a thief or a thieving dog" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Perversions" (in the Southern edition) or the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature" (the seventh chapter in the Northern edition), which says that when a person awakens to a thief, the thief can do nothing.
Furthermore, based on Kāśyapa’s inquiry regarding the four types of persons,
he raised this objection:
"World-Honored One!..."
"If even Māra and others can transform themselves into the body of a Buddha, how much more so could they not take on the form of an Arhat?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
If one conceives doubt regarding what I have taught, they should not even accept it, let alone such things as these.
Therefore, you should skillfully discern and understand them. Good son!
It is like a thieving dog that enters a person's house at night;
if the household servants or maidservants perceive it, they should immediately drive it away and scold it, saying:
"Get out quickly!"
"If you do not come out, I shall take your life.
Upon hearing this, the stolen dog immediately departed and did not return.
From now on, you all should likewise subdue Pāpīyān and speak these words:
“Pāpīyan! You should not assume such a form now.
If you do so intentionally, I shall bind you with the fivefold fetters.”
Upon hearing this, Māra will immediately depart,
just as that thieving dog never returns again.
Below, there is a detailed exposition of the characteristics of what the Buddha said and what Māra said.
This text merely serves to bring about awakening and awareness.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The profound meaning in its major part is that which is called emptiness,” this refers to the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* (Twelve Gates Treatise), with the sole modification being the replacement of the character “也” (ye) with the character “故” (gu).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “common and uncommon, etc.,” there are two meanings: the former meaning is further explained in the *Daśabhūmika*, while the latter meaning is clarified in the *Avataṃsaka* (Chapter on the Manifestation).
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, 'acting according to the intentions of others' and below" refers to the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It clarifies that the Buddha has three types of speech:
speech according to his own intention, speech according to the intentions of others, and speech according to the intentions of both himself and others.
The establishment of practice is likewise as previously cited.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "chánrán wūchā" (孱然無差), "chán" (孱) is synonymous with "xiàn" (現), meaning "manifest.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "jǔhuài liùgēn" (沮壞六根), etc., "jǔ" (沮) is also synonymous with "huài" (壞), meaning "to destroy."
Regarding the commentary’s mention of “the five kinds of evil winds” and so forth, this refers to the first chapter of the *Secret Essentials for Treating the Illnesses of Dhyāna*.

This sutra was translated by the śramaṇa Dharmamitra at the Jetavana Monastery in Yangzhou during the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; its title indicates it contains seventy-two methods for treating the mental illnesses of those in *āraṇya* retreats.
The Sūtra states that this was asked by the Venerable Śāriputra; it is excerpted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The following section concerning the matters of the araṇya is cited according to its general meaning.
It concerns certain bhikṣus of the Śākya clan who were practicing dhyāna when they were terrified and driven mad by the elephant games of King Vairūḍaka.
Ānanda ordered the door to be closed and informed Śāriputra; Śāriputra led him to question the Buddha. The Sūtra says:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will [speak] for the sake of the forest-dwelling bhikṣus of future ages who, due to five kinds of matters, will have their minds driven to madness:
first, because of confused sounds; second, because of ill repute; third, because of gain and offerings; fourth, because of external winds; and fifth, because of internal winds."
"How should these five kinds of illnesses be treated?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth, circled him seven times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
He addressed Śāriputra:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

If there is a practitioner who cultivates the twelve dhūtas in an araṇya and practices ānāpānasmṛti, then due to external harsh sounds contacting the internal sense-faculties and the four hundred and four channels, the mind becomes momentarily agitated because it is being treated with urgency. Because the force of the wind is strong, one first becomes insane; as the heart-channels shift and the five winds enter the throat, one first utters foul speech.”

"You all should instruct this practitioner to consume ghee, honey, and harītakī; then, fixing the mind on a single point, first imagine a mirror the color of crystal, and observe your own body within that mirror performing various acts of madness."
Having seen this, one should further contemplate and say:
"In a clear mirror, you see yourself performing acts of madness and folly.
There are extensive methods of treatment, which conclude with: "This is called the method for treating a mind that is chaotic and inverted."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Having already removed external sounds, one should remove internal sounds. As for internal sounds:

due to external sounds, the six sense organs are stirred, and the mental channels become inverted. Five kinds of evil winds enter these mental channels; because the winds move the mind, one may sing or dance, performing various transformations.
"You should instruct them to perform the 'mind-cleansing contemplation' (*citta-viśodhana-bhāvanā*).

As for this mind-cleansing contemplation: first, one contemplates one's own mind until it gradually becomes clear, like a fire-gem (*agnimaṇi*), while the four hundred and four channels become like *vaiḍūrya* and other precious stones. Thus he spoke extensively on the methods of treatment.
The present commentary now cites the text from the subsequent section.
However, that passage merely mentions the "five kinds of evil winds" and says no more below.
It appears, however, that based on the five preceding matters, these are treated as the five winds.
According to the *Saptatiśāstra*, there are five kinds of winds:
first, prāṇa; second, apāna; third, udāna; fourth, vyāna; and fifth, samāna.
These five kinds of winds all share the same function regarding the sense faculties.
As for the *pāna* wind, its pathways are the mouth and nose; its function is to grasp external objects, and its specific activity is that which thinks "I" and "I act."
The opponent asks:
By which faculty is this *pāna* produced?
The answer is:
These thirteen faculties share a single function, namely the eleven faculties together with the great *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").
It is like a bird in a cage: when the bird moves, the cage moves.
Therefore, these thirteen faculties perform the same function.
The *āpana* wind, upon seeing something fearsome, immediately contracts and avoids it;
if this wind is excessive, it causes a person to become timid and weak.
The *udāna* [wind] is that which thinks: "I wish to climb the mountain," "I am superior," "others are not my equal," and "I can do this."
If this wind is excessive, it causes one to become self-exalting, thinking "I am superior," "I am wealthy," and so forth; this is the matter of *udāna*.
As for the *prāṇa* wind, it pervades the entire body and also extends far beyond the body.
If this wind becomes excessive, it causes one to be separated from others and prevents the attainment of peace and happiness.
If it separates even slightly, it is as if one were dead; if the separation is complete, one passes away.
As for the vāmana wind, it resides in the heart and is able to sustain these functions.
If this wind is excessive, it causes one to be stingy and to seek wealth and companions.
These five types of wind-activities are all produced by the thirteen faculties.
The commentary states:
"These five must certainly be so.
Because they do not rely on their usual positions but enter through the channels of the mind, they give rise to madness.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "The above are all 'all-seed' dhyānas," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 43, states: "There are six kinds and seven kinds of 'all-seed' dhyānas, totaling thirteen."

Regarding the six types: first, wholesome meditative concentration; second, indeterminate transformative meditative concentration; third, śamatha meditative concentration; fourth, the category of vipaśyanā; fifth, correct and thorough reflection upon the benefit of oneself and others; and sixth, meditative concentration that can induce the qualities of supernatural powers and majestic efficacy.

Regarding the seven types: first, meditative absorption conditioned by names; second, meditative absorption conditioned by meanings; third, meditative absorption conditioned by the sign of tranquility; fourth, meditative absorption conditioned by the sign of exertion; fifth, meditative absorption conditioned by the sign of equanimity; sixth, meditative absorption for dwelling in happiness in the present life; and seventh, meditative absorption capable of benefiting others.
Now, regarding "name and meaning," these correspond to the first and second [factors] among the latter seven;
"stopping and contemplation" (śamatha-vipaśyanā) correspond respectively to the third and fourth [factors] among the sixth and seventh;
and "the two benefits" (svaparārtha) correspond to the fifth and sixth [factors] among the former six, as well as the fifth, sixth, and seventh [factors] among the latter seven.
Therefore, it encompasses the thirteen wholesome states, and there is also a commonality with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This is also the pure *dhyāna* among the nine,” the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 43, says:

“There are ten kinds: first, the pure *dhyāna* that is free from all attachment to worldly flavors; second, the supramundane purity that is without defilement; third, by means of preparatory application (*prayoga*); fourth, by means of the fundamental state (*maula*); fifth, by means of the superior progress of the fundamental state; sixth, mastery over entering and abiding; seventh, mastery over re-entering after having emerged from *dhyāna*; eighth, mastery over the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); ninth, being free from all views and tendencies; and tenth, the *dhyāna* that is tranquil regarding all afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*)."
All [of these] contain the phrase "pure meditative concentration" (*viśuddha-dhyāna*).
If one correlates this with the sūtras, it precisely refers to the ninth, tenth, first, and second [stages], because they are free from the obstacles of defilement (*mala-āvaraṇa*).
However, "purity of the great intention" arises from being free from the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
The three spheres are defined as: first, the objective sphere; second, the sphere of sentient beings; and third, the sphere of afflictions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Therefore, Śāriputra did not perceive the hand that struck him,” this accords with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says: “Śāriputra was sitting in meditation along the road when a powerful ghost named Kṣepaka (‘The Harmer’) struck him with his hand.”
Emerging from meditative concentration, he felt a slight headache.
He informed the Buddha, who said:
"It is thanks to your power of concentration that this ghost’s strength could have crushed Mount Sumeru into fine dust."
"From this day forward, do not sit upon the path. The commentary states:
"As for 'Kāśyapa did not hear the sound of Nirvāṇa,' on the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month, the Tathāgata uttered a voice, universally proclaiming to all:
'Today at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter the Nirvāṇa without remainder.'"
"If there are any who have doubts, you may now ask all of them; this shall be your final question.
By the Buddha's supernatural power, his voice pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, reaching every kind of being.

Kāśyapa, however, did not hear it; only upon emerging from samādhi did he perceive the transformations in the world. In his astonishment and inquiry, he then learned that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa.

Regarding these two matters, first, he was unable to perceive tactile sensations while in samādhi, and second, he was unable to hear sounds while in samādhi; thus, it is known that [his concentration] was inferior.
Now, the Bodhisattva possesses skillful knowledge [of both], and is therefore transcendent and superior.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Characteristics do not abide for even a single thought-moment,” and so forth: although the three characteristics or four characteristics are fully present within a single thought-moment, as already explained in the first fascicle, they are now clarified here by distinguishing between their nature (*xing*) and their characteristics (*xiang*).
If these characteristics are integrated into four, then grasping conditions gives rise to names, yet this arising is itself non-arising.
When emptiness and existence are unimpeded and the illusory characteristics are securely established, this is called abiding; yet this abiding is itself non-abiding.
The perfect fusion and mutual sublation of forms, transforming in accordance with conditions, is called "difference"; yet difference is itself non-difference.
When both characteristics are entirely exhausted and each lacks self-nature, it is called "extinction"; yet extinction is itself non-extinction.
This means that by taking the characteristics as they are, one realizes their true nature; therefore, nothing is apprehended.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “the great earth as a drum,” etc., the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* states: “Even if the great earth were made into a drum and Mount Sumeru were used as a drumstick, and it were struck right beside Subhūti’s ear, it could not give rise to even a subtle thought or cause his mind to be disturbed.”
"Why is this? Because he has entered the meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

Regarding the commentary's phrase "namely, the difficult-to-practice dhyāna": there are three types of "difficult-to-practice" according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as already cited in the "Exposition of the Dharma" (*Mingfa*). Here, I shall again extract their essential meaning.
That is to say: first, dwelling in profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one relinquishes it to benefit sentient beings by being born in the desire realm;
second, relying on meditative concentration, one gives rise to the immeasurable samādhis of the bodhisattva and the two vehicles;
third, relying on these, one swiftly realizes unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The current text corresponds precisely to the third [section].
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first phrase designates ‘all-gate dhyāna’,” the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
“Briefly, there are four kinds: first, dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra; second, dhyāna accompanied by joy; third, dhyāna accompanied by bliss; and fourth, dhyāna accompanied by equanimity.”
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding 'gate' (*dvāra*)," this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which asks:
"Why do you not simply speak of samādhi, but further speak of it as a 'gate'? The answer is:
Samādhis alone are infinite in number, like the boundlessness of space; how could a bodhisattva attain them all?"
"Therefore, it is called a 'gate.
When a bodhisattva enters one samādhi, they encompass immeasurable samādhis.
The passage beginning with 'like pulling a garment' shares this same meaning."
The Commentary states: "Not only does it not disturb the fundamental concentration, but it further increases it. This refers to the characteristics of increase explained below.

When a pig rubs its filthy body against a mountain of gold, not only does it fail to defile it, but it causes the mountain’s color to become even more brilliant and pure. This is how the pig, as an external object, enhances the purity of the mountain of concentration.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Abiding in pure mindfulness is the happiness of the present life,” and so forth: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are nine types of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) that bring happiness in both worlds.
First is the meditative absorption for taming sentient beings through the manifestation of supernormal powers;
second is the meditative absorption for taming sentient beings through the manifestation of telepathy.
Third, the meditative concentration that manifests the transformations of the three teachings to discipline sentient beings;
fourth, the meditative concentration that manifests the miserable realms for those who commit evil deeds;

fifth, the meditative concentration that can bestow eloquence upon those who have lost their power of expression; [sixth, the meditative concentration that manifests the splendors of the heavens for those who perform meritorious deeds].
Sixth, the meditative concentration that can bestow right mindfulness upon those who have lost it;

seventh, the meditative concentration that establishes and constructs non-erroneous treatises and subtle, exquisite praises of the *mātṛkā*, thereby enabling the True Dharma to abide long in the world;

eighth, the meditative concentration that, regarding the various worldly crafts and occupations, can bring about meaningful benefit for sentient beings by performing various tasks such as writing, calculation, measurement, arithmetic, sealing, and the making of beds and seats.

Ninth, for the sake of temporarily alleviating the manifold sufferings of sentient beings to be converted who are born in the miserable realms, one emits great radiance that touches them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This now merely provides a general summary of the meaning of happiness pertaining to both worlds.
The sixth is the practice of "Excellent Manifestation" (*sudarśana*).
The commentary states: "Its essence is *prajñā* (wisdom)," which likewise illuminates while forgetting the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
Regarding the three spheres of *prajñā*, they consist of the distinctions between object, wisdom, and sentient beings.
Within the section on the designation of the title, there are two parts:
first, a general revelation of the essence; second, the formal explanation of the name, beginning with the term "yoga.
Within this [second part], there are two further sections:
First, the names of the three types of wisdom are established through different citations; subsequently, their names are explained based upon them.
Within the former section, four explanations are briefly presented.
Regarding the three [explanations] from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, according to that treatise, they are listed in full as follows:
First, non-conceptual preparatory wisdom; second, non-conceptual fundamental wisdom; and third, non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom.
The treatise explains in detail: "Non-conceptual preparatory wisdom refers to the superior skillful means of knowledge prior to the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness)."
Non-conceptual fundamental wisdom refers to the cognitive wisdom that contemplates suchness (*tathatā*).
The three types of non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom refer to the various conventional cognitions that are able to initiate diverse kinds of activities.

Regarding the "three wisdoms" in the *Liang* commentary, the treatise explains: "From hearing the teaching of the signless Mahāyāna, one attains the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, thereby entering into the emptiness of conceptualized marks; these are collectively termed the non-conceptual preparatory prajñā."
If one enters the three natures of non-substantiality, non-conceptual wisdom is termed "non-conceptual prajñā.
After attaining this non-conceptual wisdom, one subsequently enters meditative observation; regarding that which has been realized, one either reflects upon it oneself or explains it to others.
This is called "non-conceptual subsequently attained prajñā.
Because it possesses these meanings, it is said that prajñā has three categories.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The *Mūlaprakṛti-karma-sūtra* [states] 'it illuminates the three truths,'" the Sūtra says: "First, the wisdom that illuminates the truth of existence; second, the wisdom that illuminates the truth of non-existence; third, the wisdom that illuminates the ultimate truth of the Middle Way."
Regarding the phrase "all clearly elucidate the meaning of the ten perfections," it is because the sutra lists all ten in full.
In the commentary, from the passage "The sutra contains the ten perfections" onwards, is the second section, which explains the names based upon them.
Regarding the statement, "Now, this is for the sake of conforming to the text," it is because [this treatise] largely accords with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The section beginning with "Although that [text] relies on the six [perfections]" serves as an explanation of an objection.
The objection states:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "If one relies on the six perfections, then prajñāpāramitā fully encompasses the three types of wisdom—namely, preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained.
If [the perfections] are ten in number, the sixth [prajñāpāramitā] encompasses only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)."
"Now, why are six cited to form ten?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
this is spoken in terms of the perfect practice (*paripūrṇa-caryā*), while also concurrently clarifying the primary meaning, as is the case in the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Activities)."
In the commentary, the section beginning with "The ancients also relied upon... first recounts the past views.
Second, the section beginning with "This attains the sequence... refutes those errors.
Third, the section beginning with "Now, based on... establishes the correct interpretation.
The preceding text was still brief; now I shall cite the three types of wisdom in full.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the characteristics of the three wisdoms as follows: "What is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing wisdom?
This is of two kinds:"
The first is mundane wisdom (*laukikī prajñā*), and the second is supramundane wisdom (*lokottarā prajñā*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds:

First is the wisdom that is able to realize and penetrate the reality of the knowable (*jñeya-tattva-anubodha-prativedha-prajñā*). This refers to the sublime wisdom of Bodhisattvas—whether they are about to awaken to the truth of reality (*tattva*), are currently awakening to it, or have already awakened to it regarding the naturelessness (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of ineffable phenomena—which is supremely tranquil, vividly manifest, free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), and devoid of all proliferation (*prapañca*). It realizes the equality of all phenomena, enters into the great universal characteristic (*mahāsāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), exhaustively reaches the limit of all that is knowable, remains far removed from the two extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), and accords with entry into the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). This is called the Bodhisattva’s wisdom that is able to enter and realize the reality of the knowable.
The commentary states:
Based on this, it is fully endowed with the three types of wisdom—preparatory (*prayoga*), fundamental (*maula*), and subsequent (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
It also possesses the essence of the three types of wisdom that illuminate existence, non-existence, and the Middle Way.
This is the first wisdom; since the wisdom of the three truths is already fully contained within the first section of the present sutra, it is identical to that.
Second, the explanation of the second wisdom above: having realized the truth and thoroughly understood the conventional, one extensively knows the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and so forth.

The treatise states: "If bodhisattvas are definitively skillful in expounding upon the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), their characteristics should be understood as previously described in the 'Chapter on the Lineage of Powers' (*balagotra-paṭala*), as well as their definitive skillfulness regarding the three categories (*trividha-rāśi*)."

That is to say, regarding the collection of dharmas that lead to what is beneficial, the collection of dharmas that lead to what is not beneficial, and the collection of dharmas that lead to neither the beneficial nor the non-beneficial, one knows them all as they truly are. By skillfully embracing the sublime wisdom present in these eight points, one is able to swiftly fulfill the vast and unsurpassed provisions for sublime knowledge and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The commentary states:
This refers to the subsequently attained [wisdom].

It consists of the extensive knowledge of the three categories of all phenomena—namely, those that lead to benefit and so forth—which include the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; when combined with the five sciences, these constitute eight.
The five sciences consist of the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement that the wisdom capable of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings is "of eleven kinds, as should be known from before," this refers to the *Paripāka-paṭala* (Chapter on Maturation) within the thirty-seven treatises.
The nature of maturation itself consists of eleven aspects: namely, first, the possession of the seeds of wholesome dharmas;
second, the repeated cultivation of various wholesome dharmas;
and third, the attainment of purity that is conducive to the abandonment of the two obstacles.
4. Possessing the capacity for the higher mind;
5. Being thoroughly disciplined;
6. The fulfillment of correct application.
Abiding therein,
whether one encounters a Great Teacher or does not encounter a Great Teacher, one possesses the sevenfold capability;
and one possesses great power as the eighth.
The ninth is the immediate realization of the abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
