4. From "The Bodhisattva, having already established firm faith" onwards, the text concludes by establishing fearlessness.
In the commentary, from "Because there is correct wisdom" onwards, it explains that [the Bodhisattva] always possesses the fundamental [wisdom].
This section has three parts:
first, a brief explanation following the text;
second, the citation of ancient interpretations beginning with "The *Śāntasiddhi* says..."; [and third, the refutation of those interpretations].
Below the section beginning with "This may perhaps be so," there is a reconciliation.
The phrase "may perhaps be so" provisionally accepts the previous interpretation;
subsequently, under the section beginning with "Now, by means of principle," examples are cited to reconcile this with the second treasury of precepts (*śīlapiṭaka*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “referring to the precepts of chickens, dogs, and so forth,” the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 24, states: “When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva upholds the prohibitive precepts, it is not for the sake of rebirth in heaven, nor out of fear; he does not even accept the precepts of dogs, chickens, oxen, or pheasants. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa, the third precept.”

Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that within the defiled lands there are many non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), including those who observe the cow-vow, the deer-vow, the dog-vow, the crow-vow, and the elephant-vow.
The commentary states:
These are all the evil prohibitions and precepts maintained by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
This false conceptualization arises generally from two causes:

First, it is because one perceives with the divine eye that there are sentient beings who are reborn in the heavens immediately after being born from chickens, dogs, and so forth; second, it is because this false conception arises through irrational reflection.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 114.
There were two non-Buddhist practitioners:
one was named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who observed the cow-vow (*go-vrata*).
The second was named Aṭṭilāśīrṣaka, who observed the dog-vow.
At different times, the two men went to where the Buddha was staying; after exchanging various kind words and greetings with one another, they sat down.
At that time, Pūraṇa had previously asked on behalf of another:
"Where will this Kheṭaka, who observes the dog-vow and has completed his cultivation of the path, be reborn?
The Blessed One replied:
"Cease, do not ask.
Although he requested again and yet again, the Buddha, with a mind of loving-kindness, addressed him, saying:
"Listen attentively."
"If one upholds the dog-precepts without any transgression, one shall be reborn among dogs;
if there are transgressions, one shall fall into hell.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, he wept with such grief and sobbing that he could not restrain himself.
The World-Honored One said:
"I previously told you, 'Stop; there is no need to ask,' yet now you have indeed harbored resentment."
Then Pūraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
it is not because this person is destined to be reborn in the realm of dogs that I weep in sorrow.”
"Yet I have observed the 'cow-vow' throughout the long night; I fear that in the future, too, it may turn out thus.
I pray only that the Great Compassionate One will explain this for me.
The World-Honored One replied:
"As with the aforementioned dog-precepts, these all arise from a failure to understand the true Path.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further asks:
"How can one maintain the pig-precepts, the ox-precepts, and the dog-precepts without deficiency or transgression?"
Answer: "In accordance with the way of an ox and in accordance with the way of a dog, it is called 'being without transgression.

Commentary: "Not like Nanda. The circumstances surrounding Nanda are very extensive and well-known to many; this specifically clarifies that his nature was characterized by great desire and that he was stained by attachment to Sundarī.
The Buddha used skillful means to lead her to the heavens, where she saw that the celestial maidens were more upright, beautiful, and exquisite than her own wife.
She saw that every male deity was accompanied by a female deity, yet in one particular place, she saw a female deity who was exceptionally beautiful and outstanding, but without a male deity.
She questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha instructed her to ask herself.
The woman replied,
"I have a husband, namely Nanda, the younger brother of the Buddha."
Nanda replied, "It is my very body.
The woman said:
"Nanda has joined the Sangha and donned the *kāṣāya*.
Upon hearing this, he immediately sought ordination and observed the precepts.
Because he originally maintained the prohibitions out of attachment to celestial maidens, Ānanda rebuked him:
"Just as rams, when about to charge each other, retreat instead of advancing, so it is with you who seek to uphold the precepts:
though the body is able to maintain the precepts, the mind is dragged away by desire."
"Since this karma is not pure, what use is there for these precepts?
His intention was:
"Just as a sheep is intended to move forward, you who wish to be born in the heavens to enjoy sensual desires are instead retreating."
"Because you maintain the precepts, your past karma is not purified," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary’s question, "Why does one maintain the precepts for the sake of *nirvāṇa*? this refers to the twenty-seventh [chapter], where Siṃhanāda asks:
"For what causes and conditions does one receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts?"
The Buddha said,
"It is because the mind does not regret.
[He asked,] "For what reason does it not regret?"
“For the sake of experiencing pleasure.
“For what purpose does one experience pleasure? “For the sake of detachment.”
"Why does one dwell in seclusion?
"For the sake of peace and security.
"Why is there peace and security?"
“For the sake of meditative concentration.
“For what purpose is meditative concentration?
“For the sake of knowing and seeing reality.”
"Why is it for the sake of knowing and seeing reality?
"It is for the sake of seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death.
"Why is it for the sake of seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death?"
“Is it for the sake of the mind being free from attachment?
“For what reason is it for the sake of the mind being free from attachment?
“It is for the sake of attaining liberation.”
“Why is it for the sake of attaining liberation?
“It is for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, great parinirvāṇa.
“Why is it for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, great parinirvāṇa?”
“In order to attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
“For what reason do you seek to attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
“In order to attain that which is neither born nor extinguished.”
"Why is it for the sake of attaining the unborn and the undying?
"It is for the sake of perceiving the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is naturally able to maintain the ultimate pure precepts.

The commentators maintain that [the teaching] culminates in *nirvāṇa* alone as the ultimate goal; therefore, they omit the final three [reliances], because those three are matters contained within *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the fifth point, "Not like Devadatta": the Buddha taught the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) in order to eliminate the four evil desires of the bhikṣus.
Devadatta added one more to make five, namely adding the abstention from butter, salt, fish, and meat for as long as life lasts.
Although the stated precepts were the same, his underlying intention was not virtuous.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, fascicle four, states: "Devadatta enticed the bhikṣus with five heterodox practices:

(1) begging for alms for as long as life lasts; (2) wearing rag-robes for as long as life lasts; (3) sitting in the open air for as long as life lasts; (4) not consuming butter or salt for as long as life lasts; and (5) not eating fish or meat for as long as life lasts."

The Commentary states: "Not contradicting *nirvāṇa*" means that it is not the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* which maintains [the precepts] through signlessness (*animitta*), but rather because they accord with quiescence (*śamatha*).

Regarding the commentary's statement, "First, one must maintain the precepts not out of a desire to vex sentient beings," this refers to cases such as when one wishes to subdue a dragon; having heard that an Arhat can dispatch a dragon by maintaining the precepts, one then proceeds to maintain them. This is precisely what is meant.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “such as the horse sacrifice,” etc.:
this refers to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) mentioned in the *Śata-śāstra*, who calculate that by sacrificing a horse to the gods, one will attain rebirth in the Brahma Heaven.
They thus inflict suffering upon the horse, claiming it to be a form of precept (*śīla*), and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “certainly existent” and “certainly non-existent”: contemporary scholars of the Vinaya mostly reckon [the precepts] as existent, while those of the Chan school speak of the precepts as being like space.
To be certain of their existence is to cling to permanence; to be certain of their non-existence is to cling to annihilation. These constitute wrong views mixed with the true precepts.

The Commentary states: “Observing that the nature of conditions is detached” means that one observes the characteristics of conditions without destroying or rigidly clinging to them; because the nature of the precepts is empty, delusion does not arise.
The Commentary further states: “As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
‘First, feigning eccentricity’” refers to those who, out of greed for gain and offerings, practice the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues.
They form this thought:
"If others perform such conduct, they shall obtain honor and sustenance; if I too perform such conduct, I may perhaps obtain it as well.
For the sake of gain and offerings, they alter their deportment.

Second, regarding "acting as one's own kin": because they desire gain and offerings, they go to the houses of donors and say to them, "You are no different from my parents, brothers, sisters, or relatives."
"If you have anything you require, I can provide it for you.
If there is anything that must be done, I can do it.
Whether you come from near or far to inquire after me, my staying here is solely for your sake."
Seeking gain and offerings, they become greedily attached to their patrons and are able to captivate people's hearts through skillful rhetoric.
Third, "agitation" refers to those who disregard the sin of greed yet desire to obtain material goods; manifesting signs of craving, they say to their patrons:
"These robes, alms bowls, and sitting mats are excellent; if I were to obtain them, I would be able to make proper use of them."
"If there were a person who could give as they please, such a person would be difficult to find.
Furthermore, someone said to the donor:
"The soup, rice, cakes, and meat in your home are fragrant and delicious; your clothing is also fine."
"If you constantly make offerings to me, I shall certainly give [this] to you as my own kinsman.
Fourth, "exalting and disparaging" refers to speaking to a donor out of greed for gain and support, saying:
"You are extremely stingy; you cannot even give to your parents, brothers, sisters, wife, children, or relatives—who else could possibly obtain your property?"
The donor, feeling ashamed and humbled, bowed his head and offered the gift.
He then went to other households and said to those people:
"You possess merit; your birth as a human being is not in vain."
"Arhats and others constantly enter your home, sitting and rising with you and conversing," he says,
wishing to make the donor believe for certain that "I am an Arhat. Fifth,
"seeking profit through profit" means that there are those who take up items for livelihood— such as robes, alms bowls, saṃghāṭī cloaks, and sitting mats— and show them to people, saying:
"This was brought by the king, the donors, and other nobles to give to me.
This causes the thought to arise in the minds of those donors:
"If even the king and the nobles make offerings to him, how much more should I not give?"
"Because one seeks further benefit based on this initial benefit, it is so named.
Third is the "Treasury of Shame" (*hrī-kośa*).

The commentary states: "Now, first, regarding the distinction between the characteristics of shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*)," which explains the heading while providing both the general and specific definitions for the two chapters on shame and dread.

Regarding the statement, "Nirvāṇa is called 'shame' (hrī) because one feels shame before the heavens," and so forth, this refers to the seventeenth fascicle of the Southern Canon, in which Jīvaka explains this to King Ajātaśatru.
The Sūtra says: "Great King!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly speak these words:
'There are two white dharmas that can save sentient beings: first, shame; second, remorse.'"
"Shame" (hrī) is when one does not commit an offense oneself; "embarrassment" (apatrāpya) is when one does not incite others to do so.
"Shame" is internal self-reproach; "embarrassment" is confessing one's faults to others.
"Shame" is being ashamed before the gods; "embarrassment" is being ashamed before other people.
This is called shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*).
Those who lack shame and modesty are not called human beings; they are called animals.
Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it corresponds to the sixth [chapter], where the treatise asks: “What is shame (*hrī*)?”
Its nature is to revere and honor the noble and virtuous based on the power of one’s own dharma;
its function is to counteract shamelessness and to bring rest to unwholesome conduct.

That is to say, by taking one’s own dharma as the object of veneration and supremacy, one honors the noble and virtuous and feels shame for faults and evils; thus it counteracts shamelessness and brings all unwholesome conduct to rest.
The commentary states:
Regarding the term "one's own nature" (*svadharma*), it refers to the predominance of respect toward oneself and the predominance of esteem toward the Dharma.
Due to these two powers, honoring the worthy and valuing the good constitutes the characteristic of *hrī* (moral shame).
The treatise states: "What is the nature of *hrī* (moral dread)?

Its nature is to feel a sense of light rejection toward violence and evil by relying on worldly power; its function is to counteract *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread) and to bring about the cessation of unwholesome conduct."

This means that based on the predominance of worldly censure and revulsion, one rejects and resists violence and evil, feels shame regarding transgressions and faults, and counteracts non-embarrassment (*anapatrāpya*) by ceasing all unwholesome actions.
The commentary explains:

"Based on the censure and disparagement of others in the world, as well as feeling shame for oneself regarding unwholesome dharmas and refraining from committing them, etc., is called 'based on the predominance of worldly censure and revulsion.'"
That which possesses evil is called "violent"; that which is the nature of defiled phenomena is called "evil.

Regarding these two types of phenomena, one who possesses evil does not associate with them; they reject evil phenomena, abandoning them and not dwelling in them. Through this superior counteractive measure, shamelessness ceases all evil karma.
The treatise further states: "To feel shame regarding faults and evils is the common characteristic of these two; therefore, the various holy teachings provisionally designate it as their essence.
The commentary explains:
This reconciles the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Mahāyāna) states that shame (*hrī*) has two aspects; these are its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

While these are provisionally posited as its essence based on their generality, in reality, veneration and rejection are its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "These two are the general characteristics."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *Abhidharmakośa* is the same,” it refers to a verse in the second section of that same commentary, the "Roots Chapter" (*Indriya-nirdeśa*), which says: "Lack of shame and lack of dread consist in not respecting [virtue] and seeing no fear in transgression."
The commentary states:
Not esteeming the virtuous and good is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame).
That is to say, toward all meritorious qualities and those who possess virtue, to have no respect, no veneration, no sense of restraint, and no sense of dependence is termed *āhrīkya*.
This refers to that which is abandoned through reverence.
The *Abhidharma* states: "Virtue consists of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
A person of virtue is one who possesses ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
"Without restraint" means being free from fear.
"Not following [the teacher]" means not performing the rites of a disciple.
"Seeing no dread in sin" means being released from shame.
The phenomena censured and loathed by those who are virtuous are called "offenses.
To fail to perceive that within these offenses there are results that can evoke fear is called "lack of shame" (anapatrāpya).
The inverse of the above is precisely the characteristic of *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (modesty), namely, the honoring of the virtuous and so forth;

thus, it is the same as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "If one speaks of shame," it explains the common characteristics of these two. First, it relies on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, as already cited above;
subsequently, it relies on the present sutra, because within each of the passages there is the phrase "not respecting one another."

The Commentary states: "To reflect upon this for oneself is precisely to feel internal shame. This is identical to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, while simultaneously incorporating the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*’s principle of relying on the power of one's own mind.
The fourth is the Treasury of Shame (*hrī-kośa*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because one does not perceive suffering or its origin, there is no knowledge or vision,” this means not knowing the fruit of suffering and not seeing the fault of its origin.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “relying on regard for the world,” this accords with the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That which arises from lust is impurity of the seed,” the commentary first explains five kinds of impurity:

(1) impurity of the seed, (2) impurity of the dwelling place, (3) impurity of self-nature, (4) impurity of specific characteristics, and (5) ultimate impurity. These are as explained in the twenty-first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, where their characteristics were already detailed in the “Chapter on the Holy Life” (*Brahmacarya-varga*).
However, regarding the impurity of intrinsic nature, there are thirty-six items which shall now be further explained.
As it is said in the twelfth chapter, "The Noble Practices," of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "From head to foot, within [the body] there are only:
first, hair; second, body hair; third, nails; fourth, teeth; fifth, impurities; sixth, filth..."
6. Excrement, 7. Skin, 8. Flesh, 9. Tendons, 10. Bones, 11. Spleen, 12.
Kidneys, 13. Heart, 14. Lungs, 15. Liver, 16. Gallbladder, 17.
Intestines, 18. Stomach, 19. Raw Digestive Organs, 20. Cooked Digestive Organs, 21. Feces.
11. Urine; 22. Nasal mucus; 23. Saliva; 24. Tears from the eyes;
25. Fat; 26. Grease; 27. Brain; 28. Meninges; 29. Bone; 30. Marrow; 31. Pus; 32. Blood.
33. The brain; 34. the bladder; 35. the various vessels; 36. [the heart].
When the Bodhisattva contemplates thus with single-minded attention, the commentary states:

Master Yuan did not distinguish that among these there were two bones, two brains, and the brain connected with its membrane; excluding two and omitting two, there were large and small intestines, one of which was also omitted; in other places there were membranes, totaling thirty-six.
To directly follow the scriptural text as it stands today:

furthermore, if one treats "filth" (*mala*) as one and "sweat" (*sveda*) as another, then the character for "impurity" (*durga*) would belong to sweat, and thus [the body] would still possess all thirty-six impurities.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, 'the defiled body is internally filthy and impure' refers to two kinds:
first, internal; second, external.
The Treatise asks: 'What is meant by internal filthiness and impurity?'"

That is to say, within the body there are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, filth, skin, flesh, bones, sinews, veins, heart, gallbladder, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, stomach (the raw receptacle), the matured receptacle (the large intestine), the abdomen, spleen, kidneys, pus, blood, hemorrhoids, fat, grease, muscle, marrow, brain, membranes, mucus, saliva, tears, sweat, feces, and urine; such categories as these are called "internal."
The commentary states:
These also consist of thirty-six items.

Regarding the "external," this refers to bluish discoloration, or putrefaction, or decomposition, or bloating, or being devoured, or turning crimson, or disintegration, or bones, or skeletons, or that which is produced by urine, or saliva, or nasal mucus, or smeared with blood, or smeared with pus, or in places of excrement and filth; such categories as these are called external impurities based on defilement.

2. Regarding "contact with suffering is impure," the *Śāstra* states: "This refers to that which arises conditioned by contact conducive to painful feeling, whether it pertains to the body or the mind, and constitutes an uneven sensation (*vedanā*)."
"Being thus comprised by sensation, it is called 'impurity of painful contact.

Third, regarding "inferior impurity," the *Śāstra* states: "It refers to the most inferior things and the most inferior realm, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); beyond this, there is nothing more inferior or more utterly vile."
The other realms may be understood accordingly.
This is called "inferior impurity.
Regarding "impurity by way of dependence," the treatise states: "For example, when there is an inferior pure thing, it appears as impure in dependence upon another superior pure thing."
Just as when compared to the superior and pure phenomena of the formless realm, the phenomena of the form realm appear impure;
so too, when compared to the nirvana that is the cessation of the *satkāya*, everything up to the peak of existence appears impure.
"Categories such as these are called impurity by way of dependence.
Regarding the fifth, the impurity of afflictions, the treatise states: "It refers to all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, afflictions, and entanglements belonging to the three realms."

Sixth, "defilement through disintegration" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); because they are impermanent, they can never be relied upon with confidence and are subject to transformation and decay. Therefore, both the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are termed "impure."
The commentary states:
Now, having briefly assigned [the categories] according to their predominance, it is sufficient to observe the cited scriptural passages themselves, for they will become naturally clear.
Fifth is the Śrutapiṭaka (Scripture Collection).

The Commentary states: "Because hearing is the foundation, one who practices accordingly will possess extensive knowledge. Thus, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
'In what regard should one train in and understand the unimpeded correspondence regarding all dharmas?'"
The commentary states:
This refers to the meaning of "knowing much.
In the Buddha’s response below, it is largely identical to this enumeration.
The Buddha said:

"All dharmas are wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and indeterminate dharmas; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; shared dharmas and unshared dharmas."
The commentary states:
These ten dharmas are merely shared; those that are unshared are omitted here because they belong exclusively to the *prajñāpāramitā* that is unshared.
That sūtra asks: "What are the shared dharmas?"

"The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless concentrations (*ārūpyasamādhi*)—dharmas such as these are called 'shared dharmas' (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "Because the birthplaces and places of meditative entry for both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) are shared, they are called 'shared dharmas.'"
The Sūtra says: "What are called the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)?
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities—these are called the unique qualities.

The Commentary explains: "The Bodhisattva discriminatively knows that these various dharmas are each without marks (animitta). Because these dharmas arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); because they lack intrinsic nature, their self-nature is empty (svabhāva-śūnya)."
The commentary states:
This is the Dharma of the Noble Ones, not shared with ordinary beings.
Just as the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and so forth, it is also not shared with those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The remainder is largely the same as this.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Based on the two gates of ‘arising’ and ‘inducing,’ they are opened into four layers of inquiry and explanation,” the sixth stage extensively reveals their characteristics, whereas the present text provides only a brief citation.
However, this section of the commentary consists of three parts:
first, a general exposition of arising and drawing forth;

second, from "Now, based on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*," onwards, an interpretation of the meaning of the scriptural passage through the lens of the three conditions for arising; [and third, the conclusion].
Third, the formal explanation of the scriptural text.
This section has two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the three conditions for dependent origination; second, the reconciliation and interpretation of the present passage.
First: However, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* asks, "What is dependent origination?
How many things are dependently originated?"
"For what purpose does one contemplate dependent origination?
This is the question; it means "by way of its characteristics" and "by way of analyzing its branches.
The commentary states:
That [dependent origination] possesses fifteen meanings, of which I shall now briefly employ one or two.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination: it is the characteristic of dependent origination because it arises through non-creative conditions, because it arises through impermanent conditions, and because it arises through efficacious conditions.
On account of these three reasons, the Blessed One said:

"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises," and so forth, as extensively set forth in the detailed exposition beginning with "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations."

Regarding the phrase "because this exists, that exists," it clarifies the meaning of dependent origination through ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya*) and so forth; this is explained in detail in the commentary (*śāstra*).

However, following the section on the differentiation of functional capacities, it further states: "Just as various formations (*saṃskāra*) arise by the power of ignorance, and so on, up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) arising by the power of birth (*jāti*)."
The Commentary states: "Now, regarding the passage 'In this present sutra... and so forth, this is the second section, which provides a detailed interpretation of the sutra text.
This section contains five parts;
the first is the formal elucidation of the two gates.

However, the principle that "this being, that exists" and so forth also encompasses functional efficacy (*śakti*), as it primarily reveals the two characteristics; therefore, the functional efficacy is pointed out as residing in the sixth stage.
Second, from the passage beginning with "Now, regarding the two gates," its implicit omissions are brought forth.

Regarding the phrase "mutually citing the preceding and following," this means that within the context of the "inducer" and the "induced," it clarifies dependent origination without action (*anabhisamskāra*), while within the context of the "produced" and the "producer," it clarifies impermanent dependent origination.
3. Regarding the passage "The first seven are permitted to share the same stage as the causal state" and below, this explains the reasons for the citation.
The term "permitted to share" (*sūn-t'ung*) is based on the meaning of the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*).

While the first two and the second five differ in terms of past and present, they are permitted to share the same period (*ekakāla*) when considered in terms of the two periods [of present and future].
However, because only five types are cited, it is not called "arising.
The fourth section, beginning with "Because of this, within the [factors] that can induce and those induced," explains the reason for the omissions and abbreviations found in this sutra.
Previously, within the context of that which induces and that which is induced, the meaning of "non-action" was manifested while "impermanence" was apprehended as its shadow;
within the context of that which produces and that which is produced, the meaning of "impermanence" was manifested while "non-action" was apprehended as its shadow.
5. Below "Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*... is the citation of evidence for the characteristics of projecting and drawing forth [birth].
In the commentary, from "However, the text contains both defiled and pure [elements]... onwards is the third section, the explanation of the text.
The text consists of three parts.
The first sentence is the heading.
Regarding those who possess the contemplation of defilement and purity, this is explained extensively in the sixth stage.
That is to say, "ignorance conditions volitional formations" and so forth; the former gives rise to the latter, and this cyclic flow of birth and death constitutes defilement.
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" and so forth; returning to the origin and source constitutes purity.
In the commentary, from "First, regarding that which can induce" onwards, there are two separate explanations, which constitute four sections.
The first section is self-evident.

In the commentary, from "Second, concerning that which is induced" onwards, regarding the defiled and pure states that are induced, following the previous pattern, it should likewise state: because consciousness exists, name-and-form exist.
The preceding text should also logically state that because ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are absent.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) pervades both the projecting [cause] and the projected [result],” this explains the above point.

While the aforementioned [passage] also encompasses the sense of both the projecting cause and the projected result, the correct interpretation specifically takes consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as the meaning of the "projected."

Now, to explain the preceding statement that [the link of] consciousness applies to both the projecting cause and the projected effect: if the link of consciousness applies to both the projector and the projected, while name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is exclusively the projected, then consciousness and name-and-form stand in the relationship of projector and projected.
Within this, first the scriptural text is explained by way of inversion, clarifying it in terms of the defiled contemplation.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness (vijñāna) pervades both the projecting [cause] and the projected [result]": if one takes the seeds of consciousness as the member of consciousness, then it is the projected; if one takes the seeds of volitional formations (saṃskāra) as the member of consciousness, then consciousness is the projector and volitional formations are the projector.

Therefore, two types of karma are now presented: the first type is that which projects [rebirth], because it takes the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of formations (*saṃskāra*) as the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*). In reality, these seeds of formations coexist with consciousness; thus, they are designated as the limb of consciousness.
This is precisely the intention of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

It correctly takes the seeds of karma as the "consciousness" link; since these seeds of consciousness are subsumed under the "name-and-form" link within dependent origination, the sutras refer to both the seeds of karma that project [the result] and the seeds of consciousness as "consciousness," encompassing both the projecting agent and the projected object.
The seed of consciousness is merely the support for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), but it is not itself name-and-form.
Now, according to the second intention, consciousness acts as the projector, which is why it is said that "it serves as a condition for name-and-form."
From the passage "namely, by means of consciousness entering the mother's womb" onwards, it simultaneously reveals the two results of manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).

From the words "but now," the meaning of the sūtra applies to both the subject and the object; thus, the *Sixth Stage* states, "planting the seeds of the mind within all formations (*saṃskāra*)," which encompasses both.
Regarding the statement on its two kinds of karma, this refers to the section on "The Self-Karma and Aided Karma" in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*).
As for those two types of karma, it is said that consciousness has two functions:
first, it causes the continuity of all states of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the generative cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Now, taking its momentum, we distinguish two types of karma by means of the "projecting" (ākṣepa) and the "projected" (ākṣipta).
In terms of maintaining the seeds of practice, it is the projector; in terms of its own essence, it is the projected.
The Commentary states: “Now, when it says ‘consciousness is non-existent,’ the preceding section was an exegesis by way of inversion, whereas this is an exegesis by way of conformity.
The two meanings contrasted with the above can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the passage beginning with “Third,” it concerns the relationship between that which produces and that which is produced.
The preceding [factors]—craving, grasping, and becoming—are the producers, while birth, old age, and death are the produced;
thus, the fourth [category] can be understood.
Regarding the phrase "the latter three gates" in the commentary, this is an analytical selection.

However, regarding the second gate concerning consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), although consciousness possesses the sense of being that which draws forth, it is specifically taken as that which is drawn forth; thus, all three are related as the agent and the object.
The question comes first and the answer follows; thus, the intent of the answer can be understood.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Furthermore, in order to reveal the 'conducive factors' (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*)," it reiterates the reason why the two preceding characteristics are combined into one.

If the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is that which is projected, then the projecting factors are only two; if consciousness is the projecting factor, then there are three projecting factors.
If consciousness takes up that which is projected, then the four subsequent cases constitute three categories:

the first case pertains solely to the projecting factor, the second pertains solely to the projected factor, and the third and fourth are explained as being common to both, because they relate to the mutual correspondence between the projector and the projected.

This demonstrates that when each of the twelve links is considered in relation to every other, the principles of "this being, that becomes" (*asmin satīdam bhavati*) and "this arising, that arises" (*asyotpādād idam utpadyate*) apply universally. It need not be explained solely through the mutual relationship of the "projecting" and "projected" factors or the "producing" and "produced" factors for these principles to hold; therefore, the commentary states: "The subtlety of the expositor."
In the commentary following the phrase "Second, the five contaminated aggregates," the text is divided into five parts:
first, the explanation of the general name, which has already been seen in the "Awakening of Light" [chapter].
Regarding the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the "fruit of the storehouse" and so forth refers to the second treatise.
The meaning of "store" (*skandha*) is largely identical to the meaning of "aggregate" (*piṇḍa*); the meanings of "burden" (*bhāra*) and "covering" (*chādana*) are likewise largely identical.
However, that treatise states: "What is the meaning of 'aggregate'?
Answer:"
Whatever form there is—whether near or far—all that, in brief, is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) because it has the sense of a collection, just like a heap of wealth;
and so on, up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The commentary states:
This refers to the meaning of "receptacle" (*skandha*), for it stores resultant phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Regarding the term "burden," the treatise says: "Because it bears the burden of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), it is called a 'heap' (*skandha*), just like carrying a load on one's shoulder."
Regarding "bearing the burden of defilement": this refers to all various defiled phenomena, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*), which all depend upon form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates.
For example, just as a single part of the body in the world can bear a burden, that very part is called a "shoulder" (*skandha*). Thus, it is called an "aggregate."
The same applies to form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates; because they are able to bear the burden of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "but as for the designation of the name," there are two explanations of the world (*loka*).
There are three meanings of "world" (*loka*):
it is called a world in the sense of being concealed or covered, referring to both the conditioned and the unconditioned, as in the "Chapter on the Formation of the World";
in the latter two cases, it refers exclusively to the conditioned world, where "world" (*loka*) is itself the "interval" (*antara*), forming a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The commentary states: "However, as for 'form and so forth'... and below, there are three types of discrimination.
To say "it also includes the untainted" (*anāsrava*) refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, since one attains permanent form by extinguishing impermanent form through the cause, it also encompasses the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Now, we take only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) aggregates; since it would be inconsistent with the meaning to include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is reserved for discussion in the subsequent section.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "How is this known?", there are four explanations of the characteristics of knowledge.

This is the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (the *Dapin*), which was already cited in the preceding text. Within the initial discussion on the characteristics [of the aggregates], it states that “form has transformation and resistance as its characteristic. Regarding this, in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, form has two meanings:
first, the sense of being subject to transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*).
The Treatise asks:
"From the eye faculty at its beginning to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) at its end, for what reason did the Blessed One designate these as 'form' (*rūpa*)?
The answer is:
"Because it is subject to transformation and decay, it is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The commentary states:
"Transformation" indicates momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇika-anityatā*), while "decay" indicates the impermanence of the homogeneous life-stream (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The treatise asks:
"Who is it that undergoes transformation and decay?

It is said that through the contact of the hand and so forth, [the body] immediately undergoes transformation and decay; this is explained in detail up to the contact of mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like."
This "changeable and decaying" (vipariṇāmadharmin) means that which is subject to destruction.
Second is the sense of "resistance" (sapratigha).
The treatise states: "Some say:..."
"Because it is subject to transformation and resistance, it is called 'form' (rūpa).
The commentary states:
"Transformation" means being subject to decay; "resistance" means physical obstruction.
"If that were so, atoms (paramāṇu) should not be called 'form' (rūpa), because they lack resistance and changeability.
This objection is not valid, for no single atom exists in isolation; it is only when a multitude of atoms aggregate that the characteristic of resistance and changeability is established."
The rest is as explained at length there.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* also presents two meanings.
First, it asks:
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of form?
Answer:
The characteristic of manifesting transformation is the characteristic of form.
This is of two kinds:
first, transformation through contact; second, manifestation through spatial direction.
Regarding transformation through contact: this refers to the fact that when one is touched by hands, feet, or even by mosquitoes and gadflies, it immediately undergoes transformation.
"Manifestation according to location" means manifestation by way of whatever characteristic corresponds to a particular location,
such as "this form is thus," or "such a form is so," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "feeling is characterized by experiencing," the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* asks:
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of feeling? Answer:
Its characteristic is that of experiencing.
Therefore, it experiences the various maturations (*vipāka*) obtained from diverse pure and impure karmas.
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: “Feeling (*vedanā*) has as its nature the experiencing of objective aspects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neither.”
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “‘Perception’ (saṃjñā) means grasping images,” this refers to a passage from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

The subsequent text states that its function is to establish various conventional designations (nāma-pada); that is to say, one must first establish the specific characteristics and boundaries of an object before one can subsequently give rise to various conventional designations.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "The apprehension of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Due to this perception, one apprehends various types of images.
According to the meanings of what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, one gives rise to various verbal expressions."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “‘Formations’ (saṃskāra) refers to that which flows on,” the *Abhidharmakośa* states: “The two meanings of ‘constructing’ (abhisamskāra) and ‘flowing on’ (prasyanda) are called formations.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states: “The characteristic of constructing is the characteristic of formations; it is by virtue of this formation that the mind is made to construct, meaning that the mind is driven and employed within the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.”
The commentary states:
Regarding the two meanings of *vijñāna* in the *Abhidharmakośa*, we now adopt the sense of "transmigration," as it is intended to be criticized and rejected here.

The sub-commentary (*śū*) says, "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) functions through discernment (*prativijñapti*)," which the *Abhidharmakośa* explains as: "Vijñāna refers to the individual discernment [of objects]."
The *Śāstra* states: "Discernment (*vijñapti*) is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); because there are six kinds of discernment that differ from one another, it is named consciousness.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "The characteristic of discernment is the characteristic of consciousness."
"By means of this consciousness, one discerns various objects such as form, sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and dharmas.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "Furthermore, knowing that all dharmas tend toward form," this is a secondary illustration of this meaning within the context of the third point.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All dharmas tend toward form; yet even form cannot be apprehended—how, then, could there be tending or non-tending?
Tiantai explains this through the three contemplations as follows:
the first phrase is the provisional (conventional), the second phrase is emptiness, and the third phrase is the Middle Way.

However, while the scriptural text merely reveals the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), the intent cited here in this commentary instead takes up the principle that "all dharmas tend toward form" to clarify the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).
Because there are infinite meanings within a single [phenomenon], this is called skillful erudition (*kauśalya-bahusruta*).
In the commentary, from "However, as for the nature of the aggregates" onwards is the fifth section, the resolution of objections; here, the general is treated as the particular.
There are two meanings to this resolution of objections:
the first can be understood [as stated].

Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, the inclusion of dharmas is extensive," this is the second explanation. Based on this, the extent to which the five aggregates include various dharmas will be briefly elucidated.

According to the hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna, the aggregate of consciousness includes only the eight consciousnesses as mental sovereigns; the aggregate of form includes only eleven types of matter; the two aggregates of perception and feeling include only two of the universal mental factors among the mental concomitants; and the [remaining] four aggregates include only twenty-one dharmas.

Excluding the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which are not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), the remaining seventy-three are all subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); thus, it is said that they are "many.
The one hundred dharmas have already been seen in the first commentary and notes.
The Commentary on "the third, the untainted" has four parts:

first, the explanation of the general name; second, from "now, as for the untainted aggregates" onwards, the manifestation of its specific categories; third, from "desiring to manifest the precepts" onwards, the explanation of the reason for establishing the general name.

Regarding the statement, "In reality, there are also mundane precepts and so forth," although the aforementioned five aggregates also include supramundane elements, mundane precepts and so forth themselves consist of two types of precepts:

first, those shared with non-Buddhists, such as the precepts of the ten wholesome actions and the concentrations of the four dhyānas; these involve the wisdom of worldly knowledge that liberates one from the afflictions of lower stages and constitutes knowledge and vision therein.

Second, within the True Teaching (saddharma) itself, it is also taught that the ten wholesome paths, the five precepts, the four dhyānas, and the eight samādhis involve cultivating wisdom through the contemplation of joy and aversion without views or pride; yet because these [states] are still subject to outflows (sāsrava) and are termed "worldly" (laukika), they cannot liberate one from the bonds of the lower realms, even though one may have a clear and distinct realization.
Commentary on the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Following the Sub-commentary, Scroll Forty-four.
Commentary on the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Following the Sub-commentary,
Scroll Forty-five.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty.
Following "Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom," the fourth section is the formal commentary according to the text.
This contains seven parts:

1. A brief explanation by way of analogy using a single finger; 2. A general explanation by citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) below; 3. Establishing the five reasons for [the teaching] starting from "However, it then transforms the preceding" and so forth; 4. Resolving and clarifying objections and difficulties; 5. Identifying the essential nature (*svabhāva*); 6. Harmonizing and explaining the general name; 7. Reconciling and clarifying the provisional and the ultimate.
The first two [points] can be understood.
Regarding the third, there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation, which follows the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*.
The commentary states, "Therefore, in the *Renwang* [Sūtra]," and so forth, citing scriptural evidence which can be clearly understood by correlating it with the following sequence.

However, this refers to the "Bodhisattva-caryā" chapter of the new translation of the sūtra, which says: "Furthermore, a Bodhisattva of the *mārgajñatā*-nature cultivates the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) and gives rise to the ten types of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*). That is to say, by observing the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness—he attains the patience of morality, the patience of concentration, the patience of wisdom, the patience of liberation, and the patience of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
by observing the causes and effects of the three realms, he attains the patience of emptiness, the patience of signlessness, and the patience of wishlessness."
"By contemplating that all phenomena, whether provisional or substantial, within the two truths are impermanent, one attains the patience of impermanence;
by contemplating that all phenomena are empty, one attains the patience of non-arising.
This present passage corresponds to the preceding five [sections]; as the text belongs to the old translation, it consequently differs from this [version].

In the commentary, following the passage "Knowledge, vision, and wisdom," the fourth section explains and resolves objections, specifically the objection regarding mutual confusion; this consists of the initial objection followed by the response.
Regarding the statement that there are three explanations in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, this is now the first explanation.
The second [interpretation] states: "All are the wisdom of liberation through unimpeded conditions, which is called the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Wisdom of liberation through conditions refers to the knowledge that takes the Truth of Cessation as its object.
"Taking other [truths] as objects" refers to the knowledge of the remaining three truths and so forth.

The third [commentary] states: "All [of these] pertain to both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*); they are partially attained in the stage of learning and perfected in the stage of no-more-learning, for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess all five."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'these five are explained individually' below, this is the fifth [section], which establishes their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they differ in terms of what is illuminated by the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) and by wisdom (*prajñā*), they are nonetheless identical in being wisdom."
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is associated with perception (*saṃjñā*), while the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) is associated with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “However, this fivefold dharma-body,” the sixth section explains the collective name as being supramundane (*lokottara*).
The citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* used as proof refers to the first treatise mentioned above.
In the commentary, following the passage "Question:
Regarding the five aggregates without appropriation," the seventh section provides a comprehensive reconciliation of the provisional and the ultimate.
Citing Cunda, as in the *Xuanzhong lun*:

"Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also states: 'Regarding the five aggregates without grasping (*anupādāna-skandha*), should they be called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?'"
Answer:
One should not say that it is either conditioned or unconditioned. Why is this?
Because all karma and afflictions are absent, it should not be called conditioned;
because they manifest according to desire, it should not be called unconditioned. Why is this so?
The aggregates (*skandhas*) that are without grasping manifest before one according to whatever one desires; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not like this, because it is eternally abiding.
The commentary states:

This is a provisional teaching of "neither-nor," which negates both essence and function in relation to one another; furthermore, it does not definitively state it to be either conditioned or unconditioned.
Furthermore, the statement "appropriating the five aggregates" reveals that ordinary beings possess the appropriated five aggregates.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "The 'appropriated aggregates' are so called because they are conjoined with appropriation."
"Grasping" refers to the various afflictions within the aggregates.
Cunda has already seen the profound discourse on the fundamental reality.
Regarding the "fourth, the conditioned," the commentary first explains the general name.

Citing two treatises, regarding the phrase "the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is connected to causes and conditions," the first fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is so called because it is produced by the collective gathering of various conditions."
If the future has not yet arisen, why is it called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
Because it belongs to that same category, it is also termed conditioned.
It is like firewood: even while in its unburnt state, it is still called "firewood" because it belongs to that same category.

Alternatively, there is no error in establishing names based on what has been or what will be, as in the case of naming lutes, harps, and the like "possessing sound," or as with the breasts, lotuses, and ponds.
All dharmas that have not yet arisen do not transcend that category; therefore, they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
That which possesses arising and ceasing—this statement is still brief.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "If a phenomenon possesses arising, ceasing, abiding, and change, it may be termed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)."
"All phenomena are conditioned, with the exception of one portion of the dharma-element and the dharma-base; this is for the purpose of abandoning attachment to a self that is impermanent.
The commentary states:
herein the treatise answers three questions, the first being the answer to "What is the conditioned?"
2. From "All phenomena" (*sarvadharmāḥ*) onwards, [the text] answers how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
3. From "In order to abandon" (*prahāṇārtham*) onwards, it answers for what purpose one contemplates the conditioned.

The Commentary states: "Now, briefly citing four matters" means that, in reality, there are many extensive teachings in such works as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* asks: "What are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? and so forth.

If phenomena arise, abide, and cease—this explains the meaning of "conditioned" (saṃskṛta). The five aggregates of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; even the feelings produced by the causes and conditions of the mental consciousness; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and that which constitutes all-knowledge—all these are conditioned phenomena.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are briefly said to have three characteristics:

first, birth, abiding, and cessation; second, the meaning of being bound to the three realms; and third, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)."
"Although there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they possess activity, they are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The characteristic of the unconditioned is what constitutes an unconditioned phenomenon.
The commentary states:

Now, because the eighteen unshared [dharmas] and so forth belong to the category of determinate dharmas (*vyākṛta*), only four of them are briefly presented; as for "sentient beings," this encompasses the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
In the commentary, the section beginning with "However, the locus upon which they depend" explains the meaning of the three realms (*tridhātu*).
The phrase "Thus the treatise says" refers to the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

The word "etc. includes the other two realms; one should say that the realm to which form belongs is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the realm to which the formless belongs is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Omitting the two characters for "belonging to," one simply uses names such as "the Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*).

This is like the expressions "sesame drink" (*tilapāna*) and "vajra ring" (*vajravalaya*): "drink" and "ring" are both general names, while "sesame" and "vajra" are specific designations. Because the specific depends upon the general, one refers to them as "sesame drink" and "vajra ring. To be fully explicit, one should say "the drink belonging to sesame" and so forth; however, by omitting the "belonging to," one simply says "vajra ring" and so on.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) is a general term for specific designations such as "desire" and so forth; by omitting the intermediate words, one speaks of the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*) and so on.
The treatise asks: "In this context, what phenomenon is expressed by the word 'desire'?"
Answer:
Briefly stated, edible food is the craving induced by sexual desire.
The note says: "Craving for sex is called *rāga* (greed); craving for food is called *kāma* (desire)."

However, the wording remains obscure; the first fascicle of the *Fenbie yehong jing* (Sutra on Distinguishing Karmic Actions) states: "The Buddha-sons see two types of karma due to being attached to all desires within the dharma-realm; because of this, the retribution arising from desire is divided into the retribution of the desire realm."

When the Buddha-sons perceive and cling to the two karmas, they become deluded regarding all matter and mind within the Dharma-realm; thus, the retribution arising from such matter and mind is categorized as the retribution of the Form Realm.

When the Buddha-sons perceive and cling to the two karmas, they become deluded regarding all meditative minds within the Dharma-realm; thus, the retribution arising from such meditative minds is categorized as the retribution of the Formless Realm.
Therefore, within a single dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there are the retributive fruits of the three realms. To make this even clearer:

because beings in the desire realm possess male and female forms and receive bodies through sexual desire, it is called the "desire realm"; because beings in the form realm lack male and female forms and possess only form, it is called the "form realm"; and because beings in the formless realm are said to be without form, it is called the "formless realm."
Regarding the previous mention of "attachment to views" in the *Mūla-karma-sūtra*, that scripture speaks of seven views and six attachments.
The sutra states: "O Son of the Buddha!

Ignorance (avidyā) is defined as the failure to comprehend all phenomena; it is through delusion regarding the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that one gives rise to the karmic fruits of the three realms."

Therefore, I say that from the storehouse of ignorance arise thirteen afflictions, namely: the seven views—false view, the view of self, the view of permanence, the view of annihilation, the view of precepts and rituals, the view of grasping, and the view of doubt—and because one seeks [objects] in all places through these, they are called "views."
Furthermore, six types of clinging minds arise—namely, greed, craving, hatred, delusion, desire, and pride—which arise at all times within the dharma-realm.
All afflictions take these thirteen as their root; ignorance takes these thirteen as its root, and ignorance gives rise to the mental formations of these thirteen.

Therefore, within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one separately establishes the conceptualization of the three realms; this refers to the two karmas of "viewing" and "attachment," as previously cited.
Regarding the commentary on the "fifth, the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), there are six sections:

first, explaining the general name; second, the classification and combination; third, explaining the text; fourth, distinguishing between the provisional and the real; fifth, identifying the essential nature (*svabhāva*); and sixth, concluding with an indication of the purpose of extensive learning.
First, the general name is explained.
Below, under "Yoga," citations are provided as evidence, with the two treatises corresponding respectively to the two preceding meanings.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "It is called 'unconditioned' (asaṃskṛta) because it is devoid of arising, abiding, and ceasing; it does not fall within the categories of enumeration."
This refers to the "Ānanda Chapter" of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, which states: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into the categories of enumeration.

Enumeration refers to the conditioned; all other meanings merely reverse the preceding notion of the conditioned. Therefore, the commentary concludes: "In all treatises, the general title and its essential purport are no different."

In the commentary, from "However, its... onwards, within the section on "opening and closing," the phrase "However, the Hīnayāna mostly speaks of three kinds" refers to what the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises state: "The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path, as well as the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena, namely space and the two types of cessation."
Regarding the term "for the most part," there are four [unconditioned phenomena] according to the *Vibhaṅga*:
first, space; second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*); and fourth, suchness (*tathatā*).

The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts nine unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), namely: the three [unconditioned phenomena], the four [formless] attainments (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), the nature of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-aṅga*), and the nature of the factors of the noble path (*āryamārga-aṅga*).

The Mahīśāsaka school also asserts nine, adding to the aforementioned three: the immovable (*āniñjya*), the three natures (*tridhātu-svabhāva*), the factors of the path, and the factors of dependent origination.
The Commentary states: "The *Mahāyāna-śāstra-tattva-saṃgraha* speaks of four" because it adds True Suchness (*tathatā*) to the three [categories] of the Hīnayāna.
Alternatively, it is said that there are six, as extensively explained below in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and other texts.

Alternatively, when expanded into eight, the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "There are eight kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*): namely, the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome phenomena, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena, the suchness of indeterminate phenomena, space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*)."
Thus, among these eight unconditioned phenomena, one should understand that they are established based on differences in their respective supports.

True Suchness (*tathatā*) is analytically designated as threefold. Regarding "the True Suchness of wholesome dharmas by way of intrinsic nature," this refers to selflessness (*anātmatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the reality-limit of signlessness (*animitta-bhūtakoṭi*), and the ultimate dharma-sphere (*paramārtha-dharmadhātu*).
For what reason is suchness called "selflessness"?
Because its intrinsic nature is immutable; that is to say, because at all times the true nature of selflessness undergoes no alteration or transformation.

Because there is no alteration or transformation, it is said to be without change; one should know that this is precisely the nature of selflessness (*anātmatā*), as it is free from the two types of self.
For what reason, then, is this further called emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Because it is not traversed by any defilements. Why is this?
Because by taking this as an object, one is able to cause all matters of defilement to become entirely empty and quiescent.
Sometimes it is said that defilement is merely adventitious; because all characteristics are quiescent, it is called "signless" (animitta).
Because it is the object of non-erroneous cognition, it is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi).
"Reality" (bhūta) means being free from inversion.
Because this is the ultimate limit, it is called the "limit" (koṭi).
Because it is the sphere of activity for the most excellent noble wisdom, it is called the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha).
Because it is the basis upon which all the sublime teachings of the three vehicles rely, it is called the "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu).
"Just as it is with wholesome *tathatā*, one should know that it is likewise for the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
The remainder is as stated in that treatise.
The passage beginning with "gradually desiring" below is the commentary’s extraction of the meaning of the treatise.
The Commentary states: "This sutra speaks of six," etc. This is the third section, the explanation of the text.
It contains two parts: first, a general clarification of existence and non-existence; [and second, a detailed analysis].
Below the section beginning with "Next, 'space'... follows a separate explanation that draws extensively from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
There are six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which constitute six sections.
The initial explanation of the term "space" is entirely based on the intent of the commentary on the *Śataśāstra*.
That is to say, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establishes the existence of objects as a mere provisional designation based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

That treatise first explains the nature of phenomena as follows: "It refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by emptiness and selflessness; it is neither existent nor non-existent, transcending the paths of mind and speech, and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena."
This dharma is the true principle; therefore, it is called the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
It is free from all obstructions; therefore, it is called "space" (*ākāśa*).
The commentary states:
That treatise clarifies that the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) merely refers to being free from all obstructions.

The *Śataśāstra* additionally includes external emptiness, stating it is "that which is manifested by the absence of things. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "In this context, emptiness is non-obstruction."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two types of *nirvāṇa*,” *nirvāṇa* is identical to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
First, the nature-purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is clarified, which is merely an incidental discussion of alternative meanings.

As for the phrase, “The thirty-fourth [topic], *nirvāṇa*, is also explained in this same way,” this refers to the interpretation in the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text), which states that it is the same as the space and *nirvāṇa* described in this sutra.

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its explanation of the four propositions regarding dependent origination, states: "That which exists but is neither dependently originated nor part of the twelve links of dependent origination refers to space and nirvāṇa."
This refers to the meaning of "purity by nature" (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*).
Of these two latter meanings, the latter is correct: the fruit of purity by nature is precisely *pariniṣpanna-vyavadāna* (perfected purity), which is *nirvāṇa*.
One should ask: [What is the relationship between them?]
If it were a fruit, how would it differ from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?

Because cause and fruit are distinct, two paths are differentiated; therefore, in the previous general explanation, this principle was taken as correct, stating that within cessation through deliberation, *nirvāṇa* is distinguished by way of the two separate paths.
The phrase "However, in the Mahāyāna" and below refutes the two preceding interpretations.

Regarding the statement "then the latter interpretation is correct": if the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) by saying, "It is not due to the power of analysis, but because it is pure by its very nature."
The Commentary states: "Third, cessation through deliberation.
The section beginning with "Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty" below presents its alternative names.
The phrase "that which is obtained through the power of discernment" is an explanation from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Therefore, that analogy states: "Just as a cart drawn by oxen is called an 'ox-cart,' where the middle term has been omitted, so too is it said simply as 'cessation through discernment' (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains: "Because one eliminates all defilements through the power of discernment and ultimately realizes [this state], it is named cessation through discernment."
The Commentary states: "Now, regarding 'this cessation has two [aspects],' this is a specific explanation of the term 'cessation.
These two meanings are designated as 'cessation.
If one includes the wisdom that is capable of effecting cessation, then that wisdom is also designated as 'cessation.'"

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The fourth is cessation not through deliberation,” the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: “That which is not due to the power of deliberation, but is naturally pure and manifested by the absence of conditions, is called cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
The commentary states:
This treatise maintains two meanings.
The first meaning differs from that of the Hinayana; therefore, the preceding commentary takes it as the definitive standard.

Regarding the phrase "deficiency of conditions," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "That which absolutely obstructs what is about to arise is separately termed 'non-analytical cessation' (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The subsequent commentary explains: "'About to arise' refers to dharmas that are destined to arise; they arise when conditions converge and do not arise when conditions are deficient. At the time when conditions are deficient, one attains non-analytical cessation."
That which obstructs dharmas destined to arise so that they never again occur is called "ultimate obstruction" (*atyantavighna*).

Regarding the term "separate acquisition" (*prāpti-viśeṣa*): it means that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) possesses a substantial nature, because a separate acquisition arises within the state where conditions are deficient. Non-analytical cessation is so named because its acquisition does not depend on analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but occurs solely due to the deficiency of conditions.

The *Treatise* (Śāstra), pointing to specific phenomena to clarify this, states: "When the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away.
The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) that would have taken those objects as their conditions abide in the future and will never arise."
"Because they cannot take past objects as their cognitive domain, and because the conditions for such cognition are incomplete, they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The commentary explains:

When the eye takes form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is also capable of taking sound (*śabda*) and so forth as its objects; however, because it is focused exclusively on form, the ear and other faculties do not take sound and so forth as their objects.
Furthermore, because sounds and other objects have already ceased in a single moment, the consciousnesses that take those sounds as their objects no longer arise.
This is because the first five consciousnesses perceive only the present and do not perceive the past or the future.

Regarding the phrase "contact and so forth," the term "and so forth" (ādi) includes those factors among mental objects (*dharma*) that exist simultaneously with their corresponding cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*) as their objective referents (*ālambana*), such as the object of a cognition of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*).

This knowledge of others' minds takes only the present mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as its object; it should also take mental factors (*caitta*) as its objects, but because it focuses exclusively on the mind-king, it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the mental factors.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The five conditions for arising,” the text has two parts:
first, a dual introduction;
second, a detailed explanation beginning with “Specifically,” which first explains the specific [conditions] and subsequently explains the general [condition].
Regarding the first [section], the text consists of four parts:
first, citing the positions established by various schools of the Hīnayāna;
second, from "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 32" onwards, citing Mahāyāna treatises to establish proof for the aforementioned meaning.
In this context, a prior section of the treatise poses a question:
"Why is it that such *dharmatā* and *bhūtakoṭi* are not taught within the Śrāvaka-dharma, whereas they are taught everywhere in the Mahāyāna?"
Answer:
These two are also taught within the Śrāvaka-dharma;
this is the same as the commentary below, which has already been cited in the Xuánzhōng [commentary].
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “The *Nirvāṇa* also says,” this is the third section, which cites Mahāyāna sūtras to establish the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
First, it cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, specifically the thirty-fourth sūtra, the "Kāśyapa Bodhisattva Chapter," which serves as the opening chapter of the Northern version.
The Southern Collection comprises thirty-one fascicles;

the Northern Collection comprises half a fascicle, followed by twenty-one treatises on controversial points. This is the sixth: the Sūtra states, "Some say that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); others say that the twelve links of dependent origination are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Upon reaching the thirty-fifth section, the commentary explains: The Sūtra states in full, "Good son!
In my sūtras, it is asked: What is called the twelve links of dependent origination?"

From ignorance arise volitional formations; from volitional formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises clinging; from clinging arises becoming; from becoming arises birth; and from birth come old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair.
"Good son!
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim: 'The Tathāgata has definitively stated that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned.'"
On another occasion, I instructed the bhikṣus, saying these words:
"The twelve links of dependent origination—whether a Buddha appears or does not appear—have their nature and characteristics eternally abiding.
O sons of good family!"

There are dependent origination factors that do not arise from conditions; there are those that arise from conditions but are not dependent origination factors; and there are those that both arise from conditions and are dependent origination factors.
There are things that arise from conditions but are not the twelve links of dependent origination;
there are things that are the twelve links of dependent origination but do not arise from conditions, namely the twelve factors of the future life.
There are things that arise from conditions but are not the twelve links, namely the five aggregates (skandhas) possessed by an Arhat.
There are things that arise from conditions and are also the twelve links of dependent origination; these refer to the five aggregates possessed by ordinary worldlings.
There are things that neither arise from conditions nor are the twelve links of dependent origination; these refer to space and nirvana.

“Good son! When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim that the Tathāgata has definitively stated that the twelve links of dependent origination are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).”
The commentary states:
If it is said in the sutra that both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are not understood, this refers to the meaning.
Regarding Master Yuanyang’s interpretation, each has its own justification, yet there are two underlying intentions.
The present commentary represents the first meaning.
The second meaning states:
