Thus, this final sentence serves as a summary, indicating that there is no separate mental factor apart from experience; it refers back to ignorance, craving, and so forth in the past, and forward to name-and-form and so forth in the future. Therefore, experience is itself the twelve links.

In this present commentary, I have cited only the first section to demonstrate that ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are the roots of the twelve links of dependent origination; these are precisely what are meant by "ignorance, craving, and so forth.
The phrase "and so forth" includes other scriptural passages.

However, the original intent of that sutra was to clarify that there is no separate mental factor (cittadharma), and not to establish that ignorance (avidyā) and craving (tṛṣṇā) are the fundamental members of dependent origination; therefore, the commentary concludes by stating, "it is also similar to this meaning."

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding 'taking ignorance as the root across the three time periods,' this is from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; it shall be analyzed in detail below in the sixth stage, but for now it is briefly explained."
It should be understood that ignorance arises adventitiously as the root, for ignorance is defined as the failure to comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
As for the statement "craving and grasping constitute the limit," this refers to what arises in the present life.
If craving and grasping arise again, then there will be the future factors of birth, aging, and death.
If they do not arise, suffering shall not come into being; since existence or non-existence depends upon them, they are called "limits" (koṭi).

Regarding the statement, "Between these two, there are the five [factors] beginning with consciousness," this refers to the five resultant factors situated between the link of ignorance and the subsequent links of craving and grasping.
Regarding the statement, "as well as birth and old age and death," this refers to the links of craving and grasping themselves.

Looking back toward the future, the branches of craving and grasping that have not yet arisen are designated as the "intermediate" stage; this is because they will arise again in the future, leading to an endless succession.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Now, awakening to ignorance,” it explains the reason why craving and grasping are established as the limit (*anta*); the meaning has been explained above.
The Commentary states: "The latter three are categorized according to purity. This is the second section, explaining the final three segments.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, an explanation based on the text;...

2. "Furthermore, knowing the śrāvaka is itself knowing suffering" integrates [the teaching] with the Four Noble Truths, as the previous heading stated that one illuminates the ten dharmas by means of the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths;
3. From "The preceding explanation integrates the cause" onwards, the two explanations are integrated.
Although cause and effect are said to be distinct, they do not differ from the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "If one definitively takes the former two as the *pariccheda* (segmented) [saṃsāra]," this is the fourth section, which summarizes and critiques the ancient interpretations; it is the explanation found in the *Kanding ji*.
The Commentary first sets forth this point; subsequently, from the passage beginning "then the three fruits of the Hīnayāna," it demonstrates the characteristics of the fault.

Regarding the latter three vehicles, they encompass both cause and fruit; if [the transformation body] were now subject to the *parinirmita-vipākaja* (transformation-retribution) birth, then the three fruits would already have undergone such transformation.
Since one only undergoes it after entering the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), how could the three fruits undergo transformation so soon?
Furthermore, these three fruits are not what is known here, because these three fruits belong to the stage of *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented existence).

Regarding the phrase "directly proceeding to the seventh stage" and so forth: those who turn back from the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and enter the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) may undergo *pariṇāmanī-kāya* (transformation body) from the first stage upward; however, for a bodhisattva who proceeds directly, it is only from the eighth stage onward that they undergo *pariṇāmanī-kāya*.
Now, because this refers generally to the transformation of rebirth (*pariṇāma-vipariṇāma*), those from the seventh stage and below are not what is known here.
Alternatively, it may be that even prior to the seventh stage, one would undergo transformation; however, each case would entail two faults, which the commentary (*śū*) has omitted for brevity.
Regarding the death of the segmented and the death of transformation, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of death. What are the two?
They are the death of segmentation and the inconceivable death of transformation."
Those who undergo death by segmentation are the deluded ordinary beings.
Those who undergo inconceivable transformation-death are the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the mind-made bodies of Bodhisattvas of great power, up to the ultimate unsurpassed enlightenment.
The commentary states:
Based on this, it is clearly known that those in the three fruits of the Hīnayāna and those from the seventh stage downward have not yet undergone the transformation of death (vaśitā-pariṇāma).
The meaning of the four types of transformation has already been explained at length previously.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It also reveals the characteristics of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-lakṣaṇa*,” the “object of knowledge” refers to the nature and characteristics discussed below; one must first reveal the object of knowledge before one can recognize the subject that knows it.
Regarding the section of the commentary beginning with “Knowing the characteristics, one knows the nature,” there are three parts therein:
first, knowing the characteristics; second, knowing the nature; and third, knowing the absence of obstacles.
There are two kinds of non-obstruction:
first, the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics;
second, the non-obstruction of the mutual interpenetration of nature and characteristics through their integration, which constitutes the four dharma-realms—these are the objects of knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "knowledge of non-knowing," this refers to the Bodhisattva’s capacity for knowing;
that is, the non-knowing of *prajñā* which illuminates in response to conditions.

As for the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, within the two sections, the preceding five categories are contained,” it means that previously, through the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), each of the five categories of phenomena was examined one by one, as is clearly evident in the text.
Now, as the meaning within the text implicitly contains the preceding dharmas, the commentary (*śū*) provides them in full.

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Dapin*) briefly lists over eighty categories, while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Da banruo*) is even more extensive. This begins with form, as it is the first of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); next, it proceeds through the four aggregates; then through the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*); then through the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced by eye-contact and so forth; then the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four truths (*satya*), the four dhyānas, the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the dhāraṇīs, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*), the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), the knowledge of all modes, the practices of the four fruits and the bodhisattvas, and finally unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
The commentary states:
"The 'above' refers to what has already been traversed.

Regarding the passage in the sub-commentary, "One perceives that all phenomena are like a mass of foam," etc., this raises the point that the five aggregates are unreal and subject to disintegration to challenge the notion of indestructibility; the intended meaning of this has already been explained repeatedly previously.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “All have already attained nothingness, etc., as a minor expedient,” the commentary explains “minor expedient” (*sāvakalpa-upāya*) by means of “non-attainment.
As the subsequent scripture says: “One takes non-attainment as the expedient.”

If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, non-arising is taken as the skillful means, non-abiding is taken as the skillful means, and non-reliance is taken as the skillful means; all of these are characteristics of prajñā.
However, as skillful means, there are briefly two intentions:
first, the means for entering existence, which brings about the non-apprehension of existence and so forth;
second, the means for entering emptiness, which likewise does not abide in non-apprehension.
Therefore, it is now correctly taken as the skillful means for entering existence.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is also like clarified butter, there is nothing it does not penetrate,” this refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* praising the wisdom of reality (*tattvajñāna*) for penetrating everything without exception.
The eighth is the "Storehouse of Mindfulness.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The eleven divisions of the teachings shall now be briefly explained," this refers to the fifth section, the "Expounding of the Teachings.
This passage consists of three parts:

First, the general name is explained; second, from "each has two characteristics" onwards, the characteristics are explained; third, the distinction between the universal and the specific is analyzed.
Within the second section, there is first a general clarification, followed by a detailed explanation starting from "The Sūtra... and so forth.
This section has two parts:
first, the distinction between the two characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "the prose composition" and so forth, it shall be understood in the following section.
Second, from "However, there are further... onwards, the different names are distinguished, thereby manifesting the three characteristics.
This section has two parts:
first, the four names are listed, as was done in the first fascicle; [the second part follows].
Below the phrase "The Dharma is Fundamental," there is a separate explanation.
This section has two parts:
first, the formal presentation of Master Huiyuan’s interpretation; [the second part follows].

Second, from "Because they are established by that" onwards, the reason is provided, namely the establishment of the three characteristics, because the latter three among the five are themselves the three characteristics of the sūtras.
Within this, there is first an enumeration and subsequently a summary.
From "not different from the former" onwards is the explanation.
This consists of two parts:

The first [section], "The Correct Explanation," provides a general exposition of the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*), which is not different from the general exposition within the preceding two characteristics.
The remaining two [sections] can be understood accordingly.
The passage beginning with "However, as for the latter two" serves to refute misconceptions and provide a comprehensive reconciliation.
In the *Kanding ji*, he establishes two levels of general and specific categories, whereas the first commentary (*shuchao*) does not permit the establishment of three.
That first commentary refutes [the threefold division] as follows:

"Although Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty speaks of three general and specific categories of the *sūtra*—first, conforming to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; second, lacking scriptural authority and contradicting correct principle; and third, violating the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*."
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "Sūtra refers to prose compositions that briefly explain the meanings that ought to be explained.
Its own commentary explains: "Briefly explaining the meanings that ought to be explained is precisely what constitutes prose composition."
There has never been an instance where a brief summary is presented first, followed by an extensive explanation later.
As for what is called "brief," it refers to the alternative names for the general [classification]: that is, one part of the Sūtra is the general, while the remaining eleven parts are the specific.

Now, the name "Sūtra" is established based on the general characteristics and functions among the various schools (nikāyas), whereas the names of the other schools are established based on their specific characteristics and functions.
Why is this so? Because the function of the Sūtras is able to penetrate and encompass [all teachings].
Therefore, that which is expounded by other Piṭakas and other schools, as well as their respective converts, only achieve their completion through being penetrated and encompassed by these [Sūtras].
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "From the beginning with 'Thus have I heard' until the end with 'rejoicing and practicing accordingly,' all are subsumed under the *sūtra*.
The commentary explains:
this refers to the establishment and refutation therein.
In this commentary, I recognize that what has been established is merely a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and thus I shall not further elaborate upon it.

Regarding the statement "it contradicts the *Saṃgrahaṇī*," I have provided a clarification of its characteristics; however, since I am actually employing the *Saṃgrahaṇī* itself, I say that there is no contradiction.
This establishes the specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa); therefore, it says: "The prose compositions that are not subsumed under these eleven [categories].

Fearing that the meaning might not yet be clear, I cite the "Chapter on the Wise Leader" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to demonstrate this: since the prose compositions that constitute the overall arrangement are themselves the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), how could the general characteristic possibly exclude the verses?
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the brief exposition of the meanings that ought to be expounded,'" this refers generally to the *Sūtra on the Brief Characteristics*.

This is the text from the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, which is divided into two sections to provide the basis for the specific brief expositions; it employs only the single passage from the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) above to simultaneously verify these two meanings.
Regarding the statement, "At that time, Mañjuśrī, having finished expounding the great merit of the pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion," this is merely a summary in prose form.
If it is said, "In order to manifest the merits of the bodhicitta," this briefly indicates its characteristics and serves as a heading for what will be explained below.
It should be understood that the subsequent clarification shows no contradiction with the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "This, moreover, pervades the twelve divisions," this clarifies that they are briefly interconnected; they do not differ in their individual characteristics, yet the eleven [divisions] do not subsume it.

In the commentary, from the passage "If, among the twelve divisions, it is the Sūtra... onwards, both the Pitaka and the Nikāya are concluded by distinguishing between the universal and the specific applications of the Sūtra.

This text specifically establishes two levels of general and specific categories for the *Kanding* [Catalogue]. It states: "However, according to the Śrāvaka schools, each category has two levels of general and specific designations:
first, the 'Three Piṭakas' and 'Twelve Divisions' serve as the general names, while the 'Sūtra' and so forth serve as the specific titles."
The second point is that "Sūtra" serves as the general designation, while "Vinaya," "Geya," and so forth, are the specific categories.
According to tradition handed down from antiquity, only the former category has been analyzed, while the latter has not been discussed.
The commentary states:
Regarding the latter general and specific [arguments], they were presented as outstanding [points], but now they are precisely refuted.
Their intention is as follows:
Since that which accords with principle and suits the faculties is called *sūtra*, then both the Vinaya and the Abhidharma must also possess such accord; how could they not be termed *sūtra*?
Therefore, it is now shown:
those among the two baskets (Vinaya and Abhidharma) that possess this accord are precisely the *sūtras* within the twelve divisions of the teachings.
Since this definition already encompasses the meaning, why must two further layers of general and specific categories be established?

Thus, while the Sūtra-piṭaka among the Tripiṭaka is restricted solely to the general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), it is nonetheless divided into three types within the twelve divisions of the scriptures (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana). Therefore, the Sūtra-piṭaka is established based on these general characteristics to distinguish it from the other two Piṭakas.
The commentary states, “But it opens the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,” etc., concluding by showing the basis for Master Huiyuan’s position.

The commentary states, “There are those who do not understand,” etc., concluding by refuting the *Kanding* [commentary] for contradicting the words of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, while instead relying on the remaining twelve divisions; the text for both cases can be understood as it stands.
However, if one were to cite the relevant sutra as proof for each individual part, it would demonstrate that this sutra possesses all twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*).
Regarding the second point, the commentary states: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
'In the past, the Buddha [spoke] to the bhikṣus,' etc. This refers to what is stated in the fifteenth sutra:
The prose version states in full: What is called a *geya-sūtra*?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, you and I were ignorant and lacked wisdom; we were unable to see the Four Noble Truths as they truly are."
Therefore, one wanders through saṃsāra, dwelling for a long time in birth and death and sinking into the great ocean of suffering.
What are the four: the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
As the Buddha formerly taught in a sūtra for the bhikṣus... [the remainder is identical to the commentary].
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" at the end of the commentary, there are two parts.
First, it refers to the remaining verses.
There is one further verse which says: "If one can perceive the Four Truths, one shall immediately attain the cessation of birth and death."
"All forms of existence being exhausted, one shall no longer undergo further existence.
This is what is called a *geya-sūtra*.
Second, it refers to other sūtra texts by way of general inclusion.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “As in the prediction for Maitreya,” the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: “What is called a ‘sūtra of prediction’?
It refers to those sūtras and vinayas in which, when the Tathāgata speaks, he bestows a prophetic prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon various devas and humans.”
"Ānanda, in the future there will be a king named Śaṅkha who shall attain the Way of the Buddha in that world, and his name shall be Maitreya.
This is called the Sūtra of the Prediction."
Regarding the four gāthās: the two aspects of the verse "Commit no evil" cited in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* are established as verses based on two intentions.

In the commentary on the fifth [section], it says: "Because one only speaks of knowing the beginning and the end once the causal events have occurred. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* asks: "What is called a *nidāna-sūtra*?"
As in the verses of various sūtras, one should expound for others the fundamental causes and conditions.

For example, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a man who caught birds with a net; having captured them, he confined them in a cage, provided them with water and grass, and then released them again.
The World-Honored One, knowing the causal conditions from beginning to end, spoke in verse:
"Do not treat a minor offense lightly, thinking there will be no calamity.
Though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel."

The Commentary on the "Seven Original Matters" (*pūrvayoga*) states that among the two types of characteristics, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, mentions only the first characteristic, saying: "As for 'original matters,' it refers to all events belonging to the Buddha’s past limit (*pūrvānta*) and events arising in his future limit (*aparānta*)."

The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* mentions only the latter [type of] intention, stating: "Regarding 'past events' (*itivṛttaka*), it refers to the proclamation of matters concerning the previous lives of the noble disciples and others."

The Commentary states: Regarding "the eight birth stories" and so forth, as for the phrase "one says that the Tathāgata," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was originally a bodhisattva, he practiced various ascetic austerities. Monks, you should know that in the past I was a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, a minor king, a universal monarch (cakravartin), a nāga, and a garuḍa."
"When practicing the bodhisattva path in such ways as these, one relinquishes the body that is so dear.
Regarding the commentary's mention of "the nine Vaipulya [sūtras]," this may be understood accordingly.
All the citations from the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* refer to the eleventh fascicle.
Regarding the opening of the general characteristics of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one should say there are four, with the general [characteristic] making five in total.
The rest can be understood.
In the commentary, the section beginning with "These twelve, regarding the Great and Small [Vehicles]" constitutes the second part: the discernment of their universal and specific applications.
Within this section, there are three parts:

first, distinguishing between the universal and the specific, as well as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; second, a general reconciliation; and third, distinguishing between the mutual presence and absence of the twelve [links].
This is the first part.

Regarding the statement, "The third [section] of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says that those who protect the Mahāyāna uphold the ninefold canon," the meaning is drawn from a sūtra which says: "If there is a bhikṣu whose requisites for sustaining the body are always abundant, and who is further able to guard and maintain the prohibitive precepts he has received, and is able to roar the lion’s roar and expound the sublime Dharma—namely, the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, and Adbhutadharma—and thus extensively explains these ninefold scriptures for others for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings," and so forth.
The Commentary states: "'The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One' refers to the 'Expedient Means' (Upāya) chapter.
The second half of the subsequent verse says: "Entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation; for this reason, I preach this sutra."
Below, it quotes the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, where there are only eleven [categories].
The commentary (*shu*) from "However, regarding the various sūtras" onwards can be understood as a reconciliation [of these differences].
The commentary from "However, regarding the sūtras and so forth" onwards distinguishes between what is mutually present and what is mutually absent; the rest can be understood.
The ninth, the *Dhāraṇī-kośa*, may be understood [as previously explained].
The tenth, the *Vibhaṅga-kośa*, elucidates the seven types of discernment (*vibhaṅga*), as extensively clarified in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
This concludes the fourth assembly.

Chapter Twenty-three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. Commentary on the Fifth Assembly of the *Bodhisattvamahāyānapiṭaka-sūtra* (or simply titled *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*), consisting of one fascicle.
It is also called "Bowing to the Buddha, Repenting, and Rejoicing," followed by an extensive explanation of the merits of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and so forth.

First, it clarifies that one might offer the seven treasures as a gift, filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within a trichiliocosm to make offerings to the Buddha; subsequently, it states that practicing this merit of dedication surpasses the former merit, thereby citing immeasurable fruits. This, however, is merely an implicit citation of their significance.

The Commentary states: "Because the mind of dedication constitutes a great benefit," it implicitly cites the verse of the Bodhisattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana from the "Buddha-way" chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
The verse says: "Possessing the seven treasures of wealth, one causes them to grow through instruction; practicing as taught and dedicating [the merit] constitutes the great benefit.
Regarding the phrase "therefore, the subsequent is clarified by the former," it means that the preceding practice is dedicated [by the latter].
The Commentary states: "There are also three meanings": first, in terms of location, it is called the Assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace;
second, in terms of persons, it is called the Assembly of Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva;
third, in terms of the Dharma, it is called the Assembly of the Ten Dedications.
In the commentary, the phrase "Regarding 'stating this in this context'" below serves as the inquiry.
From "indicating the position" below, the answer follows.
This answer contains six points of meaning:
First, previously it was in the Yāma heaven, but now, through dedication, it has surpassed that and resides above Tuṣita; this is merely according to the sequential order.
Second, it adopts the name of the Heaven of Contentment (Saṃtuṣita).
Third, it is spoken of in reference to the Lord of that heaven.
Fourth, it is explained again by way of contentment: the former was based on contentment regarding one's own benefit, while this is based on contentment regarding the benefit of others;
fifth, it is spoken of in terms of the Middle Way;
sixth, it is explained by way of impartiality.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, having been born in this heaven, one cultivates the three merits," this refers to the thirty-second [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. It should be stated that by cultivating generosity and precepts, one obtains the body of a lower or upper heaven; by cultivating generosity, precepts, and meditative concentration, one obtains the body of a Tuṣita heaven.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "Third, [the stage] fulfills through the perfection of application," etc.: therefore, at the beginning of the eighth stage, there is a general clarification of the section on the accumulation of skillful means (*upāya*), wherein the preceding seven stages are accumulated as the skillful means for the eighth stage.
The first part of the fortieth stage is precisely this "Section on Fulfilling the Ground through Expedient Means.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "It does not necessarily give rise to the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*)": this also refers to the beginning of the twelfth sutra cited previously, where each [being] manifests supernatural powers according to their respective category.
Other masters explain that there are four assemblies, and similar examples can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the second of the two major sections, the commentary states: "Alternatively, the second section clarifies dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This is because the first section is based on stages; since the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are entirely identical to the ten practices (*caryā*), the second is assigned to dedication and the fourth to the ten grounds (*bhūmi*). Thus, the vertical sequence of stages is fully complete.

Because the second section contains the intention of dedication within such qualities as "indestructible supernormal powers," and the fourth section contains the structural essence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within such qualities as "universally entering Buddha-fields," this correspondence is established.
Because [the sequence] of two and three involves alternation, while that of two and four is not manifest.
The former is the direct explanation; the latter applies generally to all stages.

Regarding the commentary on the "retribution of the primary body" (*sabhāga-vipāka*), which states, "Emotion is stirred within, therefore it is manifested in speech," and so forth: this refers to the *Preface to the Odes* by Zixia, which says in full: "Emotion is stirred within and is manifested in speech; when speech is insufficient, one sighs and exclaims."
When sighing and praising are insufficient, one composes songs.
When singing is insufficient, one is unaware that the hands are dancing and the feet are stamping.
The fifth is the contemplation of the Buddha’s supreme virtues.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “However, the meaning of this passage is both broad and extensive,” it is because at the beginning of the *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World), the Buddha is praised by name but not explained, whereas in the present text, he is explained but not mentioned by name.
The text provides a complete and sequential explanation of the twenty-one virtues over more than four pages; thus, it is said that both the words and the meaning are extensive.

Since the text spans more than four pages, its wording is broad; furthermore, because the phrases and meanings therein encompass the various divergent interpretations found in all the treatises without exception, it is said that the meaning is extensive.

For this reason, within this [treatise], various śāstras are cited; the śāstras are used to explain the sūtras, and the sūtras are used to corroborate the śāstras, which is why it is said that they are cited "as occasion demands.

The ancients also cited various śāstras in the "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*) chapter; however, since there was no corresponding sūtra text, those śāstras lacked a scriptural basis for verification.
Because these names do not exist, the ancient masters were likewise confused.

Master Zang and those who followed him summarized the ten phrases into ten sections; the *Kanding* [Commentary] correlates them with the sixteen types of the three karmas, as cited below, but neither approach shall be adopted here.

In the commentary, the statement "The 'Chapter on Transcending the World' is named 'Sublime Awakening Fully Perfected'" explains the general heading within the sutra; the following section reconciles the various alternative names for that general heading.

However, the root text of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* was composed by Asaṅga himself; both Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva wrote commentaries on it, which were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty. Both versions consist of ten fascicles each, and this [present work] corresponds to the fifth [of the five parts].

Now, according to Asvabhāva’s commentary on the *Lakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of the knowable), the reason given is: "If one wishes to explain the Mahāyāna teachings, it is done briefly by way of three aspects:
first, by explaining dependent origination; second, by explaining the characteristics of phenomena arising from conditions; and third, by explaining the meaning of the words."

The Commentary says: "To explain the meaning of the words means to state the first phrase and subsequently analyze and reveal it through further phrases, either by way of its qualities (*guṇa*) or by way of its meaning (*artha*)."
The commentary on the *Śāstra* states: "That which has already been attained resides within oneself; because it brings about perfect benefit, it is called 'virtue' (*guṇa*).
That which has not yet been attained resides within oneself; because one follows it and seeks it, it is called 'meaning' (*artha*)."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the locus of qualities,' this refers to the exposition of the Buddha's qualities, namely the twenty-one kinds of preeminent qualities.
The Explanation says: "'The most pure awakening' is the first phrase, and its meaning is elucidated by the remaining phrases."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “As Master Bandhuprabha explains,” Bandhuprabha is the author of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*. While the two versions of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* do not explain the general sentence [of the verse], this Bodhisattva [Bandhuprabha] provides three distinct interpretations. The commentary then uses logical analysis to select and determine the correct interpretation among them.
However, these three explanations have two underlying intentions:
first, the separate explanation of the general phrase; second, the explanation of the word "correct" (samyak), the word "most pure" (viśuddha), and the word "equal" (sama).
That "Wordless" (Anakṣara) corresponds in meaning to the present sutra.

Second, regarding the phenomena to be realized (*abhisambodhya-dharma*), it provides a brief summary: first, the conditioned and unconditioned as the objects to be realized; second, all things as the objects to be realized; and third, the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāva*) and so forth as the objects to be realized; thus, there is a slight difference.
Furthermore, first, it comprehensively clarifies that which is realized, as there are no more than two categories: the conditioned and the unconditioned;
second, because it exhaustively details the distinctions among all phenomena;
and third, because it universally encompasses both the subject and object through suchness and so forth.
Regarding the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*) and so forth, it shall now be briefly explained.

As stated in the eleventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*: "The object-condition of the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantālambana*) refers to the nature of all phenomena as they exist in their entirety (*yāvadbhāvatā*) and their nature as they truly are (*yathāvadbhāvatā*)."
The commentary on that passage states: "Regarding 'the limit of phenomena' (*vastuparyanta*) and so forth, there are two kinds of phenomena:
first, phenomena as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇavastu*), and second, phenomena as common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇavastu*).

The former refers to the cognitive mind that exhausts the full extent of the dharma; the latter refers to the cognitive mind that, like all things mentioned in the sūtras, shares a common essence and is thus termed a 'limit' (*paryanta*)."
In this context, "matter" (vastu) refers to the object (viṣaya).
According to the text, there are three sections:
first, the presentation of the heading; second, the opening of two meanings; and third, the detailed explanation.
The above constitutes the first two sections; what follows is the specific explanation. The Treatise states:

"As for the nature of the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), it refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). To reveal the essential substance and phenomena of all knowable objects, there is only such a measure and limit; therefore, the three categories of aggregates, elements, and bases are established."
The commentary on that [text] states: "It refers to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.

The treatise says: "'The nature as it is' (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the Four Noble Truths, suchness (*tathatā*), the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the suffering of all conditioned phenomena, the selflessness of all phenomena, the tranquility of nirvāṇa, and so forth; as well as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)."
The commentary on that passage states: "In this context, four types of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are briefly explained:
first, the gate of the truths (*satya-mukha*), referring to the Four Noble Truths;
second, the gate of practice (*pratipatti-mukha*), referring to the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) and suchness (*tathatā*)."
The third gateway of exalted utterance refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent up to being quiescent;
the fourth gateway of liberation refers to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The root treatise mentions the object but does not mention the cognizer.
The treatise states: "Because one cognizes the objects of knowledge through such categories of distinctions in meaning, it is called 'the nature as it is' (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*)."
The commentary first explains the general name and subsequently provides the specific explanation;

this is the former. That is to say, because [the objects] consist of the four truths, the sixteen aspects, and so forth, these constitute the meaning of differentiation within the nature of "exhaustive existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).
As for the cognizing mind, it is called the nature of "suchness as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) because it fully understands all the various differentiations existing among all phenomena.
The treatise states: "Alternatively, one comprehends the objects of knowledge through the gateway of the truths (*satya*).

Its commentary says: "That is to say, one should comprehend, as appropriate, those previously mentioned aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as being suffering (*duḥkha*) up to the path (*mārga*)."

That commentary divides the four distinctions into four sections; this is the first passage. It means that one contemplates, in general, the aggregates, elements, and bases within the nature of "exhaustive existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*): those which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are contemplated as suffering and its origin, while those which are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are contemplated as cessation and the path; hence it says, "according to what is appropriate."

The treatise states: "Alternatively, one may comprehend the objects of knowledge through the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*); it is taught that each of the truths has four aspects (*ākāra*), and furthermore, that all phenomena are without distinction, being solely the aspect of suchness (*tathatā*)."
That commentary states: "The preceding truths and dharma-gates receive their designations based on the objects of cognition (*ālambana*).

From here downward, they receive their designations based on the subjects of cognition (*ālambaka*"; that is, each of the four truths has its own four aspects (*ākāra*), which means that one understands the aggregates and so forth by applying the previously established general understanding of the truths."

Now, by means of a distinct fourfold analysis within each individual truth (*satya*), one gives rise to the four modes of practice; furthermore, by taking all phenomena as the object of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one gives rise to the practice of True Suchness—this is precisely what is called "thoroughly understanding impermanence," "True Suchness," and so forth.

"Practice and understanding" is termed "practice"; that is, the aforementioned sixteen modes of practice are the objects of conditioned phenomena (*prajñapti*), while the subsequent mode of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the object of the unconditioned (*aprajñapti*).

The treatise [further] explains that through the gateway of the *udāna* of all phenomena, one realizes the objects of knowledge, namely: "all conditioned things are impermanent," up to "nirvāṇa is quiescent."
Regarding that term *udāna*, it was formerly called *yōtuonà* (憂陀那), which is a corruption.
Its correct translation is "utterance" (*shuō* 說); in meaning, it corresponds to a discourse spoken spontaneously without being questioned.
Names are established according to their meaning, which is also a general summary of that meaning.

Alternatively, they are called "signifying characteristics," meaning that the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is the characteristic sign of the conditioned, while the tranquility of nirvāṇa is the characteristic sign of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The treatise states: "Alternatively, the gates of liberation comprehend the objects of knowledge, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and so forth.
Its commentary says: "That which is called liberation is nirvāṇa, characterized by the severance of fetters (*visaṃyoga*)."
The meditative concentrations on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) are the gateways for entering into nirvāṇa.

Within this context, one realizes the objects before them through the three gates of emptiness and so forth; that is, one realizes that all knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharma*) are empty and signless (*animitta*).
The commentary states:
The meaning of the two natures has been briefly set forth.

That which pertains to the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) is solely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while that which pertains to the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) applies to both truths; thus, it reveals the self-characteristic and common characteristic of the Tathāgata.

Whether it be that which is taught in the scriptures or the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there is nothing that is not realized and awakened to as it truly is; therefore, the commentary simply states: "Because of the equal awakening that simultaneously illuminates the two truths."
"However, when the two truths are equal, then the two natures are unimpeded, encompassing everything without exception.
Since there is nothing that is not known, this constitutes the meaning of 'pervasive.
In the commentary, the section beginning with 'That is, illuminating both' explains the second meaning."
Regarding the passage "That sutra lacks the correct equality" and below, the texts of four sutras are harmonized; it is said that there are omissions, yet all [elements] are contained therein.
First, the four distinct cases are exemplified, and subsequently, from "The 'wondrous' means the subtle and wondrous" onwards, they are explained through reconciliation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The names ‘wondrous,’ ‘correct,’ ‘universal,’ and ‘supreme’ are distinct both in their meanings and the distinctions they exclude”: ‘Wondrous’ excludes that which grasps at characteristics; ‘correct’ excludes the heterodox; ‘universal’ excludes that which is not all-encompassing; and ‘supreme’ excludes that which has not reached the ultimate. As explained in the first assembly, the remaining meanings may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Now each sentence is assigned accordingly”: this is because the three sections within the treatise are presented simultaneously. That is to say, first, twenty-one scriptural passages are listed; second, the root treatise simultaneously establishes the names of twenty-one virtues; and third, the explanatory commentary sequentially cites and explains them all at once. Therefore, they are now assigned and extracted individually to form twenty sections.
Each section of the commentary contains two parts:
first, the explanation of the names and meanings; second, the explanation of the scriptural text.

Regarding the first part, "Non-duality in Manifestation," within the explanation of the names and meanings, the three sections—including the citations from the sūtras, śāstras, and commentaries—may be understood accordingly.
However, in Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, he first cites the names of the qualities from the root treatise and only afterwards points to the sūtra.
As this section states: "Regarding the quality of proceeding unimpededly and invariably with respect to the objects of knowledge," this is precisely the revelation of the non-dual manifestation.
The following sections shall all conform to this principle.

While Vasubandhu first cites the sūtra [before providing commentary], the present commentary first cites the sūtra and subsequently introduces the names established in the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*). Therefore, within the explanation of these names and meanings, they are provisionally divided into two parts:
First, the title is established by citing the sūtra; second, it is explained by quoting the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the first: the five characters "immediately observing the Tathāgata" are additions made by the subcommentary (*ṭīkā*), as they accord with the contemplation of the Buddha’s virtues in this sūtra.
All that follows is from that treatise.
Here, first, regarding "the non-dual does not manifest," one should understand that the title is established by first citing the sūtra.
Below the section "Two Explanations of Non-nature" in the Commentary, this is the second part, which cites and explains the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Śāstra).
Within this, there are three sections:
first, the explanation of the absence of nature; second, the reconciliation of the two treatises; and third, the arising of the absence of nature.
Now, for the first [section], the first explanation of the internal [meaning] also has three parts:
First is the commentary on the treatise;

second, from "This refers to being free from the cognitive obscurations" onwards, the sub-commentary extracts the essential nature of the virtues by taking up the intended meaning from the section on their arising;
third, from "It is not like... onwards, the sub-commentary explains the treatise.
In the second explanation, the phrase "this explanation [applies] to two locations" and below, the commentary reconciles the two meanings.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Vasubandhu agrees with the latter explanation," the text is identical in its entirety.

However, Vasubandhu’s commentary on this consists of four parts: first, citing the name of the sūtra; second, his own explanation; third, quoting the relevant passage from the root treatise; and fourth, a further explanation. As it says in this section:

"In this context, 'the non-manifestation of duality'—first, this cites the sūtra, meaning that because there is no manifestation of duality, it is called 'non-dual manifestation. Second, this explains the meaning, which refers to the merit of proceeding toward the objects of knowledge with absolute unimpededness. Third, this quotes the relevant passage from the root treatise, for the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possesses both obstructions and lack of obstructions. Fourth, this is the further explanation."
The text is largely like this.
Below the section on "Bandhuprabha" in the commentary (*śūtra*), it reconciles Bandhuprabha’s interpretation;
the reading of the text is identical to this [present] one.

In the commentary, from the phrase "Regarding the arising of non-nature" onwards is the third section. This marks the conclusion of Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Commentary), wherein he restates the initial sequence of arising; those who do not understand this mistake it for a further explanation.

Now, I shall also extract its development into twenty sections and correlate them individually, sentence by sentence; this is the first sentence within these particulars, which follows upon the preceding general statement.

Therefore, the previous commentary states: "This sutra refers to non-afflicted ignorance [arising] from the separation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This means that the essence of the cognitive obstructions is distinguished from afflicted ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*).
In the commentary, from the words "The text has two parts" onwards, there are two explanations of the text that employ both treatises together.
The first part, on "extensive benefit and happiness," follows the intention of Bandhuprabha.
The second, on "being free from the objects of knowledge," follows the intention of Asvabhāva.
The lower [stage] is free from afflictions; this is precisely the intention of Bandhuprabha.
If one follows Bandhuprabha’s view that non-duality manifests, it is simultaneously free from both obstacles and distinct from both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Adornment with concentration and wisdom produces the roots of goodness in sentient beings,” this explains the sūtra passage from “adorned by the Buddha” up to “abiding securely in roots of goodness.

As for the terms “concentration and wisdom,” the *Lotus Sūtra*, chapter one, states: “The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; according to the Dharma he has attained, adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, he delivers sentient beings by means of this. Thus it is said.

The Commentary states: "Both the subject that abides and the object in which it abides are equally vast. That which is the object of abiding is the Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*), which pervades all places; therefore, the vast wisdom is said to be equal to the Dharma-body. Its true nature is like sunlight merging with space.
The sub-commentary states: “Possessing the two meanings mentioned above,” which concludes by returning to the general statement while also serving as an illustration for the following text.
Regarding the section beginning with “Second, wisdom,” within this second virtue there are also two parts:
first, citing the sūtra to establish the name; second, from “absence of nature” (*niḥsvabhāva*) onwards, quoting and explaining the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Śāstra).
Within this, there are again two parts:

first, the explanation of the arising of non-substantiality; the five characters "namely, the nirvana of non-abiding" are from the *Śāstra* (commentary), while all the rest are from the *Bhāṣya* (treatise).
Second, from "However, the signless dharma" onwards, the *Śāstra* adopts the explanation provided in the *Bhāṣya*.

However, the Commentary employs both explanations to interpret the treatise and the names of the Sūtra and the root treatise; thus, the underlying principles are fully exhausted. Yet, as for the wording, it may sometimes be adopted and sometimes omitted. As Asvabhāva states: "That is to say, this *tathatā* possesses the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) and lacks the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*)."
By this principle, the absence of dual characteristics is clarified: there is no characteristic of non-existence, because [the ultimate] is truly existent;
there is no characteristic of existence, because that which is grasped as such does not exist.

Regarding "the merit of entering supreme purity," this refers to the supreme purity of *tathatā* (suchness) itself, for it is the foremost among all phenomena and is far removed from all adventitious defilements.
One is able to enter this suchness through self-awakening, and also enables others to enter it; therefore, it is called the supreme merit of being able to enter complete purity.
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Those who proceed toward the signless dharma" refers to pure suchness, which is named the signless dharma.
"Access" (*gati*) means "entering," which refers to the supreme purity of the merit of being able to enter into suchness that is free from the two characteristics of existence and non-existence.
This means that this suchness does not have the characteristic of existence, because its characteristic is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in all phenomena;

nor does it have the characteristic of non-existence, because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists, as one is able to enter into this suchness which is without characteristics through supreme purity.
The commentary states:
By examining the two preceding treatises in relation to the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), the meaning becomes clearly evident.

Regarding the sub-commentary’s phrase, “the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) pervading the objects of body and mind,” there is a verse that says: “I now understand the nature of the Tathāgata; The Tathāgata is now within my own body. I and the Tathāgata are without distinction; The Tathāgata is my very *tathatā*.”
The Commentary states: “In order to attain the superior [state],” etc., is the second section, which cites and explains the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
It contains only the sense of providing an introduction, situated within the explanatory text.
The Commentary states: “Within the text,” etc., is the explanation of the text itself, which is divided into two parts.
Generally speaking, the first section explains the Sūtra and the second section explains the Śāstra, which is easy to understand from the text itself.

However, if one follows the intent of the Śāstra and cites the *Vyākhyā* in full, the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* states: "That is to say, without exerting effort, one is able to remain continuously engaged in the Buddha-deeds for the sake of sentient beings and so forth; one always correctly abides in the noble, celestial, and Brahma-abodes according to what is appropriate. This is not like the Śrāvakas, who must exert effort to be able to accomplish the work of benefiting sentient beings, nor is it like the non-Buddhists, who, despite having a place of abiding, do not possess such excellence."
The celestial abodes refer to the four dhyānas; the Brahma abodes are the immeasurables such as compassion; and the noble abodes are emptiness, signlessness, and so forth.

Vasubandhu says: "It means dwelling in the place where the Buddha dwells—the nature of non-abiding which is emptiness—and within this dwelling, constantly performing the Buddha-work without rest, which is great compassion."
Now, two treatises are employed to explain the scriptural text.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the nature of great compassion is emptiness, it belongs to the Buddha-family”: great compassion belongs to the family of benefiting others, whereas the nature of emptiness belongs to the family of self-benefit.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that great compassion is the dwelling, while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of the "house of ultimate emptiness and stillness.
Moreover, these two aspects mutually guide one toward the house of reality; therefore, they are both established together.
From "Therefore, he is able to abide nowhere" onwards, it means that he is supported by the Great Compassion and Prajñā.
Regarding the commentary's phrase "As above, the Buddha abides," this refers to the arising of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The Commentary states: "All Buddhas" and below takes up what was previously mentioned to serve as the opening for the question.
Therefore, the answer now says:
"They dwell in a state of intermingling."
This also explains the sutra.

From the passage "All Buddhas" onwards, the treatise merely provides the headings; within the text, three matters are explained in detail, each first citing the heading and providing the commentary's explanation, followed by a specific interpretation according to the sutra.

In the first [section], from "emanating great" (*mahā-vimocana*) onwards is the commentary; in the second, from "the words 'universally causing'" (*sarva-saṃcodana*) onwards is the commentary; in the third, from "first clarifying" (*pūrva-prakāśana*) onwards is the commentary.
Regarding this virtue, Vasubandhu merely provides its classification.
The passage in the Commentary beginning with "Within the benefit of others" introduces Asvabhāva’s text.
The section beginning with "Having already become habituated" explains the meaning of the term "merit," which is entirely from Asvabhāva’s treatise.
Regarding the phrase "Therefore, the treatise designates it as 'cultivation and purification' (bhāvanā-vyavadāna)," this is an explanation from the *Śāstra*.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, having already reached" is an explanation from the *Anāśraya-śāstra*.
Since the *Śāstra* intends to correlate these with the Sūtra, it concludes by stating, "The two texts mutually clarify [the meaning]."
From the section "Within the text" (*wénzhōng*) onwards, the commentary (*shū*) extracts the meaning of the *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) to explain the sūtra text.
Regarding the passage "Because there exists a superior antidote" (*yóuyǒu shàng néngzhì*) and below, the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* provides the following exposition:
From "That is to say, the teaching and the realization" onwards is Asvabhāva’s commentary.
From "Manifesting the Tathāgata" onwards is the introduction.
From "That is to say, the eight worldly winds" onwards is the explanation.

I have thus extracted the essential meaning from the commentary to provide a concise explanation, while also reconciling it with the works of Bandhuprabha; as the five sensory objects, such as form and so forth, are the domains of Māra, I shall present the full commentary only when we reach the relevant section of the explanatory text.

The statement in the text, "It is not because they are like those blind from birth who lack faith that [the Buddha] does not manifest," refers to the meaning within the first dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The commentary’s citation, "As a verse says," refers to the *Anabhāvavāda-śāstra* (Treatise on Non-nature).
The commentary states: "By relying on the aforementioned preliminary means," and so forth, [the section] introduces the subject.
From "That is to say, the twelvefold" onwards, the commentary extracts the meaning of the treatise to provide an explanation.

Wuxing’s *Vyākhyā* says: "That is to say, the twelve divisions of the teaching, such as the sūtras and so forth, are called 'that which is established,' because they establish their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)."
Established in this manner, it is not within the sphere of the cognition of ordinary fools, for it is supramundane.
This establishment is inconceivable; such is its excellence.
The Commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "From 'The above is the preparatory stage' (*prayoga*) onwards, [the text] introduces the arising.
From 'That is, regarding the three periods of time' onwards, it explains the meaning; this is the interpretation of Wu-xing."
However, there is further text preceding this which states:
"That is to say, one is able to traverse universally throughout the nature of phenomena that is equal across the three periods of time.
The section beginning with "That is to say, [the nature] equal across the three periods of time" is identical in its entirety to that treatise.

The phrase "Therefore, the subsequent sutra" and below serves as a proof, because the *Sutra on Wandering through the Three Times* is not explicit; thus, it is supplemented with other meanings within the text.
The commentary’s section beginning with "Manifesting the aforementioned benefit" and below introduces the subject matter.
The meaning is contained within the text; as it is easy [to understand], it is not further explained.
Wuxing says: "This means that according to those to be converted, one manifests two bodies throughout all worlds in order to bring them benefit and happiness."
The commentary states: From "Eleventh" below, to "Because in the ten directions above" below, it introduces the subject.
From "Regarding all objects" below, it explains the meaning, which is entirely the *Tattvaviniścaya-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Determination of Reality).
The two doubts mentioned in the text are also from the treatise itself.

The treatise contains only two phrases: "One who is not himself certain regarding all phenomena cannot resolve the doubts of others"—this is the negative explanation (*pratiṣedha*); "one cannot sever doubt apart from certainty"—this is the positive affirmation (*anvaya*).
The commentary uses only the former phrase.

According to the Liang dynasty *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, one who possesses the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) is able to resolve their own doubts, while one who possesses the four analytical eloquences (*pratibhāna*) is able to resolve the doubts of others.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The Bodhisattva Moon of Wisdom Light,” this refers to the verse from the fifty-ninth sūtra.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It may also be attributed to the aforementioned Manifest Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya),” this passage possesses two implications:

first, it is attributed to the eleventh [chapter] as a means of severing one's own doubts; second, it also applies to the tenth [chapter], where its body is disseminated throughout all worlds, which involves severing the doubts of others before being specifically attributed to the eleventh.
Since it is correct to associate [this phrase] with what follows, it is said that it may also be associated with what precedes it.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because one has deeply entered dependent origination, doubts and views are extinguished,” the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: “Deeply entering dependent origination, one cuts off all false views; regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence, no further habitual tendencies remain.”
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* verse states: "Dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent; they arise through causes and conditions.
This is because by perceiving causes and conditions, one is able to sever doubt.
The Commentary states: "Because the dispositions of those to be converted (*vineya*) differ" refers to their arising.

The section beginning with "namely, entering into various [realms]" explains the meaning; since the two treatises are easily interchanged, I have merely attributed the sūtra to the respective treatise.

The intent of this commentary is as follows: the accomplishment of great awakening is categorized under the "knowable" (jñeya), for it is differentiated according to the various distinctions of mental activities, ultimately reaching the state of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
As explained in the commentary on the text, this is therefore merely an interpretation based on the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding "opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "Because, precisely at the preceding [passage]," it introduces the subsequent section.
The passage beginning with “referring to the noble śrāvakas” explains the meaning, all of which intends that they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Like one seeking to cross [a river] who has been gathering firewood for many kalpas,” this refers to the ninth chapter of the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Great Ornament Treatise). It cites this anecdote because it was said there that making offerings to a śrāvaka yields immeasurable merit, let alone to a Tathāgata.
In the past, there was a man who, through the power of certain conditions, resolved to leave the household life. He went to a monastic dwelling but found that the Buddha was not there.
He then approached Śāriputra, who observed that the man possessed no roots of goodness whatsoever.
He approached the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus first asked him:
"Who did not ordain you?
He replied:
“Śāriputra,” [he said].
Thus, they passed him on from one to another, and none of them took him across.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata went to the gate of the monastery and spoke this verse:
"The body of all-encompassing wisdom has great compassion as its essence.
Within the triple world, the Buddha beholds all those children who are to be transformed, loving them without ceasing, just as a cow seeks her calf."
He stroked the man’s head with his hand; the man wept bitterly and related in detail the causes and conditions for why he had not been delivered.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
“Śāriputra, Śāradvatīputra, was not omniscient; He did not understand the nature of reality, Nor did he fully know the middle and lower capacities.”
"His consciousness is limited and he cannot understand deeply; there is no wisdom capable of knowing the subtle retribution of karma.
He then led him into the monastery, where he was ordained and attained the Way.
Śāriputra asked, "I observe that this person has not the slightest root of goodness; how can you grant him ordination and enable him to attain the Way?
The Buddha said:
"Your wisdom is shallow and limited.
In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, this person was a poor man who entered a forest hermitage to gather firewood. When he was pursued by a tiger, out of fear he cried out, 'Namo Buddha. "
"The seeds have now ripened; therefore, I deliver them so that they may attain arhatship.
Thus, it was said above: "It is accompanied by the seeds of even a slight root of goodness."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The eleventh, then, is for severing one’s own doubts”: according to Asvabhāva and Vasubandhu, all eleven [stages] sever the doubts of others;
however, following Bandhuprabha here, this specific explanation is given.
The Commentary states: "By means of the aforementioned skillful knowledge... and so forth, which introduces the subsequent section.

Above this, the Commentary follows the preceding point to generate the next; Asvabhāva merely says: "It is simply that, within the midst of the correct and incorrect conduct of the sentient beings to be converted, the signs that should appear are not to be distinguished."
The meaning lies within the text.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "Yet Asvabhāva says," this serves to harmonize and explain the *Vyākhyāyukti*.

However, Asvabhāva states in full: "That is to say, according to the various inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings, he manifests golden bodies and so forth; although he manifests these bodies, he is without conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*), like a mani jewel or a flute, as explained at length in that *Tathāgataguhyasūtra*."
The commentary states:
Therefore, the sub-commentary (shu) resolves this in accordance with the current text.
The sub-commentary’s passage, "Gopā contemplates the Buddha’s pores," refers to the seventy-fifth sūtra.
In the fifteenth section of the Commentary (*śāstra*), from the passage beginning "In order to induce... onwards, the [subject matter] is generated.
From the passage beginning "That which is sought by words, etc.," onwards, this is the commentary (*śāstra*) explaining the Sūtra; the meaning resides within the explanatory text.
Regarding the statement therein, "This sought-after wisdom is that upon which immeasurable bodhisattvas rely," this is the explanation by Wuxing.
The section beginning with "and yet it is called the Path" is the commentary on the sūtra.
The Commentary states: "From 'by means of immeasurable bodhisattvas' up to 'obtaining wondrous wisdom,' all [of this] is the explanation by Wuxing.

In the root treatise, following this, there is further text which says: "Bodhisattvas of diverse types receive and uphold the entrustment, passing it on in succession without interruption; through this, they realize the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas."
The commentary states:
This refers to the wisdom established within the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
It means that by relying on this wisdom, one brings about transformation and birth, causing [beings] to be born into this wisdom; therefore, bodhisattvas seek it all.
The commentary states: "In order to exclude those to be converted," and so forth, introduces the subject.
From "By fulfilling all the perfections" onwards, the commentary summarizes the intended meaning to answer the preceding doubt.
From "It is said that there is no duality," the Bodhisattva Wu-xing (Asvabhāva) correlates the text of that sūtra with this treatise.
From the section beginning with "There are two kinds of equality" onwards, the meaning is explained; both meanings concern the theory of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The treatise states: "Because it is established as the fulfillment of the fruit-stage of the *pāramitās* based upon the equal *dharmakāya*"; this refers to the previous point.
The treatise states: "Alternatively, 'equality' means there is neither decrease nor increase.
Within the dharmakāya, all pāramitās are fully perfected;
therein, there is neither increase nor decrease, unlike how the pāramitās may increase or decrease within those bodhisattva stages."
The commentary states:
This refers to the subsequent intention.
Of these two, the former sense of equality belongs to the Dharmakāya, while the latter sense of equality belongs to the various perfections (pāramitās).
However, according to the *dharmakāya*, it is that which is to be fulfilled, while the various perfections (*pāramitās*) are that which fulfill it.
Below, [the commentary by] Bandhuprabha identifies the *dharmakāya* as the *pāramitās*; this is consistent with the former interpretation of Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva.
The commentary states, “The refutation of the synthetic consciousness,” which follows the intent of the *Awakening of Faith*.
This was already presented in the preceding text and is now clarified once more below.
From the passage beginning “Because others hear,” the argument is developed.
The passage beginning with "That is, all suchness" explains the meaning.
This is the commentator’s general explanation of the non-intermingled meanings within the sūtra.
The commentary continues from "But the sūtra says 'the liberation of the Tathāgata'" onwards to reconcile the differences between the sūtra and the śāstra.
Among these, the first citation from two commentaries clarifies that the root treatise is consistent with the sutra; thus it says, "resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) is called liberation (vimukti).
Why is resolute conviction given the name "liberation"?
Resolve (adhimokṣa) has the nature of determining and maintaining an object.
For example, if one forms the resolve that the great earth is gold, it becomes gold;
if one forms the resolve that it is many, it becomes many.
This is the inconceivable function of liberation.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Having attained this liberation, one can cause Mount Sumeru to enter a mustard seed," and so forth.
2. From "Furthermore, [regarding] resolute belief" (*adhimukti*) onwards, it is understood that this applies to both those who transform others and those being transformed.
3. From "Bandhuprabha" onwards, it clarifies liberation through the removal of hindrances.
4. From "Observing the present sutra" onwards, it generally summarizes the various treatises.
5. Regarding "The Buddha adds [the phrase] 'himself free from obstacles,'" this is because Bandhuprabha only had sentient beings free them.

In the commentary, the section beginning with "The reason it is called 'unmixed'" provides a detailed explanation according to the specific difficulties raised; this constitutes the exegesis of the sūtra.
Within this, first there is the question, followed by the explanation beginning with "Therefore, that to which they belong is different.
This explains how that to which they belong is different.
This means there is no confusion among them;
like a thousand lamps that are each distinct,
they pervade everywhere in successive layers.
This is the meaning of "uninterrupted" (*anantara*).
Just as light interpenetrates with light,
the preceding summary statement says it is like a thousand lamps in a dark room.
The Commentary states: "In the superior case, the mind has high and low" refers to the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Śrīvatsa said to Śāriputra:
"O worthy one, your mind has high and low."
"Because they do not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom, they perceive this land as impure.
Now, the aforementioned transformed lands are shown to vary in height according to the mind; what is now seen as the Land of Enjoyment relies upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Commentary states: "From 'due to doubting the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata above,' [the following] arises; this merely elaborates upon the preceding meaning.
Regarding the phrase "as for the directions and locations," the Commentary below briefly reconciles that with the root treatise and the sūtra.
From the passage "In this absence of middle and extremes, there are briefly four meanings" onwards, the general commentary explains their significance.
The first four explanations all intend the meaning of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
However, regarding these four meanings: first, taking the world as a metaphor; second, the Buddha-body pervading the world—both of the former two employ the world as a model;
third, the Dharma-body pervading the stages of Buddhahood; and fourth, because it accords with the Middle Way.
However, the commentary has already fully encompassed the intended meaning.

To provide the full text of the *Nirabhilāpya-svabhāva* [Treatise], it says: "Just as the world has no center or periphery, so too is the Buddha-ground; its qualities and spatial extent are without limitation."

Alternatively, since the spatial dimensions of worlds are infinite, the three bodies of the Buddhas abide within them, pervading them equally in accordance with the measure of those worlds; for the Dharma-body dwells within such worlds and nowhere else.
Alternatively, the Dharma-body is equal to the stage of Buddhahood, pervading all things equally; it is neither central nor peripheral, and possesses no boundaries.
Alternatively, this Dharma-body pervades all places, manifesting to bring benefit to all sentient beings.
"However, it is not that there is neither middle nor limit within the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The commentary states:
By correlating this with the four sections of the *Vyākhyā*, it can be understood that Bandhuprabha’s intention accords with the latter [of the two views].

The Commentary states: "Because the body of unimpeded wisdom has no basis" refers to the citation from the "Manifestation Chapter," establishing that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the wisdom whose meaning is being without reliance.
Therefore, that text states: "All Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion; compassion, in turn, is established based upon skillful means (*upāya*).
Skillful means rely upon knowledge (*jñāna*), and knowledge relies upon wisdom (*prajñā*); the body of unimpeded wisdom has no basis."
However, unimpeded wisdom is subsumed under fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), because fundamental wisdom subsumes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
As for the remaining points regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and so forth, their meaning is as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The meaning of the four wisdoms has already been explained as previously stated.
In the commentary, the passage beginning with “taking delusion as the seed” explains the purity of the Dharma-body.
Since the word “purity” (清淨) is used twice, it says “all have already” (悉已).

This means that when the seven consciousnesses are in the causal state, they are associated with the four afflictions and are only able to grasp internal objects and undergo internal perfuming to form seeds.
Now, being devoid of the four afflictions, these very seven consciousnesses are able to give rise to mastery; they no longer undergo internal perfuming, and thus it is said as such.
The Commentary states: "In terms of the total meaning of the above points, there are ten bodies": first, by means of awakening others, one clarifies that self-awakening is the Bodhi-body;
second, the accomplishment of the Dharma-body and the manifestation of Suchness is the Dharma-body;
third and fourth, the three wisdoms are the Wisdom-body.
Fourth, the excellence of the four adornments refers to the body adorned with the primary and secondary marks;
fifth, being incapable of being eclipsed refers to the body of majestic power;
sixth, immeasurable merit refers to the body of merit.
Seventh, manifesting as bodhisattvas and so forth is the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*);
eighth, causing beings to become free from delusions is the body of aspiration (*praṇidhānakāya*);
and ninth, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The ten courses of action that constitute what appears in the world are precisely what sustain the body;
therefore, it is said that they are "complete in ten.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The above speaks of the absence of center and periphery," this introduces the following section.
The passage beginning with "That is to say, this dharma-dhātu" explains the meaning; it is an interpretation based on the *Wuxing* (Asvabhāva).

In the commentary (*shu*) following the phrase "By this, then, regarding the term 'dharma-dhātu'," the two treatises are reconciled. According to the scriptural text, "permanence" corresponds to the intent of the *Wuxing*, while "purity" corresponds to the intent of *Bandhuprabha*.

In the commentary, from the passage "The Tathāgata is also like this" onwards, the seven matters concerning the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) are presented without a strict sequential order, yet their meaning is complete in every respect.
The first three apply generally to all teachings; the fourth, from "From this point onward," follows the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Thus, within the single Buddha-vehicle, he differentiates and teaches three vehicles, using the provisional to cover the real;
when he brings the three back to the one to reveal the true aspect, he uses the real to cover the false.
The first part explains the general meaning according to the Dharma.
The fifth point, "wearing tattered and soiled garments," refers to the meaning of the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding.
This means that because he does not yet speak of the characteristics of the ten lotus-treasury worlds, it is said that he has "cast off his precious and noble robes."
To speak of the thirty-two marks and so forth is like wearing tattered, defiled robes;
to show that one has long since realized bodhi by severing the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind is like grasping a refuse-removing vessel.
The sixth is the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (*Anlehangpin*), which uses the analogy of the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) untying the bright pearl from his topknot.

The perfect principle of the One Vehicle is likened to the bright pearl; formerly it was concealed by provisional means, as if hidden within the topknot. To open up the provisional and reveal the real is to untie the topknot and give the pearl.
The seven meanings are also applicable here.
In the commentary, from the phrase "referring to the superior benefit and happiness" onwards, the subject is introduced.
From the phrase "the profound and secret Buddha-ground" onwards, the commentary distinguishes between the opening and closing [of the sections].
Within this, there are six [sections]:
first, the opening and closing according to the sūtras and śāstras;
second, the opening by Bandhuprabha;...
Third, the meaning of the three non-attachments is combined;
