first, that she might sell her son and return to her native country; second, that her son would not suffer from hunger; and third, that she and the crown prince would return early to their native country.
Śakra said, "It shall be as you have wished.
The Prince then made this vow:
"May all sentient beings attain liberation from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Śakra praised him, saying, "How great is this vow! It is beyond my power to achieve."
"What further wish do you seek?
He replied with another vow:
"For now, I wish to attain great wealth so that I may constantly practice giving."
"Furthermore, I pray that the king and his ministers shall all wish to see me.
Śakra replied, "As you wish."

The Brahmin took his son and returned home; his wife, filled with resentment, asked what use he had for a member of the royal lineage, and instead sought out slaves. He subsequently sold his son in a foreign land.
Śakra, though attempting to entice buyers, found no one to purchase him, so he eventually reached his own country.
The people of the country recognized him and informed the king. When the king wished to embrace him, the boy wept and refused to go to him.
He asked the man who had sold him, who replied first:
"For this man, [I require] one thousand silver coins and a hundred head of special oxen."
"A daughter is worth two thousand silver coins; a cow, two hundred.
The king asked, "Why is a daughter so precious and a son so base?"
He replied:
"The king's concubines have no kinship with the king; they rose from humble and lowly origins yet received his honor and favor.
The king has but one son, yet he banished him to the deep mountains and never once looked back with affection."

Knowing clearly that women are noble and men are base, the King then sent men to pursue the Prince back, entrusting him with a treasury of jewels to bestow as he pleased; thus, he attained Buddhahood.
The father was Śuddhodana; the mother was Māyā; the consort was Gopī; the son was Rāhula; the daughter was Sītā; the brahmin was Devadatta; and his wife was Ciñcāmānavikā.
"The mountain-dwelling practitioner is Maudgalyāyana; the hunter is Ānanda.
Commentary: "Manifesting as King Prabhūtaratna" is as described in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding the *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* which speaks of 'Sarvadhārīrāja giving his two sons,' this sūtra consists of three fascicles; the present section extends from the middle of the first fascicle toward the end, up to the middle of the second fascicle."
However, as for its causal origin, it closely resembles that of Sudāna;

yet whereas he gave away one son and one daughter, this [prince] gave away two sons, both male, and furthermore, his eyes were requested. Aside from the lack of the king’s invitation to return, most other details are the same.
To cite another brief example:

King Sarvadharman, who was fond of giving, presented a white elephant that walked upon lotuses and possessed the power to rival an enemy nation. The people of his kingdom and his ministers were all struck with fear; moreover, apprehensive that the enemy might invade, they subsequently banished the prince to the Snowy Mountains.
In the mountains, he gave his two children to an ugly brahmin; the brahmin sold them and reached his own country, where the ancestral king was struck with amazement.
Later, Śakra transformed himself into a brahmin and begged for the prince’s wife, and the prince gave her to him.
He then said, "Your wife is beautiful; I fear she might be abducted by bandits.
I entrust her to you for the time being, but I must take her back."
Having heard this, the prince accepted it in silence.
Then, [the deity] again transformed into a brahmin and begged him for his eyes. As the prince was about to gouge them out, [the deity] stopped him, saying:
"I do not need them yet; lend them to me for the time being, and I shall certainly take them back when I require them."
The prince said,
"How could I accept two kinds of entrusted deposits?
Śakra, knowing the firmness of his resolve, returned to his celestial form and said:
"Your wife and your eyes—these two things are my possessions.
I now entrust them to you; do not give them away to others.
Having said this, he flew through the air and departed, raining down flowers and praising [the Bodhisattva], saying that he would surely realize Bodhi.
The Commentary states: "However, as for the actual transformation performed... and so forth, this is the second section, which provides a detailed analysis.

Regarding the phrase "As in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Vaiśravaṇa," etc., this refers to the first scripture. Because the Brahmā King requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma, the Buddha declined, saying: "Sentient beings are obscured by defilements; it would not be right for me to extinguish them too quickly."
The Brahma King then cited past causes and conditions to exhort the Buddha:
"In the past, throughout incalculable kalpas, for the sake of seeking the Dharma for sentient beings, you gave even a single verse, sacrificing your body, mind, wife, and children as offerings."
Why do you not reflect on the past and instead wish to abandon this life?
Long ago in the distant past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Śūraprabha, who ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms within this world.
Initially, he provided material gifts; later, intending to provide the gift of the Dharma with steadfastness and substance, he sought out a teacher.

King Vaiśravaṇa, wishing to test him, transformed himself into a yakṣa—his complexion dark blue-black, his eyes red as blood, his fangs protruding, and his hair bristling—and went to the gate of the royal palace, saying:
"I am able to preach the Dharma."
The king invited him into the palace, wishing to request that he preach the Dharma.
He replied:
"If you first give me my beloved wife and my beloved son as food, then I shall grant you the Dharma."
The king immediately gave him his beloved queen and the most excellent of his sons.
When the yakṣa had finished eating, he spoke this verse for the king:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; that which is born is subject to suffering."
"The five aggregates are empty and signless; there is no self, nor anything belonging to a self.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy; he transcribed the teaching and circulated it widely, free from any regret.
Vaiśravaṇa then resumed his original form and praised him, saying:
"How extraordinary!
The queen and her son still remain as they were before.
The King was the Buddha; if he was thus devoted to the Dharma in the past, why does he now pass away so quickly?
The commentary states:
"In this case, the wife and children are real, while the beggar is a transformation.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "This refutes the attachment of the Bodhisattva," it is as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "Those who act as Māras throughout the worlds of the ten directions are mostly Bodhisattvas abiding in the inconceivable liberation, who manifest as Māras through the power of skillful means."
Therefore, it is said that this "destroys the attachment of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "the two beggars are treasures," the citation from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* refers to its eleventh chapter.

The Liang translation of the commentary states: "Or he manifests various jātaka tales; by means of afflicting others or afflicting enemies, he causes them to develop a mind of mutual affection, benefit, and peace."

The Commentary states: "In order to transform sentient beings with wrong views who do not believe in cause and effect, and to lead them to attain the True Dharma, abandon evil, and cultivate goodness, he manifested various Jātaka tales."
It is like King Viśvantara who gave his son to a brahmin; this was not an act of afflicting another. Why?
Because this son was a magical creation.
For what reason?
This is because the Bodhisattva does not cause affliction for one person while producing peace and happiness for another.
For example, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja caused King Mūrdhaja and King Videha to afflict one another.
This, too, is a transformation; subsequently, it causes all beings to have hearts that desire one another’s benefit and happiness.
What is the benefit of a bodhisattva performing such deeds?

The Treatise says: "First, they generate faith in others; subsequently, those roots of goodness ripen within the noble paths of the three vehicles. This is called the distinction of the bodhisattva’s profound discipline."
The three cases of simultaneous transformation can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the four types of jewels, as for those "whose two faculties have matured," it is like the case of King Sarvada, who gave his son to a brahmin; the brahmin then whipped him and took him away.
Arriving beneath a tree, he intended to strike him again; the tree deity reached out his hand toward the brahmin, and the brahmin immediately fell down.
The deity wished to take his life, but instead seized the prince and sent him back.
The prince said to the deity,
"Please do not harm them.
If I return again and cause my father, the King, to fall short in his practice of giving, I shall be an unfilial son."
The deity then released him.
This is precisely what is meant by "the wife and children traveling together.
Since one must still sacrifice one's own life, how could one decline out of a desire to avoid suffering?
Regarding the statement "the place where giving was practiced by the 'giver of births,'" this refers to the events from the past karmic conditions of the seventy-five Śākya women,
including Gopā. At that time, the maiden Sumati desired to serve the Prince,
but the Prince stipulated that she must not become an obstacle to his cultivation of the Bodhisattva path.
She thought to herself:
"I have no defiled heart; I request to be the mistress.
Among the verses she spoke to the Prince, there was a verse that said: "For immeasurable kalpas, I have borne him upon my head, like a vast mountain of adamant."
If you would graciously accept me, I shall endure this suffering with a willing heart.
Within the immeasurable ocean of birth and death, I offer my own flesh as a gift;
may I likewise attain the station of the Dharma King when you do.
"If you would deign to accept me and grant me the status of your master, I pray that in every birth throughout my practice of giving, you may always accept me as an offering.
The commentary states:
These are all those whose faculties have reached maturity.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'if one relies on the *Ābharaṇa* [Sūtra] concerning the fifteen wheel-turning kings,' this refers to the three levels of worthiness (the *tri-śukla*), the ten stages of sainthood (*daśārya-bhūmi*), and the two types of awakening—the Equal and the Sublime. These shall be analyzed in detail in the 'Chapter on the Minor Marks' (*Anuvyañjana-paṭala*')."
In this context, it refers to the Brahmā King of the Third Dhyāna.
According to the *Mahāpuruṣacaryā-śāstra*, the joy and bliss of a Bodhisattva surpasses that of the mundane world as well as the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles.

This treatise consists of two fascicles, or is simply titled the *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra*. It extensively describes the matters of worldly superior pleasures, yet none of these can equal the joy felt by a Bodhisattva upon seeing a beggar; furthermore, even the ultimate bliss of liberation mentioned at the end cannot match it, as it surpasses that of the Two Vehicles.
The Commentary states: “The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 39, says:

‘Furthermore, regarding the obstacles to giving and their remedies for all bodhisattvas. Within this, there are first the heading, second the enumeration of the obstacles, and third the explanation of the remedies.
The first two [sections] present the full treatise, while within the section on remedies, I have merely extracted the essential meaning of the treatise.

Nevertheless, the treatise is extensive and comprehensive, encompassing all meanings without omission; at its conclusion, the treatise states: "In this way, regarding the four kinds of obstacles to a bodhisattva’s giving, one should know that four kinds of remedial wisdom serve as their antidotes."
First, awakening; second, enduring all sufferings; third, thoroughly knowing perversions; and fourth, seeing that the nature of all conditioned phenomena is not solid.
By means of the first three types of remedial wisdom, these bodhisattvas are certainly capable of correctly practicing generosity;
by means of the latter type of remedial wisdom, they are able to correctly appropriate the superior fruits of the merit of giving.
"One should know that this is also called the Bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom in practicing giving while remaining detached from signs.
Regarding the commentary's phrase "first severing the notion of self," this refers to the stage of the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*).

The Commentary states: "First, not giving rise to increase or decrease regarding the essence of phenomena" means that the essence of all phenomena does not transcend existence or non-existence; to hold it as definitely existent is to exaggerate (samāropa), while to hold it as definitely non-existent is to depreciate (apavāda).

Regarding the phrase "fourthly, regarding the meaning of all phenomena, one is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence": within the single existence of a phenomenon, there are the meanings of both permanence and impermanence. That which arises from conditions is impermanent; that which does not arise from conditions is termed permanent.
The five [aggregates] and the three realms of existence are the sudden transformation of consciousness-only, termed "images" (pratibimba), which serve as the basis for their arising.

Perception (*saṃjñā*) is thus mind, yet it is neither perception nor mind; this explains the phrase: "In the six [objects], regarding the fundamental nature of phenomena, one leaves behind the mind and does not perceive them as mind."
All the preceding phrases contain the term "perception" (saṃjñā); all dharmas are sustained by perception, which generally signifies the presence of mind.
Since the mind is the root of all phenomena, the forgetting of the mind constitutes non-perception (asaṃjñā).
Now, as they are all sent forth together, it is said that "the six" refers to the mind being sent forth according to the *dharmamūla*, rather than being a mental conception.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "Because existence is identical to emptiness," this clarifies that based on conditioned existence (*pratyaya*), the two types of emptiness are of one flavor, being equal and without distinction.
From the perspective of True Suchness (*tathatā*), none of these possess any objective referent.

However, according to the established system of Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there is the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the existence of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Since we are now clarifying that [the dependent] exists as a condition, it is not the case that its nature consists of the two absences (of self and phenomena); rather, its very nature is non-existence.
Regarding the statement, "The absence of non-conception entails the presence of manifold mentalities," there are briefly five meanings;
the first dispels the negation of a non-existent entity, such as space, a tortoise’s hair, or a rabbit’s horns.

Second, it clarifies that conditioned existence is itself emptiness. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Form is itself emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness, for the nature of form is itself empty.
This clarifies that existence is itself non-existence; therefore, this [text] clarifies that it is not the cessation of form that constitutes emptiness.

The third [verse] dispels the notion that the unconditioned is non-existent; the fourth dispels the notion that the unconditioned is not non-existent. Both the third and fourth dispel [extremes] by taking emptiness as the meaning of existence.
Fifth, the preceding four [verses] clarify non-existence by dispelling errors;
this line reveals the reality, clarifying that non-existence does not obstruct existence.
"Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: 'It is neither existent nor non-existent. This is a citation of scriptural evidence.
This 'neither non-existent' is precisely 'not non-existent.
However, to say merely 'not non-existent' contains fewer implications."
To say "not non-existent" carries many implications;

however, by merely saying "not non-existent," one obtains the first two meanings. As for the latter two meanings, it is only by saying "not non-non-existent" that they are fully encompassed from beginning to end.
However, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as the ancients said:
"When I say 'it is not existent,' I merely mean it is not [inherently] existent; I do not mean it is non-existent.
This is because the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) are existence and thus non-existence, and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is existence and thus not non-existence.

The five preceding phrases merely follow the sequence of the sutra text to form two pairs; from here below, the four phrases are collectively refuted: when combined with the former, they constitute the "both" phrase, and when mutually negated, they constitute the "neither" phrase.
Since the fundamental basis of existence and non-existence lacks the category of "both," how could "neither" be established?
This does not yet address the resolution of the concluding phrase; it merely takes the fourth sense among the four alternatives within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This may also be understood concurrently with the fifth [stage], which is the non-obstructive perception (*anāvaraṇasaṃjñā*).
Regarding the "subsequent pairing that reveals bondage and liberation": conceptualization (*vikalpa*) constitutes bondage, while non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) constitutes liberation.
The Commentary states: "Next, 'pairwise revealing the two karmas' refers to volition (*cetanā*) and that which follows volition as the two.
"Finally, 'also clarifying bondage and liberation through pairs' means that where there is mind, there are the waves of birth and death; therefore, it is not the non-mind that performs dedication."
To be without mind would be identical to the non-Buddhist paths; therefore, this is not a dedication performed through the absence of mind.
This constitutes the principle that "there is nothing that does not obstruct existence.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, by means of being without mind" clears away all traces to clarify the preceding meaning.
To say that having a mind is "not having it" means there is active movement.
To say that not having a mind is "not [the case]" means there is no contemplative observation.
This is precisely stillness that does not lose its illumination; as for the latter sense, it is simply stillness within stillness. Both of these possess their own道理 (principle/reason).

The Commentary states: "If there were originally no bondage, who would seek liberation? This implicitly employs the passage from the "Dharma Gate of Non-duality" in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta says:
"'Delighting in nirvāṇa' and 'not delighting in the world' constitute a duality."
If one does not delight in nirvāṇa and does not feel aversion toward the world, then there is no duality. Why is this?
If there were bondage, there would be liberation; but if there has been no bondage from the very beginning, who could seek liberation?
"When there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither joy nor aversion; this is called entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Regarding the commentary's phrase, "Suddenly finding no point of reliance, the principle naturally accords in mystery," these words are from Master Sengzhao’s *Preface to the Śata-śāstra*.

Therein lie two pairs [of characteristics]: it is said that "in his discourses, his words are never off the mark and his refutations leave no room for rebuttal; though he remains detached and without reliance, the facts do not lose their truth, and though he is aloof and without dependence, the underlying principle naturally accords with the profound mystery."
"The way of returning to the root is clearly manifested herein.
The commentary states:
This is a general exposition of the treatise's central thesis.
The former pair concerns the non-loss of phenomena (*vastu*), while the latter pair concerns the non-loss of principle (*tattva*).
Although these do not explicitly rely on an exposition of phenomena and principle, they nonetheless accord with them.
Now, this commentary combines these two pairs; it takes only the non-loss of principle, because this constitutes dedication free from conceptual marks (*nimitta-parāvṛtti*).
"Tang" (儻) means "extraordinary" (俶儻).
The *Guangya* states: "'Extraordinary' refers to being eminent and exceptional.
This means that while having no basis for reliance, one stands out as eminent and exceptional, and in a manner of speaking, darkly accords with principle.

The commentary states: “Because seeking [birth] throughout the three periods of time is impossible,” which generally clarifies the meaning of the text; this refers to the "three-time gate" (*trikāla-mukha*) of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
“Because it arises from non-existence, it is called ‘birth’” establishes the principle of birth.
Below, the seeking of the three periods of time is distinguished individually; the characteristic of arising cannot be found.
That which has already arisen, that which has not yet arisen, and that which is currently arising constitute the three.
The fact that what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen do not arise is a principle easily made manifest.
The present moment of arising is hidden by its very nature.
Because it does not abide, once it is divided into the past and the future, there is no such thing as the present moment of arising.
This is precisely as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: "If it is a past arising, that past arising has already ceased."
If it were birth in the future, that future birth has not yet arrived.
If it were birth in the present, that present birth would have no duration.
Because there is no duration, it would necessarily belong to either the past or the future.
From the section "The Principle of Arising" onwards, the text concludes with non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "discussing the quiescence of consciousness and wisdom": one relies on wisdom (*jñāna*) and does not rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), whereas relying on wisdom is quiescence (*śānti*).
Now, as both are "neither," they cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*) nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This refers to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*); the meaning of these four reliances shall be explained in the following text.
In the commentary on the second section, "Non-obstruction in Accordance with Characteristics," there are three parts:
first, a general explanation of the purpose;
second, from the words "as for 'in accordance with characteristics,'" the explicit clarification of the characteristic of non-disruption.
The statement, "All Buddhas rely on the two truths when teaching the Dharma to sentient beings," refers to the *Catuḥsatya-parivarta* (Chapter on the Four Truths) of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
The subsequent verse further states: "First, the conventional truth; second, the ultimate truth."
"If a person cannot know and distinguish the two truths, then regarding the profound Buddha-dharma, they will not understand its true meaning.
This has already been cited above.
Third, from "However, the conventional is the true conventional" onwards, the two truths mentioned above are integrated to establish the meaning of non-obstruction.
In the commentary, from "Now, first, regarding the names that follow appearances," the text consists of two parts: first, an explanation of the purpose for introducing this section;
[and second, the actual exposition].
Second, from "Briefly Manifesting the Ten Meanings" onwards, the text correctly elucidates the departure from signs and the reception of the name "dedication.
The preceding section was a provisional inquiry; from this point on is the explanation.
This section consists of two parts:
The first part is general;
the second part, beginning with "One who transcends the eight worldly dharmas," is specific, establishing distinct "other shores" according to their respective destinations.
Regarding the former: gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—these eight dharmas are precisely the worldly dharmas.
Being unmoved by the eight worldly dharmas is called the "unmoving shore.
Because one relies on the aggregates (*skandhas*) to conceive of a self, there are two kinds of self.
To be free from these two selves is called liberation.
Third, vitarka and vicāra are the path of speech; since the path is a cause, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) transcends speech.
Fourth, the removal of mindfulness, perception, and contemplation is for the sake of true wisdom.
Fifth, because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of the afflictive hindrances, its mere severance constitutes the state with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa).

Sixth, the body that serves as the basis for suffering is the locus of reliance; when both the body and the wisdom upon which it relies have perished, this is the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Seventh, because the seven types of giving and so forth are precisely the wholesome deeds performed;
eighth, because the Bodhisattva emerges from existence and enters into non-existence without defilement, it is the "non-abiding shore";
ninth, because the realization of the Dharmakāya is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).

The ten characteristics—birth, abiding, change, and cessation—are the conditioned phenomena of the mundane world; because the mind of awakening, through direct perception, realizes that the flow of arising and ceasing has no intrinsic nature, one reaches the shore of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
In the commentary, from the phrase "the nature of bodhi is pure" onwards, there are two types of bodhi:
first, innate purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*); second, perfected purity (*pariniṣpanna-viśuddhi*).
That which arises from conditions is precisely perfected purity.
Purity is further twofold:
first, the clarification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), because the myriad practices serve as its conditions;
second, the clarification of nature-arising (*prakṛti-udbhava*), because it is entirely manifested by the pure meritorious qualities of the *tathatā* (suchness) nature.
Furthermore, because dependent origination is without intrinsic nature, it is intrinsically pure, as explained at length in the "Manifestation" chapter.

This is also the meaning of what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature; the seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; therefore, they preach the One Vehicle. This has already been cited extensively above.
From the passage beginning “If karma depends on the body,” the text explains that karma does not exist within the body.
This is the seventh dedication.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Now, first, the title is cited,” there are four parts:

First, the formal explanation of the name; second, the section beginning with "This derives from" which establishes its designation; third, the section beginning with "Thus, the *Mūla-karma-bhūmi*" which cites scriptural evidence; and fourth, the section beginning with "That is to say, non-attachment" which clarifies its essential nature.
Within these three [sections], there are three parts:
first, the citation of the sutra; second, the correlation with the present text starting from "named as non-existent" (*amūka*); and third, the explanation of that sutra starting from "some say.
Within the third part, first the divergent views are presented, and subsequently, the correct interpretation of the meaning is provided starting from "it should be said."
“Wisdom and skillful means” refers to the intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the seventy-ninth fascicle of the present sutra, which shall be explained in detail below.

Regarding “evil parents are ignorance and craving,” this corresponds to what is said in the third fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: “At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One!’”
As the World-Honored One has said:
"If a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell.
World-Honored One!
"How is it that men and women who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution do not enter the Avīci Hell?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall explain it for you."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The five deeds of immediate retribution consist of killing one's father and mother, harming an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with an evil mind shedding the blood of a Buddha."
Mahāmati! What is the mother of sentient beings?
It is craving for further embodiment, conjoined with greed and delight, which acts as the condition like a mother.
Establishing ignorance as the father and entering the village of the sense bases, one cuts off these two roots; this is called "killing father and mother.
When those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) no longer manifest—like the latency of rat-poison coming to fruition—and one eradicates them completely, this is called "killing an Arhat."
What is the schism of the Saṃgha?

It refers to the ultimate severance of that which is a collection and accumulation of the various aggregates (skandhas) characterized by distinct marks; this is called the schism of the Saṃgha, Mahāmati.

Failing to realize that external objects—whether characterized by specific or general marks—are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one perceives them through the sevenfold body of consciousness. By means of the three gates of liberation, one utterly severs those seven consciousnesses through the cessation of impure perceptions; the Buddha calls this "shedding the blood of the Buddha with an evil mind."
"If men or women perform these acts of immediate retribution, they are called the five deeds of immediate retribution, and are also called the 'Immediate [Realizations]' (*ānantarya*).

A verse says: "Craving is named the mother; ignorance is taken as the father; the consciousness that perceives objects is the Buddha; the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the Arhats; and the accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is named the Saṃgha."
"Severing [the fetters] in immediate succession is called the five immediate transgressions; one does not fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "like the onset of rat poison," there is a type of rat in the West whose bite is extremely toxic.
When poison is within the body, although the wound has healed, it will suddenly flare up again upon encountering the sound of thunder.
It is the same with the practitioner: if they suddenly encounter the "thunder" of sensory objects, their afflictions will once more be stirred and arise.
The remainder may be understood.
Below the phrase "not extinguishing delusion and craving," the meaning of the "unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) is explained; this corresponds to the chapter on Subhūti in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
Those of the two vehicles extinguish delusion to attain clarity, and by extinguishing craving, they achieve liberation.
Now that one nature is fully realized, it is not extinguished; its very essence is luminous liberation.
To know that principle is non-dual is itself to be in accord.
When there is no sign of even this "accord," only then is it true accord.
The Commentary states: "However, as for the first ten," and so forth, this is an analytical selection (*viniścaya*).

Regarding the statement, "The first eleven each arise from the middle ten": [this means that] the small and other [levels] arise from the Buddha-object; the small and other [levels] arise from the Dharma-object; and it is the same for the remaining eight.

Second, regarding the statement "the eleven in the middle can each give rise to the ten subsequent ones": from the single realm of the Buddha, the ten perfections such as *dāna* (generosity) can arise;
from the Dharma, the ten perfections arise, and the same applies to the remaining eight [realms].

Third, regarding the statement "the latter eleven may each possess all ten": this means that among the perfections such as giving (*dāna*), there are small and great varieties; they may consist of one, two, three, or four, or they may be fully complete as ten.
It is not necessary for all [factors] to be present simultaneously; therefore, it is said that they "may be complete.
The same applies to the nine perfections, beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*), in relation to the preceding ten.

Regarding the fourth point, "the eleven preceding [categories] each encompass the twenty subsequent ones," this refers to cases such as initiating a small act of giving (*dāna*) from the perspective of the Buddha-realm, or initiating a great act of giving from the perspective of the Buddha-realm, and so forth.
Whether one gives rise to the minor precepts within the realm of the Buddha, or gives rise to the major precepts and so forth from the realm of the Buddha, the principle is self-evident;
as it is said, "Contemplate this and it will manifest of itself."

The Commentary states: "The six [perfections] above all possess skillful means that are preeminent" refers generally to the seven types of supremacy that constitute the *pāramitās*, which were already fully established in the first assembly.

However, "supremacy" (*paramatva*) is also termed "preeminence" (*viśiṣṭa*); although this was previously explained, it must be understood here as the general intent in contrast to the wording of the sūtra.

Regarding the excellence of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it corresponds to the fifth [category], because it is said to be subsumed by signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*); therefore, all six preceding phrases are signless wisdom.

Regarding the statement that the fifth purity is the most supreme, it corresponds to the seventh [stage]. This means that one must not be interspersed with the two obstacles; specifically, among these, one must be free from the grasping at phenomena as real entities and realize "mind-only" to be separated from the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Third, seeing that the nature is empty and free from the hindrance of afflictions;
next, there are three minds by which one dwells in excellence, the first of which is that one must dwell securely in the bodhisattva lineage.
Next, there are two minds, namely those that are dedicated toward excellence; these constitute the sixth [stage], which means one must dedicate them toward unsurpassed enlightenment.
What is now called "thoroughly resolving all meanings and possessing the three dedications" refers to resolving wisdom, resolving compassion, and resolving the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Next is the "one-pointed mind," which refers to the excellence of intention; this corresponds to the third [requirement], namely, the necessity of having compassion for all sentient beings.
The final two minds refer to the excellence of reliance; these correspond to the second [requirement], namely, the necessity of relying upon the bodhicitta.
Regarding "the excellence of activity within the aforementioned generosity," this corresponds to the fourth [requirement], which means that one must fully carry out all activities.
The phrase "possessing the seven aforementioned [qualities]" below serves to conclude the preceding meaning.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Only when embraced by the seven kinds of supremacy can they be established as pāramitās.
This preceding exegesis of the sūtra accords perfectly with this text, like two halves of a tally.
The Commentary states: "The conduct of the foremost among those in the good destinies and the worthy stages" refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) in its perfect fusion.
"Lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

Although the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) generally encompasses all three "worthy stages," here it specifically takes up the two stages of practice and the direction toward realization (*prayoga-mārga*).

Therefore, the "mind generated through practice and understanding" (*adhimukticaryā-prasthāna-citta*) resides in the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), because it is the generation of the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The *Guhyakapuruṣasūtra* explains this fully in the second [chapter],” this also clarifies it upon reaching the tenth stage, the stage of dedication (*daśama-pariṇāmanā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement, "The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* also cites this sūtra," the treatise states in the sixth verse: "One should understand that the Bodhisattva’s own accomplishments are as previously explained.
That the voice possesses sixty qualities is said to be the activity of the Tathāgata."
In the prose commentary, the *Buddhaguhyasūtra* is cited in full; this *Buddhaguhyasūtra* is none other than the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*, both of which will be clarified below.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, there are places that speak of sixty-four phonemes,” and so forth: while the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts mention the eight case-endings (*vibhakti*), the commentary merely cites their names in the Chinese (Tang) language; here, however, we also clarify them according to their Sanskrit sounds.

According to the laws of the Western Regions, if one wishes to study the inner and outer scriptures, it is essential to understand the *śabdavidyā* (science of grammar) and these eight case endings (*aṣṭavibhakti*), for only then will one know the precise distinctions of the textual meaning.
First, *puruṣa* is a term used for direct designation; it is like pointing out a person when one says, "A man is cutting a tree"—it refers to the agent.
Second, *puruṣakāra* is the term for the action performed; as in the act of cutting a tree, it is therefore called "action" (*karma*).
Third, *karaṇa* is the term for the instrument of action; as in "cutting with an axe," it is called the "instrument.
Fourth, *sampradāna* is the term for the recipient of the action; as in "being cut for someone," it is called the "recipient."
Fifth is *pralopa*, which is the "sound of origin," as in the case of a house built by relying on a person; thus it is called "origin" (*cong*), for "origin" is that which serves as the cause.
Sixth is *pralāpa*, which is the "sound of belonging," as in the case of a slave belonging to a master; thus it is called "belonging" (*shu*).

The seventh is *pralopa* (補盧鎩), which refers to the locative case (*saptamī-vibhakti*). It is called "at" (*yu*) because it is like a guest depending upon a host; thus, "at" carries the meaning of "relying upon.

In the second chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these seven types are termed the "seven examples" (*sapta-prayoga*), as they serve as the primary paradigm for generating understanding. These consist solely of the Sanskrit grammatical cases (*aṣṭa-vibhakti*). To this, one further adds *he-pralopa* (醯補盧沙), which is the vocative sound; hence it is called "calling" (*hu*).
However, each of these eight types of voice has three varieties:
first, the male voice; second, the female voice; and third, the voice that is neither male nor female.
The above explanation was given specifically regarding the male voice, as the Sanskrit term for "man" (puruṣa) is *luśa*.

The Commentary states: "That these eight case endings each possess eight virtues" refers to the eight Brahma-voices, which were already explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*); they shall now be restated.
First, "harmonious" means that the scale is moderate, being neither too large nor too small.
Second, "soft and supple" means that the speech is free from coarseness or harshness.
Third, "clearly understood"—also called "most excellent"—is like the voice of the kalaviṅka bird and others.
Fourth, "easy to understand" (su-vijñeya) is also called "easy to comprehend," because the words and phrases are clear and distinct.
Fifth, "without error" (a-viparīta) is also called "unmistaken speech," because there is no mistake or deviation.
Sixth, "without female" (amātṛka) is also called "not feminine," because its voice is heroic and resonant.
Seventh, "vast" (vipula) is also called "venerable wisdom" (guruprajñā), because it is free from conflict and fear.
Regarding the "eight profound [qualities]," they arise from the navel-cakra (*nābhi-cakra*).
The Tathāgata is endowed with these eightfold tones.

As for the commentary’s statement, "If one takes what follows here as belonging to the preceding fruit of Buddhahood," this reconciles a divergent interpretation; namely, that according to the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text), both sections belong to the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, it is clarified here that practicing the bodhisattva path and associating with virtuous friends do not pertain to the state of Buddhahood itself.
The Commentary states: "The eighth [point] says 'neither identical nor different' refers to the Ten Penetrations (*daśa-samāpattayaḥ*).
The word 'etcetera' serves as a heading;
therefore, within those Penetrations, the meaning of being neither identical nor different is explained in detail."
From the passage beginning with "Because they understand all," it is shown that being neither one nor different is the characteristic of supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
If they were exclusively not one, each would obstruct the other, and they would be unable to act upon one another.
If they were not different in every respect, no duality could be found; what then would perform the function of mutual conditioning?
Because they are not different, the single principle is harmoniously integrated;
because they are not a single identical entity, they are able to perform functions such as mutual conditioning.

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, 'neither one nor different' should result in four propositions": (1) not one; (2) not different; (3) neither not-one nor not-different; and (4) neither both one and different nor neither one nor different. These shall be explained in the *Daśakṣānti*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first three phrases manifest superior and wondrous birth,” this refers to the explanation in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* cited within the preceding chapter on the perfections (*pāramitā*), which identifies the first three as leading to a superior rebirth (*abhyudaya-janman*), because the path brings about great wealth, a physical form, and a retinue.
That which is "superior and wondrous birth" (viśiṣṭa-utpatti) is identical in meaning to "higher birth" (abhyudaya-utpatti), though the names differ.
The latter three [perfections] constitute the path of definitive excellence (niyāma-samyak-mārga).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the six correct factors and their aids are not in conflict," this refers to the sutra’s statement: "The paths of action do not conflict with karma, and karma does not conflict with the paths of action."

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in the "Chapter on Karma," states: "It is called *śīla* (1), *sucarita* (2), *karman* (3), and *saṃvara* (4); only the first [moment] of both manifest and unmanifest [action] is called *prātimokṣa* (5), and it is also called a *karmapatha* (6)."
The commentary states:
"This has six names, and this present one corresponds to the sixth.
The sub-commentary on that treatise explains: 'Furthermore, this initial moment is also called a karmic path; it is the sixth name.'"

Originally, one seeks the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the precepts; now it is said that because this volition reaches its ultimate fulfillment through action (*karman*), the term "course of action" (*karmapatha*) is established based on the meaning of its manifestation. That is to say, the volition prior to the formal undertaking of the precepts is termed "action" (*karman*);
the first moment of the essence of the precept (*śīla-svabhāva*) is termed the "path" (*patha*), because it is that which the volition traverses.
Because it is the path of karma, it is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
Thus, at the first moment, it is termed "analytical liberation" (*prātimokṣa*), because one initially abandons evil.
It may also be termed the "analytical liberation restraint" (*prātimokṣasaṃvara*), because it is capable of preventing what is non-virtuous.
It may also be termed the "fundamental path of action" because it flows from the arising of volition.
The second moment of thought and subsequent moments are not termed paths of action because they do not flow from volition;
they are termed "subsequent actions" because they follow the fundamental [action].
The present commentary relies entirely upon the text of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; therefore, I shall not further cite the various divergent interpretations of past scholars.
Under the section of the commentary beginning with "The reason why each of these matters is without contradiction," the cause for the non-contradiction of each matter is set forth.
Briefly stated, there are three causes:

first, the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature; second, the gate of mutual dependence in dependent origination—these two constitute the meaning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena;

third, the direct statement that all share a single dependent origination, which refers to the universal application of both phenomena and principle, yet does not itself constitute the meaning of non-obstruction.
It is like seeing a single leaf fall and knowing that autumn has come to the world.

Regarding the statement, "It is also by means of the latter two sections that this lack of contradiction is established," the latter two refer to the non-contradiction between phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*), and the non-contradiction between principles themselves; it is through these that the non-contradiction among all phenomena is established.

This means that since they are of one and the same flavor, phenomena (事) are identical with principle (理). Because phenomena are identical with principle, and principle is interfused within phenomena, one attains the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon; therefore, there is no contradiction.
The Commentary states: "However, the three preceding sections are not contradictory," which serves as a further general analysis. This section contains two parts:
first, an analysis of similarities and differences; second, [an analysis of the specific categories].

Second, regarding the phrase "If this is opened, then there is," the following analysis of the number of propositions is conducted solely by means of lands (*kṣetra*) and sentient beings (*sattva*) to form the various propositions.

First, the four fundamental propositions; second, the four propositions formed by the principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*) of the lands; third, the four propositions formed by the principle and phenomena of sentient beings. The first two sets of four propositions (the second and third) consist merely of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmārthāpratighāta*).

Fourth, the four propositions formed by taking the phenomena of the lands in contrast to the principle of sentient beings; fifth, the four propositions formed by looking at the phenomena of sentient beings in relation to the principle of the lands. These latter two sets of four constitute the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the first two tetrads, [the result is established] by the first and third [factors] respectively,” this is because when phenomena and principles are compared, the result is established solely through their mutual similarity.
The statement that there are "two and four for each" does not mean they are unimpeded, yet it is also not contradictory.
As for the phrase "the meaning is as explained above," since both the two and the four are not identical [to one another], they are not unimpeded.
Regarding the statement "nor are they contradictory," it is because, as mentioned above, they share the same dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is because, through their indestructible phenomena and unchanging nature, they all constitute a single dependent origination.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Herein, the first two phrases show that there is no contradiction between principle and principle,” this means: first, that the lack of intrinsic nature in a single kṣaṇa is identical to the lack of intrinsic nature in sentient beings; second, because these two principles are the same.

Regarding the statement, "Because there is nothing to which one can conform and nothing to which one can oppose," this explains the second phrase: that this principle is non-contradictory in its own nature.

The commentary states, "The fourth phrase, although not 'unobstructed,' is also not contradictory. This means that the fourth [phrase] does not constitute "non-obstruction" because it allows both [positions] to coexist. Thus, it is not unobstructed.

Furthermore, because they are likewise the same dependent origination, there is no contradiction between the fifth and the fourth [sets of four], nor do they contradict the first two sets of four; all are consistent with one another.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The fifth four-line [verse],” and so forth, it means that this refers to the first and third lines therein.

As for the phrase, “In the second section, regarding the non-contradiction between principle and phenomena, phenomena of different categories are compared with one another,” this is because when comparing the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) to sentient beings who lack intrinsic nature, the *kṣetra* and sentient beings are of different categories.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Sub-commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Fifty Commentary on the Meaning of the Sub-commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Fifty-one
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the eighth dedication, the Commentary states:

"The name is established based on that which is relied upon; thus, its meaning applies to both the subject and the object. This means that merely mentioning the characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā) refers to the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) that serve as the basis.
The synthesis remains as before, and its meaning applies to both the subject and the object.
Within this, there are five parts:
first, the correct explanation above.
Second, from "Therefore, the *Original Karma*" onwards, he cites scriptural evidence.
Regarding the term "constantly illuminating," this implies the existence of subject and object, let alone a unified whole (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there are two meanings:
First, existence and non-existence are non-dual, which is the mark of oneness because they are identical to suchness;
second, wisdom merges with its object, transcending subject and object, whereby both subject and object are realized as the mark of suchness.
3. From "If [it were] Brahmā" onwards, the Sanskrit original is reconciled.
4. From "Thereby, through the Dharma-realm" onwards, the essence is revealed; for the union of the subject and object constitutes the Dharma-realm.
5. The section beginning with "This, together with what precedes and follows" serves to eliminate confusion.
"Preceding" refers to the seventh [stage], because it accords equally with sentient beings.
"Following" refers to the ninth and tenth; the ninth is so called because it is free from the bondage and attachment of subject and object.
Because the ten entries into the Dharma-realm are likewise in accord with it, four of its names are largely interchangeable; these may be distinguished by consulting the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "the rest is as in the fourth dedication," that [dedication] takes roots of goodness to be like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and therefore they reach all places.
Since this has already been distinguished in relation to the preceding [three vows], it is not distinguished here in relation to the fourth. The commentary states:
"Of the four, the first phrase provides a general heading. Below this, the commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the general phrase; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "The thirty-one vows."
In the commentary, first the "lovely" (iṣṭa) is explained; subsequently, from "Explaining this" (*śeṣam*) onwards, the formal analysis and explanation is clearly set forth.
This section has three parts:
first, the dual introduction; second, the brief explanation of the character "total" (*sāmānya*) from "As for 'total'"; third, the dual explanation of the two chapters from "As for 'horizontal'."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Third, the enjoyment of transformation,” it mentions only “pure” because transformation bodies also possess purity.
Being free from all afflictions constitutes the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Since sentient beings have already attained rebirth there, they all possess these [supernormal powers].

As for the statement that "the rest are matters within the land": the fourth refers to the dissemination of Dharma-gates; the fifth refers to the cultivation of bodhisattvas; and the sixth refers to the divine eye. Those born in the world of Constant Joy possess a divine eye that penetrates and sees throughout the ten directions.
Seventh, water birds, forest trees, flowering ponds, and jeweled pavilions; eighth, protecting the Dharma; ninth, realizing the Dharma; tenth, a mind free from attachment.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “the forest of untainted dharmas” (*anāsrava-dharma-vana*) and so forth, this refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, “Chapter on the Buddha-way,” which states: “The forest trees of untainted dharmas, the garden of total retention (*dhāraṇī*); this is because the subsequent sutra passage describes “samādhi as the garden.”

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “in contrast to the grasses and trees,” this refers to the three types of grasses and two types of trees mentioned in the “Parable of the Medicinal Herbs” chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, which was already cited during the first assembly. Since the distinctions among the five vehicles arise solely from differences in wisdom, the well-observing wisdom is here set in contrast to the grasses and trees.

The Commentary states: "The second section, 'The Three Vows Clarify the Fulfillment of the Three Virtues of the Fruit,' means that that which is capable of severing [afflictions] is *prajñā* (wisdom), that which is severed is *vimukti* (liberation), and the wisdom that pervades the dharma-realm is the *dharmakāya*, because it takes what is realized as its object."

Furthermore, the first [of these three] is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), the second is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), and the last is the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*). Because of this virtue of grace, it is able to manifest in the world.
Therefore, regarding the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*, the commentary states: "The body of the Tathāgata is also not *nirvāṇa*, because it includes the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*)."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the first phrase establishes the thesis' (立宗): this means that although one correctly cultivates right action (正業), one knows that the nature of action is empty.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Right action is the subject (*dharmin*); 'emptiness and existence are unimpeded' is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); the reason (*hetu*) is 'because being dependently originated entails the absence of intrinsic nature' (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); the concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is 'like an illusion' (*māyā*)."
Illusory phenomena arise from conditions; emptiness and existence do not obstruct one another.
Right action arises from conditions; like those illusory phenomena, it does not obstruct them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ten phrases consist of five pairs that cause the four minds to become even more firm,” this refers to the response to the question concerning "abiding" found within Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
According to Asaṅga, this corresponds to the first stage of the resolve (prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra).
However, in Asaṅga’s system of eighteen stages (vihāras), each stage answers three questions.
These three questions are: how one should dwell, how one should practice, and how one should subdue the mind.
The question regarding the omission of "cultivation" in the Qin translation should be included within the two preceding sections.
As for the dwelling place where the mind is first resolved, the Sūtra states: "The Buddha told Subhūti:
'A bodhisattva should subdue his mind in this manner.'"

"Whatever classes of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. This is my foremost resolve."

"In this way, although one brings immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in truth there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa"—this is the mind of permanence.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva, nor do they possess a non-perverted mind.
The verse of the treatise says: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; their mind is non-perverted; abiding in a deeply beneficial mind—this vehicle’s merit is fulfilled."

The first half of this verse indicates the four types of mind, while the second half explains the meaning of "abiding. Since these four minds possess the benefit of practicing for the sake of both oneself and others, the bodhisattva with such profound resolve should abide in the merits of the Mahāyāna until they are fully perfected.
Regarding the four minds: to fully deliver all beings throughout the nine categories of the three realms is the vast mind.
To cause them to enter nirvana without remainder is the foremost mind.
The two vehicles still possess the three remainders; since they are not said to be "without remainder," they are not called the foremost.
Now, between the two types of nirvana, that which is without remainder is the foremost.
Among the four types of nirvana, only non-abiding nirvana is truly the foremost.
What is now called "without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa) is precisely the Buddha’s non-abiding.
In the past, there were only three types of nirvāṇa; therefore, "without remainder" was not mentioned.
In that commentary, the first two mental states are categorized as the "abiding of preparatory application" (prayoga-sthiti).
Regarding the "constant mind," the treatise states: "To regard sentient beings as one's own body, never abandoning them, is called the constant mind.

The verse explains the meaning of this constancy through the context of benefiting others; that is, to deliver sentient beings while never departing from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the realization of the same essence (*samatā*), just like one's own mind—therefore, it is named "constant."
The Commentary categorizes this mind as the "concentration for cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "non-perverted mind," the Commentary categorizes it as the "mind of analytical dispersal.
As for the term "non-perverted," the Treatise states: "This demonstrates the departure from the characteristics of sentient beings who rely upon the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)."
To grasp at a self based on the body is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); to possess these four [views] and so forth is not to be a bodhisattva, for this is termed "inversion.
Now, to be free from these four is to be a bodhisattva, and not a mind of inversion.
Mahāmegha said:
"This passage is fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
The preceding passage on great compassion is subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna)."

"Because fundamental wisdom is itself free from the view of a self, the aforementioned Great Wisdom must first observe the non-existence of the mark of a sentient being before it can achieve fulfillment.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* that "there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa," there are five general meanings:
first, because the nature of sentient beings is empty, there is nothing that can be extinguished.

The compassion that is of the same essence as the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the two Bodhisattvas is such that, apart from their own selves, there are no separate sentient beings; thus, there is no "other-essence.
In fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one must first personally abandon the marks of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); thus, there is no "self-essence" either.
Since there is neither self nor other, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Third, all sentient beings are originally quiescent, for they do not undergo further extinction.
Fourth, one accords with the dharma-nature; the dharma-nature is without thought, for if the mind gives rise to thought, it immediately contravenes the dharma-nature.
Wu explains that within the dharma-realm, there are no sentient beings to be delivered.
Tianqin explains:
"In the equal and true dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings."
By means of the name "sentient beings," the name itself is the dharma-realm.
The aggregate body of sentient beings—the aggregates themselves—is the dharma-realm.
Since sentient beings and Buddhas share the same single dharma-realm, how could one deliver sentient beings by means of this principle?
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The various sages and worthies are also suchness; even Maitreya is suchness.
If Maitreya were to receive a prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive a prediction."
Because suchness is one and should not be differentiated, this principle is particularly profound.

When Vasubandhu provides this interpretation in the subsequent passage, he intends it for the instruction of the great bodhisattvas on the bhūmis; since they have fully realized true suchness from the first bhūmi onward, he thereby causes those training on the bhūmis to practice the contemplation of the Buddha’s equal dharma-realm.

Today, Vasubandhu has immediately elucidated this text; his Great Compassion being of the same essence as [the Buddha's], he provides this commentary for those who have studied the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and are contemplating the grounds themselves.
Thus, Vasubandhu’s wondrous intent is clarified today.
The commentary states:
The above are all Master Hui’s views;
however, I now maintain that this is not so.
Furthermore, I ask: are quiescence (nirvāṇa) and emptiness (śūnyatā) one or different?
If you say they are one, then the first three [truths] would not be distinct.
If you say they are different, what are their differing characteristics?
Does this not clarify that the nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty and quiescent?
Furthermore, is the expression "quiescent extinction" merely a characteristic of cessation,
or does it manifest the reality?
If this were to manifest reality, it would be identical to the fifth [category], the single Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, if compassion shares the same essence (*samāna-svabhāva*), how could it differ from the single Dharma-realm?
Moreover, what distinction is there between these five Dharma-realms and that which accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?

Wisdom devoid of mindfulness is not called true understanding; this is because the treatise clarifies that the Dharma-realm is the same when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha and sentient beings, and it clarifies that they share the same essence when viewed from the perspective of the Bodhisattva and sentient beings. Therefore, these two [distinctions] should not be dualistic.

In that case, the five aforementioned understandings should be reduced to only two; the meaning of "non-conceptualization" (amanasikāra) should be merged into the state of a non-erroneous mind. Since the Sūtra mentions only the "self" as being erroneous, is it not also an error when the attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha) has not been extinguished?

Therefore, being non-perverted, one relies on *śamatha* to sever discursive thought (*vikalpa*) and, through the contemplation of the ever-present mind of identical essence, realizes the profound truth.

Thus, the sutra text explains the aforementioned "ever-present mind" by means of "non-perversion. Why is this? Because only by being free from delusion can one accord with reality; and only by acceding to reality can one become free from delusion. Since these two meanings mutually establish one another, there is no sentient being who attains *nirvāṇa*.
First, one accords with the suchness of emptiness; because its nature is empty and quiescent, there is nothing that can be delivered.
Second, one accords with non-emptiness; because it is identical to the single dharma-nature, and the dharma-nature is equal, there is nothing that can be delivered.

This clearly demonstrates that the profound and subtle [teachings] are all based on the contemplation of the mind by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, rather than being restricted solely to abstract principle; therefore, the present commentary directly adopts the intent of the treatise as the correct interpretation.
Furthermore, in accordance with the present sutra, this sutra serves as proof that Vasubandhu’s commentary on the scripture perfectly accords with the holy intent.
Regarding the gloss, "To accord with conditions is called 'such' (tathā)," this refers to the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Dharmas follow the *tathatā* (suchness), because there is nothing for them to follow.

Now I say that *tathatā* follows dharmas, because there is nothing capable of following it; for it is precisely because the nature of *tathatā* is empty that it can follow conditions to manifest all things.

In the commentary, from the passage "And as it says in the *Awakening of Faith*," onwards, this treatise explains the section on interpretation, specifically the initial exposition of the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This consists of two parts: first, the direct manifestation of the essence of Suchness; second, the reconciliation of attachments to explain its name.

Regarding the first gate, the treatise states: "The True Suchness of the mind is the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm; that is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. All phenomena exist only through the differentiation of deluded thoughts; if one is free from mental thoughts, then there are no appearances of any objective realms."

Therefore, all phenomena, from their very origin, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible. Being solely this one mind, they are called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The commentary states:
This preceding treatise consists of three sections:

first, a brief indication according to ultimate reality; second, from "All phenomena" (*sarva-dharmāḥ*) onwards, the reconciliation of delusion to reveal the true; and third, from "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, the conclusion that the true is free from delusion.

These three all directly manifest the essence of *tathatā* (suchness): it is "true" (*satya*) because it is free from falsehood and delusion, and it is "such" (*tathā*) because it is free from differentiated characteristics.
What is cited here in the commentary is precisely an explanation of the name by reconciling [the various] attachments.
Regarding "endowment," the *Śāstra* states: "Because all verbal designations are conventionally named but lack reality, being unattainable except as they follow deluded thoughts.

That which is called 'True Suchness' (Tathatā) likewise possesses no characteristics; it is the ultimate limit of verbal expression, wherein words are dispelled by means of words. Yet this essence of True Suchness cannot itself be dispelled, for all phenomena are entirely True Suchness."
Furthermore, there is nothing that can be established, because all dharmas are identical to suchness (tathatā).
One should know that because all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable, they are called true suchness.
The commentary states:
This preceding section of the treatise has two parts:
first, the explanation; second, the conclusion beginning with "One should know that all phenomena... and so forth.
The preceding section is divided into three parts;
first, the formal reconciliation of the tenets.
Fearing that there might be those who hold such a view, [the author] says:
The preceding statement spoke of being detached from the characteristics of names; for what reason, then, is the name "True Suchness" (tathatā) established?
Therefore, it is said that this name "True Suchness" is also a provisional designation.
Second, the section beginning with "the ultimate limit of verbal expression" explains the doubt by means of the name.
An objection is raised:
"If it is merely a provisional designation, why is it not designated by other names instead of 'tathatā' (suchness)?
The explanation states:

Tathatā (Suchness) is the ultimate limit of verbal expression; beyond this, there are no further names. Therefore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Tathatā is called the "ultimate name," and thus it is described as "the extreme."
By means of words, words are dispelled; thus this ultimate name is established.
If this name did not exist, there would be no means to dispel names.
If this name were to persist, it likewise would not dispel names.
3. Regarding the passage "This essence of *tathatā* is also not something that can be discarded," the following explains "discarding" (*apavāda*) in terms of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Although there have been many ancient interpretations, none of them are followed here.
I maintain that this refers precisely to the non-established (*apratiṣṭhita*) *tathatā*.

If one were to establish this through conventional discourse, one would set aside the false to call it "true" and manifest the principle as "suchness," which accords with the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Now, however, we are precisely brushing away these two [distinctions]: since there is no phenomenon that is not true, what falsehood could possibly be set aside?
Then the true is not truly true.
Since there is no phenomenon that does not accord with suchness, what principle could be manifested? Therefore, suchness is not suchness.
This is thus neither negated nor established; it is the non-established *tathatā* (suchness).
Therefore, the commentary concludes: "It is only by means of apophatic designation (*paryudāsa*) that ultimate truth is suddenly revealed."
The Commentary states: "Second, clarifying the categories. There are six gates in total, namely: one, two, three, seven, ten, and one hundred, making six classes.
Within the second [category], there are three and six types of *tathatā* (suchness), which, together with the eight *tathatās*, comprise ten meanings in total.
The remainder is as previously explained in the *Daśadharmaka* [Sūtra] and in the preceding assemblies;
only the seven aspects of true thusness (*tathatā*) shall now be discussed.

This corresponds to the first part of the third chapter, "Compendium of Matters" (*Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*), of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which states: "Regarding the characteristics of mental attention (*manasikāra*) to true thusness: it refers to mental attention directed toward the seven kinds of pervasive true thusness, as explained at length in the Sūtra."

Regarding the mental engagement with the *tathatā* of transmigration (*pravṛtti-tathatā*): this refers to the mental engagement already seen and described as being well-cultivated by bodhisattvas through superior Dharma-practice; it consists of reflecting upon the real nature of the transmigration of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from beginningless time within the context of both defiled and purified dharmas.
Having reflected thus, one abandons the view of causelessness and the view of inequality.

Second is the mental engagement with the true suchness of the two realities; as previously described, it consists of reflecting upon the causes of defiled and purified phenomena, as well as the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena in all dharmas.
Having thus reflected, all views of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), as well as the mental engagements with the conceptualization of various signs, no longer manifest.

Third is the mental engagement with the suchness of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratātathatā*); that is to say, as previously explained, one reflects upon the nature of all phenomena as being representation-only, even regarding the basis of defiled and purified phenomena.

Having reflected thus, one understands as it truly is that it is solely because of the defilement of the mind that sentient beings are defiled, and solely because of the purity of the mind that sentient beings are pure.

This is the mental attention to the fourfold established suchness (*tathatā-vyavasthāna-manasikāra*), which, as previously described, involves reflecting upon the truth of suffering regarding the essential nature of both defiled and purified phenomena.
Having reflected thus, one speaks for the sake of sentient beings so that they may understand.

This is the mental attention to the *tathatā* (suchness) of the fivefold wrong conduct; as previously stated, it involves reflecting upon the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) as the cause of defiled phenomena, and speaking for the sake of sentient beings with the desire that these be abandoned.

Sixth is the mental attention on the suchness of purity (*viśuddhi-tathatā-manasikāra*). As previously explained, this refers to contemplating the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) regarding the essence of pure phenomena.
Having contemplated it thus, one preaches it for the sake of sentient beings in order to bring about its realization.

Seventh is the mental attention to the suchness of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti-tathatā-manasikāra*). As previously explained, this involves contemplating the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) up to the point of pure conduct.
Having performed this contemplation, one explains it to sentient beings for the purpose of cultivating that practice.
The commentary states:

The meaning of "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is precisely the contemplation of the Bodhisattva; the rest may be understood accordingly, as the sub-commentary merely lists the names and provides a brief exhortation.

Regarding the sub-commentary’s phrase "first, the function of being the basis and support," this refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) serving as the basis for both delusion and enlightenment, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
As extensively discussed in the section on the meaning of the fourfold transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is further elaborated upon in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* speaks of the three great aspects," there are four parts to the commentary:

first, citing the three great aspects from the treatise; second, correlating them with the present text; third, explaining the function of the aspect of greatness (*mahatva*); and fourth, correlating them with the *Śata-dharmaka-mukha-śāstra*.
Now, regarding the first [section], it consists entirely of the text of the treatise itself.
Within the section on "The Greatness of Essence" (*tattva-mahatva*), the phrase "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) is missing from below the first point, "The Greatness of Essence.

This refers to the explanation of "Essence" (*tattva*) provided in the commentary on the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*siddhārtha-vibhāga*), which states: "The true nature (*bhūtatathatā*) is profound and vast; because both ordinary beings and sages, as well as the defiled and the pure, all take it as their basis, it receives the name 'Great'."
Following the flow, defilement is added yet there is no increase; reversing the flow, defilement is removed yet there is no decrease.
Furthermore, reversing the flow, purity is added yet there is no increase; following the flow, purity is lacking yet there is no decrease.
This is because it is neither diminished by defilement nor purified by holiness, and remains unchanging from beginning to end; thus it is said to be "equal, without increase or decrease.
Regarding the greatness of the two aspects, the *Śāstra* states: "Because the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable innate virtues. The Commentary explains:
"Among the two types of *garbhas*, this refers to the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha."

The present commentary briefly omits the term "tathāgatagarbha" because it explains the characteristics solely in terms of *tathatā* (suchness). Since these are qualities that are not distinct from the essence itself, they are called "intrinsic virtues," just as the eight qualities of water are not distinct from the water itself.
The third, the Greatness of Function (*vṛtti-mahattva*), is entirely the same as that in the commentary.
The explanation states:

This refers to following pure karma; regarding the spontaneous great function, the coarse and subtle functions of the two bodies—the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body)—cause all sentient beings to first accomplish mundane virtues and ultimately accomplish supramundane virtues.
The characteristics of its function are fully revealed in the text below that treatise.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “However, it relies on the mind,” this is the second section, which correlates the present sutra [with other texts] and also resolves potential objections.
An objection states:
