The three mindfulnesses and four knowledges are the same as those discussed in the seventh and eighth [stages] of the treatise.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Furthermore, if the mind wanders and scatters,” this is a threefold explanation of mindfulness and awareness (*smṛti-samprajanya*), which includes the ninth [stage], the cultivation of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
It is called a "re-explanation" because the previous section explained the fundamental mindfulness and awareness, whereas the present section explains how to rouse oneself when they have declined.
Following the methods of the Western Regions, the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) presides over the assembly and constantly recites these words at dawn to spur those who are indolent.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This can lash the mind so that it returns to its original contemplation,” this reflects the intent of the *Zhuangzi*.
It is like a person driving sheep; one that lags behind the flock is called "the last," and is whipped so as to catch up with the herd—hence the expression "whipping the last.

Cultivating the mind is like the sheep: when it wanders and scatters, it is like failing to keep up with the herd; causing it to return to its original contemplation is what constitutes catching up with the herd.
Impermanence, the three miserable realms, and so forth, are the "whip.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "its impurity," this refers to the accompanying factors, self-nature, and so on.

Regarding the phrase in the *Śāstra* "according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*," etc., this explains the three contemplations within the latter three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), citing two treatises to clarify them.
First, the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi* is as follows:
Just as one contemplates the internal body above, taking the five sense faculties of one's own body as the object, contact is established in relation to them.
Because of this contact, feeling arises; the experiencing of impurity and so forth is termed "internal feeling."
One contemplates the external body above, as well as the internal and external bodies; the arising of sensation follows this same pattern.
As it is with sensation, so it is with the mental factors (*citta-dharma*).
Regarding the phrase "The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says" in the commentary, there is a slight difference in its interpretation.
Regarding the statement "Mind is exclusively internal": mind is one's own sovereign king (citta-rāja), as it is subsumed under the faculty of mind (manas).

Regarding the commentary’s statement "The dharma-realm is exclusively external": among the twelve bases (āyatana), the dharma-realm is exclusively external because it is subsumed under the dharma-base (dharmāyatana); furthermore, sensation (vedanā) must necessarily perceive the objects of the six sense-fields (ṣaḍviṣaya).

"Phenomena" (dharma) refers to perception (saṃjñā) and mental formations (saṃskāra). Perception grasps external characteristics, while mental formations consist of volition (cetanā) and so forth; because they contact external objects, they exist only externally.
As for the statement that "the body extends both internally and externally," one regards one's own person as internal and one's wife, children, and so forth as external.
The commentary states: "The answer, 'There are two types of reception,' etc., is the response from the treatise.
The commentary text has three parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the two meanings—internal and external—of the three mindfulnesses."
This means that among these three mindfulnesses, the first two each have two meanings.
Within the mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā*), there are two aspects: first, regarding body and mind; second, regarding sensation itself.

That which is experienced by the five sense-faculties is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*); that which is experienced by the six consciousnesses is called mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).
The second meaning concerns the internal and external divisions within the six consciousnesses.
Next, from "Although the mind... onwards, it clarifies two meanings regarding the mind and its thoughts.
Finally, from "Although phenomena are external... onwards, phenomena have only one meaning, namely that they are solely mind.
The first meaning is largely identical to that in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, while all others differ.
Regarding the section "Second, Right Effort" (*samyak-vyāyāma*) in the commentary, there are four parts: first, the purpose;
second, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, the etymological explanation (*nirukti*); and fourth, the word-by-word commentary.
First, this summarizes the preceding section by examining both the dharma and its analogy together.

As for the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it simply states: "Thus, because one has practiced habitually within the four foundations of mindfulness, one has already been able to eliminate the heavy burdens of coarse dysfunction (*dausthulya*) and perversion, and has already attained a thorough understanding of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; immediately following this, for the sake of causing wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen to arise," and so forth.
The Commentary states: “Vigor is its essential nature” refers to the second [section], which establishes the essence; it is diligence (*vīrya*) among the eleven wholesome mental factors.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: “Diligence is vigor; its intrinsic nature is courage and fortitude in the acts of cultivation and abandonment regarding the categories of the wholesome and unwholesome; its function is to counteract indolence and to fulfill the wholesome.”
"Valiance" (*vīrya*) signifies superior progress, thereby distinguishing it from all defiled phenomena;

"fortitude" (*dhṛti*) signifies purity and refinement, thereby distinguishing it from the pure neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). This demonstrates that diligence (*vīrya*) is subsumed exclusively within the nature of the wholesome.
The commentary states:

The courageous and clear understanding increases with every thought-moment to a state of loftiness and excellence; it is not like defiled dharmas, which, even if they increase, are all termed "retrogression" when compared to the various categories of wholesome qualities and cannot be called "progress."
"Guarding and manifesting pure essence" differs from the purity of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Therefore, it is collectively named diligence," the explanation of the name consists of three parts:
First, the formal explanation; second, the alternative names; third, the distinction between the general and the specific.
Now, for the first [section], it is divided into two parts:

first, reiterating the previous definition of its essence to explain the general name; second, [the explanation of the specific]. Regarding the first: [The text continues: First, reiterating the previous definition of its essence to explain the general name.
Following this, the section beginning with "The former two are diligence in abandoning" explains the specific names; its meaning corresponds to the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
This section has three parts:
first, the four [diligences] are condensed into two, which do not go beyond the cessation of evil and the cultivation of good.
Regarding the second point, "The two unwholesome and the two wholesome are both objects of perception," this clarifies the three types of objects of perception (*ālambana*).
The phrase "among the former, those not yet arisen" and so forth distinguishes their four specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "restraining unarisen evil so that it does not arise," "restraining" (遏) means to stop.
The Sūtra says, "for the sake of non-arising.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If [a phenomenon] has not yet combined and has not yet manifested before one, it is called 'unarisen.'"
To ensure that [unwholesome states] do not arise, one generates the aspiration: "I shall cause all of them never to arise again.
Regarding the statement, "Having arisen, evil is severed so that it does not continue," the Sūtra says, "For the sake of severing [it]."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which has already been brought together and has already manifested is called 'already arisen.
Because one has previously brought them together, in order to abandon them, one arouses the aspiration:
'I shall not tolerate any of those evils; I shall sever, extinguish, and eliminate them.'"
The commentary states:
To simply prevent [the afflictions] from continuing is itself their severance, extinction, and elimination.
Therefore, Master Huiyuan said:
"Once it has arisen and passed away, how can it be removed?

This refers to severing the continuity of the category that has already arisen, so that what exists in the future does not continue; it does not mean severing that which has already arisen and ceased."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the latter two cause unarisen virtues to arise,' the Sūtra says, 'for the sake of arising.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* says: 'That is to say, with respect to all virtuous dharmas that have not yet been attained and have not yet manifested, one gives rise to a fervent aspiration and a longing desire for their attainment and manifestation, seeking to acquire them and desiring them to appear before one.'"
Regarding the statement "to cause what has arisen to expand," the Sūtra says, "for the sake of increasing and expanding it.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It refers to all wholesome dharmas that have already been acquired and have already manifested; regarding these wholesome dharmas, one has already attained them without loss, and having already attained them, one does not regress."
Based on this, it is said that one desires to cause [the mind] to abide in these wholesome dharmas, so that they are clearly manifest before one and devoid of dullness or obtuseness.

Based on this, it is said that one causes them not to be lost; having already brought these wholesome dharmas into manifestation, one repeatedly cultivates them until they reach fulfillment and consummation.
Based on this, it is said that one "causes cultivation to reach fulfillment.
Although the current sutra text is abbreviated and merely says "increasing and expanding," it also encompasses the terms from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "abiding in clarity" and "fulfillment."
Master Yuan Gong also said:
"That which has already arisen has passed away; how can it be venerated?
This [veneration] likewise venerates that which belongs to the same category as what has already arisen, so as to cause it to continue arising in the future."
The text above states "perfection," which already indicates its category.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "also called the four right endeavors" (*samyakprahāṇa*), this is the second section, which distinguishes the alternative names.
This section contains five parts:
First, the explicit clarification;
second, the specific refutation beginning with "The latter two are cultivation";
third, the general explanation beginning with "Goodness is the locus of abandonment."
4. From "Correct Cultivation and Abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*) onwards, the objects to be abandoned are briefly indicated;
5. From "Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says" onwards, the treatise is cited as formal proof.
The latter two [sections] constitute abandonment, because all four are designated as "abandonment."

Regarding "abandonment through restraint": as for unwholesome states that have already arisen, one should practice restraint toward those arisen evil and unwholesome matters so as to cause them to be severed and extinguished; they must not be tolerated.

Regarding "the abandonment by abandonment" (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*): it refers to the abandonment for the sake of ensuring that unarisen unwholesome dharmas do not manifest; because one abandons them in order to abandon them, it is called "abandonment by abandonment."
The commentary states:
This meaning clarifies the severance of non-arising.

Regarding "severance through cultivation," this refers to wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen; because one repeatedly cultivates these wholesome dharmas, those previously unattained are brought into manifestation, thereby enabling what was to be severed to be severed. Thus, it is called "severance through cultivation."

"Four protections for abandonment" refers to the fact that regarding all wholesome dharmas already arisen, by means of abandoning negligence and cultivating non-negligence within those wholesome dharmas already attained and presently manifest, one is able to cause these wholesome dharmas to abide without being lost and to bring their cultivation to fulfillment.
The abandonment through guarding (*ārakṣaṇa-prahāṇa*) refers to the ability to abandon [defilements] by means of guarding all wholesome dharmas that have already arisen.
The commentary states:
"The preceding sub-commentary says, 'The wholesome is the locus of abandonment.'"
"Correct cultivation for abandonment" means abandoning laziness;
this is precisely that meaning, as cultivation serves as the means for abandonment.
However, the initial explanation in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* first clarifies the non-arising of unwholesome states, which is identical to the sequence in the present sutra.
Yet, while explaining the four abandonments, he first clarifies that which has already arisen as evil, but does not correctly explain the reason why.
Furthermore, the concluding summary asks: "How else can one know the summarized meaning herein?"

This means that in order to demonstrate the perfection of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) and the perfection of the application (*prayoga*) regarding the acts of relinquishing and adopting within the categories of the dark and the white, the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) are taught.
The commentary states:

This clarifies that for both the two types of evil and the two types of good, the former sense constitutes the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), while the latter sense constitutes the perfection of application (*prayoga*).

To cause already arisen evil to be abandoned is the intention; that which has not yet arisen does not arise is the perfection. Therefore, the already arisen is discussed first; this refers to the time of cultivation.

Regarding what was previously stated concerning the timing, first the unarisen is clarified and subsequently the already arisen is distinguished; that is to say, when speaking for the sake of sentient beings, one should say:
"Ensure that unarisen evil does not arise, and that which has already arisen must be severed."
When practicing, if evil arises at that time, it must be immediately severed so that it does not arise again.
Therefore, Master Huiyuan also said:
"Regarding evil, he first spoke of that which has not yet arisen; this refers to the time of teaching, not the time of practice."

Regarding the clarification of what has not yet arisen among the wholesome, since the wholesome does not exist inherently but arises only through cultivation, it is therefore said that "what has not yet arisen arises first.
Thus, the commentary further states:
"Alternatively, that which has already arisen may be considered 'first,' because the ground where ignorance dwells (*avidyā-āśraya*) is subtle."
"Later, excluding those that have not yet arisen, these are the manifest afflictions of the four abodes; because they are coarse, they are severed first.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "However, their goodness and evil are both general and specific," the third point distinguishes between the general and the restricted.
The commentary consists of two parts:

first, it clarifies the restricted [meaning]; second, from "Regarding the Mahāyāna" onwards, it distinguishes the universal [meaning] of this gate while simultaneously selecting between the provisional and the real.
The commentary reveals only the real; however, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "What are called evil and unwholesome dharmas?"

This refers to those factors that defile the body, speech, and mind through sensual desires, which are comprised within unwholesome conduct, as well as all the afflictions capable of giving rise to them.
What, then, are called all wholesome dharmas?
This refers to "that which is an antidote," "a wholesome antidote," or "an antidote to the fetters.
The commentary states:
this refers to the term "distinct" (*viśeṣa*) within the sub-commentary (*vṛtti*).
The treatise explains the characteristics of evil and unwholesome states extensively below; its general meaning does not go beyond what was stated previously.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If one refers to the Mahāyāna," these words clarify the commonality [of the teachings].
This should be understood in two ways:
first, that which is evil with respect to all matters;
second, as explained according to principle in the present commentary, where only the true mark (dharmatā) is good and everything else is evil.
Thus, even grasping at wholesome signs is called evil; this is the true teaching for cultivating the intention of right abandonment.
One should also say:
if there is anything to be abandoned, it cannot be called true abandonment.
That which is the non-interruption of abandonment is such that there is nothing not abandoned.
Diligence without exertion is alone termed diligence.
Thus the *Dharmapada* says: "If one gives rise to various forms of vigor, this is forgetfulness, not vigor."
"If one can be without delusion, diligence will be boundless.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "In each of the sections on diligence, there are four [points]," this is an explanation of the text.
The text consists of three parts:

first, the explanation of diligence; second, the section beginning with "the remaining three" which illustrates the other three [perfections]; and third, the section beginning with "if there are two evils" which demonstrates their resultant characteristics.
Within the first part, the commentary divides the scriptural text into four sections:
The first [of the four foundations of mindfulness] is the object of focus; the latter two are the cultivation; and the third is the fruit of cultivation.

The essential nature has already been established previously; here, the single category of its accompanying factors, the foundations of mindfulness, is explained in general, such that all five gates are complete.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Regarding the cultivation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), as it is said in the Sūtra: 'With desire for their arising, one exerts oneself; one initiates right effort to rouse the mind and sustain the mind.'"
In this context, these phrases clarify the cultivation of right effort and its basis.
As for the basis, it refers to the fact that one initiates diligence preceded by aspiration and delight.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "To give rise to the mind of aspiration," where "aspiration" (希願) refers to desire (*chanda*).
Following the phrase "fourfold diligent effort" in the Commentary, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*) consists of exertion and so forth."

Among the mental applications of the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), if one applies the mind through the signs of calm abiding and so forth, and does not cling to the focal object, one practices the antidote exclusively.
"At that time, it is called 'exertion' (*pragraha*)," which refers to the term "diligent effort" (*vīrya*). The commentary states:

"'The right abandonment of generating the mind' means to exert and sustain the mind. This means that when the mind sinks or when secondary afflictions arise, one exerts and trains the mind by means of mental orientations (*manasikāra*) such as the pure and the sublime, in order to diminish those [afflictions].

If the secondary affliction of restlessness arises, one immediately restrains and sustains the mind through the gateway of internal realization and concise withdrawal; at that time, it is called the arousal of right effort.
As for the commentary’s statement, “The fulfillment of the application of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya-prayoga-paripūri*),” this refers to the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Thus, that treatise concludes: “It should be understood that herein, the superior intention is fulfilled by means of desire, and the application is fulfilled by means of self-exertion, which initiates diligence and sustains the mind.”
That yogin says:

"There is only this which is rightly to be done—namely, for the sake of abandoning that which is to be abandoned and for the sake of attaining that which is to be attained—one must first give rise to aspiration, longing, and so forth."
If one carefully examines the two preceding treatises, the commentary (*śāstra*) is easy to understand.

Regarding the section beginning with "If the two evils," which constitutes the third part on manifesting the fruits: therein, among the evils already arisen and those not yet arisen, one abandons the evils already arisen;
and among the virtues already arisen and those not yet arisen, one increases and expands the virtues already arisen.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "The fruit of right abandonment refers to the complete relinquishing of all that is to be countered (*vipakṣa*).
Among the counteracting factors (*pratipakṣa*), whether they are attained or increased, this is called the fruit of cultivation."
The Commentary states: "Third, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Prior to the main text, there are five sections:
first, the purpose;
second, the explanation of the name, beginning with "Psychic power (*ṛddhi*) is [identical to] supernormal power (*abhijñā*)."
The introduction to the treatise has two parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application [of the analogy] from "By means of supramundane... onwards.
Third, from "The bases of psychic power... onwards, the objects of focus are analyzed.
4. From "the bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*) downward, the essence is set forth.
5. From "desire and effort" (*chanda-vīrya*) downward, the auxiliaries are clarified; this constitutes the analysis of their characteristics.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the brief indication and explanation; second, the presentation of the causes.
Regarding the first: the reason for merely indicating the four aids is that these four are able to directly assist.
If one were to explain the accompanying factors in general, this has already been seen at the beginning of the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness).
Regarding the term "desire" (*chanda*) mentioned in the commentary, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it refers to the capacity to generate a longing for joy.

It involves the careful and correct contemplation of the intrinsic nature, causes, conditions, defects, and remedies regarding all unwholesome states, thereby giving rise to one-pointedness of mind; and it involves mindfulness of the intrinsic nature, causes, conditions, functional efficacy, and renunciation regarding all wholesome dharmas.

When one dwells with correct investigation and examination through one-pointed mindfulness, by virtue of such extensive cultivation, one touches one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) and is able to suppress active afflictions; therefore, it is called "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*).
The commentary states: "Diligence means unremitting exertion.
This means that one should exhort and encourage oneself to arouse diligent vigor (*vīrya*), in order to sever the two kinds of evil and cultivate the two kinds of goodness.

The Commentary states: "Mind is itself concentration" means that when one focuses the mind upon evil that has arisen or not yet arisen, and good that has arisen or not yet arisen, this very act of guarding [the mind] is what is called "mind."
This is the preparatory application (*prayoga*); because it brings about one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), it is called concentration (*samādhi*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Mental samādhi refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the prior cultivation of the power of concentration."
Why is this so? Because in previous lives, they repeatedly cultivated the power of concentration (*samādhi*), causing the functional capacity of its seeds to increase.
By the power of these seeds, the mind spontaneously undergoes a transformation in accordance with *samādhi*, whereby one swiftly realizes one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
The commentary states:
This clarifies that by virtue of past seeds, the mind spontaneously inclines toward meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is itself the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, it is also referred to as "mindfulness-concentration" (*smṛti-samādhi*) in the sūtras and śāstras because the mind is bound and stabilized; thus, it is able to maintain the object.
The sub-commentary states: "By the predominant force of desire," and so forth, concludes by establishing the name of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"All receive their names from their preparatory application" means they receive specific names; that is, the name of the cause is applied to the result.
If all four are termed "concentration" (samādhi), then the cause is designated by the name of its fruit.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "These four preparatory stages," this second section clarifies their cause, as they arise from the preceding right effort (samyak-vyāyāma).
Therefore, what was previously called "desire to arise" is here termed the concentration of desire;

what was previously called "diligent effort" is here termed the concentration of effort. Since the previously mentioned arousal of the mind includes the arousal of the mind and the sustaining of the mind, there are two concentrations involving the mind and contemplation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “‘Identifying the nature of the auxiliaries to be cultivated’ means that desire serves as the auxiliary and concentration serves as the essential nature,” this is because desire acts as the support and meditative absorption constitutes the core essence.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two characters ‘abandonment’ (prahāṇa) and ‘action’ (samskāra) collectively manifest the characteristics of cultivation,” this refers to the collective explanation, as it contrasts with the subsequent detailed clarification of the specific characteristics of cultivation based on the distinct categories such as disenchantment (nirveda).
Regarding the lower [level], the accomplishment of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) clearly explains the result; therefore, it says, "also the fruit of its cultivation.
As for the "eight applications for abandonment" (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*), they are fully detailed in the commentary.

In the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, following the explanation of desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), it says: "When practicing in this manner, there are eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*). These function with distinct characteristics in order to permanently destroy all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and to bring samādhi to full perfection."
"First, desire; second, exertion; third, faith; fourth, tranquility; fifth, mindfulness; sixth, clear comprehension; seventh, volition; eighth, equanimity.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that "desire" refers to aspiration and longing.
1. At what time shall I cultivate meditative concentration to perfection and extinguish the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
2. One should exert oneself with diligence, not abandoning the application of effort.
3. One should develop deep faith and understanding regarding that which has been realized above.
Fourth, the mind gives rise to joy, gradually eliminating coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Fifth, one causes the mind to abide in *śamatha*.
Sixth, one abides in the category of wisdom (*prajñā*) within *vipaśyanā*.
The seven minds perform their functions in accordance with śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The eighth mind is undefiled throughout the three periods of time.
It concludes: "By these two causes and conditions, one analytically understands the abandonment of the latent tendencies (anuśaya)."
This means: "It is due to the volition regarding objects that are not directly perceived, and due to the equanimity regarding objects that are directly perceived.
This can be understood from the text itself.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* is the same as this; I shall further explain it based on that commentary.
The treatise states: "These eight kinds are briefly subsumed into four, namely: first, application; second, appropriation; third, relinquishment; and fourth, antidote. Regarding application:
this refers to desire, diligence, and faith. Desire is the basis for diligence, and faith is the cause of desire."
Why is this? It is because of the desire to seek.
One exerts diligent effort in order to attain this objective; such a desire to seek is not separate from faith, for it possesses the same essential nature and so forth.
Second, "appropriation" refers to the fact that pliancy must be appropriated by this [concentration], as it benefits both body and mind.
Third, "succession" refers to right mindfulness and right situational awareness, because by not losing the object of focus, the mind is settled upon a single point.
If laxity arises, because one understands it as it truly is, one proceeds according to the sequence.

Regarding the four remedies: they consist of the two powers of application—namely, reflection (*vitarka*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), exertion (*pragraha*), and mental retention (*dhāraṇa*)—because these enable one to distance oneself from laxity and excitement that have already arisen, and furthermore, because they can induce the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth, which are free from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This is largely the same as the nine types of cultivation mentioned previously.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, it reveals the characteristics of cultivation while simultaneously identifying the objects of focus”: because this collectively reveals cultivation in contrast to the aforementioned factors of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), it is termed “further revealing”; this refers to the gateway of cultivation (*bhāvanāmukha*).
Regarding "simultaneously distinguishing the objects of focus": because it takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, this constitutes the first object of focus.

As for the commentary’s statement, "When focusing on this object, one necessarily seeks to cultivate it, and thus it is called 'dedication' (*pariṇāmanā*)," in the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, this is termed "relinquishment" (*utsarga*), the meaning of which is identical to this.

The commentary states, “This also comprises the four paths, such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),” which reflects the intention of Master Yuan (Yuàngōng); this is explained in terms of the sequential stages (*avasthā*).
First is the path of preparation, which serves as the contemplation of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-bhāvanā*), because it involves transcending and turning away from [suffering].
Second, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is for detachment, because it eliminates the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Third, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is for cessation, because it abandons the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Fourth, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is for relinquishment, because one attains *nirvāṇa*.
This is also subsumed within the four meanings among the eight abandonments in the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*:
"aversion" refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*);
"detachment" refers to acceptance, because it brings about pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
"Cessation" refers to immediate succession, because the mind remains one-pointed without forgetting its object;

Because this pure faith has the sense of being predominant, it is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

faith is established through the three categories [of the aggregates, bases, and elements], and thus faith is unshakable.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In this context, mindfulness is the mindfulness within the foundations of mindfulness,” this is a fourth point that specifically demonstrates its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

The three—mindfulness (*smṛti*), exertion (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—are precisely the first three categories; because they accord with these three categories, mindfulness is explained first.

"Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the wisdom that takes the Four Noble Truths as its object" means that since it relies upon mindfulness such as revulsion (*nirveda*) and so forth, it has already been assigned to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); therefore, it is said that wisdom is the wisdom that takes the Four Noble Truths as its object.
In reality, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) pervades the first three categories, because the four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their essential nature;
the right efforts (samyak-prahāṇa) involve diligent observation of the two types of goodness;
and the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) involve meditative concentration associated with observation.
Subsequently, because the other two are merely auxiliary companions, they are not mentioned.

Although the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature, they are designated by the name "mindfulness" in the present context; therefore, it is said that the wisdom which contemplates the Four Truths constitutes wisdom itself.

Furthermore, regarding the first three categories: although the first two have not yet established the basis for revulsion (*nirveda*) and so forth, their meaning extends throughout the Four Noble Truths; therefore, it is said that "wisdom takes the Four Noble Truths as its object.
In the commentary, from the phrase "If based on the stages" (*yadi sthānam āśritya*) onwards, the fifth section distinguishes the fruit (*phala*).

The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "The fruit of the cultivation of the five faculties refers to the ability to swiftly give rise to the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) through wisdom.

"Furthermore, they are able to cultivate and refine *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, and induce *kṣānti* and the *laukikāgradharma*, because they have already entered the stage of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* in this very body.
Regarding the phrase "now in the fourth stage" and below, the second [section] is an analysis based on the sūtra.
The commentary on "The Fifth: The Five Powers" consists of two parts:

Who is unable to subdue this pure faith?
Whether it be devas, māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or anyone else in the world, there is none who can rightfully draw it away or seize it.
Even the various entanglements of the afflictions cannot subdue it; therefore, it is called "difficult to subdue.
This serves as the leader and this serves as the precursor; the other factors, such as diligence and so forth, are also termed "powers."

The Commentary states: "Furthermore, it can diminish and reduce... and so forth. This second section concerns the ability to subdue others; it cites two treatises to explain "power" (*bala*) by means of its "fruit.

Although they resemble the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) in that their essential nature consists of the objects they take as their objective range, the five powers (*pañcabala*) are established separately because there are differences in their meanings, such as being incapable of being suppressed.
The present commentary follows this very treatise while setting aside the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, explaining only the subduing of others.

The treatise states: "Because these aforementioned powers possess great majesty and authority, they crush and subdue the power of all Māra armies and enable the realization that all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted; therefore, they are called 'powers' (*bala*)."

However, according to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, this refers to the path of approach to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), a meaning that encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

If that which is called "non-arising" at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the first ground (*bhūmi*) is also a direct realization (*abhisamaya*), the commentary on the "sixth [topic], the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*)" contains six sections: [The text continues with the six sections of the commentary.]

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The wisdom of the realization of reality belonging to those individuals (*pudgala*) who have already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth takes this as its constituent part; therefore, it is called a 'factor of awakening' (*bodhyaṅga*)."
This is precisely the meaning of the term's etymology.

It is also the object of focus (*ālambana*); thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "The object of the seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four noble truths. Suchness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because it is the object of purification."
Therefore, the commentary states: "Awakening to the self-nature of phenomena.
The self-nature of phenomena refers to the suchness of the Four Noble Truths.
"Awakening" refers to the function of the aforementioned wisdom that realizes suchness.

The meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*) is established by means of the objects of observation, and the objects of observation are revealed by means of the awakening; thus, these two meanings mutually establish one another.
In the commentary, following the phrase "the essential nature of the factors of awakening," the second section identifies their essence.

However, while the preceding discussion was based on the general essence as it truly is, the present analysis concerns the distinct essences according to their specific characteristics; namely, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity—these seven each have a single dharma as their intrinsic nature.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) are among the five specific mental objects (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).
Among these five, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (*prajñā*) are included; this is because the investigation of dharmas is itself wisdom.

Diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are subsumed under three of the eleven wholesome factors: diligence is itself vigor (*vīrya*); pliancy is itself lightness-and-ease (*praśrabdhi*); and equanimity is itself the equanimity of formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).
Joy is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); feeling is subsumed within the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "The text has two [parts]," this is the third section, the explanation of the text.
This consists of three parts:
First, the general outline; second, the analysis of characteristics; third, the reconciliation of their mutual inclusion.

Among these, first there is a general clarification: while the seven [factors] each have distinct substantial entities among the mental concomitants (*caitasika*), because *vitarka* (investigation) governs the others, only the single factor of *dharmapravicaya* (discrimination of phenomena) has *vitarka* as its essential nature.
The remaining six are all categorized as "conducive" (*anuloma*) to the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*).
Below the passage beginning with "That is to say, mindfulness is... (*yad uta smṛtir iti*), their specific characteristics are individually demonstrated;
this is entirely the text of the *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Following the Sub-commentary, Scroll Sixty-two.

The Sub-commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty states:

"Regarding 'comprehensively subsuming the seven factors of enlightenment' and below, the third section is the reconciliation of mutual inclusion, which follows the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*."
Within this, there are two parts;
first, the primary inclusion.
Regarding "mindfulness pervades both concentration and wisdom," it is because mindfulness is omnipresent within both concentration and wisdom.
The four foundations of mindfulness are wisdom, because they must be attained through mindfulness.
The bases of spiritual power are concentration, for the mind must be concentrated and rely upon mindfulness in order to maintain its object.
The subsequent section, beginning with "Although these are the same as the preceding three," addresses and resolves potential objections.

"Since these are the same as the previous three, why are they stated again? [The answer is:
They are called "awakening" (bodhi) because they are augmented.

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "The fruit of cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) refers to the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the seven factors of enlightenment constitute the very essence of the path of seeing."
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because one first attains the seven factors of enlightenment, one is called a 'first-stage learner' (*śaikṣa*).

Having seen the traces of the noble ones, one then permanently eradicates all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), leaving only those afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, although [it occurs] in a single kṣaṇa," and so forth, refers to the fifth stage.

This means that although the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is swift and consists of sixteen moments of mind, in terms of its meaning, seven factors arise simultaneously within a single kṣaṇa; because their functions differ, they cannot be said to be one.
It is like seven kinds of fragrant incense being pounded, sifted, and blended together; when burned, as small as a sesame seed, the seven fragrances are released simultaneously.
From the phrase "mindfulness that eliminates deluded thoughts" onwards, distinct characteristics are specifically shown.

In the commentary, following the phrase "The Seven Factors of Enlightenment of the Mahāyāna," section six clarifies contemplation of principle (*lǐguān*), which is the intent of Chan in the Sudden Gate (*dùnmen*). Not recollecting any phenomena is itself the awakening of mindfulness (*niànjué*).
Thus, an ancient said:
"True Suchness is without thought; it cannot be attained through the recollection of dharmas."
The true mark is unborn; how could a mind that arises reach it?
When there is no one who thinks, one then contemplates True Suchness (tathatā).
When there is no one who gives rise to birth, one is born into the true mark.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one knows that, being free from thought, there is neither the one who thinks nor that which is thought of, this is called 'conformity.
If one is free from thought, it is called 'attaining entry.'"

Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If one conceptualizes all phenomena, one does not conceptualize the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Not recollecting any phenomena is, then, recollecting the Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.
The remainder may be sought out through inquiry.

First, regarding the term "concise by category," this refers to the path that arises subsequent to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) among the seven categories.

For those noble learners who have already seen the track, by means of the eightfold path of practice that subsumes the tracks of conduct, they are able to abandon all afflictions without remainder and are able to realize the ultimate liberation; therefore, it is called the Noble Eightfold Path.

Regarding the section "The essential nature of the Eightfold Path" in the commentary, this is the third part, which sets forth the essence; it can be understood.

Regarding "right effort" in the commentary, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "For one who diligently practices by relying upon right view, right thought, right speech, right action, and right livelihood, all their desire, exertion, vigor, renunciation, courageous power, and inspired application continue uninterruptedly in the stream of the mind."

"Because the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are purified, and the obstacles to supreme merit are purified.

Regarding the three types of antidotes—universal and restricted—the former is exclusively restricted to principle (*tattva*), whereas the latter pertains to the six stages (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*) and is thus profound; hence the commentary concludes: "In each stage, these are mutually abandoned," for the superior supersedes the inferior.
Furthermore, these three preceding meanings also mutually support one another.

Since that which is to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*) in the first case is restricted, that which remedies it (*pratipakṣa*) is universal; as both phenomenon (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*) are equal, why should purity apply to the body alone?
Because that which is to be remedied is universal while the remedy is specific, the single principle is equal, being devoid of both defilement and purity.
Since pure pride has not yet been eliminated, one cultivates the contemplation of equality; this contemplation of equality is already established within this fifth stage.
In the latter six stages, by entering into principle through contemplation, one establishes the middle by means of the beginning and the end.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the ten powers and so forth of the fruition stage," the term "and so forth" (等) includes other dharmas of fruition, namely the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the three bodies, the four wisdoms, and so on; it does not refer to the explanation of equality (*samatā*), as the pure mind of equality has already been explained in general above.
The Commentary states, “The preceding [sections] are combined into the three trainings,” etc., which explains the first six [sections] through two analytical approaches:
first, in terms of practice (*caryā*), and second, in terms of stages (*avasthā*).
First, a brief summary of the scriptural text:
how are the two characteristics of purity regarding view and doubt made manifest?
This is because these two are both among the six fundamental afflictions.

The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is derived from the six [fetters] above; furthermore, because it is clung to as the path and its characteristics are subtle and difficult to perceive, it is treated as a separate category.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “If one considers the stages,” the second section provides a detailed explanation according to the stages in response to the difficulties raised.
The statement "desiring to give rise to true wisdom" refers to the supramundane wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding the commentary's phrase "the next three are in the path of seeing," the explanation of these three consists of three parts: first, the direct explanation; [second, the refutation of objections; third, the summary].
2. From "At the time of entering the Path of Seeing" onwards is the interrogation;

3. From "The teaching on Nirvana" onwards is the citation of the answer to that interrogation, wherein it is stated that "the ten proclivities (*daśa-anuśaya*) are all abandoned," which, when expanded, constitutes eighty-eight proclivities (*aṣṭāśīty-anuśaya*).
The answer has two intended meanings.
First, it cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* because [the matter] is already established there by virtue of its gravity.
In the thirty-third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, while explaining the directions for contemplation, Kāśyapa asks:
“The Tathāgata has said:
‘The srotāpanna severs afflictions as if [removing] forty li of water.
What does this mean?”
"What are the three fetters that must be severed?
First, the view of a self; second, the view that what is not a cause is a cause; third, the net of doubt.
The Buddha replied:
"Because these three categories encompass all the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
It is like when a king goes out: although he is accompanied by the fourfold army, one simply says 'the king is going out.'"
It is further asked: "For what reason are these three alone designated as 'heavy'?

[The answer is: "Because they are constantly aroused by all sentient beings; because they are subtle and difficult to recognize; because they are difficult to sever; because they can serve as the cause for all afflictions; and because they are the enemies that oppose the three antidotes—namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)."
Furthermore, sentient beings would regress if they heard that many [afflictions] were abandoned; therefore, only three are taught.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Moreover, among the ten proclivities,” the second section distinguishes [the afflictions] according to those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the statement that "the remaining four [afflictions] pertain to both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation," this refers to greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance. Among these, the four that obstruct the path of seeing have already been abandoned within the path of seeing; furthermore, those that obstruct the path of cultivation are not designated with the term "abandoned" [at that stage], and thus they are omitted here.
The Commentary states: "The three roots and the three followings"—here, "following" refers to the derivative.
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is itself the self; because one considers whether this self existed or did not exist in the past, it is called the "eternalist view."
If one regards the "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*) as being produced by me in the future, then the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) arises;
therefore, it is said that extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) follow from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

As for "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it consists in the denial of cause and effect; because one wavers and fails to resolve upon the principle of the Truths (*satya*), one consequently denies them as non-existent, and thus it is said that false view follows from the net of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Since one who regards what is not a cause as a cause must necessarily grasp it as real, it is said that the grasping of views follows upon the grasping of precepts and observances.
Once the root is severed, the branches and twigs perish of their own accord.

Furthermore, regarding the term "following" (*anuvartana*): the three bases are called "turning," like a hand turning a wheel; the three [mental factors] that follow are called "following," like a wheel following the hand.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The preceding five are identical in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna," this concludes the discussion of the five purities previously mentioned and introduces the two subsequent purities.
Second, regarding the two purities (*śuddhi*), there are differences in their expansion and contraction according to the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as distinctions in their respective stages.
This section contains two parts:
first, concerning the Small Vehicle; second, concerning the Great Vehicle.
Within the Mahāyāna, there is the stage of prior practice and the subsequent stage.

Regarding the simultaneity of these practices, in terms of their meaning, the severance of obstacles constitutes the practice itself, while the purification resulting from that severance constitutes the accomplishment of virtue—the progressively superior purification of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

In the commentary, the section beginning with "If categorized by stages" addresses the second point: categorization by stages, which involves the distinction between the increase and decrease [of cultivation].
Although there is still progress from the seventh stage downward, the meaning of "increasing" refers to the severing of hindrances;
from the eighth stage upward, it is not that hindrances are no longer severed, but rather that progress is predominant.
For this reason, each of the two positions receives a distinct name.
Second, the clarification that [the stages] accord with the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “furthermore, in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtra,” the following relies on the Śāstra and accords only with the three types of mind; these—the first half and the latter two parts—are all stages of abiding mind (*sthiti-citta*), which are subsumed within the three positions.
This follows the path and subsumes the fifth dwelling.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because wisdom is pure and so forth, there is no delusion or confusion,” this refers to the subsequent scriptural passage which says: “The tenfold contemplation of the Dharma-gate of the Four Truths is called the purity of wisdom.”
This is precisely non-delusion (*amoha*), which knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
To know it as it truly is is the meaning of being undisturbed.

As for the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes the excellence of skillful means in diligently benefiting sentient beings; all these carry the sense of non-delusion, which accords very closely with the explanation of the meaning of non-delusion within that [section on] conduct.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “Because it encompasses inexhaustible virtues,” there are four fruits below; the first is specifically named the fruit of encompassing merit, as the remaining three are all fruits of merit.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because all four phrases within the summary constitute correct practice,” one asks: among these four, the first is the practice of the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmiḥ*); why, then, is it said that all of them are correct practice?
Furthermore, does the subsequent sūtra state, "Having entered the fifth stage, one has skillfully cultivated the factors of enlightenment"?
Answer:
There are two interpretations.
First, the practice that serves as the antidote must necessarily proceed through a reciprocal relationship with that which it counteracts; all such instances constitute cultivation.

Second, regarding the factors of the path (mārga-pakṣya-dharma) of the four stages, one takes their pure aspects and employs the ten pure minds to counteract [their opposites], thereby entering the fifth stage.

Having entered the fifth stage, one does not grasp at the signs of purity regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), yet it is not that they are not practiced; for it is only by practicing without grasping that one can cultivate them skillfully.
Although the ten subsequent purities are themselves objects of remediation, even as one accords with the Path, one does not abandon the ten preceding pure minds.
If Master Yuan says:
"All are practicing correctly; this treatise addresses the objections.
He fears there might be an objection raised:

If, as in the case of the path, this pure mind takes up the preceding pure mind, and that pure mind in turn takes up the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the four stages, then the factors of enlightenment should likewise arise from the three stages.
Why are they not taken up?
Therefore, this answer was given.
The answer states:
these four refer to the correct cultivation practiced from the fourth bhūmi upward.
"Since the third stage consists of worldly dharmas, it is for this reason that [the term 'pure'] is not mentioned.
This is also a valid principle.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "In the latter phrase, although various practices are initiated, one does not fall away from the previously attained pure mind of equanimity," this refers to the sūtra’s phrase, "conforming to suchness."

The Treatise says: "One who practices in accordance with the path of suchness, because they manifest the non-retrogression of a profoundly pure mind within that equality, abides in accordance with those pure dharmas of equality."
The commentary states:
The non-retrogressive mind is precisely this conformity to suchness (*tathatā*).
The meaning of the final phrase is as follows:

Having already used the preceding phrase to remedy the deep mind by grasping at pure signs, the present section uses the non-grasping of a deep and pure mind to follow along until reaching the practice of non-retrogression, constantly abiding within equality in accordance with the Way of Suchness; therefore, the Commentary states: "Although one gives rise to various practices, one does not lose the previously attained deep and pure mind of equality."
The subsequent commentary on the conclusion states: "When a bodhisattva thus dwells with a profound mind, it is called 'conforming to the path of suchness' (tathatā-mārga-anuloma).
Therefore, the sub-commentary says, "Thus one is able to conform to true suchness" (tathatā-anuloma), which precisely adopts this scriptural passage.
Regarding the statement "equality is itself suchness" (*tathatā*), this is a commentary that accords with the sūtra.
The sūtra says "in accordance with suchness," while the treatise takes up "equality. How are these two the same?
Therefore, it is said that "equality is suchness" (*tathatā*), as has already been explained previously.
Question:
The treatise states, "the profound mind dwells in composure. How does this differ from the previous dwelling in accordance with those equal and pure phenomena?
Answer:
Previously, one merely abided in equanimity; thus the commentary states, "not losing equanimity.
Now, speaking of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), its practice accords with Suchness, and this constitutes abiding in the profound mind.

In the commentary, regarding the statement, "In the subsequent detailed explanation, it is shown that there are eight kinds of 'practice in accordance with suchness' (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*)," the question is asked: Since all eight are practices of activity (*vastu-pratipatti*), why are they called "practice in accordance with suchness"?
The answer is:
There are two intended meanings.
First, these eight [factors] assist in manifesting the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness);
second, when practice arises within suchness, being entirely without attachment, one then manifests conformity to suchness.

While the distinct practices may be understood [otherwise], it is because the seventh phrase is sustained by the power of mindfulness and wisdom that this commentary follows the sutra in its explanation of the treatise.
The Sūtra states, "Because one has attained mindfulness, intention, and the power of wisdom. Here, "intention" (manas) refers to the wisdom of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā).
Master Huiyuan says:
"Mindfulness is the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), for it retains the teachings."
Intention (*manas*) is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), because it seeks out meanings through deliberation.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because it is able to transcend obstacles and achieve superior progress.
These three phrases are collectively termed the "power of knowledge" (*jñānabala*).

In this present sutra, since there is no distinction between intention and speech, mindfulness corresponds to the two types of wisdom (*prajñā*), while knowledge (*jñāna*) corresponds to cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This is the second [section], the Path of Non-Abiding.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Wisdom is purified among the dharmas that are known”: the Truths (*satya*) are the dharmas that are known; because wisdom perceives them therein and is free from defilement, it is called “purified.”
"Compassion that gathers beings is called benefiting sentient beings;
diligence without falling [into error] is skillful means.
Regarding the commentary's phrase "the *yogasthāna* chapter," it refers to the forty-eighth.

The treatise states: "In this manner, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they primarily seek the excellence of wisdom and, regarding the four noble truths, understand them as they truly are through ten aspects."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'real dharmas' (*dharmasatyāni*), there are two meanings:
first, taking 'real' (*satya*) in its literal sense, as already explained in the commentary;
second, taking it to mean 'real dharmas' because they are designated by different names according to the capacities of sentient beings within the ten subsequent sections."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, clarifying the opening and closing [of the categories],” the commentary text consists of four parts:
the first is a synthesis, and the latter three are analyses.

Within these three, the first analyzes according to the dharmas to be transformed; the second analyzes according to the benefits conferred; and the third analyzes according to the types of beings to be transformed.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the three pairs that clarify the general and the specific in relation to real dharmas': the four [categories] consisting of the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth are exclusively specific because each consists of only one [truth].
As for the tenth category, in relation to the first five categories it is called 'specific' because it contemplates only two truths—cessation and the path;
however, in relation to the sixth through the ninth, which contemplate only a single truth, it is likewise called 'general'."
Regarding the statement, "Master Yuan’s later five [treatises] are also said to be 'comprehensive' (tong)": what is meant by "comprehensive" (tong) and "distinctive" (bie)?
That which is observed is comprehensive across four [truths], yet that which is accomplished is singular; thus it may also be called "distinctive."
The Commentary states: "Regarding the statement 'the ten phrases of the initial yoga do not manifest in their literal wording,' this refers to the aforementioned *Vihāra-paṭala* (Chapter on Abiding).
The Treatise says: 'All literal wording is as explained in the sūtras; one should only take up the meaning of the sūtras.'"
The meaning established therein resembles the commentary of the present treatise, though with slight differences; therefore, it is set forth separately.

Regarding the statement in the *Śū* (Commentary), "The text has three sections," he first enumerates the names of these three sections: first, "this is said for the sake of"; second, "this is said because of"; and third, "this is said in this manner," which are fully analyzed below in the *Śū*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “should be understood in their respective order,” this refers to the sequence of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—which corresponds here to the numbers six, seven, eight, and nine.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “for the sake of teaching the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths and so forth,” this means that beneath the truth of suffering there are four aspects: namely, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Under "origination" there are four: origination, cause, birth, and condition.
Under "cessation" there are four: cessation, purity, excellence, and liberation.
The Path also has four: path, suchness, practice, and exit; therefore, these constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That is, the four pairs of the two truths,” etc.: as for the “four pairs,” first are the two truths of the provisional and the real; second, the two truths of phenomena and principle; third, the two truths of the conventional and the ultimate; and fourth, the two truths of the established and the non-established. These are explained in detail in the *Xuánzàn* (Profound Commentary).
Regarding the statement "now this is the third layer," it is because the Four Truths are taken as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Master Huiyuan also spoke of three types of two truths:

first, distinguishing them by their characteristics—wherein that which exists through the conceptualizations of the mind is called the worldly truth (*loka-satya*), and the emptiness of signlessness is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The two characteristics are in actual opposition: the phenomena of false conceptualization, which exist emotionally but lack objective reality, are termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is precisely the true dharma of the empty *tathāgatagarbha* mentioned in this sutra;
the quiescence of characteristics wherein the essence exists is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

Third, regarding the analysis according to reality: within the *Akṣayakośa*, the essence (*tattva*) is termed the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārthasatya*) and its function (*vṛtti*) is termed the "Conventional Truth" (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Now, among the various truths, this is the primary one; yet if one proceeds according to the second gate [of classification], it appears that the intended meaning is not fully grasped.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase “not the same as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,” the *Yogācāra* merely states that it is “based on awakening others,” and thus it is general.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “for the sake of expounding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*),” this refers to the third level within the fourfold classification of truths.
Together with the conventional truth of the first four truths mentioned above, these constitute the third set of two truths.
Regarding the third and fourth [truths], they clarify that the two aforementioned truths are neither identical nor different: the third is not different, and the fourth is not identical.

Furthermore, the three are identical with the two yet are not two; thus, the Sūtra says, "Awakening to self-characteristics and common characteristics," and the Śāstra says, "Abiding together in the four, they are non-dual yet dual."
The Treatise treats doubt as one, because it is non-dual;
the Sūtra clarifies distinctions, because it is dual.

Furthermore, the fourth [topic] concerns the truths, which are always inherently dual; the third concerns understanding, which is always inherently one; and the fifth comprehensively clarifies the characteristics and nature of dependent origination within the two truths.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "To penetrate this non-duality is truly to enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the sixth is right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*): among the preceding [five], the third is doubt, the fourth is error, and the fifth is the departure from right mindfulness; none of these constitute right view.

Now, being free from this error constitutes right view; thus, one may clearly elucidate the distinctions of the Four Noble Truths, thereby avoiding attachment to phenomena and the claim that all is empty and non-existent, so as to enable the realization of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the verification of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path.
"Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of suffering, because all sensations are suffering.
"The origin is able to produce suffering.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "The wisdom of one beyond training knows thus," this explains the word "wisdom" (*jñāna*) in the sutra in order to answer an external question.
Cessation is the principle of cessation; how can it be called "wisdom"? Therefore, this commentary states: "The intent lies in taking up cessation.
Regarding the phrase in the Subcommentary, "The Way is said to be non-dual," this briefly cites the scriptural text; the full passage reads: "Because it gives birth to non-duality."
The *Śāstra* on the *Sūtra* states: "Because one gives rise to non-dual conduct.
Since it is referred to as the cessation of cognition, dualistic conduct does not arise.
Regarding the passage in the *Subcommentary* beginning with "Previously, the real dharmas were listed," there should be a question as follows:
Regarding these Four Truths, what is the distinction between them and the Four Truths previously listed alongside the real dharmas?
The intent of the answer can be understood.
If one follows Master Yuan’s previous explanation, then the four gates of the real dharmas were each distinct; [whereas here they are integrated].
Now, since each [of these] is confused regarding the preceding four, there are differences;
yet this is also a single principle.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Because the fundamental substance has not been attained," there are two kinds of fundamental substance:
First, with respect to not yet having realized the Buddha-wisdom, the Buddha-wisdom serves as the essential nature (svabhāva);

second, since one has not yet realized the Tathāgata’s wisdom, regarding all phenomena known by omniscience, these are both the essential nature and the reflected image (pratibimba), because all that is to be realized has not yet been directly realized.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second [section] concerns the excellence of the skillful means of diligent effort for the benefit of sentient beings”: since one contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth for the sake of benefiting others, why is compassion (*karuṇā*) specifically elucidated?
It is because, in contrast to the aforementioned purity of the wisdom that contemplates the truths (*satya*), although various formations (*saṃskāra*) are present therein, compassion is predominant.
In the commentary, the phrase "The two characters 'false' and 'erroneous' refer to observing the internal five aggregates" serves as the topical heading.
The section beginning with "That is, conceptual construction" is the treatise’s explanation.
From "This clarifies" onwards, the commentary explains the treatise.
Regarding the phrase, “Constantly conceiving the pride of ‘I’ leads to falsehood,” this is the commentary (*śāstra*).
From the words “This explains” (*cibian*) onwards, it is the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).

In the sub-commentary, the statement “The two characters ‘fraudulent’ (*zhawei*) refer to observing the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-bāhyaviṣaya*)” serves as the topical heading; the passage “Because worldly dharmas entice and seize the foolish, they are fraudulent” is the commentary (*śāstra*).
"‘This reveals’" and below is the commentary (shu) explaining the treatise (lun).
The phrase "Because worldly dharmas are utterly destroyed, they are false" is the treatise.
"'This clarifies' and below" is the commentary explaining the treatise.

Regarding the phrase "the two objects of superior falsehood": "falsehood" (*xū*) refers to internal objects, while "deception" (*wèi*) refers to external objects; both can draw the mind toward them, and thus together they are termed "delusive" (*kuǎng*).

"Falsity" (*wàng*) refers to the internal mind, while "fraudulence" (*zhà*) refers to the external mind; both can cause confusion regarding their objects, and thus together they are termed "delusion" (*huò*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The treatise says ‘permanence, etc.’,” the preceding commentary should have paired the two objects with the two minds to correspond to deception and delusion.

In the treatise, the internal and external aspects of subject and object are explained separately; first, the internal is explained, where the apprehended object is clarified first and the apprehending subject second.

Subsequently, from the passage “the worldly dharmas are exhausted and beneficial” onwards, the external subject and object are explained, likewise clarifying the apprehended object first and the apprehending subject second.
This can be easily understood through careful investigation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The ‘foolish person’ refers to one who relies on that very grasping of the conceit of self,” the former part explains deception and delusion, while the latter part explains the foolish person.
Previously there were two pairs; now, we address only the first five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to clarify the foolish person.
The five aggregates constitute the person.
Second, a distinct contemplation of compassion (*karuṇā*) is initiated.
The Commentary states: "Correctly clarifying the meaning of generating the vow to save sentient beings.

Although the Sūtra says "seeking the Buddha-wisdom," it speaks of saving sentient beings; this precisely corresponds to the third stage (bhūmi), where one desires to save sentient beings without departing from Buddha-wisdom.
The Commentary states: "Now, first, ignorance and craving for existence are the causes of transmigration"—the meaning reaches this point.
From the phrase "therefore, birth" onwards, all [factors] are subsumed under the category of results.
If one were to extract the scriptural passage, it should extend to "therefore they are born" as the conclusion of the sentence.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "citing what precedes and rebuking what follows": this means citing the profound suffering that preceded and rebuking the heavy suffering that follows.
Regarding the phrase "the painful business of mechanisms," Master Yuan’s commentary explains:
"The place where things are contained and moved is called a *ji* (mechanism);
that which revolves within it is termed a *guan* (pivot)."
The term "cause" (*hetu*) is called "trigger" (*ki*), and the "resulting suffering" (*duḥkhaphala*) that follows it is termed "gate" (*kan*).
The intent of the present commentary is likewise; it does not separately assign these two characters.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "Among those who seek desire, there are two types of seekers of desire," the seeking of desire is divided into two.
First, those who indulge in the five desires without fearing their future retribution are evildoers;
second, those who merely dote on the five desires but do not necessarily commit evil—this person here is of the latter kind.
Attachment arises toward favorable conditions, while aversion arises toward those that are unfavorable;
delusion underlies both of these, though it is not mentioned here as one who practices wholesome conduct.
Wholesome conduct generally exists within the pursuit of existence, and because its faults are slight, it is omitted from discussion for brevity.
This is also included within the category of "experiencing desires.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "observing reality as it is" (*yathābhūta*), its meaning can be understood by contrasting it with the preceding analysis.

Regarding the commentary’s statement "being far from that cessation and not tending toward cessation," the *Śāstra* says: "They proceed toward the state of fearlessness, yet do not seek the Great Sage Teacher who possesses the Ten Powers."
The meaning is:
one desires to proceed toward the cessation that is fearless, yet does not seek to realize cessation for oneself.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "because it follows the path of the enemy": the fetters and latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are called a "dense forest"; because this is the domain of Māra, it is termed the "path of the enemy."
"Having already entered the path of enmity, one is immediately far removed from the True Path.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Briefly, old age is not explained," the preceding section relied on the *Śāstra* to contemplate birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Since the suffering of birth occurs at the beginning, and sickness can suddenly strike and applies to both the young and the old, the Sūtra clarifies these [first three].
The present mention of "birth and death" already encompasses the suffering of death.
Since the mention of "old age" is not explicit, it is said to be "omitted," yet it ought to be included as well.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "In the general [category], one who has no father is called 'lonely' (*gu*)," and so forth: within the specific [categories], the Sūtra contains eight matters, fully explaining these four characters.
The first four matters clarify that there is suffering, while the latter four matters clarify that there is evil; each pair of matters explains one of the preceding points.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because they constantly give rise to false thoughts, they constitute an obscuration”: based on the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), the arising of a mind of deluded conceptualization is termed "false thought."
Because they flow and continue in succession, they are said to "arise constantly," unlike the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*), where good and evil arise alternately.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because one has not heard the True Dharma, one is enveloped by those [afflictions],” it means that while the delusions of the four abidings may occasionally be interrupted by goodness, when there is such an interval, they do not envelop.
Because they do not hear wholesome exhortations, they are thus bound and enveloped.
Regarding the section "Second, Arousing Compassion," the Sūtra has three parts:

first, practicing the causal conditions for the sake of sentient beings; second, from "Solely giving rise to the thought of enlightenment" onwards, uniquely highlighting the great resolve; and third, from "By means of these merits" onwards, benefiting sentient beings through virtue.
First, it causes the purification of hindrances, serving as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.
What is called "ultimate purity" is also the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Finally, up until the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and unimpeded wisdom, it brings about the fruit of *bodhi*.
Although this commentary now provides a general explanation, its meaning is already complete.

Regarding the passage in the commentary that states, "First, it restates the previous [section] to generally clarify the cultivation of goodness mentioned above": while this briefly mentions the cultivation of goodness, in reality, it also encompasses the preceding wisdom-observation.

Seeing that sentient beings are subject to suffering and evil, and lack both remedy and rescue, one cultivates roots of goodness to provide them with benefit; all such acts are the marks of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), for they are able to benefit others through wholesome wisdom.

The Commentary states: "The first two are for the sake of rescuing the future" means that they cause beings to abide in wholesome causes so that they may obtain pleasant fruits belonging to the future;
this is precisely the meaning of benefit and happiness, as frequently seen in the preceding text.

The first phrase causes those who have not yet established themselves [in virtue] to do so; the second phrase causes those who have already established themselves in subtle goodness to subsequently increase it, thereby attaining the fruit of happiness.
