The Commentary states: "Furthermore, in the seventeenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the three natures as causes are contrasted with the five kinds of fruits, because even the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) can bring about fruits."

Regarding the statement, "The treatise generally takes three as the causes for the path," the beginning of the fifth fascicle of that commentary states: "It was previously said that there are five kinds of fruits; among these, which karma has how many kinds of fruits?"
The verse says:
Defiled karma on the path of abandonment possesses all five fruits.
Untainted karma has four, namely, with the exception of the ripening fruit alone.
The other contaminated wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] likewise have four, excluding dissociation.
The other uncontaminated and neutral [dharmas] have three, excluding those previously excluded. Commentary:
The path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) is precisely the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*); its detailed correlations are as described therein.
Among those, the second [section] concerns the mutual relationship between the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

The treatise states: "Having already made a general distinction regarding the fact that all karma has results, we next examine the characteristics of karma and its results through various categories; therein, we first distinguish the three results, beginning with the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth."

The verse says: "Regarding wholesome and so forth, for wholesome and so forth; in the first [moment], there are four, two, and three; in the middle, there are two, three, and four; in the last, there are two, three, and three fruits. The commentary explains: [This refers to the relationship between karma and its results. When a wholesome action is performed, it may have up to four results: the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the result of dominance (*adhipatiphala*), the result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), and the result of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*). In some cases, it has two results (the results of dominance and disconnection), and in others, three results (excluding the result of outflow). This pattern applies to unwholesome and neutral actions as well, with variations depending on the specific category of action and its timing. Thus, in the initial stage, there are four, two, and three results; in the intermediate stage, there are two, three, and four results; and in the final stage, there are two, three, and three results.
The "superior wholesome" and so forth refer to karma; the "inferior wholesome" and so forth refer to dharmas.

The former refers to wholesome karma, for which wholesome dharmas serve as four fruits—namely, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), since maturation is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Unwholesome [karma] has two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Neutral (*avyākṛta*) [karma] has three fruits, excluding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*); thus it is said that the first [category] has four, and the second and third have two and three [fruits respectively].
Regarding the statement that there are two, three, or four [fruits] within the intermediate category: the "intermediate" refers to unwholesome karma.
When taking wholesome [karma] as the cause, there are two fruits, namely the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
When taking unwholesome [karma] as the cause, there are three fruits, adding the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) to those two.
The indeterminate [dharmas] serve as four fruits, namely, excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Regarding the statement that the latter two [categories] have three fruits each, the "latter" refers to the indeterminate.
The wholesome [dharmas] serve as two fruits, namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Unwholesome [dharmas] serve as three fruits, excluding the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*).
Neutral [dharmas] also serve as three fruits, likewise excluding the maturation fruit and the fruit of disconnection.
The commentary states:
Since the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is considered in relation to the wholesome and unwholesome, and the indeterminate possesses two or three fruits, this clarifies that it does indeed have fruits.
Furthermore, since the specific does not depart from the general, there is no fault in its serving as a cause.
The Commentary states: "Or, since it does not attract a ripening [result]," and so forth. Second, this clarifies that the causes of the path are exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
That is to say, since it is said that there is no substance for the total retribution result of ripening, the meaning of "result" is absent.

The Master of the Treatise states that, while generally clarifying that the three [types of action] serve as the causes for the path, his specific intent is to take only the wholesome and unwholesome as the causes.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “The two—those with representation and so forth—are distinctions of intrinsic nature,” the following two lines refer exclusively to the distinctions in meaning according to the functional substance (*karmabhāva*).
"Self-nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the sense of "constructing"; it is the self-nature of karma. In the initial commentary, it was simply stated as "the distinction of self-nature.
From the passage beginning with "The treatise says: 'This is of two kinds,'" onwards, this is the Master of the Treatise’s subsequent re-explanation of the text.
The Master of the Treatise merely states: "First, the time of deliberation; second, the time of performing the action.
From the passage beginning "This resides in the mental ground" (*manobhūmi*), the commentary explains the first meaning.
Regarding the statement that speech resides in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), it has not yet manifested through body or speech.

As for the claim that there are two types of volition (*cetanā*)—deliberation (*santīraṇa*) and determination (*niścaya*)—the present statement that "there is only the single type of deliberative volition" precisely clarifies the intention within the treatise regarding what has not yet been performed.

Although it exists within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), because it has not yet reached certainty, has not yet become a course of action (*karmapatha*), and has not yet received its retribution, it is like the [karma] of the six grounds which, for two reasons, does not receive its fruit of retribution: first, because the action has not yet been performed.
The preceding citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* has already extensively demonstrated this.
Regarding the phrase "Second, the time of performing the action," this is the text of the treatise itself.
From the point "Explaining the character 'action' (作) in the sūtra" onwards, the commentary explains how this applies to all three types of karma.

What is called "definitive volition" (*niścita-cetanā*) is precisely mental action (*manas-karman*); it constitutes a path of action (*karmapatha*) only upon reaching definitive volition, as it is capable of summoning retribution.
The passage beginning with "If [it occurs] in body or speech" below distinguishes the remaining two types of action.
In the section following "Establishing Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), a treatise is cited as proof.

At the end of the first chapter of that treatise, after extensively refuting the external schools' positions regarding manifest and unmanifest form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*), a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) cites a sūtra and asks:
"The World-Honored One stated in the sūtras that there are three types of karma."
"If one negates body, speech, and mind, would this not contradict the sūtras?
Therefore, the treatise answers: "It does not negate them as being non-existent; it merely states that they are not form (*rūpa*).
The volition (*cetanā*) that moves the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the volition that initiates speech is called vocal action (*vākkarman*)."
"The two types of volition—deliberative and impulsive—are called mental karma because they are associated with the mind and because they move the mind.
The commentary states:
This explains the essential nature of the three types of karma.
However, there are three types of volition (*cetanā*):
first, deliberative volition; second, determinative volition; and third, impelling volition.
Of these, the first two constitute the distant and proximate preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for initiating bodily and vocal actions.
However, the volition that initiates and correctly impels body and speech constitutes the essence of the two types of karma.
Since the first two types of volition are associated with the mind and cause the mind to act and move, they are termed "mental karma" (manas-karma).
Therefore, volition (*cetanā*) is taken collectively as the essence of the three types of action.
The commentary states:

Within the category of mental action (*manas-karman*), it is necessary for both types of volition to be present for it to constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*), as has already been explained above.
Now, regarding the establishment of karma, it is simply stated as "definite"; therefore, the Jin translation says, "discriminating the non-discriminable characteristic.
Regarding the commentary’s passage, "However, since it is now said that there is representation," this merely follows the wording of the sūtra and does not reflect the intent of the treatise.
"Manifest action (*vijñapti*) is so called because it is characterized by being visible; non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is the opposite of this.

The *Abhidharmakośa*, in the 'Chapter on Karma' (*Karma-nirdeśa*), states: 'The differentiation of the world arises from karma, which consists of volition (*cetanā*) and what is produced by volition.'"
"Volition is mental action; what is performed refers to bodily and vocal [action].
The commentary explains:
This refers to a question being asked:
From what does the world arise?
The first phrase answers:
it arises from karma.
The second line indicates two types of karma:
first, the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*); second, the karma after having willed (*cetayitvā*). Thus, the latter two lines expand these two into three.
However, that mental karma (*manas-karma*) is established as karma in terms of its origination (*samutthāna*).
Since volition (cetanā) is associated with the mind (manas), that which is induced by the mind and so forth is termed mental action (manaskarma).

Regarding bodily action (kāyakarma): it is designated as "body" in reference to its basis; that is, bodily action arises dependent upon the physical body (rūpakāya), and is therefore called bodily action.
Regarding the "action of speech," it is established based on its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because speech itself is the action.

Next, these two types of action are further divided into the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). As the verse says: "These two actions of body and speech both possess the nature of the manifest and the unmanifest."
The commentary states:
The treatise’s explanation of these two points is extensive and detailed; I shall now provide a brief indication.
First, the correct reasoning for establishing the thesis of existence (*astitva*) is as follows:
It is accepted that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consists of a distinct shape; therefore, shape constitutes bodily intimation, as in the case of joining the palms and so forth.
It is accepted that there exists a distinct shape, and this shape itself is the intimation, because it manifests virtue and non-virtue.
The manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) is itself karma; because this form and color arise based upon the body, it is called "bodily karma" (*kāyakarma*).
Next, he refutes the Saṃmitīya school, stating:
"Motion is not its essence, for motion is itself conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)."
Conditioned phenomena possess momentariness because they undergo cessation at a subsequent moment.
This phenomenon of cessation does not depend on any further cause.
Bodily intimation is an effect, and every effect necessarily depends upon a cause.
The Master of the Treatise further refutes the Vaibhāṣika school, stating:
"Shape is not substantially existent, because it would have to be apprehended by two sense faculties.
That is to say, length and so forth are conventionally established based upon multiple manifest colors; since there are no distinct atoms [of shape], they are conventional and not substantial."
If it is said that there is a real entity manifested as the object of the eye, then its shape (*saṃsthāna*) should be perceivable by the body.
Now, since what is manifested is precisely the shape, it should be apprehended by two sense-faculties.
Although shape is indeed indicative (*vijñapti*), it is not karma, because karma is volition (*cetanā*).
Because it relies on bodily activity as its gateway, it is called "bodily karma.
Next, the following statement is established:
"Vocal intimation is admitted to be vocal sound."
To grant this for the moment: we accept that the vocal sound itself constitutes the essence of the action of speech (*vāg-karman*).
Furthermore, the essence of this action is also the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates speech, because it functions through the gateway of speech and is the action of speech.
Thus, it shares the same essence as the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Although unmanifest [form] has matter as its intrinsic nature just like manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), it does not communicate itself so that others may understand it; therefore, it is called 'unmanifest'."

Furthermore, a verse states: "Whether the mind is distracted or absent, [the karma] flows along as pure or impure; because it is produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is therefore called 'unmanifest' (*avijñapti*).
The above is based on the Hīnayāna; hereafter, the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) will be explained according to the Mahāyāna.

However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* sets forth the correct principle, stating: "The mind acts as the cause, causing the consciousnesses to transform and manifest the arising and ceasing, and the continuous succession, of the appearances of form and so forth; as these transition toward other locations, they appear to have movement. Because this represents the mind, it is conventionally designated as 'bodily intimation' (*kāyavijñapti*)."

"However, because of the mind, consciousness transforms and manifests as something resembling sound, arising and ceasing in a continuous succession; it appears to have the capacity for expression, and is thus conventionally designated as 'vocal action' (vāg-karman).
The commentary states:
"The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* relies solely on the transformation of the mind, which distinguishes it from the Hīnayāna."
Next, the non-informative (avijñapti) is explained: "If the informative (vijñapti) is not real, how could the non-informative be true?
Nevertheless, there is no logical contradiction in provisionally establishing the non-informative based on the limits of wholesome or unwholesome volitions and aspirations.
Next, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna views are contrasted.
According to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, only bodily and vocal actions possess both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

However, according to the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, since the unmanifest is established as a conceptual construct based upon the manifest, the commentary states: "As for the manifest, all three are volition (*cetanā*)."
If non-information (avijñapti) were defined as being neither matter nor mind, then it would also exist in the mental faculty.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states: "What is manifest action (vijñapti-karman)?"
Briefly, there are three types:
first, defiled; second, wholesome; and third, indeterminate.

If, with respect to the ten unwholesome courses of action of body, speech, and mind, there is bodily or vocal manifest karma that does not depart from the predominant force of their active manifestation, it is called defiled manifest karma.
Third is that which is to be remedied.

If one undertakes the vow to distance oneself from all bodily and vocal manifestations (*vijñapti*) within those [unwholesome states], it is called wholesome manifest karma; this refers to wholesome bodily and vocal manifestation.

If the bodily and vocal informative actions (vijñapti-karma) belonging to a portion of the modes of deportment (īryāpatha) and the arts and crafts (śailpasthānika), these are called neutral (avyākṛta) informative actions; such are the neutral informative actions of body and speech.

If one does not wish to communicate to another, but merely gives rise to a thought within oneself, deliberating internally without uttering speech, yet manifests the activity of wholesome, afflicted, or neutral mental factors, this is called mental action (manas-karman).
The commentary states:
This demonstrates that mental karma also possesses the three natures.
"Being able to understand for oneself, 'I am now performing such an action,' which specifically indicates the subsequent manifestation associated with the mind, is called mental manifestation."
"Consider that the mind is non-manifestation;
reflect upon this according to the principle.
The commentary states:
Thus, one should know that all three [types of karma] in the Mahāyāna possess informative expression (*vijñapti*);
this is explained in detail in a separate chapter. In the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma), the Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna provides a tenfold analysis:

first, distinguishing the names; second, identifying the essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, distinguishing between the provisional and the real; fourth, the number of constituent factors (*aṅga*); fifth, the boundaries of acquisition and relinquishment; sixth, the presence or absence of dependence on others; seventh, the nature of being composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); eighth, the distinctions to be established; ninth, the sequence of acquisition and relinquishment; and tenth, resolving various objections and difficulties.
It is explained in detail as stated therein.

Regarding the "differentiation of skillful means" (*upāya-viśeṣa*) in the Commentary: the mind serves as the skillful means for the arising of karma; thus the Sūtra says, "That which arises together with the mind and is not separate from it" means that karma arises simultaneously with the mind and, once arisen, does not depart from it.
This statement means that karmic actions always depend upon the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "co-arising with the motivating mental consciousness" (*samutthāpaka-manovijñāna*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "There are two kinds of motivation (*samutthāna*): causal (*hetu*) and momentary (*tatkṣaṇika*)."
It should be understood that, according to the sequence, they are termed "the primary mover" (*pravartaka*) and "the follower" (*anuvartaka*).
This citation and explanation from the treatise are as previously discussed in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmiḥ*).
However, in this present context, it specifically refers to the co-arising of conditions (*sahabhū-samutthāna*).
Because it arises simultaneously with the karma that has been initiated, it is said that "the mental consciousness arises together [with it].

As for the statement, "In accordance with its being wholesome or unwholesome, once it has arisen, it immediately perfumes and forms seeds such as names and phrases," this text is an elliptical abbreviation.
If there is the perfuming of the wholesome or the unwholesome, it immediately forms the seeds of karma.

The perfuming by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth forms the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*), because the aforementioned [seeds] arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness.
However, it is only through the perfuming of karma that the mind truly becomes a seed; thus it is said as such.
In the commentary, the term "etc. refers to the seeds of karma.
Regarding the statement that the seeds resemble the perfuming agents (*vāsanā*), there are also two meanings:
first, they resemble the wholesome and the unwholesome; from the unwholesome arise bitter fruits, and from the wholesome arise pleasant fruits.

The second [category] consists of those resembling names and words (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*): the eighth consciousness, being perfumed, becomes the seed of maturation (*vipāka*), while the seven evolving consciousnesses and so forth, acting as perfumers, become the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so on.
Regarding these two aforementioned cases, it is stated that they do not produce fruits separately.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of non-separation," this concludes by returning to the sūtra.
It means that the seeds of karma are not separate from the mind, and the attainment of the fruit is not separate from the seeds.
In the commentary, the phrase "the fourth, the exhaustion of the accumulation of fruits" refers to the second pair of three phrases below.
The first two phrases discuss karma in relation to its fruit, while the subsequent phrase concerns the distinctions among types of karma.
Within the former, this specific line clarifies that once karma has attained its fruit, it is neither lost nor destroyed.
The expression "attaining and maintaining until the fruit" refers to the meaning of "continuous maintenance" (*prāpti-prāpti*) as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The verse of the treatise states: "Acquisition (prāpti) refers to obtaining and accomplishment; non-acquisition (aprāpti) is the opposite of this.
Acquisition and non-acquisition belong only to oneself, regarding the two cessations within the continuum.

However, this acquisition of acquisition functions to maintain that karma, like a promissory note holding a debt; therefore, the ancient sūtras and śāstras call it the "dharma of non-disappearance" (avipraṇāśa-dharma).
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The non-perishing dharma (*avipraṇāśa*) is like a promissory note, and karma is like the wealth owed.

Although the Mahāyāna establishes the existence of attainment (*prāpti*), it does not allow for its substantial reality; rather, it asserts that it consists of seeds formed through perfuming (*vāsanā*). This has already been cited in the preceding passage.
The Commentary states: "Although the preceding thought has ceased," and so forth, which explains the sequential terminology of the Sūtra.
This contains two meanings:
first, it clarifies the sequence by means of the cessation of the preceding cause and the arising of the subsequent effect.
Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore, these causes also perfuse instantaneously" clarifies the sequence solely from the perspective of the fruits, as explained in the Sixth Stage.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The treatise says: 'Having already received the fruit,'" etc., this sentence clarifies the speed with which karma receives its retribution.

Regarding the statement, "Karma that was to be experienced as retribution in past lives has already been experienced in the present," this is explained for the time being by way of a single proximate aspect.

If it is experienced in the present life, it is further karma created in preceding lifetimes; thus, it may also be considered karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, and is termed "already experienced."

This refers to the fact that for karma to be experienced in a future life (*paścātkarmavipāka*), that which has already been moistened (*ārdrīkṛta*) results in retribution, while that which has not yet been moistened does not result in retribution; likewise, it should be said that what has already matured (*pakva*) has already been experienced, while what has not yet matured has not yet been experienced.

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "There is yet another principle," this follows the previous section on the six grounds of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), specifically within the protection against the three external faults, and now addresses the objection concerning karma that lacks retribution.
The preceding treatise answered: "Karma does not receive its retribution for three reasons:
first, it has not yet been performed; second, it has not yet been moistened [by craving]; and third, an antidote has been obtained.
The former refers to the second reason, while the present refers to the third reason.
"Karma not yet created" refers to that which has not been performed previously.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The first two contrast black and white," this explains the distinctions according to the *Śāstra*.
However, that treatise on the sūtras contains four propositions, stating: black karma, white karma, black-and-white karma, and neither-black-nor-white karma.
The commentary explains: "Black karma is contrasted with white karma."
"Wholesome karma (*śukla-karman*) is contrasted with unwholesome karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*);
that which is neither black nor white is contrasted with these two types of karma—the third being 'black-and-white' karma.
Therefore, it is said: "The latter two are outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) karma," for the non-outflowing is indeed karma that is both black and white.
Furthermore, the present expression "black-black" relies entirely upon the *Abhidharmakośa*, which will be cited below.
Regarding the passage in the commentary, "Of the four [types of karma], the first has both cause and effect that are evil," the following is a detailed explanation.
However, explaining "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) as "evil" (*akuśala*) is the general meaning.
Specifically, because it is defiled by evil causes, its fruit is evil, base, and loathsome, and thus cannot be cherished.
The general explanation of "white" is thus well-clarified; yet, the specific meanings also differ, because while the substance of the cause is non-defiled, the fruit of the white is desirable.
However, the aforementioned "black" is the cause, as it is capable of summoning a black fruit.
The "black below" is the fruit, because it can recompense a black cause.
The case of white causes and white fruits may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because all untainted (*anāsrava*) karma has no maturation (*vipāka*): since there is no white maturation, it is said to be "not white."
Its essence is not defiled; therefore, it is said to be "not black.
Now, because its nature as being untainted and non-defiled is readily understood, it is simply stated that it "has no maturation."
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "This is not a literal statement;
it is not spoken with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-vacana*). For in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
'All dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are purely wholesome, purely white, and entirely without fault.'"
The commentary states:
Since it is said to be "pure white," the statement that it is "not white" is an intentional (sandhyābhāṣa) teaching.
The term "not white" is employed in order to establish the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Therefore, the Commentary states: "The name 'neither' is established in contrast to the two types of karma, black and white.

If one follows the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, it merely speaks of karma that is neither black nor white, without the two characters for "neither" (*liang-fei*); thus the treatise says: "It is not black because it is free from the defilements of affliction (*kleśa-mala*)."
"White" refers to being exclusively pure.

Regarding the four types of karma mentioned above: the first two establish "black-black-white-white" based on both cause and effect; the third establishes its name solely from the perspective of the cause; and the fourth establishes its name from both cause and effect, clarifying that the cause is not black and the fruit is not white.

The Commentary states: "The 'three above have retribution' refers to the fact that 'retribution' is defined here as *vipāka* (ripening); since the untainted (*anāsrava*) lacks ripening, it is said that there are three types of retribution.
If, however, 'retribution' is defined according to the term 'fruit,' then since the untainted possesses four fruits, all four categories mentioned above would be termed 'having retribution.'"

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “If [it follows] the *Abhidharmakośa*,” etc., this is intended to introduce the subsequent explanation, as that treatise does not admit that the wholesome and the unwholesome can coexist simultaneously.

This refers to the *Kośa*’s clarification that [the relationship between karma and its fruit] is based on the continuity (*saṃtāna*) of the stream of consciousness, rather than on their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, the preceding four lines fully capture the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*; thus, that treatise states: "Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra that there are four kinds of karma: some karma is black with black maturation; some karma is white with white maturation; some karma is black-and-white with black-and-white maturation; and some karma is neither black nor white, having no maturation, which is capable of exhausting all karmas."
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Based on distinctions such as the "black" and so forth, four types of karma are taught.
"Unwholesome [dharmas], form-realm [dharmas], desire-realm wholesome [dharmas], and those that can exhaust them—
the outflow-free (anāsrava)— should be known as black, white, both, and neither,
respectively. The commentary states:
The preceding commentary has fully utilized the treatise; one may see this for oneself by examining it closely.
That is to say, the first two phrases provide a general indication.

The next phrase refers to the three types of evil karma, which are the evil karmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the wholesome karma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and "desire" (*kāma*) refers to the wholesome karma of the desire realm.
That which can exhaust those [previous karmas] is the untainted (anāsrava) fourth karma; it takes those aforementioned three types of karma as its objects of treatment.
The untainted serves as the antidote, meaning that the exhaustion of those aforementioned three is untainted karma.
The final two lines constitute the conclusion, which is self-evident.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The rest is as explained extensively in the eighth chapter of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*,” the meaning of the *Abhidharmakośa* has already been fully utilized above.
The meaning of the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* is largely identical to that of the *Abhidharmakośa*; it is now set forth in further detail. The treatise states:

"Furthermore, there are four types of differentiation among karmas: namely, black karma with black ripening; white karma with white ripening; black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening; and non-black-and-white karma without ripening, which is capable of exhausting all karmas."
Karma that is black with black ripening refers to unwholesome karma; because it is defiled, its ripening is undesirable.
Karma that is white with white ripening refers to wholesome karma of the two realms; because it is undefiled, its ripening is desirable.

Regarding "karma that is black-and-white and white-and-black with mixed maturation," this refers to karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that is mixed, because it is a mixture of both wholesome and unwholesome.
How can a single karma be both wholesome and unwholesome?

In this context, it is not on the basis of the characteristics of the moment of arising that a single type of karma is said to be both wholesome and unwholesome; rather, it is by way of the underlying intention (*āśaya*) and the preparatory application (*prayoga*) that a single karma is spoken of in general.
This is the intended meaning of this sutra.
Based on these two types, which are mutually dissimilar—either black or white—one kind of black-and-white karma is established.
There may be karma that is black by way of intention (*āśaya*) but white by way of application (*prayoga*), or there may be karma that is black by way of application but white by way of intention.

Regarding that which is black by way of intention but white by way of application: for example, there is a person who, desiring to deceive another, first manifests a certain appearance in order to inspire confidence in him, and thus practices generosity, even to the point of renouncing the household life; this is due to the application [of virtuous conduct] but the blackness of the intention.

Regarding "white" [actions]: it is as when a person, wishing to lead their children and disciples away from a place of danger and toward safety, manifests various forms of coarse and harsh physical and verbal conduct out of a heart of compassion; at that time, defilement arises.

Regarding "karma that is neither black nor white and has no ripening, which is capable of exhausting all karma": this refers to all untainted (anāsrava) karma within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of these preparatory stages (*prayoga*), because the path of immediate succession constitutes the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for the abandonment of those various karmas.
It is not black because it is free from the defilements of affliction (*kleśa*).
It is white because it is exclusively pure.
It has no maturation (*vipāka*) because it is contrary to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

"Regarding 'being able to exhaust all karma': this is because, through the power of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma, one forever uproots the three types of contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma—such as the black and so forth—along with their ripening (*vipāka*) habitual tendencies.
The commentary states:
"This is easily understood from the text."
To say merely that "what is not black" is not defiled by the stains of afflictions (*kleśa*) serves to distinguish it from the previously mentioned "black-black" karma.
To say it is "exclusively pure" distinguishes it from the previously mentioned tainted wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*), which is incited by afflictions.

Regarding the statement that it is "permanently uprooted by the power of untainted karma": this refers to the volitional karma (*cetanā*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the immediate stage (*ānantarya*) which, being untainted, are spoken of as wisdom because they arise simultaneously with that wisdom.
The phrase "permanently uprooting that which is to be uprooted" refers specifically to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three outflows (*āsrava*) and karma.
As for the remaining meanings, they are identical to those cited above from the *Abhidharmakośa* and not different; therefore, the commentary refers to them collectively.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase “distinctions in causes and conditions,” this indicates that karma is capable of acting as a condition because it can serve as the cause for seeds.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “according to the high or low nature of the field, there are differences which cause the seeds to also have many distinctions”: the first clause refers solely to the analogy, while the second clause contains both the dharma (the subject) and the analogy.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "causing distinctions in seeds," this shall first be clarified by means of an analogy: just as a grain seed varies according to whether the field is fertile or barren, it does not cause the seed-grain to produce bean sprouts.
If one were to say that it becomes a *ju* (orange) south of the Yangtze River and a *zhi* (citrus trifoliata) north of the river, this would imply only a slight change in species;
yet even this is merely a distant classification, not a complete distinction.

If explained according to the Dharma, there is no difference in the seeds of consciousness; however, because karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—induces suffering or pleasure, it causes the seeds to become distinct.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “the supramundane has not yet been accumulated,” etc., this is explained in terms of ordinary beings’ inability to accumulate the noble Dharma, thereby clarifying the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones as stated in the sutra.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* According to the Sub-commentary,
Fascicle Seventy Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* According to the Sub-commentary,
Fascicle Seventy-One

The *Commentary* composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty, concerning the "Ninety-two Sentences on the Distinctions between the Determinate and Indeterminate," etc., consists of two parts:
first, the headings above; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "The preceding sentence clarifies... and so forth.
First, the explanation of the ninth phrase has three parts:
first, the citation of the treatise; second, the explanation of the scriptural text; and third, the explanation of the meanings of "determined" and "undetermined" in the treatise.

Regarding the passage beginning with "That is to say, manifesting [karma]," the commentary explains the meaning of the three types of sensation in the scriptural text, which is already fully contained within the commentary itself.
However, the Sautrāntika masters say:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is the most powerful; it must necessarily yield its retribution in the next birth.
If karma to be experienced in the subsequent birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) is slightly weaker in power, it must necessarily yield its retribution in a later life, rather than in the present."

Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is the weakest in power; it is not experienced in the present life but only in a later life. It is designated as "to be experienced in the present" and so forth according to the stage at which its maturation first occurs.
The commentary states:

The meaning appears to be incomplete. Alternatively, there may be cases where karma for a single lifetime is created by both humans and devas; one first receives retribution as a human and later as a deva. Why, then, would it be necessary to force them to receive human retribution again?
However, regarding these three types of feeling, there are briefly three causes:

first, that which depends on the cause. For example, one who makes offerings to the Buddha, the Sangha, the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the meditative absorption of non-contention (*araṇa-samādhi*) during the paths of seeing and cultivation will obtain the retribution of happiness in the present life;
whereas one who commits acts of harm or affliction toward parents, kings, and others will obtain the retribution of suffering in the present life.

Second, by way of the nature of the karma: as with immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*), which yields the retribution of birth in a happy state; or as with the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), which yield the retribution of birth in a state of suffering.

Third, by way of practice and vows: for a person of great merit, even if they commit offenses that would normally result in birth [in a miserable realm], they receive them as light sufferings in the present life and swiftly attain Bodhi.

Those with many transgressions do not receive retribution in the present life; because they have committed grave evils that result in retribution upon rebirth in the evil realms, the karma for the various marks and signs of excellence all receives retribution in future lives, and thus one cannot attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Furthermore, most wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) receive their retribution in subsequent lives, because they cultivate the causes during the period of kalpa-decrease and receive the fruits during the period of kalpa-increase.

Regarding the passage in the Commentary, "Within these three [types], each has both the determinate and the indeterminate," this is the third section, which explains the terms "determinate" and "indeterminate."
Within this, the first two lines provide the heading, while the section beginning with "That is to say, the former two" provides the explanation.

This follows the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states in verse: "These are determinate or indeterminate; the determinate are of three types, such as those to be experienced in the present life."
"Alternatively, it is said that there are five types of karma; other masters say there are four categories.
The commentary states:

"The first phrase provides the general heading; the second phrase provides a specific explanation of karma pertaining to the present life; the latter three refer to the three types of determinate karma."
When added to the indeterminate, there are thus four types of karma.

Alternatively, some say there are five types of karma; others wish to further divide the indeterminate-karma into two kinds, namely, those that are determinate regarding maturation but indeterminate regarding time, and those that are indeterminate regarding both. These are opened into two categories:

first, that which is determinate in its maturation but indeterminate in its timing—meaning the fruit will certainly be experienced within one of the three periods of time, but the specific time is not fixed.

Second, regarding the maturation (*vipāka*), both the fruit and the time are indeterminate; that is to say, there are cases where both the fruit and the time are experienced as indeterminate, or where only the fruit is determinate while the time is indeterminate.
There is no case where the time is determinate but the fruit is indeterminate, because time has no distinct nature apart from the fruit.
Although there are differences in their formulations of opening and closing, their underlying principle is no different.
When other masters speak of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), they refer to the Dārṣṭāntikas, who divide karma into eight types and thus establish these four propositions.

That [karma] is certain as to its timing but uncertain regarding its fruit; within that uncertainty, timing is further divided into three types. When combined with the previous five types of karma, there are thus eight kinds in total.

Regarding the first category: it is certain as to its temporal period but uncertain as to its maturation (*vipāka*); this refers to the three types of karma—namely, *sāmdṛṣṭika* (to be experienced in the present life), etc.—which are fixed in their timing across the three periods of time, yet remain uncertain regarding their fruit.
If one obtains its fruit in the present life, it is experienced immediately; if not experienced in the present, it will never be experienced again.
It is certain in terms of time, but uncertain in terms of the fruit.
As it is with karma to be experienced in the present life, so it is for those to be experienced in future lives.

This is divided into three types: first, that which is certain to bear fruit in the present life but uncertain as to whether it will bear fruit at all; second, that which is certain to bear fruit in the next life but uncertain as to whether it will bear fruit at all; and third, that which is certain to bear fruit in subsequent lives but uncertain as to whether it will bear fruit at all.
The second phrase refers to karma that is determinate regarding its maturation (*vipāka*) but indeterminate regarding its timing.
That is to say, there is indeterminate karma that is certain to obtain maturation; this is the "one" case where the fruit is determinate but the timing is indeterminate.
Regarding the third phrase: there are actions that are determinate with respect to both, meaning they are certain to yield maturation in the present life and so forth.
These are of three types:
first, those determinate in yielding results in the present life; second, those determinate in yielding results in the next life; and third, those determinate in yielding results in subsequent lives.
Regarding the fourth phrase: there are actions that are indeterminate with respect to both.
That is to say, an indeterminate action does not necessarily result in maturation; this refers to only one case, namely, when both the fruit and the time are indeterminate.
The commentary states:

Regarding the three masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* mentioned above, each subsequent one provides a more detailed exposition; the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) summarizes these points while noting slight differences.
When it says "these three all possess both determinate and indeterminate [results]," this summarizes the views of the three masters while specifically incorporating the position of the first master.

As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "These [karmas] are of three types—determinate and indeterminate—along with those that ripen in the present life and so forth; including the indeterminate, there are four.
The commentary, from the words "That is, the former two," separately demonstrates their characteristics.
Although this accords with the four propositions of the third master, there are distinctions between its universal and restricted applications.

Regarding the first two cases where the time is fixed: if one receives the fruit in the present, it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*); if one does not receive it in the present, it is not "karma to be experienced in the present life."

The same applies to karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*): it must be experienced in the immediately following birth to be designated as such; therefore, it is said that for the first two [types of] timing, the period is fixed. Regarding the statement "retribution may be either fixed or unfixed":

there are cases where one performs an action that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), which ought to be experienced in the present, yet encounters superior conditions that obstruct it so that it is not experienced; in such cases, this retribution is unfixed.
The same applies to retribution in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).
Because there is no shifting this [retribution] to another time, there is no uncertainty regarding the timing.

Regarding the last one, which is common to both determinate and indeterminate: this refers to the fourth case, where both time and retribution are indeterminate; the third case, where both time and retribution are determinate; and the second case, where retribution is determinate but the time is indeterminate.

This refers to indeterminate karma to be experienced in a subsequent life; there is karma that is determinate in its experience but indeterminate in its timing, because it may be experienced in one birth, two births, or many births—thus, while the retribution is fixed, the time is not.

There is indeterminate karma that ought to be experienced in the third birth, yet it is destroyed by encountering conditions; this is what is meant by "determined as to time, but indeterminate as to retribution.

Alternatively, there may be karma for which the number of births has not been fixed, yet its fruit is experienced; if it is suddenly destroyed by encountering conditions, both [time and retribution] are indeterminate.

However, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is taught that while the retribution is fixed, the timing is not; this principle applies to all three types of retribution. Why, then, does the present discussion focus specifically on "favorable-to-feel" (*anukūla-vedanīya*) karma?
Answer:

The *Abhidharmakośa* treats karma in terms of its timing, meaning there is karma whose retribution is fixed, yet it may be experienced either in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
Now, it is clarified that karma is categorized by time: only that which necessarily receives retribution in the present is called "present karma.

If it is received in the present, it is "present determinate karma"; if it is not received in the present, it is not "present karma. Therefore, there is no such thing as "present retribution" with an indefinite time.

If it is experienced in the present life, it is karma of immediate retribution; if it is not experienced, then it is not karma of retribution in the present life. Therefore, there is no fixed time for retribution in the present life.
Taking each of these perspectives individually, they do not contradict one another.
Question:
It is observed that there are karmas that ought to be experienced as results in the present life, yet through the intervention of power, they are instead experienced as results in the next life.
Or, there are karmas that ought to be experienced as results in the next life, which, due to other causes and conditions, are instead experienced as results in subsequent lives.

For example, Queen Mallikā was so dedicated to the practice of giving and moral discipline that she ought to have been reborn in Tuṣita Heaven as a result of her merit; however, because she harbored a slight anger at the time of death, she was first born among scorpions, and only after seven days did she undergo a further transformation of retribution to be born in heaven.
Question:
According to these three types of karma, all have determinate retribution but indeterminate timing; how can it be said that they do not exist?
Answer:

Those who take rebirth through the immediate conditions of present retribution (kṣipra-vedanīya) are what constitute rebirth in the next life (upapadya-vedanīya); they are not called "present retribution" because their timing is indefinite.
The same applies to rebirth in the next life; this can be understood by reflecting upon it.
Regarding the first three masters, the intent of the commentary corresponds to that of the fourth master.
The power of karma is profoundly deep; it does not preclude a broad interpretation, and perhaps there are further sutras and treatises that clarify it.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Those who are settled are difficult to deliver,” etc.: this refers to those who are settled within their own respective domains—namely, those who do not belong to the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) and those of the two vehicles (dviyāna).
If one is already settled in the Mahāyāna, there is no further need for deliverance; therefore, it is not said that those who are settled are easy to deliver.

The Commentary states: "The various categories, such as the faculties (*indriya*), all constitute eighty thousand. This is because afflictions (*kleśa*) give rise to karma; since afflictions have gradations of superiority and inferiority, karma is likewise so.
Afflictions exist in dependence upon the faculties, and thus there are differences in their superior or inferior natures.
There are varying depths of understanding and varying degrees of desire;
each constitutes eighty thousand [afflictions].
Regarding the statement, "To reverse this is to manifest," and so forth: the following clarifies that each and every remedial factor for the afflictions reaches the other shore.
To exhaust the principles and fully realize one's nature is precisely the eighty-four thousand gates of *pāramitā*.
If one remains unmoved by the delusions and so forth, being tranquil within them, this is the eighty-four thousand samādhis.
If one perceives not even a single atom of these delusions and so forth, this is the eighty-four thousand liberations.
The fourth is the thicket of the faculties (*indriya-gahana*).
The meaning of the faculties has already been seen in the ninth dedication.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Among the particulars, the ten characteristics constitute nine distinctions,” this is the general outline.
The nine [categories] are condensed into three: first, the six [lines] distinguish according to the meaning of the Dharma;
next, the two [lines] distinguish according to persons, as the treatise states, "because of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas";
finally, the last one distinguishes their faculties based on their practice.
The first three [of these] are further divided into three:
the first three are pure faculties (*viśuddhendriya*), the fourth is defiled faculties (*kliṣṭendriya*), and the latter two are both defiled and pure.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “There is slowness or speed in receiving [the fruit],” etc.: for those of dull capacity, it is slow and slight; for those of sharp capacity, it is fast and abundant; and for those of middling capacity, the degree of depth and shallowness in the interval is likewise so.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “the faculties and natures of the three vehicles compared to one another”: the Hīnayāna is the lower, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is the middle, and the Mahāyāna is the upper.
This is also like the differences in size among the forms of sheep, deer, and oxen.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'joy, pleasure, and so forth,' joy and pleasure arise from greed; sorrow and suffering arise from hatred; and the faculty of equanimity arises from delusion.
Because these subsequently possess a predominant function regarding these categories of afflictions, they are called the 'defiled roots of many afflictions.'"

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the Mahāyāna, those who are matured are fixed,” and so forth: the preceding chapter explained fixed and unfixed [karma] in terms of karma itself, whereas this current section explains it in terms of the faculties (*indriya*); thus, they are naturally distinct from one another.

Furthermore, while the previous section clarified certainty and uncertainty based on ease and difficulty of deliverance, this present section clarifies certainty and uncertainty based on whether [the beings] are mature or immature.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the midst of leaving the world, one transforms others only by waiting for the proper time,” there are ten kinds of pure relinquishment (*śuddha-tyāga*); however, two categories therein involve waiting for the proper time, and all of these are now being addressed.

First, the fourth [verse] states: "Regarding sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma, one transforms them by waiting for the proper time; regarding those who are not vessels for the Dharma, one does not give rise to aversion, but maintains pure equanimity.
The commentary explains:
Here, we simply employ the method of waiting for the proper time for those who are vessels for the Dharma.

Second, regarding the ninth abandonment, it says: "There may be sentient beings whose faculties are already matured and who have given rise to wisdom and mindfulness, yet are unable to know the supreme Dharma; for their sake, one waits for the proper time to transform them through pure abandonment."
Now, since this [text] is used in its entirety, the Commentary states, "For the time being, it is set aside.

Regarding the Commentary’s phrase "the body relies on and acts in accordance with," the wording in this treatise is inverted; it should properly read "the body relies upon acting in accordance with," which is how the Commentary now correctly employs it.

The Commentary states: "That is to say, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are mutually and successively bound to one another. This means that as the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) universally takes the six sense organs as its objects, the phenomena of the organs likewise proceed in accordance with that consciousness.
Among these six, the eye sees its own body and the ear hears its own sound; both sound and body are subsumed within the internal sense-faculties.
Because the faculties follow consciousness in taking the eye-faculty as its object, the faculties are bound and cannot attain liberation.
Other examples may be understood accordingly;
therefore, it says "successively.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "second, the progression of arising and ceasing," this phrasing is inverted; if it were correct, it should read "the progression of arising and ceasing."
Because the faculties and the mind-king (citta-rāja) follow one another in defilement, they accord with arising and ceasing.

Regarding the phrase "easily subject to change and cessation": *jāti* (arising) and *sthiti* (abiding) explain "lightness" (*laghu*), *anyathātva* (alteration) explains "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), and *nirodha* (cessation) explains "destruction" (*bhaṅga*).

Regarding "the three contemplative practices proceed in accordance [with the flow]," this is because the mind of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) engages with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

As for the commentary’s phrase "included within the net of the faculties," the six faculties grasp the six sense objects; thus, the faculties are the net and the objects are the contents caught therein.
The six objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) draw in the six faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya); thus, the objects are a net for the faculties.
Therefore, regarding that "net of the faculties," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks of "apprehending signs.
In the commentary, from the phrase "seventh, the purity of the śrāvakas" onwards, the following two points concern persons.
Regarding the first point concerning the śrāvakas, it says:

"Because their practice is superior to that of ordinary beings and the two vehicles. However, the treatise later provides a further explanation, stating: "The purity of the śrāvaka consists in the superiority of their practice, because they are able to accomplish the cessation of hindrances."
Now, this commentary extracts the treatise to explain the sūtra.

The above explains "predominance" (*adhipati*): that is to say, when the pure faculties of the two vehicles are compared with those of ordinary beings who do not seek nirvāṇa, because [the former] are now able to seek it, they attain predominance regarding the supramundane.

From the passage beginning with "By means of the faculties of the two vehicles" (*dvayāyāna-indriya*), the text explains that [the path] cannot be destroyed, while simultaneously explaining the capacity to eliminate obstacles and achieve realization mentioned in the treatise.
The commentary’s reference to the "eight purities of the bodhisattvas" refers specifically to the Mahāyāna faculties.
The "three non-regressions" refer to abiding in right mindfulness.

In the commentary following the passage on the "nine distant followings," this section concerns practice, specifically the sūtra’s statement: "distantly following, arising together, yet having different characteristics."
The *Śāstra* states: "Deeply entering together, they manifest various distinct characteristics. "Various" means they are not identical; "deeply entering" means following [the object] from afar.
The passage beginning with "Manifesting the inclusion of all faculties" is the *Śāstra*’s commentary on the *Sūtra*.

The *Śāstra* provides a further commentary, stating: "Regarding the distinctions encompassed by all faculties (*indriya*), they differ because the initial practice, the skillful means, and the maturation of the retribution of the faculties are distinct.
From the passage beginning with "That is to say, the three untainted [faculties]," the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains the text of the *Śāstra*.
Initial cultivation constitutes the beginning of correct practice; skillfulness constitutes the means (*upāya*); and because it is ultimate, it is called the maturation of the reward (*vipāka*).
Their correspondence with the three untainted [knowledges] is as seen in the preceding text.
The passage beginning with "That is to say, the aforementioned faith and so forth" uses the treatise to harmonize with the sutra, explaining the terms "not distant" and "following.
It explains that faith and the others coexist with the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), because these faculties arise in association with the practice of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
The phrase "and follows" below explains the meaning of "not being identical.
The phrase "from beginning to end" below explains the meaning of "following from afar.

The phrase "these three faculties" below explains the meaning of "constituting a faculty," because they are designated as "faculties" (*indriya*) since their superior function illuminates and manifests the sense of predominance (*ādhipatya*).
From "And these nine above" onwards, [the text] summarizes them by way of their meaning,
as is done throughout the "Dedication Chapter.

Regarding the commentary's section "Fifth, following the three," the explanation of the three types of spiritual disposition (*gotra*) is presented briefly here as in the "Chapter on the Ten Powers" and extensively in the "Chapter on the Merits of Arousing the Mind."

Regarding the phrase "the nature and characteristics accord and enter [one another]," it means that understanding arises based on the faculties, the nature is established based on understanding, and desire arises based on the nature.
Since all these are mutually consistent, they are said to be "in accord."
The mutual correspondence of principles and meanings is termed "harmonious entry" (*suniyāta*).
Using this as a model for the faculties (*indriya*), no further detailed explanation will be given.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The sixth [section] explains the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)," it first explains the general name, and subsequently, from the words "furthermore, there are... onwards, it provides an exegesis based on the treatise (*śāstra*).

First, regarding the statement "this refers only to seeds": according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 2, it says, "Among the seeds contained within the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, those comprised within the category of afflictions (*kleśa-pakṣa*) are called both 'heavy dysfunction' (*dauṣṭhulya*) and 'latent tendency' (*anuśaya*)."

If it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*) or other categories of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is termed only "heaviness" (*dausthulya*) and not a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
If it is a seed comprised within wholesome roots such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, it is neither termed "heaviness" nor a "latent tendency."
Why is this? Because when these phenomena arise, their supporting substratum possesses only functional capacity (*samartha*), not a lack of capacity.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first six clarify where [the afflictions] follow along,” the treatise explains this for the time being based on the principle of following along (*anubandha*).
If it concerns bondage, one should also ask: where is there bondage?
By what means is there bondage?
If it concerns latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), one should likewise say: where do they lie latent?
By means of which latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Therefore, the subsequent commentary states, "the place where one has long been at ease," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "Now, first, there are five [explanations]": first, explaining the locus (*sthāna*) in terms of the mind; second, explaining the locus in terms of the realms (*dhātu*); third, explaining the locus in terms of the stages (*avasthā*); fourth, explaining the locus in terms of time (*kāla*); and fifth, explaining the locus in terms of activity (*caryā*).
Regarding the first point: the term "retributive mind" (*vipāka-citta*) refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, as it is the general retribution-body (*sarva-bīja-vipāka-ātmabhāva*).
The meanings of its subtlety and so forth have been seen repeatedly in the preceding text.

As for the statement that "it is called simply 'mind' because it arises without departing from manifest phenomena," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises designate the first seven consciousnesses as "born of retribution" (*vipākaja*), but they are not the retribution-body itself.
The recompense of past mental seeds cannot be called "retribution" (vipāka).
Rather, the seven consciousnesses all rely upon the eighth consciousness and manifest in dependence on conditions; this is termed "not departing from the present reality.

As for the seeds, they may or may not exist in accordance with what manifests, and thus are termed the "temporary locus of transformation," like a person taking a brief nap who does not necessarily remain in their own room.
In the commentary on the section "The Two: Correspondence and Non-correspondence," the first part establishes the names based on the intent of the treatise;
from "Only with" onwards, the commentary explains the characteristics of correspondence and so forth.
The section beginning with "Therefore, the treatise says" cites scriptural evidence in reference to the realms (*dhātu*).
The section beginning with "Because the afflictions of the formless realm are subtle" is a commentary on the terms "lower," "middle," and "upper" found in the treatise.
In the inclusion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are placed below; this is based on the essential nature of the afflictions.
Master Yuǎn says:
"The desire realm is considered 'below' in terms of the superiority or inferiority of the realms."
From the phrase "although they are latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*) onwards, the author addresses potential objections.
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
"Does one who resides in any single realm necessarily possess all the latent dispositions belonging to all three realms?"
Just as when one is born in a higher realm, the seeds of the afflictions of the lower realms are also fully present (*pariniṣpanna*).
How then can it be said that there are both associated (*saṃprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta* [seeds])?
Therefore, the answer is now given:
Regarding the manifest afflictions, one speaks of their association with seeds; this does not mean that when one is born into a higher realm, one loses the seeds of the lower realms.
However, examining the sūtra now, there is only mention of "association" and "non-association," and therefore I offer this explanation.

If one follows the sūtra cited in the treatise which states, "associated, non-associated, and not separated," then while manifest afflictions may be either associated or non-associated, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are always not separated from them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, up to the peak of the vajra,” this means that prior to the *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like concentration), there still exists the existence of birth and death; therefore, it is called the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because the seeds of the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are severed precisely at this time.
Although the preceding section on the "Forest of Afflictions" mentions that they extend down to the diamond-like [samādhi] (*vajropama*), it speaks specifically in terms of the seeds.
Despite these two interpretations, the intent of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) supports this [latter view]; therefore, the previous section states: "Third, the locus is clarified by way of the stages."
From the passage beginning "Now, taking the comprehensive [explanation]," the treatise reconciles the sutras.
The reason it does not mention the "Vajra" here is that it intends to encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Since the subsequent verse states, "Only when the Vajra-path is extinguished is the intention fulfilled," the former meaning is established as correct.
The term "nine stages" (navabhūmi) also encompasses two meanings:

first, in contrast to the summit of the three realms of existence, it refers to the nine stages of the triple world—namely, the four dhyānas of the desire realm and the four formless attainments (ārūpya), which together constitute the nine. Thus, there should indeed be nine.

If one follows the preceding meaning, this refers to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), as it corresponds to the tenth stage, which is the position where [fear] is completely severed.
Regarding the fourth point, [the timing], it is easy to understand.

As for the commentary’s statement, “Only wisdom can fear,” this is the intended meaning of the treatise; for the *Śāstra* explains that the Sūtra says, “Because there has been no characteristic of fear since beginningless time. This is the commentary’s explanation for that.
The treatise states: "In boundless worlds, only wisdom can bring fear; [ignorance] is feared like a hostile robber.
Because one has never yet cultivated the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, or meditation, it is therefore not extinguished."
The commentary extracts the meaning of the treatise to interpret this present sutra, which can be understood as follows.
Regarding the phrase "unable to accord with correct practice," it is because the words "correct practice" appear below "supernormal powers" (abhijñā) in the treatise’s version of the sutra.
The remainder may be understood.

Regarding the section of the *Śāstra* beginning with "The latter three realms," which clarifies by what [factors] they are pursued (*anugata*), the fourth phrase is excluded to demonstrate that the substance of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is insubstantial; the remaining five are also explained in terms of their preceding locations to clarify their pursuit, though the textual order is not sequential.
The first [point] explains "following" by means of the second [section], which clarifies the bases (*āyatana*) in relation to the realms (*dhātu*);
"non-interruption" is the characteristic of following.
The second [point] distinguishes "following" by means of the fourth [section], which clarifies the bases in relation to time.

The sutra speaks of "the characteristic of causing the continuum of the boundless mind to manifest," whereas the commentary on the sutra refers to it as "the characteristic of the accumulation of the continuum since beginningless time. In the sub-commentary (*śāstra*), both "beginningless" and "boundless" are reconciled; however, this "continuum" is precisely the characteristic of following along.
"Opening the doors of the three sense-bases" refers to the discernment of the following [of the mind] by means of the first [category], which clarifies the sense-bases in relation to the mind.
"The gathering and arising of the six consciousnesses" refers to the characteristic of that following.
The remainder is as stated in the commentary (*śū*).
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of this sūtra is contained therein," it is because among the various bases (*āyatana*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*) subsumes the *ālayavijñāna*.
Following the term "solid and real" in the commentary, [it is shown that] the essence of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is empty; this does not refer back to the preceding location.
Regarding the phrase "the unreal is substantial," the Sūtra says, "substantial and difficult to cure," while the Śāstra says, "the unreal persists.

The unreal is precisely the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that persists even into states such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); therefore, it is substantial. Thus, the fact that the unreal is difficult to cure constitutes the characteristic of persistence.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The five are the locations (*sthāna*) and so forth,” this refers to the third section, which clarifies the locations by way of their stages (*bhūmi*) to demonstrate their persistence.

As for the phrase “the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) within the nine stages,” it is because the *Śāstra* states that the *sūtra* speaks of “the characteristics of the stages and bases being conformable or non-conformable,” and the *Śāstra* explains: “Because within the nine stages, the body of afflictions (*kleśakāya*) persists within the six bases.”
The commentary states:
"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the essence (*ātman*).
The passage beginning with "However, in the ninth stage" and below is the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explaining the treatise.
Regarding the two [types of] *bhavāgra*, there remain two [obscuration-categories] across nine stages (*bhūmi*).

These two, in relation to the seeds of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the nine stages of virtuous wisdom, persist even through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), as there remain the two delusions of "equality-enlightenment" (*samatā-abhisambodha*); this is because from the entry into the first stage onward, they are abandoned dualistically at each successive stage.
Since eighteen [defilements] have already been abandoned at the ninth stage, it is said that "at this stage, there is partial abandonment.
Next, by citing the *Vajra* [Sūtra], the ultimate [abandonment] is established; these two [citations] together verify the preceding two points.
Since it is said that "the vajra stage is finally completed," it clarifies that [the afflictions] still exist up through the tenth bhūmi;
yet, since it is said that they are "finally completed," it clarifies that they have already been eliminated from the ninth bhūmi onward.

Furthermore, regarding the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because they are severed instantaneously by the vajra-like samādhi, this also establishes the sense that within each and every bhūmi described in the sūtras, there is the meaning of accomplishment.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Sixth, being pursued by suffering”: this refers to the meaning of being pursued as explained in the preceding fifth section, which clarifies the stations (*āyatana*) by way of conduct (*caryā*).

The phrase “only the supramundane noble path can bring about liberation” serves as a counter-illustration, showing that mundane paths, various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and the like cannot bring about such liberation.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Because other practices cannot bring about liberation.
This uses the inability [to liberate] as the characteristic of being "concomitant" (*anubandha*).
In the previous fifth [section], the characteristic of being concomitant was defined by the fact that [the afflictions] are fully present (*samanvāgama*).
The seventh is the dense forest of rebirth.

Regarding the statement, "The treatise generally comprises eight [sections]," among these eight, the first seven contrast causes with their results, while the final phrase distinguishes the origin that gives rise to future suffering.
Among the aforementioned seven, they are subsumed into three pairs: namely, the first two, the next three, and the final two.
Within these three pairs, in each case, the former discusses arising in terms of its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter explains arising in terms of its causes (*hetu*).
Regarding the first pair, "the variety of a single body" explains arising in terms of its own characteristics.
"The variety of karmic causes" distinguishes arising in relation to its cause; because karma is not uniform, what arises becomes manifold.
Regarding the second pair within the three statements, the first two statements discuss arising according to their specific characteristics.
As for "the various dwelling places," they do not consist merely of the six destinies, because there are immeasurable locations even within a single destiny.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The four hundred and fifty-two phrases concerning the various [states] of form-perception (rūpa-saṃjñā) above and below,” two phrases from the present sutra constitute one phrase in the treatise.
The sutra says: “The differentiated characteristics of the possessed-of-form and the formless; the differentiated characteristics of the possessed-of-perception and the non-possessed-of-perception.”
There are two realms that possess form, while the formless realm is formless; the heaven of non-perception is without perception, while all others possess perception.
As for the terms "upper" and "lower," the formless is considered upper and the possessed-form is considered lower;
the state without perception is considered upper and the state with perception is considered lower.
There should further be the inclusion of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and the Sphere of Non-Perception (asaṃjñāyatana).
However, since the treatise merely states "the upper and lower [realms] of form-perception" (rūpasaṃjñā), Master Huiyuan asked:
"How can the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) be considered 'upper' and 'lower' within the category of form?"
The commentary states:
This is because they lack coarse matter, yet possess subtle matter.
Furthermore, it asks:
Regarding how the state of non-perception (asaṃjñin) can be categorized as superior or inferior within the realm of perception:
the meaning of the answer is the same as before; it means that while those beings lack coarse perception, they possess subtle perception.
The rest is as explained in the section on the First Ground.
The Commentary states: "The fifth [point], 'the various aspects being the same as external matter,' distinguishes arising by means of its cause.
This is because it reveals the existence of the sprout by citing the cause of the past karma; this is explained in detail in the Sixth Stage."
In the third pair, "the sixfold variety of self-nature" refers to arising according to its own characteristics (*dharmatā*), as in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*).
However, because some natures consist solely of form (*rūpa*) while others possess both [form and mind], it is called "various."
In the commentary, the section beginning with “The seven fundamental factors follow birth” analyzes birth in relation to its causes;
this is the main body of the treatise.
The section beginning with “That is, delusion and craving” is the commentary following the sequence of the treatise to provide an explanation.
If Master Huiyuan says:
"The phrasing in the treatise is inverted; it should correctly read 'conforming to the causes of origination.
This means that present birth has ignorance and craving as its fundamental causes."
Based on this present life, one again gives rise to delusion and craving; therefore, it is said that "it accords with the root.
This does not contradict reason.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The last two phrases of the eighth [section]," these are designated as "the various aspects of the Truths of Suffering and Origination" because they manifest the origination of birth in relation to future results.
Regarding the passage beginning with "That is, the three kinds of seeking," the commentary extracts the meaning of the treatise to provide an explanation.
Within this, it first provides a general explanation of the title of the treatise, and subsequently, under the heading "The preceding phrase," it specifically analyzes the wording of the sūtra.
First, I shall explain the two types of seeking mentioned in the preceding phrase.
Regarding the term "desiring to receive" (*yùshòu*): "receiving" refers to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
