Therefore, the second chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* instructs one to contemplate the four propositions: namely, identity and difference; both and neither; existence, non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence; permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one forms many sets of four propositions by interweaving the various categories,” this refers to the second section, the multiple-layered four propositions.
It consists of four general sections, forming twenty layers in total.

The first section has eight layers. First, by comparing the "existence" in the first gate with the "non-existence" in the second gate, four propositions are established: first, dependent origination exists, because its true nature is wondrously existent;
second, dependent origination is non-existent, because karma and afflictions have no substantial body;
third, it is both existent and non-existent, because it simultaneously illuminates both the true and the delusive.
Fourth, it is neither existent nor non-existent, because both the true and the delusory are transcended.

Second, based on the first gate, when contrasted with the second gate, four propositions are established: first, dependent origination is existent, for karma and afflictions have functional utility in producing birth and death;
second, it is non-existent, for the one true dharma-realm is devoid of all marks.
Third, "both existent and non-existent," because it simultaneously illuminates both the true and the delusive;
fourth, "neither existent nor non-existent," because both the true and the delusive are transcended.

The third [category] establishes the four propositions by taking the "existence" mentioned in the first gate as a counterpoint to the "non-existence" in the third gate; that is to say, first, dependent origination is existent, because the true nature is existent.
Second is non-existence, because phenomena lack true reality;
third is both existence and non-existence, because it simultaneously illuminates both phenomena and principle;
fourth is neither existence nor non-existence, because phenomena and principle are mutually identical and mutually subsumed.
Fourth, by means of the first gate, there is no opposition; within the third gate, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are established: namely, first, because the characteristic of phenomena exists;
second, because the characteristic of principle is empty;
and third, because emptiness and existence manifest together.
Fourth, because existence and emptiness mutually dissolve into one another.

Fifth, regarding the formation of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) based on the presence [of existence] in the first gate and the absence [of existence] in the fourth gate: first, because the single true nature exists;
second, because phenomena are themselves empty.
Third, because the three pairs illuminate the two;
fourth, because they mutually negate one another.

Sixth, within the first gate there is no counterpart, whereas within the fourth gate there is the establishment of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, first, that the principle of non-substantiality exists; and so forth.
Second, because the principle is signless;
third, because the two meanings appear simultaneously;
fourth, because it is the true Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent.

Seventh, by means of the first category, four propositions are established in relation to the fifth category: first, because ultimate truth exists; second, because emotional conceptualization is absent within that truth; third, because there are instances where false conceptualization perceives what does not exist; and fourth, because the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the non-existence of truth, and the non-existence of truth is itself the existence of intrinsic nature.
Eighth, because there is no counterpart in the first gate, while there is the establishment of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) in the fifth gate:
first, "existence," because it exists as a conventional designation;
second, "non-existence," because in principle there are no characteristics.
Third, both exist: because the ultimate principle is without marks, it exists only as a product of deluded attachment;

fourth, neither exists: that which exists as a product of deluded attachment is non-existent because it is the truth that is without marks, yet it is not non-existent because the markless true nature serves as the basis for deluded attachment.

Above this, by taking the presence or absence of the first category and contrasting it with the presence or absence of the four categories below, eight sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are formed.

Second, by taking the presence or absence within the second category and contrasting it with the three categories below, another six sets of four propositions are formed. Third, by taking the presence or absence within the third category and contrasting it with the two categories below, four further sets of four propositions are formed. Fourth, by taking the presence or absence of the fourth category and contrasting it with the presence or absence of the fifth category, two sets of four propositions are formed. Altogether, twenty sets of four propositions are established.

One must not take what follows as the primary [category] to correspond with what precedes it, because one does not take what is not distinct from the preceding category as the primary to correspond with what follows.
Here, I have set forth the eight categories in full; as for the twelve categories, one should infer them by analogy, though I refrain from listing them here for fear of prolixity.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, in terms of similarity of characteristics,” this is like seeing a single leaf fall and knowing that autumn has come to the world, or seeing a single flower bloom and knowing that spring has arrived.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, in terms of perfect interfusion,” the text itself contains three points:
the first concerns the meaning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.

Regarding the two gates following "Harmonizing phenomena through principle": these concern the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*). The first gate is the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature (*faxing rongtong men*), and the third is the gate of the mutual conditioning of dependent origination (*yuanqi xiangyou men*).
Within the third section, the commentary is divided into two parts:
first, citing one gate; second, [explaining] their mutual identity.
The passage beginning with "Since it is so" serves as an illustration for the remaining gates.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, entering by means of the identical;
second, from "Since the distinct entities are thus" onwards, using the distinct to illustrate the identical; [and third, using the same to illustrate the different].
3. From "The Single Gate" onwards, the gates are illustrated by means of other gates.

Just as it is with the gate of the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination, so it is with all other gates, such as the gate of the absence of fixed nature and the gate of manifestation as mind-only.
Furthermore, just as it is with the mutual inclusion of characteristics, so too is it with the "Gate of Subtle Mutual Containment and Establishment" and the others.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The things that are negated may also be sequentially correlated with the preceding categories of sentient and non-sentient objects,” this is as follows: “neither male nor female” corresponds to the preceding realization of sentient beings;
“neither earth, water, fire, nor wind” corresponds to the preceding realization of lands and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because elephants and so forth are not the artifice,” this refers to the gate of the mutual difference between cause and effect: the fruit that is the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is not the object of the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
“The subsequent phrase reverses this” means that the artifice is not the elephant and so forth; this clarifies that the imagined nature is not the dependent nature.
The following section clarifies the existence of characteristics, which constitutes the mutual establishment of cause and effect.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “Movement and stillness are non-dual,” the subsequent text consists of five parts:

first, a general explanation of the scriptural passage; second, citing corroborating evidence; third, explaining the meaning of "neither existence nor non-existence"; fourth, providing analogies to substantiate the point; and fifth, a systematic analysis through various thematic approaches.
The first section may be understood as before.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Therefore the Sūtra says: ‘Wisdom does not apprehend existence or non-existence, yet it gives rise to the mind of great compassion’,” this is the second citation of scriptural evidence; it is the first verse of praise to the Buddha from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

However, that sutra praises the Buddha’s thorough realization of the three natures; its first verse states: "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet one gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
This clarifies the pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*).

The subsequent verse states: "All phenomena are like illusions, transcending mind and consciousness; since wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
"Avoiding the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is ever like a dream; though wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
These two preceding verses clarify the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Next, another verse states: "Knowing that persons and phenomena lack self, and that afflictions and the knowable are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
This verse clearly elucidates the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, this preceding verse, following the intent of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, reveals that the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*): namely, through the realization of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is established; through the realization of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is established; and through the realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the dharma body (*dharmakāya*) is established.

However, the second halves of all four verses are identical; the present sutra specifically cites the second half of the verse on "illusion-like" within the context of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while the second half concerning "dream-like" will be cited again later in the section on the patience regarding dreams (*svapna-kṣānti*).
In the commentary, the section beginning with "By realizing that the essence is empty" constitutes the third part, which explains the meaning of neither existence nor non-existence.
The section beginning with "Just as the birth of an elephant is itself its death" constitutes the fourth part, which provides an analogy to confirm the point.

The commentary states: "These two pairs correspond to form four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). This refers to the fifth section on the analytical selection of meanings. Within this, there are four parts:

first, the establishment of the four propositions by means of the second gate regarding the nature of apparent existence and non-existence; second, the clarification of neither identity nor difference through the first gate; third, applying the same logic to the remaining three gates; and fourth, applying the same logic to explain the preceding and succeeding sections.
Now, regarding the first [section], there are four propositions: first, not different; second, not one; third, neither non-one nor non-different; fourth, neither both one and different.
Regarding those illnesses sent forth, there are four types: first, difference; second, identity; third, neither identical nor different; fourth, both identical and different.
Contemplate this according to the commentary.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the second [category] is called "delusive discrimination of views"; therefore, it must be refuted.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "If one takes the two meanings upon the cloth," the second section analyzes the non-identity and non-difference in contrast to the first gate.
The commentary consists of three parts:
first, the statement of the basis;
second, from "First, with a cloth" onwards, the enumeration and explanation of the ten phrases.
Third, from "If by way of non-difference" onwards, the essential meaning is summarized.

First, regarding the phrase "the two meanings upon the cloth": first is the meaning of abiding in its own nature, and second is the meaning of forming an elephant. The former is the meaning of immutability (*avikāra*), and the latter is the meaning of conforming to conditions (*anuparivartana*).

Regarding the two meanings of "upon the elephant": first is the meaning of the identity of emptiness, and second is the meaning of differentiation; the former is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), while the latter is illusory existence.

Within the second section, the detailed explanation of the ten phrases, the first four phrases clarify that they are not different, and the subsequent four phrases clarify that they are not one; the ninth and twelfth phrases subsume the preceding two gates to elucidate neither identity nor difference.

Regarding "not different from the initial [state]," the first phrase means that following conditions is not different from differentiation; the second phrase means that non-alteration is not different from the emptiness of essence; the third phrase combines the preceding two phrases through non-obstruction; and the fourth phrase combines the preceding two phrases through mutual sublation.
Regarding the first phrase of the present section, the commentary states: "The Sūtra says, 'The Dharma-body flows forth,'" and so on, citing scriptural evidence.
Two sūtras are cited as proof; the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (Questioning Wisdom) has already been analyzed, and now it shall be further explained.
The initial statement, "The Dharmakāya flowing through the five paths is called sentient beings," refers to the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra*.

The Dharmakāya is precisely True Suchness (*tathatā*); its flowing through the five paths is its functioning in accordance with conditions; and being called "sentient beings" carries the sense of differentiation.

Next, regarding the passage "The Tathāgatagarbha experiences pleasure and pain, accompanying the causes, whether arising or ceasing," this corresponds to the fourth [chapter] of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
It says there: "O Mahāmati!..."
The seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration, nor do they experience suffering or pleasure;
they are not the cause of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati! The tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure together with their causes, arising and ceasing.
The commentary states:

The seven consciousnesses arise and perish in every moment and are impermanent; they vanish as soon as they arise, like the turning of a river. Since their own substance is not established, they do not experience suffering or pleasure.
It is neither the basis for defilement, nor is it the basis for untainted nirvana.

This Tathāgatagarbha is truly eternal and all-pervasive; yet within the six realms of existence, beings are deluded regarding it, which enables it to manifest through conditions and give rise to phenomena, resulting in the experience of the fruits of suffering and pleasure.
To be co-existent with the seven consciousnesses is called being co-existent with their causes.
Not maintaining its own nature, it forms the seven consciousnesses; depending on this, it undergoes arising and ceasing, which is described as "if arising" or "if ceasing."
This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is itself True Suchness (tathatā), which undergoes suffering, pleasure, and so forth because it follows conditions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, the meaning of the cloth remaining in its own position,” etc.: “remaining in its own [position]” refers to immutability; the characteristic of the essence being empty is precisely Suchness.

The two meanings accord with one another as phenomena converge and return to their nature; thus it is said that "one returns the derivative to the fundamental. The fundamental is precisely the nature, while the derivative is precisely phenomena.
The commentary states, "The Sūtra says: 'All sentient beings are themselves suchness,'" which is an invocation of scriptural evidence.
This refers to the Maitreya Chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
Indeed, that sūtra states: "Is one granted the prediction of enlightenment by virtue of the arising of suchness, or is one granted the prediction by virtue of the cessation of suchness?"
If one were to receive the prediction of enlightenment through the arising of suchness, suchness has no arising.
If one were to receive the prediction of enlightenment through the cessation of suchness, suchness has no cessation.
All sentient beings are suchness, and all phenomena are also suchness.
The multitude of sages and worthies are likewise so; even Maitreya is likewise so.
If Maitreya has received the prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive the prediction.
Why is this? For suchness is neither dual nor differentiated.
If Maitreya were to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, then all sentient beings would likewise have to attain it.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are themselves the mark of bodhi.
If Maitreya attains parinirvāṇa, then all sentient beings shall likewise attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas know that all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent, possessing the very characteristic of nirvana, and do not undergo further extinction.
Therefore, Maitreya!
"Do not use this teaching to entice the sons of heaven.
Now, in this commentary, I shall briefly cite the essentials of two phrases.
Regarding the word "etcetera" (等), there are two intended meanings:
First, it is equivalent to other passages in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, such as those cited above;
second, it is equivalent to all other passages stating that "all things are like [tathatā].
Therefore, this sutra says: "All dharmas are like [tathatā], and the realm of the Buddhas is likewise."
"...up to the point that there is not even a single dharma that undergoes arising and ceasing within the intermediate state," and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Third, [it shows] the fundamental source to which the branches return": this phrase combines the preceding two phrases to eliminate obstacles and form this single sentence. This is because the emptiness of the essence of differentiation and the aspect of following conditions through immutability are mutually constitutive, and thus not distinct.
Regarding the phrase "gathering the branches back to their fundamental source," this refers to the emptiness of the essence of differentiation.

In the preceding second line, the emptiness of essence is the fundamental, while differentiation is the branch; thus, the fundamental merges with the branch. By causing the branch to accord with the fundamental, differentiation is itself the emptiness of essence.

The phrase "granting the end that is derived from the fundamental essence" refers precisely to the unchanging following conditions (*ananyathābhāva-anupravṛtti*). This corresponds to the first statement above; because the unchanging manifests its entire substance in accordance with conditions to form distinctions, the derivative end merges into the fundamental essence, causing the essence to become identical with the end.
Therefore, it is said that these two are mutually fused: because the unchanging nature manifests its entire substance in accordance with conditions, the fundamental does not obstruct the derivative;
because the differentiated aspects are identical to the emptiness of the substance, the derivative does not obstruct the fundamental. Hence, they are called "unimpeded."
Precisely because the Dharma-body manifests as sentient beings, one realizes that sentient beings are identical to Suchness;
because sentient beings are identical to Suchness, one then knows that the Dharma-body transmigrates through the five paths to become sentient beings.
Thus, the first phrase is equal to the end from the beginning, and the second phrase is equal to the beginning from the end; hence it is said that "the beginning and the end are equal.
When the beginning is truly equal to the end, then the end is likewise equal to the beginning; therefore, the two preceding sūtras are also not mutually contradictory.
Therefore, it is said: "Because the texts of the preceding two [sūtras] are not separate.
Since the characteristics of the preceding two phrases are combined to constitute the third phrase, the texts of the preceding two sūtras are employed to corroborate this phrase.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Fourth, the subsumed [phenomena] are returned to their original source through their derivative aspects,” etc., this phrase also combines the previous two phrases by means of mutual negation (*parasparāpoha*) to form this sentence; that is to say, because the aspect of differentiation—which is identical to the emptiness of essence—is mutually negated with the aspect of unchangingness—which is identical to following conditions—they are not different.

However, while the first two phrases are used identically, they are separated by a vast interval; the third phrase employs the first, taking up the "following conditions without changing" (suiyuan), whereby the fundamental becomes the derivative.
Now, the fourth phrase employs the first: it takes that which is unchanging despite following conditions, thereby subduing the derivative with the fundamental;
this is merely a matter of inversion.
The third phrase employs the second: it takes that the substance of differentiation is empty, whereby the derivative becomes the fundamental.
Now, the fourth phrase employs the third phrase; it takes up the distinction of "emptiness of essence" (*tattva-śūnyatā*) and subordinates the end to the root.
This is merely an inversion.
Therefore, the meanings are vastly divergent.
The phrase "the derivative that is subsumed within the fundamental" refers to the differentiation of the essence of emptiness; this is the second clause.
The phrase "the fundamental that follows along with the derivative" refers to the unchanging nature that conforms to conditions; this is the first clause.
Because it is unchanging precisely through following conditions, one negates its distinctness; by making its essence empty, the derivative is quiescent.
Because its essence is empty precisely through its distinctness, one negates its unchanging nature; by making it follow conditions, the fundamental is quiescent.
When the whole is taken as the part, the whole becomes hidden;
when the whole is taken as the part, the part vanishes.
Thus, while True Suchness follows conditions to become sentient beings, it never loses its true essence; therefore, sentient beings are not [merely] sentient beings.
When the substance of sentient beings is empty and is precisely the Dharmakāya, it has never been that sentient beings do not exist; therefore, the Dharmakāya is not [merely] the Dharmakāya.
Thus, the two pairs are both transcended.
Since the two are mutually transcended, truth and delusion are equal, with nothing to differentiate them.
The Commentary states: "The four gates below are not one" is a general heading.

This means that the fifth gate is not one because its nature and characteristics are mutually contradictory; the sixth gate is not one because its nature and characteristics are mutually destructive; the seventh gate is not one because it combines the fifth and sixth gates to clarify that their contradictions and destructions differ; and the eighth gate is also not one because it combines the fifth and sixth gates to clarify that their non-dissolution and non-existence differ.

The fifth and sixth gates merely alternate with the second gate; that is to say, in the aforementioned second gate, because the unchanging is contrasted with the emptiness of essence, they are not different, whereas here, because it is contrasted with differentiation, they are not identical.
The sixth [point] is likewise.
Regarding the five [points], the first is the explicit explanation.

As for the statement, "Because the fundamental and the derivative are contradictory and opposed," it means that the fundamental is quiescent and devoid of dual characteristics, whereas the derivative manifests in myriad differentiations; therefore, they are contradictory.
The sub-commentary states, "As the *Laṅkāvatāra* says," and so forth; the supporting evidence can be understood from this.

The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "In this context, that which is solely subject to arising and ceasing is the seven consciousnesses, while that which is solely non-arising and non-ceasing is the Tathāgatagarbha."
Since these two meanings have been distinguished, it follows that the ālayavijñāna has no separate self-substance; therefore, it is said to "not exist within.
This is based on the sense of non-duality, not on the sense of non-conjunction.

Why is this? Because herein the Tathāgatagarbha is neither arising nor ceasing; it is the non-arising and non-ceasing of the seven consciousnesses that are subject to arising and ceasing, and thus it is not identical with their own arising and ceasing.

The arising and ceasing of the seven consciousnesses are the arising and ceasing of the Tathāgatagarbha’s non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, they are not identical to its own non-arising and non-ceasing.
Herein, it is not merely that they do not conflict or differ that clarifies their non-identity, but rather, it is precisely because they do not differ that their non-identity is established.

Why is this? If the Tathāgatagarbha, when following conditions to undergo arising and ceasing, were to lose its own nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, then arising and ceasing could not exist at all.
Therefore, that which possesses arising and ceasing by virtue of non-arising and non-ceasing is not different [from it]; thus, they are not one.
The commentary states:
The meanings cited above harmonize the doctrine of neither identity nor difference.
This current section specifically clarifies that they are not identical; if one were to harmonize "neither identity nor difference" so as to make them coincide, that would be the tenth section.
Now, I have simply cited and harmonized this based on the passage concerning the arising and ceasing of the seven consciousnesses.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “The image formed upon the six towels,” etc.: in the first sentence above, the formation of the image was not different when contrasted with its differentiation; however, it is now not identical when contrasted with the emptiness of its substance.
First, the correct explanation follows.

Furthermore, regarding the citation from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* beginning with "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate," this refers to the fourth scripture, which has already been cited previously.
Although the preceding passage was cited in its entirety, its intent lay in the *tathāgatagarbha* undergoing suffering and pleasure because it takes up dharmas formed according to conditions.

Now, although this commentary cites it in full, its intent is to take up the meaning of the seven consciousnesses not being subject to transmigration (*pravṛtti*), thereby establishing a contrast, as the latter [the *tathāgatagarbha*] is ultimately empty.
Regarding the statement "the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate," because the root destroys the branches, the branches are rendered empty; thus, there is nothing that can transmigrate.

Regarding the statement "only the Tathāgatagarbha experiences pleasure and pain," because the branches destroy the root, it does not maintain its own nature, and its pure essence follows conditions to manifest as existence.
When one first intends to establish form, it is contradicted by the emptiness that pervades the body;
when one intends to embody emptiness, it is contradicted by the established form.

Therefore, they are not identical. Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “Seventh, because the initial characteristics are opposed,” etc., this sentence combines the opposing contrasts of the preceding fifth and sixth sections.

This refers to being at odds with one another, like two enemies who take no pleasure in seeing each other; it is also like the conjunction of the lunar mansions Shen and Chen, or like a husband and wife whose eyes have turned against one another.

It refers to mutual harm, like two enemies contending for life and death, or like an avenger toward his parents' enemy with whom he will not share the same heavens; it is also like the fight between two tigers where neither can survive.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Eighth, because they are utterly mutually destructive, both are extinguished yet not extinguished,” this combines the fifth and sixth phrases.

Taking up “not extinguished” and “not existing” clarifies their non-identity; “both extinguished yet not extinguished” corresponds to the sixth phrase, while “both existing yet not existing” corresponds to the fifth phrase.
Why is this? Because the fifth [characteristic], "existence," which is contrary [to non-existence], remains, while the sixth, "annihilation," which is destructive, is extinguished.
However, within existence there is the meaning of non-existence, and within annihilation there is the meaning of non-annihilation.

If there were only cessation and no non-cessation, then both form and emptiness would vanish, and there would be nothing for them to identify with one another; because there is non-cessation, although they identify with one another, form and emptiness remain distinct and clear.
If only non-existence were preserved and existence were not, then form and emptiness would each have a fixed nature and could not be mutually identical;
because existence does not persist, they are vividly distinct yet nonetheless mutually identical.

Because its essence is empty, the seventh gate merely combines the existence and disappearance of the fifth and sixth; now, the eighth gate combines the non-existence and non-disappearance of the fifth and sixth. Thus, although the seventh and eighth gates both combine the fifth and sixth, their two meanings are different.
Regarding the statement, "This refers to the fact that formation and destruction are not identical," it means that this destruction is not preserved, yet this formation is not obliterated.
Since the ninth gate is neither identical nor different, these two gates are not identical.
The tenth gate synthesizes the preceding eight gates as a whole, designating them as the true *dharmadhātu*; therefore, they are also not different.
Since there is no principle of duality, how could there be any distinction between unity and difference?
The commentary states: "If one takes [the relationship] by way of non-difference," and so forth, which is the third section, summarizing the essential meaning.
The commentary states: "Since it is thus with the pair of the cloth and the elephant," and so forth, which is the third section, applying the analogy to the remaining three gates.
In the commentary, following the section "The various gates above and below," the fourth part provides an illustrative explanation of the preceding and succeeding sections.
According to Master Zhiyi (En), the praises of the ten similes primarily manifest the principle of emptiness.
The analogy of illusion states: "It deludes the foolish eyes, which gaze upon it incessantly, causing long-term exertion within the world.
Father and son, father and son—'I' is truly not 'I,' yet it arises from false conceptualization."
"If one realizes that [all things] are like an illusion, this mind will naturally cease.

Now, there are ten metaphors; since the moon in water and the image in a mirror already correspond to the category of "within a reflection," the further metaphor of the city of Gandharvas should likewise be subsumed under the category of "illusion."
The analogy of the city of the Gandharvas is praised as follows: "The phenomena of the world are empty and vast, like that city of spirits; at dawn their shadows spread, appearing as a great capital.
Fools rush toward it, marching with the wind, only to realize at day's end that they have cried out in despair, their voices lost."
The fifth is the patience like a flame (*pratibhāsa*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one discusses the Dharma through ten similes, each simile has many meanings,” the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the simile of the flame as follows: “Because the sunlight strikes dust stirred by the wind, it moves in the wilderness like a mirage; a person lacking wisdom, seeing it for the first time, mistakes it for water.”
The characteristics of male and female are likewise thus.

The scorching heat of the sun of fetters and afflictions, the dust of conditioned phenomena, and the wind of distorted recollections revolve within the vast wilderness of birth and death. Those lacking wisdom perceive these as having a single characteristic—either male or female—and this is called being like a mirage.
Furthermore, if one sees a mirage from afar, one perceives it as water, but when near, there is no perception of water. It is the same with those who lack wisdom:

if they remain far from the noble Dharma, they do not know non-self and do not know that all phenomena are empty; thus, amidst the elements, sense bases, and the nature of phenomena which are empty of self-nature, they give rise to the perception of a person, the perception of a man, and the perception of a woman.

When one draws near to the sublime Dharma, one realizes the true nature of all phenomena; at that time, various deceptive and false conceptualizations are entirely eliminated. For this reason, it is said that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas know all phenomena to be like a mirage.
The commentary states:
That [text] speaks of saṃsāra as a wilderness from the perspective of delusion.
Now, speaking from the perspective of the union of the real and the delusive, the empty space is used as a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Yi said: "The delusions of fire, ignorance, and craving bring such boundless pleasure that one perceives what is not the body as the body and sees what is not form as form; yet in reality there is nothing to be delighted in, which none are able to recognize."
"If there is wisdom, this mind will naturally cease.
Regarding the sixth [stage], "Patience Like a Dream," the commentary states:
"However, as for the opening of this meaning of 'dream,' the text of the commentary consists of two parts:"
First, the general meaning is established; second, the text is analyzed.

Regarding the former, the commentary states: "The first is the basis, which refers to awakening the mind as a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This is because if there were no object of perfuming (*bhāvyatā*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other afflictions would not exist.
It may also be likened to the *tathāgatagarbha*;

as for its being likened to the *mūlavijñāna*, this is because it is accepted by all schools, whereas the Dharmalakṣaṇa school clarifies that the *tathāgatagarbha* does not undergo perfuming (*vāsanā*).

The Commentary states: "The second cause is the hindrance of drowsiness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Furthermore, it is like being in a dream, where one feels joy without a joyful occasion, anger without an angry occasion, and fear without a fearful occasion."
"Sentient beings in the three realms are also like this; due to the power of the slumber of ignorance, they become angry when they ought not to be.
Regarding the commentary's point, "Fourth, these dream-objects exist though they are non-existent," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, there are five kinds of dreams."
If the body is out of balance or if there is an excess of heat, one sees fire in dreams, seeing yellow and red.
If there is an excess of cold, one sees water and white.
If wind-energy (*vāyu*) is predominant, one sees flying objects and black forms.
Furthermore, because one frequently reflects upon and contemplates what has been heard and seen, or because a deity grants a dream in order to make one know future events.
These five kinds of dreams are all devoid of substantial reality and are merely false perceptions.

The people of the world are likewise; due to the power of the causal conditions of the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) among sentient beings within the five realms of existence, they perceive four kinds of "self": that the various forms are the self, that forms belong to the self, that there are forms within the self, and that there is a self within forms.
As it is with form, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; four times five makes twenty.

Through the true wisdom attained on the Path, one awakens to the knowledge that these have no reality. Commentary: This means that just as form is empty and lacks intrinsic nature, so too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. When one attains the true wisdom of the Path, one realizes through awakening that these five aggregates are devoid of substantial reality. Thus, the total of twenty refers to the five aggregates each being analyzed into four aspects (such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self), totaling twenty characteristics through which the practitioner realizes their lack of inherent existence.
In the treatise, the power of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) corresponds to the disharmony within the body.
The sentient beings of the five destinies may also be correlated with the first five dreams:

the initial fire is like the fire of hell because it scorches the path; white is like the wholesome dharmas of humans; black is like the ignorance of animals; much thinking is like the hungry ghosts; and "heavenly" is like the devas.
However, both the *Zhouyi* and the *Liezi* discuss six types of dreams, which share some similarities with and differ from these five types.

As for the six types of dreams, they are: first, the true dream (*zhengmeng*); second, the nightmare (*emo*); third, the dream of thought (*simeng*); fourth, the dream of waking (*wumeng*); fifth, the dream of joy (*ximeng*); and sixth, the dream of fear (*jumeng*).
A "correct dream" refers to one that occurs spontaneously without prior deliberation; it is largely identical to dreams granted by celestial deities.
The remaining five types of dreams mostly consist of what has been seen or heard.
The second chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, the "Qi Wu Pian," states: "Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly; in his own exceeding of his will, he did not know he was Zhou."
Note: If one is a butterfly yet does not know that it is Zhou, this is no different from dying a separate death.
However, since there is nowhere it does not find its will satisfied, those who are attached to life while living must surely be those who cling to death when dying.
Viewed from this perspective, we know that those who grieve for the dead while still alive are mistaken.
"Suddenly he awakens, and he is alert and wide awake—this is Zhou."
Did Zhou dream that he was a butterfly, or did the butterfly dream that it was Zhou?
There must be a distinction between Zhou and the butterfly; this is what is called the transformation of things.
The Master thought:
"The dream of yesterday has already vanished today.
How can the transformation of birth and death be any different from this?"

Furthermore, speaking from the perspective of the Zhou dynasty, the butterfly was said to have attained awakening; it is not necessarily that this was anything other than a dream. This, too, can serve as a metaphor for how all phenomena are like dreams.
Moreover, in the *Liezi*, there is an account of someone who served as a subject by day but dreamed of being a sovereign by night;
while the master dreamed of being a servant at night, both possessed their own form of excellence.
The Commentary states: "Because it is merely a transformation of the mind, it is not the perception of an external phenomenon.
This refers to both the analogy and its application. Regarding the analogy, this serves to resolve potential objections.
Specifically, there is an objection that says:
If things were not real, why would one see forms, hear sounds, and so forth within a dream?
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One should not discuss matters that lack reality."
Why is this? Because consciousness arises when it encounters conditions.
The consciousness within a dream has various conditions; if there were no conditions, how could it arise?
Therefore, the present answer states:

In a dream, the five consciousnesses do not function; the five sense objects perceived therein are merely transformations of the mind. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says they do not exist, because one perceives what should not be perceived.
It is like seeing a person with horns on their head or seeing one’s own body flying in a dream; in reality, the person has no horns and the body does not fly.
Second, regarding phenomena: because it is merely a transformation of the mind, there is the sense of "conjunction" (saṃyoga);
since no external object is perceived, there is no sense of "existence through conjunction."
In the commentary, from the passage "The first part of the text clarifies that neither [of the two] applies" onwards, is the second section:
the explanation of the text. Within this, the commentary consists of three parts:
first, a general elucidation of the textual meaning to establish the four propositions; second, a detailed explanation; and third, the citation of supporting evidence.
The Commentary states: “However, these four phrases, all beginning with ‘Because it is a dream,’ constitute the second level of explanation.
Within this, the two preceding phrases serve as the heading, while the section beginning with ‘That is to say, first, because it is’ serves as the explanation.”
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the two phrases "existence" and "non-existence," and second, the explanation of "neither.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
First is the formal explanation, followed by the elimination of confusion starting from "However,
speech exists," which is further divided into two parts:
first, presenting the correct view, and second, eliminating what is incorrect.
Now, first, the correct position is set forth:
that existence and non-existence mutually penetrate; thus, the phenomena of a dream are themselves empty in nature, and this emptiness of nature is itself the phenomena of the dream.
In terms of dharmas, emptiness of nature is itself illusory existence, and illusory existence is itself emptiness of nature.
If it were determinately existent, it could not be empty;
if it were a void of annihilation, it could not be existent.
Since there is no intrinsic nature, existence completely subsumes non-existence within itself as existence.
Since they arise through conditions, emptiness completely subsumes existence and renders it non-existent.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "There are not two characteristics.
Regarding the commentary’s remark, "It is not merely that the characteristics exist while the nature is absent," the term "two" serves to exclude [the notion of duality].

This refers to the frequent assertions found in various philosophical schools that only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty while phenomena themselves are not empty; for example, the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang zong) maintains that only the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, whereas the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not non-existent.
Furthermore, those who study the Three Treatises but do not grasp their essential meaning also say:
"Phenomena have no intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are said to be empty.
This, however, renders the characteristics [of phenomena] non-empty.
Now, since there is no intrinsic nature yet they exist because they arise through conditions, their existence is itself emptiness;
because they arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature, they are empty, yet within that emptiness they eternally exist.
Only when these two mutually penetrate one another is this the "wondrous existence" of true emptiness.
Therefore, while their words are largely the same, their underlying intent differs; thus, I urge you to reflect upon this.
If you grasp this meaning, then the significance of the following two phrases will become clear.
In the commentary, from "Third, because it is a dream" onwards, within the second section—the explanation of the double negation—there are also two parts:
first, the direct explanation; second, the integration, beginning with "However, this mutual non-being."
This also serves to eliminate confusion: for if both were ordinarily affirmed, their meanings would involve contradiction;
if both were ordinarily negated, their meaning would involve frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, they are made to be mutually integrated, thereby departing from the two types of false accusation and forming a phrase endowed with perfect qualities.

This means that not only are these two non-contradictory, but the two phrases also mutually establish one another; therefore it is said: "If one does not deprive [the other], there would be no 'non-existence' by which to define non-existence."
To say that one takes away non-existence so as not to let it end is not [to affirm] non-existence;
to take away existence so as to let it end is not [to affirm] existence.
This means that if one says "it is not non-existent" while referring to non-existence, then non-existence itself is also non-existent.
Why is this? If there were no "non-exhaustion," then this would be the absence of a fixed nature; therefore, it is not a true non-existence.
The same applies to the following phrase.
If "non-existence" does not exist, then "existence" must also exist.
Because existence is not exhaustive, it is an existence of fixed nature rather than true existence.
Therefore, by means of "neither existence nor non-existence," one establishes the aforementioned "both existence and non-existence."

Furthermore, it would also be appropriate to explain that the "both" category establishes the "neither," as this is already contained within the "both" category and the subsequent conclusion; therefore, it is omitted here.
If one wishes to explain it separately, one should say:
because there is also an existence that is precisely non-existence, it constitutes "non-existence."
Because there is also no such "non-existence that is itself existence," it is established as "not non-existent.

The commentary’s statement, "When existence and non-existence do not obstruct one another and both are simultaneously obliterated, this is the freely sovereign Dharma-gate of dreams," serves as the conclusion.
Existence is "being," non-existence is "non-being," their coexistence is "both being and non-being," and their dissolution is "neither being nor non-being.
Since these all interpenetrate one another, they are said to be sovereign and unimpeded.

Furthermore, that which exists is the fourfold set of existence; that which perishes is the fourfold set of non-existence; that which is both is both existent and non-existent; and that which is merged is neither existent nor non-existent. Therefore, it is called the Dharma-gate of Sovereignty over Dreams.
Acting as pits for one another, how can this be called sovereignty?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The sutra says that the world is constantly like a dream,” etc., this is the third citation of scriptural evidence; it refers to the first chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, specifically the middle two lines of that passage.
If [the verse] is complete, it should read: "Distant from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is ever like a dream;
though wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
The previous section on the "Tolerance Like Illusion" has already been cited in full.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In each of the four preceding gates, both [aspects] are preserved and mutually negated to form four propositions,” it is as stated in the first gate concerning permanence and impermanence: first, permanence;
[second, impermanence; third, both; fourth, neither].
Second is impermanence;
third, combining the two, it becomes both permanent and impermanent, hence they are said to coexist;

fourth, by way of mutual negation, it becomes neither permanent nor impermanent: because impermanence negates permanence, it is not permanent; because permanence negates impermanence, it is not impermanent.
This means that because its substance is empty and lacks reality, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is impermanent.
The following three sections should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The final phrase clarifies the gate of awakening as both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,” the commentary consists of three parts:
The first section above is the heading;
second, from "That is, it requires awakening" onwards, explains the reason for establishing awakening;
third, from "Contemplating the many doors of the aforementioned" onwards, explains the meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the establishment of the reason why it is "during the waking state," this also serves to resolve an objection.
That is to say, there may be a question:
"This explains the patience regarding dreams; why then do you speak of the time of waking?"
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
since waking and dreaming establish one another, it is necessary to speak of waking.
Within this, first, waking establishes dreaming, because when one has not yet awakened, one does not know it is a dream.
Among these, the first point—"one must be awake to know that it was a dream"—correctly establishes the reason why awakening is necessary.

This means that during the night of a great dream, there must necessarily follow the light of that great awakening; for it is our World-Honored One who has realized that the three realms are all like a dream.
The preceding citation from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* praises the Buddha for his ability to understand dreams.
The subsequent statement, "While actually in a dream, one does not know it is a dream," means that one takes it to be real.
Because ordinary beings remain in a long sleep through the great night and do not give rise to weariness or the desire for awakening, Master Rui said:
"To dream within a dream is the state of a purely deluded mind.
Next, regarding the phrase "even if one knows it is a dream, one has not yet awakened," this addresses and resolves potential objections.

This means that there are also people who, while dreaming, know it is a dream; for instance, when a person in deep sleep suddenly experiences a dream and clearly recognizes, "This is my dream," yet because their sleep is so profound, they are unable to awaken from it.
This is analogous to the various bodhisattvas, who from the very first moment they resolve their minds [for enlightenment], know that the three realms are all like a dream; is this not awakening?
Why, then, would it be necessary to speak further of "the time of awakening"?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
This is also not yet awakening, because it is not yet great awakening.

Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If a person realizes that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment and can restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise, although this is called 'awakening,' it is still non-awakening, because it involves arising and ceasing, and because ignorance obscures the mind, rendering it not autonomous."
Next, it says: "When awake, one realizes that the dream was truly non-existent. This means that not only does one know the dream upon waking, but one also knows that the dream did not exist.
This is like the eighth-stage Bodhisattva who dreams of crossing a river, which serves as an analogy for realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
One does not perceive this shore of birth-and-death nor that shore of nirvana, for both the one who crosses over and the one who is crossed over are unobtainable;
how much more so in the case of Great Awakening?
Thus the Sūtra says: "For a long time I have contemplated the suffering of sentient beings, desiring to liberate them, yet finding no way to do so."
"Today I have realized Bodhi; suddenly, there is nothing at all. Commentary:

"However, it is because of the dream that awakening exists; therefore, the distinction between the time of dreaming and awakening is established. This means that while the previous section distinguished the dream by means of awakening, this section distinguishes awakening by means of the dream.
To speak of awakening in contrast to dreaming is to have neither dream nor awakening.
Since one has realized that the dream is no dream, in relation to what could one speak of awakening?
Therefore, both awakening and dreaming are utterly transcended.
If there is no non-awakening, then there is no initial awakening; only when both awakening and dreaming are severed together does one attain wondrous awakening.
In the commentary, from the phrase "contemplative realization" (*guanliao*) onwards, the meaning of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) is explained.
Because it illuminates the four preceding gates, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

When awakening and dreaming are both severed, one no longer grasps at the delusions of the dream; thus, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* praises the Buddha, saying: "Wisdom is tranquil and the emotions are stilled; anxieties coalesce into stillness. Intention ceases and consciousness perishes, and the mind is likewise quiescent. One forever cuts off the delusions of dreams and the thoughts of ideation, such that the various aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) no longer exist."
He immediately realized that the ultimate understanding of the dream belongs only to our World-Honored One.
Master Rui said:

"Within the long night, all that is produced by the great dream is painted by the mind; it universally fashions myriad forms, and the spirit transmigrates through the five paths, fully exhausting all its wanderings."
If one can awaken to this, ignorance is immediately shattered.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Subcommentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 75.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Subcommentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll [75].
Seventy-sixth: The Seventh [Chapter],
Endurance Like an Echo, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
The commentary is clear.
Master Rui’s eulogy says:
"Sound responds with resonance; their harmony is as one."
Responses accord with conditions; who can distinguish the false from the real?
Though karma is illusory, its retribution—whether of sin or merit—is never lost; when reflected through this illumination, it is as clear as the bright sun.
Furthermore, he praised it, saying:
"An echo has no location; sound arises through the convergence of conditions.
One does not know the self, yet joy and anger contend within."
When false thoughts harmonize with the true mind, phenomena manifest in myriad forms; one knows not their source and busies oneself all day long.
This is the eighth, the Patience Like a Shadow.
The commentary states: "The nature is not something to be cultivated, yet its characteristics are not abandoned. This explains the meaning of the dual illumination.
As the preceding text states, "It is not of the mundane world; its meaning must transcend the world.
The subsequent phrase, "not transcending the world," then sweeps away the aforementioned transcendence of the world.
Since both the mundane and the supramundane are simultaneously brushed aside, it is called "double negation" (*śūnyatā*).
In the present text, if it were said that one does not cultivate the bodhisattva practices, this would result in a general double negation;
however, since it is stated that one does not abandon the great vows, it is clearly a case of "double affirmation" (*prabhāsvara*).

This means that not practicing the bodhisattva path is precisely the illumination of reality, and not abandoning the great vows is precisely the illumination of the provisional; thus, it receives the name "double illumination.
Next, the explanation of "neither real nor unreal" follows the same principle as the double illumination of the ultimate and the conventional.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The simultaneous [functioning] of exclusion and illumination constitutes the union,” if one were to define the union based on the concurrent practice of the provisional and the ultimate, then the second section would already have completed the discussion of that union.

Now, if the negation (*pratiṣedha*) and illumination (*prakāśa*) are taken as the unified operation (*yuganaddha*), then this middle section exists; that is, the preceding two gates are combined to form this third gate.

Since it is stated that negation and illumination occur simultaneously, then total negation constitutes illumination and total illumination constitutes negation, whereby the two gates stand side by side.
When illumination supplants negation, negation ceases;
when negation supplants illumination, illumination becomes still.
Thus, both negation and illumination vanish.
Regarding the term "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*), there are two intended meanings:
first, that concealment does not impede illumination, and illumination does not impede concealment;
second, that the simultaneous affirmation of both does not impede their simultaneous negation, and the simultaneous negation of both does not impede their simultaneous affirmation.
Therefore, it is called "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*).

Only in this way can one be said to possess mastery; hence, the conclusion below states: "By this, the two preceding sections are shown to share this same unimpededness, and thus they are called 'profound and mysterious' (*gambhīra-gūḍha*)."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Now, first, if one takes the metaphor of a reflection to specifically illustrate the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s body,” the commentary consists of two parts:

first, distinguishing the scope—whether general or specific—of the object of the metaphor; second, from the passage beginning “The two kinds of rivers and springs,” distinguishing the scope of the illustrative metaphors themselves.
Regarding the statement "although it is capable of manifesting," this is because the sun and moon are seen within rivers and springs; therefore, it is said to be capable of manifesting.
Regarding the statement "and yet it is that which is manifested," this is because the subsequent sutra says, "Only when there is oil and water does the clarity become capable of manifesting."
"Now, rivers and springs serve as its manifestations.
The phrase "the long river and flying springs enter the mirror" indicates the appearance of these manifested forms.
When one ascends a tower and holds up a mirror, the entire expanse of the Yellow River enters the mirror, and a thousand-fathom waterfall appears within a span of a foot.
The Right Minister Wang said:
"Mist and clouds arise upon my robes as I look through the window; when the curtain is rolled back, mountain springs enter the mirror.
This clearly illustrates what is manifested.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Within the two [aspects of] that which can manifest, there are also both general and specific [meanings],” the commentary text consists of two parts:
first, a general exposition of the text’s purport; second, a specific analysis of the meaning of the analogies.

First, regarding the statement "separately illustrating the responsive capacity and the locus of manifestation": since the sun and moon have already been used as metaphors for the Bodhisattva, the water and other elements serve as metaphors for the responsive capacity, and they also serve as metaphors for the locus where the Bodhisattva manifests.
Just as reflections fall upon the hundred rivers, this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s body pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The hundred rivers and great streams are metaphors for the capacities of sentient beings and the locations of the lands manifested for them.

In the commentary, the passage beginning with "However, this text fully incorporates the three metaphors of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*" marks the second section, which specifically elucidates the intent of the metaphors.
These two sentences provide the general heading; the following establishment of the three meanings is then divided into three distinct parts.

The Commentary states: "First, pairing oil and water with the sun and moon above serves as the analogy of the moon in water. In this context, the sun and moon represent the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom, while the water represents the receptive mind of sentient beings.
The moon in the water is a metaphor for the objects of the meditative states (*samāhitabhūmi*), referring to the vision of the Buddha and so forth within concentration.
It is also a metaphor for the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), because the objects of concentration consist of blue, yellow, red, white, and so on.
The verse on "Manifestation" says: "Just as the pure moon in the void can eclipse the multitude of stars and display its waxing and waning;
its reflection appears in all waters, and to all who gaze upon it, it stands directly before them."

The Tathāgata’s pure moon is likewise: it can obscure other vehicles to manifest long or short durations, appearing universally in the waters of the pure minds of humans and devas, such that all perceive him as being right before them.
Master Rui said:
"The moon in the water is not real; there is only a hollow reflection.
Human beings are likewise: in the end, they never grasp this truth, but instead toil and bustle about, turning their backs on this true purity."
"If one can awaken to this, one will transcend and remain uniquely sober.

Regarding the commentary's statement, "Second, taking the body in relation to the sun and moon above as 'light and shadow'": the sun and moon are metaphors for the compassion and wisdom of the Bodhisattva; the body is a metaphor for the capacities of sentient beings; and the sun shining to produce shadows is used to metaphorize the manifestation of physical forms and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "reflecting the sun" and so forth, the "and so forth" (等) includes the word "moon" from the sutra as well as lamps and candles.

As for the commentary stating, "Because they play with shadows in manifold ways, they are likened to the various consciousnesses," the former [section] concerned the specific metaphor of the Bodhisattva manifesting his body, whereas this concerns the general metaphor for all consciousnesses.

Moving the body, looking up or down, is precisely playing with shadows; when the form is upright, the shadow is upright, and when the form is bent, the shadow is slanted—hence it is said to be "multifaceted.

This serves as an analogy for how the eight consciousnesses differ according to the body they rely upon, and it also metaphorically illustrates how the seventh consciousness differs according to the objects it encounters in relation to the eighth consciousness.
The above are all the essential points of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
Master Rui said:
"That which light does not illuminate is called shadow."
If one does not illuminate with the light of wisdom, birth and death will endure for a long time; having abandoned the level highway, one wanders through thorny thickets.
If one can awaken to this, madness will be extinguished and one will naturally regain clarity.
The Commentary states: "Third, 'using a precious mirror and so forth to face the aforementioned man,' etc., explains the third simile.
The commentary text has two parts:
first, the direct correlation with the scriptural text; second, the differentiation based on the analogy."
First, regarding the initial point:

the Commentary (*Sūtra-śāstra*) speaks from a general perspective, stating that "the metaphor refers to the retribution of non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*). This is the intention of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
It is said to be "non-concentrated" in contrast to the aforementioned meditative objects such as the moon in water.

Thus, the mirror is used as a metaphor for the cause; therefore it is said that the essence of ignorance and so forth is the metaphor for the conditions (*pratyaya*), while the reflection is the metaphor for the retribution (*vipāka*).
Hence, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "This body is like a shadow, manifested from the conditions of karma."

Furthermore, the mirror metaphor represents the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) and the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; the original object represents ignorance, karma, and so forth; and the reflected image represents the retributive fruit, as described in the "Chapter on Inquiring about Clarity" (Pṛcchāmukhaparivarta).

If one uses the mirror image as a distinct metaphor for the manifested body of a bodhisattva, then the mirror and so forth represent the bodhisattva, the original object represents the sentient being (the capacity), and the image represents the body manifested by the bodhisattva.
The Commentary states: "Because the reflection in a mirror is separate from its original substance," and so forth. This is the second pair of metaphors used to distinguish [the two cases].
It clarifies that this "mirror-image" receives the name of "attaining the fruit" because the fruit is distinct from the cause; it is as if the shadow were outside the body.
Below the phrase "the preceding reflection-substance," the text distinguishes the former case as being different from this one.
When the sun and moon are in the sky while their shadows and light are upon the body, the body serves as a metaphor for the cause; thus, the manifested phenomena can coexist with their cause.

The Commentary states: "Therefore, it is illustrated that although the various consciousnesses arise by depending on objects, the distinct self does not reside within those objects. This corresponds to the previous point that although shadows follow the sun and so forth, they actually follow the body; this is explained by employing a general analogy for all consciousnesses.

If one uses the analogy of light and shadow to represent the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s body, then just as a shadow varies according to the body and not because of the sun's rays, so too does the body vary due to its arising and not because the sun of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom causes it to vary.
Master Rui said:
"A form does not enter the mirror, yet it appears when light shines upon it; the world is likewise: one receives the shadow of one's karma.
Those who do not understand this will long remain entangled in its faults."
"If one can awaken to this, one returns to the Mother of Spirit and Qi.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Within this, the meanings of unity and difference, conjunction and separation are universally revealed through reflections," this serves to distinguish between the various pairs of universal and restricted [meanings] found within the sutra.
Since this applies to all three types of reflections, it is said to be "universally manifest.
Next, from the passage beginning with "In the flowing stream," only the reflection of the moon in water is explained.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "However, 'identity' and 'difference' refer to this reflection and that reflection," this is intended to distinguish between two pairs of meanings whose purports differ, thereby demonstrating that there is no fault of redundant repetition.
Regarding the statement "this reflection" and "that reflection": if the moon in the river were identical to the water, it could not remain in the river;
if it were different from the water, then since the river and the water are distinct, there ought to be two moons.

Regarding the statement, "The union and separation are like a reflection corresponding to water," and so forth: if the reflection in the water were to unite with the water, then as the water flows, the moon [in the reflection] should also flow;
if the reflection were to separate from the water, then even when the water is removed, the reflection should remain behind.
Furthermore, regarding conjunction and separation, the intention of conjunction is also twofold, like the joining of two palms.
Identity and difference are not thus: if they were identical, there would be no duality, just as ice becomes water;
if the reflection were different from the water, the moon could emerge from the water.
If the reflection and the moon in the water were one and the same, then wherever there is water there would be the moon, and it could not be moved.
The principle of their conjunction and separation is no different from the previous explanation.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that “it does not apply to two reflections,” this is because it refers only to the moon in the water, and does not apply to images in a mirror or reflected objects.
This is because the *Wenxuan* merely states "streams, ponds, and wells.
As for the phrase "the moon reflects in the Huai River's flow," the *Wenxuan* actually says "the moon reflects in the clear stream."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “including mirror-images,” this is because the text says, “although they appear therein”; thus, it applies to mirror-images but does not apply to reflected objects, for the shadows of reflected objects do not appear within [the mirror].
If one takes the shadow of the sun’s rays as they enter into water, it is likewise included therein, yet it is subsumed under the category of "water-shadow.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because one does not know that this shadow has no distance or proximity,” this explains the scriptural passage: “The shadow does not follow the object in having distance or proximity.”

It is like holding a mirror or standing by a pond: when the moon appears in the water, this reflection is neither close to the moon in the heavens, nor is it far from it, even though it falls into the pool at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas from the earth.

This serves as a metaphor for how a Bodhisattva, though dwelling afar in another realm, constantly abides here; and though remaining in this place, they are ever present there. How, then, could there be any distinction between near and far?
All things, whether distant or near, should be understood in this same way.
The ninth is the patience regarding the nature of transformations (*nirmāṇa-kṣānti*).
The *Renwang jing* says: [text follows].

Regarding the statement, "The Dharma is fundamentally without [intrinsic nature], yet it arises through causes and conditions," this serves as proof for the two meanings of "unreal" and "the manifestation of marks.
Furthermore, there are two senses:
first, that which arises through causes and conditions is precisely the manifestation of marks.

Because they arise through conditions, that which comes into being is immediately non-existent; thus, phenomena are fundamentally non-existent from the start, meaning they lack any substantial reality.
These two phrases together constitute a single meaning: "self" (or "originally") refers to what has existed from the very beginning.
To exist from non-existence is called "arising"; since it does not exist inherently from the beginning, it is said that "dharmas are originally non-existent.
Meeting with conditions, they immediately emerge; therefore, it is said that "all things arise through causes and conditions."

This means that by simply employing the principle of dependent origination, two meanings are established: namely, because things arise through causes and conditions, their characteristics exist; yet because those dependently arisen things lack intrinsic nature, they have no reality.
Because there is a transformation from the sudden emergence of names where none existed, this passage is cited.

This passage is from the fifth chapter, "The Universal Radiance King," in the second fascicle of the "Chapter on Protecting the State" (*Rāṣṭrapālaparivarta*), wherein the Universal Radiance King speaks a verse for the sake of the thousand kings.
Following this, there is another verse which says: "That which flourishes must inevitably decline; that which is full is ultimately empty.
The bustling world of beings is entirely like a dwelling in an illusion.
Both sound and echo are void; the lands, too, are likewise so. And so forth.
In total there are eight verses and their contextual circumstances, all of which are as found in that sutra.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two meanings of ‘purifying’ can be understood by analogy with this,” these refer to the two meanings of being unreal and the manifestation of appearances.

The Commentary states: "Compassion is further established based upon skillful means. This refers to the text from the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) below; thus, that verse says: "For example, forests exist by depending on the earth, and the earth remains indestructible by depending on water; the water-mandala depends on wind, and wind depends on space, yet that space has nothing upon which it depends."

All Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion; compassion, in turn, is established upon skillful means; skillful means rely upon knowledge, and knowledge relies upon wisdom; the body of unimpeded wisdom has no basis upon which it relies.
That [text] explains five layers of mutual dependence; here, however, it is simply that compassion depends upon skillful means (*upāya*).

Skillful means is none other than subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); compassion takes subsequently attained wisdom as its essence, because within that wisdom one bestows happiness and removes suffering.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because there is neither existence nor non-existence,” the sutra contains two phrases: “neither existent nor non-existent.
Here, the phrase “not non-existent” is explained specifically; that is to say, "not existent" is itself "non-existence."
Now, since that which is sent forth is also non-existent, it is said to be "neither existent nor non-existent"; thus it is said that there is neither existence nor non-existence.
The preceding phrase is easy to understand and therefore not explained.
Master Rui said:
“Sentient beings are like magical illusions—neither existent nor real.
Those who do not realize this revolve like the wheel of a chariot.
When one understands that phenomena are pure, being without self or person, all defilements are eliminated, like the sun when it is free from clouds.”
"The tenth is the patience like space.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The heading says 'like space,' and that which is illustrated by 'like space' applies to all phenomena," etc., the subsequent commentary consists of four parts:

first, revealing the universality or limitation of the illustration; second, clarifying the differences in the characteristics of the metaphors; third, citing treatises to provide an interpretive explanation; and fourth, concluding with the essential meaning.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text]: the first part, "The above is the meaning of the root sūtra," provides a general metaphor for all things;
the second part, "The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains purity through metaphors," onwards, cites the śāstra to clarify both the universal and the specific.
The commentary states: "Now, as for 'the characteristics of the analogies'... This marks the second section, clarifying that the characteristics of the analogies differ.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, using only the analogy of emptiness to contrast with the preceding six analogies and demonstrate their differing characteristics;...

Second, from "Furthermore, regarding these various metaphors, if one considers the analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*) themselves," below, there is a comprehensive analysis of the distinctions among the seven metaphors and what they refute;

third, from "Furthermore, the first six eliminate existence," below, there are three layers that contrast the metaphor of emptiness with the six [previous metaphors] to clarify how their meanings differ—establishing that while the various metaphors collectively illustrate emptiness, the metaphor of emptiness itself conversely becomes a form of existence;

fourth, from "Furthermore, the aforementioned metaphors apply universally to all," below, there is a comprehensive analysis of the scope and limitations of the seven metaphors regarding both the subject and the object.

Regarding the statement, "In this context, the illustrative metaphors possess manifold meanings," it means that, for example, a single space possesses the meaning of non-existence and existence, the meaning of non-arising and arising, the meaning of a single flavor, and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "The metaphors each correspond to specific meanings to illustrate a particular category of phenomena," this means that "absence of marks" (animitta) illustrates only the *dharmadhātu* of things, "non-arising" (anutpāda) illustrates only the world (*loka*), and "single flavor" (ekarasa) illustrates only the teaching (*dharma*) and so forth.
The Commentary: "However, Nāgārjuna... and below marks the third section, which cites sūtras and śāstras to provide a harmonious interpretation.
Within this, it cites one śāstra and two sūtras.
First, regarding the four meanings from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, they are presented in brief as in the full text.
Second, the ten meanings of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*;
third, the ten meanings of the *Aṣṭabhūmika-sūtra*.
Both of these sūtras contain ten meanings in their texts, yet their intended meanings differ respectively.

The ten meanings of the *Buddhabhūmi* [Sūtra] serve solely as metaphors for the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmadhātu*.
