Regarding the ten aspects of the space-body (*ākāśakāya*) known through the ten meanings of the eighth stage, they are: first, the aspect of being immeasurable; second, the aspect of pervasiveness; third, the aspect of formlessness; fourth, the aspect of non-differentiation; fifth, the aspect of boundlessness; and sixth, the aspect of manifesting the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Although the text contains only these six, by analogy there should be ten.
However, this merely speaks of emptiness and does not provide distinct analogies for the dharmas.
I shall now cite in full the ten meanings from the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, which extends from the third treatise to the conclusion of the fourth.
Regarding the ultimate truth, the Sūtra states: "O Wondrous Birth, you should know!

The pure dharma-realm is like space; although it pervades all various forms and diverse characteristics, it cannot be said to possess those diverse characteristics, for its essence is of a single flavor."

In this way, although the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm pervades all various categories of objects of knowledge, it cannot be said to possess various characteristics; its essence is of a single flavor.
The second says: "Furthermore, just as space, though pervading all forms, is not separated from them and yet is not defiled by the faults of those forms;
so too, the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, though pervading the mind-nature of all sentient beings, is not separated from it by virtue of its reality, yet is not defiled by their faults."
Third, it says: "Furthermore, just as space contains all actions of body, speech, and mind, yet this space has no activity or origination;
so too, the Tathāgata contains all the deeds manifested by omniscience for the benefit of sentient beings, yet the pure dharma-realm has no activity or origination."

At the beginning of the fourth fascicle, it says: "Furthermore, just as within empty space various forms and appearances manifestly arise and manifestly perish, yet this empty space itself neither arises nor perishes."
Thus it is said, and so forth: while the various manifestations of wisdom that benefit sentient beings appear to arise and cease, the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is neither arising nor ceasing.
Fifth, it says: "Furthermore, it is like space; although various forms and appearances appear to increase or decrease, this space itself neither increases nor decreases."
In this manner, and so forth, it is shown that while the Tathāgata’s nectar-like holy teaching has increase and decrease, the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) neither increases nor decreases.

Sixth, it says: "Furthermore, it is like space; the forms and characteristics of the ten directions are boundless and inexhaustible because the realm of space is boundless and inexhaustible, yet this space neither comes nor goes, and neither moves nor transforms."

In this manner, and so forth, he establishes the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions; his various activities are boundless and inexhaustible because the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is boundless and inexhaustible. Yet, the pure dharma-realm neither comes nor goes, neither moves nor transforms.
7. It is further said: "Just as the three-thousandfold world system appears to form and appear to disintegrate within space, yet the realm of space neither disintegrates nor forms;

so it is with the manifestation of immeasurable signs such as the attainment of perfect enlightenment or the demonstration of entering great parinirvāṇa—yet the pure dharma-realm neither attains perfect enlightenment nor enters into cessation."

8. It is further said: "Moreover, just as various forms and appearances may be seen to decay, rot, burn, and undergo transformation while depending upon space, yet the realm of space is not transformed by them nor obscured by them."

Thus, based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm, various violations of the precepts regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind may be found within the realm of sentient beings; yet the pure dharma-realm does not undergo transformation because of them, nor is it obscured by weariness.

"Furthermore, it is like how, depending upon space, the great earth, massive mountains, light, water, fire, Śakra and his retinue, and even the sun and moon—these various things can be perceived; yet the realm of space is not those various characteristics."

In this way, based upon the Tathāgata’s pure realm (*dharmadhātu*), the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation can be found; yet the pure dharma-realm is not characterized by those [phenomenal] marks.

10. It is said: "Furthermore, just as within space, through various causes and conditions arising in succession, the revolving cycle of the immeasurable worlds of the trichiliocosm can be perceived, yet the realm of space itself performs no action of origination."

In this way, within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the surrounding circles of the assemblies of all Buddhas, endowed with immeasurable marks, can be found; yet, the pure realm itself is devoid of any arising or activity.
The commentary states:

The ten points above are fully set forth in the scriptural text; beneath each instance of the word "thus" (evam), there is the phrase "the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm" (tathāgata-viśuddha-dharmadhātu), while the remainder follows the scripture.
The treatises all provide extensive explanations, and their general purports are similar; therefore, this commentary does not cite the treatises, nor does it list the scriptural passages in full.
What is meant by "the general purports are similar" refers specifically to the common meaning that [the Buddha-nature] is neither identical to nor separate from all phenomena.
In the preceding correct exposition of the five dharmas, because the One True Dharma-realm (ekadharmadhātu) is the subject, it is illustrated by ten meanings of space (*ākāśa*).

To briefly extract their specific characteristics: first, its essence is of a single flavor; second, its nature is pure and unstained; third, it is without arising or activity; fourth, it is without birth or extinction; fifth, it is without increase or decrease; sixth, it is without coming, going, movement, or shifting; seventh, it is without formation or destruction; eighth, it is without change, transformation, or weariness; ninth, it is not comprised of various marks; and tenth, it is without anything that arises or acts.

Observing the text of these sutras, the "Ten" and the "Three" are identical, yet the "Three" refers to non-arising through inclusion, while the "Ten" refers to non-arising through origination; when the two are combined, they are called "without subject or object."
If one examines the conclusion of the treatise, ten [points] should be described as "without conceptual differentiation," and three should be called "without mental application.
Now, I shall briefly cite the commentary from the treatise to explain this.

Regarding the first, it says: "Next, the characteristics of the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) shall be revealed, and the distinctions within the dharma-realm shall be explained through the resolution of difficulties."
It is said in response to an objection:
"If all Tathāgatas have the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as their nature, and the dharma-realm has true suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence,

then since true suchness is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, and all phenomena possess various distinctions, how can the dharma-realm— which conforms to them— be devoid of various distinctions?"
If the dharma-realm possessed various distinctions, how could it be pure?
It is not like a crystal that is associated with various supports; therefore, it lacks any manifold characteristics.
To resolve this difficulty, the analogy of primordial empty space is taught.
The meaning is:
although it pervades all varieties, it does not conform to their forms, for it does not abandon its own nature.
Below the section on "single flavor," the following is an excerpt from the treatise based on its essential meaning.
Second, an objection is raised:
If the *dharmadhātu* pervades all things, it would then be associated with greed and other afflictions; how is it that it does not become impure, like contaminated mental factors?
Therefore, it is now generally stated:
because its nature is pure and because it is not of that [defiled] substance, it is not stained by them.
A third objection may be raised as follows:

If the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm has true suchness as its essence, then it is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of activity; how, then, can it accommodate the work of benefiting sentient beings?
Therefore, it is now explained comprehensively:

by means of the dominant condition of former vow-power, one spontaneously abides in performing acts of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, free from conceptual discrimination and non-conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Fourth, an objection is raised:
"If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) pervades all things, is inseparable from them, and invariably evolves along with them, then the dharma-realm itself must be subject to arising and ceasing."
Therefore, it is now generally stated:

although [the nature of phenomena] pervades all things, they undergo arising and ceasing through conventional designation (*saṃvṛti-prajñapti*), whereas their true ultimate essence (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) is neither born nor extinguished.
Five people raised this objection:

If the pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) were omnipresent and inseparable from all things, then since the holy teachings of the Tathāgata currently exhibit increase and decrease, the dharma-realm would likewise have to increase and decrease.
Therefore, it is generally stated:
"While increase and decrease are spoken of according to all conventional principles, there is no increase or decrease in the true dharma-realm."
Sixth, an objection is raised:
"If the dharmadhātu is the essence of all Tathāgatas, then when a Tathāgata bestows benefit and happiness upon sentient beings or comes and goes, the dharmadhātu itself must come and go."
Therefore, it is now explained in general terms:
it is said that there is coming and going with respect to the *saṃbhogakāya*, but it is not the case that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* has coming and going.
Seventh, an objection is raised:
If there were no coming or going, how could one attain perfect enlightenment?
Therefore, it is now explained:
"attainment" is spoken of in terms of conventional reality; in the ultimate sense, there is neither attainment nor destruction.
The eighth objection states:
"If the *dharmadhātu* pervades all classes of sentient beings, how can sentient beings commit transgressions?
To this, the following general response is given:
Sentient beings may commit transgressions, yet the dharma-realm remains unchanging.
A difficulty regarding the ninth [verse] states:
"If the dharma-realm pervades all things, there should be no characteristics of the untainted aggregates, such as morality."
Therefore, it is now generally stated:
the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) increases all things, yet itself possesses no characteristics.
Ten [objections] raise the following difficulty:
If all Buddha-dharmas have the dharma-realm as their essence, there should be no enjoyment; how then could there be distinctions among assemblies?
Therefore, it is now explained:
these are obtained through various individual causes and conditions; they do not imply that the Tathāgata’s body possesses conceptual proliferation or discrimination.
The ten objections above are, in fact, easily understood in light of the preceding scriptural text.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “However, from the perspective of distinct meanings, there are these differences,” this constitutes the fourth section, which summarizes the general purport.
However, the text consists of three parts:
first, a general explanation;
second, from "Therefore, Master Rui... onwards, citations of evidence to establish that the meaning of emptiness is identical.
This is merely a summary praise based on the ten similes.
If one were to explain emptiness specifically, the praise would say:
"Emptiness has only a name; it has no function and no form. Human beings are likewise, such that none are able to recognize them."
"Creating delusions and suffering amidst a hundred urgent hardships, they race through emptiness seeking emptiness until their strength is utterly exhausted.
This also clarifies the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The subsequent statement, "The remaining meanings of non-obstruction are as explained before and after," constitutes the threefold conclusion that summarizes the great purport of this sutra.
The commentary on the sutra has already been discussed previously, such as in the section on the "patience like an illusion" (māyopama-kṣānti) and so forth.
It is also discussed later, as in the section on "virtues equal to space" (ākāśasama-guṇa).
There are many more such distant passages from the beginning and end of the text.
The Commentary states: "That which arises from the collective karma of the world" will be explained in the "Appearance Chapter. The Commentary states:

"The fourth is the reverse of this," meaning that because there is no intrinsic nature it exists, and because it is dependently originated it is empty; both points are as explained in the "Chapter on the Questions of Vimalakīrti."

Regarding the scriptural passage, it should be stated that because things exist through conditions, they serve as the basis for the world; yet because they lack intrinsic nature and are empty, they have no basis.
The four propositions merely express the meaning of emptiness, differing only in their specific formulations.
The Commentary states: "No dharma emerges from emptiness" and below, there is a separate explanation.
It is like empty space: all worlds appear before it, yet it does not appear before all worlds.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the single flavor of liberation is no different,” the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, “All are identical in the single flavor of ambrosia and the single flavor of liberation,” and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says, “The flavor of liberation serves as the drink.”
The remaining prose and verse sections may be understood accordingly.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (Daśakṣānti-parivarta).

**Commentary on the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta), Chapter Thirty:** Regarding the statement, "There are two reasons for the initial introduction," the first is general: it correlates the latter three chapters with the former three chapters.
Regarding the two distinctions, this chapter corresponds to the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences.
Therein are three intended meanings:
first, it answers the beginning of the second assembly; [the other two follow].
2. From "First, as a distant answer" below, the ten oceans within the first assembly are answered;
3. From "Furthermore, it penetrates" below, the number of sections in this one division is revealed.
The beginning and middle sections further contain two intentions:
first, a direct exposition of the Bodhisattva; second, from "Furthermore, two things are inconceivable" onwards, the elucidation of the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the Buddha’s virtues.
The verses in the subsequent section likewise possess these two intentions.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "fully incorporating a numerical designation," it is because the term "countless" (asaṃkhyeya) is itself one of the one hundred and twenty-four numbers.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "mentioning both person and dharma together," if the person and the dharma were different, they would be contradictory.
The subsequent statement, "and the calculation of what was asked by the Bodhisattvas," is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "However, the Saṃgha... and so forth, it addresses an objection.
The objection states:
The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* is neither the beginning nor the end; for what reason is it singled out?
The general intent can be understood.
In the commentary, under the section "Fourth, Explaining the Text," this first provides a general outline, which consists of two parts:

Up to this point, the explanation has been based on the categories of phenomena (*dharma*); following the phrase "However, these three categories," the text proceeds to analyze them in terms of persons (*pudgala*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The numerical expression is not separate [from the mind]," this explains the character for "mind" (*citta*).
The phrase "number and non-number" below explains the character *wang* (king); for "king" takes sovereignty as its meaning.
The phrase "further revealing this number" below clarifies both characters, *xin* (mind) and *wang* (king).
The mind governs and encompasses all phenomena because it is the most supreme of all.
A king governs the four seas because he is the most preeminent.
From the phrase "the reason for asking specifically" onwards, the text analyzes and distinguishes the question asked.
Regarding the term "transformation" (*varta*), it refers to the *asaṃkhyeya*.
One *asaṃkhyeya* constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya-varta*, and so forth. The commentary states:

"Beginning from one and two and ending at the 'correct carriage' (*samyak-carana*). From one to ten constitutes ten; next there are thirteen numerical units: ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand, followed by ten thousand, *koṭi*, *arbuda*, *nyarbuda*, *samudra*, *madhya*, *bṛnda*, *lakṣa*, *atila*, *vahala*, *kharva*, *nikharva*, *mahāpadma*, *śaṅku*, *samāpta*, and *samyak-carana*.
Regarding the term "carrying" (zài), it means that even heaven and earth cannot contain or carry [them].

As for the commentary stating, "The sixty kalpas of the Small Vehicle have already reached the incalculable," this refers to the sixty kalpas mentioned in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, after which there are further incalculable [kalpas].
This is the twelfth treatise, which cites the *Vimokṣa-sūtra* stating that among the sixty numerical units, asaṃkhyeya is the fifty-second.
That text lists them in full: from one to ten constitute ten; continuing in this manner up to a *bālākṣa*, which constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya*.
Within this enumeration, eight others have been lost, leaving only fifty-two.

As for the statement that "the sixty categories of the Hīnayāna have already reached the 'incalculable' (asaṃkhyeya)," this "incalculable" means that there is nothing further beyond this; it does not refer to the [mathematical] *asaṃkhyeya*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, a *lakṣa* is taken as a *koṭi*”: that treatise, in its eleventh chapter explaining the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), states in verse: “In establishing the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*) dwells at the very bottom; its extent is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen *lakṣas*.”
Next, regarding the depth of the water wheel: it is eleven hundred and two million [yojanas]. Below this, eight lakṣas of water remain after the condensed portion has formed gold.
It is said that "eleven hundred million" is the vernacular expression, while "lakṣa" below refers to the Sanskrit term.
If one follows this system consistently, it should be stated that eight hundred million [yojanas] below are water, while the remainder solidifies into gold.
Thus, we know that a *lakṣa* is taken here as a "hundred million.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, "there are then four instances of the word 'unspeakable' (*anabhilāpya*)," this means that taking the previous example, one should state "unspeakably unspeakable" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpya*), and one "unspeakably unspeakable" constitutes one "unspeakably unspeakable-fold" (*anabhilāpyānabhilāpyaparivarta*).
The two aforementioned "unspeakable-unspeakables" constitute one unit of accumulation, namely, one "unspeakable-unspeakable.
Two "unspeakable-unspeakables," and so on, up to an "unspeakable-unspeakable" number of "unspeakable-unspeakables," thus comprise four units.
Now, by substituting this character "again" (又) for the two instances of the phrase "inexpressible," is it not indeed marvelous?
The reason for citing this is that the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text) refutes the scripture’s use of this character "again" as being superfluous.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The fruit-virtue is profound and vast, and the cause is able to enter into it”:
“entering” refers to realization and attainment, whereas “previously thoroughly exhausting” refers to understanding.
Furthermore, regarding the virtues cited, the first pertains to non-obstruction and the second pertains to profundity and vastness; thus, the two are distinct.
However, the entry into this excellence is thorough, and it should be understood as profoundly vast and unimpeded; [the current text] is merely a concise summary.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "a single hair-pore of the Dharma-nature," the wording here is likewise a concise summary.
If one possesses all the pores of the lands, they all contain the meaning of being in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*) and possessing the characteristic of indestructibility.
Now, because we take the meaning of being in accordance with the nature from upon the hairs, it is like the fact that there is nothing external to the *dharmatā*.

Because the meaning of grasping the indestructible characteristic within the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) is intended, the phrase "hairs that do not pervade and accord with the nature" is attached as the words of an enlightened one.
Furthermore, there is another intention, which is also omitted by way of elliptical phrasing in the text.
That which is called "the hair-tip awakening" (mao-an wu) reveals that the causes of the *kṣetra* exist due to delusion.
In delusion there are divisions; in awakening there are none.
The former principle discusses the phenomenon (*dharma*) directly, while the latter principle takes the phenomenon from the perspective of the person (*pudgala*); this can be seen through reflection.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because internal and external dependent origination are neither identical nor separate,” there are two meanings:

first, that the internal and external together constitute dependent origination; because they are not identical, there is the distinction between the subject that enters and the object entered, and because they are not separate, they are able to interpenetrate one another.
Second, regarding the fact that internal and external dependent origination is neither identical to nor separate from true *dharmatā*, there are two further meanings:
first, because internal and external phenomena are not identical to *dharmatā*, there exist the subject and object of entry;
yet because they are not separate from *dharmatā*, a single hair can encompass all and a single *kṣetra* can universally enter all.
Second, as for the hair-pores, they are subsumed within the dharma-nature without being separate from it;
as for the lands, they are not identical to the dharma-nature and do not pervade the hair-pores—contemplating this constitutes the meditative observation.
However, among the ten sections, one section cites a number while another does not; the omission is intended as a condensation, whereas the citation is made for fear of losing the sequence.
The commentary’s passage beginning with "Furthermore, following what is manifest" concludes by explaining the manifestation of profundity.
Chapter Thirty-one: On the Lifespan. Commentary on the "Intent of the Chapter": This section has two parts:
first, establishing the principle; second, the actual exposition.
In the preceding section, the lifespan of the ten bodies was correctly revealed; for now, this is clarified by means of the three bodies.
That is to say, the True Body has neither length nor brevity, while the Responsive Body manifests as having both length and brevity.
Regarding "profound" (*xuan*) in the preceding [phrase], it refers to profound principle; regarding "mirror-like" (*jian*), it refers to mirror-like illumination.
When wisdom and principle are in dark resonance, they constitute the True Body (*dharmakāya*).
Because it is profound, it is void and still; because it is mirror-like, it is luminous and penetrating.
Transcending numerical categories, its lifespan—whether short or long—cannot be described;
transcending spatial domains, its physical form and location cannot be specified.
Furthermore, transcending numerical categories, it cannot be said whether it consists of a single body or many bodies.
Transcending these realms, it cannot be equated with the lifespans of humans or devas.
If one distinguishes between the subject and object of realization as described above, then the meaning of the three bodies (trikāya) is complete.
The passage beginning with "However, in accordance with beings" below clarifies its manifest transformations (nirmāṇakāya).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure as empty space; the various forms and appearances he manifests cause beings to enter into this Dharma.
It also says: "The Tathāgata’s true body is fundamentally non-dual, yet it responds to things and adapts to capacities, pervading the ten directions," and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the superior grade... and so forth. This is the second section, which correctly reveals the purpose of this chapter.
It contains two parts:
first, a detailed expansion upon the preceding chapter, including the lifespan of Bodhisattvas; [the second part follows].
The second section, "Also for... and below, provides a remote response to the first assembly, concerning only the lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Second, explaining the names" and so forth: these names are also established based upon the True (Dharmakāya) and the Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya).

However, various sutras and treatises describe the lifespan of the three bodies as follows: the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) has both a beginning and an end, with its duration varying across ten thousand different types;
the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) has a beginning but no end, being eternally constant once attained;
and the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) has neither beginning nor end, remaining steadfast and unchanging.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that being born at Gayā and passing away at the Twin Śāla Trees refers to the Nirmāṇakāya (the Transformation Body);
the lifespan accomplished when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path refers to the Saṃbhogakāya (the Enjoyment Body);
and its eternal abiding without extinction refers to the Dharmakāya (the Dharma Body).
The essential purport of this sutra is that once the three bodies are fused, the three lifespans are unimpeded; thus, the long can be short, and the short is eternally long.
There is neither long nor short, yet within this absence of length and brevity, length and brevity persist. Each is perfectly interfused, beyond the reach of words and thought.

The Commentary states: "Already adjacent to the ocean of lands in equality" implies that there is still a numerical limit, which is why the word "adjacent" is used; for the ocean of lands in equality is without measure or number.
Chapter 32: On the Abodes of Bodhisattvas. Commentary on the "Intent of the Passage," which has three parts:
first, an extensive explanation based on the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*;
second, from "Also answering at a distance" onwards, responding to the first assembly; [and third, the specific analysis of the text].
Third: "In the past, when about to present this chapter," and so forth, describes divergent interpretations; the meaning is as explained in the second assembly.
In the commentary, "The mountains and seas contain within them," and so forth, explains the intent of the "mountains and seas."
This phrase refers to actual phenomena: mountains provide concealment and the ocean provides inclusion.
To say that "the benevolent and the wise dwell therein" is an expression borrowed from non-Buddhist texts.
As the Master [Confucius] said:
"The benevolent delight in mountains; the wise delight in waters.
This means that the benevolent person loves mountains, for they are as stable and immovable as mountains.
The wise person prizes water, for its virtues are like those of a clear mirror that washes and cleanses; it flows or remains still according to conditions.
Therefore, it is not necessary that benevolence must dwell in the mountains and wisdom must stay by the water.
From the section "Manifesting Great Wisdom" onwards, the text specifically addresses that which is manifested.

This single Great Wisdom simultaneously unifies the two aforementioned aspects: it is as lofty as a mountain and as deep as an ocean; its quiescence is the mountain, and its illumination is the ocean.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It must be Mount Xiang north of the Snow Mountains,” the phrase “it must be” indicates a state of uncertainty. When a matter is difficult to reconcile, one should not attempt to force a conclusion; rather, one ought to rely on extensive learning while acknowledging what remains doubtful.

Regarding the term "north of the snows," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that there is Lake Anavatapta between the Snow Mountains and Mount Gandhamādana; therefore, it is known that the Snow Mountains lie to the south of Mount Gandhamādana.
Regarding the commentary on "The Five Cool Mountains," the text is divided into six sections:

first, a brief explanation of the scriptural passage; second, revealing what it symbolizes; third, determining its location; fourth, manifesting its spiritual sanctity; fifth, investigating its origins; and sixth, exhorting beings to practice reverence.
First, regarding the initial point: there are briefly two names.
To speak of "Wutai in Daizhou," this refers to the border between the two counties of Wutai and Fanshi.
Those who have traveled there are not few, and their accounts may be summarized as follows.
In the commentary, from "Manifesting my Great Sage" onwards, the second section clarifies that which is manifested.
Much is drawn from the *Vajraśekhara Yoga*, and there is also analytical reasoning applied.
The term "Great Sage" (Mahāmuni) refers to Mañjuśrī.

Rather than mentioning his specific name, he is directly called the Great Sage; thus, when one recites "Great Sage Bodhisattva" here in the mountains, this employs the general title while specifically indicating Śrī.

Regarding the "five wisdoms," if one follows the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the nature of great enlightenment is subsumed within five factors: namely, the four wisdoms of enlightenment and the one true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
According to the *Vajraśekhara*, the single true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is termed the wisdom of the pure dharma-realm; thus, the five wisdoms are established.
Second, the five eyes may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding the "five families": first, the Buddha family; second, the Vajra family; third, the Ratna family; fourth, the Padma family; and fifth, the Karma family.
All mantras of the devas belong to the Ratna Family, while the mantras of the spirits and ghosts belong to the Karma Family.

Regarding the "five aggregates" (skandhas): these are my own five aggregates, which signify that within these five terraces there is Great Enlightenment—that is, the Sovereign Sublime Wisdom of Acala-jñāna Buddha, who is Mañjuśrī.
Regarding the five-character phrase "wearing upon his head the crown of the five Buddhas": many of the great Bodhisattvas possess such a crown, yet the Great Sage does not mention wearing one.
Furthermore, he constantly has five topknots.
However, these five meanings are largely analogous.

Specifically, the central topknot represents the central terrace; it is where Vairocana Buddha resides, who is the lord of the Buddha Family and the pure wisdom of the Dharma-realm, which is also the Buddha-eye.
The single topknot to its east is the Eastern Terrace; it is the abode of Akṣobhya Buddha, who is the lord of the Vajra family. He is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is the Eye of Wisdom.

The single topknot to its south is precisely the Southern Terrace, the abode of Ratnasambhava Tathāgata; he is the lord of the Jewel Family, the Wisdom of Equality, and is none other than the Divine Eye.
The single topknot to its west is the Western Terrace, the abode of Amitābha Tathāgata; he is the lord of the Lotus Family, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Dharma-eye.
The single crest to its north is the Northern Terrace, the abode of Akṣobhya-vajra Tathāgata; he is the lord of the Karma-kula, the Wisdom of Accomplishment, and is the fleshly eye.

Seventh, if these are correlated with the five vehicles: the center represents the Buddha Vehicle; the east, the Bodhisattva Vehicle; the south, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; the west, the Śrāvaka Vehicle; and the north, the Human and Deva Vehicle.

If one distinguishes between the vehicles of humans and devas, the northern [region] corresponds to the human vehicle; when combined with the vehicles of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the rest follow their respective order.
As for the eight [qualities], if they are pure while the five turbidities are present, one merely takes the five as being distinct; it is not necessary for them to correspond exactly to the sequence.

If these are correlated with the five aggregates (*skandha*), the center corresponds to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); the east to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); the south to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); the west to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); and the north to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The examples follow their respective order because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the primary factor.

Nevertheless, all five Tathāgatas possess seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the specific contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) for each differ; only those who study the Secret Teaching (*guhyamantra*) understand their essential points. For now, I shall merely provide a brief attribution.
The Commentary states: "However, as for the phrase 'but simply says northeast' and below, this is the third section, which determines its location.
Since the Sūtra does not specify the name of the country but merely says 'northeast,' [the author] cites the Sūtra to determine the specific place."

If this sutra does not specify [the location], it is because, following the pattern of the eight directions, the remaining seven directions are likewise not specified, as the names of the countries appear later in the text.
Now, fearing that those of shallow understanding may be confused, I cite the sutra as proof.
This sutra is also titled the *Aṣṭākṣara-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, which extensively explains the virtues of Mañjuśrī.
The commentary’s citation was still brief; I shall now cite it further.
That is to say, in that sutra, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi asked the Tathāgata:
"In which direction does Mañjuśrī reside?
Furthermore, in which direction is he able to perform acts of benefit?"
The Tathāgata replied:
"After my parinirvāṇa," and so forth, as quoted in full in the commentary.

Below there is a verse which says: "The Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, not abandoning his vow of great compassion, manifests transformed bodies as youthful youths, sometimes wearing crowns and sometimes bare-bodied."
Sometimes they dwell among children, playing in towns and villages;
sometimes they appear as impoverished people, with haggard forms and the appearance of old age.

They also manifest the sufferings of hunger and cold, wandering through the streets and markets to beg for clothing, wealth, and treasures, causing people to give even a single gift, thereby fulfilling all their wishes and inspiring them to develop faith.
Once faith has been awakened, he expounds the Dharma of the Six Perfections.
Leading ten thousand bodhisattvas, he dwells upon Mount Wuding; emitting billions of rays of light, humans and devas all behold them, and their karmic defilements are entirely extinguished.

May they attain the dhāraṇīs of hearing and retaining, all secret and profound treasuries of the Dharma, the practice and realization of the true Dharma, and the vow for the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.
"Endowed with the gateway of the śūnyatā-samādhi, he practices the path to the exhaustion [of suffering] and nirvāṇa.
By the power of Mañjuśrī’s great vows, his realm is identical to that of the Buddha.
Below this, his virtues are praised at length; they cannot be recounted here in detail, so one should consult the sutra for them.
In the commentary, from "The numinous traces of that mountain" onwards, the fourth section reveals its sacred spirit.
This section has two parts:
first, a brief indication of various texts; second, a personal account of what was observed.
Regarding the preceding section, the original biography is very extensive; it is briefly organized into six gates: first, establishing the name and indicating the conversion;

second, the boundaries and number of *li*; third, the terraces, peaks, stupas, and temples; fourth, the various monasteries and halls; fifth, spiritual responses throughout antiquity and the present; sixth, the merit of hearing the name and paying homage. However, all of these have already been briefly covered within the current text.
The first two phrases here refer generally to all the various sections. The *Dili zhi* states:

"Its mountains rise in layered terraces and stand out in majestic beauty; its paths are winding and deep. These numinous peaks and divine streams are not dwellings for those of vulgar character, but are entirely the abodes of those who seek to settle their spirits in meditative stillness and those who search in darkness for the subtlest mysteries."
The Commentary states: "From 'I, in my youth, sought... onwards, there are two parts: first, a personal account of what was seen and heard;
within this, there are further two sections, the first of which narrates the circumstances of arriving at the mountain.

Based on the passage concerning the Bodhisattva’s dwelling at Mount Qingliang, at that time rebellious insurgents were overturning the normal order and weapons rose up like swarms of bees; with jackals and wolves filling the roads and mountains and rivers cut off, he traveled without hesitation, thus it is said, 'entrusting his life to take refuge there.'"
Although the journey was five thousand *li*, it extended back and forth over ten thousand *li*.
Having originally set out for a brief excursion, day after day I have hastened toward the sacred realm.
Fifteen years have passed since I began composing this commentary; at this point, exactly ten years have elapsed.
The commentary states: "Regarding 'its resonance and response' and below, this is the formal narration of what was seen and heard.
From 'the mountain's terrain and the temple buildings' and below, it briefly points to the excellent scenery.

This mountain lies one thousand six hundred li northeast of Chang’an, over one hundred li southeast of Dai Prefecture, and stretches majestically across several prefectures for more than seven hundred li.
To its left it borders Mount Heng, where a thousand peaks rise in majestic prominence;
to its right it adjoins the long-flowing current of Mengjin;
to the north it overlooks the remote frontier, holding back the smoke and dust of ten thousand li.
To the south it embraces Fenyang, serving as the "back of the mountain" (the eastern flank) for this great state.
It encircles and moors the sun and moon, and stores and releases clouds and dragons.
Although snow accumulates and remains frozen even in summer, there are ten thousand varieties of famous flowers;
The cold wind is fierce and biting, yet auspicious grasses flourish in a thousand varieties.
Vermilion cliffs open wide, and emerald screens rise in tiers.
Pushing through clouds and parting the mists, one occasionally encounters peaks that transcend the mundane world.
Climbing through creepers and treading upon peril, one reaches extraordinary realms at every turn.
Where white clouds gather and spread, they surpass the clarity of a ten-thousand-li river;
as the bright sun is about to rise, one beholds a great sea three fathoms deep.
Each of the five peaks is difficult to describe in full detail.

Regarding the "monastic buildings," during the Northern Qi dynasty, the Emperor held them in high esteem and established monasteries there; thus, there were over two hundred sites on the old grounds, though at that time, only eight monasteries remained as places of refuge.

Since the Zhenyuan era, several peaks have already exceeded ten in number; some emerge embraced by five ridges, some open between two ranges, some rise in tiers from within the crags, and some tower above the clouds—these cannot be described in full detail.
The Commentary states: "From 'Since the Great Master concealed his traces' onwards is the fifth section, which investigates the origins and simultaneously manifests the sacred traces.
First, it directly narrates the original source.
In the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, as the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Bodhisattvas with the task of wandering for alms throughout the trichiliocosm.

This land has many venomous dragons that cause harm, yet its people greatly cherish and delight in the Mahāyāna; therefore, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī dwells here to transform them through his practice, which is why it is said: "Mañjughoṣa spreads his radiance throughout the Eastern Realm."
The *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one merely hears the name, the transgressions of birth and death for twelve hundred million kalpas will be eliminated.
If one prostrates in worship, one shall be constantly born into the family of the Buddhas."
If one recites the name for one day or seven days, Mañjuśrī will surely descend.
If there are karmic obstructions from past lives, one shall see him in a dream.
Upon seeing his physical form, such a person will rank among the fruits of sainthood, and their transformative manifestations will be vast and great.
Therefore, it is called "Radiating Splendor" (*yānghuī*).
The following lines correspond to the two preceding phrases.
First, they establish that the Great Master [Vasubandhu] concealed his traces, while simultaneously addressing and resolving potential objections.
This refers to a question such as:
"If you have always resided on Vulture Peak Mountain and in other various dwellings, why do you say that you have concealed your traces?
Therefore, the answer is now given:
The essence of the two sages is fundamentally serene and still;
the traces of the two sages, however, have their periods of concealment and manifestation.
Today, Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is entirely obscured by overgrown brambles.
Mount Ji (Ji-shan) is precisely Mount Jizu (Ji-zu), which is also under the jurisdiction of Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa).
Regarding the phrase "manifesting [the response]," this establishes that [the Dharma] radiates its brilliance throughout the Eastern Lands (China).
Because the mountain resembles Vulture Peak, it is called "Vulture Ridge" (Jiu-ling).
The reason for this name will be explained below in the commentary.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that states, "Spiritual monks were manifested in sacred realms," the *Gantong zhuan* (Records of Spiritual Resonance) says: "During the Later Zhou period of the Yuwen dynasty, Mañjuśrī transformed himself into a foreign monk (*brahmacārin*) and came to travel in these lands, saying he wished to pay homage at the site where Kāśyapa Buddha preached the Dharma, and to go to the place where Mañjuśrī resides, known as Mount Qingliang."

During the early Tang dynasty, there was a monk from Siṃhala in Chang’an who had spent ninety-nine summer retreats and attained the third fruit of arhatship. Upon hearing of these sacred traces, he traveled here barefoot to pay homage at Mount Qingliang.
All of these were instances where divine monks manifested their spiritual power.

Regarding the statement that "Master Xuan received instructions from the various heavens," the *Nanshan Gantong Zhuan* (Biographies of Miraculous Responses from Mount Nanshan) states: "At that time, there was a celestial being named Lu Xuanchang who came to visit him and said:
'I was born in the heavens during the era of King Mu of Zhou.'"
I then asked: "Regarding a doubt within this world that has been transmitted from antiquity:
it is said that Mañjuśrī resides on Mount Qingliang, presiding over five hundred immortals as he preaches the Dharma."
"The sutras state that Mañjuśrī has long resided in the Sahā world.
Since 'Sahā' is the collective designation for a great trichiliocosm, why is he specifically located in this direction?
The deva replied:
“Mañjuśrī is the primordial teacher of all Buddhas; he appears for the benefit of beings according to conditions, manifesting different transformations as required.
The great deeds of this Great Being are beyond the realm of ordinary people, so there is no need to labor over critical evaluations.”
"It is simply known that he mostly dwells within Mount Qingliang (Wutai).
People frequently see him, so one cannot help but believe it.
Thus it is said that he receives his mandate from the various heavens above.

Furthermore, today there is Qingliang Prefecture and Wutai County to the south of the mountain, and Wutai Prefecture to the north of the mountain; these may serve as a mirror for ten thousand generations, and thus there is no cause for doubt.

The Commentary states: "Emperor Ming of Han first inaugurated the lofty foundation; the Wei Emperor [Wen] responded with sincere faith to the ultimate transformation. According to the *Gantong zhuan*, it says: "Now, thirty li southeast of Mount Wutai, there exists the Dafu Lingjiu Monastery, where the ruins of the two halls still remain."
To the south there is a flower garden, covering about two *qǐng*.
Its colors bloom throughout the four seasons, such that no one can fathom its secret. Some say:
This was established by Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty;
it is also said to have been composed by Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty.
As their accounts differ from one another,
how can this be? Tian replied,
"Both were created by the Two Emperors."
During the time of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty, the Buddha-dharma already existed; this mountain was numinous and extraordinary, being the dwelling place of Mañjuśrī.
King Mu of Zhou built a monastery there to make offerings, and King Aśoka likewise established a stūpa in accordance with that precedent.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, Kāśyapa Mātanga also perceived with his divine eye that there was a stūpa there; he requested the Emperor to establish a monastery.
Because the shape of the mountain resembled Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), it was named Dafu Lingjiu Monastery (Great Faith Vulture Peak Monastery).
"Daifu" (Great Faith) signifies vast confidence.
The Emperor, having faith in Buddhist principles, established this temple and exhorted others to do so.
The Flower Garden (Huayuan) is still located in front of the temple today; later kings may have changed its name to Dahuayuan Temple (Great Flower Garden Temple).
Upon his arrival, Empress Wutian Dasheng was translating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with the Tripiṭaka Master from Khotan.
Seeing that the Bodhisattva resided on Mount Qingliang, she consequently renamed it Dahuayan Monastery.
The five peaks encircle and embrace it, with the mountain-heart opening at its center; the trigrams Li, Kan, Qian, and Kun attain their central principle therein.
A thousand crags soar with elegance, ten thousand ravines lie in deep stillness; it extracts the immortal peaks of Vulture Peak to become a single leaf of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
"It may truly be called the central repository where all spirits soar and gather, and the profound capital where the worthy assemble and the sages are visited.
This is why the Vulture Peak mentioned previously derives its name from this land.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Several states of Northern Qi offered their stipends,” the *Biography* says: “Emperor Gao of Northern Qi deeply revered the Great Teaching; he established more than two hundred monasteries on this mountain and allotted the tax revenues of eight provinces to provide for the clothing and medicine of the mountain community.”
"Even to this day, there still remains the Five Sites of Practice (Wǔ Dàochǎng Zhuāng).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the returning radiance of the nine emperors of the Tang," from our Great Tang up to the present Sage [Emperor], nine successive reigns have passed, none of whom failed to reflect their light back upon the sacred mirror.

It is said that the present Sage is the Emperor who honors the Virtuous Ancestor; he gazes up with devotion toward Mount Ling, and his imperial edicts upon heavenly robes constantly illuminate the Five Peaks. He ensures that incense and medicinal herbs are supplied without interruption throughout the year, while the golden pavilion towers loftily amidst the clouds.

Still harboring doubts regarding the Sage’s transformation, they beheld the bamboo groves towering majestically by the cliffside, appearing as if descended from heaven; thus, the hundred officials returned in veneration and the nine provinces presented offerings.

Clouds and mists gather and merge, covering the earth and filling the mountains; this is none other than our Buddhas’ patriarchs, who accumulated myriad practices over kalpas of vast eons, such that clouds of compassion spread and universally cover all, while oceans of wisdom remain profound and serene, embracing all within them. They take the entire Dharma-realm as their domain and encompass all sentient beings as the gateway of their vows.
Who is able to respond to such inspiration?
How profound must one’s past roots of goodness be to encounter these sacred remains, such that their joyful emotion cannot cease and finds expression in verse.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Suḥrllekha Following the Sub-commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 76.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Subcommentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Seventy-Seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
In the commentary, following the passage "The people of the Five Indias risked their lives to hasten toward the wind," the sixth section exhorts beings to practice reverence.
The first two lines cite examples to encourage such practice.
As for the five countries of India (Pañcāla), it is roughly said to be two hundred thousand *li*; who knows its actual number?

If traveling by land, one must pass through several hundred kingdoms and traverse tens of thousands of layers of clouds and mountains; at times, one must climb by grasping at ropes suspended in the void, or ascend by means of flying ladders set across precipices; at times, one must travel amidst wind and snow or lie down in the snow; at times, one must subsist on wood or dwell among pine trees; and at times, one encounters swarms of ferocious beasts or a succession of bandits.

If one travels by water, there are surging billows with no shore and misty islands that swirl in concealment; spectral monsters stir the wind and leviathans drum the waves; the sun and moon rise and set from the depths of the waves, and souls drift like ghosts within dreams.
Even if the waves were stilled and the winds ceased, one would see only the waters merging with the horizon;
though the boat moves and the oars are raised, they still take the cessation of thought as their livelihood.

Despite such peril, eminent monks of the Tripitaka arrived one after another, all because the Great Sage entrusted his life to them so that they might sacrifice their own; thus it is said that those from the Five Indias rushed toward the wind at the cost of their lives.

Regarding the statement, "The eight directions vie to entrust their deluded bodies," whether from the east or west, the south or north—from the celestial extremities to the lunar caverns, and from the ocean tides to the rising sun—those with ears and eyes do not shrink from hardship, for they will surely reach even the most distant places.

The commentary states: "Those who dwell in Zhōushén" and below is the formal exhortation; it specifically cites the faults of those who do not go [to the land] in order to illuminate the merits of those who do.
This refers to the region east of the Pamir Mountains, spanning several thousand *li*, known as Chìxiàn (the Red County);
Zhōushén is none other than the Middle Kingdom of the Tang dynasty.

The journey to the realm of Qingliang is not far; the main thoroughfares are level and wide, with carriages and horses overflowing the roads. One may observe the transformations of the land in every direction without losing one’s daily routine.
Since a visit will surely evoke a spiritual response, why not go?
Thus we know that those who do not go [to the Buddha] are precisely the three hundred million followers.
Therefore, now that he wields the battle-axe and divides the fiefs, there is no one among the heavy responsibilities of regional governors who does not look up to him with reverence.
The various kings of the Western Regions regret being born in the Five Indias rather than in the Eastern Land; how could it be that they merely pay distant homage to the Great Sage?
I have often looked up to and admired this gentleman.
Thus, when anyone travels to the Western Heaven (India), they first ask whether he has ever dwelt on Mount Wutai;
if he has not, they cast him aside and pay him no heed.

The sentient beings of this land today have, through the causes of their past lives, been fortunate enough to be born in the Central Kingdom; yet they do not understand how to cultivate reverence toward the Buddhas and the Patriarchal Teachers. For this reason, I exhort them.

Regarding the "three hundred million followers," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states: "The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower, which appears only once in a long time."
Such sinful persons revolve through the three evil realms, or may exist among humans and devas; yet when a Buddha appears in the world, these devas and humans do not perceive him.

As it is said: in the city of Śrāvastī there were nine hundred million households; three hundred million households saw the Buddha with their own eyes, three hundred million households heard that a Buddha existed but did not see him with their eyes, and three hundred million households neither saw nor heard of him.
"The Buddha resided in Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, yet these sentient beings neither saw nor heard him, let alone those who were far away.
Therefore, there are people in China today who, having once gone to Mount Tai, both hear and see him."
There are those who hear of the Cool Mountain (Wu-t'ai) yet fail to reach it; they are the same as those who hear its name but do not see it.
Even those in close proximity to Mount Wu-t’ai have some who neither hear nor see it, let alone those who are far away.
Therefore, I exhort you to cultivate reverence.
If one beholds Mañjuśrī, the extent of the merit is as briefly described above; the full details are found in the sūtra text.

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "According to the *Record of the Western Regions*, fascicle seven," etc., it states: "The country of Vaiśālī is the same as Pi-ye-li (Vaiśālī); these are variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit term."
Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southeast from the City of Clouds, one arrives at a great *stūpa*, which is the site where seven hundred noble ones held a second council.

One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, there were certain *bhikṣus* in the city of Vaiśālī who had distanced themselves from the Buddha-dharma and practiced the precepts erroneously.

At that time, the Elder Yaśoda resided in the kingdom of Kośala; the Elder Subhūti resided in the kingdom of Mathurā; the Elder Revata resided in the kingdom of Karṇa; the Elder Śāradvata resided in the kingdom of Vaiśālī; and the Elder Puṣkarasārin resided in the kingdom of Sālā.

These great arhats had attained mastery over their minds; they upheld the Tripiṭaka and had acquired the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). Possessing great renown and being well-known to all, they were all disciples of the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, Yaśoda dispatched messengers to inform all the worthy sages and saints, who gathered at the city of Vaiśālī.

Yet there was still one person short of the full number of seven hundred. Then Puṣyamitra, using his divine eye, saw the great worthy sages assembled to deliberate on matters of the Dharma; exercising his supernormal powers, he arrived at the Dharma assembly. Thereupon, in the midst of the great multitude, Tripuṭa bared his right shoulder, knelt down, and proclaimed aloud:
"The assembly, do not be noisy! Be reverent! Be mindful!"
Long ago, when the Great Sage, the Dharma King, entered parinirvāṇa through his skillful means, although many years have passed, his words and teachings still remain.
In the city of Vaiśālī, indolent bhikṣus became errant regarding the precepts, and ten matters emerged that contravened the teachings of the One of Ten Powers.

"Now these worthy ones have deeply clarified the precepts on what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed; all are instructions from the Great Virtuous Ānanda. Bearing in mind our debt of gratitude to the Buddha’s kindness, we shall re-proclaim the holy intent.

At that time, the entire great assembly was moved with sorrowful emotion. They immediately convened the bhikṣus and, in accordance with the Vinaya, issued a formal censure and prohibition, expunging erroneous practices and proclaiming the clarity of the holy teachings.

Traveling eighty or ninety *li* southward from the place where the seven hundred noble ones held the council, one arrives at the Śvetapura Monastery. Its tiered terraces are brilliantly illuminated and its multi-storied pavilions soar like soaring pheasants; the monastic community is pure and disciplined, and all study the Mahāyāna.
Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites where they practiced walking meditation.
Adjacent to these is a stūpa built by King Aśoka.
"This is the site where the Tathāgata, in the past, while traveling south toward the kingdom of Magadha and looking back north toward the city of Vaiśālī, halted midway to rest.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Pāṭaliputra," the *Records of the Western Regions* (Xiyuji), fascicle 8, states: "To the south of the Gaṅgā River in the kingdom of Magadha, there is an ancient city, over seventy li in circuit. Although it has long been desolate and overgrown, its foundations still remain."

In the past, when the human lifespan was immeasurable years, there was a city called Kusumapura, which in the language of Tang means "Fragrant Flower Palace City"; it was so named because the royal palace abounded in flowers.
When the human lifespan reached several thousand years, it was renamed the City of Pāṭaliputra.
The former name, "Balianfu City," is a corruption.
Initially, there was a Brahmin of high talent and vast learning who had several thousand disciples following him to receive instruction; he would travel and tour together with his students.
There was a scholar who was pacing back and forth in dejection;
his companions said to him, "What is it that you worry about? He replied:
"In my prime, when my vigor was at its height, I wandered as a traveler, treading upon my own shadow.
The years have already accumulated, yet no achievement has been attained in my arts and studies.
Reflecting on this, my sorrowful heart grows ever more intense."
Thereupon, his disciples said to him in jest:
"We shall now seek a marriage for you with your sister-in-law.

They then arbitrarily designated two men as the parents of the groom and two women as the parents of the bride. They subsequently sat beneath a Pāṭalī tree—which is called the "son-in-law tree"—and remained there.
Gathering seasonal fruits and drawing from the clear stream, he recounted the history of their marriage and requested the date for their union.
Then, the girl’s father took a flowering branch and handed it to the young man, saying:
"This is a blessed match; I pray you do not decline."
The scholar’s heart was filled with joy and contentment.
At sunset, as he spoke of returning home, he paused out of lingering attachment.
His students said:
"I was merely joking earlier; it would be fortunate if we could return together.
I fear the fierce beasts in the forest might harm one another.

The scholar then remained there, coming and going by the side of the tree. After evening fell, a wondrous light illuminated the wilds, and elegant pipes and strings played as curtains and canopies were arranged.

Suddenly, an old man appeared, leaning on a staff, to offer his condolences. Shortly thereafter, a woman arrived leading a young girl, accompanied by a retinue filling the road, dressed in magnificent attire and playing music.
The old man pointed to the young girl and said, "This is your wife."
They sang and feasted merrily for seven days.
The disciples, suspecting that he had been harmed by a beast, went to search for him; they then saw him sitting alone beneath a shady tree as if conversing with a distinguished guest.
He informed his companions that he was returning with him, but they declined to follow his command.
Later, he entered the city on his own to pay visits to his relatives and acquaintances, recounting the beginning and end of these events.

Those who heard him were struck with amazement; together with several friends, they went to the grove and all saw that the flowering trees had become a great mansion, where servants and laborers were busily running back and forth.
The old man received them with composure; he laid out the food and provided music, and the rites between host and guest were fully observed.
The friends returned to the city and reported the matter to everyone near and far.
Ten years later, a son was born, and the man said to his wife:
"I now wish to return home.
Yet, unable to bear the separation and obstacles, I have momentarily remained here, dwelling in this transient and exposed state.
When his wife heard this, she reported it all to her father.
The old man said to the scholar, "In the life of a man, one seeks pleasure; why must it necessarily be in one's native land?
Now that I am about to build a house for you, you should have no other intention."
Thereupon, he commanded his divine attendants, and the work was completed in no time; with incense and flowers, the capital was moved from the old city to this town.
Because of that son, the deity built the city, and from that time forth it was named Pāṭaliputra (the City of the Son of the Pāṭala Tree).
The commentary states: "Mathurā" is also called Mathura; it is located within the region of Central India.
Regarding the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), Volume 4, that record names it the Kingdom of Śrāvastī, and it does not mention the account concerning the peacock.
Regarding the phrase "there are stupas containing relics and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the stupas of Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa.

Regarding the phrase "to the north of the monastery there is a cliff," the record states: "Traveling five or six *li* east of the city, one arrives at a mountain monastery. A rugged cliff serves as its chambers and a valley serves as its gate; it was established by the Venerable Upagupta (translated into Chinese as Jìn-hù)."
Within it is a stūpa containing the fingernails and toenails of the Tathāgata.
To the north of the monastery, among the cliffs, there is a stone chamber twenty-odd feet high and thirty-odd feet wide, its interior filled with fine tally-sticks four inches long.

Venerable Upagupta would place a tally-stick whenever a husband and wife both attained the fruit of Arhatship through his teaching and guidance; however, even if they attained it, he did not record it if they lived in separate rooms or belonged to different clans.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'Although placing the tally was a later matter,' etc., it is because one fears someone might raise the following objection:
'Since it was Kukkuta who constructed the cave, this must have been an event occurring during the hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.'"
Now, this is the initial establishment of the discourse on the sutra; what, then, is that cave?
Therefore, this explanation is provided.
Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "The city of Tri-kun-jina," it is largely the same as the explanation of the name Kātyāyana.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Mucilinda means ‘liberation’,” etc., the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), fascicle 8, states: “From the pool of the Naga King Cilindha, its water is clear and black, yet its flavor is sweet and delicious.”
On the western bank there is a small vihāra containing an image of the Buddha.

In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he sat here in meditative concentration for seven days. At that time, this nāga king guarded the Tathāgata by encircling the Buddha’s body with his own body seven times, manifesting many heads that formed a canopy as they hung down over him.
"Therefore, his dwelling was on the western bank of that pond.
Regarding the commentary's statement, "The location of the country of Mālavaṇḍa is not clearly known," if one further infers it according to its meaning, Mālavaṇḍa is simply Magadha.
It was established by the Dragon King Anāvaraṇa and is precisely the Hall of Universal Radiance; it is simply the place where the Dharma is being preached now.
Because it was not specifically pointed out as being here, its location is said to be unknown.

The Commentary states: "The *Mahāsannipāta* is merely named 'Cave of Compassion' (Maitrīkuṭa)" refers to the tenth section, the *Candragarbha-parivarta*, which likewise only lists the name without providing a specific location.
Below, I shall fully cite the text from the *Candragarbha-sūtra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This [term] is translated as ‘Much Contemplation’ (*bahucintā*),” the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states that *Bāshā* refers to Zhīnà, which here means Hán.
The *Xiyuji* states: "Dahan" is fully expressed as "Mahācīna.
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha says it refers to "clothing and goods.
The intended meaning is:
This is a land of people distinguished by their robes and caps;
all [the names] here are literal translations (*yi-fan*), while the *shu* (exegesis) provides the standard interpretation.

Regarding the *shu*’s statement, "It also belongs to the division of Qingzhou": when Yu divided the nine provinces, the east was Qingzhou; thus, as the world was partitioned, it fell within one of those nine divisions.

The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'now arriving at this mountain,' tradition holds that it was named because it was here that the construction of the Great Wall by the First Emperor of Qin reached its completion."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The eight [countries], such as Śule (Kashgar), are fully called Kharaśūtra,” the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), fascicle 12, states: “Leaving the Pamir Mountains for the country of Wushai, one travels more than two hundred li west of this city to a great mountain. From there, traveling north through mountainous deserts and vast wilderness for over five hundred li, one reaches the country of Kasha.”
The former designation "Shule" (Shuluo) refers to the name of its city;
in its correct pronunciation, it is fully rendered as Śrīkṣetra.
The term "Shule" is merely a corruption of that original sound.
The commentary states:
Following the ancient commentaries, Tripitaka Master Sengzhao’s explanation of the *Record of the Western Regions* says:

“The Kingdom of Khasha is over five thousand li in circuit; it consists mostly of sandy deserts with little arable soil, yet its cultivation of crops is abundant and its flowers and fruits are luxuriant.”

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, one crosses a river and traverses a desert to reach the kingdom of Jiegujia (which in the language of Tang is called Zujü), measuring over one thousand li in circuit.

On the southern border of the kingdom there is a great mountain, its cliffs and ridges towering and its peaks and crags overlapping; the vegetation withstands the cold, remaining the same in both spring and autumn. Its streams and ravines have deep gullies where flying waters cascade in four directions, and cliff-cells and stone chambers are spread out like chess pieces amidst solemn forests.
In India, those who have attained the fruits of the path frequently exercise supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), traveling light to distant places and taking up residence here.
As many Arhats have entered parinirvāṇa at this site, there are consequently numerous stūpas.

Even now, three arhats still reside within the mountain caves, having entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); their bodies appear as if those of emaciated men, and their beards and hair are always long, so that śramaṇas go there from time to time to shave them.

Within this country, the number of Mahāyāna sūtra sections is particularly numerous; among all places where the Buddha-dharma has reached, none is as flourishing as this one, with some ten collections consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas each.
From this point onward, its spread has indeed become vast. The commentary states:
According to this, scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka* were actually present in this country.

From here, traveling eastward across ridges and valleys for more than eight hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Gostana, which in the language of Tang means "Earth-Milk"; this is the refined local term for it.
In the vernacular it is called Han-na; the Xiongnu call it Yudu; the various Hu peoples call it Huodan; and in India it is called Qudan. The former name, "Yutian," is a corruption.

The kingdom of Gostana is over four thousand *li* in circuit; it is mostly sandy deserts and stony wasteland, with narrow passes. It is suitable for grain cultivation and abounds in various fruits. The people revere the Buddha-dharma; there are over one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks, most of whom study and practice the Mahāyāna teachings.
The king was exceptionally brave and martial, and he revered the Buddha-dharma; he claimed himself to be a descendant of the lineage of Vaiśravaṇa Deva.

Formerly, this country was desolate and uninhabited, serving as the dwelling place of Vaiśravaṇa Deva. The crown prince of King Aśoka, having been exiled by King Virūḍhaka for his anger, was sent away with his attendants due to the latter’s jealousy; they migrated north of the Snow Mountains and dwelt among the wild valleys.
The exiles, while herding their livestock, arrived at this western frontier; they selected the most honorable and capable among them to stand as their leader over this land.
Meanwhile, the Crown Prince from the eastern lands, having been banished and sent into exile, resided at this eastern frontier; encouraged by his subordinates, he likewise proclaimed himself king.

As the years had passed and the teachings of civilization were no longer communicated, they each happened upon one another while hunting in a desolate wilderness; when they further inquired about their lineages, they began to dispute over seniority, and as anger manifested in their words, they were on the verge of engaging in combat.
Someone offered this counsel:
"Why such haste now? You have engaged in battle through the hunt;
you have not yet exhausted the full force of your military prowess."
"It is appropriate to return to govern and train our troops, so that we may assemble again at the appointed time.
Thereupon, he turned his carriage back and returned to each of their respective kingdoms, where they inspected and practiced their warhorses and strictly exhorted their soldiers.

When the appointed day arrived, the armies assembled and their banners and drums faced one another. On the morning of the battle, the Western Lord was at a disadvantage; he was pursued by his enemies and his head was taken.

The Eastern King, seizing the advantage, pacified and gathered the remnants of the fallen state. He moved the capital to Zhongdi and began constructing city walls and moats. Fearing that there was insufficient land and that success would be difficult to achieve, he issued a proclamation far and wide, seeking anyone who understood geography.
At that time, there was an ash-smearing heretic who carried a large gourd filled with water and approached, saying,
"I know the geography of the land.
He then poured out the water in a winding stream, circling back upon itself.
Thereupon, he concealed his body and suddenly vanished from sight.
Relying on those water traces, he established the foundations for the walls; thus construction was commenced, and this became the capital of the kingdom—the city where the current king now resides.
The city was neither lofty nor formidable, making it difficult to attack or conquer; from ancient times until now, no one had ever been victorious there.

Its king, having established his capital, built his city, founded his state, and brought peace to the people, had completed these great works. Now that he was advanced in years and approaching old age, he feared his lineage would perish for lack of an heir. He therefore went to the abode of the deity Vaiśravaṇa to offer prayers and request a successor.
An infant emerged from the forehead of the divine image; he was taken up and the carriage turned back, and the people of the country celebrated with joy.
Fearing that the child would not live long because he did not drink milk, they soon went to the shrine to request that he be nurtured once more.

The ground before the shrine suddenly rose up in the shape of a breast; the divine child suckled from it and thus grew to maturity, his wisdom and valor becoming preeminent, while his influence and moral teachings spread far and wide.
Thereupon, he established a shrine for the spirit to honor his ancestors.
From that time until the present, successive generations have maintained this tradition; the transmission of the state and the succession of rulers have continued without interruption.
Consequently, the divine temple today abounds with various precious treasures, and the performance of prostrations, sacrifices, and offerings has never ceased throughout the ages.
The land was nourished by milk from the earth, and thus it became the name of the kingdom.

More than ten *li* south of the royal city is a monastery, which was built by a former king of this country for the Arhat Vairocana (translated into Chinese as "Pianzhao," meaning "Universal Illumination").

More than twenty li to the southwest of the royal city, one reaches Mount Gośṛṅga, which in the language of Tang means "Ox Horn. Two peaks rise up on either side, with precipitous cliffs and deep gorges on all four sides. Within these cliffs and valleys stands a monastery, wherein the Buddha image occasionally radiates a brilliant light.

In the past, the Tathāgata once came to this place and briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans. He prophesied that this land would establish a kingdom where the bequeathed teachings would be revered and the Mahāyāna would be practiced and studied.
This is precisely that very place.

On Ox-Horn Cliff there is a great stone chamber where an Arhat entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) to await the advent of Maitreya Buddha; for several hundred years, offerings have been made there without interruption.

Recently, a cliff collapsed, blocking the entrance and the path. The king raised an army intending to clear away the fallen rocks, but immediately swarms of black bees flew out and stung the multitude with their venom; for this reason, the stone gate remains unclosed to this day.
The commentary states:
Based on this, it is also considered a sacred dwelling (*āryāvāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "or pointing to Niu-tou on the other side of the Yangtze," there is a mountain named Niu-tou forty li south of Jinling. Because this mountain has two peaks, it is variously called Shuangque (Twin Towers), Tianque (Celestial Towers), Nanjiao (Southern Suburb), or Xianku (Immortal Grotto); these names were all changed by successive dynasties without fixed consistency.
According to the *Yudi zhi* (Records of the Geography of the Realm), it states: "This mountain is one thousand four hundred feet high and forty-seven *li* in circumference.

In accordance with the *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions) and the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas" in the old version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Cittarāja addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"In the northeastern frontier region, there is a land called Ox-Head (*Gośīrṣa*)."
According to the new sutra, it says: "In the kingdom of Śuleśa, there is a dwelling place named Ox-Head Mountain (Gokurṣa).
As cited previously from the *Record of the Western Regions*, this location differs from that in China; this passage is found in the *Record of Stupas and Temples of Jinling*.
Ancient tradition states that this is the place where a Pratyekabuddha manifested his form.
While various preceding and succeeding texts frequently state that "the Bodhisattva dwells therein," its spiritual responses have often been witnessed.
The Commentary states: "Kaśmīra" refers to the region of Northern India, as stated in the *Jì* (Record).
"Madhyāntika" is the name of an Arhat.
Formerly called Mātṛkī, it is now called Mātṛceṭa; the country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.

Its four borders are backed by mountains that are extremely precipitous; although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, such that from ancient times no neighboring enemy has been able to launch an attack, and so forth.
In ancient times, this country was originally a dragon pond.

After the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued the malevolent spirits in the kingdom of Udyāna and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he traveled through the air above this land and said to Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an Arhat named Madhyāntika who shall establish a kingdom in this place, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma."

"Fifty years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda’s disciple, the Arhat Madhyantika—who had attained the six supernormal powers and was endowed with the eight liberations—heard the Buddha’s prophetic prediction and rejoiced in his heart; he has therefore come here."
While sitting in meditative seclusion within a forest on a great mountain crag, he manifested great supernormal powers.
