Upon seeing this, the dragon developed deep faith and invited him to ask for whatever he desired.
The Arhat said:
"I pray that you will graciously allow me space within this pond for my knees.
Thereupon, the Dragon King withdrew the water and offered it to the Arhat.
The Arhat expanded his body through supernatural power; though the Dragon King exerted all his strength to withdraw the water, the pond became empty and the water was exhausted.

The dragon requested that a pond be excavated; the Arhat, to the northwest of this place, left behind a single pond measuring over one hundred li in circumference, while his other followers each resided in separate smaller ponds.
The Dragon King said, "I offer the entire site of the pond; may you accept my constant offerings.
Madhyāntika replied:
"I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Although I wish to accept your invitation, how could that be possible?
The Dragon King entreated him again:
"Five hundred arhats shall constantly receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end.
After the Dharma has ended, they shall return to take this country as their dwelling place.
Madhyāntika accepted his request.

At that time, once the arhats had obtained the land, they exercised their great supernatural powers to establish five hundred monasteries; they purchased low-born people from various foreign countries to serve as laborers to provide for the monastic community.

After Madhyāntika had entered parinirvāṇa, those low-caste people established their own chieftain; the neighboring kingdoms despised them for their low birth and would not form alliances with them, calling them Kṛttivāsas (translated into Chinese as "Bought").
Now the spring waters have already overflowed in abundance.

Regarding the "Kingdom of Gandhāra," the third fascicle of the *Xiyuji* states: "In the Kingdom of Gandhāra was King Kaniṣka; four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he assumed the mandate in accordance with the timing. His royal influence spread far, and those of different customs submitted to his rule."

In his leisure time from state affairs, he regularly studied Buddhist scriptures and invited a monk into the palace daily to preach the Dharma; however, as the doctrines differed and the ritual protocols were inconsistent, the King harbored deep doubts and found no way to dispel his confusion.
At that time, the Venerable Pārśva said:

"Since the Tathāgata passed into parinirvāṇa, the years and months have grown ever more distant; the disciples have formed various schools and adhered to their own tenets, while teachers and students hold differing views, each relying on their own hearsay and observations, resulting in mutual contradictions."
When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after lamenting for a long time, he said to the Venerable One:
"By the grace of some remaining merit, I have fortunately been able to follow in the footsteps of my predecessors; though we are far removed from the Sage, we still possess great fortune."

"Venturing to cast aside my mediocrity and obscurity, I shall inherit and propagate the Dharma teachings; I will provide a detailed commentary on the Tripiṭaka according to the various sectarian tenets.
Having spoken thus, he invited the assembly of monks for a seven-day offering, intending to deliberate upon matters of the Dharma.
He proclaimed his previous command to eliminate the ordinary and retain the holy.
Although the holy assembly was still numerous, he further eliminated those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Although those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) were still numerous, he next retained only those who possessed the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

There were still many remaining; next, those who were proficient in the Tripiṭaka internally and accomplished in the five sciences externally were selected, until four hundred and ninety-nine men had been chosen.

Later, his contemporary Upagupta, though not yet an Arhat, extensively compiled the Tripiṭaka, totaling three hundred thousand verses. The King engraved them on copper plates and sealed them within stone caskets, then relinquished this entire kingdom to the Saṃgha; for this reason, it is inhabited by many noble ones.
The commentary states: "Śambara" is translated here as "yellow variegated color.

In the first chapter of the sutra, the Asura Kings Māyāśūra and Śambara appear; there, the verses and the prose are presented alternately in both Chinese and Sanskrit, and they differ from this current explanation, as the verse refers to the deity Red Light (Raktaprabha).
Furthermore, more than ten *li* to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa containing a Buddha’s tooth approximately one and a half inches long, which is yellowish-white in color.
Because it contains many sacred sites, it is an abode of the holy ones.

The Commentary states: "Tradition says this is the place where the Buddha left his shadow" refers to what is said in the second fascicle of the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions): "Twenty-odd li southwest of the city of the kingdom of Nāgara is a monastery. To the southwest of the monastery is a deep ravine with precipitous cliffs, where waterfalls cascade and sheer walls rise up. On the eastern bank of the cliff is a large cave, which is the dwelling place of the Naga Kūvara."
The entrance is narrow and the cavern is dark; there are cliff rocks, damp walls, mountain streams, and lingering rivulets.
In ancient times, there was a Buddha-image, radiant as a true likeness, complete with all the marks and signs of perfection, solemn and as if truly present.
Since recent times, people have not seen it universally; even when they do see it, it is but a mere semblance.
When those who pray with utmost sincerity experience a response from the unseen, it is revealed briefly, yet cannot remain for long.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was still in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who, while offering curds and milk to the king, failed in his ritual decorum. Having incurred the king’s censure, he harbored resentment and anger; he then used gold coins to purchase flowers and made an offering at the stūpa where [the Buddha] had received the prediction of enlightenment, vowing to become an evil dragon to destroy the kingdom and harm the king.
He immediately rushed toward a stone cliff, threw himself down, and died.
He subsequently dwelt in this cave as a great nāga king and intended to emerge from his lair to fulfill his former evil vow.

As soon as he gave rise to this thought, the Tathāgata perceived it; out of compassion for the people of this land who were to be harmed by the nāga, he exercised his supernormal powers and traveled from Central India to the nāga’s abode.
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, the dragon’s poisonous intent ceased; he received the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma.
He then requested that the Tathāgata dwell permanently in this cave, and that the noble disciples always accept his offerings.
The Tathāgata said:
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa, and for your sake I leave behind my shadow.
I dispatch five arhats to constantly receive your offerings; even when the True Dharma disappears, this matter shall not cease."
If you should give rise to a poisonous mind or anger, you should contemplate my reflection; through the power of loving-kindness and compassion, your poisonous mind shall cease.
Furthermore, the World-Honored Ones who will appear in the future within this Bhadrakalpa have likewise out of pity for you all left behind their images.
The commentary states:
This is largely identical to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, as already cited in the first fascicle of the *Yao* (Excerpts).

However, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) says: "This country has no separate sovereign; it belongs to the kingdom of Kāpiśī and is not far from the kingdom of Gandhāra, having perhaps once been subject to it."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is fully as found in the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) and the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, Candragarbha-parivarta,” this refers collectively to all the preceding locations cited; the reference to the *Xiyuji* is not restricted to a single fascicle.
The *Candragarbha-parivarta* refers to the tenth [division].
However, the *Candragarbha-parivarta* should actually be the twelfth, consisting of ten fascicles.
Within the tenth fascicle is the nineteenth chapter, titled "Establishing Stūpas and Monasteries" (*Stūpavihāra-pratiṣṭhāna-parivarta*).

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, Śakra-devendra, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, and their retinues rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, paid homage with single-minded reverence, and spoke these words:

“The Buddha has declared that within these four continents, all the great stūpas established and maintained by the Tathāgatas of the past Buddhas—the places where the Muni Buddhas have dwelt—shall remain perpetually unfailing throughout the present and future worlds.”
The Buddha, together with the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others, sent down a great rain of Dharma that completely filled [all beings].

The first was named "Arisen by the Multitude of Sages," the second was named "Accumulation of Virtue," the third was named "Vajra Flame," the fourth was named "Fragrant Chamber," the fifth was named "Śāmbhalī," the sixth was named "City of the Worthy," and the seventh was named "Sukṣmatara."
Next is named Water Light; next is named Fragrant Incense; next is named Well-Established;
next is named Cāpala; next is named Golden Lamp; next is named Joyful Abode; next is named Mucilinda;
next is named Vajra Ground; next is named Cave of Compassion; next is named Nārāyaṇa Cave; next is named...
The Kūrmāsāra incense, next named Prajñāśekhara, next named Mahāguṇaguhya, next named Susambhava, next named Nīlavarṇa,
next named Gaganaputra, next named Gośīrṣacandanagṛha, and next named Durjayā;
these are the great stūpas established and maintained by the Buddhas of the past.
They are constantly protected by bodhisattvas and others; for this reason, we always make offerings to them.
World-Honored One, regarding all the stūpas, temples, and dwellings of your śrāvaka disciples in the present and future worlds, please grant that we may protect, maintain, and nurture them.
Now, the initial enumeration of these points is identical to that in this sutra and can be understood through reflection; therefore, it is not cited in full.
Below, I shall cite them by way of summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his face issued various rays of light.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dwelling places of Buddhas appeared throughout the four continents: eighty thousand Buddhas appeared in the eastern continent, one hundred thousand in the northern, five hundred in the western, and two hundred and fifty thousand in the southern. It is explained at length that Buddhas appeared in each of these lands, and subsequently, the various devas, nāgas, and others made vows to protect and uphold them.
33. Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha. Regarding the "Initial Intent" (of this chapter), the text is divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of objections.
Regarding the first point:
"The ancient masters held that there are only three categories" is because the latter two categories are treated separately as the equality of cause and effect.
Although their application differs in breadth and narrowness, they are equivalent in their response regarding the meaning of the fruit.
The commentary states: "Regarding the passage 'If one answers the previous question' and below, there are two explanations that resolve the objection.
First, the question is raised because the first six assemblies all answered the previous question without requesting it again; therefore, the question is asked: why is this chapter requested again?
From the phrase "the separation of cause and effect" onwards, the ancient masters provide the answer.
This contains two points:
first, the separation of cause and effect.
Because the preceding assemblies shared the same causes, they were not questioned separately;
what follows here concerns the fruit, and since the fruit is separated from its cause, it is questioned again.
Furthermore, one reflects upon the rarity of the Dharma and the inconceivability of the fruit, and thus requests [instruction] once more through reflection.
From "Due to its virtues" (*guṇa-hetu*) onwards, the signs of the marvelous nature of mindfulness of the Dharma are presented.
The preceding section provides a general overview;
from the second section, "Specific Explanation," onwards, only this particular chapter is elucidated.

The Commentary states: "There is a separate analysis in three sections within the main body of the treatise": first, a general exposition of the Buddha’s virtues; second, a specific revelation of the characteristics of the meaning; and third, the revelation of the inconceivable.
Now, regarding the initial general exposition, the phrase "one hundred and forty uncommon [qualities]" has already been seen in the "Chapter on the Light of Enlightenment.

Here, the total number is restated: namely, the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor marks, the four kinds of universal purity, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three ways in which there is nothing to guard, great compassion, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies, and the sublime wisdom of all modes—these constitute the one hundred and forty.
As for the statement "the provisional [teachings] of the Small [Vehicle]," the Small Vehicle also speaks of them, though their characteristics are inferior;
those that speak of the provisional [teachings] of the Great [Vehicle] are all entirely transcendent and superior.
This already comprises two of the five teachings.

The passage beginning with "If there are five dharmas" correctly elucidates the teaching of ultimate reality (shijiao); therefore, it is said that this [teaching] also encompasses the provisional (tongquan).

Both the provisional and the ultimate are present, yet within the teaching of ultimate reality, they are all brought back to the dharma-nature (dharmatā) without destroying their phenomenal characteristics.
"Regarding 'If one says it is of a single flavor' and below, this is second, the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).
Regarding 'If one says it possesses the inexhaustible' and below, this is third, the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).
From 'Therefore, in the subsequent text' and below, fourth, the merits of the present sutra as the Perfect Teaching are distinguished."
In the commentary, from the section "Second, specifically revealing the characteristics of the meaning" onwards, there are three parts:
first, the direct revelation of the two virtues; second, the integration through the four propositions; and third, the distinction between the provisional and the real.

Now, regarding the initial mention of "faith and so forth": this refers to the stage of universal practice (*sādhāraṇa-mārga*). Since faith is the foremost of the ten thousand practices, it encompasses the stages of diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and so on.
Furthermore, faith is taken as the beginning because every practice and virtue within all fifty-two stages possesses these two [aspects].
In the commentary, the section beginning with "These two are unimpeded" constitutes the second part, the mutual integration, which may be understood accordingly.
In the section beginning with "If [it is] as explained in the provisional teachings," the third part distinguishes the provisional from the real.
First, the provisional teaching is clarified.
Regarding the term "unmixed," as with the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are two aspects: first, that which is acquired through birth, namely the four wisdoms;
second, that which is revealed through manifestation, namely nirvāṇa.

Nirvana is inherently existent (*prakṛti-stha*), while the four wisdoms are produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-ja*). Since that which is produced through cultivation is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and that which is revealed through cultivation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the two are not intermingled.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The fourfold [classification] of Dharma and Reward bodies also has distinctions," this serves to refute a potential objection.
Fearing that an external opponent might object, saying:
"Your school also has four propositions; how does this differ from the previous integration? [The author] replies:
"The first is 'only dharmas,' which refers to the Dharmakāya while still enmeshed in afflictions."
The second is exclusively *vipāka* (maturation), namely the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*);
the third is both *dharma* (nature) and *vipāka*, referring to suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from its envelopment and possessing all merits;
the fourth is neither *dharma* nor *vipāka*, namely the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body).
The statement that there are also differences now is precisely intended to distinguish the provisional from the real.
Although there are four phrases, defilement and purity occur at different times; thus, the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are not one and the same.
Reflect upon this.
Below the section "Based on the tenet of this sūtra," the reality is revealed.

Furthermore, while the *dharmakāya* is without marks (*animitta*), here the first two [of the ten] belong to the three bodies and the last one belongs to the ten bodies. Since the ten bodies necessarily integrate the three bodies, the latter possesses the former two.
