The preceding section fully cites the scriptural text; here, the text is condensed and expanded according to my own interpretation.

That is to say, the good friend is likened to a skilled physician, the afflictions (*kleśa*) to the skin, and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) to a precious jewel. Not knowing it is to have lost it; only when delusions are exhausted does one attain clear realization and knowledge, just as that strong man saw his precious jewel in a bright mirror.
The *Jianfu* commentary explains:
"The 'poor woman with a golden store' is a metaphor for ordinary beings who do not know their Buddha-nature.
This metaphor refers to the beginning of the bodhisattvas' and the two vehicles' contemplation of the mind, wherein they conceal their Buddha-nature."
Having already resolved upon the minds of the three vehicles, they are called members of the royal family.
Because they have not yet entered the Buddha-family, they possess the power of contemplation and are thus called "powerful men.
The pearl of the Middle Way Buddha-nature resides within their hearts; as they contend with the power of inversion while contemplating mundane realms, this is called "contending."
Observing the mind to grasp objects is called "the head striking against [an obstacle].
Grasping at appearances while obscuring the principle is called "seeking [the object] which has sunk beneath the skin.
Seeking the principle through appearances and being unable to perceive it is called "not knowing its location."
To perceive emptiness through the grasping of signs is called a wound.
Seeking a friend is seeking a physician;
the Buddha is the skilled physician.
To know the jewel of the Buddha-nature by grasping its characteristic of emptiness is called "knowing this is the cause of the wound as the jewel enters the body.
The nature that definitely attains it resides within the upper characteristic; this is called "the jewel having entered the skin and immediately coming to rest."
At that time, the skilled physician descended and inquired as to where the nature resided; for the true nature had been concealed by appearances.
The strong man did not know its location, yet because he had previously resolved his mind [upon it], he thought, "Could this not be a false statement? Could this not be an illusion?"
Fearing that there would be no transmigrating nature, it was called "sorrowful weeping.

Next, the Buddha consoled him, saying, "The nature is not lost; your deluded contention has merely caused the nature to be hidden within the non-self," which is likened to a pearl entering the body and remaining inside the skin.
Because there is an underlying principle and the characteristic of that rational nature, it is called a reflection appearing externally.

When you contemplate emptiness and so forth, your mind becomes so intense that it is like a surge of fierce anger; because you fall into this state due to such intensity, you do not realize it yourself.
The fact that this "existence" (dhātu) is not seen above [the stage of the two vehicles] serves as a metaphor for their lack of faith in the teaching.
At this point, the metaphor of the strong man pushing downward represents the refusal to accept the teaching.

As for the phrase "pus and blood within the skin," it refers to being amidst the characteristics of suffering and so forth in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); while the nature is pure and ought to emerge from these impure outflows (*āsrava*), for what reason is it not seen?
If it were like sinews and so forth, and if it were the ultimate truth (*tattva*), then since the ultimate truth is without marks (*animitta*), it should not be visible.
Your statement "How is it now that... and following correctly clarifies the lack of faith in the sūtra.
At that time, the skilled physician descends and, following the instructions, provides the analogy for seeing one's nature.

As for the pearl appearing clearly and distinctly within the mirror, the nature that is certain to be attained can only be revealed by the principle and teaching of the Great Nirvana, just as a mirror reflects a face with perfect clarity.
"Those who see it after [the wrestler] has seen it" refers to sentient beings who hear and see it, while those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) see it with their own eyes.
The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "As when a poor man obtains a jewel, it was not bestowed upon him at that moment," this refers to the fourth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples. Therein, the parable of the tied jewel is taught, explaining how [the disciples] attained understanding and received their prophecies.
The Sūtra says: "Suppose, for example, there is a person who goes to the house of a close friend and lies down after becoming intoxicated with wine.
At that time, the friend has business to attend to at the official court; he ties a priceless jewel into the lining of the man's garment, gives it to him, and departs."
That person, lying drunk, was entirely unaware; having risen, he wandered away to another land, where for the sake of food and clothing he sought with diligent effort, undergoing great hardship.
If one has attained only a little and considers that sufficient,
later a friend may encounter him and say: "Alas, O man!..."
"Why do you concern yourself with clothing and food to such an extent?

In the past, wishing to enable you to obtain peace and happiness and to enjoy the five desires at will, I tied a priceless jewel into the lining of your garment on a certain day of a certain month; it remains there even now."
Yet you do not know this, and you labor with toil and distress to seek your livelihood; how utterly foolish you are!
You may now trade this treasure for whatever you require, and you shall always have as you wish, lacking nothing at all.
The inconsistency [of this] can be understood.
However, there are two ways of "tying":
first, regarding the formation of karmic conditions, the perfect understanding serves as the bead, while the preaching serves as the string for tying them together.
Intoxicated by the afflictions (*kleśa*), one possesses but a slight degree of understanding; hence it is called "the tied pearl.
Seeking pleasure within the five realms of existence involves diligent effort and hardship.
To realize a minor nirvana while not seeking the great fruit is called "being satisfied with what is little."
Later, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one meets with old friends;
they reveal their knowledge and vision to one, like finding a jewel in one's garment, whereby by means of the cause one attains the fruit, and there is no bliss that cannot be obtained.
It was already bound in the past; therefore, it is said that it is not being bestowed now.
Second, this refers to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
However, even that past binding was not newly bestowed; since it was unknown and is now made known, it is merely called "binding."
Thus, it would not constitute a complete similar example (*sapakṣa*).
Now, the commentary takes the "bead tied to the neck" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to establish that [the nature] is inherently present; hence it says, "it is not something bestowed now.
The passage in the commentary beginning with "Therefore, fearing one will not practice the *Nirvāṇa*" concludes the preceding meaning by means of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
If the fault of attachment were slight, one might tentatively say it exists; however, since the fault of false speech is grave, one cannot say it does not exist.
Moreover, since he knows without attachment, it must certainly exist.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Dafangguang Fo Huayan Jing Suoshu Yanyi Chao), Fascicle 79.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Sub-commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra (The Great Vaipulya Buddha-Avataṃsaka Sūtra),
Fascicle Eighty.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The beginning and the fundamental are non-dual, transcending the two obstacles,” there are two meanings:
first, sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-wisdom; thus, fundamental awakening does not obstruct initial awakening, and realizing it in this manner is called unobstructed wisdom.
Second, through the severing of hindrances and the manifestation of clarity, one is free from the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the known (*jñeya*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The combined production of the sūtra benefits sentient beings,” etc., the commentary consists of two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the text;

second, the citation of examples for explanation, beginning with “However, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, etc. As for the “nine similes,” the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* contains nine similes, whereas one or two differ from other sūtras, or there may be one, two, three, or four, with the number being indefinite; hence the use of the word “etc. (等).

Regarding what is called the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, it was preached by the Tathāgata at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha ten years after his attainment of Buddhahood, in the presence of one hundred thousand great bhikṣus and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty Ganges Rivers, and so forth.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upright in samādhi within the Sandalwood Multi-storied Pavilion and manifested supernatural transformations. There appeared thousand-petaled lotuses, as large as chariot wheels, in infinite numbers, perfect in color and fragrance yet not yet blossomed; within every flower was a transformation Buddha, ascending into the void and covering the world like a jeweled canopy.
Each individual lotus emitted immeasurable light, and by the spiritual power of the Buddha, all the lotuses simultaneously blossomed in splendor.
In an instant, they all withered and changed; within each of those flowers, all the transformation Buddhas sat cross-legged, each emitting hundreds of thousands of countless rays of light.
At that time, this world-system was magnificently adorned, and the entire great assembly rejoiced and leaped for joy, and so forth.
The Bodhisattva Vajramati asked a question, and the Buddha answered as follows:

"With my Buddha-eye, I behold within the afflictions of all sentient beings—greed, hatred, and delusion—the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the eye of the Tathāgata, and the body of the Tathāgata, sitting cross-legged, majestic and unmoving."
"Good son!

Although all sentient beings dwell within the various realms of existence, the Tathāgatagarbha exists within their bodies of affliction; it is eternally undefiled and fully endowed with virtuous marks, no different from my own."
Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a person with the divine eye who observes an unopened flower; seeing within all those flowers the body of a Tathāgata sitting cross-legged, he removes the withered petals and it becomes manifest.
In this way, son of good family!

Having perceived the *tathāgatagarbha* within sentient beings, the Buddha desires to cause it to blossom; for this purpose, he preaches the Dharma to eliminate afflictions and manifest the Buddha-nature.
"Good son!
It is the natural law of all Buddhas that whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the Tathāgatagarbha of all sentient beings remains eternally present and unchanging."

"However, because those sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions, the Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the Dharma for them, eliminating their defilements and bringing about all-encompassing wisdom," and so forth.
After each such parable, there is a verse.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like pure honey within a tree on a cliff, surrounded and guarded by countless swarms of bees.

At that time, there is a person of skillful wisdom and expedient means who first removes those bees and then takes the honey to eat and drink as he pleases, extending the benefit to both the near and the far."
The following summarizes the essential points:

"Honey" is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*; "bees" are a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*); "the person" is a metaphor for the *Tathāgata*; and "removing the bees" is a metaphor for teaching the Dharma to eliminate the afflictions.
"Furthermore, good son! It is like non-glutinous grain that has not yet been separated from its husks and chaff;
the poor and ignorant despise it, deeming it fit only for discard. Once the impurities have been removed and it is refined, it shall serve as food for the sovereign."

He replied: "The husk is a metaphor for afflictions; the rice grain is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, his preaching of the Dharma, and his removal of afflictions. This is the pure omniscience that, among all worlds, constitutes the most perfect enlightenment."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like pure gold that has fallen into an impure place, where it is hidden and does not appear.
Although many years and ages pass by, the pure gold does not decay, yet no one is able to recognize it."
One who possesses the divine eye says to the multitude:
"Within this impurity there is pure gold treasure; you may extract it and enjoy it as you please.
The application of this principle should be understood accordingly.
5. "Furthermore, good son!
It is like a poor man who has a treasury of precious jewels within his house, yet the treasury cannot say, 'I am here.
Since he does not know it himself and there is no one to tell him, he is unable to open this treasury of precious jewels."

All sentient beings are likewise thus: within their bodies lies the great treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, powers, and fearlessness; yet, failing to hear of it or understand it, they become mired in delusion regarding the five desires, wandering through birth and death and undergoing immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, the Buddhas appear in the world to open the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata within one's own body; with unimpeded eloquence, they act as great donors.
6. “Furthermore, good son!
For example, just as the inner kernel of an *āmra* fruit remains unspoiled and, when planted in the earth, grows into a great king of trees, so it is, son of good family:
with my Buddha-eye I behold all sentient beings; the Tathāgata-treasure lies within the shell of ignorance, just as a seed lies within its husk.
"Good son!
That Tathāgatagarbha is infinitely pure, a mass of great wisdom, and wondrously tranquil nirvāṇa; it is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a person who takes an image of pure gold and travels to another country; fearing he might be robbed while traveling through dangerous paths, he wraps it in tattered rags so that no one will recognize it."
This person suddenly passed away on the road, whereupon the golden image was abandoned in the wilderness; travelers following in his footsteps all deemed it impure.
One who possessed the divine eye saw that within this tattered object lay a true golden image, so he immediately extracted it, and everyone paid it homage and respect.
"Indeed, there is the Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous treasure-store.

8. Furthermore, good son, it is like a woman who is poor, lowly, and ugly, despised by all people, yet she carries a noble child who is destined to become a holy king and rule over the four quarters of the world."
This person, unaware of it, passes through the succession of time, constantly conceiving the thought that he is a lowly being born into a base family.
Yet, he possesses the Tathāgata-treasure within.
9. "Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a goldsmith casting an image of pure gold; once it has been cast, he turns it over and places it on the ground. Although the exterior appears scorched and black, the inner image remains unchanged. When the mold is opened and the image is revealed, its golden color shines with brilliant radiance.
The text states: "There is the body of the Tathāgata, complete with all its marks.
Below this, the merit of upholding this sutra is compared:

"If one were to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the past and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, by constructing seven-jeweled towers ten *yojanas* high—doing so every day for as long as it takes to offer fifty times as many such seven-jeweled towers to as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in the Ganges—it would not equal the merit of someone who, delighting in Bodhi, upholds this sutra; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy."

Regarding the nine preceding metaphors, the first—the metaphor of the Buddha within a lotus—is largely identical to, yet slightly different from, the metaphor of the blue lotus in the mud; likewise, the metaphor of the gold falling into an impure place is largely identical to the metaphor of the mani-jewel falling into a deep latrine.
In that [text], these are omitted—like gold existing within ore or honey within the mountains; otherwise, most [points] are largely the same.
As for the lack of sequential order, this is intended to capture the comprehensive meaning, and thus only ten items have been briefly cited.
The honey within the mountain differs slightly from the Buddha-nature within the dust, and therefore it is omitted here.

Furthermore, this citation is introduced to accord with the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*); since it encompasses all meanings from the ordinary person to the sage, it is cited in a seemingly disordered manner.

If one relies on the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* for a complete explanation of the nine similes, although it does not cite the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the sequence of its similes is entirely identical to that of this sūtra; each possesses its own specific significance, as detailed in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, which has already been cited in the separate commentary (*biechao*).
Regarding the statement, "In other sūtras, there may be one, two, or three," etc., this is taught in sūtras such as the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Śrīmālādevī*; I cannot cite them all in full.
Regarding the analogy of gold ore, the tenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, good son!
It is like gold ore which, after being washed and refined to remove impurities, is then smelted into pure gold; its value thereafter becomes immeasurable."
Good son! Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise; they all achieve the same buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because they eliminate afflictions, they are like gold ore from which all dross and impurities have been removed.
For this reason, all sentient beings possess the same Buddha-nature without distinction.
Because he had previously heard of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, he naturally came to know it upon attaining Buddhahood later.
It is like that elder who knew the single characteristic of milk. Why is this?
"Because they have severed immeasurable afflictions.
The commentary states:
This is because the analogy of the householder who milks many cows into a single color is further employed here to clarify the point.
In the fifth sutra, there is the analogy of the sweet medicine of the Snowy Mountains, which is identical in its entirety to the analogy of the pure honey within the crag.
There are many other analogies, which cannot be cited in full.
As for "the precious mani jewel wrapped in a soiled garment," this corresponds to the second chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which in the commentary corresponds to the fifth.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
In the Sūtras, the World-Honored One has said:'"
The Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature; it manifests the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a precious gem of great value wrapped in soiled clothing.

The Tathāgatagarbha is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging; yet it is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and defiled by the dust of afflictions—the unreal conceptualizations of greed, hatred, and delusion—as proclaimed by all Buddhas.
The commentary states: Herein,
Mahāmati cites a former teaching and raises an objection below,
[arguing] that it is identical to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of a self (*ātman*).
The Buddha replied below:
"Because it is not the same as the paths of the non-Buddhists, these are merely false and lack any reality.

When the Tathāgata speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha, he sometimes speaks of it as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, suchness, the limit of reality, the dharma-nature, the dharma-body, nirvāṇa, the self-nature that is neither born nor extinguished, and the original quiescence and intrinsic nirvāṇa."
Passages such as these explain the *tathāgatagarbha* and other topics found in various sutras, which may be summarized here.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In summary, the ten preceding metaphors,” etc., the commentary consists of two parts:
first, it concludes the ten preceding sections to demonstrate that [the teaching] is not yet exhaustive.
The commentary states: "Therefore, one should further [use]... and so forth, which is the formal explanation of the sūtra text.

Because the sūtra says, "By means of such immeasurable marks of knowledge," the word "such" (rú) refers back to what precedes, while "and so forth" (děng) equals what follows, further clarifying distinct meanings.
These bonds are fourfold:
first, the immeasurable; second, the unimpeded; third, the inconceivable; and fourth, the vast. These all pervade the aforementioned ten as well as those not explicitly mentioned.
The fifth is the manifestation of the sphere of activity.

Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "Correctly manifesting the boundaries," the text consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the essence; [the second, the explanation of the characteristics; and the third, the clarification of the divisions]. First, the presentation of the essence: [text follows].
2. From "Based on the first meaning" onwards, the purpose of the coming discussion is clarified by contrasting it with the previous two meanings;
3. From "By virtue of the object of cognition" onwards, the two aforementioned meanings are integrated.
The Commentary states: "The section 'Next, the actual manifestation of the object of focus' below is divided into two parts:
first, an exegesis following the text;
second, a systematic analysis by way of thematic categories, beginning with 'If one refers to the two truths'."
The sixth section: The Practice of Manifestation.
Following the phrase "The preceding explained the boundaries," the text has two parts:
first, clarifying the purpose of this section; second, from "Although [it is] an ocean of wisdom" onwards, resolving potential objections.
That is to say, if someone asks:
"If the formations (saṃskāra) exist within the cause, how can there now be a fulfilled fruit?
The explanation states:
Although practices are immeasurable, they are all subsumed within two: namely, wisdom and compassion.
When the practice of wisdom is perfected, one's own benefit is fulfilled;
yet, by mobilizing compassion that is itself wisdom, one ceaselessly benefits others.
If that is so, why does the subsequent text speak of the practice of *tathatā*? [Answer:
This is precisely the practice of the fruit.
It is about to explain the unimpeded practice of compassion and wisdom:
Therefore, it is said that True Suchness (tathatā) is the very basis of practice.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The designation ‘True Suchness’ contains both the dharma and the metaphor,” the Sūtra says, “As True Suchness is unarisen from the prior limit,” and so forth; thus, True Suchness is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s practice.
If the Buddha’s practice accords with suchness (*tathatā*), then practice is itself suchness; therefore, it is itself the Dharma.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The past and future are not conditions”: because the conditions of the past have already ceased and the conditions of the future have not yet met, they are said to be “not conditions.”

Because it does not take conditions as its object, the past has nothing that can arise, and the future has nothing that can be moved; although the present exists within conditions, it does not conjoin with them, and is therefore said to be "detached from conditions."

Therefore, in the "Dedication" [chapter], it is clarified that [the mind] "pervades the three periods of time while not being identical to the three periods of time; it pervades all things while not being all things.
Thus, although conditions arise, it remains serene and without arising.
The Commentary states: "If it is argued that 'the immeasurable is itself a measure,' this is because the immeasurable exists apart from measure.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: 'The mind-measure that is no-mind-measure—this I call the mind-measure.'"
This means that to take "the absence of mental measurement" (*amānacitta*) as being ultimate is itself still merely a form of mental measurement.

Therefore, in the passage beginning with "The mind becomes increasingly void," the preceding line clarifies that the absence of measurement does not obstruct measurement, while the line "ultimately it is called practice" clarifies that measurement is itself the absence of measurement.
The section beginning with "However, regarding nirvāṇa" cites scriptural evidence; it corresponds to the eleventh sūtra.
Master Yuan has two interpretations:
first, that it explains the basis for the practice of realization, namely the virtues previously accomplished by the Tathāgata, which one cultivates and enters into.

Furthermore, the five practices may be considered the practice of the teaching; manifesting the nature to accomplish practice is the practice of the Tathāgata, because one accomplishes practice by manifesting the Tathāgata-nature.
The meaning is this:
this single [practice] is precisely the practice of realization, for it is the accomplishment of practice through realizing the nature.
The seventh is the manifestation of bodhi.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “the fruit of perfected practice,” there are two parts explaining the purpose of its inclusion:
the first explains the purpose by referring to true bodhi; the second, from “cultivating practice in response to conditions” onwards, explains the purpose by referring to responsive bodhi.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Second, clarifying the essence,” etc., this cites two treatises which mutually corroborate one another: the ninth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the third chapter of the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The two wisdoms are the fundamental and the subsequently attained; the two abandonments are the abandonment of afflictions and the abandonment of cognitive obstructions.
Because this sutra belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), it "penetrates all.

As it says below: "Attaining the equality of the measure of all dharmas and the three wheels, such that self and other are equal and cause and effect mutually penetrate. Because of such meanings as these, it penetrates all.
The Commentary states: "Third, the differentiation of types. This section has two parts:
first, the formal exposition; second, the analytical selection.
Regarding the first:
Regarding the statement, "That which is suchness (tathatā) is neither dual nor different," this refers to the chapter on Maitreya, the meaning of which shall be explained below.
As for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s passage beginning with "inferior wisdom contemplates" and so forth, it has already been cited under the sixth stage.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Or it is divided into five, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,” the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states: “First is the bodhi of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), which is the generation of the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout immeasurable births and deaths.”
Therefore it is called Bodhi; this is speaking of the fruit within the cause.
Second is the Bodhi of subduing the mind: severing all afflictions, subduing one's own mind, and practicing the various pāramitās.

The Bodhi of the Threefold Knowledge of the Mind consists in contemplating the general and specific characteristics of the beginning and end of all Buddhas' dharmas throughout the three periods of time; through such discernment, one attains the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, which is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The fourth is to emerge and reach bodhi; because one has attained the power of skillful means within nirvāṇa, one does not cling to it.

If one extinguishes all afflictions, beholds all Buddhas, attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and emerges from the triple world to reach sarvajñā (omniscience).
"The five unsurpassed bodhis: sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), severing the residual habit-energies (vāsanā), and attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Alternatively, possessing the ten suchnesses as in the 'Chapter on Leaving the World'": this refers to the fifty-ninth scripture, wherein the ten kinds of accomplishment of the Tathāgata's powers constitute the ten bodhis.
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha!
There are ten kinds of ways in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the powers of a Tathāgata. What are these ten?"
That is to say: first, by transcending all the afflictions, karmas, and Māras, one achieves the power of a Tathāgata;
second, by fulfilling all bodhisattva practices and sporting within all bodhisattva samādhi-gates, one achieves the power of a Tathāgata.
Third, because they are fully endowed with the vast meditative concentrations of all bodhisattvas;
fourth, because they have perfected all pure factors conducive to enlightenment;
fifth, because they have attained the light of wisdom regarding all phenomena through skillful reflection and discernment.
Sixth, because their bodies pervade all worlds;
seventh, because the sounds of the speech they utter are equal to the minds of all sentient beings;
eighth, because they are able to empower all things through their supernormal powers.
Ninth, they are equal to the body, speech, and mental karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, for they comprehend the dharmas of the three periods in a single thought-moment;

tenth, they attain the samādhi of the wisdom of excellent awakening and are endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, namely, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, up to the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows.
To achieve the powers of a Tathāgata constitutes the tenth.
If bodhisattvas are endowed with these ten powers, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Every sentence contains the phrase "achieving the powers of a Tathāgata."
These ten types of bodhi are for the most part the same as those in the present sutra.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Only ten constitute the perfect [teaching],” this is the second section, which provides a critical analysis (*liao-jian*).
First, it demonstrates the distinct teaching (*bie-jiao*).
Below the section "The latter three exclude the former two," the text distinguishes and incorporates [the teachings] according to the *tongjiao* (common teaching) gate.

Regarding the commentary’s statement "Fourth, clarifying the functional activity" (*yeyong*) and so forth: since the subsequent topical outline of the scripture contains ten gates that encompass both essence (*ti*), characteristics (*xiang*), and function (*yong*), the present section only debates the function;
it consists of these ten items and does not go beyond what follows in the text.
The Commentary states: “Being free from all conditions” means that where there is contemplation, there are conditions; where there are no conditions, contemplation ceases.
The section beginning with “Like the ocean” explains the text to establish the preceding meaning.
The passage beginning with "not that there is nothing realized" establishes the meaning that the culmination of contemplation is non-contemplation (*anupalambha*).

This means that the ultimate limit of contemplative wisdom is called non-contemplation; it is the absence of that contemplation which involves conceptualization and grasping at signs, yet it is not the absence of profound non-conceptual contemplation (*nirvikalpa-bhāvanā*). Therefore, the Jin translation of the *Sarvārtha-samuccaya* is cited to clarify how these two sūtras correspond in their exposition of all meanings.
It should state:
"To understand all meanings, there is nothing to be observed.
If it is changed to "understand," then the meaning becomes complete and sufficient.
The translator of this scripture, seeing that the subsequent text mentions "knowing the minds of sentient beings," has here clarified only the meaning of non-contemplation (*anupalambha*).

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Since the contemplation of objects is thus quiescent": the preceding section explained the attainment of wisdom, which is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); the present section explains the severance of obstructions, which is the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "Non-contemplation is the essence" concludes that [the nature of the mind] possesses all three aspects.
"Non-contemplation is the essence" refers to the essence of non-thought (*amala-vijñāna*).

"Illuminating wisdom" refers to the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). "Severance" refers to the elimination of the seeds of delusive habits (*vāsanā*) as previously mentioned.
Regarding their union as a characteristic: it means that the non-duality of quiescence and illumination constitutes the characteristic of bodhi.
It is like a bright mirror, which takes non-mindfulness as its essence and reflective illumination as its function; the union of these two constitutes its characteristic.

This is precisely the function of the essence in the Chan school; one knows for oneself that the essence of this function is eternally quiescent. To know that quiescence and [function] are non-dual is the characteristic of the mind.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two are equal to all dharmas,” this explains the sutra passage, “equal toward all dharmas without doubt,” which refers to the equality of the three wheels mentioned below.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The preceding two have already subsumed the essence of the *Śāstrasaṃgraha*”: the first is true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), which severs the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the second is expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*), which severs the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Therefore, within these two phrases, the essence of both the two wisdoms and the two abandonments is already complete.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “One attaining perfection means all attain perfection,” this explains the scripture’s term “non-duality,” which refers to the mutual penetration of cause and effect discussed below.
Within this, there are two points:
first, clarifying that the sentient being and the Buddha are non-dual, such that the realization of one constitutes the realization of all. Therefore, the subsequent commentary states:

"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment," which implicitly cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "All sentient beings are themselves the aspect of bodhi."
This is precisely the characteristic of bodhi; how could it not be established?
Second, it clarifies that the subject and object are non-dual, as they are all of the same nature within the subsequent explanation.
Furthermore, it cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: "Non-duality is bodhi, because it is free from mind and dharmas."
The Dharma is the object and the mind is the subject; because the nature of the mind and its objects are one and the same, it is so for both sentient beings and Buddhas alike.
This citation from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* is from the chapter on Maitreya.

The Commentary states: "The fourth [point], 'generally indicating that the essence and characteristics of the preceding three are quiescent,' explains the sūtra’s term 'signless' (animitta), which corresponds to the passage below: 'the essence is free from deficiency or fullness.'"
The sub-commentary explains:
Whether accomplished or unaccomplished, it is eternally without increase or decrease, because Bodhi is neither a mark nor the absence of a mark.
Because it is quiescent, there is no waning or waxing; this quiescence is precisely the meaning of "signlessness" (animitta).
Therefore, it cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, saying "because all marks are extinguished," to explain "quiescent extinction.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The fifth is that the sphere of mental activity is extinguished," this explains the sūtra’s "no activity"; it means that, as stated below, there is no increase or decrease in marks, and thus it is said to be "serenely immutable."
The commentary states:
"If there are no marks, then there is neither increase nor decrease.
Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "Sixth, though awakened, one is always in samādhi," this explains the sūtra’s term "no cessation," because one does not abide in samādhi.
This refers to the passage below: "Employing both the active and the quiescent.
The subsequent commentary explains:
"Abiding in the samādhi of the wisdom of excellent awakening, one manifests many bodies; because one does not abide in stillness, one is able to employ activity."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The seven have two meanings, etc.,” this explains the sūtra’s term “immeasurable,” which refers to what follows below: “pervading the dharma-realm.
Herein there are two points, and the subsequent explanation likewise has two:
first, it clarifies that a single hair-pore contains many Buddhas, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
This refers to the first meaning herein.
Second, it says: "The Tathāgata’s body of perfect enlightenment is ultimately without arising or ceasing"; this refers to the second meaning.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The eighth also has two meanings,” and so forth, this explains the sūtra’s term “boundless” (*ananta*), which corresponds to the passage below concerning the “pervasion of all minds.
The subsequent explanation also has two parts:

first, it states that a bodhisattva should know that within their own mind, at every moment of thought, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment; this refers to the vertical boundlessness (*ūrdhvānanta*).
The second section explains: Why is this?
Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas do not depart from this mind to achieve perfect enlightenment.

This refers to the second meaning: every thought-moment should be the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), and that which is eternally constant upon its first attainment is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
From the phrase "the mind has no initial characteristic" onwards, it accords with and is identical to the *dharmadhātukāya* (Dharma-realm body).
However, this single phrase is precisely from the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.

The treatise states: "When the stages of the Bodhisattva are exhausted, the awakening-mind first arises; yet the mind has no initial characteristic, because it is far removed from subtle thought, and thus one attains the vision of the nature of the mind."
"The mind is eternally abiding; this is called ultimate awakening.
The subsequent statement, "not departing from this mind," is in profound accord with the meaning of the principle.
However, regarding the initial arising of the awakened mind, it is said that the mind has no initial characteristic; this contains two meanings:
First, awakening is that which awakens, while the mind is that which is awakened.
The mind is the primary characteristic, namely the characteristic of karma; it is subtle mentation, the initial delusion regarding reality, wherein one fails to realize that the mind is moving.

Now, because these characteristics do not exist, secondly, the awakened mind merges with clarity; that is to say, when the mind of perfect awakening arises, it lacks any characteristic of arising, and thus it is in profound accord with principle (*tattva*).
If there were a characteristic of arising, it would not accord with principle.

Taking this very intent as the basis, it is said that "the mind has no initial characteristic and is in profound accord with principle. This meaning encompasses what was stated previously; because there are no subtle thoughts, there is no characteristic of discernment.
Based on the characteristics of the dharmas, the *nirmāṇakāya* has both a beginning and an end; the *saṃbhogakāya* has a beginning but no end; and the *dharmakāya* has neither beginning nor end.

Now, in accordance with this principle, the *saṃbhogakāya* is likewise without beginning; therefore it is said: "Initial awakening is identical to fundamental awakening, such that there is no further distinction between the beginning and the fundamental; this is called ultimate awakening."
Therefore, it is said that "because there is no prior limit," there is no beginning.
That there is no end is the same as the preceding phrase regarding the absence of a subsequent limit.
Since the Dharma-body and Reward-body are thus fused, the response that is their very essence is uninterrupted from moment to moment; the three bodies are thereby unified.

The commentary states: "In the section 'Nine: Departing from Extremes within the Middle,' it explains the sutra passage 'distantly departing from the two extremes and abiding in the middle way,' which corresponds to the subsequent phrase 'pervading all minds.'"
The sub-commentary explains:
Vast and all-pervasive, it exists everywhere; inseparable and uninterrupted, it never ceases; it enters the inconceivable dharma-gate of skillful means.
The commentary consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of "leaving the extremes," and second, the explanation of "abiding in the middle.

Regarding the first, since it is not yet known what is meant by "leaving the extremes" as stated in the sutra, the Jin translation is cited and the subsequent explanation is introduced; four types are briefly enumerated to represent all others.

Defilement and purity refer to afflictions (*kleśa*); bondage and liberation pertain to both afflictions and karma; existence and non-existence pertain to both phenomena and principle; unity and difference refer to the mind and its objects. Why is this so?

It is because once one has attained *bodhi*, having departed from subtle conceptualization, delusive afflictions are exhausted, and the *dharmakāya* is manifested with wisdom that is purely immaculate.
If one holds such a view, one has not yet escaped this extreme.

Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says: "If there is a vision of perfect awakening, liberation free from all outflows, and non-attachment to any world, that is not the realization of the eye of the Way."
"Now, having realized that the essential nature of delusion is fundamentally empty, there is nothing further to be purified; thus, one is free from the two extremes.
Furthermore, because defilement and purity penetrate each other, there is no abiding or attachment; this is called 'leaving the extremes.'"

Regarding bondage and liberation: this refers to having been perpetually bound by the fetters of delusion and karma in the past, wandering through saṃsāra without end, and now, having attained bodhi, being released and liberated with ease.
To hold such a view is to dwell in an extreme.
The wisdom of Bodhi realizes that there has been no bondage from the very beginning; how, then, could there be liberation?
Since there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is no attachment or aversion; thus, one attains transcendence.
Regarding the unsurpassed words that penetrate both phenomena and principle: if it was previously thought that delusion exists, now one realizes that delusion is empty.
Formerly, one spoke of the mind as empty; now, one knows it as wondrous existence.
Furthermore, true bliss is fundamentally present, yet one loses it without realizing it;
delusive suffering is fundamentally empty, yet one acquires it without awakening to it.
Only today do I come to know that "emptiness" is a false suffering and "existence" is *nirvāṇa*. If one knows in this way, one has not yet departed from extremes.

Furthermore, such claims as "afflictions, karma, and suffering originally existed but now do not," or "bodhi and the Buddha-body originally did not exist but now exist," all concern phenomena that exist across the three periods of time.
The nature of bodhi does not belong to the three periods of time; therefore, existence and non-existence throughout the three periods are all subsumed under extremes.
True wisdom accords with reality and transcends the three periods; thus, it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
There are two ways in which "identity" and "difference" are conceived:
first, when the mind and its objects are not clearly understood, they appear as two; yet when they are in accord, they become one—this too constitutes an extreme.
Second, there is the notion that sentient beings and Buddhas are different, whereas now their single nature is realized—this is likewise called an extreme.

Now, one perfectly awakens to the fact that within this there is neither duality nor non-duality, nor even a great wisdom that perceives well, because one abides skillfully in accordance with reality.

To speak of "equality" while departing from these extremes means that the extremes are defined as the pairs of annihilation and permanence, coming and going, arising and ceasing, and the dependent and the primary; to be free from these two types of phenomena is what is called "equality."
Furthermore, duality and non-duality are also termed "extremes.
Now, because one accords with bodhi and all things are entirely quiescent, it is said that one is "far removed" from them.
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "not dwelling biasedly or attached" explains abiding in the Middle Way.
However, the general rebuttal to this objection is set forth in the subsequent section.
It addresses the objection which states:
"If one is separated from extremes, one has not yet escaped extremes, because there is still the act of accepting and rejecting."
Therefore, the commentary states:
"Not dwelling one-sidedly in attachment is called 'leaving the extremes' (*prānta-vivikta*); it does not mean that there is a 'limit' (*anta*) which can be left behind.
This means not dwelling one-sidedly in defilement, because the nature of defilement is empty."
Because the nature is itself pure, it does not abide exclusively in purity.

Since there is no purity if there is no defilement, and because the characteristic of purity is detached from it and identical to the nature of defilement, defilement and purity penetrate one another; how could it possibly abide [in either]?
Wisdom accords with this principle; therefore, it is said to be "free from extremes.
Thus it is stated: "It is not that one sees an extreme as existing, for the extreme itself is the middle.
Furthermore, there is an objection:
Where there is an extreme, there is already the middle; since the extreme is identical to the middle, there is no extreme.
If there is no extreme, in relation to what can one speak of a middle?
Therefore, the next response says:
To abide in the Middle Way by means of neither limit nor center has two intended meanings:

first, it accords with the preceding answer, which states that because there is neither limit nor center, it is called the Middle Way; if there were a center or limits, it would not be the true middle.
Second is the response that reverses the above, which states that there are two aspects to the Middle Way:
first, when viewed through mutual dependence, one leaves the extremes to abide in the middle; second, when signs are extinguished, the extremes themselves are the middle.
If emptiness is established through mutual dependence, then there are limits and a middle; only when there are neither limits nor a middle is it the true middle.
Therefore, even the transcendence of dependence is still itself dependent; though one may grasp the meaning and lose the words, words cannot fully exhaust it.
This applies to each and every category throughout the preceding discussion on defilement and purity.

The Commentary’s statement, “The ten [categories] collectively manifest that which transcends words,” explains the Sūtra’s phrase, “transcending all written characters and verbal expressions,” which refers to what follows below regarding the “profound nature of its essence and characteristics.”
This is the case where the topmost line (the ninth) uses metaphorical language to reveal the profound; here, bodhi reveals the profound by transcending language.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "there are three meanings to 'that which is manifested is non-existent': first, manifestation without mind pertains to *śamatha*; second, the emptiness of what is manifested pertains to *vipaśyanā*; third, the absence of a distinct essence pertains to the harmonious integration of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*."
Furthermore, there is first that which pertains to the mind, second that which pertains to the object, and third the mutual merging of mind and object.
Again, there is first that which pertains to wisdom, second that which pertains to principle, and third the profound resonance between wisdom and principle.

Regarding the third meaning, the commentary first provides the direct explanation and subsequently addresses an objection with the statement: "Because its own essence manifests, it is called awakening.
This means that there may be a challenge posed as follows:
"If there is no separate entity, how can it universally manifest the mental activities of sentient beings?"
Therefore, the answer says:
its own essence manifests, just as a jewel has light that illuminates the jewel's own body.
The body of the jewel is a metaphor for the mind; the light is a metaphor for wisdom.
The essential nature of the mind is the very nature of all phenomena; when it illuminates all phenomena, it is merely illuminating itself.
Thus, the citation from the *Awakening of Faith* is extremely clear.
However, the treatise asks:

"Because space is boundless, the world is boundless; because the world is boundless, sentient beings are boundless; and because sentient beings are boundless, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise boundless."
Such a realm cannot be divided; it is difficult to know and difficult to understand.
If ignorance is severed and no mental conceptions remain, how can one be said to realize all modes of knowledge? This is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā).
The answer is:
All objects of experience are fundamentally the one mind, free from conceptualization and perception.
It is because sentient beings perceive objects through deluded vision that the mind appears to have limitations.
Because they give rise to deluded thoughts, which do not accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they are unable to achieve definitive understanding.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are free from views and conceptualizations, and there is nowhere they do not pervade.

Because the mind is true and real, it is the very nature of all phenomena; its self-substance illuminates all delusive dharmas, possessing the great function of wisdom and immeasurable skillful means. According to what each sentient being should understand, it is able to reveal all manner of dharma meanings; for this reason, it is named "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā).
The commentary states:

The sub-commentary (*śū*) merely cites the middle section to prove that the self-substance is clearly manifest; since the preceding and succeeding sections can be understood by implication, they are not cited in detail.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "Since it is the wheel of the mind and so forth, what cause for doubt could there be? this refers to the heading established above which states, "There is no doubt regarding the equality of all phenomena."
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Now, first, there are thirteen bodies,” the text contains three parts:

first, a brief explanation of the text; second, a specific explanation of the character *liang* (measure/quantity) starting from “All are called measures”; and third, the conclusion of the profound purport starting from “Therefore, the Sage.”

This is from the "Pervading Antiquity" section of Master Sengzhao’s *Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa*, which follows the previous "Exhausting the Source" section, stating: "It is not without sentient beings that the Three Vehicles can be governed, nor is it without the Three Vehicles that Nirvāṇa can be realized; yet it must first be that there are sentient beings, and only afterwards is there Nirvāṇa."
If this were so, then Nirvana would have a beginning; and that which has a beginning must necessarily have an end.
Yet the Sūtra states: "Nirvana has neither beginning nor end; it is as profound and still as empty space.
Thus, Nirvana would have existed prior [to practice], and would not be something achieved only after study.
The commentary states:
This passage uses the fact that [nirvāṇa] is attained through cultivation to challenge the notion that present nirvāṇa has a beginning or an end;
it uses the fact that nirvāṇa has neither beginning nor end to challenge the idea that it is something attained through cultivation.
Therefore, Tonggu replied: "Non-action is called Nirvana.
The Perfected Person is empty and void, without form, yet there is nothing that is not the Self.
To bring all things into union so as to perfect the self—who else could it be but the Sage?"
Why is this? That which is not in accordance with principle is not sacred, and that which is not sacred is not in accordance with principle.
When one is sacred by virtue of being in accordance with principle, the sacred does not differ from principle.
Therefore, the Heavenly Lord asked:
"Where should one seek Prajñā?
Subhūti replied:
“Prajñā cannot be sought within form, nor can it be sought apart from form.
It is further said:
“To see dependent origination is to see the Dharma; to see the Dharma is to see the Buddha.”
This is the evidence that things and the self are not different.

Thus, the Perfected One (zhiren) gathers the profound mechanism before its signs appear and conceals the dark operation within the very process of transformation; he unifies the six directions to mirror his mind and transcends coming and going to perfect his being.

"Passing through past and present, beginning and end are the same; exhausting the root and reaching the extremity, nothing can be divided from it. When all is vast and perfectly balanced, this is called Nirvana.
The commentary states:
Although that passage clarifies Nirvana, it also implies that because the subject who realizes and the object realized are in accord, the self and others are one body.
Although this section now focuses on *bodhi*, it likewise takes the subject and object as a single entity; therefore, one may employ the wording [of the scripture].
Regarding the passage in the commentary beginning with "Now, within the first eight marks," the commentary consists of four parts:

first, a brief exegesis of the scriptural text; second, a reconciliation with the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*; third, a distinction from what preceded; and fourth, an extensive investigation and explanation.
The Commentary states: "This text is precisely the same," and so forth; this is the second section, which correlates [this text] with the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
It consists of three parts:
first, the explicit demonstration of their correspondence; second, the exposition of the meaning of that sūtra; and third, the formal correlation and explanation.
Now, regarding the first part, which is the "Bodhisattva Chapter":
Maitreya was expounding the practices of the stage of non-retrogression to the devaputras of Tuṣita, when Vimalakīrti challenged him, saying:
"Is it from the arising of suchness that one receives the prediction [of enlightenment]?"
Is it through the extinction of suchness that one receives the prediction?
If one receives the prediction through the arising of suchness, suchness has no arising;
if one receives the prediction through the extinction of suchness, suchness has no extinction.
All sentient beings are thusness; all phenomena are also thusness; all noble sages are also thusness; even unto Maitreya, they are also thusness.
If Maitreya receives the prediction of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should also receive it.
Why is this? Because the Suchness (tathatā) is neither dual nor differentiated.
If Maitreya were to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then all sentient beings would likewise have to attain it.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of bodhi.
If Maitreya attains parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings shall likewise attain parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas know that all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent; they possess the very characteristic of nirvāṇa and do not need to be extinguished again.
The commentary states:
Here, as we are specifically explaining the meaning of attaining perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), we cite only *bodhi*.
However, according to the scriptural text, which says "up to entering *nirvāṇa*," there is also the sense of passing into extinction; therefore, we have cited it in its entirety here.
In the commentary, from "Maitreya demonstrates his confusion regarding this principle" onwards, the second section sets forth the intent of that sutra.
Since he is the one next in line for Buddhahood (*upapadya-buddha*), how could there be any principle he does not exhaustively understand?
He merely feigns being at a loss in order to awaken those listening at that time.
The statement "merely words of logical interrogation" refers to the characteristic of delusion.
Furthermore, there are two senses to this delusion:
first, in relation to Maitreya’s reception of the challenge.

It is said that since all are equally identical to suchness (*tathatā*), it would truly contradict reason for me alone to receive the prediction of enlightenment; thus, it is called "words of logical refutation.
Second is the objection regarding Maitreya not receiving the prediction.
It is said that although the principle is indeed one and the same, one receives the prediction of enlightenment only when practice is perfected.
How can one use the principle to challenge the facts?
Therefore, it is called "interrogating the principle."
The Commentary states: "Not knowing that one has truly attained Bodhi exactly as it was questioned" refers to the third section, which correctly explains the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.

This is not to say that the questioning was false; rather, true Bodhi is indeed such that attaining it once is to attain it all. Thus, whether one accepts the challenge or does not accept it, both are equally deluded regarding this principle.
If one wishes to clarify that there is no delusion, one should respond to Vimalakīrti:
"It is indeed as you have said; I have already seen [the Buddha] receive the prediction of Buddhahood and enter into parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the commentary's phrase "Furthermore, in the previous chapter," etc., this constitutes the third point distinguishing [this stage] from the preceding ones.
Thus, the former refers to universality, while this refers to comprehensive inclusion.
As for the statement that "the equality of one nature and their mutual reinforcement alternate," the preceding chapter elucidated equality, whereas this chapter elucidates the single nature.
Therefore, in the subsequent explanation, all are of a single nature; because they are equal, they are of only one nature, and because they are of one nature, why would they not be equal?
Thus, it is said that they "mutually establish" one another.
In the commentary, from "The establishment herein" onwards is the fourth section, the extensive interrogation and explanation.
First comes the interrogation; subsequently, from "This is the great theme of the Avataṃsaka," begins the explanation.
This section has two parts:
first, a general indication;
second, a detailed explanation beginning with "However, all sentient beings," which presents the intent of the five teachings, including those for humans and devas as the sixth.

First, the Vehicle of Humans and Devas; second, the Two Vehicles (beginning with "the Lesser Vehicle"); third, the Initial Teaching (beginning with "the Mahāyāna"); fourth, the Final Teaching (beginning with "or it is said that there is only the Tathāgatagarbha"); fifth, the Sudden Teaching (beginning with "furthermore"); sixth, the Perfect Teaching (beginning with "if one relies on this school").
Within this, there are four sections:
first, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of difficulties; third, the application by analogy; and fourth, the re-explanation.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If that were so," the second section—the resolution of difficulties—consists of five parts:
First, the objection is stated.
Second, from "If one considers sentient beings" onwards, there is the explanation.
The meaning here is as follows:
Since these points are integrated through principle, they cannot be interpreted as a distinction between the principle and the phenomena.
Third, from "If that were so" onwards, the objection challenges the response:
"Since the Buddha has already attained full realization, what need is there for transformation?"
4. From "Not knowing thus" below, the reason for the transformation is explained.
5. From "Such a transformation" below, it is concluded as true transformation.
To say "there is no time when there is no transforming" means that it transforms constantly; therefore, by citing continuity, its permanence is correctly established.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'there are various differences according to the different gates,' the third section concludes by analogy, which is to categorically apply this to the remaining gates.
Although there are many gates, they are briefly divided into four:
first, in terms of nature, which is the one true dharma-realm."
Second, regarding characteristics, this refers to inexhaustible phenomena.
Third, regarding the mutual penetration of nature and characteristics, this reveals that these two gates are neither identical nor separate.
Fourth, by dissolving characteristics through nature, the functions of virtue unfold in infinite layers.
First, regarding the gate of nature (*dhātu*): Question:
Is its essence the Buddha?
Answer:
It is so. If there were no obstructions, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) would follow:
first, that one is a Buddha; for the Dharma-nature body reaches everywhere, as the Sūtra says, "The emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha."
"Second, it is neither Buddha, because it transcends both the subject and object of awakening;
its nature is the equal and singular True Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), being neither Buddha nor sentient being.
Third, it is both Buddha and not Buddha, because the Dharmatā-kāya has no self-nature."
The fourfold negation: because both nature and the absence of nature are simultaneously extinguished.
As the Sūtra says: "In non-existence there is no duality; even non-duality is likewise absent.
All things of the three periods of time are empty—this is the vision of the Buddhas."
Second, regarding the gate of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mukha*), there are two meanings:
first, the sentient; second, the non-sentient.
This is because the true mind, following conditions, transforms into both the subject and the object.

Nevertheless, these two gates are each divided into the defiled and the pure: that is to say, the permeation of True Suchness by ignorance constitutes the defiled dependent origination, while the permeation of ignorance by True Suchness constitutes the pure dependent origination.
Defilement results in the myriad classes of beings, while purity leads to Buddhahood.
Only by cultivating pure conditions to sever those defiled conditions can one attain Buddhahood.
Based on these two meanings, the states of birth and Buddhahood are distinct.
Within these pure conditions, there are further causes and effects: the causes consist of the pure and the mixed, while the effects consist of the primary and the secondary.
If categorized according to the gate of purity, each and every bodhisattva practices only a single practice throughout the bounds of the future, and this is true for all;
if categorized according to the gate of diversity, they cultivate all ten thousand practices throughout the bounds of the future.
If considered from the perspective of the cause, one is always a bodhisattva throughout the reaches of the future;
if considered from the perspective of the fruit, one is always a Tathāgata throughout the reaches of the future.
As the sutra says: "For the sake of sentient beings, in every thought-moment, one newly and ever freshly attains equal and perfect enlightenment."
If one explains it through the dual gates, one cultivates the cause and attains the fruit throughout the limits of the future;
if one approaches it through the dual negation, throughout the limits of the future it is neither cause nor fruit, and thus it is identical to true nature.
In the first two gates, compassion and wisdom are both fully present, and mind and phenomena are both harmoniously fused.
Within the third gate, "The Mutual Penetration of Nature and Phenomena," there are specifically four sub-sections:
the first, "following nature through phenomena," is identical to the second gate.
Second, the two aspects return to their single nature, which is identical to the first gate.
Third, both are preserved without obstruction, encompassing the two preceding gates.
Based on this, compassion and wisdom operate in tandem, essence and appearance advance together, and stillness and illumination flow as one, thereby achieving great mastery.

Fourth, when both are mutually negated, then both nature and appearance are utterly transcended; they submerge together into the ocean of fruition, where there is neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.

This fourth section is the "Gate of Nature Integrating Appearance": although appearances differ in myriad ways, none are not identical to nature; the virtues of nature are fully contained within all appearances.

By means of the nature’s fusion with phenomena, phenomena become identical to the nature; thus, all the aforementioned gates are rendered free from obstruction. Cause and effect interpenetrate, the pure and the mixed mutually harmonize, and each phenomenon interrelates with every other in infinite, multilayered depth.
Now, within the fourfold formulation concerning the gate of nature (*dharmatā*), this refers specifically to the Buddha-gate, and the other three are not taken up.

Within the gate of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), with respect to the gate of sentient beings, that which is pure rather than defiled, and which is effect rather than cause—this is a partial meaning and is not what is employed here.

Regarding the gate of mutual penetration (*jiaoche*), the Buddha represents the simultaneous fusion of nature and characteristics, while birth represents the convergence of characteristics back into nature.
This sutra specifically relies on the fourth [gate] to fuse characteristics with nature, such that when one is realized, all are realized.

This means that by using the Buddha’s pure nature to dissolve the defilement of birth, and by using the Buddha’s singular nature to dissolve the multiplicity of birth, one causes the many defiled births to accord with the single true nature, such that they are all like Buddhas who have already attained Buddhahood.
It is not only sentient beings who, by realizing the fusion of the myriad categories into the Buddha-body, do not fail to achieve perfection.
Thus Master Zhao said:
"Is it not only the Sage who realizes the myriad things to complete himself?"
It is further said:
"Therefore, the Perfected Person is empty and formless, such that there is nothing that is not the Self.
By merging the Buddha-nature with the nature of things, all things are realized as being identical to the Buddha and thus perfected.
By dissolving the characteristics of the Buddha through the nature of things, the three karmas are made equal to the myriad classes of beings.

This is precisely the intended meaning of the present sutra, rather than other approaches; therefore, it is said that while they differ according to their respective gates, the present one is the gate of attaining Buddhahood.

The Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) mostly accords with the four gates concerning nature; the Final Teaching (Zhong-jiao) is the mutual interpenetration and thorough penetration of the same nature. The Initial Teaching (Shi-jiao) has two aspects:
first, that illusory existence is identical to emptiness, where all phenomena are gathered back into nature as being merely manifestations of mind, which mostly accords with the second gate.

The followers of the Hīnayāna and those of the human and celestial realms all share the same perspective regarding the gate of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It is for this reason that some say insentient things attain Buddhahood; this is based on the mutual fusion of nature (*prakṛti*) and characteristics. By fusing the nature of the sentient with the characteristics of the insentient, and by allowing the characteristics of the insentient to fuse with the nature of the sentient through their shared nature, it is therefore said that there is the principle of insentient things attaining Buddhahood.

If one takes the principle that insentient things do not attain Buddhahood as a means to harmonize the characteristics of sentient beings, one may likewise say that all sentient beings do not attain Buddhahood.

This is because there is no duality between the nature of attainment and non-attainment, or between the sentient and the insentient; because the Dharma-realm is limitless; because the essence of the Buddha is universally pervasive; because form and emptiness are non-dual; because phenomena have no fixed nature; because the ten bodies are perfectly interfused; because the marks of dependent origination are mutually contingent; because the realm of birth is inexhaustible; because cause and effect are all-encompassing; because one is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence; and because the myriad dharmas are empty and interfused. Therefore, it is said that "the attainment of one is the attainment of all," which does not mean that insentient things also possess a conscious nature and thus attain Buddhahood in the same manner as sentient beings.

If one were to grant that Buddhahood is attained, then this attainment would involve the cultivation of causes such as the transformation of the insentient into the sentient and the transformation of the sentient into the insentient, which would be identical to false views.
Other meanings are fully explained as previously and subsequently detailed.
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, these sentient beings are the molds upon which the images are cast. This is explained in four ways;
this is the first meaning.

It is the same as the previous [point] regarding the scroll within the dust that shares the Buddha-mind, and the same as the tenth [point] below concerning the universal pervasiveness of all minds. By seeing one's own accomplishment, one sees the accomplishment of others, which is identical to the point below that one's own mind is constantly and perpetually the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the two explanations, first is the general explanation, etc.,” there are three points of meaning:

First, it says, “Because they are equally devoid of intrinsic nature, they attain manifest realization. This means that since there is no duality of nature, the Buddha realizes the single nature and thereby attains Buddhahood; thus, all beings who follow this single nature shall likewise attain Buddhahood.

The second point states: "The nature of delusion is fundamentally empty; that which arises is originally the Buddha. Since delusion arises from within [the mind], one perceives this arising as not being the Buddha;
yet, since the Buddha realizes that delusion is empty, how could that which arises not be the Buddha?
Regarding the third truth, "The nature cannot be attained; it is not newly accomplished for the first time": if there were something that could be attained, one would attain Buddhahood now.
Since the nature cannot be attained, the Buddha is not newly accomplished for the first time.
The Buddha is not newly accomplished; the Buddha is fundamentally the Buddha.
How does the fundamental Buddha differ from the Buddha born of birth?
Therefore, when one is accomplished, all are accomplished.
It may also be said that if one [being] does not achieve [Buddhahood], then all do not achieve it, because they share the same nature.
However, since this is the gateway to attaining Buddhahood, therefore all shall attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “The subsequent explanation of the twelve phrases on what does not exist,” the text contains two parts:
first, the exegesis of the words; second, the formation of paired correlations.
Within the former, the phrase “It is not that the false is merely empty while the true alone exists,” and so forth, serves to distinguish the school and clarify its specific character.
The Dharma-lakṣaṇa school asserts that the falsely imagined is empty while the perfected nature is truly existent,
because they maintain that the parikalpita is empty and the pariniṣpanna is existent.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Birth and death are empty, while nirvāṇa is not empty.
As it says in the *Three Treatises*:
"To falsely claim that [the conventional] exists is because the ultimate truth is empty."
Regarding these twelve phrases, "arising" is the delusive and "Buddha" is the true; since both the true and the delusive are non-existent, one should not speak of them in a biased manner.
The commentary states: "By means of the nature, phenomena are fused so that the Dharma-realm manifests perfectly"—this demonstrates the correct principle.

Sentient beings and Buddhas, as well as the true and the false, are all distinct in their phenomenal aspects; yet when these are fused into the single realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), it is said that "the perfection of one is the perfection of all.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "Because of this lack of intrinsic nature, it is called the attainment of perfect enlightenment."
If there were attainment through grasping, it would not be true awakening; therefore, the text says, "Furthermore, there is no nature of attaining perfect awakening.
In the commentary, the phrase "Moreover, subsuming the twelve" marks the second pair of correspondences.

Regarding "the relationship between the single characteristic and that which is characterized": the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) serves as the characterized (*lakṣya*), and its exhaustion is the characteristic itself.
The essence of the characterized phenomenon is precisely the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which does not transcend the categories of defilement and purity.
Regarding the statement "because they exist in mutual dependence," this explains the meaning of non-existence:
defilement exists in dependence upon purity, and therefore lacks the characteristic of defilement;
purity exists in dependence upon defilement, and therefore lacks the characteristic of purity.
Therefore, the sutra speaks of the "nature of signlessness" (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the "nature of inexhaustibility," "exhaustion" refers to the characteristic of being able to manifest; arising and ceasing, as well as defilement and purity, are entirely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
However, there are briefly two kinds of the four characteristics of arising and ceasing:
first, cessation at every moment, which is called "momentary extinction"; because it is extinguished by conditions, it reveals the nature of non-extinction.
Second, cessation over a single period, such as the exhaustion of the nature of afflictions; through the gate of the emptiness of nature, it reveals the meaning of non-extinction.
Regarding "the pair of arising-and-ceasing": because all things arise dependently, they are fundamentally unarisen;
because the nirvana of pure nature is primordially quiescent, it does not cease further.
These pairs are all based on the intent of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
The former was discussed in terms of extinguishing delusions, while this is discussed in terms of extinguishing suffering.
Since bodhi arises from the extinction of both delusion and suffering, they are now eliminated.

Regarding the statement, "In terms of the Buddha’s bodhi, it is not something that first arises," this means that the intrinsically pure bodhi is not something newly attained through cultivation; how, then, could there be its cessation?
As for the "confrontation between the three types of self and non-self," one uses conditions to dismantle the self, and uses the self to dispel non-self.
To say that "I" cannot even be apprehended means that what is not-I cannot be apprehended either;
this is the gateway to non-duality.
From the phrase "within the true reality of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*) onwards, the gateway of true reality is used to simultaneously negate both.
The first two [points] are from the text of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, which have already been cited repeatedly above.
Regarding "the four conditions are not conditions": sentient beings are conditions; since they grasp at conditions yet lack intrinsic nature, there are no sentient beings.
That which is not a sentient being is not a condition; since even a condition cannot be apprehended, how could that which is not a condition be apprehended?
This is the refutation through mutual dependence.

Regarding the "pairing of the five types of the means of realization and the object of realization," both the cause-condition gate and the door of the pair [of subject and object] refute both the agent and the object.
Therefore, the preceding scripture states: "Knowing that the nature of bodhi arises from conditions, one enters the profound dharma-realm without opposition.

Regarding the statement "the six realms are neither joined nor opposed," space has no intrinsic substance and does not join with things; yet it is through causes and conditions that the non-existence of space is revealed.

One who attains perfect enlightenment is the harmonious union of subject and object; furthermore, through the gate of causes and conditions, it is explained that there is no such thing as "perfect enlightenment. Therefore, the "single unified mark" is not a single unified mark.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Every phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature," there are two intended meanings:
