The Commentary states: Regarding the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra*, this refers to the first section among the listing of the assembly, where the Sūtra says: "At that time, there were Buddhas from other directions who, desiring to adorn the assembly at Vairocana’s place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), manifested themselves in the form of Bodhisattvas and entered the gathering to take their seats."
"Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas.
This passage is identical to the commentary (*shu*) below; it is cited here to clarify the reality [of the teaching] and to manifest the previously established traces.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "skillfully entering the limitlessness of limits," it means deeply penetrating the limitless *bhūtakoṭi* (the ultimate reality).
However, all of these are the opposite of the virtues of the śrāvaka, and their categories may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of the "nine unique qualities of a Buddha" and so forth: in the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind," it states that although a bodhisattva has not yet realized the ten powers of a Buddha, they nevertheless have no doubt regarding them.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the realization and faith that enters through the ten kinds of omniscience' (*sarvākārajñatā*): 'realization and faith' refers to the stages from the first bhūmi upward; this distinguishes them from the śrāvakas who have not yet attained such faith, because all ten bhūmis rely upon the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom."
In the commentary, following the section "The second major division: the request," the phrase "It is like Yegong’s fondness for dragons" refers to an account from the *Zhuangzi*.
Yegong’s surname was Shen and his given name was Zhuliang.
Therefore, the commentary on the *Chunqiu* states: "Ye Gong Zihao, Shen Zhuliang, received his fief at Ye and usurped the title of 'Gong' (Duke). It is also said:
"He shared the same surname as the state of Chu; the surname of Chu is Qian [pronounced with the initial q and rhyme mian/bi], with the final sound mi."
Thereupon Zi Zhang went to see the Lord of Wei, but the Lord did not treat him with full courtesy. Zi Zhang said:
"Your Majesty's fondness for scholars is like that of Duke Ye’s fondness for dragons.
Duke Ye loved dragons so much that he had their images painted everywhere, even in his latrines and privies."
The true dragon, knowing of his fondness for such things, appeared in his courtyard.
Lord Ye fell flat on his back with laughter and did not dare look at it.
Lord Ye’s fondness was for what resembled a dragon; he did not truly love the real dragon.
"Now your lordship's fondness for scholars is merely a fondness for those who *appear* to be scholars, not a fondness for true scholars.
Thus, when a śrāvaka requests the Dharma, it is like that person's fondness for dragons: if he does not behold something extraordinary, he will fail to recognize the true creature.
The Commentary states: "With the first ten phrases, the perfection of its own essence is clarified. This indicates the reason for dividing the subject matter of the inquiry into two sections.

Within the preceding thirty phrases, only the first ten constitute the dharma requested; that is, the Buddha’s realm and so forth represent the perfection of the Buddha’s own essence, and because they are clearly manifest, they are identical to the ocean of fruition, which transcends all words.
Regarding the final ten phrases on the universal application of transformation:

subsequently, thirty phrases are requested for exposition according to the capacity of the audience. Of these, twenty phrases constitute the Dharma being requested; since the preceding ten phrases concern the request for the discourse on the past, the latter ten phrases concerning the application of transformation are specifically cited here, as they properly accord with the theme of opening and transforming beings.
The Commentary states: "Therefore, the Jin version selects... and so forth, explaining that cultivation (*bhāvanā*) precedes reflection (*cintā*).
According to the Jin translation, the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*) is not lost.

Regarding the passage, "Furthermore, these ten phrases have two general meanings," etc., it means that since [the meaning] can only be known through the empowerment of all Buddhas and the like, it clearly demonstrates the profundity [of the teaching].
Since the Buddha already knows [the capacity of the audience], he requests empowerment from the Buddha to expound [this teaching].
Those who lack the vessel find it difficult to understand; those who possess the vessel may hear it.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “differences in the one wealth and so forth,” this refers to the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*), namely: (1) mastery over wealth, (2) mastery over life, (3) mastery over mind, (4) mastery over karma, (5) mastery over birth, (6) mastery over resolve, (7) mastery over vows, (8) mastery over supernormal powers, (9) mastery over knowledge, and (10) mastery over phenomena. These are explained in detail in the *Bhūmi* section on the Eighth Stage and in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The names and meanings of the seventh [assembly] are entirely identical to those of the first,” there are two matters where the names differ but the meanings are the same, and one matter where this [latter] and that [former] are mutually absent; thus, there are three categories.
Within the third category, there are two intended meanings; the latter meaning is also one where the names differ but the significance is identical.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “First, the perfection of causes and the accomplishment of fruits is the ocean of Buddhas,” the preceding section provides a general explanation, while the following section offers a detailed analysis.
Within each phrase there are two meanings: first, the explanation within the phrase itself.

For example, regarding the statement "cause and effect are established," this corresponds to the Sūtra’s phrase, "formerly seeking the mind of omniscience. Here, omniscience is the effect, and the mind that seeks it is the cause.

Regarding the second point, "it is the Buddha-ocean": "the second" refers to the convergence with the ten oceans of the first assembly; this applies to all subsequent phrases as well. However, each phrase's explanation follows upon the preceding one:

for instance, in the second phrase, "accomplishment necessarily entails the expounding of the Dharma," the two characters "accomplishment-necessarily" (成必) arise by taking up the "accomplishment of the fruit" (果成) from the previous context; the others may be inferred accordingly.
The ninth is the Ocean of Established [Realms].
Regarding the third major section, the "Section on Samādhi," the commentary states:
"Now, first, the Great Function Without Direction. Below this, the commentary consists of four parts:

First, clarifying the reason for entering meditative concentration; second, from "That is to say" onwards, distinguishing the sequence; third, from "The Buddha himself entered" onwards, distinguishing the person who enters; fourth, from "As for not answering" onwards, resolving potential objections.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “As for ‘within the causes of entry’ and so forth,” the four types of compassion are precisely the causes.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Furthermore, these four compassions also represent the gradual progression from the Buddha toward the sentient beings (the *jī*)," this means that based on the essence of compassion, one enters the gateway of compassion; employing compassion as one moves forward serves as the skillful means (*upāya*) for transforming sentient beings.
The commentary states: "The third section correctly elucidates entering meditative absorption. This commentary consists of three parts: first, a general heading;
second, the explanation of the terminology beginning with "As for 'stretching and yawning'"; and third, the explanation of the meaning beginning with "Therefore, following the ancient masters."
Regarding the two points within the second section:
first, the former part recounts the past, which reflects the intent of the *Kanding zhuan*;
subsequently, from "However, the old sūtra... onwards, it examines conformity and contradiction.
Within this, there are three parts.

First, it clarifies that Chinese and Sanskrit are not of the same class: for instance, although *sūtra*, *sūtraka*, and *sutta* differ from one another, their phonetic resonance belongs to the same category;
however, terms such as *vega* (fēnxùn) and *vīrya* (píshí) are separated by an immense gap in their linguistic force.
Second, from "Nirvāṇa 25" onwards, two passages are cited as evidence to clarify that this is indeed the term [being discussed].
Third, from "But as an adversary" onwards, even granting its establishment, the Sanskrit term is cited to mean "sovereign."
In the commentary, from "Therefore, following the ancient masters" onwards is the third section, the explanation of the meaning, which proceeds first briefly and then extensively.
Within the brief explanation, there are three parts:

first, the two initial sentences conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one; second, from "Stretching and exerting" onwards, the characteristics are explained by means of analogies; and third, from "General explanation of the characteristics" onwards, the characteristics are explained by means of the Dharma.
The sub-commentary states: “If one explains them individually,” and so forth, which constitutes the second section, the detailed explanation.
This section has two parts:
first, a general clarification of the basis [for the explanation]; second, the opening of the chapters for the formal explanation.
In the preceding section, two passages were cited to explain the term "Lion.

Now, for the first: the "Simhanāda-parivarta" (Chapter on the Lion’s Roar) of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which corresponds to the twenty-fifth fascicle of the Southern edition, or the twenty-seventh according to the Northern edition.
Regarding the phrase "extensively providing the analogy and its application," I shall now set it forth in full.

This was when the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda questioned the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata, in response to the assembly, praised him to inspire their reverence for this bodhisattva and spoke of the origins of his virtues. Therefore, it is said: "Now, before me, he wishes to let out a lion’s roar."
"Good son!

It is like the lion king, who, knowing his own physical strength and the sharpness of his teeth and claws, plants his four paws firmly upon the ground, dwells securely in his rocky cave, and roars while lashing his tail."
"If there be one who can possess all such characteristics as these, know that this person is then able to roar the lion's roar.
The commentary states:
What follows here explains eleven matters; although they are combined into one section in the sutra, we shall first separately combine them with the lion.
The Sūtra says: "Good son!

The Tathāgata’s perfectly awakened wisdom constitutes his teeth and claws; his body is perfected by the four bases of psychic power and the six pāramitās; he is valiant with the ten powers; great compassion serves as his tail; and he dwells securely in the pure cave-dwelling of the four dhyānas."
The commentary states:
This contains both the simile and its application, specifically applying it to the lion.
In the section of the *Śāstra* following "Furthermore, from the Chapter on Transcending the World," the second part cites the relevant scripture.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the body and so forth," the term "and so forth" refers to the subsequent sutra.
The subsequent sutra states: "The Four Noble Truths are its feet; right mindfulness is its neck; compassion is its eyes and wisdom its head; and the turban of liberation is its topknot."
"In the valley of ultimate emptiness, he roars the Dharma to terrify the hosts of Māras.
Regarding the statement "not necessarily fixed," this introduces the subsequent analogy and its application, as it does not rely entirely upon the textual passages of the two aforementioned sūtras.
Furthermore, the third chapter of the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* also states:
"Good son, there are ten further qualities that are like a lion.
What are these ten?"

That is to say: he is fearless and does not dread the great assembly; having departed, he never returns; he can roar the lion’s roar and is endowed with eloquence; he delights in dwelling in forests and wilds or within mountain caves; he subdues the great assembly and possesses heroic power, being well able to provide protection.
He explains this at length.

Therefore, this *Siṃha* [Sūtra] differs from the two preceding sūtras; it is clear that one need not strictly fix the correspondence between the metaphor and its application, but rather simply adopt what is convenient for the meaning.
In the commentary, from the phrase "Now, gathering together the various texts" onwards is the second section: the opening of the chapters and the formal explanation.
First, the two chapters are presented; subsequently, from "Now, first," the individual explanations follow.
However, for the sake of convenience in conveying the meaning herein, I have synthesized the various perspectives into a single exposition.
The concluding statement, "In this way, each and every hair of the lion accords with the Dharma-realm," is precisely the intent of the *Jinshizi Zhang* (The Treatise on the Golden Lion).
Just as a lion made of gold has every single hair composed of gold, so too,
how could the lion of the *dharmadhātu* not be the *dharmadhātu* itself?
This should be understood.
The commentary states: "Next, regarding the phrase 'for eleven matters,' the following explains the second chapter.
This section further consists of two parts:

first, the eleven matters are synthesized; moreover, herein both the Dharma and its metaphors are expounded together, employing the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to accord with the present scripture."
Now, I shall first cite the passages from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in their entirety, as those texts have not yet been seen and are difficult to interpret.
That sutra provides a parable, saying: "The true lion king emerges from his den at dawn, stretches and yawns, looks toward the four quarters, and lets out a roar for eleven purposes."

What are these eleven? First, because he wishes to destroy those who are not actually lions but falsely pretend to be so; second, because he wishes to test his own strength; third, because he wishes to purify his dwelling place; fourth, so that all other lions may know their proper domain; fifth, so that the members of his herd may be free from fear; sixth, so that those who are sleeping may attain awakening; seventh, so that all heedless beasts may become diligent; eighth, so that all beasts may come to rely upon him; ninth, because he wishes to tame great fragrant elephants; tenth, because he wishes to instruct his offspring; and eleventh, because he wishes to adorn his own retinue.

All birds and beasts let out lion’s roars; those belonging to the watery realm submerged themselves in the deep abysses, while those that travel on land hid away in their burrows and caves; the flying creatures fell from the sky, and the great fragrant elephants were so terrified they lost control and voided excrement.
"O sons of good family!
Just as that jackal, though it may follow a lion for a hundred years, can never produce the lion’s roar;
whereas the son of a lion, upon reaching three years of age, is able to roar like the lion king."
The commentary states:
The following section of the sūtra provides the application of the analogy.
First, the application regarding the lion has already been cited above.
Next, these are combined into eleven matters, which are stated as: "First, to roar the lion's roar for the sake of all sentient beings and to crush the armies of Māra;
second, to manifest the ten powers to the assembly;
third, to reveal the sphere of the Buddha’s conduct."
Fourth, to serve as a place of refuge for all those with false views;
fifth, to comfort the multitudes who fear birth and death;
sixth, to awaken sentient beings who are asleep in ignorance.
Seventh, to cause those who practice the seven unwholesome dharmas to give rise to a mind of repentance;
eighth, to reveal to all sentient beings with wrong views that the six teachers are not true lions, so that they may understand this;
ninth, to shatter the prideful minds of Pūraṇa and the others.
Tenth, it is to cause those of the two vehicles to give rise to a sense of remorse, and to instruct the bodhisattvas of the five stages so that they may generate great power;
eleventh, it is to ensure that the fourfold assembly of right view does not give rise to fear toward the followers of the fourfold assembly of false views, and so forth.
He emerged from his cave-dwelling—the abode of noble conduct, pure conduct, and celestial conduct—stretching his limbs in order to cause all sentient beings to break their pride;
he yawned in order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to wholesome dharmas.
He gazes in the four directions in order to cause sentient beings to attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
His four feet rest firmly upon the ground in order to cause sentient beings to fully abide in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
The Lion’s Roar refers to the definitive teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and that the Tathāgata is eternally present and unchanging. Good son!
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas may follow the World-Honored Tathāgata for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they are nonetheless unable to utter the lion’s roar.
"If a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage can practice these three spheres of conduct, it should be known that he is then able to roar the lion's roar.
The commentary states:
The preceding two sections, consisting of the citation of the scripture, the analogy, and their synthesis, complete this single thematic meaning.
Having understood his intention, I shall now provide the formal correlation.
This commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the correlation of the eleven matters; [the second part follows].

The second [section] follows accordingly; it briefly omits [the mention of] frowning, stretching, yawning, and so forth. When one compares the text of that sūtra with the present commentary, the distinction between the primary and the secondary becomes clear.
For instance, "because it first destroys [them] with a false lion’s roar" is the illustrative passage (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If one says "crushing and destroying the army of Māra," this corresponds to the text.
Since this is entirely identical to that, there is no distinct meaning.
Regarding "manifesting to the assembly" and so forth, as in the phrase "because of manifesting the power of the body," this is precisely that metaphor.

If it is said that "manifesting the ten powers to the assembly" constitutes their conjunction, then the "supernatural power" (ṛddhi-bala) and "equal power" (sāmya-bala) refer to the present sutra; these serve as examples of those [powers], though they are not identical to the wording of those [other texts].
Herein, it is precisely shown that the Tathāgata manifests supernatural powers by entering the dharma-realm concentration; therefore, he exerts his supernatural power.

As for the term "equal power" (*samartha*), while the "ten powers" (*daśabala*) clarify only ten kinds of intellectual power, the "equal power" here refers to the power of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-bala*).
Whether it be the power of samādhi or the power of merit, as long as there is the sense of "power," it is simply the power of the body.
That which appears below within the section on the causes is the characteristic of power.

Among these three [types of purity], that sutra merely uses the opening of the Buddha’s sphere of activity (*caryā-viṣaya*) to cause his sphere of abiding (*vihāra-viṣaya*) to be pure; this sutra, however, uses the purification of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and its lands, which thus differs slightly from the former in its application of the Dharma.
The similarities and differences regarding the remaining seven can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “Furthermore, the jackal,” the second section on following the lion is clear.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of the “ten kinds of *vikrīḍita* (mastery) among the fifty-seven,” the Sūtra says: “O Son of the Buddha!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of heroic strides (*vikrīḍita*).
What are the ten? They are as follows:
the heroic stride of the bull king, because it outshines all the great assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth.
The Elephant King exerts his prowess, for his mind is well-tamed and supple as he bears the burden of all sentient beings.

The Dragon King exerts his prowess, raising great clouds of the honey of the Dharma, flashing the lightning of liberation, thundering with the roar of the reality of suchness, and raining down the nectar of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis.

The Great King of Golden-Winged Birds exerts his prowess to exhaust the waters of craving and attachment, shatter the shell of ignorance, and seize the venomous dragons of affliction, thereby causing them to emerge from the great ocean of suffering in birth and death.
The Great Lion King exerts his prowess, dwelling securely in the great wisdom of equanimity as his weapon in order to subdue all Māras and non-Buddhists.

Regarding these five metaphors, the subsequent sections refer only to the Dharma: sixth, the prowess of the courageous; seventh, great wisdom; eighth, dhāraṇī; ninth, eloquence; and tenth, the prowess of the Tathāgata, wherein omniscience is fully perfected, and so forth.
The details are as explained therein.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The adorned pavilion reveals the self-substance of dependent origination,” this means that upon the substance of the *dharmadhātu*, there are the myriad virtues of dependent origination; it is because these exist within this very self-substance, amidst both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
These three conditions for dependent origination represent the intention of Master Guāngtǒng.

Regarding the phrase "to shatter emotional attachments and reveal the Dharma": this refers to the convergence with reality by means of the mind, which is the phenomenal aspect, while the convergence with reality by means of the object is the noumenal aspect.

As for the commentary’s statement, "The following three sections also separately answer the latter twenty phrases within the preceding questions," the seven directions discussed above answered only one of the first ten phrases among those twenty; the three directions below answer all three phrases among those twenty, while the two directions above and below provide both general and specific answers.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The nine phrases within the pores of the lower direction answer the previous nine questions,” this is because among the ten [questions] previously mentioned, the single question concerning supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) has already been answered by the preceding seven directions.
According to the explanation below, since five phrases answer the five questions regarding causes and four phrases answer the five questions regarding results, how can it be called "answering nine"?
It is because the question concerning supernormal powers (abhijñā) is separately manifested again.
Thus, since this has already been answered extensively above, it simply states "nine.

Regarding the commentary’s remark, "This phrase should clarify 'seeking and pursuing,'" it is because the text says, "emerging from the cloud-sound of the ocean of skillful means for the practices of all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time"; therefore, it is designated as answering "practice. Since this mutually and correctly answers "practice," the meaning of this single phrase clarifies the seeking and pursuing of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*); it is called "cultivating practice" merely because it marks the beginning of such practice.
The Commentary states: "However, the question 'as it pertains to the causal stage of the Tathāgata,' etc., serves to generally address and distinguish the differences within this context.
The section beginning with "Its auxiliary paths" explains the nature of the statement that does not answer regarding other causes.

The preceding section provided a general response concerning skillful means (*upāya*), while this section further adds the aids to the path (*mārga-aṅga*) and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*). Thus, this lower section provides a general response to three causes and a specific response to five causes; combined with the aforementioned skillful means, it also generally responds to two questions: first, the causal conditions of the fundamental matter, and second, the various stages (*bhūmi*) entered therein. Therefore, it fully answers ten causes.
Regarding the question on the *pāramitās* within the aforementioned section, its meaning is repeated for the sake of clarification.

The commentary states: "The separate response to the first phrase concerning 'entering the dwelling place of all sentient beings' and so forth" refers to the preceding general response to the two phrases within the causal stage (*hetu*), whereas from here below is the specific response to the three phrases within the resultant stage (*phala*).

In the preceding section, there were five questions and answers; here, there are three. Together with the eighth question and answer, the tenth regarding images and manifested signs concerning the buddha-fields, the ten questions are thus complete.
In the commentary, the passage beginning with "Regarding those instances where the answers to questions are not in sequential order" analyzes and distinguishes the sequence.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, they all say" provides a general explanation of the term "original matter" (benshi), which here is interpreted according to the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong).
The text contains three parts.
First is the formal explanation: because the dharma-nature is eternally abiding and the marks are identical to that nature, the marks are likewise eternal.
This means they are not different from the essence and thus do not perish throughout the three periods of time.
Being not identical with the essence, such is the nature of its characteristics;
this is the gate of the marks of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
According to how it causes [beings] to see, this is the gate of karmic function (*karma-vṛtti*).
Therefore, both are concluded as being equally capable of attaining mastery.
This is simply the nature of principle; it is merely that the functional activity is not established through the marks of qualities.
The section beginning with "Thus, in the Guhyasamāja" (Hence, in the *Ghanavyūha*) below cites scriptural evidence.
The section beginning with "first realizing the activity" and continuing through "purifying the basis" establishes the gateway of the characteristics of realized virtue.
The third section, beginning with "if one practices the principle and phenomena separately," distinguishes [this teaching] from other schools.
The statement that "in the present life, both essence and function coexist" refers to the Mahāyāna doctrine.
The phrase "how much more so for the Hīnayāna" refers to the Sarvāstivāda (You-you zong) doctrine.
The remark "because those [past and future dharmas] have no essence and no function in the future" provides the reason for this distinction.
According to this school, the past exists as a latent presence and the future exists as a potential nature; therefore, they possess substantiality (*dravya*).
However, unlike present phenomena which exist as actual entities (*vastu*), they lack functional efficacy (*kāritra*).
Now, because their essential nature is fused, both essence and function coexist.
This is precisely "being while being non-being," a being that is non-being.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Also called the three kinds of threefold action": first, the threefold action of approaching the Buddha; second, the threefold action of gathering and transforming beings; and third, the threefold action of supernormal powers.

The Commentary states: "The following four inversions clarify the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). First, the initial phrase clarifies the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Second, from "attaining all... onwards, it clarifies the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*). Third, from "in the dharma-realm of empty space... onwards, it clarifies the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*). Fourth, from "knowing all dharmas... onwards, it clarifies the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
The fifth major section: Raising the Section on Faults.
The Commentary states: "Now, first, Śāriputra. Regarding the various disciples, the translations differ between ancient and modern times; for now, we mostly follow the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva.
Regarding the term "śārika," a Mahāyāna Dharma Master stated:
"This is the hundred-tongued bird; it is also called the spring oriole.
An ancient virtuous master, citing a sūtra, also said:
"Because his mother’s eloquence was like that bird.
In this context, this is the older Sanskrit term; the newer form is Śāriputra, where *putra* means "son."
Furthermore, *śarīra* may also be translated as "body" (*śarīra*), because the mother possessed excellent physical features.
Alternatively, *śarīra* may be called "pearl," because the mother's mark of intelligence was present in her eyes.
He was also addressed as "Mother.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost among those whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolve all doubts."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 41, refers to him as "the left-hand disciple of the Tathāgata, whose father’s name was Upatiṣya.
The commentary on "Maudgalyāyana" notes that this is a transliteration from the Sanskrit; it is an ancient translation, whereas the meaning [of the name] is the new translation.
In the new Sanskrit language, he is called Mahā-maudgalyāyana.

However, according to the commentary, this name is derived from his mother’s lineage; if named after his father, he is called Kauliya, also known as Kaulita, or Kauludāya, which translates as "Auspicious Fortune."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while Maudgalyāyana was held in the highest regard as a preeminent youth; their intellectual skills were comparable, and their virtuous conduct was identical."
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "Among my disciples, as for those who possess supernormal powers and can fly light as they travel to the ten directions, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 41, refers to him as the "right-hand disciple."

He burned down the Hall of Virtuous Victory, kicked away the chariot of Jīvaka, and crushed the five hundred followers of Devadatta; his voice seeking the Buddha reached across worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—his virtue is difficult to extol.

The Commentary states: "This is translated as 'Drinking Light' (Kāśyapa). Paramārtha and others likewise translated it as 'Drinking Light,' while ancient translators called him 'Turtle-clan' (Kauruṣya).
His ancestors practiced the Way, and a numinous turtle responded by bearing a divine chart; consequently, he took this as his clan name."
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In Rājagṛha there was a wealthy householder named Kapila; his wife’s name was Dhanā; his son’s name was Piṇḍola; and his daughter-in-law’s name was Bhadrā."
His family was a thousand times more prosperous than that of King Bimbisāra, such that none among the sixteen great nations could rival them as neighbors.
"Pippala" is the name of Kāśyapa; it was given because his father prayed at this tree when he was born.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Fu fazang zhuan*) states: "After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the golden image within his stūpa became damaged and tarnished.
At that time, there was a poor woman who obtained a gold bead and requested a craftsman to beat it into a thin leaf of gold."

The goldsmith was filled with joy; having finished polishing and refining the Buddha image, he and his wife made a vow that for ninety-one kalpas, throughout their lives in the heavens and among humans, their bodies would always be golden in color and they would constantly experience happiness.
Finally, it was the turn of the Kāśyapa couple.
Fearing that they would incur the King’s displeasure by being surpassed, they reduced their plow by one and used only nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of oxen for the golden plow.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "In that household there was felt wool; even the lowest grade was worth a hundred thousand taels of gold.
If one were to drive a nail ten feet into the ground, the felt would not be pierced or torn, remaining exactly as it was."
"Sixty storehouses of gold and grain, with each storehouse containing three hundred and forty *hu*.

Furthermore, a sutra states: "By offering wheat porridge to a Pratyekabuddha, one will perpetually ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for a thousand rebirths each time to enjoy bliss; though their body possesses the thirty-two marks, it is spoken of only as being golden in color."
The Jāmbūnada gold lies at the bottom of turbid water; its radiance penetrates through the water, yet it vanishes in the deep darkness.
The bodily radiance of Kāśyapa surpasses this golden light, illuminating an area of one yojana.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among those who practice the twelve dhūtas and difficult ascetic practices within the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost.
As for the phrase "distinguishing him from other Kāśyapas," this refers to such individuals as Daśabala-Kāśyapa, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, and others.
The Commentary states: “Revata is here translated as ‘Śi-xīng’ (Room Star); this interpretation is consistent with both ancient and modern explanations.
The *Lotus Sūtra* renders it as Lípóduō, while the new translation gives Xié lì fá duō; these correspond to the variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation.
The phrase "some say 'that which is offered'" is an explanation of the phonetics and meaning.
"Provisional combination" is the same in both ancient and modern usage.

Regarding the commentary’s reference to "the matter of the two ghosts eating people in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*," it refers to a person traveling through an empty pavilion who stayed overnight and saw two ghosts struggling over a corpse, each claiming, "I brought this here first."
The two ghosts said together,
"Let us divide it.
This man actually saw the small ghost bring it, and when he was questioned by the ghosts, he thought to himself in secret:
"I have brought this according to my word; if he does not obtain it, he will surely harm me.
It is better to die speaking the truth than to die having spoken a falsehood."
He then answered truthfully, and the younger one brought it.
The great ghost tore off his hands and feet and ate them as he went along; the ghost who had obtained the corpse then took the dead man’s hands and feet and restored them accordingly.
After the ghost had finished eating, it wiped its mouth and departed.
When dawn came, [the king] was filled with grief and distress; he could not discern whose body it had been, and spoke of it as a mere provisional combination.
He initially harbored constant doubts, saying:
"If it were my own body, I would see it being pulled out with my own eyes;
if it were another's body, it would still follow me wherever I go or stay.
Thus, filled with doubt and hesitation, he questioned everyone he encountered:
"Do you see my body?
When the assembly of monks saw him, they said,
"This person is easy to deliver."
He then said to him:
"Your body was originally the remains of another; it is not your own.
Upon realizing that this was a mere composite, he immediately attained the Way.
Because he constantly asked [questions], it is said that he "constantly makes sounds.

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "born into an empty room": the physiognomist’s divination declared this to be an auspicious sign; thus he was called Śubhavyūha (Auspicious) and also called Ākāśagarbha (Empty-Womb), the meaning of which is one and the same.

He was foremost in the realization of emptiness and attained the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention). Because he manifested the granting of merit to those who made offerings to him, he is called Śubhūti (Good Fortune).

Regarding the passage in the commentary concerning "Aniruddha" and so forth: it is also called Aniruddha, or Āniruddha, or Āniruddha; these are all variations of the Sanskrit sound according to regional dialects.
All say it is "without cessation," and also say it is "without poverty.

Regarding the phrase "the gift of a single meal," the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "During a famine at the end of the era of Buddha Puṣya, there was a pratyekabuddha named Liṭa who went begging with an empty bowl and obtained nothing."
A certain poor man saw him and felt pity; he said, "Noble sir!
Would you be able to accept some millet?"
He immediately offered her what he had been eating.
After she had finished eating, he performed the eighteen transformations.
Later, while gathering wild millet, a rabbit leaped up and embraced his back; it then transformed into a corpse, and having no companion, he was able to escape.
When he waited for darkness to return home, he laid it upon the ground, and it became a man made of gold.
As he pulled out his fingers, they grew back immediately; though he used them, they emerged again, inexhaustible.
An evil person informed the king of this, wishing to come and seize it, but saw only a corpse.
"What he beholds is precisely gold and treasure.
This refers to the present retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*).
"Ninety-one times" refers to the karmic fruition (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, "after his birth, the family's wealth became abundant and increased day and night.
His parents, wishing to test him, sent away empty vessels; upon opening them to look, they found them filled with a hundred flavors."
Furthermore, daily there were sixteen thousand people under his tutelage collecting debts and sixteen thousand returning their principal.
After he had left the household life, wherever he went, people saw him with joy; whatever they wished to obtain was no different from being in their own homes.
"He was the younger brother of the World-Honored One and the second son of King Droṇodana.
Regarding the commentary on "Nanda" and so forth, this refers to Nanda the Cowherd.

Regarding the commentary on "Kapphiṇa": the commentary explains that according to the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations) and other older translations by the Mahāyāna school and Tiantai masters, this is rendered as "Housing Star" (Fángxiù).
However, there are two meanings:
first, because his parents prayed to this lunar mansion star and were moved to give birth to this son; second, it is said that he shared the same room and stayed under the same roof as the Buddha.

This refers to when he first went forth as a monk and had not yet seen the Buddha; setting out toward the Buddha’s dwelling, he encountered rain at night and took shelter in a potter’s hut, using grass as his seat.
Later, another bhikṣu arrived seeking lodging, whereupon he pushed his grass seat aside to give it to him and sat upon the ground himself.
In the middle of the night, they asked one another,
"Where do you wish to go?
They replied:
"I seek the Buddha.
Thereupon, the latter bhikṣu preached the Dharma and departed; [the seeker] attained the Way with sudden clarity.
The latter bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, regarding those who well know the stars, the sun, and the moon, Kapphiṇa is foremost.
Thus, his name is likewise derived from that which he knows.

The commentary states: "Kātyāyana" refers to the Mahāyāna master’s explanation; it means that in ancient times there were many sages who lived for a long duration in quietude within the mountains. As their hair and beards grew somewhat long, no one would shave them, yet according to the Brahmanical law, shaving the hair is essential.
A certain seer had two sons who both came to visit their father; the younger one then shaved the heads of the various seers for them.
The seers vowed to protect him, and later he attained the Way of the Seers. From that time on, this lineage has been called the "Shaving" clan.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Pūrṇa is fully called Maitrāyaṇīputra,” the Sanskrit name is Maitrāyaṇīputra.
“Pūrṇa” (Full) is the father’s name.
When the father was praying to Brahmā by the riverbank for a son, it happened that the river was at its full.

Furthermore, he dreamed that vessels made of the seven treasures, filled with jewels, entered his mother’s womb; his mother subsequently conceived a child, and because his father’s wishes were fulfilled thereby, the name was established from this.
His mother’s name was Maitrāyaṇī, which translates as "Compassionate Conduct."
It is also said that this name exists within the four Vedas; his mother recited it, and thus it became his name.
"Ni" is a feminine suffix.
By applying the mother's name to the son, he is called "Maitreya" (the Son of Maitrī).
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "In being able to extensively explain and analyze the principles of meaning, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is the foremost.
Regarding the commentary’s reference to what is "explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Yinyi*," the *Yinyi* provides a brief explanation, which has already been cited above.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* frequently discusses dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), citing such sūtras as the four Āgamas.
However, when listing their names, it does so either according to the superiority or inferiority of their virtuous conduct, or according to the chronological order of their renunciation.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was among those at the very beginning.

The *Kṣāranirdeśa-sūtra* (or *Bao'en jing*) says: "First he converted the five bhikṣus; next he converted fifty disciples of Yaśas; next he converted five hundred disciples of Uruvilvākāśyapa; next he converted three hundred disciples of Gayākāśyapa; next he converted two hundred disciples of Nadīkāśyapa; next he converted one hundred disciples of Śāriputra; and next he converted one hundred disciples of Maudgalyāyana. Now, taking these large numbers together, they total one thousand two hundred and fifty people."

If the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra* also provides the specific years, it states: "In the first year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he converted the five bhikṣus; in the second year, the three Kāśyapas; and in the fifth year, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana."
Consequently, there were many more thereafter;
thus, at the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were twelve thousand arhats, followed by two thousand who were both learners (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Here, only five hundred are mentioned, arranged according to their superior and inferior status, which corresponds to the first part of the third assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Because the essential nature and virtues of the recipients are largely identical, their Buddha names and titles are likewise the same;
yet, with respect to the present "Sudden" (Honmon) teaching, they are all great Bodhisattvas, and thus they are singled out for mention.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The many shared recollections [refer to] the first ten phrases among those requested regarding the fruition”: the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is identical to the aforementioned power of the Tathāgata, and the majestic adornments are identical to the aforementioned body of the Tathāgata; thus, the spheres of activity are entirely the same.
"Play" refers to the aforementioned sovereign miraculous transformations, which are also samādhis because they manifest through samādhi.
"Sublime Excellence" refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, for the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the most supreme.

Sublime conduct (*sucarita*) is identical to the aforementioned "conduct of wisdom" (*jñānacaryā*); majestic power (*tejas*) is identical to the aforementioned "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*); and sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is identical to the aforementioned "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
thus, they are all the same. Regarding the mental reflections mentioned previously, the Buddha has already shown them to you, yet you have failed to perceive them.
Below the phrase "The multi-storied pavilion is like space," there is a brief indication of the aforementioned miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi*) and modes of play (*vikrīḍita*).

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "the *Lotus Sūtra*’s playful supernatural powers" (*dharmaparyāya-vikrīḍita-abhijñā*), this cites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to distinguish [this teaching] from others; it also serves as a general rebuttal to potential objections.

Regarding the present statement on "distinguishing differences," this refers to what the four great śrāvakas themselves recounted in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:

"When the World-Honored One had been preaching the Dharma for a long time in the past, I was seated there with my body weary and exhausted; I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and my mind took no pleasure in the Bodhisattva teachings, the playful exercise of supernormal powers, the purification of Buddha-lands, or the maturing of sentient beings."
This refers to "hearing it but not rejoicing.

The following verse provides the reason for this lack of joy, stating: "All dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent; they are without arising and without ceasing, without large and without small, and without outflows and unconditioned."
"Reflecting in this way, joy and pleasure do not arise.
The commentary states:
Since one has realized non-arising, there is no joy or pleasure.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "Do not stagnate in profound stillness.
Thus, the eighth stage says: "The true permanence of all dharmas transcends mental conceptions; even the followers of the Two Vehicles can attain this."
Regarding the response to the objection concerning pervasion: why would this prevent them from hearing [the sound], and how could that cause them to hear it?
This point will be explained below.
The section beginning with "Since it is fundamentally... concludes by exhorting the cultivation of reality.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "that which was absent previously," this refers to the fact that previously there were no such roots of goodness, no such eye of wisdom, and so forth.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This section is also like the *Lotus Sūtra*’s own explanation,” etc., this also refers to the "Parable of the Faithful Son" (*Śraddhāparivarta*).
As for the phrase “its own explanation of not finding joy,” it refers to how the preceding passage describes the mind not finding joy, followed by the words “For what reason? and so forth.
As the commentary intends to convey:

"The World-Honored One previously stated that the Śrāvakas possess a final, ultimate fruit, which I have now realized; therefore, the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is not what I study, and thus I do not delight in it."

Having already attained realization, one abides in one's own vehicle; thus, although Śāriputra, who possesses superior faculties, delights in the Ten Powers and other qualities, he nevertheless laments to himself, "I do not possess these things.
Regarding the phrase "one path" in the commentary, it explains the scriptural passage: "accomplishing the path of the śrāvaka."
The phrase "viewing, cultivation, and so forth" includes, by the term "and so forth," both the path of skillful means (*upāya*) and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The phrase "the collection of the abandonment of delusions" refers to "collection" (*samudaya*), which is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); it encompasses both karma and delusion.

Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva’s non-abiding," etc., the term "etc. includes the path of teaching (*śāstramārga*), the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*), the single path, the two paths, and even immeasurable paths.
While names such as the path of teaching and the path of realization are also found among the Two Vehicles, that which distinguishes them is precisely the path of non-abiding.
If one examines their meaning, the teachings and realizations also differ; thus, the word "equal" (*sama*) is used.

In the second section, which clarifies through analogies, there are three parts: first, a general analysis; second, an explanation following the text; and third, a reverse correlation of the ten phrases concerning the deficiency of causes.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a summary of the previous general concession; second, from "Now there are two interpretations" onwards, the presentation of the present correct meaning.
This serves to critique the ancient interpretation in order to establish the present correctness and thereby demonstrate the inadequacy of the former.
Within this, first is the general explanation of the pervasive [nature], which has two parts:

first, the general discussion that establishes the pervasiveness. There are two meanings of "pervasiveness": [1] the meaning of being common to all; and [2] the meaning of being universally applicable.
First, the general application of cause and effect; second, the general application as a metaphor for all subsequent phrases.
Following this, under the section "By means of the harmonizing text," citations are introduced to demonstrate this general application.
This passage consists of three sections:

1. First, the direct citation of the text as proof, which applies generally to Bodhisattvas; 2. Second, from "Furthermore, it is not comparable" onwards, the proof is established through the reverse application of the meaning, showing that it applies generally to Bodhisattvas; 3. Third, from "Furthermore, within the combined text" onwards, the direct citation of the text as proof, which applies as a metaphor for all virtuous qualities.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second is the specific analogy,” etc., this also cites the correct [view] to distinguish it from past errors.
Within this, there are eight parts:
first, the general presentation of the reason for the specific analogy, which is an indirect clarification (*prasaṅga*).
1. "However, although they are distinct," and so forth, distinguishes [the present teaching] from past errors; 2.
"Yet, as for the preceding nine," and so forth, generally clarifies the distinct characteristics of the ten metaphors; 3.
"Among the preceding nine," and so forth, collectively demonstrates the virtuous characteristics of each individual metaphor.
5. From "Furthermore, regarding the first fifty" onwards, the characteristics of the metaphors are distinguished based on those who are deluded and those who have awakened;
6. From "Furthermore, it concerns only the śrāvakas" onwards, the distinct characteristics of the deluded are specifically shown;
7. From "For now, regarding the preceding nine" onwards, as one prepares to explain the text, the individual characteristics of the third set of metaphors are again distinguished.
8. Regarding the passage "Among the preceding nine virtues," it encompasses both the general and specific meanings.
In the commentary, under the section "Now first, the hungry ghosts face the Ganges," the text has two parts:
first, a general exposition of the metaphorical meaning; second, beginning with "As for the hungry ghosts, etc.," a word-by-word explanation of the scriptural text.
The same applies to all ten similes.
Regarding the statement, "one whose portion of birth is exhausted becomes a ghost," it is like a ghost who has already abandoned [that state] and is thus born as a human.
As for the commentary’s remark, "this is the remainder of karma," the meaning of the "three remainders" has already been seen in the preceding text.
However, speaking in general terms, that which consists of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*) is designated as "karma with remainder.

At present, not having attained non-arising (*anutpāda*), not having attained the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and not having realized true liberation, all of these involve conceptual differentiation.

Regarding the phrase "transformed by the suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*): this refers to the remaining suffering, namely the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) within the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*). This is explained from the perspective of those who have already entered the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).

Now, from the perspective of those who have not yet entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* but have already attained *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), it refers to the physical basis upon which the remaining sufferings depend; this is precisely the "suffering of conditioned existence."
In the commentary, the passage beginning with “The view of emptiness is like crows and vultures” and following consists entirely of the remnants of afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, these remnants of afflictions are universally the ground where ignorance dwells (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which is precisely the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
There are two types of cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
first, the obscuration regarding that which is to be known; this is illustrated by the analogy of the karmic obscuration, as it is said to "veil the eyes.

Second, the object of knowledge itself constitutes the obscuration; thus the Sūtra states: "The cognitive obscuration is profoundly blind and dark, referring to the separate adherence to the ultimate and the conventional."
"To now form a definitive understanding regarding existence and non-existence is itself a separate clinging to the ultimate and the conventional; therefore, it is an obscuration to knowledge.
Because a bird returns to the void, it is used as a metaphor for the view of emptiness."
Because beasts rely upon the earth, they are used as a metaphor for those with views.
This differs from the *Lotus Sūtra*, where owls, crows, hawks, and vultures are used as metaphors for the afflictions within the realms.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning "Although they behold the World-Honored One," this clarifies that the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive only their own respective spheres of experience.

When Pañcaśikha and others first received the Way, did they see that the World-Honored One’s body, having just attained perfect enlightenment, pervaded the ten directions and his wisdom entered the three periods of time?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The following [passage] corresponds to the naked ascetics and so forth”: the robe of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the food of practice within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are both the roots of goodness of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The eleven phrases from ‘and the great assembly of bodhisattvas’ onwards,” these refer to: (1) the great assembly of bodhisattvas; (2) the universal entry of bodhisattvas; (3) the universal arrival of bodhisattvas; (4) the universal approach; (5) supernatural transformations; (6) playful sport; (7) retinues; (8) locations; (9) the adornment of the lion throne; (10) palaces; and (11) the dwelling places of bodhisattvas.
Now, the dream of going to Mount Sumeru is, in reality, to go everywhere, to visit everywhere, and to enter everywhere;
the great city of Sudarśana and its various palaces are, in reality, the palaces of bodhisattvas;
the moats, cities, gardens, and groves are, in reality, their dwelling places.
The devas and devīs are their retinues;
the blooming of flowers and the playing of music constitute their supernormal transformations;
and singing, chanting, and playful enjoyment constitute their sporting.
"Wherever one dwells or moves about, there is a seat.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Now, these eight similes below," it also performs a discernment based on the Two Vehicles.

This is because the first simile [of the śrāvaka] possesses only the single virtue of not attaining the joy of the Dharma; therefore, these eight [similes] below possess both the general and the specific.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The samādhis entered by Bodhisattvas, as well as their observations, yawns, and heroic offerings, should be contemplated according to the analogy,” the application of the analogy is self-evident within the text itself.

If explained by way of analogy: the hidden treasure is like samādhi; discernment through wisdom is observation; taking what one desires is stretching and yawning; possessing the power of merit is being courageous; and supporting one's parents is making offerings.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “An analogy for the bodhisattva receiving the prediction,” etc.: if one cannot gather [the fruits], there is no vigor; if one cannot obtain their enjoyment, there is no sense of accomplishment through receiving the prediction.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The five phrases beginning with ‘Analogous to the Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva’,” these refer to: the purity of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s Wisdom-body, the manifestation of the Vow-body, the accomplishment of the Form-body, and the complete endowment of all the marks of a Bodhisattva.

The commentary states: "The five phrases do not go beyond the physical forms and majestic deportment of a bodhisattva. Regarding the phrase "pervasive bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth in the sub-commentary, there are three parts to the text: 1. A general explanation of the term "pervasive bases"; 2. An explanation of the specific characteristics of each of the ten pervasive bases; 3. A summary of their essential meaning. Regarding the first point, the sub-commentary says: "As for the statement 'pervasive bases,' etc., there are three [parts to the explanation]. This refers to the following: first, defining the nature of these meditative attainments; second, explaining how they are cultivated; and third, clarifying their function and purpose. As for the first, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "These are called 'pervasive bases' because they take as their object a single, uniform aspect of a thing and cause it to pervade all directions without obstruction. This means that by focusing on a single characteristic—such as the color blue—one causes that characteristic to extend throughout all space, without limit or hindrance. Thus, they are termed "pervasive" (*kṛtsna*). Because they serve as the basis (*āyatana*) for this mental cultivation, they are called "bases" (*āyatana*). Furthermore, because these attainments are free from the afflictions of the desire realm and are characterized by a state of tranquility and clarity, they are also referred to as "liberations" (*vimokṣa*).

However, since they lack the power to suppress the afflictions of the higher realms, they are not classified as "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*). It is precisely because they can suppress the afflictions of the desire realm that they are established as "bases of totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*). This is the primary reason for their designation. As for the second point, the sub-commentary explains that these ten pervasive bases are categorized according to two principles: first, the distinction between internal and external objects; and second, the distinction between the four primary colors and the four derivative forms. Specifically, one first cultivates the pervasive base of the internal blue color, followed by the external blue color, and so on through the other colors and forms. By practicing in this manner, one gradually eliminates the perception of diversity and attains a state of uniformity. This is the method for their cultivation. As for the third point, the sub-commentary clarifies that the function of these pervasive bases is to stabilize the mind, eliminate distractions, and provide a foundation for the subsequent attainment of the spheres of mastery and the formless absorptions. By mastering these bases, the practitioner gains the ability to transform the environment and the objects of perception at will, thereby advancing toward the ultimate goal of liberation. This is their essential purpose. Thus concludes the explanation of the first part of the sub-commentary.
First, the explanation of the names; second, the interpretation of the names; third, the reconciliation of the meaning of the sutras.
Now, for the first: A verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "There are ten kinds of universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*); eight are like the pure liberations (*śubhavimokṣa*)."
"The latter two pure [attainments] of the formless realm take the four aggregates of their own level as their object.
The treatise states: "That is to say, the eight intrinsic natures are all non-attachment; if accompanied by their associates, they have the five aggregates as their nature."
Furthermore, it is said: "Other masters maintain that the *vāyu-kṛtsnāyatana* (the sphere of totality of wind) has as its nature the wind element among the objects of touch.
As for the statement 'eight,' these are blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, and wind."
As explained in the current sutra, the *Śāstra* states:
"Those who rely on the fourth dhyāna take as their object the visible forms of the desire realm, just like the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
The latter two [liberations] correspond respectively to the two bases of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)."

If formlessness (*ārūpya*) constitutes their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it should be understood that all [meditations] taking intrinsic nature as their object each take the four aggregates (*skandha*) of their own level as their nature.

In this context, the practitioner enters the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) from the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and enters these spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) from the spheres of mastery, because each subsequent knowledge is superior to the preceding one.
In order to cultivate liberation, one merely grasps the general mark of purity regarding the object of focus, yet is unable to differentiate between blue, yellow, red, and white.

Regarding the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), although one is able to differentiate between blue, yellow, red, and white, one is not yet able to produce the mental aspect of "boundlessness."
The first four spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) refer to contemplating each [of the colors] blue and so forth as being boundless.
The remainder is explained in the commentary.

Regarding the spheres of transcendence (*abhibhvāyatana*), the verse states: "There are eight spheres of transcendence; two are like the first liberation, the next two are like the second, and the final four are like the third."

This means that the first two liberations each divide into several categories, making four; the latter four refer to blue, yellow, red, and white. Because they are able to subdue the mind as it takes these objects as its focal point, they are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The Commentary states: “Now, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,” and so forth; this is the second section, which cites the treatise to provide an interpretive explanation.
This section contains five parts:
first, the dual presentation of the Sūtra and the Śāstra; second, from “First, one contemplates blue and so forth” onwards, the explanation of the characteristics based on the *Abhidharmakośa*.
3. From "The first eight rely on the fourth" onwards, the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) upon which they depend are explained, as already cited above.
4. From "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states in the twelfth [chapter]... onwards, their formal establishment is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer beginning with "By these two kinds.
Regarding the phrase "visible form and tangibility," what is the intent of the question?

Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), these are based solely on two: namely, blue, yellow, red, and white belong to the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*); earth, water, fire, and wind belong to the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), because solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are what are touched by the body.
The answer has two parts:
first, clarifying the reasons for establishing the two categories, which involve three points that will be understood below;
second, from the passage beginning with "the eye and so forth," clarifying why the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases) are not established among the ten bases.
There are also three sections, which correspond sequentially to those above.

First, regarding the statement that "the material sense organs such as the eye belong only to one's own body," this corresponds to the previous point that they pertain to both one's own and others' bodies.

Second, regarding "the two objects of fragrance and taste do not pervade all [realms]": this is in contrast to the aforementioned pervasive realm of form; because from the second dhyāna upward there is no nose-consciousness or tongue-consciousness, the two objects of fragrance and taste likewise do not exist.
Third, regarding "the sense-object of sound has intervals": this is said in contrast to the aforementioned constant continuity.
Because sound is heard as soon as it is produced and is not heard when it is not produced, there is the statement that it is "intermittent."

Regarding the phrase "therefore it is not mentioned," this generally concludes the preceding three sections, indicating that among the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), the eight bases of form are not mentioned as *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities).
From the section on the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*) onwards, the explanation of the latter two [sections] is clear.
The Commentary states: "Now that the schools have been distinguished," etc., which is the third section, reconciling the intent of the Sūtra.
This section has two parts:
first, reconciling the Treatise with the Sūtra; [the second part follows].
Below the section "In this manner," the treatise uses the sūtra as an illustration to re-explain the aforementioned celestial *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities).
That is to say, what was previously excluded by the treatise is now all included; by this analogy, the celestial totalities may also be understood to apply to what was excluded.
The Commentary states: "The ninth [section], 'the two heavens following humans,' can be understood.

Regarding the Commentary's statement, "The tenth, the analogy of non-functioning in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)," the meaning of this meditative attainment has already been briefly explained in the sixth stage; it shall now be further discussed.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, this meditative absorption arises exclusively based on the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); all lower stages are termed "possessing ideation" (*saṃjñin*), as their mental formations are coarse and agitated, making them difficult to still.

This level of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*); because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle and easy to bring to rest, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) exists only at the Peak of Existence.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The name and essence of the attainment of cessation are for the sake of dwelling in purity at the Peak of Existence."

This means that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) has twenty-two factors as its essence. This is because prior to the cultivation of this meditative absorption, there are twenty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*) together with the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

Regarding the "twenty-one mental concomitants," these consist of the ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and either interest (*pragraha*) or aversion (*daurmanasya*), for the purpose of entering the attainment of cessation.
There are twenty-two factors of dissociated formations that serve as the locus for this state, which is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The essence of this meditative attainment consists in the successive cessation of that many mental states and mental factors.
If the sixteenth chapter of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, "The Chapter on the Cessation Attainment," states: "Question:

If the intention here is that nirvāṇa constitutes cessation, this contradicts your previous statement that within the nine successive attainments, the cessation attainment is the cessation of mind and mental factors."

Answer: There are two types of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): first, that in which all afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted; second, that in which afflictions are not yet exhausted. That in which afflictions are exhausted belongs to liberation (*vimukti*); that in which afflictions are not yet exhausted belongs to the sequential [attainment] (*anupūrva*).
First, it is called the "attainment of cessation" because it extinguishes the afflictions;
second, it is called the "attainment of cessation" because it extinguishes both the mind and its mental factors.
The extinction of the afflictions constitutes the eighth liberation and is also termed the fruit of arhatship.

If the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 7, states: "The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; or alternatively, it refers to those in training who have realized the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) among the three fruits of the Anāgāmin. Having already suppressed the afflictive obstructions, they are said to have 'nothing left' (*ākiṃcanya*), meaning that all greed for the realms from the 'sphere of nothingness' downward has been extinguished. As for 'greed for the higher [realms],' this is not fixed, as greed for the realms above has not yet been extinguished."
By means of the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*), preceded by mental attention (*manasikāra*), the six non-perpetually active consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are rendered inactive.

Because the perpetually active, defiled seventh mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) cease together with the aforementioned two types of consciousness, they do not function; thus, the body becomes tranquil and harmonious. Therefore, this is also called "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). Just as in the case of a meditative absorption with mind (*sacittaka-samādhi*)—which brings equality to the body and mind, making them peaceful, stable, harmonious, and joyful—the present absorption without mind (*acittaka-samādhi*) likewise brings equality and harmony to the body and mind through the power of the mind prior to the absorption. Thus, it is also called "meditative absorption."
Because it arises from a specific aversion toward perception and feeling, it is also called the "extinction of those" (nirodha-samāpatti), which refers to the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*).

The first fascicle of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (*Xianyang lun*) states: "The attainment of extinction (*nirodha-samāpatti*) refers to one who has already become detached from the desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), or enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), or further ascends into the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), or further ascends by means of the preliminary application (*purataḥ-prayoga*) consisting of the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that conceives of a temporary cessation; thereby, the objects of focus are stilled, and the non-constant mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*), as well as a portion of the constant mental states and mental factors, are extinguished."
The remainder of the text may be understood.

Regarding the commentary’s statement: “Furthermore, the ten preceding metaphors are assigned in reverse order from the end to correspond with the preceding ‘lack of causes,’ while the subsequent ten phrases [correspond to the latter]”—the commentary only cites three of these: first, the metaphor of the hungry ghost facing the Ganges, which illustrates the absence of joy in the Dharma, as they take the joy of the Dharma as their food;
second, the metaphor of dreaming of traveling to a celestial palace, which illustrates not knowing that Bodhisattvas are like dreams and illusions; this aspect is very clear.
The analogy of the three types of fools facing the Snowy Mountains illustrates that [the vision] does not arise from the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the application of this analogy, the Sūtra states: "Because bodhisattvas enter the realm of wisdom and possess sovereign power, they are able to see the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual transformations; this is precisely the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment."
"As for those who hunt, there is no empowerment.

This is the fourth parable of the hidden treasure that is difficult to know; it illustrates how, when the great power of the vows of all bodhisattvas is not initially aroused, one is said to lack the power of merit, which is precisely the absence of the great vow.

The parable of the five blind men who do not see the treasure illustrates that because they originally did not seek the uncommon roots of goodness for supramundane enlightenment, they lack the "eye" to see the treasure; this signifies their deficiency in uncommon roots of goodness.
The sixth is the metaphor of the pure eye being unobstructed; it illustrates that [ordinary people] originally do not obtain the objects of knowledge known by the eyes of the bodhisattvas.
This metaphor further clarifies that [ordinary] people do not see, illustrating that those of the two vehicles do not see the objects of the pure eye.
The analogies for the objects of the seven universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) serve as metaphors because one has not yet attained the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) to purify a Buddha-field.
The pervasive purity of blue and so forth is itself the pure field.

The eighth is the parable of the medicinal ointment that renders the body invisible; it illustrates how, fundamentally, the various roots of goodness for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world have not yet been accomplished.
The "medicinal ointment that renders the body invisible" refers precisely to these supramundane roots of goodness.
The second section, "Heaven Follows Man," is a metaphor for the fact that one who has not originally cultivated the various roots of goodness that give rise to all-knowledge cannot attain it.
When the two heavens see him, he is immediately recognized as a person of all-knowledge; because they do not see such a heaven [in him], this [recognition] does not occur.

The analogy of the ten meditative absorptions not functioning illustrates that, while originally existing during the time of cyclic existence, they do not encourage sentient beings to seek the supreme eye of great wisdom.
If the various consciousnesses do not function, how could there be an eye?
Therefore, one neither sees nor knows any of the six objects.
Thus, the ten similes correspond to the ten preceding reasons; their textual meaning is very clear, so one should reflect upon them according to reason.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The first ten phrases serve merely as general causes for not seeing [the Buddha],” this refers to the fact that one has fundamentally failed to cultivate the roots of goodness for perceiving the mastery of the Buddhas, and has fundamentally failed to praise and explain the specific characteristics of the pure merits of all Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The "non-manifestation" and "contrariety" are not paired with one another, because neither fully resembles the other.
They are merely presented as general causes for non-seeing, intended to demonstrate that they possess both general and specific meanings.
Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with “Third, for what reason,” this serves as an inquiry to establish the conclusion.
The commentary is divided into two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the text; second, the resolution of potential objections.

Regarding the first point: as for the statement "the rest are all according to their respective order," (1) the profundity of the Tathāgata’s realm is concluded by the analogy of the hungry ghost facing the Ganges;
(2) its vastness is concluded by the analogy of dreaming of traveling to a celestial palace;
(3) its difficulty of being seen is concluded by the analogy of the fool facing the Snowy Mountains.
The fourth is difficult to know, illustrated by the simile of hidden treasures that remain concealed;
the fifth is difficult to fathom, illustrated by the simile of the blind who do not see jewels;
the sixth is difficult to measure, illustrated by the simile of the pure eye being free from obstruction.
Seventh, "surpassing all worlds" concludes with the analogy of the meditative objects of the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) concentrations;
eighth, "inconceivable" concludes with the analogy of the wondrous medicine that renders the body invisible;
ninth, "none can destroy it" concludes with the analogy of the two deities following the person.

The ten [non-outflows] are not the domain of all two vehicles; they are compared to the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) because the functions of the six sense faculties are all suspended therein.
This is because the meaning of the text within that section is perfectly consistent with this point.
The Commentary states: "The section 'The preceding dharmas and metaphors' below" marks the second part, which reconciles and resolves potential objections.
This section has three parts:
first, concluding the preceding text to serve as the basis for the objection; second, the objection itself; and third, the explanation.
Within these two [sections], three sūtras are cited to present two difficulties:
first, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to challenge the absence of present conditions.
