Regarding the commentary’s statement, “All are matters among the five fears,” this is based on the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which holds that the five fears encompass all fears.
If this were a new translation of the sutra, there would be verses in the following text that provide a verse for each of these eighteen fears.
The verses on Avalokiteśvara in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise do not depart from these fears; however, fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.
Now, I shall briefly clarify the five types of inclusion.
While these five mostly pertain to the fruit, they are briefly derived from two causes:
First, because one falsely grasps at a self through perverse wisdom and becomes attached to it, there is the misfortune of being unable to sustain life; this is called the cause of the fear of death.
Second, because one’s roots of goodness are meager, there is the cause for the fear of the majesty of the great assembly and the fear of the evil realms.
Now, regarding these eighteen [factors], some possess causes; however, there are two kinds of perilous paths:
if they are worldly perilous paths, they are subsumed under the fears of non-sustenance and death;
if they are perilous because they serve as the cause for evil destinies, they consist of false wisdom.
There are three kinds of distressing heat:
first, the distressing heat of losing wealth, which is subsumed under the fear of not being able to survive;
second, the distressing heat of being among the multitude, that is, the great assembly, which is subsumed under the fear of ill repute.
The feverish affliction of the three poisons is itself the cause of fear.
There are two kinds of delusion:
if one is deluded regarding directions and so forth, this constitutes the various feverish afflictions, which are subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance (*ājīva-śāradya*).
If the mind is deluded, the fear of the great assembly due to bondage is also subsumed under the fear of non-sustenance.
Killing is subsumed under the fear of death.
Regarding the transition into darkness, there are two interpretations:
The fear of being deprived of one's livelihood and the transmigration into darkness are both subsumed under the fear of not surviving.
Transmigration into the dark realms of the three miserable destinies is subsumed under the fear of the evil paths.
The fear of separation from loved ones is essentially the fear of death itself, while also encompassing the fear of not surviving.
The fear of association with the disliked pertains exclusively to the evil realms, while it also includes the fear of failing to subsist.
The fear of physical oppression consists of death and the failure to subsist.
The fear of mental oppression is comprised of the majesty and power of the great assembly as well as ill repute.
The characteristics of the fears of death and non-subsistence—which constitute sorrow, lamentation, and terror—also apply to the other three [fears].

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "that which is capable of abandoning the causes," this refers to the three types of action (karma) of taking refuge in my three [jewels]; these are capable of bringing about liberation and establishing one in right mindfulness, precisely because they are free from the notions of self, what belongs to a self, and false wisdom.

Regarding "The Eighth, the Bodhisattva Rightly Proceeding, Entrusted with the Aspect of True Suchness as a Virtuous Friend": this means that because the roots of goodness accord with suchness, they achieve dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding "The Ninth, Without Bondage and Without Attachment": this means not being bound by signs (*nimitta*) and not being attached to views; because its activity is sovereign, it is called liberation (*vimukti*).
Regarding the phrase "The tenth is the immeasurable entry into the dharma-realm," it is because one dedicates the roots of goodness of the dharma-realm back to the dharma-realm.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Sub-commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
Fascicle 87.6 *Commentary on the Meaning of the Sub-commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle [87].
The Eighty-eighth [Chapter],
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty:
"The Fifth Major Section."
"There are ten virtuous friends who correspond to the ten stages.

Regarding the statement, "The first night goddess, Vāsantī, corresponds to the first stage, the Joyous (Pramuditā)," it is because she has for the first time attained the nature of a noble one, fully realized the two kinds of emptiness, and is able to benefit both herself and others, thereby giving rise to great joy.
Regarding the phrase "Because in the spring season one presides over [the realm]," etc.: flourishing virtue is like spring, for it is harmonious, expansive, and generative.
Regarding the phrase "The sun of manifest conceptual views has already set": on the first bhūmi, one abandons the delusions of view, which are precisely the afflictions of conceptualization.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase “mastery of both the doctrine and its exposition,” this has already been cited previously; it refers to the intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
Thus, the third fascicle of that sūtra states: “The Buddha told Mahāmati:
‘The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of mastery: namely, mastery in exposition and mastery in the fundamental doctrine.’”
The "penetration of teaching" (*deśanā-prativedha*) refers to preaching various sūtras in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings; this is called the penetration of teaching.

The "penetration of one's own school" (*sva-śāsana-prativedha*) refers to practitioners who, having abandoned the various delusions manifested by their own minds, do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither; they transcend all mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), personally realizing the realm of the noble ones (*ārya-gocara*), and because they are free from the characteristics of views produced by causes, they cannot be known by any heterodox teachers, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas who fall into the two extremes. I call this the penetration of the dharma of one's own school.
The commentary states:
This refers to first realizing that there is only mind.
It means not falling into lower [realms], whereby objects of perception are extinguished.
Transcending all that is inferior, even the "grasper" (the subject) does not exist.
Regarding the phrase "the noble self-awakening," one correctly awakens to one's own mind without relying on awakening through another.
Because it is free from establishment by the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is free from establishment by causes.
All non-Buddhists are inferior; [this teaching] manifests superiority in contrast to them.

The sutra concludes with an exhortation, saying: "This is called the characteristic of the penetration of one's own school (svapratyātmagatigocaralakṣaṇa) and the penetration of verbal teaching (deśanāgatilakṣaṇa).
You and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this."

The verse says: "My two kinds of penetration are the penetration of the principle and that of verbal expression; the verbal expression is for the sake of instructing the ignorant, while the principle is for the practitioner.

The commentary states: Although this was already cited previously, it is stated again here. In the previous instance, the focus was on the speaker who is capable of teaching; therefore, the penetration of the principle was explained first.
Now, as we are discussing cultivation and realization according to the teachings, we first clarify the "Exposition Common to All" (shōtō).

Furthermore, previously we proceeded from the fundamental [wisdom] to the subsequently attained wisdom, whereas now we proceed from the preparatory application (prayoga) into the fundamental [wisdom].
Because the phrasing differs slightly, the first commentary already cited the preceding passage; now it cites the subsequent one again.
An ancient said:
"The teaching is universal, but the source is not; it is like the sun obscured by clouds."
"The principle-vehicle (zongtong) and the teaching-vehicle (shuotong) are like the sun situated in the void.
In the commentary, "The Dharma-gates are like the stars and constellations," both the dharma and the metaphor are explained here together:
the body represents the essence (*tathatā*), while the stars and constellations represent the Dharma-gates.
The celestial phenomena do not depart from a single body, just as the Dharma-gates do not depart from the essence of Suchness (tathatā).
The same applies to what follows below: "teaching and transforming" represents the great function, while the "pores" serves as a metaphor for true nature.
Regarding the two types of folly and the two types of non-self, these are all as explained in the "Earth" chapter.

As for "the second night goddess, Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, who represents the Vimalā-bhūmi," this means that she possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), because she is free from the defilements of afflictions (*kleśa*) that could give rise to even subtle transgressions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Among the distinct [categories], three are the light of the dharmas of wisdom,” the commentary merely follows the difficulty by explaining three; these shall now be explained again.
Briefly, there are two intentions:
first, an explanation in terms of the general and the particular, where the first is general and the remaining nine are particular.

Among these distinctions, there are nine: first, contemplating external marks; second, recollecting internal virtues; third, knowing that which has been realized; fourth, emitting light; fifth, constant radiance; sixth, transformations; seventh, the perfect voice; eighth, names and titles; and ninth, the maturing of sentient beings.
Second, the explanation according to the ten bodies:
first, the Bodhi-body;
second, the Body of Marks and Signs; [and so forth].
Third, the wisdom body;
fourth, the dharma body;
fifth, the vow body, as in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*), where the emission of light from the pores is due entirely to past vows.
Sixth, the body of merit;
seventh, the transformation body;
eighth, the body sustained by power, because it sustains the Dharma with a perfect voice throughout the future.
Ninth, the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), so named because it is established according to the will;
tenth, the body of majestic power (*anubhāva-kāya*).
The conclusion states: "Because of its sovereign power (*prabhāva*)."
The ten bodies are simultaneously manifested, with both internal and external aspects fully present; if one focuses one’s mindfulness solely upon this, what practice could not be accomplished?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, it clarifies that the *pratyavekṣaṇā-yathābhūta-dhyāna* is identical to the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna,” the second chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* explains that there are four types of dhyāna. The sūtra says: “Mahāmati!...”
There are four kinds of dhyāna.
What are the four? They are:
the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna that examines meanings, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
What is the meditation practiced by fools?

It refers to practitioners among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who take as their primary focus attachment to the marks of selflessness of persons, intrinsic nature, common characteristics, skeletons, impermanence, suffering, and impurity.
Thus, by observing without differentiation and progressing further and further, yet without eliminating mental conceptions, this is called the dhyāna practiced by fools.
What is the dhyāna that contemplates the meaning?

This refers to the selflessness of persons regarding both their intrinsic nature and common characteristics; the absence of intrinsic nature in both self and other according to the non-Buddhists; and having already contemplated the selflessness of phenomena, the progressive advancement in the meaning of the characteristics of those stages—this is called the dhyāna of contemplating meaning.
What is the dhyāna that takes reality as its object?
It refers to the non-arising of conceptual constructions regarding the two kinds of selflessness within the realm of reality; this is called the dhyāna that takes reality as its object.
What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna?

It refers to entering the practice of the Tathāgata-stage, abiding in the three kinds of bliss through the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization, and accomplishing inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna.

Therefore, the verse says: "The dhyāna practiced by ordinary beings, the dhyāna that contemplates the meaning of signs, the dhyāna that takes reality as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
The commentary states:
Regarding the ancient correlations of these stages, there were two masters.
One interpretation states:
first, ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle; second, from the first to the seventh bhūmi; third, from the eighth bhūmi upward; and fourth, the stage of Buddhahood.
A second interpretation, the Great Cloud, states:

"Furthermore, from the initial stage of ordinary beings and śrāvakas, through the twenty stages of faith up to the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the third is the stage of application (*prayoga*), and the fourth is from the first bhūmi up to the Buddha-bhūmi; because they have realized suchness (*tathatā*), they are all called Tathāgatas."
"If one practices contemplation, an ordinary person may directly employ the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
In this passage, the third [case] is identical to the fourth, and differs from the first two.
The first two stages are those of ordinary beings and small vehicles; this is because they have not yet abandoned the notion that dharmas lack self-nature (*dharmanairātmya*).

Consequently, the third and fourth stages involve the mutual penetration of cause and effect: seeing the Buddha-dharmadhātu is the meaning of taking the Suchness as one's object, and being without grasping or entering is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "Moreover, Tathāgata-dhyāna does not obstruct... and below, the text extensively explains benefit and bliss; therefore, the commentary contains ten sections.
As for the phrase "not entirely the same as the eight negations in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*," it is called "largely the same" because it is not identical in every respect.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and other texts are for the most part entirely identical; because the principle is fully encompassed by the "eight negations," they are said to be entirely the same.
The first four [negations] are entirely identical, while the latter six are condensed into four.
Regarding the statement, "That which is neither real nor false is precisely the non-eternal," there are two meanings of "eternal":
first, the false conceptualization that birth and death are eternal; now, by saying it is not false, it means it is not eternal.
Second, supramundane real dharmas are called "permanent"; yet now you say they are not real, and thus they too are impermanent.
This is because, within the true mark of all dharmas (*dharmatā*), there is neither reality nor unreality.
Regarding the statement, "That which neither transmigrates nor perishes is precisely non-interruption," there are two types of interruption:
first, the transmigration of worldly phenomena, which constitutes cessation; second, the destruction of afflictions, which constitutes the virtue of abandonment.
Now, these are not refuted, and therefore they are not severed.

Furthermore, regarding these ten phrases, the majority of the headings concern the essence (*tattva*), while the majority of the explanations concern the function (*vṛtti*); this clarifies that essence and function are both non-dual.
These may also be summarized as five pairs of essence and function:
first, neither coming nor going, which is the essence-function of the self-substance;
second, non-arising and non-ceasing, which is the essence-function of the characteristics.
Third, non-substantiality and emptiness are the nature and function of the essence;
fourth, non-transience and non-destruction are the nature of the essence and function;
fifth, the single characteristic and the absence of characteristics are the virtues of the essence and function.
As explained in the "Ten Practices" (*Daśabhūmika*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The section beginning with ‘subsequently contemplating’ correctly reveals the four dhyānas,” this means that the Tathāgata-dhyāna guides the four dhyānas; it is not the same as the four dhyānas that serve as provisional stations in the third stage.
The four dhyānas differ from one another, thus constituting four distinct types.

Although they vary in scale—whether great or small—the number of their constituent factors (aṅga) and the names of their qualities are identical in all cases, totaling eighteen branches, as detailed in the third stage.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) subsumes all [factors] into four categories:
first, the obstacles to be abandoned; second, the factors of antidote; third, the factors of benefit; and fourth, the samādhi that serves as the basis for both.
Among the four [dhyānas], the latter three are factors (*aṅga*), while the first one is not a factor; this is as previously explained.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "having abandoned one's own sorrow" (*sva-śoka-vigata*): this is stated in terms of the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*); in the first dhyāna, one has already abandoned the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
Now, through great compassion and protection, one takes on the suffering of sentient beings as one's own.
Since suffering is that which must be abandoned, yet one now feels joy upon considering the suffering of others, this constitutes a benefit.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In the second dhyāna,” etc.: the second dhyāna possesses four factors—inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
First, it clarifies the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), which are the obstacles to be abandoned.
The Commentary states: "Next, 'gathering all sentient beings into one mind' means because they are gathered by the one mind.

However, the term "one mind" appears in the *Sūtra on the Three Stages*; thus, that sūtra says: "With the cessation of applied and sustained thought, internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, one dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss."

However, "one-pointedness of mind" (ekāgratā) signifies the meaning of internal tranquility (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); "without vitarka and vicāra" signifies the meaning of purity. Possessing these two factors is called internal purity.

Furthermore, while internal purity in the Hīnayāna consists merely of faith (*śraddhā*), internal purity in the Mahāyāna comprises the three factors of the second dhyāna: equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).

These three mental states are still obscured by joy; their functional power is not yet predominant, as they can only abandon external vitarka and vicāra. Therefore, they are combined into "internal clarity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
Now, in gathering sentient beings, because they are gathered with a single mind, the sense of "combining" is already present.
In the commentary, regarding the phrase "within the third dhyāna," it possesses five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, joy, bliss, and concentration; the rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "within the fourth dhyāna," the fourth dhyāna has four factors: equanimity, mindfulness, neutral sensation (adukkhamasukhā vedanā), and concentration.
Now, the simultaneous disappearance of these four factors constitutes the obstacle to be abandoned.
The factor of "purity of equanimity and mindfulness" serves as the remedial factor.
Since there is neither suffering nor pleasure, this constitutes neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which serves as the factor of benefit.

However, even the equanimity that abandons [suffering] for the sake of worldly benefit is regarded as a form of feverish affliction from the perspective of the supramundane; therefore, the present commentary states: "Within lower suffering, one perversely gives rise to the perception of pleasure."
Since all things have been extinguished, even relinquishment itself is relinquished; this is true relinquishment.
The rest is as explained in the third stage (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “cultivating the contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth,” the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness refers to impermanence, suffering, impurity, non-self, and so on; the phrase “and so forth” includes the ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*), as these are largely identical to the ten perceptions in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding the "ten perceptions," the treatise states: "First, the perception of impermanence; second, the perception of suffering; third, the perception of non-self; fourth, the perception of the impurity of food; fifth, the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; sixth, the perception of death; seventh, the perception of impurity; eighth, the perception of abandonment; ninth, the perception of detachment; and tenth, the perception of exhaustion."
Now there are thirteen [deities], hence it is said they are largely the same.

"The third, the Night Goddess Observing Beings with Joyful Eyes, who is entrusted to the Radiant Ground (Prabhākari-bhūmi)," means that she has accomplished supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇī of the Dharma, and is thus able to emit the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of “the bodhipākṣika factors for delivering sentient beings through supernormal powers” and so forth: since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* sets forth four types of bodhisattva practice—the first being the practice of the pāramitās, which has already been explained at length above—the remaining three are now enumerated.

The Commentary states: "The subsequent category applies to other practices. This refers to those who fully possess the four types of bodhisattva practice. First is the practice of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); because from the initial generation of the mind one accumulates merit that all assists toward enlightenment, these are the factors of enlightenment.
"Second, entering all samādhis" and below refers to the practice of samādhi.
"Third, attaining the pure divine ear" and below refers to the practice of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Attaining the liberation of a bodhisattva" and below refers to the practice of maturing sentient beings.
Therefore, the concluding summary states: "To analytically demonstrate the maturation of sentient beings.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "not yet understanding the self-nature of the mind": in the previous kalpa, one had not yet attained the stage of self-maintenance (*svabhāva*) of the ten abodes; in this kalpa, one has not yet attained the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*) of the ten abodes.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “not yet having attained the profound conforming patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) of the sixth stage,” this is because one attains the superior grade of conforming patience at the sixth stage.

From the passage “the wondrous and victorious eon” (*vimalakalpa*) onwards, there is no concluding statement regarding attainment; thus, it should be understood that one has not yet attained the seventh stage.
In the preceding kalpa, it was merely stated that he "practiced the most supreme path," which implies he had already attained the sixth bhūmi.
Regarding the commentary’s remark, "Therefore, the name of that kalpa also accords with the meaning of the bhūmi," this is another explanation provided by the author of the sub-commentary (shu).
The first eon is named Śāntanirghoṣa; having attained the first bhūmi therein, it is so called.
The second is Devottara; "deva" here carries the sense of "pure," which likewise accords with the removal of stains (*vimalā*).
The third is Brahmajyotis, which accords with the Radiant (*prabhākārī*) bhūmi.
The fourth is the Moon of Merit (*Guṇacandra*), which accords with the stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*), because the moon possesses radiance and emits blazing flames.
The fifth is Tranquil Wisdom (*Śāntamati*), which accords with the increase of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The sixth is Skillful Manifestation (*Sudarśana*), which accords with the stage of Good Manifestation (*Sudurjaya*).
Seventh is the stage of the King of Firm Accumulation (*saṃbhāra-dṛḍha-rāja*), because his application of effort is perfected and he has already attained unshakable skillful means (*upāya*).
Eighth is the stage of the Exquisite Kalpa (*praṇīta-kalpa*), because it accords with the immovable state (*aniñjya*) and is free from effortful application (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
There are nine thousand merits because of the rank of the Dharma Master.
There are ten adornments of non-attachment, for the two adornments—the non-attachment of wisdom and [the non-attachment of merit]—are fulfilled.

Regarding "The Fourth, the Night Goddess Subhūṣaṇā Praṇidhānavatī, who is entrusted with the Stage of Blazing Wisdom": this means that by abiding in the most excellent factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), she burns the fuel of afflictions, and thus the flames of her wisdom increase.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The latter two phrases refer to Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi),” the reason it does not mention the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is that the ten stages are already manifest in the text of the preceding two phrases;
since the meaning of the remaining stages is obscure, they are specifically pointed out here.

The Commentary states: "Manifest true diligence arises from meditative concentration. True diligence is so called because it is detached from body and mind; without meditative concentration, this does not exist.

Regarding the "Fifth Night Goddess, Ocean of Silent Sounds, who represents the Ground Difficult to Conquer": this means that the practices of the two wisdoms—of the ultimate and the conventional—are mutually contradictory, yet they are brought into union and made to correspond, which is extremely difficult to achieve. Thus, it is called "Difficult to Conquer."
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "In the latter response, it is divided into four," the commentary text consists of three parts:
first, a general outline; second, a detailed analysis starting from "In the question"; and third, the explanation of the text starting from "Now, the first."
Regarding these two [sections], because the answers do not follow the sequence of the questions, there are four points within them:

first, the formal resolution of the objection regarding the lack of sequence; for the first answer corresponds to the third question, the second to the first, the third to the fourth, and the fourth to the second, thus constituting a non-sequential order.
The present explanation clarifies the intent as follows:

among the questions, the first two concern that which is to be established (*sādhya*), while the latter two questions are both means of establishment (*sādhana*). The third question establishes the first [point], and the fourth establishes the second.
Therefore, in the present response, the third [reason] that establishes serves to establish the first [point] to be established; thus, the third is answered first, followed by the first.
The fourth [reason] that establishes serves to establish the second [point] to be established; thus, the fourth and the second are answered last.
Second, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, by virtue of being able to give rise to that which is produced" serves as a general rebuttal to an objection.
The objection states:
"The sequential pairing of terms is very clear in terms of their logical relationship; why, then, in the two pairs of questions, is that which is produced explained first?"
Why, in the response, is the "capable of establishing" (the proof) answered first?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
because the object to be established is established by means of that which is capable of establishing it, the "capable of establishing" is answered first.
Furthermore, one should ask:
"Why does the question not first inquire about the capacity?
Therefore, one should answer as follows:
Question: This is because one observes that which is produced and seeks that which produces it.
One infers the cause by seeing the effect, just as with the Four Noble Truths.
The reason the commentary does not explain this is that its meaning is easy to perceive.
Third: Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore, observing within," this is the third response to the objection concerning confusion.
It refers to a question such as:
"If observation (*vipaśyanā*) is that which accomplishes [the goal], why is it that within the answer there is that which is observed (*ālambana*)?"
If that which is practiced is what is to be accomplished, how can there be the practice that accomplishes it within the object?
Therefore, the answer is now given:

although there is an object of observation within the process of contemplation, this is for the sake of accomplishing the observing subject; just as within the *prajñā* there is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), yet this is for the sake of accomplishing wisdom.

Within the sphere of activity, both the subject that acts and the object acted upon are the sphere of activity; just as when Bodhisattvas practice profound prajñā, both the subject who contemplates and the object contemplated are the sphere of activity.
4. "Therefore, the four questions are entirely distinct" concludes [the section]. This citation of evidence serves both to conclude and to critique the ancients.

The ancients held that the first [question regarding] the arising of skillful means (*upāya*) and the second [question regarding] activity (*kriyā*) both answer the question concerning the first activity;

that the third answers observation (*vipaśyanā*), thereby answering both the second and fourth questions simultaneously because the object of observation and the act of observing are inseparable; and that the response to the fourth question—"What is the object of practice?"—in turn answers the third question regarding the arising of skillful means.
If one were to provide this interpretation, not only would the characteristics of the four answers fail to be distinct, but the answers would also be disordered and out of sequence.
Therefore, having completed the commentary on the sub-commentary (*śū*), it now concludes by stating: "The four questions are entirely distinct."

The passage beginning with "Therefore, in the Jin [translation] of the Sūtra" cites the scripture to provide direct proof that within the object of practice (*pratipadya-viṣaya*), there exists the sense of a subject who practices (*pratipattr*).

That is to say, if the known object (*jñeya-viṣaya*) were exclusively the object of practice, whereas the delimited object (*pramāṇa-viṣaya*) possesses the subject who practices; therefore, the commentary states: "It is not merely the observed object, because the 'Jin' realm (*jin-jingjie*) includes the observing subject."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The two texts are mutually abbreviated”: the preceding text contains the name of the *mahākalpa* (great eon) but lacks the enumeration of the *antarakalpa* (intermediate eons); therefore, one should implicitly take the small eons from the subsequent text.

In this passage, only the number of *antarakalpas* (small kalpas) is clarified, while the term *mahākalpa* (great kalpa) is omitted; therefore, one should implicitly understand it from the preceding text as referring to great kalpas.
Thus, there are in total kalpas numbering as many as the atoms within two Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*).

The Commentary states: "If one takes the *Samantaprabhāsa* eon as a single dust mote of a buddha-field," this means that above, the *Samantaprabhāsa* was identified as a great eon (*mahākalpa*), within which already exist small eons (*antarakalpa*) as numerous as the dust motes of a buddha-field.

The present term refers to the designation of a "small kalpa" (*antarakalpa*). The number of such small kalpas, beginning with the "Universal Light" (*Samantaprabha*), passes through as many eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra-rajas*).

Regarding the statement that "two characters are missing," it should properly read: "From here, at the end of his life, he will be reborn again in this very world-system after passing through as many eons as there are atoms in two Buddha-fields. Therefore, by citing the Jin translation, it is established that the character "two" (*er*) is indeed present.

Regarding the statement "The Buddhas are exceedingly numerous": previously, Universal Radiance was taken as the great unit, and within that greatness there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.

Now, Universal Radiance is taken as a small kalpa; within a single small kalpa there are already Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, and thus there have been Buddhas throughout two such small kalpas of atomic proportions.
Because there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within two *kṣaṇas* of minor eons, the Buddhas are thus exceedingly many.

Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the four questions prior to [the section on] *Gen* (艮) all concern karmic activity," this is said in view of the Bodhisattva’s gates of liberation; thus, "deeds and activities" constitute but one among these four.
The Commentary states: "A single profound dharma has many categories" refers, for example, to the nine gates of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and so forth.
"Within each category there are many specific dharmas" refers, for example, to the various types of material wealth within the aforementioned external giving.
"The fifth is 'A Single Gift of Food Having Many Branches.

Regarding "The sixth is the Night Goddess Sarvapura-rakṣā-pramardinī (Guardian of All Cities, Increasing Power), who dwells on the Ground of Presence," this means that by abiding in the wisdom of dependent origination, she brings forth the manifestation of the most excellent non-conceptual prajñā.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The twenty-five existences are non-dual in principle,” the verse says: “The four continents and the four evil destinies, the Brahmā kings and the six heavens of desire, the non-conceptual beings and the five *anāgāmins*, the four formless realms and the four dhyānas.”
The meaning is as explained previously.

Regarding "the seventh night goddess, Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamaya, who represents the Far-reaching Stage (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi)": this refers to having reached the final limit of the stage of effortful cultivation within the signless dwelling (*animittavihāra*), thereby transcending the paths of both the mundane world and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
The Commentary states: "The five turbidities act as the cause that brings about the fruit of the three calamities. Regarding the fruit of the three calamities, there are two types:
first, the minor three calamities, namely famine, pestilence, and warfare, which last for seven years, seven months, and seven days respectively—each being one period of seven;
second, the major three calamities, namely water, fire, and wind, which destroy the physical world (*bhājanaloka*).
This is what was previously stated in the full text of the sutra:
first, it clarifies famine, because Heaven does not send down rain;
second, there are many pestilential diseases, which refers to epidemics.
Third, "running about in the four directions with no one to rely upon" also encompasses the calamity of war.
Furthermore, these three calamities have two meanings:

first, they refer to the time when the kalpa is about to end and human lifespan is ten years; second, they often arise as minor occurrences. Here, it is explained in terms of the latter, the minor calamities.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, one deeply arouses great compassion,” the *Chao* (Excerpts) explains the scriptural text as follows: this compassionate mind is largely identical to the "Accumulation of Results" (*saṃbhāra*) in the Second Ground.

The first [of the ten] provides a general clarification, meaning that sentient beings who undergo the three types of seeking all fall into the bottomless pit of birth and death, from which it is difficult to escape;
the remaining nine are specific instances.
This is further divided into two parts:

first, the refutation of false reasoning through external investigation, which is collectively termed "false" because it involves the arbitrary conception of permanence, bliss, self, and purity within the world, thereby giving rise to afflictions such as craving; thus, [the teaching] causes one to abide in wholesome karma.
The remaining eight lines concern those who practice wrongly; therein, the sentient beings who pursue three types of seeking are specifically revealed and divided into three groups:
first, compassion for those who seek through desire; second, compassion for those who seek through existence; and third, compassion for those who seek through wrong holy practices.
The first two [types of suffering] also have two aspects:
the first three pities concern the faults arising from the enjoyment of the five sensory desires once they have been attained through active manifestation;
the latter two pities concern the faults arising from the pursuit of the five sensory desires when they have not yet been attained.
The preceding section is further divided into three parts:

first, regarding sentient beings who possess no common wealth and who, desiring to sustain their bodies and lives, are oppressed by the sufferings of birth, old age, and so forth, and find no peace; [the Bodhisattva] causes them not to cling to wealth, whereby their minds will find peace.

Second, regarding compassion for sentient beings who never tire of receiving [offerings]: their inner minds are difficult to satisfy, and fearing ill repute or the loss of wealth and profit, they are led to attain the causes of Buddhahood.

Third, regarding compassion for sentient beings who hoard wealth: unable to realize that great wealth brings great calamity, they are called those lacking the eye of wisdom; resolving their doubts and views constitutes the skillful means.

The second [section], "Deluded by the Darkness of Ignorance," consists of the following two gates: the first expresses compassion for those who, not yet having attained the five sensory desires, give rise to faults through their pursuit of them;
the latter three express compassion for those who give rise to delusions, while these two express compassion for those who create karma.

The former gate concerns those who, out of compassion, seek future retribution by performing tainted wholesome deeds; they are like those traveling at night in the dark who lose their way, for whom the torch of wisdom should be shown.

The latter gate concerns those who, out of compassion, seek present retribution while committing various evil acts; they deceive themselves regarding their possessions, envy those superior to themselves, and are turbid with delusions as they seek wealth through flattery and deception.
If one cuts off all evils, the Dharma-body becomes pure.
The second section, consisting of two sub-sections concerning the long-term drifting and drowning [of beings], concerns compassion for sentient beings who possess craving.

The former sub-section concerns the differentiation of the paths; that is, the cycling through the five destinies, wherein the *ālaya-vijñāna* drifts and drowns in the great ocean of delusion and suffering, and thus causes [beings] to ascend to the other shore.

The "rear gate" refers to the differentiation of the realms (*dhātu-viśeṣa*); that is to say, being dragged by the six sense objects and the various faculties such as the eyes, one lacks self-mastery and has no prospect of escape, until one is drawn out by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.

Third, by means of the tenth gate, one brings into the gateway of wisdom those sentient beings who seek false brahmacarya; they practice unrighteous paths, are deluded regarding the principle of non-self, and follow after ninety-five distinct types of false views. Therefore, they are led into the gateway of wisdom.
In the ten types of compassion mentioned above, there are respective antidotes that counteract them, which have been briefly displayed;
the rest is as described in the second stage (*bhūmi*).

"The eighth great vow, the power of diligence, entrusted to the Night Goddess Unmoving" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) flowing on spontaneously, because its characteristics and functions cannot be disturbed by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Now, first, ‘arising from the preceding as being equal to oneself,’ etc.,” the commentary text consists of three parts:
first, the cause for attaining equality;
second, from “equality has four meanings” onwards, the demonstration of the characteristics of equality.

Regarding the statement, "Because one perceives the first, it is not different from the other two," this means that because one realizes and perceives that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is identical, one is thus equal to all Buddhas above and equal to all sentient beings below.
If it is said that [this stage] is no different from the other two, then for the Bodhisattva, it constitutes ultimate identity.
The section beginning with "Precisely because of the eighth stage" specifically explains the reason why this text clarifies their identity.

Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "the thousand Buddhas whom he saves," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the "Tathāgata-āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta," states: "In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas have passed. Thus it is.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “First, clarifying the internal seal of principle and phenomena,” this meaning is entirely identical to the “all-form body wisdom-attainment” (*sarvarūpakāyajñānābhijñā*) within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*; as it has already been explained at length previously, I shall here merely provide a brief outline to present its general purport.
Now I shall explain this further: because one realizes the truth within, external forms manifest. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Question:
'If the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is free from the marks of form, how can it manifest forms?'"
He replied:
"This very Dharma-body is the substance of form; therefore, it is able to manifest as form.

That which has been so from the beginning is the non-duality of form and mind. Because the nature of form is identical to the nature of wisdom, the substance of form is formless and is termed the 'Wisdom-body' (jñānakāya)."
Because the nature of wisdom is identical to the nature of form, it is said that the Dharma-body pervades all places.

The forms manifested therein have no boundaries; according to the mind, they can manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions the infinite bodhisattvas, infinite reward-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and infinite adornments, each distinct from the others. All of these are without boundaries yet do not obstruct one another.
"This cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of mind-consciousness, because it is the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (tathatā). Commentary:
Although that [previous passage] referred to the Buddha, this present stage is at its ultimate limit and is largely identical to Buddhahood.
Next, I shall explain the scriptural text, which consists of three sections:
first, clarifying that the internal seal of principle and phenomena shows that form is itself emptiness;
second, clarifying the manifestation of the physical body through vast great function, because emptiness is itself form.
The subsequent conclusion is profound and vast because it is not obstructed by compassion. Regarding the first [point]:

because one realizes that the dharma-realm has no fixed, substantial form, the entire body is emptiness, yet it is not a nihilistic void; within emptiness there is no form, yet form is not obstructed. Because form and emptiness are unobstructed, and both existence and non-existence, manifestation and concealment, are entirely sovereign, one is then able to manifest various forms according to the inclinations [of beings]. Therefore, one first clarifies the internal realization of phenomena and principle.
In this sutra, the realization of the signless nature of reality is first clarified, followed by the simultaneous understanding of both nature (dharmatā) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa).
Regarding the first part, the phrase "awakening to the equality of the self-nature of all phenomena" provides a general explanation; how, then, is this equality defined?

Next, it says: "Because one enters into the true nature (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. This means that within the true nature, there are no marks of differentiation, no marks of variety, and no marks of multiplicity; since the myriad phenomena are one, how could there be inequality?
Upon what is this true nature established?
Therefore, it is further explained that the means of realization relies on no support; that is to say, it does not rely on form, nor does it rely on emptiness.
If all phenomena relied upon emptiness, then emptiness would have nothing upon which to rely.
Now, the myriad dharmas rely upon the Truth, yet the Truth has nothing upon which it relies; this is the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Non-reliance.
Having abandoned the world, the world itself possesses various distinctions; since even its nature cannot be established, how much less so its characteristics?

Nor does one establish form based on emptiness, nor establish emptiness based on form; there is neither difference nor non-difference, neither identity nor non-identity. When even this view is severed, it is conventionally termed "inner realization."
"Subsequently, one fully knows the distinctions among the characteristics of all phenomena" refers to the simultaneous realization of both nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
First, one clearly understands that characteristics are emptiness, because emptiness is form;
subsequently, "one is also able to penetrate" refers to this nature of clear understanding, because form is emptiness.
Furthermore, in the first phrase, there is no emptiness within form; in the second phrase, there is no form within emptiness.
Moreover, in the first phrase, form can contain emptiness; in the second phrase, emptiness can contain form.
Furthermore, in the preceding phrase, emptiness can manifest form; in the following phrase, form can manifest emptiness, being without obstruction or hindrance.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The second [phrase], ‘yet always... clarifies the boundless great function”: the first phrase in the sutra, “yet it is able to manifest immeasurable form-bodies,” cites what precedes to introduce what follows; thus it says “yet it is able” because, due to the non-obstruction of emptiness by form, it is able to manifest form.

Furthermore, if one regards form as form, one cannot manifest form; now, because form is itself non-form, there is nothing that is not manifested. Moreover, it is precisely form-as-emptiness that constitutes wondrous form;

thus, following from the above, it clarifies that form and emptiness are non-dual. Establishing the aforementioned non-duality of true emptiness and [form], wherein "the non-dual is dual," this is wondrous form. The fusion and identity of form and emptiness constitute the true Dharma-realm; the inexhaustibility of dependent origination means that within the one, the many are manifested.

Regarding the statement that "treatises such as the *Awakening of Faith* clarify that the eighth stage corresponds to mastery over form," the *Awakening of Faith* says: "The fourth is the defilement of the non-correspondence with manifested forms; this can be abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over form."
The commentary states:
How is it known that this treatise belongs to the eighth stage?
Because there are seven stages preceding it and a ninth following it.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. This means that because one realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*) in the aforementioned eight stages, one is severed from the burdens of form; thus, one attains the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) and the activities of the ten bodies (*kāya*), which manifest universally like reflections—this is mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The preceding night deities’ praises of profundity all follow this pattern of dharma and metaphor,” it is because although they mostly inquire about the duration and proximity of the time when [the Bodhisattva] first resolved his mind, the answer concerns the wheel of wisdom, which is the very essence and function [of that resolve].
Nevertheless, these five metaphors are not without meaning; since they have all already been discussed previously, the commentary does not explain them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “‘Bìn’ refers to the amputation of the feet”: in common parlance there are five punishments—*ni* (cutting off the nose), *mo* (branding), *gōng* (castration), *gé* (cutting off the hands), and *bìn* (the great execution).

The Commentary states: "In meaning, he had already attained the fourth bhūmi at that time," because there are one hundred [qualities] in the first bhūmi, one thousand in the second, ten thousand in the third, and one million in the fourth.

Regarding "The Ninth: The Lumbinī Grove Goddess Entrusts [the Teaching] to the Stage of Good Wisdom," it means that she has accomplished the subtle fourfold analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is thus able to skillfully preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “These ten penetrate all six stages,” the sub-commentary contains five sections:
first, a vertical correlation by way of the stages, also termed the "explanation of sequential arrangement" (*xingbu*);
second, from “However, based on sequential arrangement” onwards, which concludes the preceding section and gives rise to the subsequent one, giving rise to the "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*).
3. "If one considers them in terms of perfect interfusion" (*yōu-yūng*) and below provides an explanation that applies to all stages; this is also called the "explanation of perfect interfusion. 4.
"If it is strictly necessary to possess all ten" and below concludes the preceding vertical arrangement.
5. "If it is strictly vertical" and below concludes the necessity of the horizontal arrangement.

In reality, the intended meaning here is that there is no obstruction between the horizontal and vertical [dimensions of practice]; therefore, both interpretations are preserved, as the textual meaning is clear.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Also, the family of birth at the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*)," one might fear this is mistakenly taken to mean the family of birth at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). However, there are briefly six stages of such "families of birth": (1) the family of generating the bodhicitta at the first dwelling;

(2) the family of the holy teachings at the fourth dwelling; (3) the family of *tathatā* at the first stage; (4) the family of birth in the supramundane at the fourth stage, considered according to the provisional positions; (5) the family of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) at the eighth stage; and (6) the ultimate family of birth at the stage of the Tathāgata.
This present stage is the first dwelling, which is precisely the birth into the family of bodhicitta for the first time.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It is the Stage of Pure Mind,” the commentary explains it in response to the specific difficulty; now I shall provide a more detailed explanation.
To speak of attaining the light of the Tathāgata’s bodhi refers to the bodhi of the enlightened mind.
To enter the ocean of a bodhisattva’s skillful means means that, by realizing the ultimate truth and understanding conventional reality, one abandons all realms of existence.
Furthermore, it is because they have already abandoned the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Regarding the accomplishment of mastery, it is because they manifest their bodies in hundreds of lands.
Regarding the cultivation of the bodhisattva’s sublime practices, it is because they constantly cultivate the ten practices that purify the stages (*bhūmi*).
One who possesses the faculties of a bodhisattva achieves all other faculties through the realization of faith.
Furthermore, because great compassion is primary, compassion serves as the faculty.
Since the objects of knowledge have already been severed, the mind is luminously pure.
Because the ten vows have reached maturity, his vows are unshakable.
Because he realizes suchness (tathatā) equally with the Buddhas, he receives the protection of the Buddhas.
When conceptual discrimination is suddenly exhausted, it is called the destruction of all hindrances.
Possessing all these aforementioned virtues, he serves as a refuge for sentient beings.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "precepts, patience, diligence, etc.," the term "etc. includes one [perfection] each from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as they are each increased.
As for the final two lines: the first line concerns skillfulness in the three types of action (*trikarma*), such that all who see him will surely rejoice.
The second phrase concerns the fulfillment of the practice of effort, as all practices are attained through non-effort.
Regarding the commentary’s section from "Sixth, the first of the latter [part]... to 'becoming born into the Buddha-family,'" there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the heading; second, the detailed interpretation.

Regarding the first two phrases: "attaining the patience of non-arising" explains the family of birth, while "conforming to and abiding in the dharma-nature" explains abiding with all Buddhas, because the Buddhas abide in the profoundly deep true dharma-nature.
The preceding section concerns the accomplishment of the stage of pure patience (*śuddhakṣānti*).

From the phrase "all profound dharma-gates" (*sarvagambhīradharmamukha*) onwards, all pertain to the stage of superior practice (*viśeṣacaryā*); since this sentence serves as a general heading, the commentary does not explain it.
Since all that follows consists of profound dharma-gates,
the section on "the excellence of the perfection of aspiration" explains the scriptural passage beginning with "having fulfilled [the practices] throughout the three periods of time.
The section on "the single essence of roots of goodness" explains the scriptural passage beginning with "attaining [the state of] all Buddhas."

This means that they share the same roots of goodness characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*), and they equally accord with the essence of the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From the phrase "from delusion, etc. onwards, it explains the possession of supramundane pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*).
The above constitutes the meanings of the preceding sūtra that were not previously explained.
From "abiding securely" (*anusthita*) onwards, it corresponds to the vastness of the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) in the preceding sūtra.
From "entering the various samādhis" onwards, it corresponds to the cessation of obstacles (*vighna-vinivṛtti*) and quiescence (*śānti*).
The final three phrases constitute the benefit of transformation through the three wheels; as these are straightforward, they are not explained.
Regarding the passage in the Commentary beginning with "Seventh, by the power of the Buddha," both the sutra and the commentary are easy to understand.
If one wishes to explain this: because of the Buddha’s seven exhortations, it is called "entering the power of all Buddhas"; this is the general statement.
From "wandering through lands" onwards, there are two specific lines concerning the swiftness of initiating practice.
From "having fully realized" onwards constitutes the section on the Pure Land, because one attains mastery over the three worlds.

Specifically, the first two [mastery] refer to mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); the next two refer to perfect enlightenment; and the final three refer to preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings.

The Commentary states: "The phrase 'the gate of observing universal wisdom' refers to the virtue of the Dharma Master" means that this is also the accomplishment of the Dharma Master’s skillful means.

Regarding the phrase "in the three natures," the three natures are themselves the transformative teachings (dharmas of transformation), serving as the basis for the accomplishment of wisdom and so forth.
The word "etc. includes the eleven thickets of entry, practice, accomplishment, and gnosis.
Under each of these gates, there is the accomplishment of verbal karma, which possesses the forty kinds of unimpededness; therefore, one is able to expound at length.
The others are all the masteries accomplished by the Dharma Master: first, mastery over samādhi, because he can suddenly expound [the teachings] at will;
second, mastery over rebirth;
third, from the phrase "in the differentiated" onwards, mastery over the Dharma, because phenomena and principle penetrate one another.

From the phrase "knowing principle through phenomena" (*jìshì zhīlǐ*) onwards, the commentary explains this first pair, clarifying how one enters into principle through phenomena (*jìshì rùlǐ*) and enters into phenomena through principle (*jìlǐ rùshì*).
Furthermore, the former phrase indicates that phenomena can manifest principle, while the latter phrase indicates that phenomena are established based on principle.
Furthermore, previously, one spoke of the true mark without destroying conventional designations; subsequently, one established all phenomena without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Moreover, in the former case, movement did not depart from stillness; in the latter, there is stillness without any lack of illumination.
Regarding the "immeasurable" below, there is mastery over the unconditioned.
Regarding the "limited object" below, there is mastery over the vast and the narrow.
Having attained penetration below, one illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional simultaneously.
Because it is made manifest through the text, it is said that one may "contemplate and apply its principles.

Regarding the ninth section, "Universal Manifestation of Adornments," the commentary first explains the title and then, from the words "Having already attained" onwards, provides a general explanation of its overall meaning.
If explained individually, the first phrase adorns the basis, while the remainder all adorn the primary [body].

Within the primary [body], the first three phrases constitute the secret of the body; "manifesting purity" and those following constitute the secret of speech; and "according to their minds" and those following constitute the secret of the mind.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "Among the ten," the scriptural text is explicit; as all [points] accord with the doctrinal principles of their respective positions, to provide no such explanation would truly be to suppress the meaning of the scripture.
The rest is easily understood.

Regarding "the tenth, the daughter of a śreṣṭhin, Gopā, who is entrusted with the Dharmameghā-bhūmi": this means that the great cloud of Dharma-wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues; it covers the coarse residues (dausthulya) as if they were the sky, and fills the Dharmakāya.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase, “the practice of the unimpeded dual cultivation of compassion and wisdom, the inverse and the conformative, the provisional and the real, and quiescence and function,” there are herein four kinds of non-obstruction, which are also termed the four kinds of dual cultivation.
Among these ten statements, each one consists of a pair of practices.
While there are ten distinctions based on these paired practices, within them, the paired practices themselves comprise only four distinct types.

As stated in the first sentence: "How is it that one is not defiled by the afflictions of birth and death while remaining within birth and death? This refers to the non-obstruction of compassion and wisdom; that is, because one possesses great compassion within birth and death, one is not defiled by the afflictions of birth and death, which is due to being endowed with great wisdom.
Second, having realized the self-nature of phenomena, one does not abide in the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; this is the simultaneous practice of quiescence and function.
Third, this is the simultaneous practice of the real and the provisional.
Fourth, this is the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real.
Five is the simultaneous practice of both the contrary and the compliant;
six is the simultaneous practice of both quiescence and function;
seven and eight are both the provisional as it is identical to the real.
The nine and ten both involve the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real; the nine refer to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the ten refer to making offerings to the Buddha.
The eleven involve the simultaneous practice of the ultimate and the conventional, each having its own distinct characteristics.
The Commentary states: "Now, as for the phrase 'the preceding prose section merely names it the Indra’s Net' and so forth, this is intended to clarify the meaning of the Indra’s Net.
Regarding the phrase "first, the complete marks," the Sūtra contains the thirty-two marks; the preceding text refers to these and explains them in detail because they are fully present there.

Now, this shall be explained in brief, following the exposition in the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the three hundred eighty-first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. However, the sequence of those sūtras differs from that of the present one; therefore, I shall list the names according to the sequence of those sūtras and annotate them below with the text of the current scripture.
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha said:
'Subhūti, what are the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata?'"
"Subhūti!

First, the soles of the Blessed One’s feet are level and full, resting with exquisite stability like the bottom of a casket; though the ground be uneven, wherever his feet tread, it becomes entirely level, touching the earth without any inequality. This is the third mark."
2. On the soles of the Blessed One’s feet are the marks of thousand-spoked wheels, with their rims, hubs, and all other features perfectly complete.
3. The hands and feet of the Blessed One are all exceedingly soft, like *tūla* cotton, surpassing all others.

Fourth, between the fingers and toes of the Blessed One’s hands and feet, there are webbed membranes like those of a king of geese, golden in color and interlaced, their patterns like exquisite embroidery. (6)
5. The fingers and toes of the Blessed One’s hands and feet are all perfectly rounded, slender, and long, being exceedingly lovely; this corresponds to the second [mark]. 6.
The Blessed One’s heels are broad, long, and perfectly rounded, being in proportion with his insteps, surpassing those of other sentient beings; this is the seventh [mark].
7. The soles of the Blessed One’s feet are long, elevated, and full; they are soft and exquisite, and well-proportioned to his heels—this is the fifth.
8. The Blessed One’s calves are gradually tapered and rounded, like those of the king of the *eṇeya* antelope—this is the ninth.
9. The World-Honored One’s two arms are long, straight, and well-rounded, like the trunk of an elephant king; standing upright, his hands reach down to touch his knees. 14. 10.
The World-Honored One has the mark of the concealed organ; its member is hidden within a sheath, just like that of a dragon-horse or an elephant king. 11.
11. Each pore of the World-Honored One’s body grows a single hair, which is soft, lustrous, deep blue-black, and curls to the right (29).

12. The tips of the World-Honored One’s hair and body hairs all point upward and curl to the right; they are soft, lustrous, deep blue-black, and adorn his golden-hued body, being most lovely and delightful (30).
13. The skin of the Blessed One’s body is fine, thin, and smooth, such that dust, dirt, water, and the like do not adhere to it.
(27) 14. The skin of the Blessed One’s body is of a true golden color, radiant and brilliant, like a magnificent golden pedestal adorned with various jewels, which all people delight to behold. (28)
15. The World-Honored One’s two feet, the palms of his two hands, his neck, and his two shoulders—these seven places are full and rounded.
16. The World-Honored One’s shoulders and neck are perfectly round, sublime, and exquisite. 13.
17. The space between the shoulders of the World-Honored One is completely filled. (15) 18.
The World-Honored One’s deportment is majestic, full, upright, and straight. (31) 19.
The physical marks of the World-Honored One are refined, expansive, and dignified; in meaning, they are foremost.
20. The body of the World-Honored One is equal in height and breadth, being perfectly symmetrical all around, like the *nyagrodha* tree (32).
21. The neck, chest, and upper torso of the World-Honored One are majestic and expansive, like those of the lion king (12).
22. The World-Honored One’s constant radiance extends one fathom on each side of his face; this mark is included within the second [mark], that of being "delightful to behold.
23. The World-Honored One’s teeth are forty in number, even and level, pure and closely set with deep roots, and whiter than white jade or snow—this is the eighteenth [mark].
24. The Blessed One’s four canine teeth are brilliant white and sharp. 25.

The Blessed One always experiences the supreme taste among all tastes; because the channels of his throat are straight, he can draw up the vital energies through all the joints and channels of his body, such that no disorders of wind, bile, or phlegm can corrupt the supreme flavors.

Because they are unmixed, the channels are free from defects such as sinking, floating, stretching, contracting, impairment, obstruction, or curvature; thus, they are able to properly swallow and circulate the vital fluids (rasa), causing physical and mental well-being and the constant attainment of superior flavors. This meaning is analogous to the three lines on the neck, which correspond to sixteen [channels].
26. The Blessed One’s tongue is thin, pure, broad, and long; it can cover his face up to the hairline. (21) 27.

The Blessed One possesses a Brahma-voice with harmonious and elegant diction; whether the assembly is large or small, all hear him equally, and his voice resounds magnificently like a celestial drum, while his speech is refined and gentle like the call of the kalaviṅka bird. (22)
28. The Blessed One’s eyelashes are like those of a bull king, deep blue and even, without being disarrayed. (24) 29.
The Blessed One’s eyes are deep blue with a bright white sclera, adorned with a crimson ring, pure and distinct. (23)
30. The World-Honored One’s facial orb is like the full moon; his eyebrows are bright and pure like the bow of Śakra; and his cheeks are like those of a lion—this constitutes the seventeenth [mark].

31. Between the eyebrows of the World-Honored One is the mark of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which curls to the right and is as soft as *tūla* cotton; it is fresh, white, and pure like crystal or snow—this is the twenty-fifth [mark].
32. On the crown of the World-Honored One’s head is the *uṣṇīṣa*, lofty, prominent, and perfectly round, like a celestial canopy.
Subhūti, these are called the thirty-two marks of a Great Being.
The commentary states:
The preceding passage has been cited in full according to its sequence.
Compared with this current scripture, it lacks the detail that his circular halo extends one fathom; this is included within the phrase "that which people delight in beholding."
If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the forty teeth are distinguished from the quality of their brilliant whiteness; thus, there are thirty-two marks.
Now, following the sequence of this present sutra, they are listed below, with the order from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* annotated beneath.
1. His appearance is exceptionally handsome and distinguished (the nineteenth).
2. He is pleasing to behold by all people, which includes the fifth mark, being "extremely lovely," and the twenty-second mark, the halo extending one fathom.
3. The soles of the feet are level and full (1).
4. The wheel-marks are complete (2).
5. The insteps are high-arched (7).

16. There are three lines on the neck; this corresponds to the twenty-fifth [mark].
17. The cheeks are like those of a lion; this corresponds to the thirtieth [mark].
18. He possesses forty teeth (23). 19. His four canine teeth are all perfectly even and closely set.
[In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, these two are combined into one, thus also corresponding to number 23; here, they are both expanded according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.]
20. His four canine teeth are brilliant white (24).
21. His tongue is long and broad (26).

The eyelashes are like those of a bull king (aṣṭāviṃśati).
