Commentary:
The above briefly synthesizes two sūtras.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and causes (*hetu*) differ from one another.
Furthermore, there are minor discrepancies, as detailed in the first assembly [of the commentary].

Regarding the gloss on "The Three Jewels and the Woman Seeking Refuge": in the case of women, marriage is termed "returning" (*gui*); thus, the *Zhouyi* contains the hexagram "Return of the Younger Sister" (*Guimei*).
The second major section: "Converging Conditions to Enter the True Aspect.
This commentary contains five parts:
first, the general topical analysis and explanation;...
2. From "However, although people... onwards, there is a critical examination; 3.

From "Since Māyā had already met [the Buddha]... onwards, there is the resolution of obstacles and difficulties, consisting first of a question and subsequently the explanation beginning with "Is it not the case that...";
4. From "Furthermore, this one... onwards, there is a specific presentation of the doctrinal gates.
5. From "The Original Lord of Devas" (*ādideva*) onwards, there is a general explanation of the various assemblies.
This contains two intended meanings.
The first is the meaning of the Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) entering into the mundane world.
The "two" refers to the previous detailed explanation of the convergence of conditions, which ultimately returns to these two.
Under the heading "Now, first," the text provides an exegesis of the passage.
Within the first five [sections], each cites what was attained therein.
“First, Lord, you must maintain right mindfulness without loss” means that he has attained the bodhisattva liberation called ‘Pure Adornment of Unobstructed Mindfulness.’
Second, "He can serve as a teacher of the world" refers to the *Sarvamitra* (Universal Friend) not attaining the Dharma-gate.

Third, from "thoroughly exhausting" (*sarvaparīkṣita*) onwards, it refers to the "Skillful Knowledge of All Arts" (*Sarvaśilpajñāna*); the youth attained liberation and was named Skillful Knowledge of All Arts, wherein he extensively explains the alphabet.

Fourth, regarding "Non-reliance and Inexhaustibility," this refers to the noble and eminent upāsikā who attained the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) that is free from reliance, and further attained the samādhi named "Inexhaustible."
Fifth, "Unattached Purity" refers to the elder Sthira-vimukti (Firm Liberation), who has attained liberation because he is adorned by the purity of unattached mindfulness.
Sixth, "Purity is the Radiance of Pure Wisdom" refers to the elder Sunetra (Wondrous Moon), who attained the liberation named "Radiance of Pure Wisdom.
Seventh, "The Radiance is the Inexhaustibility of the Marks of Wisdom" refers to the elder Anabhibhūsenāpati (Invincible Army), who attained the liberation of inexhaustible marks.

8. Regarding the phrase "If there is no exhaustion, then one’s sincere vow will not be violated": this refers to the most tranquil Brahmin who has attained liberation; his speech is called a "sincere vow" because it is truthful.
9. Regarding the phrase "only then able to return to the illusory abode": this refers to Devasaṃbhava and Guṇākara attaining the Dharma-door of the illusory abode.
The section beginning with "Therefore, although... serves as the conclusion.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the first point, 'Māyā was formerly called the Queen of Heaven': she is referred to as 'formerly' because in the new translations she is rendered as 'Illusion';
she is also called 'Born of Illusion' because she has attained the gateway to illusory wisdom."

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Already able to secretly accord with the illusory gate of vow-knowledge,” this is because the present text says that one possesses the pure *dharmakāya*, manifests the *nirmāṇakāya* through illusion-like karma, and contemplates the world through illusion-like wisdom, and so forth.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “It secretly accords with what will appear below as the Heavenly Queen,” this means that while one will see her manifest physical retribution (the *sambhogakāya*) below in the form of clouds of immeasurable bodies, at this point she has not yet been seen;
nevertheless, it is already known that she manifests her body, hence the term “secretly accords.”
This commentary provides only the general meaning; if one were to allocate them specifically, these seventeen bodies subsume the forty bodies mentioned in the subsequent sutra.
Each of these forty bodies consists of two phrases: the first serves as a heading, and the second provides an explanation.
First, the body born according to one's will, which generally manifests the fulfillment of vows.

Second, the body free from arising and ceasing, which refers to the latter two types of form bodies: namely, the non-arising form body because there is no origination, and the non-ceasing form body because it is eternally quiescent.
The three bodies that neither come nor go refer to the latter two bodies: namely, the body of form that does not depart, because it is not extinguished in any realm of existence;
and the body of form that does not arrive, because it does not emerge from any world.
The fourth is the body that is neither unreal nor real; it also subsumes the two bodies. As the subsequent sutra states: "It is not a real form-body, because it attains suchness;
it is not an unreal form-body, because it manifests in accordance with the world."
Fifth is the unchanging body, which is the indestructible form-body (*rūpakāya*); because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is indestructible.

Sixth is the body without arising or ceasing, which is the non-arising form-body; because it manifests in accordance with the bodies of sentient beings and in accordance with the karma of sentient beings, constantly manifesting a form-body that remains inexhaustible throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.

In the first two phrases above, both are characterized by their "nature" (xing) and explained by their "characteristics" (xiang), which differs from the previous [section] where there was exclusively no arising or ceasing.

All the various characteristics that exist are the body of a single characteristic; as it says below, "the color-body of a single characteristic," because non-characteristic is itself the characteristic.
The eighth is the body that is free from the two extremes; this refers to the pervasive meaning, as both phenomena and principle are without obstruction.
If one were to assign them specifically, it is as stated below: the *dharmatā-rūpakāya* (dharma-nature form-body), because its nature is pure like space;
and the *mahākaruṇā-rūpakāya* (great compassion form-body), because it constantly protects sentient beings.
The first phrase avoids the extreme of existence, while the second phrase avoids the extreme of emptiness.
Furthermore, the first phrase indicates that through wisdom one does not abide in saṃsāra, and the second phrase indicates that through compassion one does not abide in nirvāṇa, and so forth.
Ninth is the body without a basis of support, which is the form-body without a lower locus, because it constantly transforms sentient beings without interruption.
Tenth is the inexhaustible body, which is the inexhaustible form-body, because it reaches the limit of the births and deaths of all sentient beings.

Eleventh, being free from all conceptualization, it manifests like a reflection; this refers to the aforementioned non-conceptual form-body (*rūpakāya*), which arises solely in accordance with the conceptualizations of sentient beings.
Furthermore, as a form-body like a reflection, it manifests birth in accordance with their vows.
Twelfth is knowing the body as being like a dream; that is, the dream-like form-body (*rūpakāya*), because it manifests in accordance with the mind.

Thirteenth is realizing the body as being like a reflection; that is, the form-body that universally appears before others, because it is manifested through great sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*), just as images arise when facing the substance of a clear mirror.

Fourteenth, it is like the body of the pure sun; that is, the pure form-body (*rūpakāya*), because it is identical to suchness (*tathatā*) and free from discrimination, just as the bright sun is impartial.
Fifteenth, it manifests transformed bodies throughout the ten directions; that is, the form-body that transforms all beings below, appearing before sentient beings in accordance with their minds.
Sixteenth is the body that abides without change throughout the three periods of time; this refers to the immovable form-body (*rūpakāya*) below, because it is forever free from arising and ceasing.

Seventeenth is the body that is neither mind nor body; this refers to the general manifestation of its essence below, which states that such a body does not belong to form, for the characteristics of form are like shadows.

Up to and including the Bodhisattvas who have transcended consciousness, because they manifest wisdom as empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, because the verbal expressions of all sentient beings have been cut off, and because they have already attained the accomplishment of the body of quiescent extinction; therefore, the conclusion now states that their conduct is unimpeded like space, surpassing the eyes of all worldly beings, and is visible only to the pure eyes of Samantabhadra.
This brief correlation is provided; although other points may not be fully exhausted, they can be subsumed by analogy.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “That is, the ten kinds of superior practices for purifying the ground in the first stage are abbreviated and out of order,” it continues: “O Son of the Buddha!...”

In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes ten methods for purifying the stages, namely: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity; being free from weariness; knowing the various sūtras and śāstras; skillfully understanding worldly dharmas; possessing the firm power of shame and remorse; making offerings to all Buddhas; and practicing in accordance with the teachings.
The commentary states:
"Making offerings to the Buddhas and practicing according to the teachings is simply the single practice of 'acting as one speaks.
Regarding the phrase "Thus, the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*," etc., the circumstances concerning Aṅgulimāla have already been cited in the *Xuánzhōng*.
Now, I shall directly explain the meaning of the cited passage.
However, following the second sutra, the World-Honored One instructed him to take the three refuges, to which he replied:
"I have only one refuge; the Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Sangha."
This clarifies that there is but one training.
In the third fascicle, the Buddha asks:
"What is this one training?"
The verse says: "The lives of all sentient beings depend entirely upon food and drink; this is the Śrāvaka vehicle, not the Mahāyāna.
What is called the Mahāyāna is eternally steadfast, being free from food."
What is meant by "one"?
It refers to the fact that all sentient beings are ultimately and eternally abiding within the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The second [category] refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the third refers to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*); and the fourth refers to the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), and so forth—all being likewise.
This is what is meant by: "What are the five?
They are the aforementioned five faculties; these belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle and are not the Mahāyāna.
That is to say, the faculty of the eye perceives the Tathāgatas as eternal, seeing them with certainty and clarity, fully perfected and without diminution."
The same applies to hearing with the ear, smelling with the nose, tasting with the tongue, and touching with the body as it does for the eye.
However, there are two versions:
one version reads "clearly and distinctly," while another version reads "definitively and distinctly."
Next, it is asked: what are the six that are so named?
They are the six bases of entry (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); these belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle and are not the Mahāyāna.
That which is called the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is eternal in all Tathāgatas; they clearly perceive the gateway of the six bases, fully possessing them without deficiency in their cultivation.
Hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching are all the same as seeing.
Regarding the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*), it says:
"What is called the sense base of mind clearly explains that the Tathāgata is eternal; one hears no contrary thoughts, and enters the gateway through pure faith."
The meaning is as explained in the commentary.

Throughout the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the nine meditative concentrations, and the ten powers, [the text] consistently subordinates the lesser to the greater and expounds upon the Tathāgatagarbha; thus, the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity are shown to be without deficiency.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "The rest may be understood.
There are two ways in which they may be understood:
first, by analogy with the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*; second, by analogy with the other samādhis mentioned herein.
Regarding the phrase "the flowers of Samantabhadra," although the quantity of these flowers is not specified here, the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra* (Ten Stages) states that they are "without limit."

The Commentary states: "The preceding two are both the substance of abiding and universally pervasive. This refers to three meanings within the gate of the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination:
first, the meaning that all conditions are distinct; second, the meaning that they mutually pervade and support one another; and third, the meaning that essence and function are without obstruction.
What is now called the "substance of abiding" refers to the distinctness of each individual condition.
What is called "pervasive response" refers to their mutual pervasion and reciprocal support.
That the substance of abiding is itself pervasive response constitutes the third [characteristic]: the non-obstruction between essence and function.
However, while Māyā above manifested myriad distinct responses— which constitutes multiplicity within difference—
this single body of Sudhana here faces Māyā everywhere, which constitutes multiplicity within identity.
If we consider Māyā and Sudhana, they are both undivided and pervasive.
Although their modes of identity and difference differ, there is no distinction in the meaning of their abiding essence being universally responsive.
Māyā is likewise a single essence that is many-in-one; because she manifests differently according to what is appropriate, she possesses no dual essence.
Below, it is stated that [the Buddha] does not dwell in a single place nor in many places.
Sudhana likewise shares the same essence such that the many are one; for the Sudhanas in all locations are none other than the Sudhana present before one’s own eyes.
Furthermore, when these two sages are viewed in relation to one another, they both contain the aspects of being of the same substance and of different substances.
Since a single Māyā responds to many Sudhana-s, this Māyā is thus of the same substance [as Sudhana].
Because Sudhana is contrasted with Māyā, Sudhana is therefore of a different substance [from her].
The commentary states: "Without destroying smallness, it contains vastness," which refers to the gate of the non-obstruction between the broad and the narrow.
"Arising without arising" refers to the gate of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "I vow to gather Samantabhadra," the former was based on specific vows, whereas the present is a universal vow; there is no vow that does not encompass all.

Regarding the passage "not encompassed by ignorance" and so forth: the vows and wisdom are mutually integrated, and all are the Great Illusion; thus they constitute the unique *prajñā*, whereby Buddhas arise.

As for the commentary’s statement, "Originally non-dual because it is called the single nature": the commentary follows the preceding point—that these many bodies are precisely this [single reality]—and states that they are originally non-dual because the multiplicity is entirely designated as being in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).
If explained according to the phenomena themselves, it may also be fundamentally only one.
Regarding the statement that it "does not abide in a non-single place nor abide in multiple places," there are four interpretations in total:
the first explains the dual negation solely from the perspective of its essence; therefore, it is not many.
The phrase "it is not like the phenomena" means that principle is of a single flavor, unlike the multiplicity of phenomena.

This second pair is explained in terms of the non-destruction of nature and characteristics: the upper clause refers to the non-destruction of characteristics, and the lower clause refers to the non-destruction of nature; this is also a discourse on the non-destruction of the one and the many.
This first pair refers to the unity of phenomena in relation to their particulars.

The third pair concerns the mutual correspondence between phenomena and principle as previously explained; "correspondence" (*xiangru*) simply means the sense of non-obstruction, and it also signifies the mutual pervasion of phenomena and principle.
The fourth pair is explained solely in terms of the mutual interpenetration of phenomena, which is the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

However, it possesses both the gates of "identity" (*ji*) and "entry" (*ru*), encompassing the characteristics of dependent origination through the fusion of the principle of nature (*lixing*) and the distinction between identical and different bodies (*tongti yiti*).

Regarding the statement, "This explains the meaning of 'wisdom-illusion' within the title," it is because the title refers to "the great vow-wisdom-illusion. Having already extensively cited the vows as the mother of all Buddhas, this concluding summary here explains the meaning of "wisdom-illusion" from the aforementioned title.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The father of the goddess Candraprabhā was named Samprajanya,” this refers to the third assembly, where he questioned the King of Brahma-conduct (*Brahmacaryarāja*).

Furthermore, concerning the mention of “going to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,” this is the heaven where Māyā was reborn after relinquishing her physical form; thus, one knows that Māyā was not exclusively in heaven.
Therefore, the *Jin jing* (Jin Scripture) simply states, "In the city of Kapilavastu.
Regarding the second, Bandhumat, it may be understood.
Within the third section on Viśvāmitra, concerning the phrase "the two 'I's constantly descend to manifest their functional activity," the commentary (*shu*) contains three parts:
First, the indication of the heading and the establishment of the intent; second, the general outline; third, the commentary on the text.

Regarding the first: the statement that "the alphabet is the preeminent script among all arts and the foundation of all teachings" serves to provide the specific reason for this presentation, as it indicates that while [the text] makes known all arts, it specifically explains [this one].
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All dhāraṇīs arise from the differentiation of speech.
The forty-two letters are the root of all letters. Based on letters there is speech;
based on speech there is name; and based on name there is meaning."
If a bodhisattva hears these syllables and is even able to comprehend their meaning—
these syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *ḍa*, with forty syllables in between—
they will attain this syllable-dhāraṇī, which brings about great accomplishment and benefit.
...and so on, as explained at length.

Furthermore, the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Pūrṇāvadāna*) states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva distinguished for each of the youths the origins and endings of their characters, and even instructed and transformed thirty-two thousand youths, exhorting them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."

Thus, one knows that characters (*akṣara*) are the foundation of all arts; therefore, within the *Daśabhūmika*, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are used as a metaphor for being the foundation of all dharmas.
Second, from "There is a heading" onwards, is the general illustration.
Third, from "All say Prajñā" onwards is the commentary on the text.
First is the explanation of the general heading, which contains three parts:
first, an implicit citation of the *Vairocanasūtra*; second, an explicit citation of the *Vairocanasūtra*; and third, a citation of the *Pañcākṣarasūtra*.

Now, first of all, there is a verse therein which says: "The profound characteristic of signlessness is beyond the capacity of those with inferior wisdom; for the sake of transforming such as these, the teaching provisionally maintains both existence and non-existence."
The commentary states:

Since the syllable is existence and the wisdom of its signless nature is non-existence, those who practice the yoga of recitation first contemplate the form of the syllable and subsequently enter into its meaning.

Regarding the contemplation of the form of the letter A, it says: "An eight-petaled white lotus opens all at once, brilliantly manifesting the pure white radiance of the letter A. This is the *akṣara-rūpa* (the form of the letter).

Furthermore, wisdom represents the bodhicitta; realizing that [all things] are fundamentally unborn and being perfectly complete like the lunar disc—this is the *akṣara-artha* (the meaning of the letter).
Because appearance exists while meaning is non-existent, it is said that they are "combined.
Therefore, when this sutra utters the syllable *A*, it is precisely appearance;
entering the gate of Prajñāpāramitā is precisely the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "These characters are the gateway to the true mark (*dharmatā*). They reveal that the three kinds of *prajñā* are inseparable: the characters themselves are the *nāma-prajñā*; entering the gateway of *prajñāpāramitā* is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*; and awakening to non-arising and so forth is the *dharmatā-prajñā*."
Commentary on the Meaning of the Subcommentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Eighty-Eight Commentary on the Meaning of the Subcommentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Scroll Eighty-Nine
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang, the Great Huayan Monastery of the Tang Dynasty.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore, Vairocana... and below: the second section clarifies the citation of Vairocana.
Furthermore, while the preceding section provided proof through meaning, this section provides proof through the text itself.
The phrase "unobtainable" (*anupalabdhi*) is precisely the characteristic of *prajñā*.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures extensively explain that non-attainment constitutes *prajñā*.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī," this is the third section, which cites the *Pañcākṣara* to prove that [this teaching] is a gateway to *prajñā*.
Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “However, as for the first five characters,” this is the second section, the explanation of the individual [terms].
Within the enumeration, these are combined into forty-two sections; the present commentary contains three parts:
first, the individual explanation of the five characters; second, the explanation of the remainder; and third, the concluding summary and indication.
Regarding the first five characters, they are cited according to the *Pañcākṣarī-dhāraṇī-sūtra* to facilitate the phonetic interpretation of Amoghavajra.
However, the ancients did not provide much explanation for this sūtra; the Master Jingfa composed a treatise titled *Xuanfu* (The Whirlpool), which analyzes it through six sections:

first, the definition of the name; second, its essential nature; third, its establishment; fourth, the explanation of its characteristics; fifth, its benefits; and sixth, questions and answers. Even in its explanation of the characteristics, it extensively cites various sūtras, though not in their entirety.

Furthermore, the phonetics of the various sūtras are intermingled; because the weight of the Sanskrit sounds was disregarded, the Tripiṭaka commentators failed to examine the underlying meanings and merely took those characters that were identical in form, resulting in many errors and discrepancies.
For instance, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the syllable *a* is used for *aḥ* and the syllable *ra* is used for *ta*;
such cases are not fixed by semantic meaning, and thus many errors have occurred.
Now there is also a separate chapter that collectively cites ten sūtras and one śāstra:

(1) the *Forty-two Letter Gate of the Avataṃsaka* translated by Xingshan; (2) the four hundred and ninetieth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; (3) a citation from the eighth fascicle of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*; (4) the sixth fascicle of the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā*; (5) the tenth fascicle of the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*; (6) the third fascicle of the *Lalitavistara-sūtra*; (7) the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñā-akṣara* separately translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xingshan; (8) the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-akṣara* separately translated; (9) the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; and (10) the present sūtra itself.

The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the five characters; second, their synthesis into a harmonious whole. Regarding the first part, the *Chao* (Excerpts) extensively cites the five characters and divides them into five sections, each of which contains three elements: 1. The character itself. 2. Furthermore, these fifteen points are subsumed under four categories: the essence, the characteristics, the function, and the ultimate reality. Each of these four categories also possesses three aspects, resulting in twelve points. Together with the aforementioned fifteen, this makes twenty-seven points. These twenty-seven points are further condensed into ten gates, and these ten gates are ultimately unified within the single gate of the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). This is the meaning of the phrase "the five characters are the complete and perfect Dharma-realm. Regarding the second part, the synthesis into a harmonious whole: the five characters are not merely five distinct entities; rather, they are mutually inclusive and interpenetrating. Because the five characters are mutually inclusive, the ten gates are also mutually inclusive. Because the ten gates are mutually inclusive, the twenty-seven points are also mutually inclusive. Because the twenty-seven points are mutually inclusive, the four categories are also mutually inclusive. Because the four categories are mutually inclusive, the single gate of the Dharma-realm is also mutually inclusive. Thus, the five characters, the ten gates, the twenty-seven points, the four categories, and the single gate of the Dharma-realm are all perfectly interfused and non-obstructive. This is the meaning of the phrase "the five characters are the complete and perfect Dharma-realm. This concludes the explanation of the five characters. The commentary states:
In the two preceding sūtras, "arising" (qi) has the meaning of "birth" (sheng).

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The syllable 'a' is the sound of impermanence.

This is because the character *a* (阿) is pronounced with a high tone and a short duration; therefore, it was translated as the character *’o* (噁) at the beginning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Although the terminology differs slightly, the meaning is the same.
Therefore it is said: "The sound 'A' refers to non-destruction.

Fifth, from "If it conforms to the absence of dust" onwards, the letter *ra* is used to interpret the scriptural text, because in many sūtras, the second syllable of a word's meaning is predominantly identical.

The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "'Double-ra' refers to the appearance of defilement; regarding all phenomena, there is no dust."
The *Prajñāpāramitā-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Guangzan) states: "The gateway of RA is that phenomena are free from dust and defilement.
The *Vajraśekhara* states: "RA signifies that all phenomena are detached [from conceptualization]."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Ra signifies that which can destroy greed, hatred, and delusion; it refers to the teaching of the true Dharma, and also carries the meaning of destroying defilements.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one hears the syllable Ra, one immediately understands through its meaning that all phenomena possess the characteristic of being free from defilement, because 'rajas' (ra) is a term for 'defilement' (mala)."
The above sūtras all share the same meaning of "free from defilement" regarding the second letter *ra*; therefore, there is no doubt [regarding this].

Regarding the phrase in the commentary, "The third *pa*," other translations and other sūtras mostly use the letter *ba*; here, we follow the explanation of the meaning for the letter *ba* according to the *Five Letters*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states: “*Pāda* refers to the teaching on the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* says: “*Pāda* is so called because it is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).”
The *Prajñāpāramitā-āloka* (Fàngguāng) states: "The 'lame' refers to the supreme ultimate meaning of the nirvāṇa of all dharmas.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "It utters the sound of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
The commentary states:
The aforementioned sūtras all exclusively clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
however, these merely negate it, whereas only the *Vajraśekhara* says: "The term 'pa' [indicates] that the ultimate truth is unattainable."
This constitutes the complete characteristic of *prajñā*.

Therefore, the commentary states: "That is to say, both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously negated. Following this, it interprets the first two characters of the preceding sutra passage, using the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to dispel the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Now, since there is also no ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the "real" is further dispensed with; when both the real and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are absent, this is the true *dharmadhātu*.
The former refers to that which is illuminated.
From the phrase "all phenomena are equal," the sense of universal illumination is implied.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one hears the syllable *pa*, one immediately knows that all dharmas enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for *paramārtha* is what this [syllable] signifies."
The commentary states:
"This, too, merely enters into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) alone.

In the text, the meaning is first explained; subsequently, from the passage "Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty" onwards, the scripture is correlated.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The letter-gateway 'A' is the entry into the realization that all phenomena are far removed from birth and death, such that neither birth nor death can be apprehended."
The commentary states:
"All conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the very substance of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The meanings of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* correspond to the character "negation" (zhē), as both clarify the gateway to transcending the world.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Regarding the character 'negation,' cultivation is unattainable."
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "To 'restrain' is the meaning of 'cultivation,' for it tames all sentient beings.

The commentary states: "As for 'the five *na*s,' they are separately translated as the character 'nà' (曩), and the meaning is entirely the same.

Within the text, first the meaning is explained according to the *Five Characters* (*Wuzi*), and subsequently, from "that is to say, nature and characteristics both perish" (*wei xingxiang shuangwang*) onwards, the scriptural passage is interpreted and harmonized.
In most sutras, this is the syllable "Na. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states:
"By hearing the gateway of the syllable 'Na,' one enters into all phenomena and remains far removed from names and characteristics."
"Whether it be names or characteristics, all take non-apprehension as their expedient means.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The letter-gateway 'Na' [indicates that] all dharmas are free from names; because their intrinsic nature and characteristics are not identical, they do not lose [their true nature]."
The *Prabhāsa* states: "That which is 'na' refers to the intrinsic nature of the syllables of all phenomena; it is neither attained nor lost. The *Prajñāpāramitā-prasphuta* states:
"'Na' is the gateway to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of names and words; when one calculates their fundamental purity, they cannot be apprehended."
The *Lalitavistara* states: "As for the word 'not' (*na*), it is uttered because it does not follow after sentient beings, being free from the sounds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "The syllable *na* is the sound that universally knows name-and-form."
The *Vajraśekhara* states: "Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is also unattainable.
The aforementioned three sutras all speak of name-and-form; "name" refers to the designation, and taking these two characters together constitutes the intrinsic nature of birth and death.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is 'na' refers to the Three Jewels abiding securely without any movement or shaking, like a door-sill.
The commentary explains:
The true Three Jewels are eternally free from names and characteristics.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one hears the syllable 'na,' one immediately knows that all phenomena are neither gained nor lost, neither coming nor going; for 'na' in the Prakrit language signifies 'not'."
The Commentary states: "Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'by means of the letter Na,' etc., this is the second section, the collection and integration of the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*).
Within this, there are four parts;
the first is the reverse collection from the end."
This means that by virtue of the fifth pair, the characteristic of non-existence (*abhāva-lakṣaṇa*), how could there be the fourth, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
Since conditioned phenomena are themselves characteristics, if characteristics exist, then the third must also exist.
Since, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), conditioned phenomena do not exist, how could there be an ultimate truth?
Because of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), there is a second [nature] that is primordially pure.
Since a third does not exist, how could there be a second?
Because of the primordial purity of the second, one speaks of non-arising; since a second does not exist, how can there be non-arising?

The Commentary states: "Because the letter A signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, the letter NA is devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics. This refers to their revolving and mutual inclusion.
Since the initial letter A gives rise to the fifth letter NA, they form a continuous circle like a ring.
This means that within non-arising, how could there be any nature or characteristics?
Therefore, the five characters cause one another to arise, revolving without obstruction.

Regarding the commentary’s passage beginning with “You know this is the essential point,” it concludes the meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*): by awakening to fundamental purity, one accomplishes the contemplation of the three emptinesses, stating, “free from self and what belongs to the self. Here, “what belongs to the self” refers to phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, the aforementioned three sections are all the text of the *Pañcākṣarī-sūtra*.

Since its distinct translation in meaning is identical to that of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, it is based upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; however, because there are minor differences in the phonetic values of two or three characters, the word "based on" is not explicitly stated.

However, according to the *Five-Syllable [Treatise]* and that translation of the *Forty-Two Letters*, among the first twelve letters, only the fifth contains the phrase "unobtainable" (*anupalabdha*);

This phrase "unobtainable" is itself the characteristic of *prajñā*.
Furthermore, such qualities as "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are also characteristics of *prajñā*.
Therefore, there is non-arising, yet one need not rely on the expression "unobtainable.

As previously stated, there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within the "negation" (*pratiṣedha*); if there were no negation, it would not exist. It is merely spoken of as "negation.
Since negation is itself a phenomenon, it is simply that which serves as the basis.
That form is itself emptiness is the characteristic of Prajñāpāramitā.
If one speaks only of "form," it is merely that which is empty.
This principle applies to all the other terms as well.
Furthermore, as in the fifteenth letter, *ka*, it says: "An agent cannot be found. If there were no such thing as "cannot be found," it would merely be an agent; for *ka* is itself the agent.
The remainder should all be understood by analogy.

Now, this [text] possesses both [characteristics]: first, it cites that [earlier] commentary; subsequently, from "Transcending the World" (*lokottara*) onwards, one can see how it harmonizes and explains the present sutra.

Within this, there are three parts:

This gateway of syllables is that by which one can penetrate to the very limit of the dharma-realm; beyond this gateway of syllables that expresses all dharmas, nothing else can be found. Why is this?
Thus, the meaning of these words cannot be proclaimed, cannot be displayed, cannot be grasped, cannot be fully known, and cannot be observed, because they are free from all marks.
"Good son! Just as space is the destination to which all things return, so too are these gateways of syllables;
it is only by entering these gateways that the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena becomes fully manifest."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains skillful wisdom regarding such entry into the gates of all syllables, they will be without obstruction in all spoken sounds and their expressed or indicated meanings; they will be able to fully realize and maintain the equal emptiness of all phenomena, and they will attain skillfulness in all forms of speech and sound.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to hear such entry into the gates of all syllables—which reveal the seal of syllables—and having heard them, receives, maintains, recites, masters, and explains them to others without craving for fame or profit, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall attain twenty kinds of merit.
What are these twenty? They are: attaining powerful mindfulness; attaining superior shame and remorse; attaining firm strength; attaining the essential purport of the Dharma;
attaining supreme awakening; attaining distinguished wisdom; attaining unimpeded eloquence; and attaining the gateways of dhāraṇī.
He attains freedom from doubt; he attains the state where neither aversion nor attachment arises toward the disagreeable or agreeable;

he attains dwelling in equality, free from high and low; he attains skillfulness regarding the vocal expressions of sentient beings; he attains skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana*), and skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*);

he attains skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), skillfulness regarding causes (*hetu*), and skillfulness regarding conditions (*pratyaya*); and he attains skillfulness regarding phenomena (*dharma*).

He attains skill in the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties; he attains skill in the knowledge of others' minds; he attains skill in the observation of the stars and constellations;

he attains skill in the knowledge of the divine ear; he attains skill in the knowledge of recollecting past lives; he attains skill in the knowledge of supernormal powers; he attains skill in the knowledge of death and rebirth;
he attains skill in the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; and he attains skill in explaining what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
"Skillfulness in the wisdom of abiding, and skillfulness in the establishment of the majestic deportment of coming and going—
these constitute the attainment of twenty kinds of sublime merits.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Pao-kuang*, and the *Kuang-ts'an* are largely identical to this.

Regarding the third, the ritual for the practice of contemplation: the title of that text is *The Ritual Manual for the Yoga of the Syllable-Wheels of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana, Entering the Dharma-Dhātu Chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Its commentary states: "Now, those who wish to enter suddenly into the practice of the contemplation of the Dharmakāya of Tathāgata Vairocana according to the One Vehicle must first give rise to the subtle and wondrous vows and practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; furthermore, they should empower their body and mind through the three secrets, whereby they will be able to awaken to and enter the great ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom."

If one is able to practice, first in a secluded place, one should collect the mind and settle it in tranquility; with eyes closed and body upright, sit in the full lotus posture, directing the mind to universally take as its object the boundless ocean of lands, and clearly contemplate all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time as they appear before each and every Buddha and Bodhisattva.
With earnest devotion, one should prostrate, circumambulate, and offer various clouds and oceans of ritual implements to all such assemblies of noble beings.

Having performed this vast offering, one should further contemplate one's own mind: that the mind is fundamentally unborn and spontaneously accomplished, its luminosity pervading everywhere like space.

Furthermore, one should deeply give rise to compassion and pity for sentient beings who do not realize that their own minds revolve through the various realms of existence; I shall universally transform and rescue them, causing them to attain awakening until none remain.

Furthermore, one should observe that one’s own mind, the minds of all sentient beings, and the minds of all Buddhas are fundamentally non-different, being of a single equal aspect. They constitute the Great Bodhicitta, translucent and pure, vast and pervasive, perfectly luminous and pristine, forming a great lunar disc whose magnitude equals space and is without limit.

Furthermore, within the lunar disc, forty-two Sanskrit syllables are arranged in a clockwise sequence; they are all golden in color, emitting great radiance that shines through and illuminates the ten directions, appearing with perfect clarity.

Within each and every ray of light are contained infinite oceans of lands; within each and every ocean of lands are infinite Buddhas; and each and every Buddha is surrounded by infinite assemblies of holy ones before and behind, seated at the site of enlightenment and having attained perfect awakening.

With wisdom they enter the three periods of time and their bodies pervade the ten directions; they turn the Great Dharma Wheel to deliver all classes of beings, causing them all to realize for themselves the nirvana of non-abiding.

Furthermore, they contemplate and awaken to the forty-two letter-gates of the Prajñāpāramitā, comprehending that all phenomena are ultimately unattainable, and are able to perceive the dharma-realm as entirely equal, without distinction or differentiation.

If a practitioner of yoga can bring this Svadhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī into correspondence with their contemplative practice, they will be able to directly realize the wisdom-body of the Tathāgata Vairocana and attain non-obstruction regarding all phenomena.

The fifth is the elder Sthira.
Regarding the phrase 'binding the mind through non-thought' (wúniàn yuēxīn), the character 'non' (wú) is employed in two ways."

Furthermore, by being free from the two obstacles, one adorns the Dharma-body through wisdom and severance; thus, the three virtues are complete.
The sixth, the Elder Subhāṣita-candra, may be understood [from other sources].
Regarding the seventh, the Liberation of Anabhibhū-sena, there are two interpretations:
First, it concerns the inexhaustibility of function; second, from "Furthermore, all mental objects and the mind" onwards, it concerns the inexhaustibility of essence.
From "Having seen the Buddha" onwards, the name is explained by means of the Dharma.

Regarding the first two meanings: the former explains that there is no delusion from beginning to end; the latter, starting from "Good son, because I abide in this," explains the mind that is not in vain in accordance with practice.
Because his conduct accords with his words, what he undertakes is brought to fulfillment, encompassing the perfection of both self-benefit and benefit for others.

Following this, from the passage "Words are the pivot of the gentleman" (*yan xing jun zi zhi shu ji*) downward, he explains the name of the city.
Now, this single sentence is from the *Xici* (Appended Statements) of the *Book of Changes*.
The Master said:
"When a gentleman dwells in his chamber, if the words he utters upon leaving it are good, they will be responded to even beyond a thousand li; how much more so those who are near?"
If one dwells in their chamber and utters words that are not good, those thousands of li away will oppose them; how much more so those who are near!
Words issue from the person and reach the people; conduct originates nearby and is seen afar.
Speech and action are the pivot and trigger of the gentleman. The pivot and trigger are the source of motion; the activation of the pivot and trigger is the source of honor and disgrace.
Speech and action are that by which the gentleman moves Heaven and Earth—how can they not be treated with caution?
"Although these are external scriptures, their intent accords with this [teaching]; it is only that their words and practices differ between the internal and external.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, 'The culmination of the convergence of conditions is the fulfillment of these two,' this refers to the fulfillment of compassion and wisdom."
Regarding the statement, "He shall see Maitreya succeed to the rank of Buddha," it means that Maitreya is perfected in compassion, whereas the rank of Buddha is perfected in wisdom.
This is the ninth virtue: the possession of virtue by one who has been born.
Regarding the phrase "Within the three [categories] and five classes of phenomena," etc., the commentary consists of three parts:
first, it explains that all phenomena are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The section beginning with "All [phenomena] are unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) provides the reason for excluding the unconditioned.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*: "Because true reality is empty of the conditioned.
From the "ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and so forth," the remaining four categories of results emerge.

Ripening refers to the mind; "and so forth" includes the other seven consciousnesses, as well as mental factors (*caitta*), material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), and non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Second, from the passage beginning "From the beginningless," the causes that establish the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth are explained.
There are, however, two types of the view of self:

first, that which is associated with the seven consciousnesses, which grasps the eighth [consciousness] as the internal self; therefore, it is said that the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) is associated with the four afflictions (*kleśa*).
The phrase "the view of self and so forth" mentioned here includes, by way of the term "and so forth," craving and pride.

Second, there is the self-clinging associated with the six consciousnesses, which, together with external grasping at delusive objects as "mine" and the arising of other afflictions, is why it is called "various."
Third, from "therefore it is induced" onwards, the causes are distinguished.
The induction of the fruit can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The fourth and fifth phrases separately clarify the non-associated [factors]," there are twenty-four types of non-associated factors; here, within these two gates, four are briefly excluded, while the remainder are treated as equal.

Among the four [sections], the phrase "at that very time" explains the three periods of time (*trikāla*) mentioned in the Sūtra, as these three periods constitute one "time" within the twenty-four [categories].
From the passage beginning with "namely, based on conduct," the reason why the three periods of time are like an illusion is set forth.

Formations (*saṃskāra*) are precisely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which arise and perish moment by moment in a continuous succession. That which has already ceased is the past; that which has not yet arisen is the future; and that which has arisen but not yet ceased is called the present. Apart from these formations, what other state could there be that constitutes the three times?
How much more so when the basis—the formations—is empty; how could that which depends upon it exist?

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The five are impermanence, birth, old age, and so forth,” these are three of the twenty-four [factors]: first, impermanence; second, birth; and third, old age, etc.
This corresponds to the aforementioned sūtra which states that birth, cessation, and death are all subsumed under impermanence (*anitya*).
The two characters "birth" and "aging" constitute two distinct dharmas, though "abiding" (*sthiti*) is omitted for brevity.
Furthermore, many of the holy teachings combine birth and cessation, naming them collectively as impermanence.
The reason for this is that birth is called "existence," yet existence is not permanent existence, unlike the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Cessation is called "non-existence," yet non-existence is not permanent non-existence, unlike a rabbit's horn.
Because it differs from those two types of permanence—the unconditioned and the rabbit’s horn—it is called "impermanent.
The commentary states, "That is to say, based on perishing after having arisen," which clarifies the reason why [phenomena] are like illusions.

Therefore, the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "However, because conditioned phenomena arise through the power of causes and conditions, they were originally non-existent and now exist, and having existed for a time, they return to non-existence; to distinguish them from unconditioned phenomena, the four characteristics are provisionally established."
That which was originally non-existent now exists; this state of existence is called "arising" (*jāti*).
When the state of arising momentarily halts, it is termed "abiding" (*sthiti*).
When abiding differs between earlier and later moments, it is further designated as "alteration" (*anyathātva*).
"Temporarily existing and then returning to non-existence—this state of non-existence is termed 'cessation'.
This establishes [the concept] based on the stage of destruction following arising.
The statement "all are false conceptualization" precisely reveals the cause of illusion.
However, that which constitutes sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction is precisely the matter of birth and old age; its essence is not a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, the four [links] mentioned above—namely, ignorance, formations, craving, and grasping—are also specific aspects of the preceding twelve factors of dependent origination; these four merely clarify the arising and aging-and-death across the three periods of time.
The Commentary states: "Because there are deluded thoughts, both mind and views are inverted. This refers to the three types of inversion:
first, inversion of thought; second, inversion of mind; and third, inversion of view.
However, this has already been analyzed in detail in the "Chapter on the Ten Practices.

While that passage contains many meanings, the present one concerns a single point: seeing with the mind is not a perverted view; it is because of the confusion of perception (*saṃjñā*) that the other two [views] become perverted.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “illusory phenomena are not existent,” and so forth: here, for the time being, it is based on existence and non-existence, identity and difference; furthermore, by incorporating the Middle Way, these constitute the three contemplations.
It should also include the transcendence of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Furthermore, by means of the phrase "neither one nor simultaneous" regarding the nature and characteristics of conjunction, the meaning of "not different" corresponds to the phrase "not simultaneous.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “In accord with the true source of the dharma-nature,” there are ten phrases.
The first four are explanations in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), which exclusively accord with reality.
Of these, the first three concern phenomena and the last one concerns persons; for a person may also be designated as the "perfectly established nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The next four analogies clarify that the phenomenal marks accord with reality.
This is because phenomena are empty in their very nature, as they share the same principle of reality.
In each case, the first phrase indicates the mark, while the second phrase provides the explanation.

The latter two phrases summarize their nature and characteristics in terms of the Dharma. When the Sūtra states that "there is no arising through successive emergence and cessation," it means that because there is further emergence and cessation, there is no fixed arising.
Since the latter phrase arises from conditions, it clarifies that there is no fixed nature; this absence of nature is precisely the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “These three non-obstructions are the three contemplations within a single mind”: the first is the provisional (*prajñapti*), the second is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the last is the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

Regarding the statement that there is a sequence of before and after, Sudhana’s contemplation of the mind realizes its instantaneous perfection; it is not a process of entering emptiness from the conventional, and so forth.
As for the phrase “now first, recompensing good and evil,” the text contains ten sentences, yet only four matters are explained because their characteristics overlap.
Karma is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of various karmas.

The fruit is maturation (*vipāka*); through the seeds of names and words (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-bīja*), one gives rise to faith, whereby the Buddha’s powers manifest as both the True and the Responsive.
"Faith is the source of the Way," for it necessarily leads one to the stage of Buddhahood.
When a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) manifests in response, a heart of reverence will immediately evoke a response.
While the stimulus of the practitioner's capacity evokes the Buddha—what is termed "evoking another’s transformation body"—attaining Buddhahood through faith is precisely one's own Buddha.
The remainder is easily understood, and thus the commentary does not explain it.

this view is itself causeless. Regarding the fourth phrase, "reckoning the impermanent as permanent" is the inversion of the Two Vehicles, who fail to perceive the profound reality of the wondrous existence of Nirvana.
To reckon the impermanent as permanent is the inversion of ordinary beings; how could they know the reality of the principle of the two kinds of emptiness?
The commentary’s phrase "those with the view of a creator" refers to the fifth point: the false claim that a sovereign being (*īśvara*) can produce all things.
Now, knowing that [happiness and suffering] arise from karma, one does not depend on others.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "As for those who come and go among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they should not come and go if they are permanent, nor should they come and go if they are impermanent; the same applies to sentient beings."
Existence and non-existence can thus be known.
Regarding the vision that transcends all dharmas, there are three statements in the commentary.
First, as for dispelling [delusions] through principle: within the emptiness of the dharma-nature, dharmas are themselves no-dharmas.
Second, because things must arise when conditions converge and must cease when conditions disperse, all phenomena lack autonomy.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The three assemblies return to the Middle Way,” there are two parts:

Regarding the preceding section, the statement "following any single phrase, one is free from all the aforementioned faults" means that, for example, by following the seed, the arising of the reed is immediately free from the errors of nihilism, eternalism, causelessness, and so forth.
Now, as for the general explanation: this does not address specific objections, but merely explains the meaning of the Middle Way through its general characteristics.

In the commentary, from the passage "like a seed producing a sprout" onwards, there is a specific explanation that demonstrates the characteristics of the Middle Way solely by means of the seed and the sprout.
The rest is omitted.

By expounding this Madhyamaka, the previous two [positions] are subsumed; that is to say, it reveals that emptiness and the conventional are precisely the emptiness and the conventional of this Middle Way, rather than entering this Middle Way from those [other] forms of emptiness and conventionality.

Regarding the phrase "Thus, it is free from [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence," etc., this serves as an illustrative explanation of the preceding text, summarily distancing itself from all faults.
As for the commentary’s statement, "The seed and sprout serve as a horizontal metaphor for the myriad dharmas," this refers to the knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
This means that whether wholesome or unwholesome, internal or external, all arise from their own seeds through the conjunction of conditions.
Regarding the phrase "just as a seal produces its impression, so are all dharmas illustrated by this analogy": "this aggregate also ceases" refers to the cessation of the present aggregate.
Regarding the phrase "those aggregates continue to arise," this is because they are viewed in relation to the three periods of time.
This is from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, specifically the "Chapter on the Summit of Mount Sumeru," which has already been cited; it is now briefly presented once more.
When it is said that "this aggregate also ceases," this refers to the arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Yet these five aggregates do not reach the intermediate state, nor do the five aggregates of the intermediate state come from any other place; rather, because of the present aggregates, there are the aggregates of the intermediate state.
Regarding the phrase "like a wax seal impressed upon clay": the wax seal is a metaphor for the present aggregates (*skandha*).
The pattern formed upon the clay represents the intermediate state aggregates (*antarābhava-skandha*).
The destruction of the seal signifies the cessation of the present aggregates.
The formation of characters refers to the arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) aggregates.
Just as a seal does not reach the clay [directly], so too the present aggregates do not reach the subsequent aggregates.
These characters arise through the causal conditions of the seal, just as the intermediate state aggregates exist by virtue of the present aggregates.
That the present aggregate does not reach the subsequent aggregate means it is not eternal;
that the subsequent aggregate does not come from another place but exists because of the present aggregate means it is not annihilated.
This non-annihilation and non-eternality is the meaning of the Middle Way.
The rest is as previously explained.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “To realize that the world is mind-manifestation is also the contemplation of Mind-only,” the word “also” (亦) is used because this precisely constitutes the Middle Way.

One may thus distinguish the three contemplations based on the principle of Mind-Only: that which is provisionally established by the mind as it conditions phenomena is the Contemplation of the Provisional; that phenomena appear while lacking intrinsic nature is the Contemplation of Emptiness; and the non-duality of these two aforementioned aspects is the Contemplation of the Middle Way.
The subsequent section on the dharma and its analogy can be understood by reference to what precedes it.
Regarding the "Praise of the Abiding Pavilion," since its principles are vast and its scriptural text is extensive, the general pattern is self-evident; therefore, it will not be explained in detail.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “*Jñeyabhūmi* means ‘the ground of the knowable,’” etc., the commentary briefly cites the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. The treatise states:

“The Bodhisattva possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits; having reached the *jñeyabhūmi*, he is oriented toward Nirvāṇa, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, he returns to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). For incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he manifests the endurance of diligent suffering, surpassing all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and becomes fully endowed with all merits and wisdom.”

Therefore, having transcended the stage of *jñeyāvaraṇa* (the veil of the knowable), it is said that the Bodhisattva dwells within the ocean of birth and death: during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, they cultivate the practice of purifying the stages (*bhūmi*) to seek pure liberation; during the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, they cultivate the practice of purifying meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and during the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, they cultivate the practice of purifying wisdom, thereby removing the obstacles of the stage of *jñeyāvaraṇa*.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva is said to ride the vehicle of mastery; having fulfilled the ten stages and attained that which is unimpeded and unobstructed, with everything fully complete, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Therefore, by means of *jñeya-jñāna* (knowledge of the knowable), one attains the great fruit.
The commentary explains:

*Jñeya* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "mother of wisdom," also as "perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*), also as "objective sphere," and also as "that which is known. Furthermore, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is also termed *jñeya*.

Because the Sūtra states, "causing them to pass beyond the ocean of *jñeya*," the Commentary employs only the single meaning of "the knowable" (*jñeya*), which corresponds to the third eon in the Treatise: passing beyond the ocean of birth and death.

The treatise further states: "Upon entering the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to permanently sever [ignorance]. Based on this, it is taught that in the ten stages one severs two types of ignorance along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*); all of these take the cognitive objects (*jñeyālambana*) as their objects of knowledge.

If one relies on the initial statement that [the practitioner] "reaches the stage of *jñeyabhūmi*," and the concluding summary which states that "one attains the great fruit by means of the wisdom of *jñeya*," these already contain further implications.
Now, taking the intent of the sūtra, I have cited only one instance.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, “There have been many ancient exegeses on the one hundred and ten spiritual friends,” three interpretations are briefly outlined:
the first is the ancient interpretation;

the second is the interpretation of Xianshou (Fazang), which first presents his own view and then—under the section beginning with “If one relies on this”—the *Kanding* (Jingying Huiyuan) refutes that master.
Third, the section beginning with "Some say" is the explanation from the *Kanding ji*.
This also has two parts: first, the presentation of that explanation; [second, its refutation].
Below the section beginning with "If that were so," the commentary refutes that interpretation, clarifying that its established positions are internally contradictory.
The preceding portion entirely recounts the views of former scholars.
From the section beginning with "If one seeks to reconcile [the contradictions]," the commentary provides a harmonizing explanation.
There are three ways to synthesize [the text], which will be explained in reverse order from the end.

Second, regarding the section beginning with "However, below it says again," this synthesizes the intention of Master Zang, taking the number one hundred and ten as representing the Dharma in its wondrous perfection.
Regarding the statement, "Even if there are three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), they likewise possess only ten," this is because each of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) subsumes three positions.

If even a single stage can comprehensively subsume the ten, how much more so when the three stages of worthiness are compared to the [ten] stages, as their analogies are similar; thus, their subsumption is well-established. Therefore, within the ten stages, each practices one degree, and the positions of the ten practices (*daśa-pratipatti*) likewise each constitute one degree.
Regarding the stages of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), the first is the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), and the last is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).

Since one initially realizes the arousal of the mind and finally receives the rank through consecration, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*) is opened [as a separate abiding], while faith is subsumed under the [Ten] Abidings.
If one merges with Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), one immediately opens up the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā).
Opening the faiths represents regression, while opening Equal Enlightenment represents progression; thus, one must cause the eleven stages to become one hundred and ten.
Regarding the doctrine of the first master: even if the scripture were not yet complete, it would likewise consist of one hundred and ten [sections].

The commentary states, "The 'city of realms' refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). Because the eighteen realms constitute the causal characteristics of birth and death, the Jin translation refers to them as the "three realms" (*tridhātu*).
The three realms constitute the city walls, because they are defined by their resultant characteristics (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "the realms and stages are the four elements, such as earth," the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the four elements; namely, earth, water, fire, and wind."
"Because they can accomplish the functions of upholding and so forth, having the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
Furthermore, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth are all as described in the second stage (*dvitīyabhūmi*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "That is, one lifetime of an ordinary body," this is explained from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).
The section beginning with "Also, regarding the practice and the single lifetime" explains this in terms of sequential progression (*xingbu*).
The passage starting with "Therefore, the crow of a thousand years" establishes the meaning of the first [category], that of a single lifetime for an ordinary body (*fan-shen*).
The section beginning with "For one who practices according to reality" serves to preemptively address potential objections.
One might fear that someone would ask:
"While it may be so if one speaks in terms of the perfect interfusion of dharmas,
how can it be achieved within a single lifetime in an ordinary body?"
Therefore, this explanation is provided.
It is not only for Sudhana; how could a practitioner obtain [the fruit] immediately?
The rest is as described in the "Chapter on the Merits of Generating the Bodhicitta."
Regarding "the three entries and ten abodes," these ten phrases herein consist of three sections:
the first two generally encompass both practice and stages; the final four are likewise comprehensive; and the intermediate four phrases possess three distinct meanings.

First, these three alone subsume the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), because these three represent the meaning of entering the dharma-realm through wisdom and dwelling therein; the fourth and fifth are both practice; and the sixth is aspiration.
Second, from "Furthermore, the four above" onwards, these four are again used to encompass the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Third, they are the realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) of the ten stages, because they realize the ten dharma-realms;
fourth, they are the practices of the individual stages.
Fifth, it is because one practices in accordance with the principle;
sixth, it is because great vows guide all practices.

Regarding the third point, "Furthermore, the meanings of the four above and the one below encompass both the specific and the general": the specific refers to the initial assignments, while the general refers to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The text of the commentary contains two hundred and twenty-one sentences. The following section is divided into two parts:
first, a general outline; second, a detailed explanation.
Within the former, there are four general points:
First, the general clarification of the arousal of the three types of resolve;
second, the division into two [sections];
third, from "Furthermore, the preceding section primarily clarifies... onwards, the division into two based on the three types of arousal of resolve.

4. Furthermore, from the section "Moreover, the preceding explanation of the sublime merits of the bodhicitta" onwards, the text is categorized according to its height and breadth; this follows the interpretation of Master Guāngtǒng, and thus the commentary is based upon it.
If one follows the third intention, then the preceding section consists merely of the Three Worthies (triyāna-piṭaka), which is divided into three parts to encompass the twelve [stages] above:

the first three sections correspond to the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the next five to the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and the final four to the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*). Both intentions apply universally.
The Master Zong of Youzong established distinct names for all two hundred and twenty-one metaphors, yet he neither provided a systematic classification nor offered a specific rationale for them.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “Because the Vajra-wisdom ultimately culminates in Bodhi,” since the sequence begins from the *gotra* (spiritual lineage) and ends with the Vajra-Bodhi-wisdom, the vertical correspondence with the underlying principle is clearly established.
That the initial resolve (ādikṣānti) instantaneously possesses the merits of all stages accords precisely with the core tenet of this sutra.
Thus, the "Vairocana Chapter" states: "All merits abide within the initial bodhicitta"; this is its meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the one hundred and three phrases within the section on the virtues of mastery (*vaśitā-guṇa*), if they are to be correlated solely with the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they may likewise be grouped as follows:

the ten abodes (*vihāra*) constitute the first stage; the ten practices (*caryā*) constitute the second stage; the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the third stage; the first, second, and third [sets] together constitute the fourth stage; the fourth and fifth constitute the fifth stage; and the final five are to be judged according to the preceding sequence.
This also accords with the original text; fearing prolixity, I have not detailed the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) therein.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “The Sanskrit equivalents for these are as extensive as those in the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Terms),” this is a reference made out of concern for excessive detail.
In the commentary (*śāstra*), two [of these] have already been explained in response to specific difficulties—namely, Vigama and Varuṇa. Those not yet explained shall now be set forth in full.
As for "Mahāsaṃgha," *saṃgha* means "body" (*kāya*).
However, the body has four names:
first, *gaya*; second, *śarīra*; third, *deha*; and fourth, *aṅga*.
Now, *aṅga* is also called "division," meaning a limb or constituent part.
Next, it says that the tree is named *santāna*; this is translated as "conjunction" (*hehe*) or "reconnection" (*duanxu*).
This means that this medicine can cause severed or injured parts to reconnect and join together once more.

Next, regarding the medicine named Ālambā—this is translated as "medicinal juice"—it originates from Mount Gandhamādana and the Snowy Mountains (Himavat), where it is produced by nature within stone mortars.
Some say it is called "attaining joy" because one experiences great delight upon obtaining this medicine.
Regarding the virtues of the four lands beneath Mount Sumeru, there is the *pārijātaka* tree; *pāri* here means "universal," and it is also called "circumferential."
Citrā is translated here as "interspersed adornment.
This means that this tree is adorned all around with flowers of various mixed colors; alternatively, it is called "perfectly wondrous adornment."
Next, it mentions the *vārṣika* flower; its full name is *vārṣikā*.
Regarding the term *vārṣi*, this translates as "rain.
*Ka* refers to *kāla*, which translates as "time"; it is so called because it blooms during the rainy season.
Campa-kā flower: this is translated as "yellow flower.
This flower has a fragrance and its shape resembles that of the *jizi* (daphne) flower.
Sumana flower: this is translated as "pleasing flower."
Its flowers and forms are both charming, causing those who see them to feel joy in their hearts.
Fifth, the section on coconuts clarifies the virtues of the fifth stage (*bhūmi*).
The medicinal juice is called *hṛtaka*, which translates here as "golden water," and its power exceeds that of the nine-times-refined elixir of immortality (*navakṛta-rasāyana*).
The kalaviṅka bird has already been explained previously.
It is called "Beautiful Voice" (Meiyin) here, or alternatively "Exquisite Sound" (Miaosheng).
This bird originally comes from the Snowy Mountains; it can chirp even while still within its shell, and its voice is so harmonious and elegant that listeners never grow weary of it.
Mahānāga means "Great Dragon" in this language, and is also called "Great Elephant.
This present athlete possesses strength like that of a dragon or an elephant.
Among the eight virtues of descending to the eighth stage of a human being, the makara fish is here translated as "Great Body."

This refers to creatures such as the giant tortoise (kūrma) found in these regions; their two eyes are like the sun, their gaping mouths are like dark valleys, and they are capable of swallowing large ships.
Whenever they emerge from the turbulent currents, it is as if the tide is rising.
They swallow water as if it were a ravine and traverse heights and depths as if they were mountains.
The largest can reach over two hundred li in length.
Anjana is a blue medicinal herb.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Following the Sub-commentary,
Scroll Eighty-nine Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* Following the Sub-commentary,
Scroll Ninety
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty, this is the commentary on the seventy-ninth scripture.
Regarding the statement, "However, these six are all contained within compassion and wisdom," it is because the pavilion symbolizes compassion and wisdom.

The Commentary states: “Sixth, the analogy of the city of Gandharvas depending on space. However, among the ten analogies, the first six have their [subjective] counterparts, while the seventh, eighth, and ninth do not.
Within the tenth analogy of illusion, the counterparts are combined all at once, following a reverse order from the end.
First, by virtue of the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, [the assembly] was joined with the illusionist.
Second, by virtue of the inconceivable power of illusory wisdom, they were joined with the great ocean; for the meaning of the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgaramudrā) is precisely the Ocean of Wisdom.
Third, because they are able to know all phenomena through illusory wisdom, yakṣas and humans are made to be mutually invisible to one another, as all things are like illusions.
Fourth, because they have attained the power of mastery of all bodhisattvas, they cause the city of *gandharva* to appear with unimpeded freedom within space, manifesting sovereign power.
Because they follow the section on illusion, all of them include the character for "illusion.
Since there are two layers of meaning, there are ten distinct metaphors with differing characteristics.
If one were not to provide this interpretation, one would have to claim that the scriptural text is redundant and unnecessary.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “previously attaining the essential meaning” and so forth: previously, it took meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the gateway; here, it takes function (*vṛtti*) as the gateway. Since movement and stillness are non-dual, one truly enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “arising from the conditions of dharma-knowledge,” the commentary takes the initial dharma-knowledge as the condition to explain the scriptural passage beginning with “such a self-nature. It clarifies that this self-nature is like an illusion, being the manifested appearance; it then shows that all subsequent [phenomena] are “not established,” thereby concluding that self-nature is like an illusion, a dream, and so forth.
The first pair concerns the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the perspective of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*).
Because things arise through conditions, they lack intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they arise from conditions.

The subsequent pair, beginning with "Because they do not maintain their own nature," distinguishes the true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); this is the meaning of the Dharma-nature school (*Faxingzong*) regarding the unchanging True Suchness (*tathatā*) that accords with conditions.
The preceding explanation that [the Buddha-nature] is entirely unaccomplished clarifies that both its essence (xing) and its characteristics (xiang) are quiescent;
